# Quarto design-decisions catalog (better-for-Taliesin)

**Date:** 2026-07-03

An exhaustive, adversarially-verified registry of Quarto design decisions above the Markdown syntax substrate (the syntax stays), so the owner can question and rule on each one. Each entry was drafted against the Taliesin codebase, then attacked by a skeptic that steelmans Quarto and pressure-tests the proposal against Taliesin's fixed invariants.

Status legend: Taliesin already better (we win today), Proposed change or Proposed (revised) (a change to make), Open question (owner judgment), Quarto choice stands (the skeptic found Quarto is right or we already match).

## Executive summary

Taliesin's deepest, already-shipped wins cluster in the engine and the authoring loop. A warm server, a warm Jupyter kernel with a forkserver pool, and one cumulative-content-hash freeze cache (execution) combine with block-level content-hash diffing, live-DOM state preservation, click-to-source, reverse-sync, and in-preview located diagnostics (authoring-ergonomics) to deliver the load-bearing promise Quarto structurally cannot: no per-edit startup cost and incremental everything. Replacing the Pandoc runtime with in-process comrak plus an own sourcepos-stamping emitter, and collapsing Pandoc's writer matrix to a single HTML target, is what makes the rest web-native: server-side KaTeX with memoized re-typesetting, single-sheet OS-follow dark mode with a pre-paint bootstrap, a reader-side Display panel, an offline search index that works under file://, and a native camera-map slide engine. Strict closed-vocabulary validation and check-as-publish-gate round out a diagnostics story Quarto has no equivalent for.

The highest-value unfinished work concentrates in three clusters. First, chapter-scoped numbering: figures, tables, equations, and listings are still flat per page while only theorems are chapter-scoped, and @sec- does not yet resolve to a real hierarchical number that agrees with its heading; closing this across crossref, book, and math is the single largest coherent win. Second, the config-cascade tension: the strict two-level model is clean, but authors keep needing inheritable defaults, so a small enumerated set of project defaults plus a narrow whitelisted project-to-page cascade (and an honest author: field) would relieve real pain without importing Quarto's _metadata.yml sprawl. Third, citations are the thinnest area in the catalog: hardcoded IEEE-numeric, .bib-only, a silently ignored csl:, no author-date and no nocite, so ruling on the citation-style engine unblocks most of that area.

Several individually high-impact proposed-changes are close to shippable and each removes a visible rough edge: honoring fig-align and out-width on computational figures (and no longer strict-flagging them), closing the format: sub-key validation hole so deck and html options get the same did-you-mean as everything else, user-definable reusable math macros, a lite brand accent and font knob that maps onto --tali-* tokens, preserving reader UI state (active tab, open callout) across incremental container updates, and an explicit computed-table policy with an opt-in df-print. Two structural open questions deserve an early ruling because they shape everything downstream: whether interactive kernel output such as Plotly or ipywidgets should survive live-preview mounting, and whether a committed _freeze/ becomes the build-without-a-kernel CI story.

To navigate the catalog, read status first, then impact. Every entry is tagged taliesin-already-better, proposed-change, or open-question, and high, medium, or low impact. Roughly half of the decisions already stand as wins, about forty are concrete proposed-changes, and around thirty are genuine open questions. The already-better entries are the case for the architecture and the invariants to protect, not action items; the proposed-changes are the roadmap; the open-questions are where the owner's judgment is actually required and should be read first. The suggested area order leads with the differentiators (the authoring loop, execution, and the rendering pipeline), moves through the config surfaces and the scholarly-content features, then presentation, then project-scale (site, book, publishing), and closes with the extensibility and safety areas.

**Cross-cutting themes:**

- Warm-process architecture is the moat: a warm server, a warm kernel plus forkserver pool, one cumulative-hash freeze cache, and memoized math and block rendering all serve a single invariant (no per-edit startup cost, incremental everything) that Quarto's per-render Pandoc process cannot match.
- One block model is the universal spine: data-block-id plus data-sourcepos powers click-to-source, reverse-sync, block-diff live-state preservation, the cheap cross-page xref registry, content-gated asset inclusion, and incremental math from a single data structure.
- HTML-only is a feature, not a limitation: collapsing Pandoc's writer matrix to one target is exactly what buys native details-based collapse, scroll-native wide tables, reader-side display preferences, single-sheet OS-follow dark mode, lightbox galleries, and the camera-map deck.
- Located, actionable, closed-vocabulary diagnostics are a consistent posture: every mistake should carry a did-you-mean and a click-to-source location and surface in the browser, not just the terminal; the recurring gap is extending validation from key names to enumerated value domains and into the format: sub-keys.
- Chapter-scoped numbering is the largest unfinished frontier, recurring across crossref, book, and math (figures, tables, equations, listings, sections), where today only theorems are chapter-scoped.
- The config-cascade tension recurs: the clean two-level model keeps meeting a real need for inheritable defaults, and the through-line is a small, enumerated, whitelisted cascade rather than Quarto's open-ended _metadata.yml directory cascade.
- An offline, self-contained guarantee is a design constant: server-side KaTeX with inlined fonts, self-hosted fonts, a window-global search index for file://, no CDNs and no telemetry; the open frontier is how far that promise extends to author-imported heavy libraries and interactive kernel output.
- A compiled-binary trust and extension model: no _extensions install path, no Lua filters, shortcodes as a line-preserving Rust text pass, so the only data-only extension surfaces are theming and a proposed shortcodes template map, and every executed byte is the binary plus the author's own repo.
- The single read-only editing surface is a hard invariant: the preview never writes back, click-to-source only navigates, and ergonomics come from editor commands rather than preview gestures, with WYSIWYG deliberately rejected.
- Accessibility, privacy, and reader agency are defaults rather than add-ons: prefers-reduced-motion honored everywhere, no analytics or telemetry, an OS-follow theme with a persisted toggle, and reader-side display controls Quarto's author-only knobs cannot match.
- Citations and bibliography form the thinnest area relative to Quarto and the clearest concentration of proposed-changes plus one high-impact open question, making it the most leveraged single area to invest in.

**Highest-impact decisions to rule on first:**

- Chapter-scope figure/table/equation numbering ('Figure 2.3'), not just theorems
- Whether @sec- resolves to the section's real hierarchical number, and agrees with the heading
- Whether to stay hardcoded IEEE-numeric or offer configurable citation styles (author-date), and stop silently ignoring csl:
- Keep a strict two-level config model (project file plus page front matter) with no _metadata.yml directory cascade
- Add a small enumerated set of inheritable project defaults (bibliography/csl/theme/execute) to _site.yml, and make the dead author: field honest
- Decide the stance on interactive kernel output (Plotly/Altair/folium/ipywidgets), which does not survive live-preview mounting today
- Explicit //| input dependency annotations plus a compile-time reactive validator, instead of implicit free-variable reactivity
- Honor fig-align / out-width (and fig-width / fig-height) on computational figures, and stop strict-flagging them
- Committed _freeze/ so CI can build without a kernel vs. gitignored local-only cumulative-hash cache
- Close the format: sub-key validation hole so deck/html options get the same did-you-mean the rest of front matter gets
- Re-render on file-save (disk watch) vs streaming the editor buffer on keystroke

Total decisions catalogued: 165.

## Authoring ergonomics and the edit loop

### D1. Re-render on file-save (disk watch) vs streaming the editor buffer on keystroke (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's preview watches the rendered inputs on disk. You must save the .qmd (VS Code render-on-save, or a manual re-render) before the preview updates; there is no unsaved-buffer preview. Each save re-runs pandoc on the whole document.
- **Critique:** Even Taliesin, whose whole thesis is 'no per-edit startup cost', still charges a Ctrl-S per visible change. The warm server and warm kernel mean the render itself is near-instant, but the author's loop is still gated on an explicit save action, so the tool leaves its own strongest promise partly on the table.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Save is a deliberate coherence boundary, not a missing feature. Markdown/Pandoc syntax is block-structured and catastrophically sensitive to incomplete input: a half-typed unclosed ``` fence swallows the entire rest of the document into one code block, an open `$$` swallows everything into math, an open `:::` div reflows the tail. Rendering on save means the author almost always renders at a syntactically coherent point, so the preview never flickers through globally-broken intermediate parses. Save also keeps disk as the single source of truth shared by the preview, the static build, git, format-on-save, and every other tool, so what you see is always exactly what exists on disk and what will ship. (Quarto's per-render pandoc+Lua+execute cost of seconds is a separate, Quarto-specific reason keystroke rendering was never viable, but the coherence-boundary argument is the durable one and it survives even against Taliesin's near-instant render.) The critique is accurate and not a strawman (it correctly states Quarto watches disk and charges a save), but it is really a critique of Taliesin's own unmet promise rather than a steelmanned engagement with Quarto: it omits the save-as-commit-boundary rationale entirely.
- **Taliesin today:** Disk watch only. crates/server/src/serve/mod.rs spawns a notify::recommended_watcher on the base dir, filters events via relevant_path, debounces 80ms (Duration::from_millis(80)), then re-renders. serve_site/mod.rs does the same per page. Nothing reads the editor's unsaved buffer; the on-disk file is the sole trigger and sole source.
- **Proposed better:** Add an opt-in keystroke channel through the VS Code companion: onDidChangeTextDocument streams the unsaved buffer text (debounced ~120ms) to the server over the existing websocket/relay, and the server renders THAT text instead of re-reading disk while a buffer feed is active. Plain-browser previews keep the disk watch. This turns the buffer into the previewed source, extending 'no per-edit startup cost' to 'no per-edit save cost' and beating Quarto decisively on loop latency.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the idea, ship it narrowed and idle-triggered rather than pure-keystroke. (1) Debounce on typing PAUSE, not every keystroke: fire ~150-250ms after the last edit, which is when the parse is most likely coherent and collapses the ~8Hz whole-doc-reparse cost. This already captures nearly all of the 'no per-edit save cost' win over Quarto. (2) Split prose from execution: re-render markdown/math from the buffer, but keep code-cell EXECUTION save-triggered, so you never run half-typed side-effecting code or pollute `_freeze/` with uncommitted hashes. (3) Guard the catastrophic-parse case: detect an unbalanced fence/`$$`/`:::` count and hold the last good render (or mark the tail pending) instead of reflowing the whole document, so the block-diff/DOM-survival advantage is preserved during typing. (4) Feed every open source buffer, not just the active doc, and teach the include resolver to prefer a buffer over disk when one is registered, or explicitly scope v1 to single-file docs and say so. (5) Suspend the disk watcher for a doc while its buffer feed is active, and fall back to disk-watch the instant the feed drops. (6) Since a corpus doc cannot pin it, make the companion round-trip e2e (buffer edit -> rendered op with correct sourcepos -> Alt-click lands on the buffer line) a required CI gate and name it as the regression net in the entry. Framed this way it becomes 'no per-edit save cost' without surrendering block-level incrementality, execution safety, or the disk-as-build-truth guarantee.
- **Tradeoffs:** Introduces a buffer-vs-disk divergence exactly like the write-path conflict that got drag-to-reorder removed, though here it is read-only so it is safer. Click-to-source line math must key off the buffer the preview was rendered from, not disk, or Alt-click lands on stale lines after unsaved edits. Freeze-cache keys (content hash) still work, but code execution on every keystroke needs its own debounce/gate so a half-typed cell does not spam the kernel. Two rendering-source modes to keep coherent. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's tradeoffs only cover kernel-spam and click-to-source line math, and miss the three costs that actually reshape the design. (1) Broken intermediate parses: at keystroke cadence the author is constantly mid-fence, mid-$$, mid-:::, mid-link. Each such state makes comrak reparse the whole doc into a globally-wrong block list, which maximizes the block-level diff and forces a near-full re-mount. That defeats the exact load-bearing advantage the live-edit benchmark sells (83x smaller payload, DOM survives via diff) precisely during the moments the feature is active. (2) Whole-document reprocessing cost: there is no incremental parse. Every ~120ms tick reruns full comrak parse + full syntect highlighting of every code block + server-side KaTeX on every math block. On a large chapter with heavy code/math, sustained ~8Hz typing can saturate a core and echo latency back into the editor, so 'near-instant' (true for a save every few seconds) is not guaranteed under continuous keystrokes. (3) Includes/multi-file: feeding only the single active buffer breaks the story for `{{< include sub.tmd >}}`; editing an included file's buffer would render nothing (include resolver still reads disk) unless every open source buffer is fed and the include resolver is taught to prefer buffers. Also: executing code cells from an unsaved buffer runs side-effecting, never-committed code, and populates `_freeze/` with hashes for document states that never hit disk. And the benefit is thin for anyone with VS Code autosave on (disk-watch already fires ~1s after a pause), so the audience that gains most is exactly the save-as-commit-boundary crowd that may not want it.)
- **Invariant check:** Preview stays strictly read-only (buffer flows editor->preview, never back), so the single-editing-surface invariant holds; the .tmd buffer in the editor is still the only place you type. HTML-only, block-level diff, warm server, and corpus-pinning are untouched. Must be corpus/manually pinned by a companion round-trip test. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation. The read-only letter holds (buffer flows editor to preview only, click-to-source still navigates, HTML-only and warm-server untouched). But two soft tensions the drafter under-weighted. (a) The previewed source becomes the editor buffer, not the on-disk .tmd, so 'what the preview shows' diverges from disk, build output, and git. The single-editing-surface invariant is stated as 'the .tmd file is the single editing surface'; keystroke mode quietly makes the buffer the source-of-truth for the view, an ambiguity the project has been careful to avoid (and the disk watcher must be actively suspended while a feed is live or a background autosave/format-on-save/checkout races it). (b) Corpus-plus-roadmap: this behavior lives in the companion plus a new server inbound protocol path, so it cannot be pinned by a corpus .tmd document rendered by `cargo test`; it is only exercisable through the companion e2e harness. The 'corpus is the arbiter of done' discipline can only partially apply, giving this feature a weaker regression net than everything around it.)

### D2. Block-level content-hash diff with live-DOM state preservation vs whole-page reload (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto re-renders the entire document and its livereload triggers a full browser reload (or full body swap) of the preview page. Nothing on the page is diffed; every DOM node, scroll position, and any live widget is rebuilt from scratch on each update.
- **Critique:** A full reload throws away scroll position, playing video, open <details>, and the runtime state of any interactive widget on every edit. For a long doc or a live visualization, one-character edits cause a visible flash and reset, which is the opposite of a tight authoring loop.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Full re-render plus reload is correctness-by-construction, not laziness. Because the preview is byte-identical to `quarto render` output, it structurally cannot suffer the bug class a diff engine invites: stale patched attributes, wrong-node replacement, id collisions, leaked GL contexts, or a DOM that silently drifts from a clean render. Quarto is a multi-format publishing system (HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs, epub, book) delegating layout to pandoc, which emits no stable content-hash block ids or sourcepos; a Taliesin-style block model would require replacing pandoc wholesale. A full reload also handles the genuinely hard cases uniformly (global CSS/JS changes, added dependencies, header edits, format switches) that any diff engine must anyway fall back to full reload for. For the dominant Quarto workload (static prose, math, figures with no live runtime state), the reset is a sub-second flash the author tolerates, and livereload restores scroll from sessionStorage so even that is usually kept. The interactive-widget-heavy live document is a minority case Quarto reasonably does not optimize for.
- **Taliesin today:** Fully built and better. crates/core/src/diff.rs diffs two block lists by content-hash id via an LCS (reduced to patience-sort LIS, O(n log n)) and emits Update/Insert/Remove plus a SetMeta op that patches ONLY data-sourcepos when a block merely shifted lines, so its live DOM (video playback, {js}/WebGL widget, open <details>) survives an edit above it. client.js applies ops under keepScroll() (pins window.scrollY, forces instant behavior) and coalesces the per-save op burst into one afterChange on a rAF. teardownJs resolves {js} invalidation so WebGL/RAF cells do not leak across edits.
- **Proposed better:** Keep as-is; the one documented gap (diff.rs tests reorder_reconstructs_via_remove_plus_insert) is that a MOVED live block is rebuilt as Remove+Insert and loses runtime state. Optionally add a Move op keyed on the stable content-hash id to preserve state across reorders. Otherwise no change.
- **Revised recommendation:** Verdict: Taliesin is already better here, and the assessment is verified against diff.rs and client.js. Keep the current design exactly as-is. Sharpen two things. First, in the critique, concede that livereload usually restores scroll position from sessionStorage, so scroll is the one thing Quarto often keeps; the fair, unassailable claim is that a full reload re-runs all page JS from scratch and so cannot preserve widget runtime state, in-flight video, or open <details> that are not in the initial HTML. Leading with scroll slightly weakens an otherwise airtight critique. Second, decline the optional Move op rather than list it as a live refinement. It targets an atomic reorder that the cut/paste-through-the-editor workflow almost never produces as a single diff, it cannot help multi-sourcepos stateful divs without replicating SetMeta's guard and falling back anyway, and its benefit is invisible to the corpus net that decides done. Note explicitly that a Move op would NOT reintroduce the removed drag-to-reorder write path (it is a source-driven preview optimization, never a second write into source), so single-editing-surface is not the reason to skip it; the reason is cost-for-marginal-value. If a future corpus document ever pins a real reorder-a-live-cell scenario via a browser assertion, revisit then; until such a pin exists, the roadmap discipline says do not build it.
- **Tradeoffs:** The Move-op refinement adds diff and client complexity for a niche case (reordering a stateful cell like a Three.js scene). SetMeta already carries a subtle correctness constraint (falls back to full Update when a block carries more than one data-sourcepos, so inner sourcepos never go stale), which must be preserved by any change. (skeptic-found downside: The Move op is far more marginal than "niche reordering" admits, for a workflow reason the drafter missed. With the single text-editing surface, reordering is a cut then a paste, which the file watcher sees as two separate debounced saves: save 1 diffs to a Remove (block gone), save 2 diffs to an Insert (block back elsewhere). The diff never sees the block present in both old and new at once, so no atomic reorder ever reaches diff_blocks and a Move op would essentially never fire for the actual reorder workflow. It only fires on an atomic editor command (e.g. Alt-Up move-line) captured in one save. Worse, a Move that preserves live DOM must inherit SetMeta's exact single-sourcepos guard: relocating a multi-sourcepos block (a stateful :::scrolly or panel-tabset) leaves its inner data-sourcepos stale, breaking click-to-source inside it, so Move would have to fall back to Remove+Insert for precisely the composite stateful blocks, leaving it useful only for single-sourcepos leaf cells like a lone {js}/Three.js widget. Finally its whole payoff (runtime state surviving a move) is a live-browser behavior the static corpus render net cannot pin, so it clashes with corpus-as-arbiter-of-done: you would add diff + client complexity for a case that neither commonly occurs nor can be regression-locked.)
- **Invariant check:** Directly upholds the load-bearing block-level-incremental-update goal and the data-block-id/data-sourcepos invariant; HTML-only and read-only preview untouched; corpus.rs already pins sourcepos totality and block identity.

### D3. Alt-click a rendered block to jump to its source line (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Nothing. Quarto has no preview-to-source navigation: a rendered element carries no source position, so there is no way to click output and land at the line that produced it. You navigate by scrolling the editor and re-finding the text yourself.
- **Critique:** For any non-trivial document the preview-to-source gap is a constant tax: you see the wrong sentence in the output and have to hunt for it in the source by string search. This is the single biggest edit-loop affordance Quarto lacks.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a pandoc-AST-to-many-writers compiler whose job is one source rendered to a dozen targets (HTML, PDF, docx, epub, revealjs, beamer). A preview-to-source jump is only coherent for HTML (you cannot Alt-click a PDF page or a docx), so it would be a one-format affordance grafted onto a format-neutral architecture. Worse, pandoc's AST does not preserve reliable source positions through most block and inline constructs, so Quarto would have to fork or heavily patch pandoc just to carry sourcepos to the output, an enormous cost for one writer. Quarto is also deliberately editor-neutral (RStudio, Positron, VS Code, Neovim, plain text), and a rendered-HTML-to-source bridge is intrinsically editor-specific and needs a live, single-format dev server bound to one editor, exactly the niche Quarto chooses NOT to occupy. Its coherent alternative is to delegate navigation to the IDE (the RStudio/Positron visual editor gives source-to-WYSIWYG sync) and keep its own investment in format-neutral rendering. So Quarto's omission is a rational consequence of the multi-format, multi-editor mandate, not an oversight.
- **Taliesin today:** Fully built and load-bearing. Every block carries data-sourcepos (and data-source-file for includes). client.js's click handler (altKey gated) resolves the nearest locatable() ancestor and opens vscode://file<abs>:<line>:<col>, or relays a qmd-goto postMessage when inside the VS Code webview (editor/vscode/src/extension.ts maps it to revealRange). A held-Alt affordance (html.tali-alt) outlines the exact block a click would resolve to, so highlight and jump can never drift.
- **Proposed better:** Two concrete refinements: (1) resolve to the clicked position within the block (map the caret/character offset to a source column) instead of always the block's start line:col, so Alt-clicking a word in a long paragraph lands on that word; (2) see the separate editor-scheme entry. Otherwise keep.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's status (taliesin-already-better is correct: this IS the load-bearing click-to-source goal, fully built, corpus-pinned). Keep the pointer to the separate editor-scheme entry (refinement 2). But narrow refinement (1): drop the general-prose caret-to-column ambition (understated cost, unreliable exactly where aimed, and a confidently-wrong landing is worse than the current predictable block-start). Replace it with the cheap, deterministic, always-correct subset: line-precision inside VERBATIM blocks (code cells and fenced code blocks), where the clicked line equals block.start_line + N, with N counted from newlines in the verbatim literal. That needs no comrak inline sourcepos, emits no inline attributes (so no reverse-sync coupling and no reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total burden), and delivers the one genuinely valuable case: Alt-clicking line 30 of a 40-line cell lands on line 30, not line 1. The code path is half-present already (wrap_code_lines emits per-line spans on the code-line-numbers path; generalize it to all code blocks or compute the line from the caret offset). Record prose word-precision as an explicit non-goal with the anticorrelation rationale, and pin the code-line case with a corpus document. Net: revise, not keep, not drop.
- **Tradeoffs:** Caret-level resolution needs inline sourcepos or an offset->source mapping that comrak only partially provides at inline granularity; for prose it may require re-deriving column from the text run, adding emit-side bookkeeping for a modest precision gain. (skeptic-found downside: Refinement (1) aims caret-to-column precision at long prose paragraphs, but those are exactly the blocks whose rendered text has no reliable character-preimage in source: inline emphasis/links/inline-code shift columns, and citations ([@key] rendering as "(Author 2020)"), shortcodes {{< >}}, KaTeX math ($x^2$ becoming nested span soup), footnote refs, entities, and smart typography have NO source characters at the clicked glyph at all. A rendered paragraph also wraps across many visual lines and spans multiple source lines, so caretRangeFromPoint's rendered-text-node offset cannot be mapped to the right source line without an inline source map comrak does not reliably provide. The benefit (word precision) and the failure mode (mapping drift) are perfectly anticorrelated: precision is weakest precisely where it is invoked. And a confidently-wrong landing (mid-word, or on the wrong line past some inline markup) is worse than today's predictable, trustworthy block-start caret, whose reliability is itself a feature. The tradeoffs note undersells this as "modest precision gain" plus "emit-side bookkeeping"; the real cost is an inline source map plus a reliability regression on the target case.)
- **Invariant check:** This IS the click-to-source load-bearing goal; it navigates (preview->editor) and never writes, so the read-only-preview invariant holds. HTML-only untouched. Pinned by corpus reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total. (possible violation flagged: As stated (compute the column at click time from the caret), no hard invariant is violated: it still navigates preview-to-editor and never writes (read-only surface holds), HTML-only is untouched, and Markdown syntax is unchanged. But the tradeoff's hinted implementation path (emit inline data-sourcepos so comrak's partial inline positions are carried on spans) WOULD entangle two invariants: highlightAtLine scans every data-sourcepos and picks the smallest-span covering block, so inline spans would silently take over reverse cursor-sync (highlighting a word instead of the paragraph), and each such span would have to satisfy reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total (L:C-L:C totality). So the block-level/reverse-sync coupling is a conditional violation to flag, avoidable only by keeping the refinement click-time-only with no emitted inline attributes.)

### D4. Persistent warm server + warm Jupyter kernel + freeze cache vs per-render process boot (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's preview keeps a process alive and can hold an execution daemon (execute-daemon / jupyter kernel reuse), but each save re-runs the document's rendering pipeline and, without careful per-cell cache config, re-executes cells; its per-cell cache is variable-state-blind and can go stale. Cold operations pay pandoc + engine startup.
- **Critique:** Quarto's cache is fragile: it caches per-cell but never captures kernel variable state, so cache hits can be wrong, and authors are told to clear it by hand. The warm path is real but the render pipeline still re-does whole-document work each save.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's cache design serves a genuinely harder constraint set that Taliesin deliberately opted out of, so the choice is coherent, not lazy. (1) Quarto renders MANY formats (PDF, docx, revealjs, HTML) from one execution result and must do it in cold CI containers and on other people's machines where no warm server and no warm kernel exist at all. In that world Quarto's document-level `freeze:` (re-run a doc only if its source changed, stored in `_freeze/`, the very directory name Taliesin borrowed) is stale-safe BY CONSTRUCTION: any source change re-runs the whole document, so it cannot serve a wrong hit. The opt-in per-cell `cache:` (jupyter-cache/knitr) is a separate, coarser lever for the one case the freeze cannot help: skipping a single very expensive cell inside a doc when every render is cold and there is no live kernel to lean on. Its variable-state-blindness and the documented `--cache-refresh` escape hatch are the honest, advertised price of a mechanism that must work with zero warm-process assumptions, not an oversight. (2) Quarto re-executes documents top-to-bottom on each render, which guarantees the published artifact matches a clean linear run (the reproducibility contract computational-science authors depend on) rather than an incrementally-mutated kernel that may carry hidden state from edited or deleted cells. Taliesin's warm-incremental model buys latency by explicitly NOT re-running the prefix, which is faster but reintroduces exactly the hidden-state hazard Quarto's full re-execution eliminates. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Built and stronger. AppState + a single Executor + the warm ZMQ kernel (kernel.rs) live for the whole session across every edit. exec.rs re-runs only the edited cell plus downstream via cumulative-hash keys; freeze.rs persists cell outputs in _freeze/<page>.json keyed by (this cell + all upstream same-language code + interpreter id), so an unchanged doc replays from disk without booting the kernel and there is nothing to clear by hand (a change busts everything downstream, no stale hits). Errors and cache:false cells are never persisted. Kernel variable state is deliberately never cached, so a cold start only skips work when the whole doc is unchanged.
- **Proposed better:** Keep. Marginal add: surface warm/cold and per-cell replay state more prominently in the dev menu (the build-state/cell-state progress chip already exists) so the author trusts what re-ran.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the warm-server/warm-kernel/freeze design: it is verifiably built and stronger than Quarto for Taliesin's actual constraint (single-author, HTML-only, preview-first). Sharpen the entry on two fronts. First, correct the critique's framing: compare freeze-to-freeze, not freeze-to-cache. Quarto's document-level `freeze:` is stale-SAFE (whole-doc re-run on any change), so Taliesin's real, honest wins are (a) CELL-granular cold replay and warm-session incrementality where Quarto's freeze is all-or-nothing per document, and (b) no stale hits versus Quarto's opt-in per-cell `cache:` and its `--cache-refresh` manual clear. Credit that Quarto's design pays for cross-format, cold-CI, cross-machine reproducibility that Taliesin sidesteps by being HTML-only and warm-preview-first. Second, keep the marginal add but reframe and constrain it: its job is to expose warm-vs-cold divergence risk (surface, per cell, whether the live kernel actually HOLDS this cell's state versus merely replaying its output from disk), so the author can tell when the preview is trusting retained state a cold build will not reproduce. Ship it as an on-demand dev-menu detail (not always-prominent, to respect the low-chrome reading-first direction), add the new cell-state signal for "restored," and note it cannot be pinned by a static corpus doc: like live-edit-bench it needs an e2e/browser harness to assert the live websocket cell-state, which is the correct home for its regression net.
- **Tradeoffs:** The honesty of never caching variable state means a cold restart cannot skip a changed-upstream cell; that is the correct tradeoff but it does mean big pipelines pay full replay after a kernel restart. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's tradeoffs section names only "big pipelines pay full replay after a kernel restart," but the deeper and more insidious cost is warm-vs-cold OUTPUT divergence. Because the warm session retains kernel variable state by design and never re-runs the unchanged prefix, a downstream cell that depends on a variable from an edited-or-DELETED upstream cell can render green in the live preview while the same cell fails or differs on a cold `build`/fresh run (the classic notebook hidden-state / out-of-order-execution reproducibility trap). Taliesin's cold `build` and the corpus (which always render cold) are the source of truth and will catch it, but mid-session the preview can silently mislead. This actually REFRAMES the value of the proposed marginal add: a warm/cold + retained-state indicator is worth far more as "your preview is leaning on in-kernel state a cold build will not reproduce" than as the drafter's weaker framing of "trust what re-ran." One trap in the add itself: a naive "cached/replayed" badge that does not distinguish "kernel actually holds this cell's state" (warm prefix) from "output merely replayed from disk while the kernel is cold and holds nothing" would re-create the very false confidence Quarto's stale cache is criticized for. The badge must encode that distinction. Two smaller costs: cached cells currently emit no cell-state message at all (an all-cached page reaches `idle` emitting nothing), so surfacing replay state needs a NEW protocol signal plus client rendering, not a free relabel; and "more prominent" pushes against the reading-first, low-chrome design direction, so it should be on-demand detail in the dev menu, not always-prominent.)
- **Invariant check:** This IS the no-per-edit-startup-cost load-bearing goal. HTML-only and read-only preview untouched. Freeze correctness is corpus/exec-tested.

### D5. Editor cursor position highlights and scrolls the matching preview block (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Nothing. Quarto's preview has no awareness of the editor caret, so moving the cursor in the source does not indicate or scroll to the corresponding output.
- **Critique:** Without reverse sync, a large document forces the author to manually keep two scroll positions aligned. You edit at source line 400 and must hand-scroll the preview to find the same place.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** For the rendered HTML preview the critique is accurate, so it is fair rather than a strawman: Quarto's preview (VS Code webview or browser tab) re-renders on save and has no caret awareness. The strongest case FOR Quarto's choice: (1) Quarto is multi-format, so its "preview" may be PDF, reveal.js, docx, or a whole website where source-position-to-output is not 1:1 (or is undefined). A caret-agnostic preview is the only surface that behaves consistently across every format, so Quarto keeps the render as a stable read-only fidelity view that never scrolls out from under you while you edit. (2) Where source-cursor correspondence genuinely helps navigation, Quarto invests it in the ProseMirror VISUAL EDITOR (source position vs visual position sync), which is the appropriate home for editor/output cursor coupling, rather than overloading the final-render view. A preview that chases the caret can feel jumpy and can fight the reader's own scroll. So Quarto's non-implementation is a coherent consequence of format breadth plus the visual-editor bet. The rebuttal that justifies Taliesin: both of Quarto's reasons dissolve under Taliesin's invariants. HTML is the only target, so sourcepos-to-output is total and corpus-pinned (reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total), and the single-read-only-surface rule removes the visual editor as an option, so a caret-following preview is the ONLY way Taliesin's single author gets the navigation Quarto hands its users through the visual editor. Taliesin also gates scroll on out-of-viewport (r.top<0 || r.bottom>innerHeight), so it does not jump gratuitously. Verified in code: extension.ts posts a debounced (80ms) qmd-cursor{file,line}; client.js highlightAtLine picks the smallest sourcepos-covering block (else nearest preceding), adds .tali-hl, recenters if offscreen, and jumps decks via TaliesinDeck.slide.
- **Taliesin today:** Built, but gated on the VS Code companion. extension.ts's onDidChangeTextEditorSelection posts a debounced (80ms) qmd-cursor {file,line} into the webview; client.js highlightAtLine finds the smallest block whose sourcepos range covers the line (else the nearest preceding block), adds .tali-hl, and scrollIntoView/center (or TaliesinDeck.slide for decks). In a plain browser with no editor there is no cursor source, so only forward click-to-source works; reverse sync needs the companion (currently Phase-1, pending author F5 acceptance).
- **Proposed better:** Ship/finish the companion so reverse sync is a default, not a pending acceptance; and make the buffer-vs-disk line basis explicit if the keystroke-preview change lands (the cursor line must be interpreted against the same source revision the preview rendered).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry; it is correct that Taliesin has reverse sync for a read-only HTML preview and Quarto's HTML preview does not. Sharpen four points. (1) Honesty: "taliesin-already-better" is gated on an unshipped companion (Phase-1, pending F5), so the real win exists only once the companion ships; make "finish/ship the companion" the actual deliverable, not a nice-to-have. (2) Add a highlight lifecycle: clear .tali-hl on preview blur/visibility-loss or after a short timeout so a stale outline does not linger, and make the Alt-click-recenter interaction intentional (it is currently an emergent side effect of the forward round-trip). (3) Decouple the buffer-vs-disk concern from keystroke-preview: the drift already exists whenever the buffer is dirty, so either accept it (self-heals on save, fine for one author) or tag qmd-cursor with the document revision/version and have client.js soft-match or skip when the preview's rendered revision differs. Do NOT bundle keystroke-preview (rendering from the live buffer) into this entry; that is a separate roadmap decision with its own tradeoffs and would only widen the same drift. (4) Note the genuine strengths worth pinning in the corpus: reverse sync is include-aware (relativeKey returns null for the main doc so null-source blocks match, and included blocks match by data-source-file), and the containing-div fallback means a cursor on a fenced-div fence/blank line highlights the whole div rather than a wrong sibling, so the "nearest preceding" caveat is milder than stated. Impact medium and confidence high are both right.
- **Tradeoffs:** Reverse sync is only as good as the editor integration, so it is inherently VS-Code-first and absent in a bare-browser preview; the highlightAtLine 'nearest preceding block' heuristic can point slightly off inside large fenced divs, which is acceptable but not exact. (skeptic-found downside: Three things the drafter missed. (1) The buffer-vs-disk drift is present TODAY, not just "if keystroke-preview lands": the preview renders from an on-disk read (serve/mod.rs std::fs::read_to_string on a notify Modify/Create/Remove event), while the cursor line comes from the editor buffer (onDidChangeTextEditorSelection). So whenever the buffer is dirty (i.e., during active typing, exactly when the cursor moves most), the qmd-cursor line is buffer-space but sourcepos is the last-saved render, so the highlight lands off by however many lines were inserted/deleted above. It self-heals on save, so it is minor, but it is a live edge, not a future one. (2) The .tali-hl outline has no clear/blur lifecycle: it is only removed when the NEXT qmd-cursor arrives, so a stale outline lingers on a block after you stop editing or focus the preview. (3) A benign feedback loop: an Alt-click posts qmd-goto, extension.ts sets the editor selection, that fires onDidChangeTextEditorSelection, which posts qmd-cursor back, so highlightAtLine now also adds the persistent .tali-hl (on top of the transient tali-hl-flash pulse) and may recenter the preview on a block you only clicked to navigate source. No infinite loop (highlightAtLine never posts back), but it is an unintended recenter-on-click that should be deliberate.)
- **Invariant check:** Read-only: cursor drives a highlight/scroll in the preview, never a source write. HTML-only untouched. The sourcepos totality it relies on is corpus-pinned.

### D6. Read-only preview + editor-command ergonomics vs a two-way visual (WYSIWYG) editor (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto ships a visual editor (a WYSIWYG surface backed by ProseMirror) that writes changes back to the .qmd via a pandoc markdown round-trip, alongside the source editor, with two-way sync.
- **Critique:** The visual editor is a genuine feature some authors want, but its markdown round-trip canonicalizes the source: it can rewrap prose, reorder/rewrite link references and attributes, and normalize syntax, so opening the visual editor mutates a hand-formatted .qmd in ways the author did not ask for. Two write paths (visual + source) also contend for ownership of the file.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's visual editor is the answer to concrete pain that snippet-style editor commands do not touch. (1) Markdown tables: editing a multi-column table by hand in source is genuinely miserable, and a grid editor is a decisive, not marginal, win. This is the single strongest case for the feature and the one Taliesin's proposal has no answer for. (2) Citations and cross-refs: the insert-citation UI with Zotero/DOI/PubMed search inserts a correct [@key] and manages the bibliography, which no keystroke command replicates without reimplementing a reference manager. (3) Equations, figures, embedded code, callouts via a menu: direct manipulation lowers the floor for authors who do not know Pandoc markdown, widening the audience. (4) Architecturally it is defensible: it is ONE editor with two synchronized views over a single in-memory buffer (VS Code or RStudio), not two processes racing over a file on disk, and the canonicalization is configurable (wrap: preserve keeps line breaks, references/canonical settings bound the rewrite), so the churn the critique describes is a default, not an inevitability. Quarto also gains a portability the read-only stance loses: the visual editor works for a bare user with no companion, whereas Taliesin's ergonomics are locked to a VS Code extension.
- **Taliesin today:** Deliberately rejected. The .tmd file is the only editing surface; the browser preview is strictly read-only and must never write back (a drag-to-reorder-slides feature was removed precisely because it created a second write path). Click-to-source navigates preview->editor but never writes.
- **Proposed better:** Do not build a WYSIWYG. Instead invest in editor-side commands (in the companion) that make common source edits ergonomic without a preview gesture: insert-callout, wrap-in-div, promote/demote heading, reorder-slide-in-source, insert-figure. This gives the ergonomic wins authors reach a visual editor for, while keeping one write path (the editor buffer) and never canonicalizing the source.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the stance, sharpen the framing. Rejecting WYSIWYG and delivering ergonomics through editor commands is the invariant-clean choice and it survives scrutiny, so do not build a two-way visual editor. But the entry must stop reading as a settled win and add four corrections. (1) Concede Quarto's real wins honestly: table editing above all (the entry has no substitute for it), plus Zotero/DOI citation insert; frame Taliesin as choosing not to serve the table-heavy and non-markdown-author segments, not as strictly dominating. (2) Scope the commands to what needs Taliesin's AST knowledge and cannot be a generic snippet: insert-figure (asset-path aware), reorder-slide-in-source, insert-cross-ref against the label index; do not reinvent heading promote/demote. (3) Require every source-rewriting command to be minimal-diff (touch only the lines it must, never reflow the rest) so it does not reproduce the canonicalization it criticizes; that minimal-diff, opt-in-per-invocation property is the actual advantage over Quarto's on-open reflow, and the entry should say THAT rather than a blanket no-canonicalization claim. (4) State plainly that this capability lives outside the .tmd corpus net and carries its own test story (companion node:test + e2e), and that it deepens VS Code lock-in that click-to-source deliberately avoids. Note the commands are Phase 2 and unbuilt, so keep impact at medium and mark it roadmap, not delivered.
- **Tradeoffs:** Some authors genuinely prefer direct-manipulation WYSIWYG and will see the read-only stance as a missing feature; editor commands are VS-Code-bound and do not help a bare-browser user. This is a real segment Taliesin chooses not to serve. (skeptic-found downside: Four costs the entry glosses. (1) It is unbuilt: editor/vscode/package.json registers exactly one command, qmdFast.openPreview; there is no insert-callout/wrap-in-div/reorder-slide/insert-figure. The entry reads as if the ergonomic parity is in hand, but it is a deferred Phase 2, so the win is aspirational, not shipped. (2) Redundancy: heading promote/demote, wrap, and callout snippets are already VS Code snippet or Markdown-All-in-One territory, so the marginal value of Taliesin-authored versions of the trivial commands is small; only the AST-aware ones (insert-figure with asset-path awareness, reorder-slide-in-source, insert-cross-ref against the doc's label index) genuinely need Taliesin. The entry lumps trivial and non-trivial together. (3) reorder-slide-in-source re-treads the exact ground: as a source rewrite it must move a slide's whole block (heading + fenced content + #| options + notes) without corrupting fenced-div nesting, and a naive version reproduces the very unrequested mutation the entry criticizes Quarto for, just triggered by a keystroke. Any source-rewriting command is a mini-canonicalizer and must be minimal-diff. (4) It deepens VS Code lock-in the entry only half-admits: click-to-source works with any editor that opens a file at a line, but every editor command is bound to the VS Code API, a strictly narrower surface. And the entry has no answer to the table case, Quarto's strongest.)
- **Invariant check:** Squarely upholds the single-editing-surface invariant; editor commands write the .tmd from the editor, not from the preview, so no second write path. HTML-only untouched. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation. Single-editing-surface is upheld (commands write the .tmd from the editor buffer, the sanctioned surface; preview stays read-only, verified: client.js emits only qmd-goto navigation messages, the companion does only revealRange/highlightAtLine, no WorkspaceEdit anywhere). HTML-only, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, block-incremental, and warm-server are all untouched. One SOFT tension the entry's invariant_check missed: corpus-plus-roadmap. editor/vscode/ is outside the cargo workspace and a .tmd corpus doc cannot exercise a VS Code command, so this is the one capability that cannot be pinned by the corpus (the stated arbiter of done); it would rely on the companion's separate node:test + Electron e2e suite, a weaker and non-standard net. The entry should say so rather than claim clean invariant coverage.)

### D7. In-preview click-to-source diagnostics + panic-guarded hot reload vs terminal errors (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto reports render/execution errors to the terminal (and can halt the preview update); the browser is left showing stale content or a generic error, with no in-page jump to the offending source line.
- **Critique:** When a render fails you must switch to the terminal, read a stack/pandoc error, and manually locate the line. A crash in the render path can also stop preview updates for the rest of the session, breaking the loop until you restart.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's terminal-only error channel is the honest lowest common denominator for a MULTI-format compiler, not laziness. Quarto renders to PDF, docx, revealjs, epub, book, and HTML; a large share of its errors originate in downstream tools (LaTeX, pandoc, knitr, jupyter) whose diagnostics are inherently log/line oriented and cannot map to a live HTML DOM, because for a PDF or docx render there IS no live HTML view to annotate. The terminal is the only surface that works uniformly across every target. Quarto also has no sourcepos/block-id model, no editor bridge, and no single-editing-surface guarantee, so in-page click-to-source is simply not available to it at any price. An in-preview located-diagnostics panel with jump-to-source is a luxury only an HTML-only, block-mapped, single-source tool like Taliesin can afford; framed that way, Quarto's choice is the correct tax of format-generality rather than a defect. (One nuance: the critique slightly overstates the crash risk. `quarto preview` normally catches render/execution failures and keeps its watch loop alive, recovering on the next save; only a genuine process-level crash breaks the loop, which is rare, so terminal-report plus stale-browser is the accurate everyday failure mode, not a dead session.)
- **Taliesin today:** Built and better. rebuild_guarded wraps render+exec in catch_unwind so one pathological document cannot kill the hot-reload task; on panic it logs, marks the doc errored, and pushes an error diagnostic, and the next good save fully re-mounts (clearing the overlay). Diagnostics (broken YAML front matter with a code_frame, unresolved includes, unresolved xrefs, kernel-unavailable, missing bibliography/theme) surface in the floating dev menu; a located diagnostic is a clickable jump-to-source row. Cell errors get their own scroll-to-cell chip.
- **Proposed better:** Keep. Optional: also render an in-page inline marker at the failing block (not just the dev-menu list) so a located error is visible where the output should be, mirroring the cell-error affordance for prose/front-matter errors.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the shipped core as verified 'taliesin-already-better': panic-guarded hot reload (rebuild_guarded catch_unwind + errored flag + forced re-mount recovery, unit-tested), located jump-to-source dev-menu diagnostics with code frames, inline-in-place cell errors, and the scroll-to-cell chip all confirmed in code. Do NOT build generic inline markers for front-matter or fatal errors: they have no anchor block and the DOM is stale, and the fatal-error overlay already covers them. The higher-leverage move is the inverse of the drafter's: make MORE diagnostics located by attaching a line to the currently-unlocated warnings (include-not-found already has line info in includes.rs IncludeWarning but serve.rs drops it; bibliography/theme file-missing could carry the front-matter key line), so the EXISTING dev-menu jump-to-source covers them uniformly. Only if an inline affordance is still wanted, restrict it to the narrow class that already renders degraded output in place and carries a line (unresolved xref, broken citation) as a subtle gutter/underline on that block, errors-not-warnings, and pin it with a dedicated corpus document (the current guard is unit-tested, not corpus-pinned, so any new inline behavior must add a corpus doc to satisfy corpus-plus-roadmap).
- **Tradeoffs:** More inline error chrome risks visual noise on a doc with many warnings; the dev-menu list keeps the reading surface clean, so inline markers should be reserved for errors, not warnings. (skeptic-found downside: The optional inline-marker add-on names the exact cases it cannot serve. (1) Front-matter errors have no anchor: front matter emits no rendered block in the body DOM, so there is no data-block-id element to attach an inline marker to. A cell error is inline precisely because a cell IS a block that produces output in place; front matter is not, so 'mirroring the cell-error affordance for front-matter errors' is architecturally unavailable. (2) A fatal render/panic keeps the LAST GOOD (stale) content mounted, whose block IDs no longer correspond to the current broken source; an inline marker would attach to mismatched stale blocks or to nothing, which is exactly why the unmissable full-screen fatal-error overlay already exists. (3) Diagnostics carry a source LINE, not a block-id, so the client would need new fuzzy line-to-block mapping (a fresh mis-anchoring failure mode) for a line that falls in front matter or between blocks. (4) The only located diagnostics that CAN anchor (unresolved xref renders raw @fig-x in place, broken citation renders raw [@key] in place) already show visibly-degraded output at the spot AND already jump-to-source from the dev-menu row, so the marginal value is low. (5) Most diagnostics are UNLOCATED (include-not-found, kernel-unavailable, missing bibliography/theme, citations-without-bibliography all use Diagnostic::warn with no line), so inline markers would appear for a small inconsistent subset, arguably worse than the uniform dev-menu list.)
- **Invariant check:** Diagnostics navigate to source (read-only), never write. HTML-only untouched. Panic-guard behavior is unit-tested (rebuild_guard_catches_panic_and_recovers_message).

### D8. Click-to-source hardcodes the vscode:// URL scheme instead of a configurable editor (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Not applicable (Quarto has no click-to-source), so there is no comparison; this is a Taliesin-internal limitation surfaced while cataloguing.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's forward click-to-source in a bare browser always builds window.location.href = 'vscode://file...' (client.js lines 1045 and 1074). An author on Cursor (cursor://), Zed (zed://), or any non-VS-Code editor gets a jump that opens the wrong app or fails, even though the webview-relay path is editor-agnostic. This quietly ties the single-author's headline feature to one editor.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto emits no editor deep-link into the browser at all. Source-to-preview navigation lives entirely in the editor-side integration (the Quarto VS Code and RStudio extensions), which inherently knows which editor it is running in, so the "which URL scheme" question never arises. That is arguably the cleaner boundary: never bake machine-specific editor knowledge into served HTML, because the page cannot know which editor opened it and any scheme it hardcodes is wrong for someone. Tellingly, Taliesin's OWN editor-agnostic webview-relay path (the qmd-goto postMessage handled by the companion host) is exactly this Quarto-style pattern. The bare-browser vscode:// fallback is the compromise that reintroduces precisely the editor-coupling Quarto avoided by construction. So "Quarto's choice" here (keep navigation in the editor layer, never in the page) is defensible, and it is the pattern Taliesin should lean into, not paper over with per-editor URL presets.
- **Taliesin today:** vscode://file is hardcoded in two places in client.js; there is no config key for the editor URL scheme or a generic file+line command. The webview/companion path (qmd-goto postMessage) is editor-agnostic, but the plain-browser fallback is VS-Code-only.
- **Proposed better:** Add a front-matter/_site.yml key (e.g. editor: vscode|cursor|zed|<custom-uri-template>) that the server injects into window.TALIESIN_DOC, and have openSource build the URL from a template like '{scheme}://file{abs}:{line}:{col}'. Default to vscode:// to preserve current behavior.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the fix but change the mechanism. (a) Prefer an ENV VAR (e.g. TALIESIN_EDITOR_URI), matching the existing QMD_FAST_*/TALIESIN_* family, over a front-matter/_site.yml key, because editor choice is machine-scoped, not document-scoped; this also dodges the strict-schema addition and the front-matter corpus-pin. (b) Make the single knob a URI TEMPLATE string with documented placeholders ({path}, {line}, {col}, plus a url-encoded variant for query-style schemes), defaulting to the current vscode://file{path}:{line}:{col}. Drop the vscode|cursor|zed enum, or treat named editors as pure sugar over built-in templates, because a curated list is a maintenance treadmill and cannot express JetBrains/TextMate/terminal editors. (c) Handle URL-encoding explicitly (encodeURI for path-suffix schemes, encodeURIComponent for query-embedded ones) and keep it distinct from js_str JS-literal escaping. (d) DRY both fallbacks (gotoSource line 1045 and openSource line 1074) through one URL-building helper so they cannot drift; update web-client/README.md which still says "vscode:// by default." (e) Frame it honestly as a pragmatic patch for the bare-browser preview; the durable answer is to make the already-editor-agnostic companion webview the default preview surface, which retires the scheme question entirely (the Quarto-style boundary).
- **Tradeoffs:** Another config key to validate against the strict-config contract (schema.rs must know it or it gets flagged); custom URI templates are a small injection surface that needs the same js_str escaping already used for paths. (skeptic-found downside: Four things the drafter missed. (1) The template shape {scheme}://file{abs}:{line}:{col} does NOT generalize: VS Code, Cursor, VSCodium fit, but JetBrains uses jetbrains://idea/navigate/reference?project=NAME&path=... (needs a project, not a bare file path), TextMate uses txmt://open?url=file://{path}&line={line} (query-embedded, needs encodeURIComponent not encodeURI), and terminal editors (vim/neovim/emacs) have no OS URL handler at all. So the named enum vscode|cursor|zed is perpetually incomplete and gives false completeness, and one template with {abs} cannot express these shapes. (2) Wrong config scope: which editor you use is a property of the previewing MACHINE, not of the committed document; putting it in front-matter/_site.yml bakes machine state into version control, so a committed editor: zed mis-navigates on any other machine or editor. Taliesin already has the right home for this: the QMD_FAST_PYTHON / QMD_FAST_R / QMD_FAST_CELL_TIMEOUT env-var family. (3) The tradeoffs conflate two unrelated escaping concerns: js_str only makes the value safe as a JS string literal injected into the inline script; it does nothing for URL-encoding the path inside the template (encodeURI vs encodeURIComponent), which the current code does separately via encodeURI(abs). (4) Scope of impact is narrower than "medium" implies in one axis: TALIESIN_DOC is injected only by the preview servers, never by the static build (page.rs), so this is preview-only, and the webview companion path is already editor-agnostic. It is real, though, because the companion is still pending acceptance, so the bare-browser preview is the common path.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure navigation target (read-only); HTML-only untouched. New key must be added to the strict schema so it is not flagged, and pinned by a corpus doc per corpus-plus-roadmap. (possible violation flagged: None. The vscode://file:line:col fallback and any replacement template only NAVIGATE the editor; they never write to source, so the single read-only editing surface holds. HTML-only, Markdown syntax, block-level incremental, and warm-server invariants are all untouched. One honesty caveat on corpus-plus-roadmap: a corpus test can pin that the server injects the configured template into TALIESIN_DOC and that the client builds the expected URL string, but it cannot pin that the OS actually opened Zed/Cursor (no editor in CI), so the invariant_check's "pinned by a corpus doc" is only partly real. Note also that routing this to an env var instead of front-matter removes the strict-schema key entirely, so the "must add to schema.rs or it gets flagged" burden and the front-matter corpus-doc obligation both disappear.)

### D9. Granularity of what stays incremental vs forces a reload (decks, site structure) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto reloads the whole preview page on essentially any change, so there is no notion of a partial vs full update; slide decks and multi-page sites reload wholesale.
- **Critique:** Wholesale reload on a slide deck loses the current slide and overview state; on a multi-page site it reloads even for edits that only touched the current page's prose.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A wholesale reload is correct by construction: it can never show a stale or wrong DOM for ANY change (content, structure, config, theme, cross-page nav, listings, includes, shortcodes), so it carries zero classifier bug surface. That is exactly where Taliesin's two deck gaps live (`---`/`<hr>` breaks and h2 to h3 level changes silently leave stale section grouping); Quarto pays none of that cost. Second, Quarto runs one format-agnostic re-render+reload pipeline across HTML, PDF, reveal, docx, epub, and books, which guarantees the preview equals the final artifact byte-for-byte; Taliesin can only afford incrementalism because it sacrificed multi-format scope for HTML-only + a block model + content-hash ids. Third, Quarto delegates state restoration to the format: reveal.js writes the current slide to the URL hash, so a preview reload usually returns you to the same slide, meaning the critique overstates 'loses the current slide' for decks; the accurate loss is overview mode, in-slide fragment step, scroll, and runtime JS state (and, on multi-page, the current page's scroll/JS). Fourth, simplicity and maintainability: no diff engine, no per-format 'did this edit change the section grouping' heuristics to keep in sync as the renderer evolves.
- **Taliesin today:** Built with deliberate granularity. Single-doc decks stay incremental for within-slide edits and only full re-mount when an Insert/Remove touches a slide HEADING (is_slide_heading), and even then the deck's JS preserves current slide + overview across the DOM swap. In site mode (serve_site/mod.rs), a content edit rebuilds only the affected page and diffs it (diff_blocks per PageState); a structural change (add/remove a page, _site.yml edit) re-discovers the site and reload_open_tabs; theme/.css edits hot-swap the <style> with no reload. The watcher marks a batch structural only when a .qmd/.tmd was created/removed.
- **Proposed better:** Keep. Minor: a _site.yml edit currently reloads all open tabs even when the change (e.g. a footer tweak) could be a targeted chrome hot-swap; a finer classifier could keep more edits incremental, but the current conservative reload is safe.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the direction: deliberate reload granularity genuinely beats Quarto's wholesale reload within the HTML-only, single-author, live-authoring scope, and preserving running {js}/WebGL cells, open <details>, and scroll through a block-level diff is load-bearing and structurally impossible for Quarto's re-render+reload. But sharpen the entry: (1) Fix or document two deck-classifier gaps: extend the structural test so a full deck re-mount also fires when an Insert/Remove touches an `is_slide_break` (`<hr>`) block, AND when an Update flips a block's slide-boundary classification (`is_slide_heading(old) != is_slide_heading(new)`, covering h2<->h3). (2) Pin both with a corpus deck that uses `---` breaks and a level change, closing the coverage claim. (3) Soften the Quarto critique on decks: reveal restores the slide from the URL hash, so the honest losses are overview mode, fragment step, scroll, and runtime state, not the slide itself; the multi-page critique stands. (4) Lower confidence from high to medium until (1) and (2) land. Keep the site-side conservative reload as-is and do NOT pursue the _site.yml footer hot-swap: _site.yml drives navbar, footer, listings, ordering, search index, xref resolution, mounts, and favicon, so a 'footer-only' classifier must prove the touched field is chrome-local and identical across every open page, which is far more than the 'minor' label implies and is exactly the class of change where a wrong guess leaves stale nav.
- **Tradeoffs:** Finer structural classification risks getting a case wrong and leaving a tab showing stale nav/listings; the conservative 'structural -> reload' rule trades a little flash for correctness, which is the right default. (skeptic-found downside: The entry presents deck state preservation and structural detection as fully solved, but the incremental deck path has two un-caught correctness holes. (1) `is_slide_heading` only matches `<h1`/`<h2`, so an Insert/Remove of a `---` slide break (an `<hr>` block, which deck.rs treats as a slide boundary) is NOT flagged structural; the live deck applies flat ops that never re-slice `<section>`s, showing a stray `<hr>` mid-slide or slides that fail to merge until a reload. (2) A heading level change across the slide threshold (`## ` h2 to `### ` h3) manifests as a diff Update, and `deck_structural` inspects only Insert/Remove, so the deck swaps the heading element in place and keeps stale grouping. Also, `sync()` preserves the current INDEX (clampIndices), not slide identity, so a structural insert/remove above the viewport shifts which slide you land on. Corpus coverage does not exercise any of this: corpus/deck.qmd uses only `##` slides, and no live-serve test drives `deck_structural`.)
- **Invariant check:** All updates are server->preview (read-only); block identity preserved through diffs; HTML-only untouched. Deck and site reload behavior are exercised by the corpus/site tests. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is broken (all updates stay server to preview and read-only, block identity is preserved through diffs, HTML-only and Markdown syntax are untouched, click-to-source and the warm server are unaffected). But the corpus-plus-roadmap invariant is under-served: the entry's 'exercised by the corpus/site tests' claim is not backed for the live deck classifier that the entry is about, since the only corpus deck is heading-only and no test drives the `---` or level-change structural paths.)

### D10. Should an included partial retain per-file source provenance so click-to-source and the block-diff cross file boundaries, or is an include a provenance-erasing text splice? (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `{{< include partial.qmd >}}` is a pre-parse text splice: the partial's raw bytes are concatenated into the parent buffer before Pandoc parses, so the resulting AST (and every HTML element it emits) carries no record of which source file a given block came from. Provenance is erased at the seam. This is fine for Quarto because Quarto has no click-to-source at all: there is nothing that would ever need to map a rendered element back to `partial.qmd:12` rather than to a flattened offset in the parent. Its preview reload is whole-document re-render, and `_freeze` caches at the notebook/document grain, so a partial has no independent identity anywhere downstream of the splice. Quarto's separate visual (WYSIWYG) editor likewise does not round-trip edits cleanly across an include boundary.
- **Critique:** Multi-file authoring is normal (shared preamble, book chapters composed from subsection partials, a reusable Three.js scene definition). With a provenance-erasing splice, the moment you click a rendered block that actually lives in a partial, there is no correct answer to "where do I edit this?" because the compiled artifact has thrown away the file identity. Quarto never hits this wall only because it never offers the round-trip in the first place. For a tool whose load-bearing promise is Alt-click-a-block-jumps-to-its-source-line, a plain text splice is a silent correctness hole: it would send you to the wrong file, or to a meaningless line in the parent. It also defeats scoped incremental updates: without per-file line numbering, editing a partial looks like a large diff (every downstream line number shifted) instead of a small one confined to the partial.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Pre-parse text splicing is the correct design for a multi-format, context-merging compiler, not an oversight. Because the concatenation happens before Pandoc parses, the included fragment participates fully in the parent's document context: cross-references, footnotes, labels, and citations defined in a partial resolve against the parent, a partial need not be an independently valid document, and YAML merges. A parse-each-file-then-stitch-block-trees design would break all of that. Provenance erasure is inherent to producing ONE coherent document across LaTeX/PDF/Word/ePub, where there is no live view and no editor round-trip to consume per-block file identity, so a source map would be dead weight plus extra bookkeeping surface (per-file line arithmetic, labels, cycle-plus-map edge cases) with zero downstream consumer. Document-grain _freeze matches Quarto's notebook-as-unit execution model. Critically, Taliesin does NOT beat this by abandoning the splice: includes.rs ALSO splices-then-parses and merely keeps a parallel LineOrigin side map, so it retains every context-merging benefit and only refuses to throw the map away. Quarto's choice is right FOR QUARTO's constraints; it is not a design Taliesin proved wrong, it is one Taliesin extended for a load-bearing feature (click-to-source) that Quarto deliberately does not offer.
- **Taliesin today:** Already built and threaded end to end. `includes.rs` resolves `{{< include >}}` into one expanded buffer while emitting a per-line source map (`Vec<LineOrigin { file, line }>`: `None` = primary doc, `Some(label)` = partial, path relative to the primary base), recursing through nested includes with consistent labels, guarding cycles, and refusing path-traversal escapes via `safe_join`; an unresolvable include is left literal AND reported as a located `IncludeWarning` (click-to-source diagnostic), never silently dropped. `render/mod.rs` carries `source_file` into every `Block` and `source_file_attr` emits an escaped `data-source-file="…"` on leaf blocks and fenced-div containers alike (generated blocks like title/footnotes are `None`). `diff.rs` carries `source_file` in `BlockOp::SetMeta`, and `eq_ignoring_sourcepos` treats `data-source-file` as load-bearing (must match exactly), so the block-diff patches provenance across edits while content-hash ids keep unchanged partial blocks stable. `client.js` (`blockRef`/`openSource`/`gotoSource`) resolves an included block to `baseDir + "/" + source_file` and navigates the editor there via `vscode://file` or a webview `qmd-goto`, so Alt-click on a partial's block lands in the partial at the right line; a11y diagnostics use the same `data-source-file` ancestor. Both dev servers watch `includes::dependencies()` so editing a partial hot-reloads without a restart. Because sourcepos resets per file, editing a partial shifts only that partial's line numbers, leaving the primary doc's own blocks untouched, which is exactly the minimal-churn behavior the splice model cannot produce. Corpus/tests pin emission and ordering: `includes_are_resolved_with_origin_files` (pca-geometry pulls `_includes/three-scene.qmd`; bayesian-website pulls 5+ subsection files), the per-file monotonic-sourcepos invariant in `corpus.rs` (keyed by `source_file`), `include_relative_base.rs`, and `located_warnings.rs`.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the per-file source map and the "`data-source-file` on every emitted block" design exactly as verified: it is the right choice and it is a genuine beat-Quarto property that the catalog had not recorded. The one open increment is to close the test-net gap so the property is corpus-pinned rather than only unit-verified. Today's corpus asserts that provenance is emitted and that lines are monotonic per file, but no corpus document pins (a) the live reverse-sync round-trip (Alt-click a block that lives in a partial actually lands the editor in the partial at the right line, exercised through the browser/relay harness) or (b) the scoped incremental diff when the partial itself is edited (an edit to the partial yields Update/SetMeta ops carrying the correct `source_file`, and leaves the primary doc's own blocks untouched because sourcepos is per-file). `incremental.rs` has only a synthetic SetMeta-with-source_file case, not a corpus-pinned edit-the-partial scenario. Add a dedicated corpus document (a parent plus a partial it includes) and pin both behaviors, so this capability moves from "true in code" to "guarded by the arbiter of done."
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the design and the catalog verdict: taliesin-already-better is verified in code. Splice-then-parse plus a LineOrigin side map is a strict SUPERSET of Quarto's splice (it keeps context-merging while adding per-block file provenance that click-to-source and the block-diff consume end to end via source_file on Block, SetMeta, eq_ignoring_sourcepos, and client.js blockRef/gotoSource). Record that superset framing explicitly so the catalog does not read as if Taliesin traded away the splice's benefits. Then sharpen the increment by splitting it rather than adding one heavy browser 'corpus document': (1) add a CHEAP pure-Rust pin against an existing include doc (pca-geometry or bayesian-website) asserting that a partial-sourced block's sourcepos line EQUALS its line within the partial file (presence and per-file ordering are already covered by includes_are_resolved_with_origin_files and the monotonic-per-file invariant; only the line VALUE is unpinned, and it is exactly what click-to-source correctness hinges on); (2) add the genuinely-missing pure-Rust scoped-diff test (the highest-value gap): render parent-plus-partial v1, edit ONLY the partial, re-render with includes, diff, and assert the resulting Update/SetMeta ops carry Some(source_file) for the partial while the primary doc's own blocks show no id drift and no ops, proving 'editing a partial is a small, file-scoped diff'; (3) treat the live editor-landing round-trip as ALREADY covered by the existing vscode relay-harness plus e2e suite, and do not rebuild it as a corpus document or a new browser harness. This delivers the load-bearing regression protection in fast, deterministic pure-Rust tests and avoids the flaky, redundant browser pin.
- **Tradeoffs:** The core capability is already shipped, so the proposed increment is test-net hardening, not new behavior: its payoff is regression protection, not a user-visible feature, and it costs maintenance. Pinning the live round-trip (a) needs the browser/relay harness rather than a pure render unit test, which is heavier and slightly flakier than the existing pure-Rust corpus assertions; the `reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total` invariant already proves sourcepos is parseable but not that file+line resolves to the correct editor location, which is precisely why the round-trip needs its own pin. One inherent limit to note (not a defect to fix): because line numbering is per file, a partial included in two places points both rendered copies at the same partial source line; that is correct (there is only one source line) but a user might momentarily expect distinct provenance per inclusion site. (skeptic-found downside: The pin-(a) prescription conflates 'corpus-pinned' with 'browser/relay-harness pinned.' The corpus (cargo test) can cheaply pin the EMISSION half of the round-trip (a partial block's data-source-file plus its per-file line VALUE), but the 'lands the editor at the right line' half is not a corpus concern at all: it is the VS Code relay's job and is already covered by the existing editor/vscode relay-harness.cjs plus @vscode/test-electron e2e tests (per project memory). So building a fresh browser 'corpus document' for it risks duplicating existing coverage while importing exactly the flakier browser dependency the drafter itself flags. Also, 'add a dedicated corpus document' slightly over-scopes: pca-geometry and bayesian-website are ALREADY parent-plus-partial include docs exercised by includes_are_resolved_with_origin_files, so the two genuinely-missing pins (the per-file line-VALUE assertion, and the edit-the-partial scoped-diff) can attach to them without a new fixture. Separately, on the drafter's 'benign nuance': same-partial-included-twice is safe (dedup_with_suffix gives identical-content blocks distinct positional -N ids, so the duplicate-data-block-id uniqueness invariant in corpus.rs is not tripped), but a consequence they omit is that editing a twice-included partial yields N ops (one per inclusion site), not literally one small op, and the -N id suffix is document-order-dependent.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: provenance is inert metadata on HTML blocks, no new output format.
