Single read-only surface: reverse-sync into a partial only NAVIGATES the editor, it never writes the partial; the preview stays read-only, honoring the removed-drag-to-reorder lesson. Keep-Markdown: `{{< include >}}` remains the unchanged Pandoc/Quarto-lineage shortcode; nothing about the syntax changes, this layers strictly above it. Click-to-source: this IS that invariant, extended across file boundaries rather than stopping at the primary document. Block-level incremental: `SetMeta`/`Update` carry `source_file`, and content-hash ids keep unchanged partial blocks identity-stable, so the diff crosses partials. Warm-server: `includes::dependencies()` watching keeps partials hot with no per-edit restart. Corpus-plus-roadmap: the proposed increment is literally adding a pinning corpus document, tightening the net rather than outrunning it.

### D11. How to view a live HTML preview on a real phone: an auto-detected, token-gated --host with a terminal QR, vs. Quarto's raw unauthenticated LAN bind (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto preview binds localhost by default. `quarto preview doc.qmd --host 0.0.0.0 --port N` will expose it on the LAN, but it is a raw bind: Quarto does not auto-detect or print your machine's LAN IP, prints no QR code, and applies no access control (any peer on the network that finds host:port gets in). Hot reload works over the LAN, but you type the address into the phone by hand, and the exposed surface is unauthenticated.
- **Critique:** Two frictions. (1) Discovery: to open the preview on a phone you must know the dev machine's LAN IP and type `http://192.168.x.y:port` in by hand every session. (2) Safety: `--host 0.0.0.0` is all-or-nothing exposure. The preview is reachable by any LAN peer with no authentication, and (for a tool that runs code cells on your machine) there is no in-product warning that you have just opened an executing surface to the network.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's raw `--host` bind is the universal dev-server convention: vite, hugo, jekyll, webpack-dev-server all expose an unauthenticated 0.0.0.0 bind and assume you are on a trusted network. That predictability is a real virtue. There is no session token to lose, a bookmarked phone URL works forever, and no experienced dev is surprised by a 403 where the page should be. Quarto also accepts an explicit interface, `quarto preview --host 192.168.1.5`, which sidesteps the multi-homed interface-guessing that a single-probe auto-detect gets wrong. On safety, the critique's "you just opened an executing surface to the network" framing is loose: in both Quarto and Taliesin a LAN peer hitting the preview does NOT trigger code execution (code runs at render time on your own machine regardless of who connects); the real LAN risks are a peer reading your unpublished draft and, in Taliesin's case, driving the websocket control channel, not remote code execution. Quarto's livereload socket only pushes reload events and exposes no restart-kernel control, so its unauthenticated bind is arguably a smaller attack surface than Taliesin's richer ws. Finally, Quarto is a general multi-format compiler whose preview is often a plain static file server for pre-rendered output; a blanket "executing surface" warning would be wrong for the majority of its documents, so declining to print one is defensible for a general tool.
- **Taliesin today:** Built and verified from code. `--host` (or the `QMD_FAST_HOST` env var) binds 0.0.0.0 in both the single-doc server (crates/server/src/serve/mod.rs) and the multi-page site server (serve_site/mod.rs); `local_ip()` auto-detects the LAN address via a UDP-connect probe, then the console prints the LAN URL and a scannable terminal QR (`print_qr`, the `qrcode` crate rendered as unicode half-blocks). Security is a clean, separate layer (serve/security.rs): a fresh per-session UUID token is minted ONLY under `--host` and embedded as `?t=` in the QR/URL; `lan_token_guard` middleware waves loopback peers through token-free (so the local workflow is byte-for-byte unchanged) but returns 403 to any non-loopback peer lacking the token, and the first `?t=` load sets an HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie so later asset/websocket requests authenticate silently. The websocket also checks origin (`ws_origin_ok`). Without `--host` the guard is never installed. It additionally warns "code cells run on this machine; only serve documents you trust over --host", and warns if no LAN address was found.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the current design (auto-detected LAN IP + terminal QR + loopback-token-free, LAN-token-gated exposure); it strictly dominates Quarto's raw `--host`, so no code churn is warranted. Two small refinements worth pinning by a doc/test note rather than a rewrite: (a) surface the session-token tradeoff next to the QR so the author knows a bookmarked phone URL dies with the session (a new token is minted each launch), which reads as a mysterious 403 otherwise; (b) document the plain-HTTP secure-context ceiling (clipboard API, service workers, getUserMedia, and similar are unavailable on the phone over http://LAN) so a future on-device browser-behavior feature is not specced expecting APIs the phone cannot grant.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the status (taliesin-already-better is correct and every code claim verified) and keep the token-gated + QR + loopback-free design, which strictly dominates Quarto on discovery and access control. But revise the "no code churn" stance: add one small, invariant-safe fix in the advertising layer so multi-homed and offline-LAN authors get a usable QR, either make `--host`/`QMD_FAST_HOST` accept an optional interface/IP value (matching Quarto's one real advantage) or enumerate and print all private-range LAN IPs and fall back gracefully when the 8.8.8.8 probe returns None. Keep doc refinement (a) verbatim (surface that the per-session token means a bookmarked phone URL dies each launch, so a stale link 403s by design). Correct doc refinement (b): drop clipboard from the "unavailable" list (it already has an execCommand fallback) and scope the secure-context note to service workers, getUserMedia, and PWA/sensor APIs. Pin all of this by the existing security unit tests plus the documented invariant note; a rendered .tmd corpus doc is genuinely not the right net for a preview-workflow feature, and saying so explicitly (a reasoned exception, not a silent skip) satisfies corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Tradeoffs:** The per-session token means a phone bookmark breaks on the next launch (you re-scan); a stable token would fix that but weakens the security model, so the current session-scoped default is the right call. The terminal QR assumes a unicode-capable terminal and degrades to the printed URL otherwise (already handled). `local_ip()` picks a single route via one UDP-connect probe, so a multi-homed machine (VPN plus Wi-Fi) can advertise the wrong interface. Plain HTTP means traffic is unencrypted on the LAN and no secure-context browser APIs are available on-device, acceptable for the stated trusted-home-network use but not for a hostile network. (skeptic-found downside: The "no code churn is warranted" conclusion is too strong because of the interface-advertising layer. `local_ip()` does one UDP connect to 8.8.8.8, which has two real failure modes the drafter under-weighted: (1) on a multi-homed machine with a VPN up, the probe routes out the tunnel and advertises a VPN IP the phone cannot reach, while 0.0.0.0 IS listening on the phone-reachable Wi-Fi IP that never gets printed; (2) on a LAN with no internet default route (travel router, conference or air-gapped network, the exact trusted-home case) the connect returns ENETUNREACH so `local_ip()` returns None and NO QR prints at all, even though the preview is reachable. And unlike Quarto's `--host <ip>`, Taliesin's `--host` is a boolean and `QMD_FAST_HOST` is presence-only (`var_os(...).is_some()`), so the author has no override to pin the right interface. This is the one axis where Quarto is genuinely better, and it is a small, in-scope advertising-layer fix (enumerate/print all private-range IPs, accept an optional interface value, or fall back when the probe yields None), not a rewrite. Separately, refinement (b) is partly stale: Taliesin already ships an execCommand clipboard fallback for the plain-http --host case (code-enhance/01-registry.js, 08-copy-buttons.js), so "clipboard API unavailable" is wrong; only service workers, getUserMedia, and PWA/sensor APIs are the real secure-context ceiling. Minor: the token rides the first load in the URL query, so it lands in the phone's history and server logs (acceptable session-scoped on a trusted LAN, but an unnamed property).)
- **Invariant check:** Respects every invariant. HTML-only: the phone loads the same built HTML view, no new output format. Single read-only surface: the phone is strictly a viewer with no write path back to source, and click-to-source is a desktop-editor bridge (vscode://file) that simply has no target from a phone, so read-only is enforced by construction rather than by policy. Warm server: `--host` only changes the bind address (0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1) and adds a guard layer on the existing warm dev server plus Jupyter kernel, with no per-edit startup cost. Block-level incremental: the same websocket block-diff drives the phone as drives localhost. Keep-Markdown: no syntax touched. Corpus-plus-roadmap: this is preview-workflow process, not document output, so its regression net is the existing security unit tests (lan_access / origin checks) plus a documented invariant note, not a rendered .tmd corpus doc.

## Code execution and caching

### D12. One cumulative-content-hash cache instead of Quarto's two-tier freeze + per-cell cache (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto ships two separate mechanisms: project-level `freeze: auto|true` stores whole-document outputs in `_freeze/` (refreshed on content change), and per-cell `cache: true` (jupyter-cache or knitr cache) keyed roughly by that cell's own code.
- **Critique:** Per-cell `cache` does not capture kernel variable state, so a cell whose own text is unchanged but whose upstream state changed can serve a stale hit; users learn to clear caches by hand. The two systems interact confusingly (freeze vs cache vs neither), and knitr's dependency tracking is famously brittle.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** freeze and cache are two mechanisms because they solve two orthogonal problems on purpose. freeze decouples WHO executes from WHO renders: the author runs the doc once on the machine that has the data, credentials, GPU, and kernel, commits _freeze/ to git, and a CI or publish server with no Python/R renders without executing at all. It is a reproducibility and deployment boundary, not an incremental-build cache. cache is a deliberately author-controlled dependency graph: with knitr cache=TRUE plus dependson, an author can declare that an expensive 40-minute training chunk does not depend on a downstream plotting chunk they keep editing, so it is not re-run. Crucially, knitr also writes the chunk's R objects to a cache database and lazy-loads them, so on a fully cold render it can skip the expensive chunk AND still make its variables available downstream. Taliesin's unified content hash expresses neither: it cannot skip an expensive upstream cell when an unrelated upstream cell was edited (the cumulative key moved), and because it caches only rendered output HTML and never kernel variable state, a cold start after editing any late cell must re-execute the entire prefix up to that cell just to rebuild state. For an author with an expensive early cell, that is a real, repeated cost that Quarto's cache plus dependson plus object persistence was specifically designed to avoid. So the two-tier design is not accidental redundancy; each tier buys something the single scheme gives up. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** A single cache. `freeze::cumulative_hashes` seeds with the interpreter id then folds every same-language cell's code left to right, so cell i's key encodes every byte the kernel ran to reach it (freeze.rs). Editing a cell, anything upstream, or the interpreter moves its key and every downstream key, so a stale hit is impossible by construction. Cache is on by default; `#| cache: false` opts out; errors and truncated outputs are never stored.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the scheme; it is the right call. The one refinement worth making is orthogonal to the hashing itself (see the interpreter-identity entry about not folding in the absolute program path).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the unified cumulative-hash cache: for a single-author, correctness-first, HTML-only tool with a warm in-session kernel, it is the right call and Taliesin is genuinely better here (it gets freeze's cross-session restore for free, makes code and upstream staleness impossible, needs no manual dependency declaration, and has nothing to clear by hand; the warm loop hides most of the cold-start cost because state persists in-session). But sharpen the entry so the catalog is not a strawman: (1) Narrow the claim from "stale hit impossible by construction" to "impossible for code, interpreter, and upstream-code changes; external-input staleness (data files, imported modules, env, clock, unseeded RNG) remains, same as Quarto, with #| cache: false as the escape." (2) Fix the critique to distinguish jupyter-cache (invalidates on ANY code change, so no upstream-stale hit) from knitr (chunk dependson/autodep brittleness), rather than describing both as "keyed by the cell's own code." (3) Reframe the tradeoff as an honest capability sacrifice, not just a safety win: Taliesin gives up knitr's disk-persisted, lazy-loaded variable state, so it cannot skip an expensive upstream cell on a cold start or when an unrelated upstream cell is edited, and it re-runs the whole prefix up to any edited cell on a cold start; the warm-kernel session is what makes this acceptable. Leave the interpreter-absolute-path fold to the orthogonal interpreter-identity entry as the drafter already noted. Conclusion (keep the scheme) is unchanged; only the framing needs tightening.
- **Tradeoffs:** Because variable state is never cached, a cold start can only skip work when the whole document is unchanged (one upstream edit re-runs from that cell down). That is the honest price of never serving a stale hit; Quarto's per-cell cache 'skips more' precisely by risking staleness. (skeptic-found downside: "Stale hit impossible by construction" is an overclaim. Verified in code: cumulative_hashes (freeze.rs:57-65) folds ONLY the interpreter id and each same-language cell's code, and exec.rs:387-395 adds only a fig-export marker to the hashed code. External inputs are never in the key, so a cell that reads a data file (pd.read_csv), imports a local module, reads an env var, uses the wall clock, or draws from an unseeded RNG will serve a replayed, now-stale output exactly as jupyter-cache would; #| cache: false is the only escape. Impossibility holds only for code, interpreter, and upstream-code changes, not staleness in general. Second missed cost: because variable state is never persisted, a cold start after editing any late cell re-runs the WHOLE prefix, not just "from that cell down." The plan (exec.rs:830-853) returns shared=0 on a cold kernel, so cells 0..k all execute to rebuild state even though their outputs are already on disk; knitr's lazy-loaded object cache would let Quarto skip an unchanged expensive upstream chunk there. The tradeoffs section frames the sacrifice as a pure safety win and misses that it is also a capability sacrifice (no state caching, no author-pinned dependency skip).)
- **Invariant check:** Content-hash keying is the block-level-incremental and warm-server story at the execution layer; outputs are self-contained HTML (inline data URIs), so there are no sidecar assets, preserving HTML-only. Corpus documents with cells pin the behavior and the freeze round-trip is unit-tested.

### D13. One warm kernel per session plus a forkserver warm pool, with warm-prefix incremental re-execution (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto starts a Jupyter kernel per render; `execute-daemon` keeps a kernel alive across renders (and Julia has a server) to amortize startup cost. Each render still re-executes the notebook subject to freeze/cache: it does not hold a live kernel's variable state across edits and re-run only the changed cell.
- **Critique:** The daemon reduces boot cost but not the per-edit work: saving re-runs the document from the top (or from freeze), so a one-line change to the last cell still pays to re-establish state. There is no 'the kernel already holds the unchanged prefix, run only downstream of the edit' path, because each render is a fresh execution.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto deliberately favors reproducible, fresh top-to-bottom execution over edit latency, and that is a defensible choice, not an oversight. It targets many published output formats (PDF, Word, HTML, revealjs, books) where the rendered artifact must reflect a clean run, so it structurally avoids the classic out-of-order/stale-state Jupyter hazard that a live-held-state model invites. Its three cost-amortizers are all PERSISTENT and SHAREABLE, unlike Taliesin's session-local in-memory prefix: execute-daemon kills interpreter+import startup; `freeze` is committed to the repo (cross-machine, CI-friendly) and skips whole unchanged documents, which is the dominant cost in the multi-doc sites/books Quarto is built for (rebuild the site after editing one page); per-cell `cache` (jupyter-cache / knitr) skips unchanged cells across sessions and machines. Taliesin's warm prefix evaporates on restart and cannot be committed. Finally, Quarto's uniform 'execute the notebook' contract works identically across knitr/jupyter/julia engines, whereas a live-prefix planner must be re-proven correct per engine's state model.
- **Taliesin today:** exec.rs keeps one live `Kernel` per language for the whole session (`LangState.ran` records the executed prefix). `plan()` computes the longest common prefix the warm kernel already holds and re-runs only `[shared, run_end)`, the edited cell plus downstream, notebook-style. A forkserver warm pool (warm_pool.rs, Linux) preloads numpy/matplotlib/torch by copy-on-write so the first cold kernel is near-instant, and a cold all-cached page replays from `_freeze/` without booting a kernel at all.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it; this is the core 'no per-edit startup cost' win. Natural extensions: make the preload set configurable per project (today `PRELOAD_CANDIDATES` is a fixed numpy/matplotlib/torch list) and add an R warm pool (the forkserver path is Python-only today).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the warm-kernel + warm-prefix planner: it is a genuine, code-verified win (plan() + LangState.ran in exec.rs) that Quarto structurally lacks, and the critique of Quarto is fair (it correctly credits daemon/freeze/cache and correctly identifies the absent run-only-downstream-of-the-edit path). But sharpen the entry on three points. (1) State the honest boundary: the differentiator is the warm in-session edit; the cold build path is roughly at parity with Quarto's freeze+daemon (all-cached replay, or full re-run on any change since kernel variable state is never cached), and the live preview's warm reuse can transiently diverge from a fresh run via intra-kernel state, while the cold build keeps the PUBLISHED artifact reproducible, that is the deliberate and correct split. (2) Rescope 'R warm pool': R already has warm-prefix reuse and a warm single kernel; only the forkserver cold-boot pool is Python-only, and closing it for R is a new mechanism (no multiprocessing.forkserver analog), so bill it as a project, not an extension. (3) Make 'configurable preload' reconcile with one-daemon-per-process + mounts, and guard the import-time-state surface. Per corpus-plus-roadmap, land each extension pinned by a corpus document plus a determinism test: cold-vs-warm output equivalence for R, and preload-on-vs-off equivalence for the configurable set.
- **Tradeoffs:** Warm-prefix reuse assumes cells communicate only through kernel state captured by running them in order; a cell with an external side effect the planner cannot see (a file it mutates out of band) can still surprise, as in any notebook. The forkserver adds Linux-specific machinery with a cold-start fallback to maintain. (skeptic-found downside: The two 'natural extensions' are mis-scoped. (1) 'Add an R warm pool' is presented next to a trivial config flip, but it is a new subsystem, not a parameter: the forkserver relies on Python's `multiprocessing.forkserver` + `set_forkserver_preload` + COW fork + in-process `IPKernelApp`, none of which R has; warming R needs a different mechanism (parallel::mcfork + in-process IRkernel re-init, Unix-only, with its own warmth/exec pitfall). Crucially R ALREADY gets warm-prefix incremental re-execution and warm single-kernel reuse (LangState/plan() are per-language), so the only R gap is the cold-boot POOL. (2) 'Configurable preload per project' collides with the one-forkserver-per-server-process model (warm_pool_for_preview boots one daemon; set_forkserver_preload bakes one list) plus mounts: different mounted projects cannot diverge their preload without multiple daemons and more RAM. It also widens a determinism surface the entry's 'identical preambles' claim glosses: preambles are identical, but a preloaded lib is already IMPORTED in the forked child, so a library with import-time side effects (torch CUDA context, numpy/OMP thread count read at import, matplotlib backend selection, RNG) can make a pooled kernel diverge from a cold one. Also unstated: the warm-prefix win is the WARM in-session edit only; on a cold build a mid-doc edit still re-runs from cell 0 (freeze restores outputs, not variables), matching Quarto, and the live preview's prefix reuse can transiently diverge from a fresh run via intra-kernel mutable state (module globals, lru_cache, RNG), which the tradeoffs note undersells by citing only external file mutation.)
- **Invariant check:** This is the warm-server invariant itself, and the warm prefix is block-level-incremental at the execution layer. HTML-only and single-surface are untouched; determinism is preserved because a pooled kernel runs identical preambles to a cold one. Corpus pins output equivalence.

### D14. Adopt an explicit computed-table policy: theme-normalize kernel-emitted table HTML and add an opt-in #| df-print with a vanilla-JS interactive table, instead of splicing pandas/Styler HTML verbatim (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto exposes a document/format-level df-print enum (default | kable | tibble | paged, plus gt via gt) that selects how printed data frames render. For HTML it ships a .dataframe CSS reset that normalizes pandas/knitr table markup into its Bootstrap-styled tables and applies its own light/dark theming to them; df-print: paged swaps in rmarkdown's jQuery paged-table widget (client-side row pagination, column paging, sortable headers), bundling the jQuery/CSS/JS that widget needs. One knob thus bundles two orthogonal concerns: a static-styling policy and a client-side interactive widget.
- **Critique:** Computed tables are the single place where a document's authored-vs-computed look diverges and where dark mode silently breaks: a pandas df.style Styler emits an inline <style> block with light-baked colors that do not adapt, so a computed table can render dark-text-on-dark. There is also no browser-native interactive (sort/paginate) table, which is precisely the "richer live-HTML behavior" the wider-than-Quarto mandate points at. Quarto's own answer conflates static styling and an interactive widget into one document-level enum (awkward for per-table control) and drags in jQuery for paged, so it is not a design worth copying wholesale.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's df-print is intentional restraint, not conflation. It ships a thin, document-level DEFAULT that normalizes the common case (plain pandas .dataframe / knitr markup) into themed tables via a targeted .dataframe CSS reset, so plain computed tables DO adapt to light/dark, then gets out of the way. For anything richer, Quarto's real answer is the escape hatch: render the table explicitly with a purpose-built library (gt/great_tables, DT, reactable, itables) that emits a self-contained, far more capable widget than any built-in enum, with Pandoc wiring the widget's JS/CSS into the page so it actually runs. That division of labor (thin default plus delegate to mature widgets) is arguably wiser than a framework hand-rolling half of DataTables. Preserving Styler's inline colors verbatim is also defensible: the author explicitly chose that gradient, so re-theming it would silently override intent. And df-print: paged is a legitimate zero-config convenience for the 90 percent case. A single knob for the DEFAULT look, plus code-level control for the exceptional table, is coherent, not awkward. The critique omits this philosophy and leans on a Styler dark-mode hook that its own layer-1 fix then punts on, and it mis-attributes jQuery to the paged widget (rmarkdown's pagedtable is largely self-contained). (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Verified from code: render_media (crates/server/src/kernel.rs) picks the richest MIME repr in fixed priority text/html > png > svg > jpeg > text/plain and splices the kernel's text/html VERBATIM into <div class="tali-output"> (exec.rs output_block). There is no df-print key (absent from schema.rs and validate.rs), so under the strict clean-break validation an author who wrote df-print: would get an unknown-key flag: Taliesin has neither the feature nor tolerance for the spelling. base.css styles ALL <table> (border-collapse, --tali-border borders, .35/.6rem padding, tabular-nums, wide-table horizontal scroll), so a PLAIN pandas _repr_html_/to_html already inherits themed borders and adapts across light/dark/sepia, roughly matching authored Markdown tables. What is absent: any .dataframe/Styler-specific normalization (Styler inline light-baked colors are passed through unchanged), the deprecated border="1" attribute is left on, there is no interactive/paged/sortable table, and there is no knob to choose. table_wrap injects the @tbl- caption/anchor into the first <table> regardless of source.
- **Proposed better:** Two layers stacked above the existing #| syntax, not a syntax change. (1) A conservative normalization pass on kernel-emitted table HTML in the output path: strip the deprecated border="1" and tag the plain .dataframe repr so base.css owns its look in every theme, WITHOUT touching author-intentional df.style Styler output (detect the Styler scoped <style> block and either leave it alone or theme it by substituting --tali-* variables). This costs nothing at author time and closes the dark-mode gap. (2) An opt-in #| df-print: cell option, schema-validated with did-you-mean-on-typo click-to-source like every other cell option, with values default (normalized static table), interactive/paged (a bundled, offline, vanilla-JS progressive enhancement that adds column sort + client-side pagination to the SAME server-rendered <table>), and plain (force the text repr). The interactive table is pure client-side enhancement over server-emitted markup: it degrades to a static themed table with JS off and is the browser-native win where Quarto ships jQuery.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the opt-in #| df-print plus a native vanilla-JS interactive table (the genuine jQuery-free wider-than-Quarto win) pinned by a light+dark DataFrame corpus doc, but restructure. (1) Drop the Rust-side HTML-normalization and heuristic Styler-vs-plain detection entirely; instead register a pandas DataFrame text/html formatter in the kernel, reusing the existing matplotlib Figure-formatter pattern (kernel.rs ~174), that emits Taliesin-native theme-driven markup with data-attributes at the source where the type is KNOWN, and leave Styler's own repr untouched by construction (author colors preserved, no misfire). (2) Reframe layer 1 honestly as cosmetic hygiene (drop leftover border="1"), not a dark-mode fix, since plain tables already theme via base.css and Styler is deliberately left alone. (3) Scope the interactive table to modest row counts (client-side sort+paginate, no endpoint), as one idempotent taliEnhanceCode enhancer nested strictly inside .tali-output, with type-aware comparators and aria-sort, and content-gate its JS fragment so table-less pages pay nothing. (4) Keep sort/page state strictly ephemeral (never persisted to _freeze or any sidecar the build reads) so it stays a read-only view op categorically unlike the removed drag-to-reorder. (5) Document that R (kable/gt) already emits clean HTML, so df-print is a per-language normalizer, not a uniform cross-kernel abstraction: do not over-claim uniformity.
- **Tradeoffs:** Normalizing kernel HTML means mutating arbitrary strings from the kernel, which is fragile: Styler output carries generated class names and a scoped <style>, and over-normalizing erases the author's intentional styling, so the Styler-vs-plain-repr detection is heuristic and can misfire (both false-strip and false-leave). The interactive table adds a JS bundle (dead weight on every table-bearing page unless content-gated) and a client-enhancement path that must re-apply on block-level swaps (keyed to data-block-id) and must preserve data-sourcepos so Alt-click still lands on the cell; client-side sort reorders DOM rows, a read-only view mutation that must never be conflated with a source edit. It adds a cell-option key plus a pinning corpus doc to maintain. Languages diverge: R kable/gt already emit clean HTML, so the R default may differ from the pandas default, meaning the policy is not uniform across kernels. (skeptic-found downside: The interactive client table cannot server-paginate: Taliesin builds static, self-contained HTML with no data endpoint, so it must render every row into the DOM and only page/sort client-side, capping it at modest row counts and bloating the block-swap payload for large frames (no better than Quarto's paged on scale). Because the incremental client mounts blocks via template.innerHTML (client.js fragment helper), any kernel-emitted widget script never executes in live preview, so the feature MUST be a taliEnhanceCode enhancement with an idempotency guard (surviving un-swapped tables must not be re-wrapped on each afterChange burst) and can never be a spliced third-party widget. Robust vanilla-JS sort is also under-scoped: type-aware comparators for integers, floats, "1,234", "12.3%", "$4.00", dates and NaN, plus aria-sort/keyboard/stable ordering, are exactly the long tail DataTables exists for. And client-side sort reorders rows so rendered order no longer matches data/source order, which can make prose referencing "the top row" wrong: an opt-in author footgun.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only preserved: a client-side table enhancement over existing markup, no new output target. Single editing surface preserved: df-print is set in the #| cell option in the .tmd (the only editing surface); sort/paginate are read-only view operations that never write back, categorically unlike the removed drag-to-reorder. Click-to-source preserved: output_block still emits data-block-id + data-sourcepos and the enhancement wraps but does not strip them, so Alt-click still resolves to the cell source. Block-level incremental preserved: the enhancement re-runs on block swap like other code-enhance.js features. Warm-server preserved: normalization is a cheap string pass in render with no per-edit startup cost. Corpus-plus-roadmap honored: ships pinned by a DataFrame corpus doc exercising each df-print value in light and dark. Wider-than-Quarto satisfied by the interactive table being richer live-HTML behavior, not a new format.

### D15. Run every language through one Jupyter-ZMQ path instead of Quarto's engine matrix (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto picks an execution engine per document: knitr (R, the default when R is detected or for .Rmd), jupyter (Python and any Jupyter kernel), or julia (QuartoNotebookRunner). An `engine:` front-matter key can force one. Each engine parses cell options and inline code differently (knitr's `` `r expr` `` inline execution, chunk hooks).
- **Critique:** The engine matrix is a large source of Quarto's complexity and of behavioral drift: the same `#|` option can mean different things under knitr vs jupyter, and R authors silently get knitr semantics while Python authors get jupyter semantics. Diagnosing 'why did my option not apply' first requires knowing which engine ran.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The engine matrix is not accidental complexity, it is the price of serving two mature execution cultures and many output formats at once, which Taliesin deliberately does not do. knitr is a 12+ year ecosystem that R authors and textbooks (R for Data Science, bookdown lineage) already depend on: inline R splicing `r nrow(df)` into prose, chunk hooks, results='asis', child documents, and figure-device control, none of which the Jupyter protocol expresses. Crucially, knitr runs R in the SAME session model as the author's console/RStudio, so what renders matches what they see interactively; IRkernel is a separate process with subtly different top-level auto-printing, graphics-device, and last-value display semantics. Forcing one Jupyter path would either strip knitr's inline+hook ecosystem (alienating the R world) or degrade native notebook semantics. The dedicated julia engine (QuartoNotebookRunner) is direct evidence that 'just use Jupyter for every language' was found wanting: Julia's precompilation and world-age startup pain pushed Quarto to build a purpose-made runner. So per-document engine selection is Quarto honoring existing tooling across R, Python, and Julia and across HTML/PDF/Word/Typst, rather than imposing one culture's model on all of them.
- **Taliesin today:** One execution path. `kernel_lang` in exec.rs maps only `python` (ipykernel) and `r` (IRkernel), both driven over the same Jupyter ZMQ protocol in kernel.rs. There is no `engine:` key, no knitr, and no julia; any other `{lang}` renders as highlighted source.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the single Jupyter-protocol path. If breadth is wanted later, add Julia the same way (a third `KernelSpec` plus a `kernel_lang` arm), so the warm-kernel, freeze, warm-prefix, timeout, and cwd machinery is inherited unchanged rather than reimplemented behind a second engine abstraction.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the single Jupyter-ZMQ path, it is genuinely better for a single-author HTML-only tool that needs none of what the engine matrix buys, and the code confirms a third language is a two-line extension (one kernel_lang arm + one KernelSpec) that inherits freeze/warm-pool/timeout/cwd. Sharpen the entry in two ways. (1) Reframe the win honestly: the claim is not 'no execution drift', it is 'one engine and one strictly-validated #| option contract regardless of language' (Taliesin owns its cell-option semantics via schema.rs rather than adopting jupyter's), while acknowledging that R runs via IRkernel and therefore will not match a knitr/console-R author's auto-print, graphics-device, and figure-size expectations. That is the real trade, and naming it pre-empts a confused R author. (2) Downgrade the Julia note from 'inherited unchanged' to 'inherited, with Julia-specific startup/timeout tuning', and credit that the warm-kernel design is precisely the mitigation for the startup pain that pushed Quarto to a dedicated Julia runner. Also record the steelman so the catalog credits Quarto's cross-community/cross-format rationale, not just 'complexity'. The lost knitr inline-R prose splicing is the one capability with no Taliesin substitute for R (there is no inline execution for python or r today, only {js}); if any R breadth is pursued later, that gap, not raw execution, is the thing to weigh.
- **Tradeoffs:** R runs through IRkernel, so knitr-only features (chunk hooks, `` `r ` `` inline execution, some caption conventions) are unavailable, and Julia is not executable today. An R-heavy author expecting knitr parity is not served. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's implicit 'one path, no drift' framing oversells: collapsing to a single engine does eliminate inter-engine drift, but it silently SUBSTITUTES a different drift the drafter did not surface. R run through IRkernel does not behave identically to R in the console or under knitr: top-level auto-printing/invisible() handling, the default graphics device, figure sizing, and last-expression display all differ. An R author porting a knitr document to Taliesin can get different rendered output (missing auto-prints, differently-sized plots) with no error to explain it. So Taliesin trades Quarto's inter-engine drift for tool-vs-expectation drift, which should be stated honestly rather than framed as drift-free. Secondly, 'add Julia the same way, inherited unchanged' is slightly optimistic: Julia-over-Jupyter is exactly the case Quarto built a separate runner to avoid (tens-of-seconds cold starts, precompile/world-age pain). Taliesin's warm-pool is actually the right answer to that pain, but Julia would still need language-specific warmup/timeout tuning (and possibly sysimage handling), so it is inherited-with-tuning, not inherited-unchanged.)
- **Invariant check:** A single code path is exactly what keeps the warm-server and block-level-incremental invariants tractable to reason about; HTML-only and single-surface are untouched. Adding Julia as another KernelSpec stays corpus-pinned.

### D16. Honour eval / output / warning / error cell options, not just echo / include / cache (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto honours a full per-cell vocabulary: `eval` (run or not), `echo` (show source), `output` (true/false/asis), `warning` (show warnings), `error` (tolerate errors), and `include` (suppress everything).
- **Critique:** Taliesin honours only echo, include, and cache. Because the validator is strict (any unknown key is flagged with a did-you-mean), `#| eval: false` and `#| warning: false` do not just get ignored, they raise an 'unknown cell option' warning. `eval: false` (show an illustrative cell without running it) and `warning: false` (hide noisy deprecation or stderr chatter) are genuinely common, useful patterns.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The full option set is not Quarto invention or bloat; it is the de facto standard inherited from knitr (2012) and Jupyter. `eval`, `echo`, `output`, `warning`, `message`, `error`, `include` are a decade-plus lingua franca that R Markdown and notebook authors already have in muscle memory, and they map onto real distinct channels: `error: true` shows a deliberate exception's traceback in teaching material without failing the build; `warning: false`/`message: false` hush the library-load and deprecation noise that is pervasive in R; `output: asis` lets a cell emit raw Markdown/tables. Because Quarto's job is to render the huge existing corpus of .Rmd and .ipynb across many formats, honouring (and permissively passing through) the whole vocabulary is a load-bearing compatibility goal, not laziness. For Quarto's audience the choice is correct.
- **Taliesin today:** `CELL_OPTION_KEYS` in validate.rs is echo, include, cache, label, the *-cap keys, fig-export, code-fold/-summary/-line-numbers, and the {js} keys. `detect_execute_defaults` in cell_extract.rs handles only echo/include/cache, with a code comment stating 'eval/output/warning are not yet honoured'. So `eval`, `output`, `warning`, and `error` are all flagged as unknown.
- **Proposed better:** Implement `eval` (skip execution but keep the cell as highlighted source and skip it in the cumulative hash chain so downstream keys stay stable), `warning: false` (drop `Output::Stream{stderr:true}` warning items in render_outputs/exec), and `output: false` (run for state, emit no output block, like `include` but keeping the echoed source). Add each to `CELL_OPTION_KEYS`.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship, but split it and never whitelist ahead of implementation. Tier 1 (clean, do first): `output: false` = run for state, keep the echoed source, drop the output block. It is the one genuinely missing echo/include combination, the hash chain is untouched, and it is a true pure filter. Tier 2: `warning: false` = drop only `Output::Stream{stderr:true}`, never `Output::Error`; document that it also suppresses non-warning stderr (fig-export/tooling messages), or scope it to warnings by pattern. Tier 3: `eval: false` = keep the source block, exclude the cell's code from `cumulative_hashes` so downstream keys stay stable, remove it from the executor list, and either handle `{js}` (skip reactive registration) or scope `eval` to kernel languages for now; note it overlaps a plain non-braced fence for the trivial "show, do not run" case, its value being paused-but-still-executable semantics. Drop `error` from this entry: Taliesin already tolerates cell errors by default (traceback baked in), so `error` only makes sense paired with a per-cell interaction with --strict; spec that separately, do not whitelist it here. If you implement `output`, either implement `asis` too or extend the validator to reject unknown values for these keys, so the strict did-you-mean identity holds at the value level, not just the key level. Add each key to CELL_OPTION_KEYS only in the same change that implements it, each pinned by a corpus cell.
- **Tradeoffs:** A plain non-braced fence already covers the simplest 'show, do not run' case, so `eval: false` overlaps with it; its value is keeping executable-cell semantics (options, the downstream chain) while paused. A `warning: false` that swallows stderr must filter warnings only, not real tracebacks, or it hides genuine failures. (skeptic-found downside: The entry over-reaches in one line ("Add each to CELL_OPTION_KEYS") relative to what it implements, and that creates a silent-no-op trap that is worse than today's flagging. (1) It lists `error` in the title/critique but never gives it semantics, yet says to whitelist it; a whitelisted-but-unimplemented `#| error: true` would pass validation and then still bake a traceback / fail under --strict, silently defeating the author's intent. (2) Quarto's `output: asis` is a real value; Taliesin's validator is key-level only, so `#| output: asis` would pass validation but the code (which only tests `== "false"`) would silently render normally, an unpoliced value-space. (3) `warning: false` dropping all `Output::Stream{stderr:true}` also swallows genuine non-warning tooling stderr (e.g. the "fig-export failed" message emitted as a stderr stream), so it can hide a real failure. (4) `eval: false` is mis-described as a "pure render/exec-time filter": to keep downstream cache keys stable it must be removed from `cumulative_hashes` membership AND pulled from the executor's cell list while its source block stays, which touches the render/exec boundary and the cache-correctness core, plus it needs a defined behaviour for `{js}` cells (skip reactive-graph registration) or an explicit scope to kernel languages.)
- **Invariant check:** All four are pure render/exec-time filters over the existing block model and Jupyter outputs: no new output format (HTML-only), no write-back to source (single-surface), and every cell still carries data-block-id and data-sourcepos (click-to-source plus incremental intact). Ship each pinned by a corpus cell. (possible violation flagged: None of the seven fixed invariants (HTML-only, single read-only surface, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, block-level incremental, warm server, corpus-pinned) are broken: all three features are render/exec filters over the existing block model, and every cell keeps data-block-id/data-sourcepos. The only tension is with the strict-validation clean-break identity (not itself a fixed invariant): whitelisting a key or value that is not fully implemented turns a helpful did-you-mean warning into silently-wrong behaviour, which undercuts the very selling point of validate.rs.)

### D17. Render cell errors inline and continue, never halting the build (and never caching them) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's default `error: false` makes an execution error abort the render; you must set `error: true` per cell (or globally) to let the document build with the traceback shown as output.
- **Critique:** Halt-on-error is hostile to iterative authoring: one broken cell blocks the entire preview, and you must remember to flip `error: true` while drafting. The flip side is that Quarto's `error: true` is also the mechanism that lets you deliberately teach a traceback and have it appear in the rendered output.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A publish-oriented, multi-format tool's core promise is that a rendered artifact is trustworthy, so a broken computation must never ship silently. Halting by default guarantees a failed cell produces a loud non-zero exit that CI catches, and you cannot accidentally publish a page with a stack trace where a figure belongs. This matters more for Quarto than for Taliesin precisely because Quarto targets PDF, Word, book, and ePub, where a "visible error block" may render as garbage, be clipped, or be silently dropped by the format, so there is no reliable in-document signal that something broke: failing the whole render is the only format-agnostic safety net. Requiring an explicit error: true turns "I intend this traceback to be output" into a conscious, auditable, greppable declaration rather than an accident. Halt-on-error is the correct default for a reproducible-research compiler; Taliesin only earns the right to relax it because it is HTML-only (an error block always renders visibly) and live-preview-first, so its never-halt is a different-tradeoff-for-a-different-workload, not proof that Quarto is wrong.
- **Taliesin today:** An execution error becomes a `tali-error` `<pre>` spliced inline where the output would go (exec.rs, render_outputs), the build continues, and `is_uncacheable` guarantees errors (plus timeouts and truncated output) are never persisted to `_freeze/`, so a transient failure never sticks and the cell re-runs next time.
- **Proposed better:** Keep never-halt as the default (correct for a live preview). Consider two small additions: an opt-in `#| error: expect` that treats a raised error as the cell's cacheable expected output (for teaching a traceback), and a build-time gate that fails the static `build` on an unexpected error so a broken cell cannot ship silently.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry cleanly. (1) KEEP never-halt inline rendering as the live-preview default and keep is_uncacheable refusing to persist errors/timeouts/truncation: verified correct and genuinely already-better than Quarto. (2) DROP the "add a build-time gate" recommendation as new: it already exists as --strict (report_cell_errors counts every tali-error block; strict_exit exits non-zero), and even a non-strict build already logs a located per-cell warning to stderr, so the only thing --strict adds is CI-enforceable exit. Correct the taliesin_current field to say so, and reframe the one open question as: should failing on an unexpected cell error be the DEFAULT for the publishing `build` (currently opt-in), matching Quarto's safe instinct, while preview stays never-halt? That is the sharp, non-redundant design decision. (3) Sharpen error: expect into a proper expect-error ASSERTION, not a bare cache hint: it must (a) use a non-colliding name such as #| expect-error: true to avoid clashing with Quarto's boolean error:, (b) mark the block cacheable AND excluded from the --strict failure count, (c) FAIL under --strict if the cell does not raise, (d) emit a distinct class (e.g. tali-error tali-error-expected) so the traceback reads as intentional, and (e) add the CELL_OPTION_KEYS entry plus schema update or strict validation will flag it, and ship a new corpus doc that pins a deliberately-erroring kernel cell (the current js-error.qmd does not cover this path).
- **Tradeoffs:** Without `error: expect`, an intentionally-erroring teaching cell re-runs every build (never cached) and is indistinguishable from a real failure. A never-halt static build can publish a page containing a visible error block if the author does not look; the proposed build-time gate is what addresses that. (skeptic-found downside: As written, error: expect is a one-way caching hint, not a two-way assertion, and that is the real trap. (1) A teaching cell that stops raising because a dependency changed would silently succeed and ship empty/wrong output with no failure, since nothing checks that an expected error actually occurred; a proper design must FAIL (under --strict) when an error: expect cell does not raise (pytest.raises semantics). (2) Caching a raised error freezes whichever traceback happened, so a cell that errors for the WRONG reason (a typo, a changed API, a different exception) gets frozen as "expected" until the cumulative hash busts it; the hash key bounds this but does not eliminate the "cached the wrong error" surprise. (3) The keyword collides with Quarto: error already means a boolean halt/allow in every author's muscle memory, so #| error: expect (and a Quarto refugee typing #| error: true) invites exactly the confusion Taliesin's clean-break strict validation was meant to kill; a non-colliding spelling (expect-error / raises) is safer. (4) The proposal never connects error: expect to the EXISTING --strict gate, which today fails on ANY tali-error block, so a teaching doc could never build under --strict unless expected errors are excluded from the count, and unexpected ones still counted. (5) A rendered expected-error block is visually indistinguishable from a real crash; a first-class concept should carry a distinct class/affordance so a reader reads it as intentional.)
- **Invariant check:** Inline error blocks are ordinary blocks carrying data-block-id and data-sourcepos (click-to-source plus incremental intact); no new output format; the proposed `error: expect` changes only what is cached, never the editing surface. Corpus already pins error rendering. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is violated (HTML-only, single read-only editing surface, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, block-level incremental, and warm server all hold; verified that tali-error blocks carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos and are ordinary blocks, build.rs test at ~line 1476). The soft breach is corpus-plus-roadmap: the entry asserts "corpus already pins error rendering", but the only error corpus doc is reactive/js-error.qmd, which pins the CLIENT-SIDE {js} .qmd-js-error box, a different code path from the server-side kernel tali-error &lt;pre&gt; the entry describes (that path is pinned by unit tests in exec.rs/build.rs, not a corpus doc). The proposed error: expect capability ships no corpus document at all, so per the corpus-is-the-arbiter-of-done rule it is not admissible until a deliberately-erroring kernel cell with error: expect is added to the corpus.)

### D18. Cap and interrupt runaway cells (time and output size) and self-heal a dead kernel (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto has no per-cell wall-clock timeout by default: a runaway or hung cell blocks the render until you kill the whole process, and there is no built-in output-size cap, so a cell printing millions of lines can swamp the render and the browser.
- **Critique:** For a long-running live server this is fragile: one infinite loop or one accidental huge print wedges the preview, and recovery means restarting the process (losing any warm daemon state).
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general, multi-format BATCH document compiler (HTML, PDF/LaTeX, Word, book, ePub), not a long-lived live server, so its failure model is genuinely different and its no-cap default is defensible FOR QUARTO. (1) A batch render is a disposable, one-shot process usually invoked from CI or a Makefile, where the OS/CI job already imposes a wall-clock limit; there is no warm daemon state to protect, so kill-the-process-and-rerun is the correct, simple recovery. (2) For a reproducible-research tool, silently TRUNCATING a cell's output or interrupting a legitimately long scientific computation (an MCMC chain, a large model fit, a slow query) would bake a subtly WRONG artifact into the published PDF/HTML, which is worse than hanging visibly: completeness and determinism of the rendered document outrank liveness. Hanging is a loud, correct failure; a truncated figure or table is a silent, corrupt one. (3) Quarto does not forbid caps, it defers to the executor: nbclient/knitr expose their own per-cell `timeout`, so an author who wants one sets it, rather than Quarto surprising the scientist with a default that cuts off real work. The whole runaway-protection layer is therefore a requirement that FALLS OUT of Taliesin's live-preview-plus-warm-kernel architecture, not a defect in Quarto's; the two tools optimize for different things.
- **Taliesin today:** kernel.rs enforces a per-cell wall-clock cap (`QMD_FAST_CELL_TIMEOUT`, default 120s, `0` disables) via SIGINT so the warm kernel and prior cells survive; a mid-cell kernel death is detected within about one second and reported as a distinct `KernelDied` instead of hanging the full budget; stream output is capped at 512KB and 4096 items with a truncation marker, and truncated output is treated as uncacheable so it is never frozen.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Small refinements: surface the truncation or timeout as a click-to-source diagnostic anchored on the offending cell (not only an inline `<pre>`), and make the output caps configurable for the rare cell that legitimately emits a large table.
- **Revised recommendation:** Status is correct and verified: Taliesin is already better here (per-cell SIGINT timeout with warm-kernel survival, ~1s KernelDied detection, 512KB/4096-item caps, truncated-output-is-uncacheable), and Quarto's no-cap default is right for a batch compiler but wrong for a warm live server. KEEP the mechanism. Fix the two refinements before cataloguing them as wins: (1) Drop or downgrade the click-to-source refinement: the diagnostic is ALREADY inside a `data-sourcepos` block and Alt-click already jumps to the cell (exec.rs:955). At most, add a distinct visual affordance or a problems-list entry, but do not claim click-to-source is missing. (2) Reframe configurable caps as a per-cell `#|` option (e.g. `#| output-max-bytes:`, `#| output-max-items:`) validated by schema.rs, NOT a global env var: it is the invariant-aligned, targeted form (raises the cap for the one cell, not the whole doc), it lives in the .tmd editing surface, and it fits the strict-config philosophy. Keep it BOUNDED (reject a `0`/unlimited opt-out) so it cannot reopen the memory/DOM-swamp failure, and correct the motivating example (a large stdout dump, since rich HTML tables are not byte-capped). Pin any new option with a corpus document per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Tradeoffs:** A default 120s cap can cut off a legitimately slow cell (the author raises `QMD_FAST_CELL_TIMEOUT` or sets it to 0); the 512KB stream cap can truncate a genuinely large intended output, which then also will not cache until trimmed. (skeptic-found downside: The two refinements are weaker than stated. (a) The click-to-source refinement is largely ALREADY implemented: the timeout/KernelDied/truncation `<pre class="tali-error">` is the `inner` of `output_block` (exec.rs:955), wrapped in a `tali-output` div carrying `data-block-id` + `data-sourcepos` = the cell's position, so Alt-click already navigates to the offending cell. The drafter's "not only an inline `<pre>`" premise misreads current behavior. (b) The configurable-caps refinement conflates the two caps: only `StreamContent` (stdout/stderr) is byte-capped at 512KB; a legitimately large rich HTML table returns as ONE `ExecuteResult`/`DisplayData` item and is byte-uncapped already, so raising `MAX_STREAM_BYTES` does nothing for the "large table" case (the real beneficiary is a giant stdout dump, a weaker claim to legitimacy; only the 4096-ITEM cap could bite rich output). (c) Making the cap unbounded (a `0`-disables opt-out like the timeout has) reopens the exact failure the cap prevents: the output is cloned into the block model + `_freeze/*.json` + the warm-state record and HTML-escaped, and it ships whole in the block-level live-update diff, so a raised cap trades one truncation for freeze-cache bloat and heavier per-edit diff payloads, cutting against the cheap-incremental-update goal. Any configurable cap must stay BOUNDED.)
- **Invariant check:** This is purely a robustness layer around execution: no output format change (HTML-only), no source write-back (single-surface), and cells keep their ids (click-to-source plus incremental). The kernel-died and interrupt paths are unit-tested.

### D19. Always run cells in the document's own directory, with no execute-dir: project switch (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto exposes `execute-dir: file | project`. In a project the default is the project root, so a cell's relative path resolves from the root rather than from the document, and authors must know which mode is active.
- **Critique:** The project-root default is a recurring surprise: `pd.read_csv('data.csv')` next to the document fails because the cwd is the project root, and figures or audio a cell writes land somewhere unexpected. The config option largely exists to paper over that ambiguity.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto actually ships the intuitive file-relative default (the input file's own directory, matching author expectation and matching Taliesin) AND an opt-in escape hatch, `execute-dir: project`, for the one topology where file-relative genuinely hurts: a website or book with many pages in subdirectories that share a single top-level data/ folder. There, resolving every page from one stable project root is more robust, not less: moving a chapter between folders does not break its reads, and you avoid ../../../data chains. This mirrors established reproducibility practice (R's here::here(), Python's pyprojroot), which exists precisely because project-root-relative resolution beats fragile per-file setwd(). Defaulting to the safe file-relative option while offering the opt-in is strictly more expressive than file-only, and costs authors who never enable it nothing. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Always file-relative. The single-doc server runs the kernel with cwd = the document's parent dir (serve/mod.rs `in_dir(base_dir)`), the site builder does `in_dir(base)` per page, and even a warm-pool kernel is `os.chdir`'d to match (exec.rs `set_kernel_cwd`), so relative reads and writes (fig-export, ggsave, audio) land beside the source.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the single file-relative rule and no `execute-dir` key. If shared project-root data becomes a real need, prefer an explicit resolver helper (resolve a path against the project root by name) over reintroducing a cwd mode, so the cwd itself stays unambiguous.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep exactly what Taliesin does (always file-relative, no execute-dir key), but rewrite the entry, whose reasoning is unsound. (1) Fix the fact: Quarto's default is ALREADY file-relative (execute-dir: file), so pd.read_csv('data.csv') next to the document works under Quarto's default too; it breaks only if the author explicitly sets execute-dir: project. Reclassify status from "taliesin-already-better" to "matches Quarto's default, deliberately narrower": the real, defensible difference is that Taliesin declines Quarto's execute-dir: project opt-in, not that Quarto's default is confusing. (2) Lead with the load-bearing architectural reason: parallel per-page builds are race-free only because each page's cwd is its own directory; a project-root cwd would let concurrent pages clobber shared output filenames. Add always-unambiguous-cwd and single-author simplicity as secondary. (3) Drop the bespoke resolver helper; if shared-root data ever bites, point authors at the language-native idiom (here::here(), pyprojroot), which needs nothing from Taliesin and keeps cells portable and the kernel namespace clean. (4) Restate the tradeoff honestly as fragility-under-move for deep book/site trees (in-scope: Taliesin's docs are books), still outweighed by the parallel-build isolation.
- **Tradeoffs:** A multi-page site with one shared data/ at the project root must reference it relatively (`../data.csv`) from each page; there is no opt-in to resolve from the root. For a single-author site that is usually fine, but a deep page tree makes those relative paths longer. (skeptic-found downside: The "explicit resolver helper" future-direction is the missed cost. Such a helper would have to inject a Taliesin-specific function into both the Python and R kernel namespaces, but Taliesin deliberately keeps that namespace clean: the only thing it injects today is a transient os.chdir that is immediately del'd (exec.rs:800). Cells calling taliesin.root('data.csv') also stop being portable Jupyter/Pandoc-lineage code, which cuts against the owner's "keep Markdown/Pandoc familiarity" direction. The language-native idiom (here::here(), pyprojroot, Path(__file__)) already solves shared-root data with zero Taliesin surface, so the bespoke helper is a bigger, worse commitment than the execute-dir key it is meant to avoid. Separately, the tradeoff is understated: the real cost is not "longer paths" but fragility-under-move for deep trees, and that case is in-scope because Taliesin's own docs are books (chapters in subdirs). The entry also omits the strongest reason FOR file-relative: parallel per-page builds (build_one_page runs many pages at once, build.rs:683-685) are race-free only because each page's cwd is its own dir; a project-root cwd would let concurrent pages clobber shared output filenames.)
- **Invariant check:** cwd resolution is an execution-time concern only: no output format (HTML-only), no write to the .tmd source (single-surface). File-relative writes preserve the per-page file isolation the freeze determinism tests rely on. Corpus pins media-writing cells.

### D20. Key the cache on interpreter version, not the absolute interpreter path (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `_freeze/` is designed to be committed and reused across machines and CI, so a collaborator without the full toolchain can still render from frozen outputs; it does not bind the freeze to a specific interpreter binary path.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's cache correctly refuses to serve outputs computed by a different interpreter, but it seeds the cumulative hash with the interpreter's absolute program path. Recreating or relocating a venv to a new path, even the same Python at the same version, changes the path and busts the entire document's cache. For this workflow (the author recreates venvs), that is a recurring, avoidable full recompute.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's _freeze is a committed, shared artifact whose whole purpose is reproducible publishing WITHOUT re-execution: CI runners, Netlify build bots, and collaborators who never installed Python or R must render the exact frozen outputs. Binding the freeze key to an interpreter version, let alone an absolute path, would bust the cache on essentially every such machine (different home dirs, different toolchain builds) and defeat the feature entirely. Quarto therefore keys on source content and pushes the is-this-output-still-valid judgment onto the author (regenerate freeze when your environment changes), buying portability and deterministic CI publishes in exchange. For a multi-author publishing pipeline, interpreter-binding would be the bug, not the feature. Taliesin binds precisely because it optimizes the opposite case (one author, one machine, correctness-per-run), so this is not Quarto being wrong, it is a different objective, which the entry itself concedes is out of scope.
- **Taliesin today:** exec.rs `interp_id` runs `<program> --version` and returns `format!("{lang}::{}::{version}", program.display())`; freeze.rs folds that string in as the chain seed, so every per-cell key depends on the absolute program path (not just the version).
- **Proposed better:** Drop the absolute path from the seed: key on `lang` plus the `--version` string (optionally plus a short hash of pinned package versions), so a same-version interpreter at a different path reuses the cache while a real version change still busts it. Bump `FORMAT_VERSION` when the seed recipe changes.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the goal but reframe the key: make an environment fingerprint the seed, not the bare version string. Probe the interpreter once per process (memoized exactly like interp_id, and like it computed up front before the kernel boots so cold replay still keys) for version PLUS a hash of its installed-distribution manifest (Python: importlib.metadata over pip freeze, with editable-install paths stripped and entries sorted; R: installed.packages/renv, its own probe). Drop the absolute program path from the normal seed but RETAIN it as the fallback ONLY when the probe fails, preserving today's discrimination between two bogus non-booting interpreters (the existing bogus-interpreter test relies on that). This simultaneously (a) lets a relocated same-environment venv reuse the cache (the target win), (b) correctly busts when packages change even at the SAME path (a hole that exists today and that version-only would leave open), and (c) still refuses another interpreter's outputs. Bump FORMAT_VERSION per the existing convention (accepting the one-time full recompute on first render after the change). Pin it primarily with a unit test on the seed recipe (two paths / same env yields the same seed; changed package fingerprint yields a different seed), since the cross-path case cannot be exercised hermetically by a single corpus render; the corpus doc plus freeze round-trip is a secondary net, not the real pin. Note the mild tension with the warm-server goal (the fingerprint adds a per-session subprocess probe), but it is per-process and memoized, not per-edit, so no invariant is violated.
- **Tradeoffs:** Two genuinely different interpreters that report the same `--version` (say two 3.11 builds with different compiled extensions) would then share a cache; folding in a small package-version fingerprint mitigates this at the cost of some startup probing. This still will not match Quarto's cross-machine `_freeze` portability, which is out of scope for a single-author tool anyway. (skeptic-found downside: The recipe as written (swap the absolute path for the bare --version string) opens a stale-output hole the drafter under-weights. python3 --version is byte-identical across venvs with completely different installed libraries, so recreating a venv at a NEW path with an updated requirements.txt (e.g. pandas 2.1 to 2.2) would serve outputs computed against the OLD packages. Today's path-in-seed accidentally catches SOME of these (any rebuild that also lands at a new path busts the chain); the proposal removes that accidental guard, so in the moved-venv-with-changed-packages case version-only is a net correctness regression, not just an imperfection. That makes the package fingerprint the load-bearing correctness mechanism, not the optional add-on the entry frames it as. Two further missed edges: (1) under pyenv/conda the interpreter path already ENCODES the version (~/.pyenv/versions/3.11.5/bin/python), so path-change approximates version-change and the proposal is a no-op there; the real win is narrowly the python -m venv relocation case, so impact medium is workflow-contingent and likely overstated. (2) A naive pip freeze fingerprint re-leaks absolute paths through editable installs (-e /path/...), quietly reintroducing the exact path-sensitivity being removed, and it also fails to normalize ordering, so the fingerprint needs canonicalization.)
- **Invariant check:** Only the cache-key recipe changes; determinism (never serve another interpreter's output) is preserved for real version changes. No effect on output format, editing surface, click-to-source, or incremental updates. A corpus doc plus the existing freeze round-trip test pin it.

## Rendering pipeline and architecture

### D21. Replace the Pandoc runtime dependency with in-process comrak plus an own sourcepos-stamping HTML emitter (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto shells out to Pandoc (a large external Haskell binary, ~150 MB, pinned per Quarto version) as a hard runtime dependency. Pandoc parses the Markdown into its AST and its HTML writer produces the output HTML. The rendered HTML carries no per-element source-position data, so the pipeline is a batch process: source in, HTML file out.
- **Critique:** A separate process per render adds spawn latency and a version-drift surface (the Pandoc pinned to Quarto can diverge from a system Pandoc). More fundamentally, Pandoc's HTML writer emits no data-block-id or source-line attributes, so there is no seam for click-to-source or for diffing individual blocks: you can only re-run the whole thing and reload.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Pandoc is the most spec-complete document engine in existence, and Quarto's whole value proposition is one source rendering to a website AND a PDF AND Word AND ePub AND revealjs AND journal-template LaTeX. That is impossible without an engine of Pandoc's scope, so the subprocess boundary is the correct architecture, not a wart: it isolates enormously complex, format-agnostic conversion behind a stable CLI contract, lets Quarto pin an exact Pandoc build for byte-reproducible output, and lets the Haskell engine (with its own GC and fifteen years of edge-case fixes for entities, table alignment, smart typography, and dozens of input dialects) evolve independently of Quarto's TypeScript and Lua. The Pandoc AST is also what powers the entire Lua-filter ecosystem (crossref plus thousands of community extensions); owning your own parser and emitter discards all of it. The absent per-element sourcepos is a non-goal, not a defect: emitting source spans into a LaTeX or docx writer is meaningless, and for a batch publish to PDF a one-time tens-of-ms Pandoc spawn is negligible against seconds-to-minutes of LaTeX. Quarto optimized for reproducible multi-format publishing; the subprocess is exactly right for that job and only looks costly through the narrow lens of a live single-format HTML preview loop, which Quarto never claimed to own.
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/src/render/mod.rs parses .tmd with comrak (a Rust CommonMark library, in-process, sourcepos tracked on every AST node via parse_options), then deliberately does NOT use comrak's own HTML formatter. render_internal_impl walks the top-level AST and emit.rs (emit) hand-writes HTML, stamping every block's root element with id, data-block-id (a content hash from make_id), and data-sourcepos. No Pandoc, no subprocess, no external binary.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the decision exactly as-is; it is the load-bearing foundation. The one hardening step worth naming: the pipeline runs on a 256 MB worker thread (render_internal) specifically because deeply nested input overflows the default stack and aborts the process. Treat that stack guard and the sourcepos-totality corpus test (reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total) as permanent invariants, and keep the comrak pin explicit (0.52.0) so a parser upgrade is a reviewed event, not silent drift.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the architectural verdict unchanged: comrak-in-process plus an own sourcepos-stamping emitter is genuinely the load-bearing foundation, and Pandoc-as-subprocess is the wrong architecture for a live HTML previewer (all specifics verify: 0.52.0 pin, sourcepos-on-nodes with comrak's formatter deliberately unused, single attr-injection seam at mod.rs:421, hand-rolled bare-math and labelled equations). But downgrade the proposed_better from a no-op to real work, because as written it just restates three things that ALL already exist in code. Concretely: (a) reframe the 256 MB stack as best-effort, not an invariant, and add a bounded-depth guard that rejects pathological nesting with a located diagnostic rather than relying on a stack that its own fallback path abandons; (b) add a golden-output corpus test pinning comrak's smart-typography and entity output so a future comrak bump that shifts it against the Pandoc-lineage baseline is caught, not silently shipped; (c) treat the pin as a standing maintenance commitment (track upstream security/conformance fixes on a cadence), not a one-time freeze. Keep reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total and the own-emitter-forever framing as the true permanent invariants.
- **Tradeoffs:** comrak is CommonMark-plus-a-fixed-extension-set, not Pandoc-Markdown, so any Pandoc construct comrak lacks must be hand-rolled (see the pandoc-markdown-breadth and string-surgery entries). Taliesin owns its HTML writer forever: every correctness detail Pandoc handles for free (entity edge cases, smart typography, table alignment) is now Taliesin's to maintain and test. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal's own headline hardening, the 256 MB worker thread, is not the permanent invariant it claims: mod.rs:167 falls back to rendering on the default small stack whenever spawning the big-stack worker fails (e.g. under a strict ulimit -v), which reintroduces the exact deep-nesting overflow the guard exists to prevent. So the guard is best-effort, not a guarantee, and a memory-limited host can still abort the process. Related and unnamed: the own emitter (emit.rs) also recurses on nested AST/inline structure, so enlarging the stack papers over unbounded recursion instead of bounding depth with a diagnostic. Two more untested surfaces the entry treats as settled: (1) parse.smart = true is relied on to match Pandoc output, but comrak's and Pandoc's dash/quote/entity heuristics are not guaranteed byte-identical and no corpus doc pins a golden baseline, so latent typography divergence is likely already present and uncaught; (2) pinning comrak 0.52.0 (pre-1.0, which ships breaking changes in minor releases) is not a free reviewed event but an ongoing manual-tracking cost, since upstream CommonMark conformance and bug fixes no longer arrive automatically.)
- **Invariant check:** This IS the invariant enabler: the own-emitter is the only way data-block-id + data-sourcepos land on every block, which is what makes click-to-source, block-level incremental diff, and HTML-only output possible. Fully consistent with keeping Markdown/Pandoc syntax as the substrate (comrak parses that substrate).

### D22. Collapse Pandoc's many output writers to a single HTML target (Html plus a native Reveal scaffold) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto treats the parsed document as format-neutral and renders it through Pandoc writers to many targets: HTML, LaTeX/PDF, docx, epub, revealjs, beamer, gfm, and more, selected by the `format:` key. One source, many outputs is a headline promise.
- **Critique:** Format-neutrality caps HTML-native richness at the lowest common denominator. A feature has to have a sensible rendering (or a graceful no-op) in docx and LaTeX too, so browser-only affordances (live reactive widgets, a real DOM, scroll-driven behavior, per-block data attributes) are either impossible or bolted on as HTML-only special cases fighting the neutral abstraction. The revealjs writer also inherits reveal.js wholesale rather than being designed for the live-preview loop.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** One source, many outputs is a genuine, hard-won value proposition Taliesin is deliberately forgoing, not a design mistake. Quarto's neutral Pandoc-AST core does NOT actually cap HTML richness at a lowest common denominator: its HTML target ships first-class browser-only affordances (OJS interactivity, Jupyter widgets, tabsets, code-folding, hover cross-references, full-text search, listing pages) built with HTML-specific Lua filters and post-processing, and it lets authors opt into per-format content explicitly (`::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}`, raw `{=html}`/`{=latex}` passthrough, per-format YAML). So a feature does not have to no-op in docx/LaTeX: it can be HTML-only by construction while the neutral core still delivers what a multi-author, multi-venue academic audience actually needs, namely the SAME manuscript becoming a submittable PDF via a mature LaTeX path with real pagination and typesetting, a docx for co-authors and journal review systems, and a rich website, with citations and cross-references resolving correctly in each. For that audience the neutral core is decisive, and Taliesin's single-author HTML-only scope is the reason it can walk away from it, not proof the choice is wrong. The critique's structural point still holds (a neutral AST cannot natively carry per-block live-loop attributes, and the revealjs writer inherits reveal.js wholesale), but its "impossible or bolted on / lowest common denominator" framing overstates the case and understates how rich Quarto's HTML genuinely is.
- **Taliesin today:** model.rs DocFormat has exactly two variants, Html and Reveal, and Reveal is Taliesin's OWN HTML deck engine (reveal.js removed), so both are HTML. page.rs page_from_doc routes to html_page_from_doc or the native deck page. There is no LaTeX/docx/epub path anywhere. Because HTML is the sole target, blocks can carry data-block-id, lightbox wrappers, {js} reactive cells, scrollytelling, and panel-tabset that a neutral AST could never express.
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line: HTML-only is a fixed invariant and the source of Taliesin's 'wider than Quarto in the browser' advantage. If print/PDF is ever needed, render it FROM the built HTML (headless browser print, or a print stylesheet plus the existing #| fig-export hook that already writes vector figures for a separate LaTeX doc), never as a parallel writer. Keep DocFormat closed to HTML-shaped variants only.
