- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's core stance, which is correct and already implemented (model.rs:113 has exactly {Html, Reveal}, both HTML; page.rs routes only to html_page_from_doc or deck_page_from_doc; grep confirms no LaTeX/docx/epub/Pandoc-writer path and no @media-print or headless-print track exists yet). Sharpen two things. (1) Narrow the Quarto critique: drop "lowest common denominator / impossible." The unassailable version is that a format-neutral Pandoc AST cannot natively carry Taliesin's LIVE-LOOP invariants (per-block data-block-id and data-sourcepos, block-level diff, click-to-source), because those describe the editor round-trip, not the document, so no neutral writer can emit them, and Quarto's revealjs writer inherits reveal.js wholesale rather than being built for a block-diff preview. That is the real, format-independent reason HTML-only wins for THIS tool, and it holds without pretending Quarto's HTML is feature-poor (it is not). (2) Re-frame the tradeoff honestly: HTML-to-PDF is a permanent quality ceiling versus LaTeX for submittable print, not a "not yet built" gap, and fig-export is a manual out-of-band bridge, not a print track. State the keep-closed rule as "resist DocFormat variant proliferation," noting Reveal already forks emission so even all-HTML variants cost. With these edits the entry stands.
- **Tradeoffs:** No PDF/Word/epub today is a real capability gap versus Quarto for users who need a submittable artifact, and 'later, from HTML' is not yet built. Authors with a hard PDF requirement are not served. This is an accepted, invariant-backed cost, not an oversight. (skeptic-found downside: The "print later, FROM built HTML" escape hatch is weaker than the entry implies. Headless-browser print-to-PDF plus a print stylesheet yield a passable "print this page" artifact but structurally cannot match LaTeX for submittable academic output (controlled pagination, running headers/footers, page-numbered cross-references, float placement, hyphenation and microtypography), so the hard-PDF gap is a PERMANENT quality ceiling of any HTML-derived approach, not merely "not yet built" as the tradeoffs section frames it. And `#| fig-export` is cited as if it de-risks print, but it only drops print-clean figures into a LaTeX document the author still writes and maintains by hand, out-of-band: it is a manual bridge, not Taliesin producing a PDF. Second, even inside HTML-only the model is not as costlessly "closed" as claimed. Reveal is not a pure page-scaffold swap: it already forks block emission (heading-level slide-splitting, a11y differences in validate_a11y), so any future HTML-shaped "print" variant would reopen the same emission-forking cost the entry treats as settled. "Keep DocFormat closed to HTML-shaped variants" should therefore be stated as "resist variant proliferation," since each variant, even an all-HTML one, taxes emit.rs.)
- **Invariant check:** Directly encodes the HTML-is-the-only-output invariant. A future print track derived from built HTML is explicitly allowed and does not reopen the multi-format model. No conflict with any other invariant.

### D23. Offer no user-scriptable AST-filter hook; implement every transform as hardcoded Rust (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's core extension mechanism is Lua filters over the Pandoc AST. Shortcodes, crossref, callouts, and most Quarto features are themselves Lua filters, and users can drop their own .lua filters (or install _extensions that bundle them) to rewrite the AST before the writer runs. It is a full second scripting surface.
- **Critique:** Lua filters are powerful but costly: the author must learn Lua plus the Pandoc AST shape, filters run per output format and are awkward to debug (opaque failures, ordering effects between stacked filters), and a bundled community filter is an unaudited code path in your build. For a single author they are usually overkill, yet they are the ONLY sanctioned way to add a construct.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Lua filters are the correct design for what Quarto IS, not laziness. (1) Quarto's value proposition is one-source-many-formats, and the Pandoc AST is the single format-neutral seam: a filter written once rewrites HTML, LaTeX, docx, and revealjs from one implementation. Hardcoding every construct per-format in the core is infeasible at Quarto's breadth, and doing it format-neutrally means you have reinvented an AST-filter API anyway. (2) The load-bearing asymmetry: Quarto users install a compiled binary and cannot recompile Pandoc/Quarto, so a scripting surface is the ONLY extension path that does not require forking and rebuilding the toolchain. Taliesin's single author IS the compiler owner, so 'edit Rust and recompile' is free for him and structurally unavailable to a Quarto user. That asymmetry, not filter quality, is why the same choice flips. (3) Implementing Quarto's own features (crossref, callouts, shortcodes) as filters keeps the shipped binary small, makes them inspectable and user-overridable, and lets them version independently of the core. (4) A composable, ordered pipeline lets independent third-party extensions coexist without the core enumerating them. So for a binary-distributed, multi-format, multi-audience tool, the AST-filter surface is close to the only tenable extensibility model; the entry's critique is fair only because it is explicitly scoped to the single-author case.
- **Taliesin today:** There is no filter/AST-transform hook. Built-in shortcodes are hardcoded in crates/core/src/render/extension/mod.rs (render_shortcode: literal `if name == "embed"` / `"video"` / `"input"`); callouts, columns, theorems, figures, tabsets are hardcoded in the pipeline (divs.rs, figure.rs). The old third-party _extensions system was removed; _extensions now resolves ONLY a theme.css (theme.rs). Adding a new construct means editing Rust and recompiling.
- **Proposed better:** For a single-author tool where the author is also the Rust developer, hardcoded-in-Rust is the right default (type-checked, corpus-pinned, no second runtime, no unaudited code). The genuine gap is the missing lightweight tier: a project-local declarative shortcode, e.g. a `_shortcodes/<name>.html` template dir expanded by extension/mod.rs's existing `{{< name args >}}` scanner with simple `${arg}` substitution, would let the author add a project snippet without recompiling, while staying line-preserving so the source map holds. Deliberately NOT a Turing-complete filter: no AST access, no arbitrary code.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's core verdict, which is right and which Taliesin already implements: reject any Lua-style user-scriptable AST-filter hook and keep every transform hardcoded in Rust (type-checked, corpus-pinned, no second runtime, no unaudited code path). For a single author who owns the compiler, recompiling is the cheapest and safest extension path, and the binary-user-cannot-recompile asymmetry that justifies Quarto's filters simply does not apply. But downgrade the _shortcodes/&lt;name&gt;.html 'genuine gap' from a recommendation to an explicitly deferred non-goal: its near-identical predecessor was removed on 2026-07-02 with a still-valid rationale, there is no recorded recurring demand, and it serves DX rather than web-native breadth. The honest default the drafter themself named, do nothing now, is the answer. IF it ever returns on concrete repeated demand, gate it on four preconditions: (1) HTML-escape substituted args by default; (2) feed the _shortcodes/ name set into the strict did-you-mean validator so the open set does not defeat strict validation; (3) wire _shortcodes/*.html into the include-style watch-dependency and block-hash so edits hot-reload; (4) pin it with a corpus doc. Until then the entry should present hardcoded-Rust as the settled answer, not an open question with a pending template tier.
- **Tradeoffs:** Any declarative shortcode tier is new surface to spec, validate (it must feed the strict-front-matter-style did-you-mean channel), and keep from becoming a backdoor to arbitrary HTML that dodges the block model. It also risks re-growing the very _extensions ecosystem that was just removed. The honest alternative is to do nothing: recompiling is cheap and the author controls the compiler. (skeptic-found downside: The proposed _shortcodes/&lt;name&gt;.html tier is a near-verbatim revival of the shortcode_templates / gather_shortcodes mechanism the owner deleted ONE DAY before this audit (commit f5239cb, 2026-07-02): that removed code already did exactly a name-to-HTML-template map with {{1}}/{{2}} positional and {{key}} named substitution, collapsed to one line to stay line-preserving. So 'new surface to spec and validate' overstates the build cost (the code existed and was tested) while hiding the real cost: reversing a fresh, still-valid, reasoned owner decision ('not this stage; return demand-driven') with zero recorded recurring demand. Concrete misses beyond that: (a) the removed impl substituted with a raw unescaped html.replace, so ${arg} into an HTML template is an injection edge unless args are escaped by default; (b) a .html template dir IS arbitrary author HTML, which contradicts the entry's own 'not a backdoor to arbitrary HTML' claim, the honest distinction is arbitrary STATIC HTML with no code execution, not 'no arbitrary HTML'; (c) the dev-server watcher and the block content-hash must treat _shortcodes/*.html as build inputs (the way includes::dependencies does) or a template edit will not hot-reload downstream pages; (d) the strict 'any unknown key is flagged' philosophy collides with a user-defined OPEN set of shortcode names, a missing template file and a genuine typo become indistinguishable unless the dir scan feeds the did-you-mean channel.)
- **Invariant check:** A declarative, line-preserving text-expansion tier respects the single-editing-surface and source-map invariants (it expands before parse, like {{< include >}} and existing shortcodes). It must NOT introduce a write-back path or a runtime that emits blocks without data-block-id/data-sourcepos. Refusing a Lua-style AST hook keeps the clean-break, HTML-only stance intact. (possible violation flagged: No HARD invariant is broken: expansion happens pre-parse into HTML that comrak assigns data-block-id and data-sourcepos (confirmed by the input_shortcode 'Raw-HTML, passed through' path), there is no preview write-back, output stays HTML-only, the {{&lt; &gt;}} syntax is already part of the Markdown substrate, and one-line-collapse keeps click-to-source and block-level incremental valid. Two SOFT tensions worth flagging, neither disqualifying: it introduces a second author-edited surface (_shortcodes/*.html) sitting outside the .tmd, mildly diluting the 'the .tmd file is the single editing surface' framing (the invariant is really about preview-not-writing-source, and template files are author-side, so this is dilution not violation); and it advances authoring DX rather than the roadmap's stated axis of 'wider = richer BROWSER behavior in a live HTML view', so it is a weak fit for corpus-plus-roadmap's growth direction.)

### D24. Re-parse the whole document on every save and diff block lists; consider memoizing expensive per-block rendering by block hash (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** On a preview edit Quarto re-runs the whole Pandoc pipeline (parse plus every filter plus the writer) and, for computational docs, the compute engine unless frozen, then the browser reloads the page (a coarse refresh). There is no per-block diff of the rendered output; scroll position and live DOM/widget state are lost on reload.
- **Critique:** Full-pipeline re-run plus full page reload is the visible-latency, state-loss problem the whole live-preview loop is trying to avoid. Even with freeze caching the compute step, the Pandoc process spawn and page reload dominate the edit-to-pixels time.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's full-pipeline-re-run plus full-page-reload is the correct engineering choice for what Quarto actually is: a MULTI-FORMAT compiler (HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs, epub, beamer). Its whole value rests on ONE Pandoc AST that Lua filters (crossref, callouts, citations) transform once and dozens of writers emit. A block-level incremental HTML differ is a single-format optimization that either has to be reimplemented per writer or bypass Pandoc, forfeiting the filter ecosystem, so a uniform full-reprocess keeps one code path correct across every target. Second, correctness over latency: a from-scratch re-render guarantees the preview is byte-identical to the published artifact, with zero risk of incremental-diff drift or stale-cache divergence, which for a reproducibility-first scientific/publishing tool is worth more than sub-100ms edits. Third, the full page reload always exercises the real production load path, so there is no gap between the patched-DOM view and a fresh load, a gap Taliesin must separately guarantee. Fourth, freeze already caches the genuinely expensive part (computation); Pandoc spawn is fast for typical docs and the batch-publish audience renders occasionally, not on every keystroke. Fewer moving parts (no block model, no diff, no invalidation matrix, no DOM-state-preservation edge cases) is itself a correctness asset.
- **Taliesin today:** The warm server also re-parses the WHOLE document each save (serve/mod.rs calls render_document_with_includes, a fresh comrak parse and full emit), but then runs diff_blocks (diff.rs, LCS over content-hash ids) and broadcasts only Update/Insert/Remove/SetMeta ops, so unchanged blocks (and their live {js}/video/<details> state and scroll) survive. Warm server plus warm kernel means zero per-edit startup. comrak parse is microsecond-fast, so full re-parse is cheap; there is no render-level memoization, so every save re-runs syntect highlighting (highlight.rs) and KaTeX server-side math (math.rs) for EVERY block, changed or not.
- **Proposed better:** Add a render-level per-block memo keyed by the content hash that make_id already computes: cache each block's emitted HTML (crucially the highlighted-code and KaTeX-rendered outputs, the two genuinely expensive passes) and, on re-render, reuse the cached HTML for any block whose source hash is unchanged. This turns the whole-document re-highlight/re-math into work proportional to the edited blocks only, mirroring at the render layer what _freeze already does for cell execution. The diff stays identical (same ids), so the wire protocol and DOM behavior are unchanged.
- **Revised recommendation:** Reframe the entry around the one real gap and drop the block-level HTML cache. The observation that survives is narrow and true: syntect re-highlights every code block on every save while KaTeX already does not, because math.rs memoizes and highlight.rs does not. The right fix is to mirror the existing, proven pattern exactly: add a process-global bounded memo to highlight.rs keyed on (code, lang), a near-verbatim copy of math.rs's MathCache (FIFO eviction, cap). This is a ~15-line change that automatically covers both call sites (emit.rs and cell_numbered.rs), needs zero cross-block invalidation because the output is a pure function of its inputs, is untouched by theme changes (class-based highlighting), and matches the leaf-level _freeze/KaTeX discipline the project already commits to. Explicitly do NOT build a per-block HTML cache keyed by make_id: it double-caches the already-memoized math and imports a numbering/xref/id-dedup invalidation matrix that the leaf memo makes unnecessary. Correct the entry's taliesin_current to state that KaTeX is already memoized. Pin the change with a code-heavy corpus chapter (many fenced blocks) so a regression in the highlight memo is caught; the diff ops, data-block-id, and data-sourcepos are all unchanged, so click-to-source and incremental update are untouched.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adds a cache to invalidate correctly (theme changes, cross-reference number shifts, and xref registry mutations must bust affected blocks, since a block's rendered number can change even when its source did not, e.g. figure renumbering upstream). Whole-doc comrak parse is already fast, so on small docs the memo saves little; the win is concentrated in large math-heavy or code-heavy book chapters. Risk of a subtle stale-render bug if invalidation misses a cross-block dependency. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's premise is factually wrong on half its motivation: KaTeX is ALREADY memoized. math.rs holds a process-global bounded FIFO cache keyed on (latex, display_mode), cap 8192, that persists across saves and across a site's pages, so unchanged math is already a hashmap hit every save. Only syntect highlighting (emit.rs:65, cell_numbered.rs:111) lacks a memo. So the proposal's incremental win over the status quo is the code-highlighting pass ONLY, not the two passes it claims. Worse, the chosen mechanism is the wrong altitude. A block's emitted HTML is NOT a pure function of its own source: sec_count, eq_count, figure/theorem counters, the xref_registry, and the dedup_with_suffix id-suffix are mutable state threaded through the emit loop, so caching whole-block HTML keyed by the make_id content hash is only correct if you also bust every block whose rendered number or deduped id shifts when an upstream block changes (figure renumbering, equation/section counters, citation order, footnote numbering, a duplicate-source suffix flipping). That is exactly the stale-render risk the drafter flags, and it is self-inflicted by caching at the block level. The leaf-level memo math.rs already uses avoids ALL of it: (code, lang) and (latex, display) fully determine their output, so no invalidation logic is ever needed, only bounded eviction, which is a capacity policy not a correctness one. The drafter also over-counts the invalidation burden in the other direction: theme changes never need to bust anything, because highlighting emits scope CLASSES (tali-hl-*) not inline colors and the light/dark toggle restyles with no re-highlight (highlight.rs docstring), and KaTeX output is likewise theme-independent.)
- **Invariant check:** Purely an internal speed optimization beneath the block model: same data-block-id, same data-sourcepos, same diff ops, so click-to-source and incremental update are untouched. It reuses the existing content-hash, matching the _freeze cumulative-hash discipline. No new output format, no write-back, no syntax change.

### D25. Drop the Pandoc template language plus Bootstrap/SCSS theming for one Rust page shell, CSS custom properties, and fixed include slots (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto assembles HTML from Pandoc templates (the $body$/$if$/$for$ template language plus a large partials tree) and themes it with Bootstrap 5 via bslib: SCSS variable layers, ~25 bootswatch themes, and a SCSS compilation step. Customizing layout means template partials; customizing look means SCSS layer files.
- **Critique:** This is heavy and multi-language: Bootstrap ships a large CSS/JS payload and legacy patterns, SCSS needs a compile step, and the template language plus partials plus SCSS layers are three separate things to learn to change a page. It also drifts from 'self-contained offline' because the theming machinery is substantial.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Bootstrap 5 + bslib + Pandoc partials is not accidental bloat; it is the deliberate price of being a GENERAL, multi-format, multi-author publishing system, and every part earns its keep for that audience. (1) One mechanism across every target: the template/partials model and the SCSS-layer model are identical whether you emit HTML, revealjs, beamer/PDF, or docx, so an author or an institution learns theming ONCE and it transfers. Taliesin only gets to be simple because it discarded every output format but HTML. (2) Override without forking: a Quarto user drops a single `title-block.html` partial, or a `theme.scss` with a `/*-- scss:defaults --*/` block, to restructure or restyle ANY region of the page, with zero toolchain access and no rebuild of the engine. Taliesin can only match that by editing and recompiling the Rust binary. (3) Instant breadth: `theme: darkly` is a complete, accessible, professionally designed restyle in one line, times ~25 bootswatch themes, plus Bootstrap's tested responsive grid and accessible components (tabs, dropdowns, accordions) that Taliesin must now re-implement one at a time (panel-tabset, callouts, lightbox...). (4) SCSS layers (defaults / functions / mixins / rules) are a more expressive, documented override surface than a flat list of CSS variables. For Quarto's real market (many authors, many formats, publishers enforcing a house style across a catalog) that breadth and format-uniformity IS the product, and a large Bootstrap payload is an acceptable, still-offline-capable cost of it. The honest point Taliesin should concede: none of these four benefits is load-bearing for a single author shipping HTML only, which is precisely why dropping the machinery is correct for Taliesin and would be wrong for Quarto. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** page.rs assemble_html_page is a single Rust format-string shell (the one source of truth for <head> ordering and body frame), with no template language. Theming is `--tali-*` CSS custom properties: base.css plus a runtime-flippable dark.css (theme.rs), and a custom theme: is just a plain .css file inlined after the base, no SCSS, no Bootstrap, no build step. The only author injection points are include-in-header / include-before-body / include-after-body / css (model.rs PageIncludes), merged site-then-page. Everything is inlined for offline use.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the CSS-variable plus include-slots model; it is leaner, buildless, offline, and theme-swappable by editing variables. The one gap to watch: because there is no template language, a structurally different page layout (not just restyling) requires editing Rust. That is acceptable for a single author, but keep the include-in-header/before/after slots as the sanctioned escape hatch and make sure the `--tali-*` variable surface is documented as the theming contract so a custom theme.css never needs to fork the shell.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the model; the status (taliesin-already-better) is correct and the single-Rust-shell + `--tali-*` variables + additive include slots is genuinely leaner, buildless, and offline. Sharpen with three fixes before cataloguing. (1) Trim the inaccurate critique clause: 'drifts from self-contained offline' conflates payload weight with offline capability. Quarto with `embed-resources: true` produces fully self-contained offline HTML, so the honest critique is payload size + a required SCSS compile step + a higher concept count (template language, partials, SCSS layers), NOT loss of offline. Also soften 'three separate things to learn to change a page': a simple restyle in Quarto touches only one (a bootswatch name or an scss:defaults block). (2) State the escape hatch's real limit precisely: include-* is additive-only and cannot override or restructure the emitted skeleton; do not present it as a layout escape hatch, present it as an injection hatch, with 'restructure = Rust edit + rebuild' as the accepted single-author cost, and name Quarto's genuine edge (partial-level override without forking + one-line bootswatch breadth) as the thing knowingly traded away. (3) Make the theming contract explicit AND fix the wart: document 'a custom theme is plain CSS that overrides the `--tali-*` variables; it is inlined after base.css and never compiled' AND either drop `.scss` from resolve_theme's accepted extensions or clearly warn that `.scss` is inlined raw (not compiled), so the extension never implies SCSS support Taliesin does not have. The verbatim-unescaped PageIncludes footgun the entry already flags is a pre-existing trust-model choice, not a new risk, and needs no change beyond the note it already carries.
- **Tradeoffs:** No template language means non-trivial layout changes are code changes plus a recompile, and there is exactly one page skeleton (three OutputMode variants of it, not arbitrary layouts). Authors coming from Quarto's partials/bootswatch ecosystem lose that breadth. The PageIncludes strings are injected verbatim and unescaped (trusted-author model), so they are a footgun if ever fed untrusted input. (skeptic-found downside: The entry oversells the sanctioned escape hatch and misses a latent wart. (a) include-in-header / include-before-body / include-after-body is strictly ADDITIVE: it can append head tags or wrap chrome around the body, but it canNOT override or restructure the emitted skeleton the way a Quarto partial can (you cannot move the TOC, replace the title block, or reorder main/aside through it). So the drafter's framing that layout changes 'require editing Rust' understates it: even the escape hatch does not cover restructuring, only addition; the only real answer to 'reshape the page' is a Rust edit plus rebuild. (b) resolve_theme (theme.rs:28) accepts a `.scss` theme file but inlines it verbatim via std::fs::read_to_string with NO compiler, exactly like a `.css` file. A genuine SCSS file ($variables, nesting, @use) therefore inlines as invalid CSS that browsers silently drop. The clean 'no SCSS' win thus ships a misleading half-open door: an extension that promises support that does not exist.)
- **Invariant check:** Fully HTML-only and offline-consistent. CSS-variable theming and include slots do not create a second editing surface or a write-back path. Keeping include-* verbatim matches the existing documented trust model; no invariant is stressed.

### D26. Emit HTML by string concatenation and post-process Pandoc attributes with string surgery, rather than handling them at the AST level (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Pandoc parses Pandoc-Markdown attribute syntax (heading {#id .class}, bracketed spans [x]{.class}, link/image attributes) directly into typed AST nodes (Attr), and its HTML writer emits them structurally. Attribute handling never touches already-serialized HTML.
- **Critique:** Not applicable as a Quarto pain; this entry critiques Taliesin's OWN internal choice. Because comrak does not model these Pandoc attribute extensions, Taliesin recovers them by rewriting emitted HTML strings after the fact, which is inherently fragile.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Pandoc's typed Attr on AST nodes is not a stylistic nicety, it is forced by its mission: one AST feeds 40+ writers (LaTeX, Docx, HTML, ePub...), so an id/class/key-val MUST survive as structured data through every writer, never as format-specific text. The reader fully parses the Pandoc-Markdown attribute grammar once, and each writer serializes it in its own idiom. The cost (a large rigid AST, a reader that owns the whole extension grammar) buys the format-independence Taliesin explicitly renounces. Taliesin chose comrak precisely because it is a fast CommonMark/GFM parser, and comrak DELIBERATELY does not implement Pandoc's attribute extensions, so an Attr field is simply not on offer. Given that constraint and a single HTML target, recovering the residual attributes near serialization is the pragmatic, correctly-scoped trade. Crucially, the highest-value attribute, the heading id, is ALREADY recovered structurally from source and written by emit into the opening tag, so Taliesin has in fact adopted the AST-level pattern exactly where it pays, and reserved string handling only for the leftovers.
- **Taliesin today:** emit.rs builds HTML by pushing strings, and mod.rs then does post-emission string surgery: parse_heading_attr/strip_heading_attr for `## T {#id}`, apply_link_attrs + inject_attrs_into_last_tag for `[t](u){.class}`, strip_trailing_hardbreak for a dangling `\`, apply_heading_bg for deck backgrounds, and divs.rs group_divs re-scans emitted blocks to regroup them into containers. These use find('>')/rfind("</h")/tag_end scanning; code comments record real bugs already fixed here (strip_trailing_hardbreak notes 'the previous global replace could corrupt it'; tag_end exists precisely because a naive find('>') split inside a quoted attribute value).
- **Proposed better:** Move attribute recovery earlier, before serialization, so surgery over serialized HTML shrinks. Concretely: run a small pre-parse or post-parse pass over the comrak AST (or the raw block source, which is already captured as block_src) that extracts the trailing {#id .class} / bracketed-span / link-attr into a typed structure attached to the block, then have emit.rs write those attributes into the opening tag as it builds it, instead of re-opening the finished string to inject them. Keep the current string helpers as a narrow fallback, but stop them being the primary mechanism.
- **Revised recommendation:** Do NOT do the blanket 'move attribute recovery to the AST' refactor; it is partly redundant, overstates current fragility, and risks regressing corpus-pinned helpers (explicit_heading_id_is_applied_and_stripped, dedup, panel_tabset, render-fixes/) for robustness-not-a-feature payoff. Rewrite the entry around three sharpened points: (a) correct the premise: heading-id, deck section-attr, and div grouping are ALREADY source-derived and structural via `attrs`+scan_div_spans; only apply_link_attrs and apply_heading_bg are true post-serialization injections, and the leftover-text strippers are best left html-level for opaque-text robustness. (b) The one cheap, corpus-safe win: make apply_heading_bg (mod.rs:1146) and inject_attrs_into_last_tag (mod.rs:1240) use the existing quote-aware `tag_end` instead of `find('>')`, as defence-in-depth so the injection no longer relies on the implicit 'all callers escape_attr' invariant (~2 lines, no AST work). (c) Only pursue AST-level link-attr handling if a concrete bug appears (a comrak split of `{...}`, or an escaping gap), pinned by a new corpus doc first. Downgrade impact to low.
- **Tradeoffs:** comrak's AST does not expose these Pandoc extensions, so the pre-pass must re-derive spans from source text (extra parsing logic, its own edge cases) or maintain a comrak fork. There is real risk of regressing behavior that the current, corpus-pinned string helpers get right today, so this is a refactor to do behind the existing corpus tests, not a rewrite. The payoff is robustness, not a user-visible feature, so it competes with feature work. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal is partly redundant and its headline mechanism does not fit the residual cases. (1) Its own prescription (derive from source, attach typed, let emit write the opening tag) is ALREADY how heading ids and deck section-attrs work (parse_heading_attr/heading_section_attrs feed the structural `attrs` string at mod.rs:421), and group_divs already regroups by source-derived spans, not by scanning HTML. So the entry overstates how much is 'string surgery over serialized HTML.' (2) The two remaining strippers (strip_heading_attr, strip_trailing_hardbreak) are NOT opening-tag injections; they remove literal text comrak tokenized into the element's TEXT content or a trailing backslash. 'Write attributes into the opening tag' does not touch them. Moving them before serialization means mutating comrak's INLINE AST text nodes, which is arguably LESS robust: comrak can split a leftover `{.a b=\"*x*\"}` across multiple typed inline nodes (Emph/Code/Text), whereas the current html-level strip treats the trailing `{...}` as opaque text and is immune to that tokenization. (3) Handling link attrs structurally is a real cost the drafter waved past: emit passes `attrs` only to the ROOT element, every inline child gets \"\" (emit.rs:264), and comrak's Link node has no Attr field, so you must thread a node-identity attribute map or a side-channel through the inline path. (4) The 'inherently fragile' claim is overstated: the two naive find('>') sites are safe because every value Taliesin writes is escape_attr'd (>→&gt;, mod.rs:1724), and tag_end is already used exactly where raw author HTML could carry a quoted `>`. The find('>')-vs-tag_end split is coherent, not accidental.)
- **Invariant check:** Internal only: same emitted attributes, same data-block-id/data-sourcepos on the same root element, so click-to-source and diff are unaffected. It strengthens (does not touch) the sourcepos-totality invariant. Keeps the Pandoc-Markdown attribute syntax exactly as authored (no syntax divergence).

### D27. Bound the input grammar to comrak's fixed extension subset plus hand-rolled Pandoc constructs, leaving some Pandoc-Markdown unsupported (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto feeds Pandoc-Markdown, whose extension set is broad and toggleable (+/-ext): definition lists, native fenced divs and bracketed spans, grid/multiline tables, line blocks, example lists, and more are all parseable out of the box.
- **Critique:** The fair critique cuts the other way here: Pandoc-Markdown's breadth is a real capability Quarto gets for free, and Taliesin's comrak-based parser supports only a fixed subset, so several Pandoc constructs an author might reasonably write are silently mis-rendered or dropped rather than flagged.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto delegates all parsing to Pandoc, so it inherits a mature, single-canonical-implementation, fully-documented grammar (definition lists, grid/multiline tables, line blocks, example lists, native divs, bracketed spans) at zero maintenance cost, and every construct is a first-class SEMANTIC node in the Pandoc AST. That semantic model is not incidental: Quarto's mission is many output targets (LaTeX, Typst, docx, epub, HTML), and a definition list or grid table must lower correctly to each. A fixed parser subset would be a real regression for a multi-format compiler, and authors get a stable, portable, well-specced surface they can rely on across formats. For Quarto's job, delegating to Pandoc is the correct, low-risk choice. The entry is honest about this: its critique explicitly says the breadth is a genuine free capability and that Taliesin silently mis-renders where Quarto succeeds, so it is a steelman, not a strawman. The only Taliesin-side rejoinder is that this same Pandoc dependency is the source of the costs Taliesin exists to remove (no sourcepos-driven click-to-source, no block-level incremental, a per-render process spin-up), so "the whole grammar for free" is not free in Taliesin's terms.
- **Taliesin today:** parse_options() enables exactly front_matter, strikethrough, table, autolink, math_dollars, footnotes, and smart typography. Everything else Pandoc-flavored is hand-rolled: `:::` fenced divs (divs.rs preprocess/scan_div_spans), heading/link attribute blocks (string surgery), bare `\begin{env}` math. Constructs comrak does not model and that are NOT hand-rolled, e.g. definition lists (`Term`\n`: def`) and bracketed inline spans (`[text]{.underline}` with no URL), are unsupported: a bare bracketed span renders as literal `[text]` text, and there is no did-you-mean for it the way there is for front-matter/cell keys.
- **Proposed better:** Since the owner has fixed Markdown/Pandoc as the substrate, decide deliberately which Pandoc constructs are in-grammar and pin each with a corpus doc. Two are worth first-classing because they are common and browser-meaningful: definition lists (comrak has a description_lists extension that could be enabled and mapped to <dl>) and bracketed spans (`[text]{.class}`), which give inline styling hooks the same way link-attrs already do. For anything explicitly ruled out-of-grammar, emit a located, click-to-source diagnostic (reuse the strict-validation channel) instead of silently passing it through as literal text, so the clean break is honest rather than a silent gap.
- **Revised recommendation:** Revise and split the bundle, because the two constructs have very different economics. (A) Definition lists: enable comrak's description_lists, but SPEC Taliesin's grammar as comrak's loose (blank-line) form and document that explicitly rather than claiming Pandoc parity; add a corpus doc; add emit arms for the four new node kinds and confirm no path silently drops them; retest sourcepos + the div corpus for interaction with the ':::' preprocess and smart typography. To make the clean break honest, add ONE targeted diagnostic for the tight Pandoc spelling (a ': ' line directly under a non-blank line with no blank between), which is the single high-signal, low-false-positive pattern. (B) Bracketed spans: treat as a SEPARATE, higher-cost item, not a cheap analog. It is inline-level, needs a real inline pass with link/ref-link disambiguation, and must only fire when {.…} is immediately adjacent to a closing bracket to avoid corrupting literals; pin it with its own corpus doc and adversarial cases (span inside emphasis, span next to a real link, literal [x] then {.y}). Do NOT enable comrak's underline extension (it redefines __bold__); route {.underline} through the bracketed-span machinery instead. (C) Scope the 'diagnose unsupported constructs' goal DOWN to a small allowlist of unambiguous signatures (tight definition list, adjacent bracket+{.…}); do not build a general 'detect any Pandoc construct we lack' net, since that cannot exist without intent-guessing. Keep impact at medium and note it is genuinely optional for a single author, so it should not preempt more load-bearing roadmap work.
- **Tradeoffs:** Every construct added is more parser/emitter surface and more corpus to maintain, and enabling a comrak extension (description_lists) risks interactions with the existing preprocessing passes (fenced-div stripping, smart typography) that need retesting. Turning silent passthrough into diagnostics could be noisy for authors who intentionally write literal brackets. Doing nothing is defensible for a single author who simply avoids the unsupported constructs. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter missed or understated. (1) Dialect mismatch: comrak 0.52's description_lists REQUIRES a blank line between term and definition (Term\n\n: def); Pandoc allows the tight Term\n: def, which is exactly the form the entry's own taliesin_current shows as broken. So enabling the extension does NOT make the described construct work; it adds comrak's loose-only dialect and leaves the canonical tight Pandoc spelling still mis-rendering, i.e. partial support wearing the 'Pandoc definition lists' label, and an inconsistency where one spelling works and the standard one silently fails. (2) Bracketed spans are NOT analogous to the existing link/heading/figure attribute handling: those are BLOCK-level, line-anchored string surgery on block_src; [text]{.class} is INLINE-level, can nest inside emphasis or sit adjacent to a real [text](url) / [text][ref] link, and comrak may already have emitted [text] as literal text from a failed reference link, making post-hoc detection lossy. Taliesin does no inline rewriting today, so this introduces a new and harder processing class, not 'the same way link-attrs already do.' Note also comrak's underline extension is __x__, which would REDEFINE __bold__ and break the corpus, so it is not a usable path for {.underline}. (3) The 'route unsupported constructs to the diagnostic channel' pitch is not a clean reuse of the strict-validation surface: that surface fires on closed-vocabulary self-announcing slots (a #| key, a ::: class, a front-matter key), where a typo is unambiguously detectable; 'the author wrote a Pandoc construct we lack' has no such anchor and requires intent-guessing (is {.underline} after a bracket a span the author meant, or literal prose?), so it is a heuristic with false positives, which the drafter waves off in one clause but is actually the crux.)
- **Invariant check:** Adding first-class handling stays within the Markdown/Pandoc substrate (no syntax divergence, just more of the existing syntax supported) and every new block still flows through the block model with data-block-id/data-sourcepos. Routing unsupported constructs to the diagnostic channel reuses the existing validation surface and respects HTML-only, single-surface, click-to-source. (possible violation flagged: None. I verified that comrak 0.52 populates parse-level AST sourcepos on DescriptionList nodes (the sourcepos test asserts 1:1-7:11 for the top-level node), and Taliesin reads parse-level data.sourcepos, not comrak's render.sourcepos formatter (whose known incompatibility is therefore irrelevant here), so a top-level dl block can carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos like any other block; inline spans live inside a paragraph block and need no block id. HTML-only, single read-only surface, keep-Markdown, and click-to-source are all respected, and the proposal pins each construct with a corpus doc per the corpus-plus-roadmap rule. The real risk is integration, not invariant breach: comrak emits four new node kinds (DescriptionList/Item/Term/Details) that Taliesin's own emit path must add arms for (Taliesin does not use comrak's HTML formatter), and the description_lists pass must be retested against the fenced-div line-blanking preprocess and smart typography, since a leading ': ' line could interact.)

### D28. Record an explicit English-first default and centralize the chrome/crossref label strings behind a narrow front-matter override, rather than shipping Quarto's ~30 bundled locales or attempting RTL (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto ships ~30 built-in translation catalogs (crossref prefixes like Figure/Table, callout titles, toc-title, section titles, "References") selected by the document's `lang:`, plus a `language:` front-matter map that overrides any single UI string, plus `dir: rtl` and RTL-aware/bidi CSS for right-to-left documents. Localization is a first-class, drop-in feature.
- **Critique:** Two different things are bundled together here. Shipping and maintaining ~30 locale catalogs (and corpus-pinning each) is dead weight for a single author who writes in one language, and full RTL touches essentially every layout rule in base.css (logical properties, mirrored chrome), so it is a rendering-wide project, not a string swap. But the small, genuinely useful slice is real: a monolingual author writing in, say, Finnish or Spanish wants "Figure" to render as "Kuva"/"Figura" and the auto "References" heading as "Lähteet"/"Referencias", and Taliesin currently gives them no way to do it at all. The gap is not "no 30 locales", it is "no override and no centralization".
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general, multi-author publishing system used by institutions, journals, and textbook authors worldwide, so drop-in localization is table stakes for its scope, not gold-plating. A Spanish research group should get "Figura"/"Cuadro"/"Referencias" from `lang: es` alone with zero config, and RTL support for Arabic/Hebrew/Persian/Urdu is a correctness requirement for that scholarship, not a nicety. The ~30 catalogs are cheap for Quarto to carry: they are small YAML files contributed by native speakers, not maintained per-language by the core team, so the marginal cost of each is near zero while the market-reach payoff is large. For a tool whose whole premise is broad out-of-the-box usability, shipping localization is the correct default and NOT shipping it would be the mistake. The entry concedes exactly this (it calls Quarto's localization "a first-class, drop-in feature") and only argues the ROI inverts for a single-author tool, so it is a fair steelman rather than a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** `lang:` is a recognized front-matter key (frontmatter.rs:26) but is used only to emit `<html lang="…">`, defaulting to "en" (page.rs:149,389); no `dir` attribute is ever emitted and there is no RTL/bidi handling anywhere in the source. Every chrome and crossref string is a hardcoded English literal scattered across files: "Figure" (figure.rs:120, cell_numbered.rs:87, cite/render.rs:13), "Table" (cite/render.rs:14 plus the executor's injected "Table N"), the auto "References" heading (cite/render.rs:78), "Proof" (divs.rs:554), theorem display names (divs.rs theorem_meta), callout titles via capitalize(kind) yielding Note/Tip/Warning/Important/Caution (divs.rs:363), TOC aria-labels "Contents" and "Table of contents" (page.rs:216,267), and the search placeholder "Search this document…"/"Search…" (web-client/search.js:146,168). There is no override map and no locale table: the localization and RTL stance is an unrecorded fork.
- **Proposed better:** Record English-first as the deliberate default (this alone closes the unrecorded fork). Then centralize the ~15 label strings into a single `Labels` table with English defaults, and expose a narrow override in front-matter and `_site.yml` (a `labels:` map keyed by a fixed slot vocabulary: fig, tbl, references, proof, the theorem kinds, toc, search) that a non-English author sets once, ideally in shared site config. Validate the override KEYS with the existing strict, did-you-mean, click-to-source machinery. Do NOT bundle locale catalogs. For direction: derive `dir="rtl"` from a known RTL `lang` subtag (or an explicit `dir:` key) as a cheap correctness win, but keep real RTL CSS gated as a corpus-led roadmap item, built only if and when the author actually writes RTL.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry into a do-now half and a corpus-gated half. Do now, because both are cheap and honest: (1) record English-first as the deliberate default, closing the unrecorded fork; (2) centralize the ~15 scattered literals into one internal `Labels` table with English defaults, threaded through render. That is a pure refactor with zero new front-matter surface, corpus stays green, and it de-risks everything downstream. Defer the user-facing `labels:` override until the author actually writes a non-English document, so its pinning corpus doc is genuine rather than a synthetic doc that exists only to justify the feature (localization is a static string swap, not the "richer browser behavior in a live HTML view" that defines wider-than-Quarto, so it ranks low against the differentiators). When the override is built: keep it a CLOSED fixed-slot object (no schema carve-out; existing did-you-mean machinery handles it), and update `is_manual_references_heading` to match the configured references label or it will emit a duplicate heading. For direction, drop the auto-derive-from-lang idea entirely: expose an explicit opt-in `dir:` key only (author knowingly accepts LTR layout) and keep real RTL CSS as a separate corpus-led roadmap item built only if the author writes RTL.
- **Tradeoffs:** Centralization is a real refactor across ~6 Rust files plus the Rust-to-JS seam: the search placeholder lives in web-client, so overriding it means threading labels to the client (a `window.TALIESIN_LABELS` global or data attribute), extra plumbing. The override is an open string-to-string map, exactly the free-form shape the clean-break strict validator normally rejects, so the schema needs a carve-out that validates keys against the fixed slot vocabulary rather than allowing arbitrary keys. Staying English-default means a non-English author must set overrides (a papercut, mitigated by putting them once in `_site.yml`). Emitting `dir="rtl"` without full RTL CSS yields partially-correct output (text direction right, layout still LTR), which can read worse than nothing when half-done, which is why RTL styling stays behind a corpus doc. (skeptic-found downside: Localizing the `references` label breaks the duplicate-heading guard: `is_manual_references_heading` (cite/render.rs:145) matches only English "references"/"bibliography", so an author who overrides references to "Lähteet" AND writes a manual `# Lähteet` heading to place the list gets a SECOND auto `<h2>Lähteet</h2>`. The override must also feed that detector, which the proposal never mentions. Two smaller misses: (a) the claimed "schema carve-out" is unnecessary work, a fixed-slot `labels:` is a closed object (`additionalProperties:false` over the slot names), exactly the existing schema.rs pattern, so it needs no special-casing and is cheaper than stated; (b) deriving `dir="rtl"` automatically from an RTL `lang` subtag is a net-negative, not a cheap win: it turns a metadata/hyphenation hint (lang: fa/ar/he) into a half-mirrored broken layout the author never requested, which the entry's own tradeoff admits "reads worse than nothing.")
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only preserved: no new output format, only string substitution in the existing HTML. Single read-only surface preserved: labels/dir are source front-matter and config; the preview never writes them back. Keep-Markdown preserved: `labels:` and `dir:` are YAML front-matter keys, no change to prose/div/shortcode syntax. Click-to-source preserved and reused: a mistyped label slot gets the same did-you-mean diagnostic that navigates to the offending front-matter line. Block-level incremental preserved: labels resolve at render into the same block model, so every block keeps its data-block-id and data-sourcepos. Warm-server preserved: a label lookup is a cheap map read with no per-edit startup cost. Corpus-plus-roadmap honored: ship pinned by a corpus doc that sets `labels:` in a non-English language and asserts the rendered prefixes; RTL is a separate roadmap item pinned only when built.

### D29. Diagram rendering: keep client-side Mermaid as the sole engine, or add a Graphviz/dot engine (and make Preview offline-honest)? (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto ships two first-class diagram engines addressed by the same fenced-cell syntax: ```{mermaid} and ```{dot} (Graphviz). For HTML it renders both in the browser by default, but it can also pre-render a diagram to a static SVG or PNG at compile time (mermaid via a headless-browser mermaid-cli path; dot via the system graphviz `dot` binary), controllable per format and per cell, so the same source works for HTML and for the non-HTML formats Quarto also targets. Diagram theming, width/height, and file-based (`%%| file:`) sources are supported for both engines.
- **Critique:** Taliesin renders exactly one diagram language. A ```{dot} or ```{graphviz} cell (the natural choice for the architecture and dependency graphs an internals/technical book constantly needs, and something Taliesin's own docs/internals book would benefit from) silently degrades to a highlighted code listing rather than a graph, with no diagnostic that the engine is missing. Separately, even for the one supported engine, Preview is not offline-honest: it fetches the library from a pinned public CDN by default, so a diagram in live preview simply fails (shows the error banner) with no network, even though the full library is already vendored in-tree and inlined at Build. This whole diagram surface (a common doc need, and one where Quarto is measurably wider) is currently uncatalogued.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's dual-engine choice is correct FOR QUARTO and is not bloat. (1) Dot is not redundant with Mermaid: it is the lingua franca for machine-GENERATED graphs (build-system, dependency, profiler, automaton, phylogenetic tools all emit .dot), and Graphviz's layout engine auto-lays-out large or generated graphs that Mermaid cannot. A second engine covers a genuinely different niche plus an import path for the huge existing .dot corpus, for a broad user base that already has those files. (2) Quarto's compile-time pre-render-to-SVG/PNG is a NECESSITY of being multi-format, not overhead: the same diagram source must also land in PDF/LaTeX/docx where client-side JS cannot run, so static pre-render is the only way one source serves every target. Given Quarto's format matrix, two engines plus %%| file: sources plus per-format pre-render control is the coherent minimal design. Taliesin is HTML-only and single-author, so it can legitimately decline the pre-render machinery and (arguably) the second engine, but Quarto's own choice is well-justified and the entry describes it accurately without caricature.
- **Taliesin today:** Only ```{mermaid} cells become diagrams. In `crates/core/src/render/emit.rs:52` the emitter branches on `lang == "mermaid"` and writes `<pre class="mermaid">` (skipping the `<code>`/highlight/copy path); a labelled/captioned mermaid cell instead goes through `figure.rs:110 emit_mermaid_figure` for a numbered `<figure>` + `#fig-` anchor. Rendering is 100% client-side: `assets/js/mermaid.js` registers through `window.taliEnhancers` and lazy-loads the library only when a `pre.mermaid` is present, bakes theme colours into the SVG at run() time and re-renders every diagram from its stashed `dataset.src` on `qmd:themechange`, and on load failure inserts a visible `[data-mermaid-error]` banner (never a silent blank), keeping the source below. Build inlines the vendored `mermaid.min.js` (assets/js/mermaid.min.js, ~2.57 MB, content-gated to pages that actually have a diagram) so a built page is offline-complete; Preview lazy-loads from the pinned CDN `mermaid@11.4.1` (`mod.rs:859 MERMAID_DEFAULT`) unless `QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL` is set. No ```{dot}/```{graphviz}/```{d2}/```{plantuml} path exists anywhere in the tree. Pinned by corpus/render-fixes/index.qmd (offline banner + label/caption), corpus/bare-draft.qmd, corpus/reader/hovercards.tali. Note (61) in notes/FEATURE-IDEAS.md already flags the Preview CDN dependency.
- **Proposed better:** Keep Mermaid as the primary client-side engine (theme-reactive, no server binary, correct default for a live HTML view), and close the two real gaps without new architecture. (1) Add a ```{dot}/```{graphviz} engine backed by a small vendored WASM Graphviz (for example @hpcc-js/wasm or viz.js), mounted through the SAME `taliEnhancers` registry and the SAME `<pre class="...">` + emit_*_figure path as Mermaid, so it inherits data-block-id/data-sourcepos, the numbered-figure/@fig-xref wiring, theme re-render on qmd:themechange, the [data-...-error] banner, and content-gated build inlining for free. (2) Make Preview offline-honest by serving the already-vendored mermaid.min.js from the dev server by default (keep the CDN only as the QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL override), so a diagram renders with no network in preview exactly as it already does in a Build. Leave any headless-Chrome build-time pre-render-to-SVG mode as a later, opt-in flag (Taliesin is already eyeing headless Chrome for OG cards / a print track), never the default, since the browser render is the point.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry into three independently-shippable items ranked by confidence, do not ship them as one change. (1) SHIP NOW, high confidence: offline-honest Preview. Serve the already-vendored mermaid.min.js from the dev server as the default (add one static-asset route to serve/mod.rs and serve_site, lazy-fetched only when a pre.mermaid is present), keep the CDN only as the QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL override. This closes a real Preview-vs-Build WYSIWYG inconsistency and corrects note 61 (which is itself stale about Build). (2) SHIP NOW, high confidence, on-brand: a strict validator diagnostic for unknown cell engines. Make check.rs / the front-matter-style validator flag any {lang} cell whose lang is not an executable kernel lang (python/r) or a known diagram engine (mermaid), with a did-you-mean and click-to-source. This closes the "no diagnostic / silent degrade" half of the critique using Taliesin's signature strict-validation pattern and also catches general cell-language typos, whether or not dot is ever added. (3) GATE behind a real author need: the WASM Graphviz {dot} engine. Ship it only when pinned by a corpus doc reflecting a diagram the author genuinely authors and cannot express in Mermaid, and budget the real costs up front: a theme-reactive path that rewrites DOT color attributes on qmd:themechange (default dot is broken in dark mode), WASM-Graphviz font/typography matching, and a genuine emit_diagram_figure(class) + emit.rs engine-match refactor (not "for free"). Keep any headless-Chrome build-time pre-render out entirely, or strictly opt-in, as the entry already says. Net: the offline fix and the diagnostic fix are unambiguous wins and Taliesin does NOT already match them; the dot engine is defensible only conditionally, so the catalog entry should record it as gated-on-demand rather than a co-equal recommendation.
- **Tradeoffs:** A WASM Graphviz is a second vendored heavy asset (~1-3 MB) to inline at build; the content-gate means only pages with a dot diagram pay it, but that is another large binary in the repo and CI. Two engines means two theme-mapping surfaces, and Graphviz theming is cruder than Mermaid's themeVariables, so dark-mode dot graphs may need per-diagram attribute hints rather than a clean token map. Serving vendored Mermaid from the dev server adds the 2.57 MB asset to the preview server's served set (again only fetched when a diagram is present). Client-side-only rendering (both engines) keeps diagrams out of any future non-browser consumer, but that is consistent with, not a violation of, the HTML-only invariant. An opt-in server pre-render mode, if ever added, reintroduces a headless-Chrome/binary dependency and a slower cold build, which is exactly why it stays a flag. (skeptic-found downside: The entry bundles three items of very different confidence and misses the cheapest, most on-brand fix. It correctly NOTICES the "no diagnostic" gap but only proposes to fix it by adding the whole dot engine, missing the standalone fix: a strict did-you-mean flag in check.rs for any {lang} cell whose lang is neither an executable kernel lang (python/r) nor a known diagram engine (mermaid). That single change closes the "silent degrade" half of the critique using Taliesin's established strict-validation brand AND catches typos like {pyton}/{grafviz} generally, independent of dot. Second, Graphviz theming is worse than stated: with no color attributes a dot graph renders Graphviz defaults (black text/edges on transparent), invisible/ugly in dark mode, so the qmd:themechange path must REWRITE DOT bgcolor/fontcolor/color at render time, not just re-init a config as Mermaid's themeVariables does; that is not a graceful degrade. Font/typography matching in @hpcc-js/wasm is a known pain (its own font handling, CJK/emoji gaps) unlike Mermaid's browser-native text. Third, emit_mermaid_figure is mermaid-specific (hardcoded pre class="mermaid") and emit.rs:52 is a lang=="mermaid" branch, so dot needs a real emit_diagram_figure(class) + engine-match refactor, not "for free." Fourth, "serve vendored mermaid from the dev server" requires adding the FIRST static-asset route to BOTH serve/mod.rs and serve_site (currently only /, /favicon.ico, /ws), small but not literally free. Fifth, note 61 is mis-cited (it flags a stale BUILD-offline concern the code already fixed; the live gap is Preview). Sixth, the corpus doc corpus/diagrams/graphviz.qmd satisfies corpus-plus-roadmap only in LETTER: the justification ("docs/internals WOULD benefit") is speculative, and for a single-author tool a 2.5MB WASM engine plus a second theming surface must be pinned by a diagram the author ACTUALLY authors and cannot express in Mermaid, not a synthetic one manufactured to pass the gate.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: diagrams are DOM/SVG in the live view; no new output format is introduced, and any future pre-render would render FROM the built HTML, not as a parallel format. Single read-only surface: ```{dot} and ```{mermaid} are authored only in the .tmd; the browser renders, it never writes back. Keep-Markdown: both use the existing fenced-cell syntax with %%|/#| option lines, so nothing about the substrate syntax diverges. Click-to-source: the diagram block carries data-block-id (content hash) + data-sourcepos via the shared emit path, exactly as the mermaid <pre> does today, so Alt-click still jumps to source. Block-level incremental: a diagram is a single block re-rendered by its enhancer on swap, no full-page rebuild. Warm-server: pure client render, zero per-edit or kernel cost. Corpus-plus-roadmap: the dot engine ships pinned by a new corpus doc (for example corpus/diagrams/graphviz.qmd) in the same change. Wider-than-Quarto stays defined as richer live-view browser behaviour, not a new format.

### D30. De-duplicate heading anchor ids against a global used-set, not a per-base counter (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto inherits Pandoc's auto_identifiers algorithm: slug the heading's plain text (strip formatting/links, keep alphanumerics plus underscore, hyphen and period, spaces-to-hyphens, lowercase, drop everything before the first letter, empty falls back to "section"), then guarantee GLOBAL uniqueness by tracking every identifier already emitted on the page. A repeat probes base-1, base-2, ... against that used-set until one is free and then registers THAT id too, so a machine-generated suffix can never collide with a heading whose natural slug happens to be the same string.
- **Critique:** Taliesin dedupes with a per-base COUNTER, not a used-set: dedup_with_suffix keys a HashMap by the base slug and returns base-N from that base's count, but it never registers the suffixed string it just handed out. So headings "Intro", "Intro", "Intro 1" resolve to "intro", "intro-1", and "intro-1" (the third's natural slug), and the page ships the id "intro-1" TWICE. getElementById then finds only the first, so a deep link to #intro-1, an @sec- cross-reference, and Alt-click-to-source all silently land on the wrong heading with no warning (the duplicate-id warning only fires on the explicit-{#id} path, whose base counter is still 0 here). This is precisely the "collision suffixing is a decision" hazard: the scheme is invisible until two authors' slugs alias, then it breaks inbound links permanently. A secondary, lower-stakes divergence: slugify keeps only is_alphanumeric, so it drops underscores and periods that both Pandoc and GitHub preserve (My_Var to "my-var" not "my_var"; 3.2 to "3-2"), and a heading containing a link folds the URL text into the slug because Taliesin slugs the raw markdown line rather than the plain text.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto inherits Pandoc's uniqueIdent, which is provably collision-free: it tracks every id already placed on the page and, for any candidate, probes base-1, base-2 against that set until one is free, then registers the winner. Because it checks against emitted ids rather than a per-base tally, a machine-generated suffix can never alias a heading whose natural slug is the same string, so getElementById, the TOC, in-page anchors, and internal links always resolve to the intended element. In practice it is O(1) amortized (Pandoc keeps the set plus a per-base hint) and the algorithm is identical and stable across every writer, which is why Quarto never had to think about it: correctness is inherited. There is no honest defense of a per-base counter here; the entry is proposing to adopt Quarto's algorithm, and on this point Quarto is simply right. The only place Quarto is genuinely defensible-not-just-inherited is the char-class (keeping _ . and dropping leading non-letters): that grammar is what makes ids match GitHub/Pandoc and stay stable across tools, so the entry is correct to leave it alone.
- **Taliesin today:** Verified in crates/core/src/render/mod.rs. slugify (line 1032) walks chars, keeps is_alphanumeric (Unicode-aware, .to_lowercase()), collapses every non-alphanumeric run to a single '-', trims trailing separators, empty falls back to "section" (matches Pandoc). dedup_slug (1052) then calls dedup_with_suffix (1065), which does counts.entry(base).or_insert(0): first hit returns base, later hits return format!("{base}-{n}") and only ever bumps the BASE key, never inserting the suffixed result. Explicit {#id} headings (mod.rs:397-408) go through the same map and DO emit a "duplicate heading id" warning, but a natural-slug-vs-generated-suffix collision produces no warning. The deck engine (render/deck.rs:292) has its own parallel counter with the identical shape.
- **Proposed better:** Replace the per-base counter with a used-set that mirrors Pandoc's guarantee: keep one HashSet of every id already emitted on the page and, for any candidate (autoslug, explicit {#id}, or a generated suffix), if it is taken, probe base-1, base-2, ... until free and insert the winner into the set. The heading_slugs map already threads through both the autoslug and the explicit-id branches, so this is a localized rewrite of dedup_with_suffix plus its one deck twin, not a pipeline change. Deliberately KEEP the existing slug character class as-is: aligning to Pandoc's underscore/period retention would itself rewrite ids on already-published pages and break inbound links, and it is far lower impact than the duplicate-id class. Pin the fix with a corpus document that contains the Intro / Intro / Intro 1 collision so the used-set property is regression-tested, and keep the existing explicit-{#id} duplicate warning.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the fix; it corrects a real, code-confirmed duplicate-id bug (intro-1 emitted twice) by adopting Pandoc's provably-correct used-set. Sharpen four things: (1) Scope: do NOT rewrite the shared dedup_with_suffix; it also backs make_id's data-block-id dedup, which is bug-immune by grammar. Add a heading-only used-set deduper and point the three heading-slug sites at it (mod.rs 398/409/410 + deck.rs 292), leaving the block-id counter as-is. (2) Perf: retain a per-base hint counter as the probe start plus the used-set as the authority so n identical headings stay O(n), not O(n^2). (3) Warning: re-express the explicit-{#id} duplicate warning as "candidate already in used-set." (4) Corpus: pin BOTH the counter-bump order (Intro/Intro/Intro 1 to intro-1-1) AND the reordered order (Intro 1/Intro/Intro to intro-2), since only the reordered case regressions the skip-taken-slug property. Keep the deferral of the char-class/underscore/period/link-in-heading divergence exactly as written. Also correct the entry's invariant_check wording: this strengthens @sec- cross-refs, in-page anchors, and TOC scrollspy, not click-to-source itself, which rides data-sourcepos/data-block-id and is untouched.
- **Tradeoffs:** In the collision case the third heading's id changes from the currently-duplicated "intro-1" to "intro-1-1", so any external link that meant that specific heading via #intro-1 now misses, but it was already ambiguous and effectively broken (it hit the wrong element). Slightly more memory: a set of all emitted ids instead of a map of bases, negligible for any real document. The proposal does not touch the underscore/period/link-in-heading char-class divergence, so those still differ from Quarto; that is an accepted deferral because fixing it now would break more existing links than it repairs. The deck-side counter must be migrated in the same change or the two paths drift. (skeptic-found downside: dedup_with_suffix is shared by THREE callers, not the "heading-slug plus one deck twin" the entry claims: it also backs make_id (mod.rs:1523), the data-block-id content-hash deduper. So a straight rewrite of dedup_with_suffix would silently convert the block-id path too. That path is immune to this bug by grammar (its base is always b- + 12 hex chars and the -N suffix can never alias a natural base, since hyphen is not a hex digit), so the sharp fix is a HEADING-ONLY used-set deduper wired to the three heading sites (mod.rs 398/409/410 + deck.rs 292), leaving the block-id counter untouched, rather than rewriting the shared function. Second miss: dropping the counter for a pure probe-from-1 loop is O(n^2) for n identical headings; keep a per-base hint counter as the probe start index with the used-set as the authority (Pandoc's own shape). Third: the explicit-{#id} warning must be re-expressed as "candidate already in the used-set" rather than "counter != 0," and the corpus should also pin the REORDERED collision (Intro 1 before the two Intros, which must resolve to intro-2 by skipping the taken intro-1), not just the counter-bump order, since only the reordered case actually exercises probing-against-the-set.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure server-side render change, HTML remains the only output. Making every emitted heading id unique is exactly what keeps click-to-source and @sec- cross-refs resolving to the right block, so it strengthens the data-block-id/data-sourcepos load-bearing invariant rather than touching it. The preview stays read-only (ids are computed at render, nothing writes back to source). Markdown/Pandoc syntax is untouched: ## heading and {#id} still mean what they meant, only the collision-resolution of the generated id changes. Corpus-plus-roadmap honored by shipping the fix pinned to a new collision corpus doc that fails on the current code.

### D31. Keep smart typography ON by default, but record the decision, document the backslash escape hatch, and stop the strict validator from trapping a document-level opt-out (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto inherits pandoc's `smart` extension, on by default for HTML, which converts straight quotes to curly, `--`/`---` to en/em dashes, and `...` to an ellipsis. It is toggleable at the format level (`format: html: from: markdown-smart` turns the extension off) and honors pandoc's per-character backslash escapes (`\'`, `\"`) to keep a literal. So Quarto users have both a global switch and a fine-grained escape, and the pain point is that the global switch is blunt (all-or-nothing) and the escape is under-documented.
- **Critique:** Smart substitution mangles technical prose that authors write outside backticks: `--foo` becomes an en dash `-foo`, `--version` becomes `-version`, and measurements like `6'2"` become curly quotes instead of primes. Verified empirically against comrak 0.52. Taliesin turns this on with no recorded rationale, no documented way to defeat it per token, and (given the clean-break strict validator) no document-level opt-out either: a user reaching for the Quarto habit `smart: false` gets an unknown-key warning and no effect. Default-on with a silent, undocumented behavior and a validator that punishes the obvious escape is an unrecorded default-behavior decision.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's choice is the mature, well-trodden one and is currently more complete than Taliesin's. It inherits pandoc's `smart`, which is on by default precisely because polished prose (curly quotes, real dashes, ellipses) is what readers expect and what almost every author wants without configuring anything. Crucially, Quarto gives BOTH controls the entry treats as a weakness: a global reader-extension toggle (`from: markdown-smart`) AND native per-character backslash escapes. The toggle is not a bespoke YAML key; it composes uniformly with every other pandoc reader extension through one well-documented mechanism, so there is nothing special to learn or maintain. The escapes are standard pandoc/CommonMark, not a Quarto invention. So Quarto authors already have exactly the two-tier control (coarse global, fine per-token) that the proposal wants Taliesin to build, and they get it without adding a compatibility-committing config key. The entry's "blunt switch" knock cuts the other way: turning smart off globally and hand-curling the few quotes you want is a legitimate, predictable workflow, and Quarto additionally lets you keep smart on and escape the exceptions. The honest comparison is that Taliesin today offers strictly LESS than Quarto here (no switch at all, and a validator that actively rejects the attempt), so Quarto's design is the baseline the proposal is trying to catch up to, not a mistake to beat.
- **Taliesin today:** `crates/core/src/render/mod.rs:33` sets `options.parse.smart = true` unconditionally in `parse_options()`, with only a comment ("to match Quarto/pandoc output"). Nothing reads a toggle: there is no front-matter field, no `_site.yml` config, no per-cell option. Two mitigations exist but are undocumented: (1) comrak smartens text nodes only, so inline `` `code` `` spans and fenced code blocks are already exempt (verified: `` `--foo` `` stays literal); (2) CommonMark backslash escapes defeat it per token (verified: `\"`/`\'` yield clean straight quotes, `-\-` yields literal `--`, `..\.` yields literal `...`). Neither the exemption nor the escape is mentioned in `docs/guide/using/writing.qmd` or `reading.qmd`, and `frontmatter.rs` `KNOWN_KEYS` does not list `smart`, so any document-level opt-out is currently impossible and would itself warn.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the default ON (it delivers the "quiet typographic polish that needs no configuration" the guide already promises, and code is auto-exempt, so the real exposure is narrow prose). But close the three gaps: (1) Record the decision in the render pipeline comment and in `writing.qmd`, including that code spans/blocks are never touched. (2) Document the per-token backslash escape as the primary opt-out (`\"`, `\'` clean; `-\-` and `..\.` for dashes/ellipsis), which is finer-grained than Quarto's global switch and is native CommonMark, not new syntax. (3) Resolve the validator trap: rather than resurrect Quarto's blunt global flag, add `smart` to `KNOWN_KEYS` and honor `smart: false` at parse time as a first-class Taliesin field, so a per-document opt-out both works and passes validation. Taliesin's live preview plus Alt-click click-to-source already make any mangled literal instantly visible and one click from its source line, so the fine-grained escape is the better-fit primary path and the document flag is the escape valve. Pin all of it with a corpus doc that exercises a prose `--flag`, a `6'2"` measurement, the backslash escapes, and (if added) `smart: false`.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep parts (1) and (2), drop part (3). Do document the behavior AND the escapes, but reframe the priority: (a) code spans/blocks (and math) are already exempt, so put technical tokens like `--version` in backticks, which is idiomatic Markdown and the correct primary path for the motivating CLI-flag case; (b) the backslash escape (`\"`, `\'`, `-\-`, `..\.`) is the fine tool for one-off literals like a `6'2"` measurement outside code. Then do NOT add `smart` to `KNOWN_KEYS`: a first-class `smart: false` field grows the config surface, is a permanent compat commitment, is as blunt as Quarto's switch, and is dominated by backticks + backslash for the real cases, so it re-imports the very Quarto-habit tolerance the clean-break strict validator exists to redirect. If the validator dead-end (a user typing `smart: false` gets an unhelpful "unknown key" with no near suggestion) is the concern, solve THAT directly: special-case `smart` in the did-you-mean path to emit a hint pointing at the escape docs WITHOUT honoring the key, so the UX is a clear redirect rather than a silent trap, and the clean break holds. If a genuine need for a real off-switch later appears, prefer it once at `_site.yml` level (one place, site-wide) over per-page front matter, and only then. Pin the whole thing with a corpus doc exercising a prose `--flag`, a backticked `--flag`, a `6'2"` measurement, and the backslash escapes; add `smart` to the corpus only if the author actually adopts an off-switch.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adding a recognized `smart` key grows the config surface Taliesin is otherwise trying to keep tight, and a global off is a blunt instrument that loses the polish everywhere to fix a few tokens (the escape hatch is usually the right tool, so the flag risks being reached for too readily). The backslash escapes for dashes and ellipsis are genuinely clunky (`-\-`, `..\.`) and easy to forget. Documenting the behavior does not remove the surprise for authors who never read the guide. If we add the field, it needs a corpus pin and a place in the parse plumbing (a per-doc parse option threaded from front matter into `parse_options`, which currently takes no arguments), which is a small but real change to a hot path. (skeptic-found downside: The recommended PRIMARY opt-out (backslash escape) is worst-served exactly for the case that motivates the entry: CLI flags like `--version`/`--flag` recur constantly in technical prose, and writing `-\-version` every time is a real, forgettable tax. The idiomatic and already-exempt fix for that case is a code span (`--version`), which is also semantically correct (a flag IS code) and needs zero new machinery, yet the entry only mentions code exemption in passing and never connects it to the motivating example. Second, the threading plan is understated: `parse_options()` is called from TWO sites (`mod.rs:179` and `cell_numbered.rs:22` `caption_inline_html`), and the caption sub-parser carries no front-matter context, so a per-doc `smart: false` that is threaded only into the main parse would still smarten `fig-cap:`/`lst-cap:` captions, a silent inconsistency the "thread it into parse_options" sentence hides. Third, toggling `smart` in a warm preview flips every quote/dash in the document, so every block's content hash changes at once, forcing a whole-document block-swap on that single edit (acceptable but worth noting as doc-wide invalidation). Finally, a config key is a forever compatibility commitment for a single-author tool whose author can already reach for backticks and backslashes.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: unaffected, this is parse-time text substitution feeding the same HTML emitter. Single read-only surface: unaffected, the escape hatch is authored in the `.tmd` source and the preview never writes back. Keep Markdown/pandoc syntax: the backslash escape IS CommonMark, and `smart: false` is a YAML front-matter field, so no syntax divergence. Click-to-source and block-level incremental: neutral, the substitution happens inside text nodes before block-model assembly, so `data-block-id` and `data-sourcepos` are untouched (a per-doc `smart: false` only changes text content, not block boundaries). Warm server: parse-time only, no kernel or startup impact. Corpus-plus-roadmap: the change ships pinned by a corpus doc that asserts the exemptions, the escapes, and the toggle.

### D32. Keep raw HTML / {=html} passthrough unsanitized (trusted author), but harden the deploy/LAN boundary the passthrough now reaches with a default self-contained CSP plus a build-time remote-origin lint, instead of leaving the trust model as a comment (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto (Pandoc) also passes raw HTML and ```{=html} blocks through verbatim and executes code cells, with no sanitization pass and no Content-Security-Policy on its HTML output.
