Its trust model is the same "you author your own docs" but it is implicit and undocumented, and there is no enforced network boundary: even a self-contained (embed-resources) page can silently bake a CDN script or a youtube.com iframe, so "self-contained" is a convention, not something the browser enforces. `quarto preview` binds localhost and has no LAN-exposure access model comparable to a token gate.
- **Critique:** The unsanitized passthrough itself is correct and must stay: sanitizing would break legitimate authoring (audio/video, custom widgets, injected head CSS) and directly contradict the single-author trusted-source model. The real gap is that Taliesin's OWN differentiators widen the blast radius past a local render, yet nothing enforces the offline-first promise the rest of the architecture works hard to keep. `--host` serves the page (and any pasted third-party snippet, analytics tag, or remote iframe) to every device on the LAN, and `build` deploys static HTML to public hosts where that raw HTML/JS runs in visitors' browsers, not just the author's. The trust model is documented in lib.rs but only as prose ("do not point it at an untrusted .qmd"); there is zero enforcement or reminder at the moment it matters most, build/deploy time, and no CSP at all, so a page that claims to be self-contained can talk to any origin with nothing catching it. The extension-system spec already noticed half of this (a self-contained page silently depending on youtube.com) and specced a remote-URL lint that was never wired into the base renderer.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A default CSP baked into the document is the wrong layer and the wrong strength. CSP is a deployment concern that belongs to the hosting layer (Netlify/GitHub Pages/nginx response headers), which the author controls per-site, not something a renderer should stamp onto every page. For a static build the ONLY vehicle available to Taliesin is `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">`, and meta-delivered CSP is the strictly weaker form: browsers ignore `frame-ancestors`, `sandbox`, and `report-uri`/`report-to` in meta context, and the deploying host cannot loosen a meta-CSP it never set. Worse, because any document tool injects inline scripts and inline styles, a shipped CSP must carry `'unsafe-inline'` for script-src and style-src, so it buys essentially zero XSS protection: only a network boundary. And a network boundary is a poor default for a publishing tool, because legitimate documents routinely embed remote content on purpose (YouTube/Vimeo iframes, hosted plots, remote images, web fonts, live-data fetches). A tool that shipped `default-src 'self'` by default would break a large fraction of real documents on deploy and spray un-diagnosable CSP-violation errors into visitors' consoles. So emitting NO CSP is the correct, honest default for a general publisher: the author who wants offline enforcement adds a header at their host, where the strong form lives and where it can be relaxed. Quarto is also right that trust is a per-document-source property, not something to relitigate at deploy time: if you authored the doc, you already trusted every embed you wrote.
- **Taliesin today:** Verified from code. lib.rs carries an explicit "Trust model" doc: raw HTML (HtmlBlock/HtmlInline), ```{=html} passthrough, include-in-header/-before-body/-after-body/css, and site page-footer text are all emitted without HTML-escaping by design; cells execute against a live kernel. emit.rs confirms verbatim passthrough (emit_html_block; HtmlInline pushed raw). No CSP or <meta http-equiv> is emitted on any served or built page (grep finds none). `--host` DOES already gate LAN access beyond Quarto: serve/security.rs installs a per-session token guard (loopback always allowed, LAN peer needs ?t= token then HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie), a websocket Origin check, plus a printed "only serve documents you trust over --host" warning. But that gates who may connect, not what the content may do. The {{< embed >}} iframe (render/extension/mod.rs) has loading + allowfullscreen but no sandbox attribute. The page template (render/page.rs) injects styles and scripts inline (including {js} payloads as <script type="application/qmd-js">), which constrains any future script-src.
- **Proposed better:** Do not touch the content path: raw HTML stays unsanitized (the trusted-author capability is load-bearing). Instead formalize the deploy/LAN boundary the passthrough now reaches. (1) Emit a default, self-contained-friendly Content-Security-Policy on both served and built pages, tuned to what the inline runtimes actually need and verified against page.rs, roughly: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; frame-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' ws: wss:. Its real value is the network directives (default-src/connect-src/frame-src 'self'), which turn offline-first into a browser-enforced invariant and block silent exfiltration from a deployed page or a phone on the LAN. (2) Wire in the already-specced build-time remote-URL lint: when raw HTML, an injected head, or a shortcode bakes an absolute http(s):// origin into a page that claims self-contained, warn through the existing sourcepos-keyed diagnostic path so it navigates via click-to-source like every other Taliesin validation. (3) Provide an explicit escape hatch (a front-matter/_site.yml csp:/remote-fetch opt-in) so the author who genuinely wants a youtube embed or a CDN relaxes it deliberately. This upgrades the trust boundary from a comment into an enforced, click-to-source-diagnosable rule, exactly the pattern Taliesin already uses for strict front-matter validation, and it composes with the existing --host token gate rather than replacing it.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry and invert the defaults. (1) SHIP the remote-origin lint as the primary, default-on deliverable: it is on-brand (reuses the strict-validation + click-to-source pattern and the existing `is_local_ref` classifier), stays offline+deterministic, and informs without breaking. Make it ADVISORY (a warning, not a `--strict` failure) with a front-matter/_site.yml opt-out, since existing diagnostics deliberately leave external refs alone. Note the extension `remote-fetch` capability it was originally gated on is GONE (commit f5239cb removed the whole extension/capabilities system), so the front-matter/_site.yml opt-out is the correct successor. (2) Do NOT ship a default-on CSP. Make CSP OPT-IN (`csp:` / a strict-offline mode). Two exceptions where a real header-CSP is safe and high-value: emit it as an HTTP response header (the strong form Taliesin controls) ONLY on the `--host` preview server, where the LAN-exfiltration worry is real, where breaking a remote embed only affects the author's own screen, and where connect-src must include the live-reload ws. For static `build`, opt-in only, because meta-CSP is the weak form, is un-relaxable by the host, and the deploy target is exactly where remote embeds are most legitimate. (3) If any CSP ships, FIX the recipe: add `font-src 'self' data:` (KaTeX), and document that `img-src`/`script-src`/`connect-src` at `'self'` deliberately disable remote images and remote `{js}` import/fetch, which is why it is opt-in. (4) Independently, add `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-fullscreen"` to the `{{< embed >}}` iframe (extension/mod.rs:357): that is a targeted, no-regret hardening the entry noticed but did not act on. Corpus-pin: one doc exercising the advisory lint (remote ref warns + opt-out silences) and, if CSP ships, one exercising the opt-in strict-offline page including a math block to catch the font-src regression.
- **Tradeoffs:** Because the page template injects scripts inline (client.js, STATIC_ENHANCE, {js} runtime payloads, TOC scripts), the CSP must ship 'unsafe-inline' for script-src, which blunts XSS defense: the CSP buys the network boundary, not inline-script hardening. Real script-src hardening would require nonces threaded through every injected script AND the live block-swap path, which is meaningful plumbing and a live-reload footgun (a stale nonce silently kills hot updates). The remote-URL lint has false-positive risk (a legitimately remote <img>, a mailto:, an author's deliberate CDN) so it needs the opt-in and careful classification, and it adds a new warning class the corpus must pin. A too-strict default CSP could silently break an author's hand-rolled raw-HTML widget that fetches another origin, so it must ship with the escape hatch and a corpus doc pinning both the enforced default and a relaxed opt-out. None of this removes the underlying reality that a trusted author can still ship arbitrary JS in their own source; it is defense-in-depth for the surfaces the passthrough newly reaches (LAN + static deploy), not a sandbox, and it should be scoped and sold as exactly that to avoid a false sense of safety. (skeptic-found downside: The default-ON CSP, unlike the advisory lint, BREAKS shipped/supported Taliesin capabilities at runtime rather than warning about them, and the drafted recipe is not actually "verified against page.rs." Three concrete misses: (1) The recipe has NO `font-src`, so it inherits `default-src 'self'`, but crates/core/build.rs inlines KaTeX fonts as `url(data:font/woff2;base64,...)`. `'self'` excludes `data:`, so the drafted CSP would block KaTeX's own fonts and silently break math rendering. It needs `font-src 'self' data:`. (2) `{js}` reactive cells are first-class and the js-import spec explicitly supports remote `import("https://esm.sh/...")` and authors routinely `fetch()` live data; `script-src 'self'` blocks the module import and `connect-src 'self'` blocks the fetch, so a default CSP breaks a documented feature, not just "a hand-rolled widget." (3) Remote `<img>`/mermaid-from-`QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL` break too. Note the framework's offline-first is ALREADY enforced by bundling (every asset is include_str!'d; there is no CDN in the template), so the CSP mostly polices AUTHOR content, where remote refs are frequently deliberate. The proposal also conflates meta-CSP with header-CSP ("a response header / meta") though only the header form is strong and only preview can emit it. Net: the value is oversold and the default-on blast radius lands on the author's legitimate content, not on a real framework leak.)
- **Invariant check:** Respects every invariant. HTML stays the only output target (CSP is a response header / meta; the lint is build-time). Single editing surface is untouched: the preview still never writes source, and the lint navigates via click-to-source like all diagnostics, it does not mutate the .tmd. Click-to-source, block-level diff, and data-block-id/data-sourcepos are unaffected (CSP is out-of-band; the lint reuses the existing sourcepos-keyed diagnostic path). Warm server + warm kernel unaffected. Keep-Markdown honored: no syntax diverges, the opt-out reuses existing front-matter/_site.yml keys, not new markup. Corpus-plus-roadmap honored: ships pinned by a corpus doc exercising the enforced default plus a relaxed opt-out. Wider-than-Quarto holds in the intended sense: a browser-enforced network boundary and a click-to-source security lint are richer live-HTML-view behavior, never a new format, and this hardens rather than weakens the Do-NOT-touch discipline. Crucially it does NOT sanitize content, so the trusted-author raw-HTML capability the whole tool depends on is preserved. (possible violation flagged: None violated as scoped. But two nearest-misses to flag: (a) Block-level incremental updates + live reload survive ONLY because the CSP keeps `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` and `connect-src ... ws: wss:`; the proposal itself names nonces as the "real" hardening, and nonces WOULD break hot block-swap and live reload, so the load-bearing invariant is quietly pinned to never doing the stronger thing (this dependency should be corpus-pinned, not left implicit). (b) The remote-URL lint reverses an established, deliberate diagnostics decision: links.rs/assets.rs/media.rs all scope external refs OUT to keep `check` offline+deterministic. The lint stays offline+deterministic (it classifies scheme/host, never fetches), so it does not break that property, but it flips the INTENT and so must be advisory, not a `--strict` hard-fail, or it breaks authors who embed remote content on purpose.)

## Project and configuration model

### D33. Keep a strict two-level config model (project file plus page front matter) with no _metadata.yml directory cascade (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A _metadata.yml dropped in any subdirectory sets defaults for every document beneath it. Resolution is _quarto.yml then each nested _metadata.yml (deep-merged, nearest directory wins) then document front matter, so a value like execute: freeze: auto can be set once in posts/_metadata.yml for a whole subtree.
- **Critique:** The cascade is powerful but is Quarto's most confusing feature: a rendered value can originate in any of four files across the directory tree and nothing tells you which, and the deep-merge rules (maps merge, arrays replace) routinely surprise. Debugging 'where did this setting come from' is a manual tree walk.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The cascade is the industry-standard model (Jekyll, Hugo, Astro, Zola all cascade config by directory), so it costs Quarto users zero learning and zero extra syntax. Directory structure IS the natural grouping unit for a content tree (posts/ vs talks/ vs notes/), so keying defaults on the filesystem is more intuitive and more discoverable than a glob map: the _metadata.yml file physically sits next to the content it governs, whereas a glob string is an indirection you must mentally resolve. For the large multi-author, multi-format books and blogs Quarto targets, DRY subtree defaults (one execute: freeze: auto, one shared bibliography, one author for a whole posts/ tree) are load-bearing ergonomics, not a nicety, and a flat model forces you to repeat them across dozens of files. The provenance cost is real but bounded and partly mitigated: quarto inspect dumps the fully resolved metadata for any file, and the deep-merge rule (maps merge, arrays replace) is at least consistent and documented. For Quarto's audience the power is worth the complexity.
- **Taliesin today:** Explicitly no cascade: site/mod.rs:13 states 'there is no _metadata.yml cascade'. Exactly two levels exist, _site.yml (project) and a page's own front matter (page overrides project). Verified that in practice only toc actually inherits project to page (page_toc, mod.rs:652); most keys do not inherit at all.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the two-level model because it directly serves click-to-source and the single-surface story: a value's origin is always one of two named files, greppable in one step. If a subtree default is ever genuinely needed, prefer a single explicit defaults: map keyed by path glob inside _site.yml over a filesystem-walked cascade, so provenance stays inspectable in one place.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the strict two-level model (this is what Taliesin already does, and it is correct for a single-author, click-to-source, corpus-gated tool: a value's origin is always one of two named files, greppable in one step). Sharpen the entry on three points. (1) Fix the accuracy nit: state that toc AND site-wide image/card_image inherit project to page (meta.rs:30), not toc alone. (2) State the tradeoff correctly: execute/bibliography/csl are not project-level keys at all, so the current cost is you repeat them on every page site-wide, which is the honest pain point, and note that adding just a site-level (not glob) default for a couple of high-repetition keys like execute would remove 90 percent of that pain far more cheaply than a glob map. (3) Do NOT build the defaults: glob map speculatively. Gate it behind a corpus document (a real multi-post blog that actually needs a shared execute or bibliography), and when built require it to run the front-matter did-you-mean validator on the values inside each glob entry and to define one explicit precedence rule (single most-specific glob wins, no deep-merge across globs) so it stays a lookup, not a cascade.
- **Tradeoffs:** With no cascade, a 50-post blog cannot set one execute or bibliography default for posts/; each page repeats it. A path-glob defaults: map reintroduces some merge complexity, but confines it to one file instead of an unbounded directory walk. (skeptic-found downside: Three things the drafter glossed. (1) The stated tradeoff is understated, not wrong: execute, bibliography, csl and theorems are document-front-matter-only keys and are NOT in the project NATIVE_KEYS set (title/author/description/url/favicon/image/output/toc/css/head/body-start/body-end/nav/footer/chapters/mounts, config/mod.rs). So today you cannot set an execute or bibliography default even once for the WHOLE site, let alone a subtree. The pain is global, not just no-subtree. (2) The defaults: glob map does not eliminate merge complexity, it relocates it: precedence among multiple matching globs, and map-merge-vs-array-replace, are the SAME semantic questions the cascade raises, just in one file. Greppable provenance is a real win; a simpler mental model is not. (3) It is real new plumbing, not a schema tweak: you must inject document-level keys into each page's front matter before render, AND extend the strict did-you-mean validator to the values inside the defaults block, or you silently lose typo-catching there. That interaction with the clean-break strict-validation feature is the biggest unmentioned cost.)
- **Invariant check:** A single-file defaults: map preserves the single-editing-surface and click-to-source provenance (one config file, not a walk); the preview still never writes back to source, and nothing here adds an output format. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation. HTML-only, single read-only editing surface (config files are edit surfaces; preview still never writes back), and Markdown-syntax invariants are all intact, and a single greppable config file preserves click-to-source-style provenance. The one real tension is corpus-plus-roadmap: building the defaults: map speculatively would ship a capability with no pinning corpus document, so it must stay gated ("only if a real doc needs it") and, when built, must preserve the strict unknown-key-flagged / did-you-mean invariant for keys inside the map.)

### D34. Add a small enumerated set of inheritable project defaults (bibliography/csl/theme/execute) to _site.yml, and make the dead author: field honest (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** The format: html: and execute: blocks in _quarto.yml set theme, toc, bibliography, csl, and execute: echo/freeze/etc once for the entire project; every document inherits them unless it overrides.
- **Critique:** Concrete pain: demo-book/'s chapters cannot share a bibliography because _site.yml has no bibliography key, so each chapter would repeat bibliography: refs.bib. Worse, I verified SiteConfig.author is parsed into a field with no reader anywhere in the codebase (no config.author consumer in grep), so the author: line in demo-book/_site.yml is effectively dead: the config surface advertises inheritance it does not actually deliver.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's cascade is not a fixed two-level enumerated set; it is an open, recursive, arbitrary-depth deep-merge (_quarto.yml, then per-directory _metadata.yml, then page front matter) over ANY metadata key. That generality is the point: adding a new inheritable option costs zero schema work because it just cascades, whereas Taliesin's closed set must extend NATIVE_KEYS plus the strict validator plus the drift-locked JSON schema in lockstep for every new inheritable key, forever. The format: html: nesting the proposal flattens exists precisely because Quarto is multi-format (each output target carries its own defaults); flattening it is only safe because Taliesin is HTML-only. Quarto also solves book-wide citations with a dedicated single References page aggregating every chapter's works, a model per-page bibliography inheritance does not reproduce. Quarto knowingly traded provenance clarity for zero-friction extensibility, the right call for a general multi-format publishing system with a huge option surface.
- **Taliesin today:** NATIVE_KEYS has no execute, bibliography, csl, or theme. Only toc genuinely inherits project to page. author is a SiteConfig field (config/mod.rs) that is stored and never read (page meta uses page.authors from per-page front matter, meta.rs:84-88).
- **Proposed better:** Add a small, explicitly enumerated set of inheritable project defaults to _site.yml (bibliography, csl, theme, and execute: {echo, include, cache}), each merged as 'page front matter overrides project' exactly as toc already is, and either wire author to a real page fallback or delete it from the schema so the surface is honest. Extend NATIVE_KEYS, the strict validator, and the JSON schema in lockstep.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry into two independently shippable pieces. (A) Fix the dead author field now: either delete it from SiteConfig plus NATIVE_KEYS plus the site schema, or wire it as a page-author fallback in the meta.rs citation_author path. Low-risk, honest, independent of (B). (B) Add the enumerated inheritable defaults (bibliography, csl, execute:{echo,include,cache}), but: drop the false 'exactly as toc' claim and state that these merge at the render entry (thread a ProjectDefaults into render_document_with_includes_scoped) because they are consumed in the core render, unlike toc; resolve project-level file paths relative to the site root, reusing the existing includes_from_parts(..., Some(root)) precedent, and document the two resolution bases; scope theme: narrowly or drop it, since inherited css: already delivers project-wide styling and theme: only adds the default-mode/pre-paint knob; make an explicit decision on the book references model (per-chapter vs single References page) and pin it; route inherited-value warnings to the _site.yml source location; and actually add the corpus pin (demo-book with a shared refs.bib, a citing chapter, and a project execute default), extending NATIVE_KEYS plus the validator plus the blessed JSON schema in lockstep.
- **Tradeoffs:** Every inheritable key is a new merge site and a new place a value can come from, a mild return of the cascade problem, but bounded to one file and a fixed key list rather than a directory walk. The closed-set validator and the drift-locked JSON schema must be extended together (schema.rs bless test enforces this). (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter missed. (1) Merge-site mismatch: the entry says these inherit exactly as toc, but toc merges POST-render in the site layer (page_toc needs the block count), whereas bibliography, csl, theme, and execute defaults are all consumed INSIDE the site-agnostic core render (render/mod.rs:269 for bib, theme.rs, cell_extract.rs for execute). Inheriting them requires threading a ProjectDefaults value into render_document_with_includes_scoped, making the core render project-aware, or splicing front matter at the site layer. That is larger and structurally different from toc. (2) Two resolution bases: a project-level bib/csl/theme file must resolve relative to the SITE ROOT, while a page-level one resolves relative to the PAGE dir; the entry never mentions this second base (feasible, since config css/head/body already resolve from root via includes_from_parts(..., Some(root)), but it is real). (3) theme: overlaps the existing inherited css: key, which is already a NATIVE_KEY applied to every page and resolved from root; a project brand stylesheet is ALREADY achievable, so project theme: only buys the default-mode/pre-paint knob (e.g. force dark), a smaller win than framed. Also unaddressed: the book citation model (per-page inheritance yields a per-chapter References section, not Quarto's single book-wide References page) needs an explicit decision.)
- **Invariant check:** Two-file provenance (project plus page) is preserved so click-to-source origin stays a one-step lookup; theme/bibliography/csl/execute are all inputs to the HTML render, so no new output target is introduced and the preview remains read-only. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation. All four keys are HTML render inputs (HTML-only holds), it is YAML config with no preview write-back (single read-only surface holds), Markdown syntax is untouched, and freeze is correctly omitted from the execute set so the hash-keyed cache invariant is safe. Two near-edges to satisfy, not violations: (a) corpus-plus-roadmap requires the entry to actually COMMIT to the pin, add a shared refs.bib plus a citing chapter plus a project execute/theme default to demo-book/_site.yml, which the entry names but does not commit to, and the corpus is the arbiter of done; (b) click-to-source provenance for an inherited value's diagnostic (a missing inherited bib/csl/theme file) must point at _site.yml, not the page front matter line where such warnings currently land, or the one-step lookup points at the wrong file.)

### D35. Keep the flat single-file _site.yml schema instead of Quarto's nested project:/website:/book:/format: blocks (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** _quarto.yml splits config across levels: project: { type:, output-dir:, render: }, a website: block (navbar/sidebar/search), a book: block (chapters/downloads), and a format: { html: {...} } block. A key's correct parent (output-dir under project, navbar under website, toc under format: html) is something you must memorize, and a key placed under the wrong parent is silently ignored.
- **Critique:** For a single-author HTML site the multi-level nesting is ceremony with a footgun: there is no validation that a key sits under the right parent, so a misplaced key (e.g. toc: at top level instead of under format: html:) is dropped without warning, which is the exact confusion the nesting was meant to organize away.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's nesting is not ceremony for Quarto's job; it is load-bearing information architecture for a MULTI-format compiler serving books and teams. The `format:` block exists because one source renders to many targets (html, pdf, docx, revealjs), each with its own option set and many same-named keys (toc, number-sections) that need different values per format, which you cannot flatten without collisions. The `project:` block separates build-orchestration (output-dir, render list, pre/post-render hooks, resources, execute-dir) from content, genuinely different concerns with different lifecycles. The `website:`/`book:` blocks group a large, independently-growing feature surface (navbar, sidebar, search, page-navigation, comments, announcement, cookie-consent, open-graph) that reaches dozens of keys, so namespacing keeps `search` at website scope distinct from format scope and signals intent. Crucially, Quarto ships a full JSON schema with editor completions and validation (RStudio + VS Code), so the "no validation" charge applies only to the render-time CLI, not the authoring experience. For Quarto's actual scope the nesting buys collision-free grouping and discoverable structure a single flat namespace could not sustain. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Flat top-level schema in crates/core/src/site/config/mod.rs NATIVE_KEYS (16 keys: title, author, description, url, favicon, image, output, toc, css, head, body-start, body-end, nav, footer, chapters, mounts). No project:/website:/format: nesting; HTML-only removes any need for a format: block at the project level. Unknown top-level keys warn with a did-you-mean via validate_keys.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the flat namespace. Lean on the existing taliesin schema CLI (schema.rs emits tali-site.schema.json) so an editor's YAML language server autocompletes and validates the 16 keys, making the flatness self-documenting rather than something to remember.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the flat top-level namespace (correct at this scale: HTML-only removes the multi-format axis, 16 keys fit one namespace with no parent-lookup cost), but sharpen three things. (1) Reframe the win: the anti-footgun advantage comes from RUNTIME strict validation plus did-you-mean (`validate_keys`), not from flatness itself. Quarto could bolt strict validation onto a nested schema; flatness's honest, separate advantage is right-sizing to the actual key count. State both. (2) Fix the critique's inaccuracies: drop the `toc:`-at-top-level example (Quarto generally lifts top-level format metadata to each document, so that key is usually honored, not dropped) and replace it with a genuinely-dropped case (a `website:` sub-key such as `navbar:` placed at the top level, or a `project:` key placed under `website:`); soften "there is no validation" to "no render-time strictness," since Quarto ships editor schema validation. (3) Close Taliesin's own nested gap before claiming "already better": add `deny_unknown_fields` plus a did-you-mean pass to nav/footer/mount item keys, and give `nav`/`footer`/`mounts` typed closed sub-schemas in `tali-site.schema.json` (currently `{}`), pinned by a corpus doc containing a typo'd nav item. Until that ships, downgrade status from "taliesin-already-better" to "better at the top level, equal footgun at the nested level."
- **Tradeoffs:** A single flat namespace cannot grow to Quarto's breadth without key collisions or grouping pressure; if the project ever needs many more keys they compete in one namespace instead of being sectioned. HTML-only caps that growth, so the risk is small. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's own anti-footgun claim leaks at the level it never inspected. Taliesin's config IS nested where the domain needs it (nav.left/right, footer.left/center/right, mount.at/path), and BOTH guards only cover the top level. Runtime `validate_keys` warns only on unknown top-level keys; a typo inside a nav item (`txt:` instead of `text:`) is deserialized by serde with no `deny_unknown_fields`, producing a blank/dropped item with no warning and no did-you-mean (config/mod.rs `nav_item` uses `from_value(...).ok()`; `items`/`footer_from`/`mounts_from` filter_map failures away). The emitted `tali-site.schema.json` types `nav`/`footer`/`mounts`/`css`/`head`/`body-*` as `{}` (any), so the language server autocompletes and validates only the 16 top-level names and gives zero help below them, exactly where the config is most structured. So "self-documenting via the language server" and "unknown keys warn with a did-you-mean" hold only at the top level; the very silent-drop footgun the entry attacks Quarto for lives one level down in Taliesin, uncaught by both the validator and the schema.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only is precisely why the format: nesting is unnecessary, so this respects the single-output-target invariant; it adds no output format and does not touch the single editing surface or click-to-source.

### D36. Infer project type from config shape (chapters: present means book) instead of an explicit project: type: with a manuscript type (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Requires project: type: website | book | manuscript | default. A book needs type: book plus a book: chapters: list; manuscript is a first-class type that binds a computational article to supplementary notebooks and emits a MECA bundle; default renders a loose set of files.
- **Critique:** The explicit type: is boilerplate for the common case, but it does document intent and gate layout, and Quarto's manuscript type does real work (article plus linked executable notebooks plus a submission bundle) that a plain website or book config cannot express.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto serves an open, extensible set of project archetypes (default, website, blog, book, manuscript, plus extension-defined types) where distinct archetypes can share config keys and some have no distinguishing key at all (a bare `default` loose-file project versus a `website` can look identical except for `type:`). In that world an explicit `project: type:` is the only stable, unambiguous selector: it picks the pipeline deterministically, documents author intent at the top of the config for any human or tool reading it, lets Quarto validate that the rest of the config matches the declared type (a `book:` block under a `website` becomes a catchable error), and scales to new archetypes without inventing a fresh disambiguating heuristic each time. Inference-from-shape carries a silent-flip failure mode: adding one key silently changes the entire layout with no explicit signal, which is exactly the kind of implicit magic that becomes hard to reason about across a large user base copy-pasting configs. And `type:` cleanly supports archetypes whose whole point (manuscript binding an article to linked executable notebooks and a submission bundle) is not reducible to a single presence-of-key test. For Quarto's breadth and audience, explicit typing is a defensible engineering choice, not mere bureaucracy.
- **Taliesin today:** No type: key exists. is_book = !chapters.is_empty() (config/mod.rs:159): a directory with _site.yml and no chapters: is a website (navbar), with chapters: it is a book (centred reading column plus chapter drawer). A single .tmd with format: deck is a deck; any other single .tmd is an article. There is no manuscript type.
- **Proposed better:** Keep implicit book detection (only two multi-page shapes exist, so a type: switch would be pure ceremony). Treat manuscript not as a new project type but as an ordinary website page that {{< embed >}}s executable pages, which already works and keeps the model to two types.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep status taliesin-already-better on the actual question the entry is about: inferring website-versus-book from `chapters:` presence is the right call and genuinely beats Quarto's mandatory `project: type:` for a tool with exactly two multi-page shapes. Two corrections sharpen it. (1) The "mildly magical silent flip" concern is weaker than the drafter grants and should be downgraded: `chapters:` is a strict-validated known key whose presence IS the book declaration (the chapter ordering is the intent), and the strict validator flags any misspelling, so you cannot fat-finger into or out of book mode without a warning. The chapters list alone is arguably MORE legible than Quarto's redundant `type: book` plus a separate `book: chapters:`. Lead with this strength. (2) Correct the manuscript claim: do not assert the embed path "already works." Taliesin correctly declines the manuscript OUTPUT type (MECA/PDF bundles are out of scope by the HTML-only invariant), which is the sound part. But an article that inlines live outputs from linked executable notebooks is a legitimate FUTURE browser-view capability that Taliesin's deck-only `{{< embed >}}` does not provide today, so it must be framed as roadmap pinned by a corpus doc, not as an existing substitute. Net: the two-type inference recommendation stands; the manuscript sub-claim needs the accuracy fix.
- **Tradeoffs:** Implicit typing is mildly magical: adding a chapters: list silently flips the layout from navbar to reading-column with no other signal, where a one-line type: book would make intent legible. Acceptable while exactly two types exist; revisit if a third layout appears. (skeptic-found downside: The proposed embed-based manuscript substitute overstates current capability. Taliesin's `{{< embed >}}` is deck-only: extension/mod.rs:119-123 iframes another document's DECK view (deck_href maps the target to its built deck .html, embed_html builds a 16:9 deck stage), and discovery.rs:68-78 resolves every embed target to a DeckRef and warns "embedded deck not found" for anything that is not a deck. It does NOT inline a specific computed output (a figure or table by label) from a linked executable article into an article's prose, which is the actual Quarto-manuscript authoring pattern (article-plus-linked-notebooks with cell-level output reuse). So the claim that manuscript is "an ordinary website page that {{< embed >}}s executable pages, which already works" is inaccurate: that pattern is not implemented today. It would be a new browser-view capability needing its own corpus-pinned entry, not a description of the status quo.)
- **Invariant check:** Declining a manuscript output type upholds the HTML-only invariant (MECA/PDF bundles are out of scope by definition); the embed-based alternative is browser-view breadth only and writes nothing back to source.

### D37. Close the one deliberate hole in strict validation: give format: deck: its own linted option schema (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** format: is Quarto's largest config surface (dozens of typed html/revealjs options) validated against a published schema, so a mistyped format option is caught.
- **Critique:** Because Taliesin is HTML-only, format: collapses to a single question (is this a deck?), and its sub-keys are the one deliberate carve-out from the otherwise clean-break 'any unknown key is flagged' contract. A typo in a deck option like format: deck: { tranrsition: fade } passes silently, which is exactly the class of error the strict validator exists to catch, so the guarantee has a quiet exception.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's format schema is the right call FOR QUARTO because format is literally its product surface: a multi-target compiler with hundreds of typed options that differ per output (html, pdf/latex, revealjs, docx, epub). An auto-generated published schema is the only tractable way to validate that combinatorial space, and because it is generated from the same definitions that drive the renderers and Pandoc templates, it stays drift-locked to actual behavior, so a typo like tranrsition is caught precisely because each format's option set is large, typed, and machine-described. The instant a tool is HTML-only and single-author, that justification evaporates: format collapses to one bit (deck or not), leaving no combinatorial typed surface for a schema to protect. Quarto's choice was load-bearing only because Quarto's complexity lived in format; it does not transfer.
- **Taliesin today:** format is in KNOWN_KEYS but its children are unvalidated by design (frontmatter.rs:17-18 and the format_subkeys_are_not_linted test at :504-511); schema.rs overrides format to fully permissive ({}). detect_format (fm_extract.rs:48) is only a line-scan that checks whether a sub-key name selects a deck.
- **Proposed better:** Give the deck its own small closed-set option schema listing exactly the keys deck.rs honors (transition, theme, incremental, and so on) and lint format: deck:/format: html: children against it, closing the hole while keeping format itself permissive for extension-owned <name>-deck formats that register their own key set.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the goal (close the silent hole), reject the mechanism. Since the engine reads no format: children, the honest fix is to WARN on any child under format: that is not a recognized format-NAME key (deck / html / <name>-deck), with a message pointing to where the knob actually lives (top-level theme:, per-slide attributes), rather than whitelisting phantom options. That closes the exact reported case (tranrsition: fade warns) without pretending options exist, and needs a corpus deck showing the SUPPORTED knobs to pin it. If instead the author WANTS format: deck: { transition, incremental, slide-number } to take effect, that is a deck-engine FEATURE, not a validation task: wire those through TaliesinDeck.initialize, pin with a corpus deck that sets them and browser-verify they change behavior, and THEN generate the closed schema drift-locked to exactly what initialize() reads. Either way the schema is a byproduct of first deciding the option surface; the entry currently inverts that dependency, treating schema-authoring as the deliverable when there is no honored surface to describe.
- **Tradeoffs:** Requires enumerating the deck options the engine actually reads and keeping that list drift-locked against deck.rs (another bless-style test like the schema tests), and it makes experimental/undocumented deck keys warn until registered. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal's central instruction, list exactly the keys deck.rs honors (transition, theme, incremental, and so on), rests on a false premise I verified in code: deck.rs honors ZERO format: deck: sub-keys. The engine's runtime options are hardcoded (TaliesinDeck.initialize({ hash: true, slideNumber: 'c/t', center: false }) at deck.rs:103, the only initialize call in the whole tree), deck theme comes from the top-level theme: key, and per-slide behavior (backgrounds, auto-animate, fragments) comes from Markdown heading/block attributes, not front matter. transition/incremental/slide-number are read nowhere in core or server. So the set of honored keys is empty, and any schema built from it is unsound both ways: (a) whitelisting transition/incremental/etc would PASS options the engine ignores, which breaks the strict validator's real contract (if it passes, it is honored) far worse than today's honest silent carve-out, converting unvalidated into validated-as-supported for no-op keys; (b) an empty/near-empty schema flags every format: deck: child, a surprising break. Compounding it: format: html:'s only honored child, toc, is picked up by an indentation-blind global line-scan (detect_toc), not a real nested read, so a closed schema for format: html: children would have to encode or fix that quirk too. The tradeoffs field gestures at enumerate the deck options the engine actually reads but never notices that enumeration yields nothing.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure validation: no source write-back, no new output target, and it strengthens rather than weakens the clean-break strict-validation stance and its click-to-source diagnostics. (possible violation flagged: corpus-plus-roadmap. No corpus deck sets format: deck: sub-keys (corpus/deck.qmd is inline format: deck; the only nested-format corpus docs set format: html: toc:). A closed deck-option schema would validate a surface no corpus document exercises, so nothing pins it, and the invariant says done means a corpus doc renders correctly. It does NOT violate HTML-only, single read-only surface, keep-Markdown-syntax, click-to-source, block-incremental, or warm-server; it is pure validation.)

### D38. Keep implicit filesystem page discovery with draft:-only exclusion instead of a project: render:/resources: include list (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** project: render: takes globs of files to render and resources: lists assets to copy, so you can enumerate exactly which files build, exclude whole directories, or render only a subset.
- **Critique:** Taliesin auto-discovers every .tmd under the site root as a page, and the only way to keep a file out is draft: true in its own front matter (or making it an include partial). There is no project-level 'do not render drafts/' or 'render only these' control, so a stray .tmd anywhere in the tree silently becomes a published page.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's default IS implicit discovery too: it auto-renders every input under the project root and skips `_`/`.`-prefixed paths, exactly like Taliesin. `project: render:` is an OPT-IN escape hatch layered on top of that convenient default, not a replacement for it, and it buys three things Taliesin's walk-plus-draft cannot express. (1) Directory-level exclusion without touching each file: `render: ["*.qmd", "!drafts/"]` keeps a whole folder of half-finished pages out of the build while those files stay normal, editable, and still shippable as assets. (2) Partial/ordered builds: the list is ordered, so you can render only the section you are editing (a real perf lever on a large site) and control render order where a downstream artifact (search index, aggregated listing) depends on it. (3) `resources:` ships files NO rendered HTML references: a `robots.txt`, a `CNAME`, a downloadable dataset, or a file fetched at runtime by client JS (`fetch('/data/x.md')`) that no `src=`/`href=` scan will ever see. That is genuine deploy-correctness control a reference-driven copier structurally cannot provide. For a multi-author repo or a monorepo where docs are one subtree, that explicitness is the difference between a reproducible publish and a surprise.
- **Taliesin today:** discovery.rs walks the tree for pages; draft: true excludes a page from output, nav, and listings (discovery.rs:19-21); _-prefixed directories (e.g. _includes) and embed-only decks are already kept out of nav and search. There is no render: key in NATIVE_KEYS.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the walk-plus-draft: model: it fits a single author and keeps config minimal. If directory-level exclusion is ever needed, extend the existing _-prefix convention (already used for _includes and _site) rather than adding a render: glob list, since a naming convention is more legible and needs no new config key.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the walk-plus-draft default (do NOT add Quarto's `render:`/`resources:` now; YAGNI holds for a single-author, corpus-pinned tree), but drop the pre-commitment to "extend `_`-prefix rather than a render: list." Instead: (1) Answer the surfaced stray-file risk in Taliesin's own grain, with a build/`check` DIAGNOSTIC. The build already prints a page count; add a warning that lists discovered pages reachable from no nav entry and no inbound link, so an accidental publish is loud, not silent. That fits the existing strict-validation + did-you-mean discipline far better than any glob and catches the failure neither draft: nor `_`-prefix prevents. (2) If real directory-level exclusion is ever needed, frame it honestly as exclude-list vs `_`-prefix, NOT as Quarto's allow-list. An allow-list inverts the footgun (forget to list a new page, it silently never publishes); a small native `exclude:`/`drafts:` glob keeps publish-by-default while adding the escape hatch AND, unlike `_`-prefix, can exclude pages while still mirroring their assets. (3) Corpus-plus-roadmap caveat: verify a corpus doc actually pins `draft:` exclusion; if none does, the "keep" rests on an unprotected feature and a pinning doc should ship with the decision. (4) Split off the `resources:` half as its own entry: the only thing Quarto's `resources:` does that Taliesin cannot is ship a SKIP_EXT file or a `_`-dir file fetched at runtime by JS (never referenced in HTML); everything else is already covered because `mirror_assets` ships all non-source files by default.
- **Tradeoffs:** No fine-grained include list means a large tree full of non-page .tmd files would need draft: on each or an _-prefixed directory; this is convention-over-config, which trades flexibility for a smaller config surface. (skeptic-found downside: The `_`-prefix is a blunt instrument the drafter treated as clean: `mirror_assets` also skips `_`-prefixed dirs (build.rs:1089), so `_drafts/` hides a folder from BOTH page discovery AND asset mirroring at once. It therefore cannot express "do not render these pages but still ship their referenced images/data", the exact case Quarto's `render: ["!drafts/"]` handles. Worse, neither `draft:` nor `_`-prefix actually solves the critique's own surfaced risk: a stray or forgotten `.tmd` auto-publishing is precisely the file the author never marked, so the proposal restates current behavior rather than closing the hole. The drafter also ignored render ORDER: website listing/default order is pure lexical path order (discovery.rs:12,45), so reordering needs numeric filename prefixes, whereas Quarto's ordered `render:` gives it directly (books already dodge this via `chapters:`). Finally the entry conflates `render:` (page discovery) with `resources:` (unreferenced-asset shipping) but the proposed_better only answers the discovery half; the `resources:` half is a separate, narrow, still-open gap.)
- **Invariant check:** Discovery reads source only and writes nothing back; draft: exclusion and the _-prefix convention add no output format and leave click-to-source and the single editing surface intact.

### D39. Solve the one real dev-vs-prod need (url:) with a build flag rather than adopting Quarto config profiles/environments (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Supports profile groups plus _quarto-<profile>.yml overlays selected by QUARTO_PROFILE or --profile, letting one project switch site-url, draft visibility, or dev-vs-final settings between local preview and CI/production.
- **Critique:** For a single-author tool general profiles are largely overkill, but there is one genuine case: url: in _site.yml feeds absolute og:image and canonical links that are correct for production yet wrong under local preview, and today there is no clean switch for it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto serves thousands of heterogeneous projects across many output formats and audiences, so it cannot enumerate every axis a project might vary between environments: draft visibility, analytics snippets injected only in prod, private vs public content, execute/freeze toggles for fast local iteration vs full CI renders, staging-vs-production deploy URLs, multi-audience variants, and secret injection. Rather than accrete N bespoke one-off flags (the very fragmentation a config system should prevent), Quarto gives one composable orthogonal primitive: named profiles selected by QUARTO_PROFILE/--profile that deep-merge _quarto-<profile>.yml overlays over the base. It is declarative (recorded in files, reproducible in CI, not hidden in shell history), it composes (profile groups), and it generalizes to needs the authors never anticipated. For a general document compiler that is the correct level of abstraction, and url: retargeting is just one instance of it.
- **Taliesin today:** No profile mechanism exists (no profile/environment/QUARTO_PROFILE handling in the config path). A single static _site.yml; url: is a fixed string. The site already suppresses absolute social cards when url: is unset (mod.rs:261), which partially masks the preview-vs-prod gap.
- **Proposed better:** Do not build general profiles (they are the config scope-creep the tool deliberately avoids). Solve the concrete need directly: keep treating url: as production-only, and if a real gap appears add a single narrow build flag (e.g. --base-url) instead of a profile/overlay system.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the no-profiles stance and keep url: production-only; this is the right minimal answer and the strict clean-break validator already reinforces it (a Quarto-style profile: block in _site.yml would be flagged, and a build flag sidesteps the config surface entirely, so no validation surface grows). But sharpen the justification and fix the errata: url: is Option<String>, suppression is in meta.rs and is total when url: is unset, and it covers canonical/og:url/og:image/twitter:image/citation, not just cards. Reframe the "genuine case": it is not "correct-for-prod-but-wrong-in-preview" (that harm does not materialize) but "retargeting the absolute base URL per deploy target," which is uncommon for one author with one domain, so defer even the flag until a concrete staging deploy actually needs it. If ever built, make --base-url a build-time-only flag that DEFAULTS to config.url (preserving reproducible-from-source output), keep it out of _site.yml, and ship it pinned by a corpus doc per corpus-plus-roadmap. Also tighten the entry's invariant_check wording: a --base-url flag does change output CONTENT (the emitted URLs), it just does not change the source file or the output FORMAT (still HTML), which is why no invariant is actually broken.
- **Tradeoffs:** Without profiles there is no dev/prod content divergence beyond draft:, which is acceptable for one author. A single build flag covers the realistic canonical-URL case but not arbitrary per-environment config, which is an intentional limit. (skeptic-found downside: Three things the drafter missed. (1) The entry's factual basis is loose: config.url is Option<String> (config/mod.rs:36), not a "fixed string"; the actual suppression lives in meta.rs:20-24/53-78, not mod.rs:261 (which is only the warning); and suppression covers canonical, og:url, og:image, twitter:image, and citation_public_url, not just "social cards". (2) The "genuine case" is thinner than claimed: with url: unset there is ZERO prod/preview divergence (no absolute tags emitted at all), and with url: set, canonical/og pointing at the prod domain during local preview is benign (preview is never indexed; og cards are not viewed in-browser). The only real residual need is retargeting the absolute base URL per deploy target (staging vs prod), which for a single author with one production domain is rare. (3) A --base-url flag introduces invocation-time config that lives outside the source file, so the same _site.yml can produce different output depending on an unrecorded flag; unless the flag defaults to config.url and the corpus pins the default path, output stops being reproducible-from-source, which matters for a corpus-arbitrated tool.)
- **Invariant check:** A build-time flag touches neither the source nor the output format and leaves the single editing surface and click-to-source untouched; it is strictly HTML-render configuration.

## Front-matter and metadata ergonomics

### D40. Validate front matter against a closed key set with did-you-mean and click-to-source, instead of silently ignoring unknown keys (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto merges front matter into a large permissive metadata bag. An unknown or misplaced key (typo `titel:`, `eco: false` instead of `echo: false`, a key nested one level wrong) is silently accepted and no-ops. The doc renders, the option just never takes effect, and nothing tells you.
- **Critique:** Silent-ignore is the single worst property for correctness: the failure is invisible until you notice the output is wrong, and even then you have no pointer to the offending line. For code-execution options a typo means echo/cache silently stay on their default.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's permissive metadata bag is a structural consequence, not laziness. Quarto is multi-format (HTML/PDF/Word/ePub/reveal/beamer), multi-engine (knitr/jupyter/ojs), and template-driven through Pandoc, with a third-party extension and Lua-filter ecosystem. Any Lua filter, custom format, or Pandoc template can define and consume its own metadata variables that Quarto core has never heard of, so a closed key set would false-positive on every legitimate extension or template variable and break the ecosystem. Metadata also merges across _quarto.yml project config, format blocks, profiles, and the document, so a key valid at one scope looks orphaned at another. Being permissive inherits Pandoc's correct "the template author owns the variables" model for an open, composable, multi-target system. And Quarto does NOT actually leave you blind: it ships schema-driven YAML diagnostics and completion in its editor integrations (VS Code/RStudio/Positron, schemas in quarto-cli/src/resources/schema), which catch many typos at edit time. Closing the set at render time is the one thing its architecture cannot do.
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/src/frontmatter.rs validate_front_matter walks a real serde_yaml parse and flags every unknown top-level key against KNOWN_KEYS plus unknown immediate children of execute:/listing:/about:/hero:/prose-lint:/theorems:, each with a levenshtein-distance-<=2 did-you-mean, each located to its source line (block_key_line/nested_key_line) so the preview warning is Alt-clickable. validate_theorem_values even catches value-level mistakes (numbered: never renders the opposite of intent, so it warns). It only warns; the key still renders.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the mechanism; it is a decisive win. The one thing to add is coverage of the remaining silent-ignore holes (see the format-subkey and severity entries). The did-you-mean + click-to-source pairing is exactly the ergonomic Quarto cannot offer because it has no source map.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's core verdict, taliesin-already-better is accurate and verified in frontmatter.rs, but sharpen it four ways. (1) State the ROOT reason this is structurally unavailable to Quarto and available to Taliesin: a single output format (HTML-only) plus a single-author tool with no third-party extension or Pandoc-template ecosystem consuming arbitrary metadata makes a closed key set tractable; the argument is "different architecture," not "Quarto is careless," and Quarto already mitigates via editor-side schema diagnostics. (2) Re-prioritize the follow-on work: the highest-value gaps are deeper-than-immediate nesting (about.links / hero.actions item keys, which silently no-op today) and value-level enums beyond theorems (title-block-style, page-layout, toc), NOT just format-subkeys. (3) Treat format-subkey closure as a distinct, harder item requiring an extension-declared key schema (a per-extension registry), because a flat KNOWN_KEYS cannot own extension-defined keys; this is the one spot where Taliesin faces Quarto's own extensibility tradeoff, so pin it to a corpus doc that actually uses a format extension. (4) Audit did-you-mean for confidently-wrong suggestions on a tiny candidate set, and keep any "severity" split a CI/check-gate concept that preserves render-anyway. Each addition stays corpus-pinned.
- **Tradeoffs:** A closed set means every genuinely new key must be added to KNOWN_KEYS in the same change (already the corpus-plus-roadmap discipline). A clean-break stance can annoy anyone pasting Quarto front matter, but that is an accepted decision. (skeptic-found downside: The one place Taliesin stays permissive (format: subkeys) is permissive for the SAME structural reason Quarto is permissive everywhere: an extension owns those keys and can define arbitrary ones, so "closing" it needs an extension-declared key schema (a registry), not a flat KNOWN_KEYS append, and the entry undersells that as just another "hole." More sharply, there are two bigger, under-named holes than format-subkeys: (1) validation is immediate-children-only, so deeper item schemas silently no-op: parse_about reads about.links[] item keys text/href/icon and hero.actions[] items, but the validator never checks them, so a mistyped `txt:` in an about link is silently dropped; (2) value-level enum checking exists ONLY for theorems (validate_theorem_values), so a wrong value for title-block-style (only literal `none` is honored) or page-layout (only `full` widens) silently falls back to the default with no warning, exactly the failure mode the entry indicts Quarto for. Also the did-you-mean is double-edged: levenshtein-<=2 against a tiny closed set can emit a confidently-wrong suggestion for a key that is real in some other tool but simply unsupported here, steering the author to the wrong fix. Finally, note check.rs already exits non-zero on ANY diagnostic, so front-matter warnings already hard-fail CI while preview keeps them non-blocking; a "severity" tier is really about making some CI diagnostics advisory, and must not turn preview warnings into build-blockers.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure read of source; warnings navigate preview->editor and never write. Located via data-sourcepos line, so it rides the existing click-to-source bridge. HTML-only unaffected. (possible violation flagged: None as written: it is a pure read, it warns through the existing data-sourcepos click-to-source bridge (navigate, never write), HTML-only and Markdown syntax are untouched, and each new closed-set key stays corpus-pinned per the corpus-plus-roadmap discipline. Caveat, not a violation: a "severity=error" tier must stay a CI/check gate; escalating it to block preview render by default would fight the render-anyway and read-only-preview ergonomic (today the offending key still renders and the doc still shows).)

### D41. Close the format: sub-key validation hole so deck/html options get the same did-you-mean the rest of front matter gets (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto owns hundreds of format:html: / format:revealjs: options and (in the extension) offers completion for them, but at build time an unknown one is silently ignored like any other key.
- **Critique:** Taliesin markets strict validation as its headline metadata win, yet KNOWN_KEYS includes `format` while the linter deliberately skips all of its sub-keys (comment: 'An extension owns them'), the schema leaves format as `{}` fully permissive, and the test format_subkeys_are_not_linted pins this. So `format: {deck: {slide-nmber: true}}` or `format: {html: {toce: true}}` silently no-ops, the exact class of bug the linter exists to catch. Because Taliesin is HTML-only, the real option surface here is tiny (deck options plus a handful of html options), and Taliesin owns the deck engine, so these are not really extension-owned.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto targets many output formats (html, pdf, docx, revealjs, beamer, epub) whose options come from Pandoc, Lua filters, and third-party extensions and change with every Pandoc/extension version, so the option space is genuinely open and version-dependent. A hardcoded closed validator would false-positive the moment a newer Pandoc or an extension ships a new key. Crucially, Quarto does NOT merely "silently ignore" bad format options: it ships a large machine-generated YAML schema that drives editor completion AND surfaces render/`quarto check` validation warnings for many misspelled format keys (revealjs options are in that schema, so `slide-nmber` is likely flagged, not silently dropped). So the critique's "silently ignored like any other key" understates Quarto. Where Quarto is deliberately lenient at render, that is an extensibility choice appropriate to an open, multi-format, extension-driven surface. A closed enumerated validator only works because Taliesin is HTML-only and single-author; it is not a free win Quarto foolishly skipped. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/src/frontmatter.rs never descends into format:. detect_format (render/fm_extract.rs) reads only the top-level format key/sub-keys as format NAMES (deck/revealjs/<name>-deck). The deck option surface lives in render/deck.rs but is not enumerated for validation. schema.rs emits ('format', json!({})) with no properties.
- **Proposed better:** Enumerate the built-in deck/html option set (the keys deck.rs actually reads: slide-number, code-line-numbers defaults, transition, etc.) as a closed child set and lint format: {deck|revealjs|html: {...}} against it with the same unknown_key_message. Leave a genuine escape hatch only for a `format:` key that names a third-party extension format, not for the built-in ones. Regenerate the JSON Schema's format branch from the same const so it can't drift.
- **Revised recommendation:** Reframe, do not implement as written. Drop the "enumerate the deck/html options deck.rs reads" mechanism: deck.rs reads none (initialize flags are hardcoded; code-line-numbers is a cell option), and html options are already hoisted to linted top-level keys, so the claimed closed child set is empty and would couple the linter to a non-existent per-deck-config feature. The only genuine residual gap is that a migrator pasting Quarto-style nested YAML (`format: html: {toce: true}` or `format: revealjs: {slide-nmber: true}`) gets no warning. If worth closing, do it as a STRUCTURAL lint, not a vocabulary enumeration: when the built-in `html:`/`deck:`/`revealjs:` format carries sub-options, emit a located hint ("HTML options are top-level in Taliesin, move `toc` up" for html; "deck options are not per-document configurable yet" for deck), while leaving a bare empty-body format-name selector and any `<ext>-deck`/extension format untouched. Downgrade impact from high to low, pin it with a corpus doc if pursued, and consider that `qmd-fast check`'s existing migration guidance may already be the better home than new linter machinery.
- **Tradeoffs:** Couples the linter to the deck/html option surface, so adding a deck option means adding it to the const (acceptable, same discipline as KNOWN_KEYS). Must keep an unlinted path for extension-defined formats so the clean-break strictness doesn't block a legitimate extension. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal enumerates "the keys deck.rs actually reads," but deck.rs reads zero format sub-keys: the TaliesinDeck.initialize flags (hash/slideNumber/center) are hardcoded in deck.rs, and code-line-numbers is a per-cell option (validate.rs CELL_OPTION_KEYS), not a format default. So the closed child set is empty today, and the const would drift-lock the linter to a per-deck-config FEATURE that does not exist yet (validation ahead of the capability it guards). For html, the option surface was deliberately hoisted to top-level keys (toc/theme/css/page-layout) that are already linted, so most claimed value is already delivered. The block-form format-name selector (`format:` with an empty-body `html:`/`revealjs:` child) is legitimate and must not be flagged, and `<ext>-deck` extension formats run the SAME native engine, so the "lint built-ins, exempt extensions" boundary the proposal draws is illusory (an extension deck would honor the identical, nonexistent options).)
- **Invariant check:** Metadata-parse-only change; render-anyway warning, no write-back, HTML-only (deck output is still HTML). The new closed set is drift-locked to the schema exactly like KNOWN_KEYS, and warnings stay click-to-source located.

### D42. Add a small explicit _site.yml -> page cascade for a whitelist of keys instead of only cascading toc and SEO fallbacks (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto cascades metadata from _quarto.yml and per-directory _metadata.yml into every page: execute defaults, theme, author, bibliography, format options, etc., all deep-merged, with page front matter overriding. Set once project-wide, inherited everywhere.
- **Critique:** Quarto's version is opaque (deep-merge across _quarto.yml + _metadata.yml + front matter makes 'where did this value come from' genuinely hard), but the underlying capability is real and useful. Taliesin currently gives a single author almost none of it: to get consistent code-echo policy or one theme across a book you must repeat `theme: dark` / `execute: {echo: false}` in every page's front matter, and there is no place to set project-wide author/bibliography/csl.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format compiler with an open-ended, unbounded metadata surface: pandoc variables, dozens of format-specific option keys across html/pdf/docx/revealjs/epub, and metadata contributed by third-party extensions. A closed whitelist is untenable there because new formats and extensions constantly add keys, so a general deep-merge across project (_quarto.yml), per-directory (_metadata.yml), and document is the only model that scales. The precedence is actually deterministic and documented (project < directory < document, later wins, maps deep-merged), so it is not arbitrary. Per-directory _metadata.yml is genuinely valuable on large multi-author books where one subtree (an appendix, a guest-authored part) needs different defaults such as echo: true or a different bibliography without editing every file, and deep-merge of nested maps lets you set format.html.code-fold once project-wide and override a single sub-key on one page. The provenance-tracing pain the critique names is the unavoidable cost of an open, multi-format metadata surface, not a design mistake; for Quarto's scope this cascade is the correct engineering choice.
- **Taliesin today:** Only two things cascade. (1) toc: config.toc is the fallback default in page_toc. (2) SEO fallbacks in site/meta.rs social_head: page title/description/image fall back to config.title/description/card_image. NATIVE_KEYS (site/config/mod.rs) has no theme, execute, bibliography, csl, or author-as-default-for-pages beyond the og:site meta. So theme/execute/citation config genuinely cannot be set project-wide.
- **Proposed better:** Add a closed, documented whitelist of cascadable keys to _site.yml (theme, execute defaults, author, bibliography, csl, lang) with a single, flat precedence rule: page front matter overrides _site.yml, full stop, no directory-level _metadata.yml deep-merge. Keep it tri-state per key so an explicit page value (including false) beats the project default, exactly as toc already does. Surface the resolved source in preview if useful.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship the cascade, it fills a real gap (project-wide theme mode and execute defaults have the clearest single-author-book payoff and genuinely cannot be set today), but revise the entry: (1) Drop csl from the whitelist. It is a no-op key today; only cascade it if and when per-doc csl is actually honored. (2) Correct the mechanism. This is not a post-hoc override like toc. Thread a small ProjectDefaults struct into render_document_with_includes_scoped and apply it at the front-matter extraction site (mod.rs:263-276) with per-key tri-state precedence: an explicit page value including false wins, else the _site.yml default, else the built-in default. Leave toc as its existing post-hoc special case. Start with theme + execute, then add lang, author, bibliography (all cheap and meaningful). (3) Frame it as extending an existing pattern, not inventing one: css/head/body-start/body-end already inject site-wide (mod.rs:270-278), and note that a custom-CSS theme is already project-wide, so the true new capability is the built-in theme MODE default plus execute/bibliography/lang/author. Keep title and description page-only (they already have their SEO fallback in meta.rs). (4) Make the preview watcher re-render all pages on an _site.yml cascade-key change and confirm execute flips invalidate _freeze. (5) Pin with a corpus book doc that sets theme + execute once at project level and overrides one chapter, proving the tri-state and the all-pages invalidation.
- **Tradeoffs:** Any cascade reintroduces a precedence model and the 'where did this come from' question; the mitigation is keeping it a tiny closed whitelist with one override rule and no multi-file deep-merge. Adds keys to NATIVE_KEYS and to the site schema. Must decide per key whether cascade is even wanted (theme yes; title almost certainly page-only). (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter missed. (1) csl is a dead key: it sits in the front-matter linter whitelist (frontmatter.rs:49) but is never read anywhere; citations use a hardcoded shipped ieee.csl (cite/author.rs). Cascading csl from _site.yml ships a project-wide knob that silently does nothing until per-doc csl is actually honored, so it must be dropped from the whitelist (or gated behind first implementing csl). (2) The 'tri-state per key, exactly as toc already does' framing is architecturally wrong for the keys that matter. toc is a special case: it is a post-hoc page-assembly boolean, resolved AFTER render by page_toc overriding doc.toc (mod.rs:436, 652). By contrast theme, execute defaults (echo/include/cache), bibliography, lang, and author are extracted INSIDE render_internal_impl from the page's own front matter during the render pass (mod.rs:263-276), and execute in particular has already been applied to emitted cells by the time RenderedDoc exists. So the cascade cannot be a post-hoc override; it requires threading a project-defaults value INTO the render entrypoint (render_document_with_includes_scoped and callers) and applying per-key tri-state precedence at the extraction site. That is a signature/plumbing change, not the cheap toc-style patch the entry implies. (3) Warm-server invalidation: in preview an _site.yml edit to a cascaded key must re-render ALL pages (not the single edited page the hot-reload path assumes), and an execute-default flip must correctly bust the affected pages' _freeze entries so no stale cell outputs survive. Minor: a project-wide bibliography means every page re-parses the shared .bib and emits its own references section.)
- **Invariant check:** Read-only metadata resolution feeding the existing block model; HTML-only. No preview write-back. Each cascaded key stays validated by the same closed-set linter, preserving strictness. Corpus-pinned by a book doc that sets theme/execute once at project level.

### D43. Decide whether format: should stay a full nested block or collapse to a bare deck-vs-page selector now that HTML is the only target (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `format:` block is deep (`format: html: toc: true, code-fold: true`) because it is multi-format: the same source can emit html, pdf, revealjs, docx, and each output format namespaces its own options under its own key. The nesting is load-bearing there.
- **Critique:** Taliesin is HTML-only, so `format:` has exactly one real job: pick page vs deck. Yet Taliesin accepts the full `format: html: {...}` nesting AND honors flat top-level keys (toc, theme, css) at the same time, giving two ways to say the same thing and a nesting level that carries no information (there is only ever one output format). A single author has to remember which options go flat at top level (toc, theme) and which Quarto muscle-memory puts under format:.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's nested `format: <name>: <options>` is not incidental ornament, it is the exact construct that lets one source fan out to N outputs where each output namespaces options that would otherwise collide: `toc`, `theme`, `code-fold`, `fig-width` all mean different things (or take different sub-options) under `html` vs `pdf` vs `revealjs` vs `docx`. Flattening would force per-target keys like `html-toc`/`pdf-toc`, which is uglier and less discoverable than a self-documenting namespace where the reader sees at a glance which options belong to which target. The nesting is also the single most muscle-memoried line in the entire Pandoc/RMarkdown/Quarto lineage, so keeping it lowers the on-ramp for every author arriving from that world. Even for a single-format tool the namespace is a cheap forward-compatibility hedge: Taliesin explicitly reserves a future print/PDF track (rendered from the built HTML), and a `format:` block is the natural, already-understood home for per-target options if that day comes.
- **Taliesin today:** detect_format (render/fm_extract.rs) only reads format:'s top-level name/sub-key names to choose DocFormat::Reveal vs Html; it ignores the nested option values. Flat keys toc/theme/css/page-layout are the honored top-level ones (KNOWN_KEYS). So `format: html: toc: true` nesting is tolerated but the toc it honors is actually the flat top-level toc:. `format: revealjs` and `format: deck` both select the deck.
- **Proposed better:** Since syntax stays Pandoc-lineage and clean-break is already the posture, consider demoting format: to a single selector value (`format: deck` / omit for a page) and moving every HTML option to flat top-level keys, then flagging `format:` used as a nested option block with a did-you-mean toward the flat key. This removes the dead nesting level and the two-ways-to-say-it ambiguity.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep it as an open-question but split it and correct it. Fact-fix first: the flat top-level form is ALREADY canonical (docs teach it, code honors it, `format: deck`/`format: revealjs`/`format: html` already work as bare selectors, and omitting format defaults to html), so there is nothing to 'demote' and no 'move every option to flat' work to do, that is shipped reality. The only genuinely new and contested move is whether to actively FLAG the nested `format: html: {options}` block. Recommend NOT adding a blanket flag: it collides with the deliberate extension-owns-format-sub-keys contract (and its passing test), warns on the current corpus, and cuts against keep-familiarity for the most-typed Quarto line. The lower-risk, sharper win is to (a) fix the real inconsistency by deciding whether toc+theme should become top-level-only like css/page-layout so all HTML options read from one consistent place, and (b) document flat-canonical / nested-accepted in the frontmatter reference. If the owner still wants a nudge, gate it as a NARROW lint that fires only on the exact built-in `format: html:` / `format: revealjs:` block and never on any `<name>-*` extension format, presented as a navigate-only did-you-mean, and pin it with a new corpus doc. Rewrite the entry's taliesin_current to state the loose-scan mechanism accurately.
- **Tradeoffs:** `format: revealjs` / `format: html` is the single most muscle-memoried Quarto line; flagging the nested form is a real migration cost and cuts against 'keep Markdown/Pandoc familiarity'. The deck-vs-page selection genuinely needs a key, so format: cannot disappear entirely. This is a judgment call between familiarity and removing a vestigial construct, hence open-question. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter missed. (1) The entry's own mechanism claim is wrong: detect_toc AND detect_theme are loose whole-file scans (line.trim().strip_prefix), so a nested `format: html: toc: true` is honored DIRECTLY, not via a separate flat key. corpus/posts/born-machines.qmd and corpus/bayesian-website/index.qmd carry ONLY the nested toc and render a TOC, proving the nesting is not dead. The real, subtler inconsistency is that toc+theme accept nested-or-flat while css, page-layout, include-*, title, author, date read top-level-only (extract_field / site val.get), so 'two ways to say it' applies to exactly two keys, not the whole block. (2) format: sub-keys are DELIBERATELY unlinted because an extension owns them (frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS comment + the passing format_subkeys_are_not_linted test). The extension format namespace is `<name>-deck` / `<name>-revealjs` with extension-owned options. A blanket 'flag format: used as a nested option block' cannot distinguish the built-in `format: html:` (flag) from a legitimate `format: my-ext-deck:` block (must stay legal), so as written it would either break extension formats or need a carve-out the proposal never specifies. (3) Flagging the nested form warns on the current corpus (the two docs above), so the change is not free: it forces migrating those regression-net docs, churn the entry does not budget.)
- **Invariant check:** Selector-only change is metadata parsing; no output format is added (still HTML + deck-in-HTML). Single editing surface and click-to-source untouched. Flagging is a warning, render-anyway.
