(possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is broken (no new output format; a warn-and-render did-you-mean never writes back, so the read-only single-surface rule holds as long as the suggestion navigates and never auto-rewrites source). Two soft tensions the entry underweights: it bumps the owner's explicit 'keep Markdown/Pandoc FAMILIARITY' directive since `format: html` / `format: revealjs` is the most muscle-memoried Quarto line to flag; and corpus-plus-roadmap requires re-pinning, migrating born-machines.qmd + bayesian-website/index.qmd off the nested form AND adding a corpus doc that exercises the selector-only form plus the new flag, which the entry does not account for.)

### D44. Auto-gate the table of contents by heading count and page kind rather than rendering a TOC whenever toc: true (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto renders a sidebar TOC whenever `toc: true` is set (site- or page-level), even on a two-heading page or a landing/listing page, producing a near-empty TOC rail.
- **Critique:** A blanket `toc: true` at project level puts a stub TOC on pages that don't warrant one (short posts, landing pages, listing/about pages), which reads as clutter and wastes the reading column. The author then has to sprinkle per-page `toc: false` to undo it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's uniform rule ("toc: true renders a TOC, full stop") is a rational consequence of being a multi-format compiler, not laziness. A content-length heuristic tuned to an HTML reading column does not generalize: in PDF/LaTeX the TOC is a whole page, in a book it is front matter, in revealjs it is meaningless. The one rule that behaves identically across every target is the literal one, so predictability, not a magic threshold, is the correct default for Quarto's brief. Two more points blunt the critique. First, Quarto decouples layout from content on purpose: whether a page has a TOC column is a template decision that stays stable as you write, so a book's chapters all share one grid rather than flipping columns as their length crosses a boundary. Second, the "sprinkle per-page toc: false" cost is overstated: Quarto's directory-level `_metadata.yml` sets `toc: false` once for an entire `posts/` or landing directory, and its about/listing templates are separate, so the correction is one line per section, not per file. The critique is still fair (a project-wide `toc: true` genuinely does land near-empty rails on short and landing pages), but it reads Quarto's uniformity as a flaw when it is the only format-agnostic choice available to a tool that is not HTML-only.
- **Taliesin today:** Site::page_toc (crates/core/src/site/mod.rs) treats toc as tri-state (detect_toc returns Option<bool>): an explicit page-level toc: wins; otherwise the site-wide config.toc default applies ONLY when the page is not a listing/about/hero page AND render::toc_entry_count(blocks) >= MIN_TOC_HEADINGS. The tri-state is pinned by detect_toc_is_tristate_so_explicit_false_can_override_a_site_default. Standalone single-doc default is toc: false (render/mod.rs).
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. The tri-state (unset vs explicit false) plus the NN/g heading-count auto-gate is a strictly better default than Quarto's all-or-nothing. Only refinement worth considering: surface why a TOC was suppressed on a page the author expected one on (a preview hint), so the auto-gate is not mistaken for a bug.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the auto-gate: for an HTML-only reader it is a strictly better default than Quarto's all-or-nothing, and being HTML-only is precisely what earns Taliesin the right to a reading-column heuristic Quarto cannot afford. But sharpen the refinement rather than shipping it as stated. (1) Do NOT emit a broad "TOC suppressed" hint; scope it to a single near-miss: a non-listing/about/hero article that sits exactly one heading below MIN_TOC_HEADINGS while the site enables TOCs, the only case where the author plausibly expected a rail. Make it a preview-only, click-to-source nudge to the front matter ("2 headings; a TOC needs 3, or set toc: true"), never a persistent warning. (2) Name and handle the reflow: the one-column/two-column flip at the boundary reflows the live preview mid-edit, which is the same "looks like a bug" failure the hint was meant to prevent, seen from the other side. Either accept it as rare or hold the layout stable within a preview session once the rail has appeared (hysteresis), and document it so it is not filed as a regression. (3) Leave MIN_TOC_HEADINGS=3 / level<=3 counting as-is unless a corpus document surfaces a genuine long-but-gated-off page, in which case pin the fix with that document per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Tradeoffs:** The heading-count threshold is a fixed heuristic; an author who genuinely wants a TOC on a short page must set toc: true explicitly (which the tri-state already supports, so cost is low). (skeptic-found downside: The auto-gate couples the page's column grid to its content, so crossing MIN_TOC_HEADINGS mid-authoring flips the live preview from one column to two (the TOC rail appears, the reading column narrows and reflows). That flip lands in exactly Taliesin's flagship context, a warm server doing block-level incremental updates, where a content-driven layout change is most visible: adding the 3rd heading is a chrome-level change, not a single block swap, so the boundary edit likely forces a fuller re-render than a normal keystroke. The drafter frames the only cost as "an author who wants a TOC on a short page must set toc: true," missing both this reflow jank and the cross-page inconsistency it creates in a book (some chapters get a rail, some do not, purely by length, which itself can read as a bug). The proposed refinement also has an unbudgeted cost: a broad "TOC suppressed" hint would fire on every short post, listing, about, and hero page under a site-wide toc: true, i.e. on the common case where the gate is working as designed, training the author to ignore it. Separately, `toc_entry_count` only counts anchored headings at level <= 3, so a deeply subsectioned page (many h4) reads long yet gates off, a proxy that can misfire.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure render-time decision from the block model; HTML-only; no write-back. An optional 'TOC suppressed' hint would be a preview-only warning, click-to-source friendly.

### D45. Align the front-matter and _site.yml key vocabularies so head/body injection is spelled the same on both surfaces (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto uses one vocabulary across _quarto.yml and front matter: include-in-header / include-before-body / include-after-body work identically at project and document level, so what you learn in one place transfers to the other.
- **Critique:** Taliesin, having designed the two surfaces separately, diverged their names for the SAME concept. Front matter uses the long Quarto-inherited include-in-header / include-before-body / include-after-body; _site.yml uses the short native head / body-start / body-end. A single author who learns the site config cannot guess the front-matter spelling and vice versa, and the did-you-mean can't bridge them because they are different closed sets. Same divergence applies to image handling and any future shared key.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's single vocabulary is not just a naming coincidence, it falls out of a deeper design: project config and document front matter are ONE merged metadata namespace (project supplies defaults, the document accumulates onto or overrides them, key by key). Because it is literally the same schema being cascaded, the two levels MUST share key names, and any key an author learns is guaranteed to work at either level AND to compose predictably. That is a stronger guarantee than mere knowledge-transfer. The long names are also a self-consistent, self-documenting position-triple: include-in-header / include-before-body / include-after-body all read as include-(where-it-goes), stating both the mechanism (an include) and the exact injection point. Taliesin's native triple is internally LESS consistent: head names an element (the head element) while body-start / body-end name positions, mixing two mental models, and bare head is mildly ambiguous. These are also Pandoc-lineage names, so they carry the Pandoc familiarity the owner explicitly chose to keep. So Quarto's stance is defensible on three fronts the entry underweights: guaranteed compositional parity, more internally coherent names, and Pandoc continuity.
- **Taliesin today:** frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS has include-in-header, include-before-body, include-after-body (resolved by render doc_includes). site/config/mod.rs NATIVE_KEYS has head, body-start, body-end (SiteConfig.head/body_start/body_end). Verified both lists; they do not overlap on these three concepts.
- **Proposed better:** Pick one spelling and accept it on both surfaces. The short native head/body-start/body-end is the better long-term name for a Pandoc-lineage-but-independent tool; teach front matter to accept those too (keeping the long forms as recognized aliases through a deprecation window, consistent with the tool's existing alias posture). Either way both closed sets should list both spellings so the linter and schema agree.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the finding, tighten the fix. Ship the CHEAP, complete version: dual-accept all six spellings on BOTH surfaces (add head/body-start/body-end to KNOWN_KEYS with resolve_doc_includes reading them, and include-in-header/before-body/after-body to NATIVE_KEYS mapping to head/body_start/body_end), and wire each surface's did-you-mean to suggest across the now-unified set. This alone eliminates the cannot-guess divergence, is auto-covered by the schema generator, and preserves the compositional accumulate-merge already in place (page.rs:366, model.rs:238). Then make canonical-for-DOCS a deliberate, stated choice rather than a linter distinction: teach ONE spelling in the guide (short-native head/body-start/body-end is the defensible pick GIVEN the owner's separate-from-Quarto direction, but name it as an independence-vs-Pandoc-familiarity tradeoff, and if you keep it, rename nothing on the site side). DROP the deprecation-window ambition: keep the long forms as permanently accepted aliases rather than building a deprecated-key tier the strict linter does not have; only retire a spelling if/when the owner actually asks. Pin BOTH directions in the corpus (head: in front matter AND include-in-header: in _site.yml), plus a test that the did-you-mean now bridges the vocabularies. Downgrade impact from medium to low-medium: this is a rarely-used escape hatch for a single author who already knows both spellings, so the justification is craft (no gratuitous divergence Quarto lacks), not user pain.
- **Tradeoffs:** Aliases mean two accepted spellings for a while (mild vocabulary bloat) until the deprecation window closes. Front-matter resolution code (doc_includes) must map the short names to the same include slots. Small risk of surprising anyone who learned the long Quarto names. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter glosses. (1) The DIRECTION of canonicalization is under-argued. The entry asserts short-native head/body-start/body-end is the better long-term name, but the long form is arguably more internally consistent (a uniform include-(position) triple) and is the Pandoc-familiar spelling the owner said to keep, whereas head/body-start mixes an element noun with two positions. Choosing short-native is a defensible INDEPENDENCE move (it sheds a Pandoc/Quarto spelling), but it is a tradeoff, not the obvious win the entry implies. (2) The deprecation window is over-scoped. The front-matter strict linter today has exactly two states, known (silent) and unknown (warn); there is no deprecated-but-accepted tier. Actually retiring a spelling therefore needs NEW linter infrastructure that does not exist. The cheap, complete fix is permanent dual-accept on both surfaces (add all six spellings to KNOWN_KEYS and NATIVE_KEYS, teach both resolvers to read both) which fully kills the cannot-guess problem with no deprecation machinery. (3) The corpus pin as written only covers head:/body-end: in front matter; it should also pin the REVERSE (include-in-header: in _site.yml) and the did-you-mean bridge, since the fix makes both surfaces accept both. One thing the entry OVER-states as a cost: the JSON Schema is auto-generated from KNOWN_KEYS/NATIVE_KEYS (schema.rs:116,158), so schema+drift-lock update for free once the consts change.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure metadata naming; HTML-only head/body injection already exists. No write-back. Both spellings remain inside the closed-set linter so strictness holds. Corpus doc pins that head:/body-end: work in front matter.

### D46. Make the JSON-Schema editor completion zero-config instead of requiring a manual magic comment with an absolute path (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** The Quarto VS Code extension ships live YAML completion and hover docs for front matter and _quarto.yml with zero per-file setup: install the extension and completion just works on .qmd/_quarto.yml.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's schema is arguably more trustworthy (auto-generated from the same closed-set consts the validator uses, drift-locked by schema.rs tests, so it cannot lie), but the on-ramp is high-friction: the author must know `taliesin schema` exists, run it with --out, then hand-paste `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<dir>/tali-site.schema.json` atop each file with an absolute path (query.rs prints exactly this instruction) that breaks if the schema dir moves or on another machine. Discoverability and portability are both poor compared to Quarto's install-and-go.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto ships its OWN self-contained YAML intelligence engine inside its VS Code extension; it does NOT lean on the third-party redhat.vscode-yaml extension. That engine delivers context-aware completion, hover docs, and diagnostics keyed off the same schema that drives Quarto's validation, and critically it fires INSIDE the embedded YAML regions of a .qmd: the front-matter block AND `#|` cell options, plus standalone _quarto.yml. Generic YAML tooling (a `yaml.schemas` association) fundamentally cannot reach embedded YAML inside a Markdown-family file; only a language service that understands the document's structure can. So Quarto's decision to build and bundle its own engine is not bloat or laziness: it is the necessary and only way to deliver as-you-type completion where config actually lives in a .qmd, with docs and format-conditional schemas, in a single install. That is a genuine, hard-won advantage the entry rightly credits.
- **Taliesin today:** schema.rs bundles FRONTMATTER_SCHEMA + SITE_SCHEMA (Draft-2020-12), generated from KNOWN_KEYS/NATIVE_KEYS/nested consts and asserted against committed files. query.rs cmd_schema writes the two files and prints the manual yaml-language-server comment with the given dir. No auto-association, no served schema URL, no init scaffolding.
- **Proposed better:** Three low-cost moves, any subset: (1) have `taliesin init` scaffold the yaml-language-server comment into a new _site.yml/front matter automatically; (2) since the dev server is already warm, serve the schema at a stable localhost URL and reference that (portable, survives dir moves); (3) Taliesin already owns a VS Code extension for the .tmd grammar, so bundle the schema there and auto-associate _site.yml / .tmd front matter (yaml.schemas contribution) to get Quarto-style zero-config completion, backed by a schema that provably matches the validator.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but sharpen it. (a) Correct the premise: the CLI does not force an absolute path; `taliesin schema --out .schemas` already yields a portable relative `$schema`, and the current comment already needs redhat.vscode-yaml to do anything at all, so the true gap vs Quarto is not "absolute path" but "generic tooling can't reach embedded front matter + cell options." (b) Demote option 2: never bake a localhost URL into committed source; a served schema URL is acceptable only as a live, extension-registered convenience while preview runs, never persisted to a .tmd. (c) Make option 3 the real Quarto-parity move and cost it honestly: to cover embedded `.tmd` front matter (and, to actually beat Quarto, `#|` cell options), you cannot rely on `yaml.schemas`; you need either a redhat.vscode-yaml dependency (which only covers standalone `_site.yml`) or a small YAML completion provider inside Taliesin's own extension, backed by the drift-locked schema and gated by a CI check that the shipped copy equals schema.rs output. (d) Keep option 1 as the cheap default, but have init write the committed schema files AND a relative `$schema` comment together (so the reference resolves offline and on any machine); guard against clobbering an existing comment. (e) State the honest impact: strict validation + did-you-mean + click-to-source already covers correctness, so this is an ergonomics/discoverability win that pays off mainly if the extension is ever published for non-author users.
- **Tradeoffs:** Option 3 puts schema shipping in the extension's release cycle and must stay in sync with the crate's bundled schema (add a CI check that the extension copy equals schema.rs output). Serving from localhost only helps while the dev server runs. init scaffolding must not clobber an existing comment. (skeptic-found downside: Three misses. (1) `yaml.schemas` is a redhat.vscode-yaml contribution point, NOT native VS Code, so option 3 is only "zero-config" if the user also installs redhat.vscode-yaml (two installs, not the one-install parity claimed) OR Taliesin builds its own YAML provider like Quarto (real work, not low-cost). And even with redhat.vscode-yaml installed, a `yaml.schemas` glob can associate a schema to the standalone `_site.yml`, but it will NOT provide completion inside a `.tmd` front-matter block (embedded YAML in a Markdown-family document is outside redhat YAML's jurisdiction). Option 3 as written over-promises the front-matter half. (2) Option 2 bakes a `http://localhost:<port>/...` URL into a committed magic comment, trading the current portable relative path for a reference that is port-pinned, server-must-be-running, http-not-https, and network-fetched: a broken/stale pointer for anyone (or any machine) not running preview on that exact port. That is worse for a committed repo than the status quo, not better. (3) The entry ignores that Taliesin's strict validator already flags unknown/typo'd keys with did-you-mean AND click-to-source at warm-preview speed (frontmatter.rs), so the real cost of having no editor completion is a discoverability nicety, not a correctness gap; for a single author who wrote `taliesin schema` themselves, "medium" impact is overstated.)
- **Invariant check:** Editor-side completion is upstream of the single editing surface (you edit .tmd; the schema only assists). No preview write-back. HTML-only unaffected. The served-schema option reuses the existing warm dev server. (possible violation flagged: None hard. Editor completion is upstream of the single editing surface (you still edit .tmd; the schema only assists), init scaffolding is a CLI file-create not a preview write-back, HTML-only and Markdown-syntax are untouched, and option 2 reuses the warm server. One soft tension worth flagging: corpus-plus-roadmap. This capability cannot be pinned by a render corpus document (it lives in the VS Code extension and its npm/CI build, like the companion which is deliberately "NOT in the cargo workspace"), so its arbiter of done is a CI check that the shipped schema equals schema.rs output, not a corpus doc. That is a gap in the regression net, not an invariant breach.)

### D47. Decide the default severity of metadata mistakes: warn-and-render vs fail-the-build, and how far value-level checks extend (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto renders through metadata mistakes by default (unknown keys ignored, no build failure); strictness is not really offered at the metadata level.
- **Critique:** Taliesin correctly makes mistakes visible in preview, but the default posture is warn-and-render-anyway: an unknown key still renders, and a plain `build` (without --strict) will happily produce output from a doc whose typo silently changed behavior. The theorems case is instructive: validate_theorem_values had to be added specifically because `numbered: never` renders the OPPOSITE of intent, which a key-only linter would pass. That same class (a recognized key with an unrecognized/ignored VALUE) likely exists elsewhere and is not systematically covered.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's metadata is a deliberately OPEN namespace: the same YAML bag is read by Pandoc, Lua filters, dozens of output formats, project types, extensions, and downstream tools. Quarto cannot enumerate the valid key set, so an "unknown" key is frequently a key some filter/extension legitimately consumes, not a typo. Hard-failing on unknown keys would break the extensibility contract that lets third parties add metadata without patching core, and would make a single multi-format source un-buildable when a key valid for one target (e.g. pdf) is meaningless for another. Warn-and-passthrough is thus the only coherent default for an open, multi-target namespace. Crucially, Quarto does NOT merely ignore mistakes: it ships JSON-schema validation surfaced in the editor (VS Code / RStudio LSP) at authoring time, so metadata errors are made visible exactly where the author is typing, just not as a build-blocking gate. Taliesin can afford strictness only because it made the opposite bet (HTML-only, single-author, a closed OWNED key set) and it deliberately does NOT lint format: subkeys because an extension owns them. The strictness is bought by surrendering Quarto's open extensibility, not by Quarto being careless.
- **Taliesin today:** validate_front_matter returns Warning only; rendering proceeds. Value-level checking exists only for theorems (number-within must be chapter; numbered must be bool or unless-unique). Site build promotes malformed _site.yml to a --strict failure (MALFORMED_CONFIG_PREFIX in config/mod.rs, honored by build.rs). No general 'build is strict on my own corpus' default; --strict is opt-in.
- **Proposed better:** Introduce two explicit severities: 'warn' (unknown key that still renders harmlessly) vs 'error' (a recognized key whose value the parser silently ignores, i.e. behavior-changing typos like numbered: never), and make the error tier fail a plain `build` by default while preview keeps rendering with the located warning. Extend value-level validation to the other enum-like keys (page-layout, title-block-style, listing type/sort) so the behavior-changing class is covered systematically, not one-off.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the genuine insight, drop both mechanisms as written. The insight is real and theorems proves it: a recognized OWNED key whose wrong VALUE the parser silently ignores (inverting intent) is a distinct defect a key-only linter misses, and it deserves systematic coverage. But: (A) Do NOT make it a default-build hard-fail. Those value checks ALREADY feed --strict (build.rs: problems += doc.warnings.len()), and --strict is the codebase's single coherent gate that malformed-config and crashed cells also use. Keep that gate. If a hard error tier that fails a plain build is truly wanted, define it coherently across ALL diagnostics (crashed cells, broken refs/includes, malformed config, bad owned-key values) via a Severity field on Warning, not bolted onto front-matter values alone. (B) Do NOT blanket-extend to page-layout/title-block-style/listing type/sort: they are boolean-shaped, so first make the PARSER strict/explicit about the one value it honors, then add a value check only for keys with a genuine closed branch-set where a wrong value inverts intent (theorems-style). The correct systematic step is a small audit: enumerate owned keys whose parser branches on a closed set, add a value check (feeding --strict) for each mirroring exactly the honored set, and pin it with a corpus doc showing a behavior-changing bad value is flagged while a harmless unknown key only warns. Net: the value-coverage idea is worth doing; the default-fail lever and the specific extension list are not, since the audience is a single author whose warm preview already shows the located warning, making the marginal safety of default-fail over preview-plus-strict modest (impact medium at most).
- **Tradeoffs:** A stricter default build could block on a genuinely intended-but-unusual value if the accepted set is under-specified, so each value check must mirror exactly what the parser honors (as validate_theorem_values already does). Deciding which keys are 'behavior-changing on a bad value' is manual per key. Risks friction for anyone building third-party-extension front matter, so the error tier must stay scoped to keys Taliesin fully owns. (skeptic-found downside: The four keys named for extension (page-layout, title-block-style, listing type, listing sort) are boolean-shaped in Taliesin's parser, NOT closed enums like theorems. The parser honors exactly one distinguished string (page_layout == "full" at site/mod.rs:398, title-block-style == "none" at fm_extract.rs:33, listing type == "grid" at site/frontmatter.rs:180, sort = anything-not-containing-"asc" = descending at frontmatter.rs:171) and treats every other value as the default. theorems is special only because parse_theorem_config branches on a small closed set where a wrong value INVERTS intent. To "mirror exactly what the parser honors" (the entry's own required discipline) for these four, the valid set is a singleton, so a faithful check would either false-green Quarto-vocabulary values the parser silently drops (table, plain, article) or false-fail legitimate default-intent values. So the "extend systematically" half is largely unsound as written: those keys first need their PARSER tightened before any linter can mirror a real accepted set. Two further missed costs: (1) Warning (render/model.rs:146) has no severity field and is the shared diagnostic type across cite/a11y/links/media/math/headings/anchors, so "introduce two severities" is a cross-cutting change, not frontmatter-local; (2) the dichotomy does not track harm: an unknown key such as toc-depth: 2 is equally behavior-changing (intent silently dropped) yet must stay in warn for extensibility, so the error tier covers a subset, not "the behavior-changing class systematically.")
- **Invariant check:** Preview stays warn-and-render (single editing surface, click-to-source located warnings). Only `build` severity changes, no new output format, no write-back. Value sets stay inside the closed-set discipline. A corpus doc pins that a behavior-changing bad value fails build while a harmless unknown key only warns. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is violated: preview stays read-only and located (single editing surface, click-to-source), HTML-only untouched, Markdown syntax untouched, block model untouched, and a corpus doc can pin the behavior. The real conflict is with an established (non-invariant) design convention: today both a malformed _site.yml (MALFORMED_CONFIG_PREFIX) and a crashed code cell whose traceback is baked into output fail ONLY under --strict, never a plain build. Making a typo'd enum value hard-fail the default build while a crashed cell exits 0 inverts the severity ordering and breaks the "default build renders through, --strict is the gate" posture the codebase already committed to.)

### D48. Standardize date: on ISO-8601 in source, render it as a semantic browser-localized &lt;time&gt; element, and reject today/last-modified/git-derived date keywords (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto recognizes `date` and layers a formatting/derivation system on top: `date-format` takes a named width (short/medium/long/full/iso) or a strftime-style pattern; the literal values `today`, `now`, and `last-modified` are resolved at render time (`last-modified` from the file mtime or git history); and month/weekday names are localized through the document `lang`. Quarto also auto-derives a page's listing date from this field. The rendered output is a formatted plain-text string with no machine-readable `<time>` element.
- **Critique:** Two distinct problems. (1) The derived keywords (`today`, `last-modified`, git date) make the rendered date a function of wall-clock time and filesystem/git state rather than of the source text: the value that appears in the document is not written in the document, and it silently changes on rebuild. (2) The output is a lossy, localized human string with no machine-readable companion, so feeds, SEO, and Google Scholar meta have to re-parse a formatted string, and any listing that "sorts by date" is really sorting formatted text.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Part 1 of the critique (derived keywords make the rendered value a non-reproducible function of wall-clock/mtime/git state) is fair and correct. Part 2 contains a strawman: it says "any listing that sorts by date is really sorting formatted text" and that "feeds ... have to re-parse a formatted string." That is true of Taliesin's CURRENT code (site/mod.rs:809 does a raw lexicographic `String::cmp`), but it is FALSE of Quarto. Quarto parses `date` into a real internal date object and sorts listings and emits RSS/Atom feed dates from that parsed value, so its sort is chronological and its feed dates are RFC-compliant. The genuinely Quarto-specific gap is narrower: its rendered HTML title block is plain text with no `<time>` element. Quarto's strongest justification: (a) it is a MULTI-format compiler (PDF/LaTeX/Word/revealjs), where `<time>` is meaningless, so a format-neutral, author-controlled formatted string keyed off the document `lang` is the correct lowest-common-denominator, and emitting `<time>` is only sensible because Taliesin is HTML-only; (b) `date-format` with named widths plus `lang` localization gives ONE deterministic, author-chosen rendering (not reader-locale-dependent) without hand-formatting; (c) for its core market of CI-built living docs and books, `last-modified` from git is the semantically CORRECT value (the page genuinely was last edited then) and hand-typed dates reliably drift stale, especially across a 50-page book where no author remembers to bump every page. So Quarto's choices are rational for Quarto's constraints; the critique understates Quarto's internal machine-date handling and overstates the consequences of the missing `<time>`. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `date` is a recognized top-level key (frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS; schema `"date": {}` accepts any value) but there is zero date logic behind it. The single-doc render calls `extract_field(fm, "date")` (fm_extract.rs:128), a raw line scan that strips surrounding quotes and returns the string verbatim; `title_block_html` (render/mod.rs:704) HTML-escapes it into a plain `<span>` inside `.tali-title-meta`. The site path is `scalar(val.get("date"))` (site/frontmatter.rs:46), also verbatim (serde_yaml keeps `2026-07-03` as a String; it has no timestamp type). There is no `date-format`, no `today`/`last-modified` keyword, and no localization: `lang:` exists but only feeds `<html lang>` (page.rs:149) and never touches the date. No chrono/time-formatting crate is in the workspace. Listing order is a lexicographic string compare on the raw field (`items.sort_by(|a,b| a.date.cmp(&b.date)...)`, site/mod.rs:809), and scholar `citation_publication_date` receives the raw string verbatim (meta.rs:92), so a non-ISO date such as "July 3, 2026" both mis-sorts and emits non-compliant meta with no warning.
- **Proposed better:** Keep `date:` in the source but move the layer above the syntax to be browser-native and machine-anchored. (a) Parse the value and emit a semantic `<time datetime="2026-07-03">` element carrying the canonical ISO form, so feeds, SEO, scholar meta, and listing sort all key off a real machine date while the reader still sees a friendly rendering. (b) Localize and prettify the visible text with `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in the browser, keyed off the document `lang:` (zero payload, no new Rust date crate, degrades to the ISO text when JS is off); an optional `date-format` front-matter key overrides the display width. (c) Lint a non-parseable date with a did-you-mean, click-to-source warning (Taliesin already runs strict front matter), nudging toward ISO so listings sort correctly and scholar meta is valid. (d) Explicitly REJECT `today`/`last-modified`/git-derived dates: an author who wants today's date types it, and an editor command (the in-scope way to make a source edit ergonomic) can insert the current date into the source.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry, revised. KEEP as-is: (a) emit a semantic `<time datetime="ISO">` in the title block (durable, HTML-only-appropriate, machine anchor for future relative-time/locale enhancements); (c) lint a non-parseable `date:` with a did-you-mean, click-to-source warning; (d) REJECT `today`/`now`/`last-modified`/git-derived as a block-content date value, with an editor command that inserts today's literal into source (moves the wall-clock dependency to a deliberate author edit captured in the .tmd). REVISE one piece: do the human-readable formatting SERVER-SIDE off the document `lang` plus an optional `date-format` key (small Rust month/weekday table, reusing the parser you already need), and DROP the client-side `Intl` step, this removes the hydration flicker, the ICU-version cross-reader nondeterminism, the no-JS degradation, and an extra JS fragment, and is strictly more aligned with "served HTML is the deterministic artifact." SHARPEN the framing: (i) sell the parse-to-real-date fix as the concrete correctness win, it fixes the live lexicographic mis-sort at site/mod.rs:809 and the non-compliant `citation_publication_date` at meta.rs:92, both of which consume the server-parsed normalized ISO, not the `<time>` element; (ii) note feeds are a prospective beneficiary (no RSS/Atom generator exists yet), not a current one; (iii) note migration cost is ~0 because the entire corpus is already ISO; (iv) restate the git-date rejection reason as the block-hash coupling, not "wall-clock." CONSIDER (as a follow-on, not required here) serving the legitimate "last updated" docs/book use case via a git-derived string in page CHROME/footer, which lives OUTSIDE the block model and so regenerates per build with zero block-hash churn, preserving the invariant while recovering the one Quarto convenience worth keeping. Update KNOWN_KEYS/schema to add `date-format` (a coupled edit) and pin the whole thing with a corpus doc exercising ISO input, `<time>` emission, chronological listing sort, valid scholar meta, and the lint on a prose date.
- **Tradeoffs:** Client-side `Intl` formatting means two readers with different browser locale data could see slightly different long-form strings; the `<time datetime>` ISO value is the canonical anchor, and the server can additionally emit a default long form so no-JS readers still get something friendly. It needs a small ISO parser in Rust for the `<time>` emission and the lint, but that can be hand-rolled for `YYYY[-MM[-DD]]` (allowing partial dates for scholarly citations) with no heavy dependency. The non-ISO lint is a mild clean break from Quarto tolerance that will flag existing prose-date documents, which then have to migrate (pin the migration with a corpus doc). Dropping `last-modified`/`today` removes a Quarto convenience some authors like, and the compensating editor-insert command is not built yet. (skeptic-found downside: The client-side `Intl.DateTimeFormat` step (option b) is the weak link and is largely unnecessary. The proposal already concedes it needs a Rust ISO parser for the `<time>` emission and lint; once the date is parsed to Y/M/D integers server-side, formatting a friendly string for the one-to-three locales a single author writes in is a trivial month/weekday name table, no heavy crate. Pushing formatting to the client instead buys little and costs three things the drafter understated: (1) FLICCKER/hydration mismatch, if the server emits a friendly default (as the drafter proposes for no-JS) and then client JS overwrites it with a possibly-different browser-formatted string, the reader sees a visible swap; (2) `Intl` output still varies by the browser/OS ICU-CLDR data VERSION even keyed to the same document `lang`, so the visible string is non-reproducible across readers, which is exactly the determinism the proposal champions elsewhere; (3) it adds a JS fragment to bundle, maintain, and test, and degrades no-JS readers to raw ISO. Server-side formatting off `lang` + `date-format` is deterministic, flicker-free, JS-free, and MORE aligned with Taliesin's "served HTML is the deterministic artifact, browser is a read-only view" thesis, while the `<time datetime>` anchor still carries the machine date for any future progressive enhancement (relative-time, locale toggle). Two further precisions the drafter blurred: the listing-sort and scholar-meta fixes consume the server-PARSED normalized ISO string (fed to meta.rs:92 and the sort key), NOT the `<time>` element, so they must be called out as the concrete correctness payload independent of the cosmetic `<time>`; and "feeds" is prospective since Taliesin ships no RSS/Atom generator today.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: satisfied (emits `<time>` and formats in the browser; no new output format). Single editing surface: strengthened rather than merely satisfied, because rejecting derived dates keeps the .tmd the sole source of the value. Block-level incremental plus content hash: this is the load-bearing reason for the rejection. A `last-modified`/`today` date makes the title block's content a function of mtime or wall-clock, so its `data-block-id` content hash would change with no source edit (spurious block churn on every save, and _freeze/incremental-diff determinism lost); an ISO-in-source date keeps the hash a pure function of the .tmd, and the browser-side localization is cosmetic-only over stable server HTML. Click-to-source: the `<time>` lives inside the title block that already carries data-block-id and data-sourcepos, and the lint warning itself navigates to source. Corpus-plus-roadmap: pin with a corpus document exercising an ISO date, the `<time>` emission, listing sort, scholar meta, and a localized render. Warm server: no impact. Wider-than-Quarto: richer live-HTML behavior (a machine-readable semantic date plus in-view localization) that Quarto's static formatted string lacks. (possible violation flagged: None hard. The reject-derived-dates decision (d) actively STRENGTHENS the block-hash invariant: a `today`/`last-modified`/git-injected value would make the title block's rendered content vary with no source edit, so its `data-block-id` (a hash keyed to block source) would either go stale or churn on every build, and _freeze/diff determinism would be lost. One reasoning correction: the invariant_check lumps git-derived dates under "function of wall-clock time," which is imprecise (a git-commit-date build is reproducible from repo state, not wall-clock); the precise and stronger reason to reject even git-date as a BLOCK value is the block-hash coupling, not non-reproducibility. Sharpen the stated rationale accordingly. The client-Intl display in (b) is in mild TENSION with (not a violation of) the determinism ethos: it makes only the visible DOM string, never the served HTML, reader-dependent, which is the same class as the already-shipped code-enhance/toc-spy cosmetic JS, so it is permitted but avoidable.)

## Cross-references and numbering

### D49. Whether figure/table/equation/listing numbers are chapter-scoped in books (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** In a book, Quarto numbers floats as chapter.counter ("Figure 2.3", "Table 5.1", "Equation 4.2"), so every float number is globally unique and `@fig-x` reads "Figure 2.3".
- **Critique:** Without a chapter prefix, chapter 2 and chapter 3 each contain a "Figure 1", and a cross-chapter `@fig-x` renders "Figure 1" ambiguously with no way for the reader to know which chapter. This is a real correctness problem specifically for multi-chapter books.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's chapter.counter numbering is the LaTeX book/report convention (\thefigure = \thechapter.\arabic{figure}), battle-tested for decades in scholarly publishing. In a book, each chapter is a separate document that resets its float counter to 1, so a prefix is the only thing that makes a float number globally unique and self-locating: "Figure 2.3" tells the reader the float lives in chapter 2 without them having to hunt, and a cross-chapter "see Figure 2.3" is unambiguous where a bare "Figure 3" is not. It composes correctly with cross-references that span chapters (the number a reader sees in the caption is the same token the ref renders), and it degrades cleanly: a single article with no chapters falls back to continuous numbering automatically. Quarto also ties this to the same book structure that already numbers sections (2, 2.1, 2.1.1), so headings and floats share one coherent numbering regime rather than two different ones. The choice is the correct default for the multi-chapter book target, not a quirk.
- **Taliesin today:** `fig_count`/`tbl_count`/`eq_count` in `render/mod.rs` are continuous per-PAGE counters that reset each chapter with NO chapter prefix. Only theorems honor `theorems: number-within: chapter` (`number_theorems` + `TheoremConfig.chapter_scoped`). `harvest_xref_numbers` stores the bare per-chapter number, so a cross-chapter `@fig-x` resolves to "Figure 3", never "Figure 2.3".
- **Proposed better:** When `chapter_for(page)` is Some (a numbered book chapter), prefix float numbers with the chapter number, computed via the same lineage the headings already use (`chapter.rs::section_number`), so "Figure 2.3" appears in the caption, in same-page refs, and in cross-page refs alike. Leave single-doc numbering continuous.
- **Revised recommendation:** Adopt chapter-scoped float numbering, but sharpen three things. (a) Make it AUTOMATIC in a numbered book chapter (follow the already-auto section numbering and Quarto), not a per-float toggle; if a knob is wanted, make it ONE book-level `number-within` in _site.yml that governs headings, floats, AND theorems together, so a book never mixes scoped floats with continuous theorems. Reconcile the theorem default in the same change (flip theorems to chapter-scoped-in-book, or route both through the shared knob) so the two never disagree by default. (b) Apply the prefix as `format!("{chapter}.{n}")` mirroring number_theorems, sourced from the `chapter` already in scope; drop the section_number lineage reference. (c) Thread the chapter into ALL float caption producers, not just the inline fig/eq path: exec.rs (executed figure + table captions) and apply_table_captions, plus keep the xref-registry number (used by same-page @fig-x resolution and by harvest_xref_numbers for cross-page) in lockstep so caption text and ref text always match. Preserve `(2.2)` paren style for equations. Pin it by extending the EXISTING corpus/demo-book (already multi-chapter, already uses `number-within: chapter` for theorems in methods.qmd) with figures/tables/equations plus a cross-chapter @fig-/@tbl-/@eq- ref, asserting the caption, same-page ref, and cross-page ref all read "N.n". Accept that in live preview cross-page refs stay bare (harvest is build-only), which is the current behavior and not a regression.
- **Tradeoffs:** The chapter number must be threaded into the per-page float emit path (today only `number_theorems` receives it). Some authors prefer continuous numbering, so it may warrant a toggle. A two-chapter book corpus doc is needed to pin it. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter understated. (1) Theorem/float DEFAULT inconsistency: Taliesin's theorem chapter-scoping is opt-in (`number-within: chapter`, default continuous), but the proposal makes float scoping AUTOMATIC whenever chapter_for is Some. In one book with default config you would then get "Figure 2.3" but "Theorem 5" side by side, which is jarring and worse than either uniform choice. Headings are already auto chapter-scoped, so floats-follow-headings is defensible, but that makes theorems the lone outlier and the mismatch must be resolved deliberately, not left to per-float toggles. (2) The threading is BOTH easier and harder than "only number_theorems receives it": the inline fig/eq/lst path lives in render_internal_impl, which ALREADY has `chapter` in scope (near-trivial), but the real cost is the EXECUTOR path (crates/server/src/exec.rs ~L990/L1021 builds executed-cell "Figure&nbsp;{fig.number}" and "Table&nbsp;{tbl.number}" captions from cell.figure/cell.table numbers), plus apply_table_captions for Markdown tables, neither of which currently sees the chapter. Those are the sites that actually need plumbing. (3) The proposal says to compute the prefix via chapter.rs::section_number's heading lineage, but a float prefix is just the chapter number (Quarto: "2.3", never "2.1.3"); it should mirror number_theorems's `format!("{c}.{n}")`, not invoke section_number (which advances heading counters). Minor: equations render `({num})`, so scoped becomes `(2.2)` and the paren style must be preserved.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML caption text and xref number only, no parallel output format; numbers still derive from the block model at render time; preview stays read-only; pinned by a book corpus doc with cross-chapter float refs.

### D50. Whether @sec- resolves to the section's real hierarchical number, and agrees with the heading (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** With `number-sections`, `@sec-x` resolves to the section's actual hierarchical number ("Section 1.2") and the heading itself shows the same "1.2", so reference and target always agree.
- **Critique:** Taliesin gives `@sec-x` a sequential count of labelled headings, so the 3rd labelled section renders "Section 3" even if it is really subsection 1.2. Worse, in a book a same-page `@sec-x` still uses that sequential number while `number_chapter_headings` prefixes the heading with "2.1", so the reference text ("Section 3") disagrees with the heading it points at ("2.1"); the cross-PAGE `@sec-x` is correct ("2.1"/"Chapter 2") because it comes from `scan_xref_targets`/`section_number`. Same heading, two different numbers depending on which page references it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto derives a section cross-reference number from the SAME single numbering pass that numbers the heading, and it refuses to resolve @sec- unless number-sections is on (quarto.org: "when using section cross-references, you will also need to enable the number-sections option"). This is a principled one-source-of-truth coupling, not an accident: because the reference text and the heading text read from one computed number, they cannot disagree by construction. And by gating on number-sections, Quarto never shows a reader a number ("Section 1.2") that appears nowhere in the rendered document. Taliesin's bug exists precisely because it is MORE lenient than Quarto (it invents a flat "Section N" with no numbering switch and from a second, independent counter), which is exactly the leniency that lets the ref drift from the heading.
- **Taliesin today:** `sec_count` is a flat sequential counter in `render/mod.rs` (the code comment calls hierarchical numbering "a separate `number-sections` feature"). There is no `number-sections` toggle for single docs; book heading numbers are computed separately in `chapter.rs::section_number`; the per-page xref registry that `cite::process` consumes carries only the sequential value.
- **Proposed better:** Compute the section's hierarchical number during the main render pass and register THAT for `sec-` anchors, sharing one counter implementation with `chapter.rs::section_number`, so heading + same-page ref + cross-page ref all agree. Add a `number-sections` front-matter toggle so single docs can opt into visible hierarchical heading numbers too.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the fix but reframe it around Quarto's one-source-of-truth coupling rather than "add a toggle too." (1) Compute the section's hierarchical number ONCE at render time (reusing chapter.rs::section_number so it equals the cross-page authority) and register that identical string for the sec- anchor AND stamp it on the heading, so heading, same-page ref, and cross-page ref are the same string by construction. (2) Gate the number on a single switch: number-sections front-matter for single docs, already-on for numbered book chapters. When numbering is OFF, do NOT invent "Section N"; render the section's title text or a bare "Section" link, so a ref never shows a number the heading lacks (this is the actual fix, and it matches Quarto). (3) Generalize the counter for the no-chapter case: a single doc's first ## is "1", a numbered chapter's is "N.1"; do not claim section_number is drop-in. (4) Decide {.unnumbered} explicitly: honor it across heading + both ref paths, or document that Taliesin numbers all headings. (5) Watch the block-level-incremental cost: numbering is inherently non-local, so an edit that inserts/removes a numbered heading must re-emit downstream headings and their same-page refs (already true of the flat counter, so not a regression, but note it), and inject the number span without disturbing data-block-id/data-sourcepos. (6) Pin it: update the existing sec_label_makes_at_sec_resolve_to_a_number test, and add a nested single doc tested with number-sections both on and off, plus a book page with a same-page @sec- to a subsection asserting the ref matches the "2.1" heading.
- **Tradeoffs:** Section numbering currently runs as a book-only post-pass; unifying means moving counter logic into the per-page pass and passing chapter context. It changes output for existing single docs that showed the flat "Section N". Interacts with chapter-scoped floats (same lineage), so best done together. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal frames the number-sections toggle as an additive nicety ("so single docs can opt into visible heading numbers too"), but it is actually load-bearing as a GATE, and missing that re-creates the very bug in a new place: if render computes a hierarchical "Section 1.2" for a single-doc @sec- ref while that doc's heading shows no number (single docs are unnumbered by default), the ref and heading disagree again. Agreement requires that a @sec- ref shows a number ONLY when the heading it points at shows the same number. Second, "share one counter implementation with chapter.rs::section_number" understates the work: section_number is chapter-scoped (level<=1 returns the chapter number, level 2 becomes "N.1"), so it is not drop-in for a single doc, where the first ## must be "1" with no chapter prefix; a no-chapter mode is needed. Third, neither the current heading pass nor the scan honors {.unnumbered}; unifying is the moment to respect it (Quarto excludes unnumbered headings from both numbering and cross-ref numbers), or the new toggle will stamp numbers on headings the author marked unnumbered. Fourth, there is now a THIRD number source (scan_xref_targets for cross-page in preview) that must keep agreeing with the render-time string; it already calls section_number, so reusing that exact fn at render time keeps them in lockstep, but the drafter should say so explicitly. Impact is also likely closer to medium than high: the defect only bites nested single docs or same-page refs to a book subsection, which are not the common case.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML text only, derived from heading structure and block sourcepos; read-only preview; click-to-source unaffected; pinned by a nested-section single doc plus a book same-page `@sec-` ref.

### D51. Whether reference prefixes (Figure/Table/Section) are author-configurable (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto exposes a `crossref:` config block with `fig-prefix`, `tbl-prefix`, `sec-prefix`, `eq-prefix`, `fig-title`, `lof-title` etc., plus `lang:`-driven localization, so `fig-prefix: "Fig."` renders `@fig-x` as "Fig. 3" and a French doc says "Figure"/"Tableau" automatically.
- **Critique:** Hardcoded English labels forbid "Fig.", forbid any non-English rendering, and forbid a house style. Fair caveat: a single-author English tool rarely needs this, and Quarto's crossref block is large and silently mis-typo-able (an unknown crossref sub-key is ignored, not flagged).
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto targets a global, multilingual academic audience where cross-reference labels are not cosmetic. Journals mandate specific forms ("Fig." vs "Figure", "§" vs "Section", "Eqn." vs "Equation"), and a French, German, or Chinese document that renders "Figure"/"Theorem"/"Table" in English is simply wrong and often unpublishable. Quarto ships a full translation table across roughly thirty languages driven by the `lang:` key, plus per-prefix overrides, so a document localizes automatically and a house-style tweak is a single line. The `crossref:` block is "large" because cross-references genuinely are a large, coherent surface (figure, table, section, equation, listing, the whole theorem family, appendix, list-of titles), and centralizing them in one declarative, project-inheritable block is the correct normalization, not sprawl. The silent-typo tolerance the caveat dings is a general Pandoc metadata-inheritance property (it also buys forward-compatible and partial configs), not a crossref-specific design flaw. So Quarto's configurability is the more capable choice for its audience, and the entry is honest to concede that a single-author English tool rarely needs it.
- **Taliesin today:** Labels are hardcoded in `cite/render.rs::xref_label()` (Figure/Table/Section/Equation/Listing plus the theorem kinds). There is no `crossref:` config key anywhere; English only; the `# References` list title is likewise fixed (only reused if the author writes a manual heading).
- **Proposed better:** Add a tightly-scoped `crossref:` map (front matter + `_site.yml`) of prefix -> {ref-label, list-title} that overrides the hardcoded defaults, run through the same `schema.rs` strict validation + did-you-mean + click-to-source used for every other key. Keep the defaults so zero-config output is byte-identical.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep it an open question, but sharpen the shape if built. (1) Narrow the schema to `crossref: { <prefix>: <label> }` over the closed prefix set {fig,tbl,sec,eq,lst} plus the theorem kinds; drop `list-title` entirely. (2) Treat the "References" heading as a separate concern; the existing manual-heading override (cite/render.rs:71) already covers most of it. (3) Refactor first: merge `xref_label` and `theorem_meta` into ONE label table both read from, so config threads through a single source of truth; that converts the "two sites to thread" tradeoff into a net dedup worth doing even without the config. (4) Lead with the real differentiator: not "we can configure labels too" but "labels are strict-validated with did-you-mean + click-to-source", which is exactly the silent-ignore gap the caveat correctly pins on Quarto. (5) Defer localization, but if ever built, drive it off the existing `lang:` key with a per-language default table (and fix the current latent lie that `lang:` implies localization), never a per-prefix hand-roll. (6) For a single-author English tool the honest impact is medium-low: the concrete near-term win is only "Fig."/section-symbol house style, so shipping is optional, but if shipped, ship it as the unify-then-override refactor, not a bolt-on that copies Quarto's block shape.
- **Tradeoffs:** New config surface and schema entries; two label sites to thread (`xref_label` and `theorem_meta`); real risk of drifting toward Quarto's sprawling crossref block. Localization is a bigger commitment (a full label table per language) that could be deferred. (skeptic-found downside: The proposed `{ref-label, list-title}` schema is half a category error, and "two label sites" is an undercount. `list-title` has no crossref meaning in Taliesin: there is no list-of-figures/tables feature (HTML-only, LoF/LoT was never built), and the `# References` heading is a bibliography artifact (cite/render.rs:78), not a cross-reference prefix, so folding it into a `crossref:` map is wrong-layer. The clean map is prefix -> label only. Configurability also touches more than two sites: `xref_label` at the inline `@fig-x` use site (cite/render.rs:11), the separate `theorem_meta` table (divs.rs:320), the hardcoded "Proof" head (divs.rs:554), and the fixed `<h2>References</h2>` are each distinct strings. Both label functions return `Option<&'static str>` / `(&'static str,&'static str)`, so config forces owned Strings threaded through `process` -> `transform_html`, which runs per block on the incremental path. Finally, unnoticed by the drafter: Taliesin already accepts `lang:` but wires it only to `<html lang>` (page.rs:389), so `lang: fr` today silently promises French and delivers English labels, and any future localization must hang off that same key rather than a hand-rolled per-prefix map.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure HTML label text, no new output format, no preview write-back; validation reuses the click-to-source did-you-mean machinery; pinned by a corpus doc that sets a custom prefix.

### D52. How cross-page and cross-book references resolve under an incremental warm-server preview (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto resolves cross-references with a project-wide Lua filter at render; any cross-ref number requires a project render, and cross-book / cross-project references historically need a book project type and often break outside it.
- **Critique:** Correct for batch builds, but it couples cross-ref resolution to a full project render, which is exactly what a warm-server incremental preview is trying to avoid. Fair: Quarto was never built for a live single-file edit loop.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's project-render coupling is correct for Quarto's goals, and the critique concedes as much ("never built for a live single-file edit loop"), so it is a fair steelman, not a strawman. The strongest case FOR Quarto: it must emit many formats (HTML, PDF/LaTeX, docx, epub, revealjs) in which global cross-reference numbering ("Figure 2.3", "Section 4.1") must be identical, and the numbering is format-dependent (LaTeX resolves \ref at compile; HTML needs precomputed numbers). A render-time Lua filter that writes a project-wide crossref index is the format-agnostic single source of truth, and a number can only be assigned once the full float/section sequence is known, which is after all content is processed. Quarto optimizes for reproducible batch publishing (render the whole book once for deploy), where a few seconds of project render is irrelevant and correctness of numbering across a 400-page artifact is paramount. Crucially, Taliesin can source-scan section numbers without a render ONLY because it abandoned multi-format output (the HTML-only invariant): with one target and no LaTeX passthrough, numbering is computable from source alone. That decoupling is a benefit Taliesin bought with its narrower scope, not a free win Quarto left on the table.
- **Taliesin today:** `site/xref.rs::scan_xref_targets` does a lightweight SOURCE pass (no render; it resolves `{{< include >}}` first) mapping every anchor to its page url plus a section number, and `harvest_xref_numbers` fills float numbers from a one-time per-page render. `cite` emits `data-qmd-xref` markers that `rewrite_cross_refs` resolves per block; first-definition-wins with a duplicate-across-pages warning. Cross-book links are plain relative `.html`.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. The improvement worth banking is making the scan incremental: on an edit, rescan only the changed page's anchors instead of every page, so a large book's cross-ref registry updates in step with the warm server rather than doing a full O(pages) rescan.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's core claim: the lightweight source-scan (scan_xref_targets, include-resolved, no render, first-definition-wins with a cross-page duplicate warning) genuinely beats Quarto's project-render coupling, and it is a benefit bought by the HTML-only invariant, so status "taliesin-already-better" stands. But REPLACE proposed_better and tradeoffs, which are misdiagnosed. Correct framing: the warm server already avoids any per-edit xref rescan (the registry is built once in Site::discover and reused), so there is no O(pages) rescan to make incremental. The improvement worth banking is a CORRECTNESS/FRESHNESS fix, not a scale optimization: on a content edit that touches an anchor, re-scan only the changed page's anchors (the scan is already per-page, so this is cheap) and splice the result into the live xref_targets, so cross-page refs stop resolving against a stale registry mid-session. Guard the first-definition-wins winner: for any label the changed page shares with another page, deletion/rename must reconsult the other definers, so that case is not purely local. Note explicitly that this only refreshes section numbers and link resolution; cross-page float numbers stay bare in preview because harvest_xref_numbers is build-only. Pin it with a serve_site integration test (edit-then-assert), since the static corpus cannot exercise the warm-edit path the entry claims covers it. Impact stays medium; confidence on the "already-better" verdict is high, confidence on the original proposed optimization was misplaced.
- **Tradeoffs:** Incremental invalidation adds bookkeeping (which page owns which anchor) and cache-coherence risk. The current full rescan is simple and is likely fast enough until books get large, so this is a scale optimization, not a correctness fix. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal is diagnosed backwards. The warm server does NOT do a full O(pages) rescan on a content edit; it does NO rescan. scan_xref_targets runs only inside Site::discover (startup, _site.yml change, or a .qmd file add/remove); a plain content edit rebuilds affected pages via finish_blocks -> resolve_cross_refs against the EXISTING xref_targets. So there is no per-edit rescan cost to optimize. The real latent gap is the opposite of what the entry claims: an edit that adds, renames, moves, or renumbers a {#sec-}/{#fig-} anchor leaves the registry STALE until a structural/config event or restart, so cross-page refs from other open pages resolve to a wrong or missing number mid-session. That is a correctness/freshness issue, not the "scale optimization" the entry states. Two further costs the drafter missed: (1) first-definition-wins makes a "rescan only the changed page" invalidation non-local, if the changed page shares a label with another page, recomputing the winner still has to consult every other definer, reintroducing O(pages) coupling for duplicates; (2) build-time harvest_xref_numbers is already skipped in preview by design, so cross-page fig/eq/tbl NUMBERS are bare in the live view regardless, meaning a "fresh registry" in preview would still not deliver cross-page float numbers without the extra render pass. So the freshness fix helps section numbers and link resolution only.)
- **Invariant check:** Source-scan only, no write-back, per-block `data-qmd-xref` markers preserved, HTML-only; already exercised by the multi-page book corpus docs. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant (HTML-only, single read-only surface, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, block-level incremental, warm server) is broken; the design stays source-scan-only with no write-back and preserved data-qmd-xref markers. But the entry's invariant_check overclaims on corpus-plus-roadmap: "already exercised by the multi-page book corpus docs" is false for the incremental/live path this proposal targets. The static corpus renders each doc once and cannot exercise a warm-server edit sequence, so any per-edit rescan/refresh work would ship unpinned unless a serve_site integration test is added. Under corpus-plus-roadmap that test is a precondition, not optional.)

### D53. How unresolved and duplicate references are surfaced to the author (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** An unresolved `@fig-x` renders as the literal "?@fig-x" token in the finished page, with no source location; duplicate labels are not consistently reported.
- **Critique:** The "?@fig-x" token ships silently into the rendered output and gives no line to jump to, so the author hunts for it by eye, and a duplicate label can quietly point a ref at the wrong element.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a batch multi-format compiler whose crossref resolution is a Pandoc Lua filter operating on an AST that has already dropped .tmd source positions, so a located, click-to-source warning is architecturally expensive there in a way it is nearly free for Taliesin, which threads sourcepos onto every block by construction. The visible "?@fig-x" token is a deliberate cross-format signal, not neglect: it surfaces a broken reference inside the delivered artifact itself (PDF, docx, revealjs, HTML) where a co-author who never runs the build, reading offline with no warm dev console, still sees exactly which ref failed. For a render-and-email workflow with no persistent diagnostics panel, the artifact is the only channel that reaches every reader, so putting the marker in the output is a coherent choice for Quarto's constraints even though it is the wrong one for a live-preview, single-author tool.
- **Taliesin today:** `cite::validate_xrefs` flags unresolved cross-refs as LOCATED warnings (file + line via `sourcepos_start_line`) in the dev diagnostics; an unresolved anchor degrades to a readable bare-label link, not a "?@" token; `register_xref` warns on a duplicate label within a doc (first-definition-wins) and `scan_xref_targets` warns on the same label defined across pages. Every warning carries a source position, so click-to-source can jump to it.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Add a did-you-mean on an unresolved `@fig-x` that is one edit away from a known anchor, reusing the `schema.rs` suggestion machinery, turning the located warning into a one-click fix in the editor.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the unresolved-ref handling (a located warning plus a readable bare-label degrade genuinely beats Quarto's silent "?@fig-x" token). Correct the attribution: the helper is frontmatter::closest / levenshtein (re-exported as crate::closest), with diagnostics/reactive.rs::closest_owned as the exact precedent for closest-over-a-runtime-name-set, NOT schema.rs (which has no suggestion logic). Add the did-you-mean, but (a) run it after site-wide resolution over the project-wide anchor set by threading the registry / scan_xref_targets map into validate_xrefs, which today receives no candidate set, so legitimate cross-page refs are neither flagged nor mis-suggested; (b) keep surfacing navigate-only, confining any auto-apply to an explicit editor-buffer quick-fix in the companion, never a preview write-back. Most important, fold in the gap the entry missed: LOCATE the duplicate-label warnings. register_xref (Warning::new, no .at) and scan_xref_targets (a bare Vec<String>) both emit UNLOCATED duplicate warnings, so Taliesin half-reproduces the Quarto flaw it critiques; give them file+line and a corpus pin (there is a located-warning test for the unresolved case but none for duplicates). That plus the did-you-mean makes "taliesin-already-better" fully true instead of true only for the unresolved case.
- **Tradeoffs:** Suggestion over the anchor set is cheap; the only risk is noisy suggestions for deliberately-external anchors, mitigated by an edit-distance threshold. (skeptic-found downside: The did-you-mean needs the known-anchor set, which validate_xrefs does NOT currently receive (it only sees the rendered blocks' data-qmd-xref markers); the registry (single-doc HashMap<String,String>) or scan_xref_targets' project map must be threaded in, so the tradeoffs' "suggestion over the anchor set is cheap" glosses real plumbing. It must run AFTER site-wide resolution over the PROJECT-wide anchor set, or a legitimate cross-page @ref (which validate.rs already warns must not be flagged pre-resolution) gets a spurious same-page suggestion. A distance-2 threshold over prefixed anchors misses the common wrong-prefix typo (@fig-x for @sec-x is distance 3) while many same-prefix anchors (fig-plot1 vs fig-plot2) risk a confidently-wrong suggestion, so the noise surface is wider than the "deliberately-external anchors" the entry names. Biggest miss: the entry rates this medium-impact polish on the ALREADY-strong unresolved path while ignoring that Taliesin's duplicate-label warnings are UNLOCATED (register_xref uses Warning::new with no .at; scan_xref_targets pushes a bare Vec<String>), so they carry no line to jump to and partially reproduce the exact Quarto flaw the entry critiques; that is the higher-value fix.)
- **Invariant check:** Diagnostics only, located to source for click-to-source, no preview write-back, rendered HTML unchanged; unresolved and duplicate cases are already corpus-pinned. (possible violation flagged: Single-editing-surface, conditionally. The proposed_better phrase "turning the located warning into a one-click fix in the editor" contradicts the entry's own invariant_check ("no preview write-back"): if "one-click fix" means auto-applying the suggested anchor into the .tmd from the preview, that is a preview to source write, the same class as the removed drag-to-reorder gesture, and is out of scope. It is only in-scope if constrained to navigate-only click-to-source (jump to the dangling @ref line, author edits by hand) or an explicit editor-buffer quick-fix inside the VS Code companion (the sanctioned "editor command" path), never the preview writing back.)

### D54. Whether a code listing is a first-class numbered crossref float, and through which door (executable cell only, or also a plain static fence) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto treats code listings as a first-class numbered crossref float alongside figures, tables, and equations. Two entry doors: (a) an executable cell carrying `#| lst-label` + `#| lst-cap`, whose source (and optionally output) becomes "Listing N"; and (b) a STATIC, never-executed code block via Pandoc attributes on the info string, ```` ```{#lst-foo .python lst-cap="..."} ````. `@lst-foo` renders a linked "Listing 1" that shares the same numbered-float and crossref machinery as figures/tables. The static form (b) is the primary documented pattern: you routinely cross-reference a config, SQL, schema, or shell snippet you are showing but not running.
- **Critique:** Taliesin already makes the listing a first-class float, and on the executable-cell door it beats Quarto (server-side syntect highlighting, data-block-id + data-sourcepos on the wrapper for click-to-source, block-level diff). The gap is the OTHER door: a static, display-only snippet has no clean path to a numbered listing. A plain non-braced fence (```` ```sql ````, ```` ```python ````) cannot carry a `lst-` label at all, because `#| label:`/`#| lst-cap:` are only parsed for braced cells. To get a Listing you must brace it (`{sql}`), which reads as "executable cell" and, for python/r, actually runs the code (kernel + freeze cache) when you only wanted to display it. And a doc written Quarto's canonical static way mis-parses: `code_lang` reads the leading `#lst-foo` token as the "language", so there is no kernel, no label, and no listing at all.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a format-agnostic compiler, so `@lst-x` must resolve to a linked "Listing N" identically in HTML, in PDF (a native listing float), and in docx. Promoting code listings to a first-class numbered float beside figures, tables, and equations is therefore the minimal correct design, not bloat: one crossref machine, one mental model across formats. The static door costs Quarto essentially nothing, because Pandoc already parses `{#id .class key=val}` attributes on fenced code blocks, so Quarto invented no syntax, it leaned on Pandoc's native code-block attributes. The `{python}`-executes versus `{.python}` / `{#id ...}`-static split is a clean, learnable rule, and cross-referencing shown-but-not-run code (an algorithm, a config, a schema) is a common, legitimate authoring need. For Quarto's mission the two-door listing float is elegant and right, and the critique is fair: it verifies each code citation and even concedes Taliesin already beats Quarto on the executable door.
- **Taliesin today:** First-class and verified from code. render/mod.rs numbers listings (`lst_count`) and gates the role on a braced cell: `cell` is `Some` only when the fence info starts with `{` (mod.rs:294), and the `CellRole::Listing` arm requires `cell.is_some()` (mod.rs:316-333). cell_numbered.rs::emit_code_listing emits a semantic `<figure class="tali-listing">` with a "Listing&nbsp;N" `<figcaption>` and a `#lst-` anchor, interpolating the orchestrator's data-block-id + data-sourcepos (invariant preserved), and honoring `code-fold`. cite/render.rs `xref_label("lst") = "Listing"` so `@lst-x` resolves to a linked "Listing&nbsp;N"; site/xref.rs:159 carries `lst-` across pages; render/validate.rs lists `lst-cap` as a valid cell option. Pinned by corpus/posts/pca-geometry/index.qmd (a `{python}` executable cell with `#| label: lst-data-generation` + `#| lst-cap`, cross-referenced by `@lst-data-generation`). Static/plain-fence listings are entirely unpinned and unsupported: code_lang (cell_extract.rs:165) splits the first token of `{#lst-foo .python ...}` to `"#lst-foo"` and returns it as the language, so the Quarto static form yields a bogus `language-#lst-foo` source block, not a listing.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the executable-cell listing exactly as is (it already beats Quarto). ADD a static, never-executed door WITHOUT new syntax: let a plain fenced code block carry the existing `#| label: lst-x` + `#| lst-cap:` directives in its body, by relaxing the Listing detection so it also fires for a non-braced fence whose body opens with those recognized directives, routing straight to emit_code_listing and never touching the executor. That gives a clean numbered-listing path for config/SQL/schema/shell snippets, reuses the one `#|` cell-option vocabulary the owner chose to keep, and adds zero syntax. Secondary (optional, larger): teach the info-string parser real Pandoc attribute handling so `{#lst-x .python lst-cap="..."}` is recognized too, since that form is Pandoc-native and would smooth Quarto imports; defer it because it requires reworking code_lang's naive first-token split.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the executable-cell listing as is (it already beats Quarto). Add the static door, but make the Pandoc attribute form the PRIMARY mechanism, not the relaxed `#|`: recognize a fenced block whose info string is a Pandoc attribute list carrying `#lst-` / `lst-cap` (e.g. ```{#lst-x .sql lst-cap="..."}) as a static listing, gated so an id-or-dotted-class attribute form is treated as static and never reaches the kernel (mirroring Quarto's `{python}`-runs versus `{.python}` / `{#id}`-static split). This keeps Markdown AND Pandoc familiarity (an owner value), matches Quarto exactly so imports just work, reuses the existing `{#sec-x}` heading-attribute parsing seam, and above all does not collide with the guide's `#|`-in-plain-fence teaching idiom (a doc teaching it nests the attributed fence one level down inside a plain display fence). Accept the real cost the drafter deferred as the actual work: reworking code_lang's naive first-token split and adding the executable-versus-static gate. The one hazard to guard is that gate: a `{#lst-x .python}` must never boot the kernel (currently `{.python}` DOES execute because the info starts with `{`), so preserving warm-server and no-surprise-execution is the load-bearing test, and the static wrapper must still carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos so Alt-click jumps to the fence. Reject or shelve the `#|`-in-plain-fence door given the documented collision. Pin with a new corpus doc cross-referencing a static ```{#lst-x .sql} listing via `@lst-x`.
- **Tradeoffs:** A `#|`-looking first line inside a genuinely plain fence currently renders as literal shown text; consuming it as a directive changes that rendering, so the relax must be scoped to only the recognized directive keys at the very top of the block (the `#|` sigil is Taliesin-specific and unlikely in real SQL/shell, so the ambiguity is small but real). Two doors to the same float widen the test surface (the corpus must pin both the executable and the static path). The Pandoc info-string form, if pursued later, is a nontrivial rewrite of info-string parsing and risks regressing braced-cell language detection, which is why it is deferred rather than bundled. (skeptic-found downside: The relax-`#|`-into-plain-fences mechanism collides with Taliesin's own guide. The docs deliberately DISPLAY `#|` directives at the top of plain (non-braced) fences as teaching text: docs/guide/using/code.qmd:92-97 opens a ```python fence with `#| label: tbl-summary` / `#| tbl-cap:`, and docs/guide/reference/cell-options.qmd:38-52 opens ```python fences with `#| echo` / `#| label: fig-loss`. That is the guide's established idiom (plain fence so the reader SEES the syntax rather than executed output). By corpus-plus-roadmap the static-listing feature must itself be documented, and its own doc would show `#| label: lst-x` + `#| lst-cap` inside a plain fence as an example, which the relaxed detector would then eat and render as a live listing: a self-referential trap where the feature's documentation triggers the feature. The drafter's tradeoffs checked only "real SQL/shell" and called `#|` "unlikely", missing that `#|` is the guide's core teaching vocabulary shown literally inside plain fences. Secondary miss: the `#|` door hands the sigil a second context that current validation does not cover (validate_cell_options runs only when cell.is_some()), so a `#| labl:` typo in a plain fence would silently fail to lint or fire.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: a listing is a `<figure>` in the single live HTML view, no new output format.
