Single read-only surface: pure render, no write-back; the wrapper still carries data-block-id + data-sourcepos so Alt-click on a static listing jumps to its fence (click-to-source preserved). Keep-Markdown: reuses the existing `#|` cell-option vocabulary on a plain CommonMark fence, no syntax divergence. Block-level incremental: still one content-hash-keyed block, diffs like any other. Warm-server: the static door needs NO kernel and never enters the freeze cache, so it is strictly faster than today's brace-it workaround, never colder. Corpus-plus-roadmap: ships pinned by a new corpus doc (a plain ```` ```sql ```` listing cross-referenced by `@lst-x`), the arbiter of done.

### D55. Whether authors can declare custom cross-reference / float types beyond the built-in set (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto `crossref: custom:` lets you declare a new category (e.g. Video, Exhibit) with its own reference-prefix and auto-numbering, so `@vid-1` becomes "Video 1" without touching Quarto's source.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's prefix set is closed AND duplicated: `cite/render.rs::xref_label()` and `site/xref.rs::is_ref_anchor()` are two hand-maintained lists that must agree, so even a first-party new kind is a two-file code change and a drift hazard. Fair caveat: a single-author tool seldom needs arbitrary float types, and every custom kind still needs a numbering source and an emit path.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto serves a huge multi-domain, multi-FORMAT audience (biology "Exhibit", legal "Statute", engineering "Plate") where authors genuinely need first-class float types Quarto's maintainers never anticipated, complete with a reference-prefix, a caption-prefix, an auto-incrementing counter, and a list-of-floats. Exposing that through declarative `crossref: custom:` config (data, not a code fork) is the textbook-correct extensibility design for a general tool: it keeps one numbering engine as the sole owner of counters while letting the type set stay open. Because Quarto must number the same float consistently across HTML, PDF/LaTeX, and docx, a config-declared kind consumed by the shared cross-ref engine is far safer than per-format hacks. For Quarto's scope, a closed built-in set would be an arbitrary ceiling, so open-by-config is a virtue, not over-engineering. The entry's critique is fair precisely because it aims at Taliesin's own duplicated closed lists, not at a caricature of Quarto, and grants that any custom kind still needs a numbering source and an emit path.
- **Taliesin today:** Fixed set: sec/fig/tbl/eq/lst plus theorem kinds thm/lem/cor/prp/def/exm/rem. `is_ref_anchor` (the site anchor scanner) and `xref_label` (the inline renderer) are independent literal arrays; no extension point exists.
- **Proposed better:** First, cheap and worth doing regardless: drive both lists from ONE shared const table (single source of truth) so they cannot drift. Then, if custom types are pursued, let `crossref:` append a kind bound to a named counter, reusing that same table.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry into a do-now refactor and a deferred, corpus-pinned capability. DO NOW: replace all three kind tables (xref_label, is_ref_anchor, divs.rs theorem_kind) and the scattered `starts_with("fig-")` checks with ONE const array of kind descriptors, each carrying id, short prefix, anchor prefix, display label, optional div kind-name, optional amsthm style, and counter key. This is a behavior-preserving refactor, it removes real (three-way, not two-way) drift, and it is the prerequisite that makes any future custom kind a one-place extension instead of a four-place edit. DEFER custom types until pinned by a corpus doc; when built, treat it as a single COUPLED change touching xref_label + is_ref_anchor + the render/mod.rs counter pre-count + the emit path + validate_xrefs + the schema export together, with prefix-collision/shadowing rejection, so the strict-validation clean break stays intact (a declared kind is recognized, an undeclared one is still flagged). Keep impact low and note that the payoff of the config feature is thin for a single author, so the unification is the part worth committing to now.
- **Tradeoffs:** Numbering for a custom kind needs a defined counter and emit path (genuine work for a rarely-used feature). The list-unification refactor is nearly free and de-risks the two-file drift immediately even if custom types are never built. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter undercounts the drift surface and misses the strict-validation coupling. (1) It is not "two-file": there are at least THREE heterogeneously-keyed tables plus scattered literal checks. `cite/render.rs::xref_label` keys on the short prefix (`thm`), `site/xref.rs::is_ref_anchor` keys on prefix+dash (`thm-`), and `render/divs.rs::theorem_kind` keys on the long kind-name (`theorem` -> ("Theorem","plain") amsthm style); on top of that, `figure.rs` and `render/mod.rs` hardcode `starts_with("fig-")`. So "drive both lists from ONE const" is really "unify a multi-facet kind registry" (id, short prefix, anchor prefix, display label, optional div kind-name, optional amsthm style, counter key), which slightly deflates the "nearly free" framing while making the case for it stronger. (2) Custom kinds collide with Taliesin's clean-break strict validation, which the tradeoffs never mention: an unknown prefix in `xref_label` returns None via `?`, so `@vid-1` is silently left as literal text and is NEVER flagged by `validate_xrefs` (which only sees `data-qmd-xref` markers that were emitted for KNOWN kinds). To make custom kinds work AND stay honest, the same author-declared kind must simultaneously reach four touch points, xref_label, is_ref_anchor, the numbering pre-count in render/mod.rs, and the emit path, and the exported `qmd-fast schema` JSON Schema plus the strict config validator must become config-aware so a declared `vid-` anchor is neither dropped nor mis-flagged as a typo. (3) `is_ref_anchor` matches by `starts_with`, so a custom prefix must be rejected if it collides with or shadows a built-in one (e.g. an author declaring `se` would swallow `sec-`).)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only anchors, block-model `data-block-id`/`data-sourcepos` unchanged; the shared-list unification is a behavior-preserving refactor; a custom-kind corpus doc would pin any new capability.

### D56. The labeling mechanism for computed outputs (#| label:) vs prose targets ({#id}) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Computed outputs are labelled with a `#| label: fig-x` cell option; prose elements with a `{#fig-x}` attribute. Two mechanisms, with the subtle rule that the label prefix must match the intended float type or no crossref is produced.
- **Critique:** The two-mechanism split is inherent, but Quarto validates it weakly: a typo'd cell label, or a `fig-` label on something that is not a figure, tends to fail silently (no number, no error), so the author only notices via a broken ref downstream.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's prefix-as-declared-type is a principled choice for a multi-FORMAT compiler, which is its whole architecture. The same .qmd targets LaTeX/PDF, docx and HTML; in LaTeX a figure is a `\begin{figure}` float and a table a `\begin{table}` float, and the float TYPE must be declared BEFORE the content is known so the engine can place the float and build \listoffigures/\listoftables. Quarto therefore treats the author's `fig-`/`tbl-`/`lst-` prefix as authoritative INTENT and does not second-guess it against the executed output. That is defensible for two more reasons: (a) cross-typing is sometimes legitimate (a gt/kable table you deliberately want called a Figure, a heatmap that is table-like), so 'reclassify by content' would fight real authoring choices; and (b) reliably detecting 'the produced kind matches the declared prefix' would need a canonical kind-detector across every engine and MIME (pandas, gt, kable, matplotlib, plotly, altair, Observable) and every output format's float model, a large, fragile surface with genuine false-positive risk. Finally, Quarto is not fully silent: it emits 'unable to resolve crossref @x' warnings at render and warns when a figure crossref lacks a caption, so the critique's 'no error' is mildly overstated. The narrow true gap is that a mistyped or type-mismatched PREFIX is surfaced only downstream via a failed reference, never validated against the content, which is a reasonable price for format-agnosticism.
- **Taliesin today:** Taliesin honors BOTH: cell options (`#| label:`, `lst-cap` via `cell_extract`/`cell_numbered`) and prose `{#fig-x}`/`{#tbl-x}`/`{#eq-x}`; `apply_table_captions` numbers a computed table and registers its anchor. Cell options are strictly validated in `schema.rs` with did-you-mean + click-to-source, so the label surface matches Quarto and is checked harder.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it, and close Quarto's silent-mismatch gap: when a labelled cell's prefix does not match the kind it actually produced (e.g. `#| label: fig-x` on a cell that emits a table), raise a located warning instead of silently not-numbering.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the instinct (close Quarto's silent-mismatch gap) but retarget the mechanism. Do NOT compare declared prefix against a sniffed output kind (fuzzy, false-positive-prone, and the fig-on-a-table example is not even a real failure). Instead add the target-side mirror of the existing `validate_xrefs`: a post-exec anchor-existence pass. For every registered crossref anchor (fig-/tbl-/lst-/eq-/sec-/thm-), verify an `id="..."` for it exists in the final assembled block DOM; if not, emit a located click-to-source warning at the labeling cell's source line ("cell labelled `tbl-x` produced no table / no output; `@tbl-x` will not link"). This is exact (zero false positives, fires only when the anchor is truly missing), general (catches the two real cases, tbl- on non-table output, and any crossref cell with empty output at exec.rs:352, plus any future wrapper that drops an anchor), and reuses the xref registry. Cost the drafter must budget: thread the cell source-loc into the xref registry (anchor -> number + location), run the pass in the SERVER after exec splices outputs (not the core emit path), and add a new located-warning channel from exec to the diagnostics panel. Cheapest immediate wins with no plumbing: a guard at exec.rs:352 (crossref-labelled cell with empty output -> warn) and at table_wrap's no-`<table>` else branch. Pin with a server exec test under a live kernel plus a kernel-free core case for the static/standalone-anchor variant. Also fix the entry's attribution: the located did-you-mean cell-option validation lives in render/validate.rs, not schema.rs.
- **Tradeoffs:** The emit path must know the produced kind to compare against the declared prefix; a small extra check. Low risk of false positives if it only fires when a number would otherwise be dropped. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal's literal example (`#| label: fig-x` on a table-emitting cell) is the ONE case that does NOT silently break in Taliesin: `figure_wrap` (exec.rs:983) unconditionally wraps any output and injects `id="fig-x"`, so `@fig-x` both resolves and has a live anchor. Detecting 'this figure output is really a table' needs fuzzy MIME/HTML sniffing that is false-positive-prone (plotly/altair/Observable figures are `<div>`, not `<img>` or `<table>`), which the tradeoffs understate. The genuinely broken, cheaply-detectable cases are different: (1) a `tbl-` label on non-table output, table_wrap (exec.rs:1004) drops the anchor while the number/xref were already registered, leaving `@tbl-x` linking to a `#tbl-x` that is absent; (2) ANY crossref-labelled cell with empty output, exec.rs:352 skips the output_block, orphaning the pre-registered number/anchor. Also architecturally: the produced kind is unknown in the core 'emit path' the tradeoffs name, it is only known in the SERVER exec path after the kernel runs, and exec today has no located click-to-source warning channel (only a kernel-state `diagnostic()` string), so this is a new seam, not 'a small extra check'. And it is execution-gated: with no kernel there is no output and nothing to check.)
- **Invariant check:** Cell-option parsing and HTML emit only, validated with click-to-source, read-only preview; a mismatched-prefix cell would be corpus-pinned. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is violated (read-only, HTML-only, Markdown-syntax-preserving, click-to-source-compatible via cell.sourcepos). Soft tension with corpus-plus-roadmap: the check is execution-gated, so it cannot be pinned by the kernel-free `cargo test -p taliesin-core` corpus render the way static validate.rs checks are; it needs a server exec test with a live kernel (ipykernel-gated). The entry's 'would be corpus-pinned' is therefore optimistic and should be scoped to the static-anchor variant plus a server-side kernel test.)

### D57. Whether an author can suppress the prefix and get a bare linked number (-@fig-x) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `-@fig-x` renders just the number ("3") without the "Figure" prefix, for prose like "see (3)" or "Figures 2 and 3", and adjusts prefix capitalization by sentence position.
- **Critique:** Minor but real: without suppression you cannot write a clean bare parenthetical number or a shared "Figures 2 and 3" without the prefix repeating. Fair that this is a small stylistic nicety, not a correctness issue.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto reuses Pandoc's existing `[-@key]` suppress-author syntax verbatim for crossref prefix suppression: one orthogonal, already-learned convention that behaves identically for citations and cross-references, with zero new syntax invented. It keeps the full prefix ("Figure 1") as the DEFAULT and makes the bare number strictly opt-in, which is the correct default: a naked "(1)" is ambiguous in running prose, and "Figure 1" is self-describing and better for screen-reader users following the link. Its capitalization control is a deliberate, deterministic, explicit pair (`@Fig-` vs `@fig-`) rather than a fragile sentence-position heuristic that would misfire on abbreviations, quotation marks, or list items, and it only becomes relevant once you have reconfigured the prefix to lowercase. So Quarto's choice is minimal, composable, accessible-by-default, and heuristic-free. NOTE: the entry's `quarto_does` mischaracterizes this as Quarto adjusting "capitalization by sentence position." Quarto does no such thing: the docs say the capitalized `@Fig-` form "makes no difference for the default output, but would indeed capitalize the first letter if the default prefix had been changed via an option to use lower case." That factual slip is worth correcting even though the critique's argument does not rely on it.
- **Taliesin today:** Taliesin supports bare `@fig-x` and bracketed `[@fig-x]`, both rendering "Figure&nbsp;3" as a link (`cite/render.rs`). In `render_citation_group` a leading `-` is stripped (`trim_start_matches('-')`) but has NO effect for an xref key, so `[-@fig-x]` still renders "Figure 3"; there is no bare-number mode and no capitalization control.
- **Proposed better:** Honor a leading `-` on an xref key as prefix suppression (emit just the number, still a link), mirroring the citation suppress-author convention the parser already recognizes. Leave capitalization alone (the English default already capitalizes).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but revise it. (a) Fix the `quarto_does` text: Quarto capitalizes via explicit `@Fig-`/`@fig-` syntax that only matters under a lowercase-prefix config, not by sentence position; the punt on capitalization is well justified because Taliesin has no configurable lowercase prefix and `parse_xref` cannot even parse `@Fig-` (prefix is `is_ascii_lowercase`-only), so the feature is moot. (b) Drop the "tiny change" framing and enumerate three surfaces: the bracketed `render_citation_group` path (detect the leading `-` before `trim_start_matches` and thread a suppress flag into `xref_link`/`xref_anchor_link`), the bare path (either relax `at_word_boundary` to admit a boundary-anchored `-` and keep the email/mention regression tests green, or explicitly emit a did-you-mean diagnostic so bare `-@fig-x` never silently renders literal), and the cross-page `site/xref.rs` resolver (carry the suppress flag on the `data-qmd-xref` marker so the label and the sec->"Chapter" override are skipped). (c) Add a label fallback so a suppressed unresolved ref is never an empty invisible link. (d) Pin with a corpus doc covering same-page bracketed suppression, cross-page suppression (especially `-@sec-`), and the unresolved fallback, plus a regression assertion that the email/@-mention boundary guard still holds. (e) Lower confidence from high to medium given the boundary-guard and cross-page surfaces; keep the sequencing note that this follows the reliable-numbering fixes.
- **Tradeoffs:** Tiny change, but only meaningful once the numbers themselves are reliable, so it should follow the chapter-scoped-float and hierarchical-section fixes. Must not collide with the citation `-@` suppress-author meaning (disambiguated by the `fig-`/`tbl-`/... prefix already routing to `xref_link`). (skeptic-found downside: The "tiny change / high confidence" framing understates the surface. (1) The entry scopes only to the bracketed `render_citation_group` path where the `-` is already stripped. Bare `-@fig-x` (which a user WILL type by analogy to the working bare `@fig-x`) currently renders as LITERAL text with no link and no diagnostic, because `at_word_boundary` treats a `-` immediately before `@` as a non-boundary (that guard exists to reject `word-@x` and anchor-internal hyphens, and has adversarial email/@-mention tests). So after a bracket-only fix you get an inconsistency: `@fig-x`, `[@fig-x]`, and `[-@fig-x]` all work, but bare `-@fig-x` silently emits garbage. Supporting it means carefully relaxing that guard (allow a `-` that is itself at a boundary) without breaking the `bob@rem-server.com` / mid-word tests. (2) Cross-page suppression is not automatic: `site/xref.rs::rewrite_one_xref` rebuilds `{label}{number}` from the link's inner text and OVERRIDES the label to "Chapter" for `sec-` refs, so a suppressed cross-page `-@sec-x` would still print "Chapter N" unless a suppress marker is threaded onto the `<a>` and the resolver taught to honor it. (3) Fallback: a suppressed ref to an unresolved/unknown anchor would render an EMPTY-text link (an invisible clickable target), strictly worse than today's visible "Figure" fallback, so the fix needs a "fall back to the label when no number is available" rule.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML link text only, no output format, read-only preview, click-to-source intact; pinned by a `-@fig-x` corpus line.

## Figures, tables, and page layout

### D58. Honor fig-align / out-width (and fig-width / fig-height) on computational figures, and stop strict-flagging them (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `#| fig-align: center|left|right`, `#| out-width: 70%`, and `#| fig-width`/`#| fig-height` are standard cell options: fig-align/out-width control how the executed plot is displayed, fig-width/fig-height set the figure size passed to matplotlib/knitr before capture.
- **Critique:** This is the single most jarring asymmetry in the current figure story. A standalone Markdown image honors `{width= height= fig-align=}` (figure.rs emit_figure, lines 72-93), but the identical intent on a computational cell does nothing AND is actively rejected: these keys are not in CELL_OPTION_KEYS, so the strict validator (validate.rs, the clean-break 'any unknown key is flagged' policy) emits a click-to-source warning for a plotting cell that any Quarto author writes reflexively. So the tool both ignores the option and scolds you for it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's four-key split is principled, not accidental, and the entry actually treats Quarto as the sensible baseline (the critique targets Taliesin's current ignore-and-scold behavior, not Quarto's design). The keys occupy three distinct layers: fig-width/fig-height are PHYSICAL (inches passed to matplotlib figure.figsize / knitr fig.width before rasterization), which fixes the font-to-data ratio, tick density, aspect, and the actual pixel dimensions of the captured raster; out-width/out-height are DISPLAY (CSS scaling of whatever was captured); fig-align is layout. This separation is load-bearing: you cannot recover a crisp, correctly-proportioned plot with CSS out-width alone, because upscaling a small PNG is blurry and the font/data proportions are baked in at figure-creation time. Quarto pushes fig-width/fig-height into the kernel precisely because that is the ONLY place physical size can be honored, and it uses the same #| out-width on cells that it uses via width= on markdown images, so authors get one mental model across both figure sources.
- **Taliesin today:** figure_wrap (exec.rs line 983) hardcodes `class="tali-figure tali-figure-center"` and ignores alignment/width entirely. fig-align/out-width/fig-width/fig-height are absent from CELL_OPTION_KEYS (validate.rs lines 18-33), so each is flagged as an unknown cell option. Only the Markdown-image path (figure.rs) reads width/height/fig-align.
- **Proposed better:** Add fig-align + out-width to the cell vocabulary and honor them in figure_wrap: fig-align selects tali-figure-left/right/center (reuse the existing classes), out-width sets a max-width on the img/output wrapper. Add fig-width/fig-height as recognized keys and forward them to the kernel as the figure size (matplotlib rcParams / R chunk size) so capture matches. This closes the asymmetry with the Markdown-image path in one move.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split into two corpus-pinned steps. STEP 1 (ship now, high value, low cost): honor fig-align + out-width in figure_wrap (fig-align reuses tali-figure-left/right/center; out-width sets an escaped max-width inline style on the outer <figure>, which naturally covers both tali-fig-light and tali-fig-dark imgs), and add ONLY fig-align + out-width to CELL_OPTION_KEYS. No freeze change and no kernel change: figure_wrap runs on every render, so alignment/width edits take effect without busting the PNG cache, and click-to-source is untouched because data-block-id/data-sourcepos stay on the .tali-output wrapper. Pin a corpus doc with an executed matplotlib plot carrying fig-align + out-width. STEP 2 (separate, later, its own corpus doc): fig-width/fig-height. Correct the cache reasoning first: because options are stripped from the cumulative hash (freeze.rs:55), fold fig-width/fig-height into the hashed code exactly like fig-export (exec.rs:389) so a size change re-runs; forward the size to the kernel while respecting the pristine-rcParams design (set at figure-creation or save/restore figure.figsize), add R support via IRkernel repr.plot.width/height (the R preamble is currently empty), and decide the explicit-figsize-wins behavior deliberately so a recognized key never silently no-ops. Until Step 2 lands, do NOT add fig-width/fig-height to CELL_OPTION_KEYS; keep flagging them so the validator's "recognized means implemented" contract holds.
- **Tradeoffs:** fig-width/fig-height require threading size into the executor and the freeze cache key (a size change must bust the cached output, which it will since the cell's option text is part of the code fed to the hash). out-width on a dual light/dark matplotlib pair must apply to both variants. A corpus doc must pin fig-align/out-width on an executed plot. (skeptic-found downside: The "one move" framing hides that the proposal is really two very different-cost changes, and its central cache claim is wrong. fig-align + out-width are cheap and correct: figure_wrap regenerates on every render (exec.rs:355 wraps cached inner too), so they take effect with NO freeze-cache change and NO kernel work. But fig-width/fig-height are materially more work than stated: (1) the freeze claim is false. Cell code is stripped of #| options before hashing (render/mod.rs strip_cell_options; freeze.rs:55), and only fig-export is explicitly folded back in (exec.rs:389). A fig-width change would NOT bust the cached PNG automatically; it needs the same fig-export-style explicit fold. (2) R has no knitr here. The R preamble is empty (kernel.rs:305), so honoring fig-width/fig-height in R means new IRkernel repr.plot.width/height plumbing, not a free chunk option. (3) Python's kernel deliberately keeps global rcParams pristine (kernel.rs:71-93); setting figure.figsize needs save/restore, and an author's explicit plt.subplots(figsize=...) silently overrides the option, reintroducing a subtler version of the exact honored-sometimes/ignored-sometimes asymmetry the entry complains about. (4) Adding fig-width/fig-height to CELL_OPTION_KEYS before honoring them would make them recognized-but-inert, which contradicts the validator's own stated stance that its vocabulary is what Taliesin actually implements (validate.rs:7-10), trading a loud no-op for a silent one. (5) out-width must be escaped into the inline style (the markdown path already escape_attr's width/height); and the entry's "closes the asymmetry" overstates it, since the markdown path honors width=/height= while the cell path would honor out-width, so the two surfaces still speak different vocabularies (mirroring Quarto's own split rather than unifying it).)
- **Invariant check:** Keeps the `#|` Markdown cell-option syntax; changes only emission and the validator vocabulary. Server-side, so click-to-source and block-diff are untouched; the freeze hash already covers option text. HTML-only.

### D59. Support subfigures (sublabelled child figures under one parent number) instead of only a flat grid of independent figures (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A figure div with a `#fig-parent` id whose children are themselves figures (each `![](x){#fig-a}`), or a computational cell with `#| fig-subcap: ["a", "b"]`, renders ONE parent 'Figure N' with children lettered (a), (b), (c). `@fig-parent` links to the group; `@fig-parent-1` / `@fig-a` link to a specific panel. Combined with `layout-ncol`/`layout` this is Quarto's standard multi-panel figure.
- **Critique:** Subfigures are the natural unit for 'three views of one result', and the lettered sublabel plus a single parent number is exactly how papers and posts cite them. Without it, three related panels each burn a top-level figure number and cannot be referenced as parts of a whole.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Subfigures are not a nicety, they are the citation grammar of scholarly and technical writing: "three views of one result" is ONE result, and readers cite it as "Figure 3a", not "Figures 1, 2, and 3". LaTeX codified this decades ago (subfigure/subcaption), and Quarto's whole value proposition is one source producing correct output across formats, so it needs a single abstraction (the fig-parent div, or one cell with fig-subcap) that lowers to \subfloat in LaTeX, a grid in HTML, and a nested block in Word. The lettered-child-under-one-number model is the ONLY design that keeps the parent number stable when panels are added or reordered (adding a fourth panel doesn't renumber the rest of the document), gives one caption for the composite plus per-panel sublabels, and makes @fig-parent link the group while @fig-parent-1 links a part. Crucially, Quarto's fig-subcap on a computational cell is the load-bearing case: one code cell emits several plots that are inherently parts of one figure, and only a parent/child abstraction can letter them without the author hand-numbering. Quarto's choice is correct for its audience and is not a strawman here.
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. `::: {layout-ncol=3}` wrapping three images (divs.rs line 391) emits a CSS grid, but figure_parts/emit_figure number each image independently (mod.rs line 447 increments fig_count per image), so corpus/media/gallery.qmd produces Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, each with its own `#fig-` id. There is no parent number, no (a)/(b)/(c) sublabel, and no `@fig-x-1` addressing. `fig-subcap` is absent from CELL_OPTION_KEYS (validate.rs), so `#| fig-subcap:` on a cell is flagged as an unknown key.
- **Proposed better:** When a `::: {#fig-parent}` div (or a `layout-ncol`/`layout` div carrying a `#fig-` id) contains child figures, assign ONE parent number, letter the children (a)(b)(c) in document order, register `fig-parent` plus `fig-parent-1..n` (and any child `#fig-` ids) in the xref registry, and render the parent `<figcaption>` as 'Figure N: caption'. Add `fig-subcap` to the cell vocabulary for the computational path. All server-side, so click-to-source on each child block and the parent survives.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the capability but split it into two entries and fix the sequencing. Entry A (do first, tractable): DIV-based subfigures where a ::: {#fig-parent} div contains explicit child figures (![](x){#fig-a}). Implement it by giving figures a post-grouping renumber pass (mirroring number_theorems, which already runs after group_divs precisely to see div structure) rather than eagerly numbering in the flat loop, so the parent gets one number, children are lettered (a)(b)(c), the registry stores fig-parent→"3" and fig-a→"3a" (the existing label+&nbsp;+value join already renders "Figure 3a"), and the downstream counter ripple is handled in one place. Emit id="fig-parent-1..n" on the children so @fig-parent-N has a real href target alongside the explicit #fig-a ids. Pin with a NEW corpus doc (do not disturb gallery.qmd, whose id-less {layout-ncol=3} correctly stays a flat grid). Entry B (defer, bigger): computational fig-subcap, one cell emitting n outputs lettered under one parent number, which is an executor change to partition display outputs and share a parent number/caption; only add fig-subcap to CELL_OPTION_KEYS as part of THAT entry so the strict validator never accepts a key it ignores. Downgrade this combined entry's confidence from high to medium given the phase-ordering refactor, and make explicit that the executor path is out of scope for the first cut.
- **Tradeoffs:** New numbering pass that must interleave with the existing per-figure counter and apply_table_captions ordering; a corpus doc must pin the sublabel format and the `@fig-x-1` resolution. Edge cases: a mixed div (some children figures, some prose), and nesting a subfigure group inside a panel-tabset. (skeptic-found downside: The entry treats this as "a new numbering pass that interleaves with the per-figure counter," but the real cost is a phase-ordering conflict it never surfaces. Figure numbering is EAGER in the flat top-level loop (mod.rs 447-456 bakes "Figure N: caption" into each child's HTML before divs exist), whereas div grouping is a post-pass (group_divs, which receives neither fig_count nor the xref registry). So the three children are already "Figure 1/2/3" with fig-no-pooling→"1" registered before anything knows they share a parent. Collapsing them to one parent number forces (a) HTML surgery on already-emitted child figcaptions, (b) re-registering the xref entries, AND (c) a global counter ripple so every downstream figure and its registry entry shift down by n-1. The clean fix is to give figures a post-grouping numbering pass like theorems/tables already have, which is a real refactor, not an interleave. Worse, the COMPUTATIONAL fig-subcap path (Quarto's main case) is dismissed as "add fig-subcap to the cell vocabulary," but that only un-flags the key. Actually implementing it means the executor must split ONE cell's multiple display outputs into n lettered subpanels under one shared parent number, yet CellFigure.number is a single scalar assigned pre-execution (mod.rs 492) and consumed by figure_wrap (exec.rs 983) which wraps the whole output as one figure. That is a substantial executor change, not a vocabulary edit. Also, @fig-parent-1 positional refs need generated element ids as href targets (href is #fig-parent-1) even though the div children carry their own #fig-a ids.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure HTML emission over the existing Markdown `:::`/`#|` syntax (no syntax divergence). Server-rendered numbering keeps click-to-source and block-level diff intact; each child stays its own data-block-id block. Pinned by a new corpus doc. HTML-only, no write-back. (possible violation flagged: No FIXED invariant is broken: it is pure server-side HTML emission over existing ::: and #| syntax, each child keeps its own data-block-id and data-sourcepos so click-to-source and block-diff survive, HTML-only, no write-back, corpus-pinned. One near-invariant tension the entry misses: Taliesin's clean-break strict-validation contract means every RECOGNIZED key must actually work (there is no silently-ignored tier). Adding fig-subcap to CELL_OPTION_KEYS before the computational subpanel path is implemented would make the validator lie: the author writes fig-subcap, gets no warning, and the option silently no-ops. So the "add fig-subcap to the vocabulary" step must NOT ship ahead of the feature that honors it.)

### D60. Add page-width / full-bleed column classes so a wide figure or table can break out of the 46rem text column (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `.column-page`, `.column-screen`, `.column-screen-inset`, `.column-body-outset`, `.column-page-inset` let a figure, table, or any block extend wider than the reading measure, up to full viewport width, while prose stays at the comfortable text width. Widely used for large plots, wide tables, and hero visuals.
- **Critique:** Taliesin fixes the body at `--tali-maxw: 46rem` (base.css line 21) and offers only the margin direction (.column-margin/.sidenote). There is no outward direction: a 12-column correlation matrix, a wide facet grid, or a data table with 15 columns is trapped at 46rem and must scroll inside its own box even on a 27-inch monitor where there is ample room to just show it. This is precisely the kind of richer-in-a-browser layout the 'wider than Quarto' goal calls for, and it is currently absent.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The description of Quarto is accurate, and Quarto's real strength is not "it has .column-page" but the mechanism behind it. Quarto models the whole article as ONE named CSS grid with lines from screen-start through body-start/body-end to screen-end, and every layout role (body, body-outset, page, screen, each with -inset and left/right variants) plus margin content and the TOC rail is placed by naming grid lines, not by ad-hoc negative margins. That is a deliberate, load-bearing choice: negative-margin breakouts do NOT compose with a persistent side rail (sidebar/TOC/margin), whereas a page-spanning named grid does. So an author learns one coordinate system once, and breakout content, margin figures, and full-bleed heroes all live in the same grid and stay mutually consistent even with a sidebar present. The vocabulary is also memorable and self-documenting (body < body-outset < page-inset < page < screen-inset < screen), and the -shaded/inset variants cover the common "wide but not edge-touching, with a tinted band" case. The thing worth stealing from Quarto is that grid mechanism and the coherent named taxonomy, not merely two class names bolted on with margins.
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. grep for column-page/column-screen/outset/inset finds nothing in src or CSS. Only `--tali-maxw` (46rem) and the margin float (`.sidenote`/`.column-margin`/`.aside`, base.css lines 598-610). Wide tables are handled by an in-box scroll-shadow (base.css line 418), which is a good fallback but never lets the content actually use the page.
- **Proposed better:** Add `.column-page` and `.column-screen(-inset)` classes usable on a `:::` div (and as a fig/tbl option) that widen the block beyond the text column via a centered grid track or symmetric negative margins clamped to the viewport, with a responsive collapse back to full-width flow below the current 73rem breakpoint. Prose keeps 46rem; only the tagged block breaks out.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but revise it on mechanism and scope before it ships. (1) Replace "symmetric negative margins clamped to the viewport" with the container-aware approach: define breakout relative to the ACTUAL layout container per context, and adopt a Quarto-style page-spanning named grid (or CSS subgrid) so breakout composes with the TOC rail and the book sidebar instead of fighting them. (2) Enumerate all four contexts (single-doc no-TOC, single-doc has-toc grid, book with sidebar, site-main) and define precisely what .column-page and .column-screen mean when a persistent side rail is present: .column-page = the layout container's outer width (72rem/62.5rem), and .column-screen = true edge-to-edge only when there is NO persistent rail, otherwise degrade to page width, so nothing ever overlaps the TOC or the drawer. (3) Compute full-bleed with scrollbar-gutter compensation (margin-left:calc(50% - 50vw) style with a scrollbar allowance) and explicitly re-assert the no-horizontal-scroll clamp so .column-screen cannot regress the mobile guard. (4) Since a raw CommonMark table has no attribute slot, be explicit that page-width tables are opted in by wrapping in ::: {.column-page} (existing syntax), while figures can take it as a fig option. (5) Expand the corpus pin from two docs to at least a page-width figure AND a page-width table each in BOTH a has-toc single-doc page and a book page, plus a mobile-width regression assertion, so the multi-context centering and the horizontal-scroll guard are both locked by the net. Impact medium and confidence high both stand; the value (wide plots/tables on a large screen is real, verified pain and is genuinely "richer browser behavior in a live HTML view") is not in doubt, only the mechanism and the corpus scope are.
- **Tradeoffs:** Breaking out of a centered max-width column via negative margins interacts with the has-toc two-column grid (base.css line 676) and with scroll containers; needs testing at the three viewport sizes in the memory matrix. A corpus doc must pin a page-width figure and a page-width table. (skeptic-found downside: The proposed MECHANISM (centered grid track or "symmetric negative margins clamped to the viewport") is the naive one that does not compose with Taliesin's actual layouts, and the tradeoffs section names only the has-toc grid while the real surface is four containers. Whenever a TOC is present, the content column is deliberately offset LEFT of viewport-center (grid sized to the exact 46+2.5+14 column sum and centered: base.css 676, site.css 80, site.css 203), so a breakout centered on the content column lands visibly off-center relative to the page, and a true full-bleed .column-screen computed from that column will overlap or collide with the sticky 14rem TOC rail and, worse, with the book's persistent left sidebar drawer. This is exactly why Quarto uses a page-spanning named grid instead of negative margins. Second missed cost: a full-bleed width of 100vw includes the vertical-scrollbar gutter, reintroducing ~15px of page-level horizontal overflow, the precise mobile breakage the codebase already guards against by clamping canvas/svg/video/iframe/img/table to max-width:100% (base.css 408-419); .column-screen would need an explicit clamp or the margin-left:calc(50% - 50vw) trick with scrollbar compensation. Third: in the 60-72rem window the has-toc grid is still two columns, so "page width" is ill-defined (there is barely any room to break out to while dodging the TOC), making the proposed 73rem collapse breakpoint arbitrary and leaving an awkward middle band. Also unmentioned prior art: site.css already has a page-level .tali-wide (60rem) toggle, which is a whole-page lever, not the per-block breakout being proposed.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure CSS plus the existing `:::`-div/attr syntax (no new syntax). Read-only layout, click-to-source and block-diff unaffected. HTML-only, and this is exactly 'richer browser behavior in a live HTML view'. Corpus-pinned. (possible violation flagged: None of the enumerated fixed invariants is broken: it is pure CSS over the existing ::: div/attribute syntax (no new syntax, keeps Markdown), HTML-only, read-only (no write-back), the breakout div stays one normal block carrying data-block-id + data-sourcepos so click-to-source and block-level diff are unaffected, warm server is irrelevant, and the corpus-pin commitment satisfies corpus-plus-roadmap. The nearest tension, not a listed invariant but a de-facto one enforced repeatedly in base.css, is the "never force a horizontal scroll on mobile" discipline that a naive .column-screen (100vw scrollbar gutter, or a fixed-pixel full-bleed plot) would violate; that risk must be designed out, not left to the author.)

### D61. Extend layout-ncol to relative-width rows (layout=) rather than only equal columns (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Beyond `layout-ncol`, Quarto accepts `layout="[[2,1],[1,1,1]]"` (rows of relative widths), plus `layout-nrow`, `layout-align`, and `layout-valign`, so panels can be sized and arranged asymmetrically (e.g. a big plot beside a small legend, then a row of three thumbnails).
- **Critique:** `layout-ncol=N` only makes N equal columns. The common 'one large panel plus two stacked small ones' arrangement is impossible, so authors either accept equal cells or fall back to raw HTML, which breaks click-to-source and the block model. This is a modest but real expressiveness gap for figure panels.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's `layout` attribute is not a gratuitous knob, it is the price of being a multi-format panel system. By expressing arrangement as relative weights in nested rows (`[[2,1],[1,1,1]]`) rather than raw CSS, Quarto keeps one authoring syntax portable across HTML (flex/grid), LaTeX (minipage widths), and Word, with each writer translating the same weights. It normalizes weights to explicit percentages with gutters subtracted via calc(), which honors the intended ratio even when panels contain intrinsic-width images (something raw `2fr 1fr` does not do reliably). It also composes with subfigure caption numbering (fig-1a/1b) and `layout-align`/`layout-valign` for real dashboard and figure-plus-legend needs, and defines a documented narrow-viewport collapse. Asymmetric layout is a genuine, recurring document need, and Quarto's weight-based model is the correct abstraction for solving it once across many targets.
- **Taliesin today:** Only `layout-ncol` is handled (divs.rs line 391): it emits `grid-template-columns:repeat(N,minmax(0,1fr))` with a fixed 1rem gap. No `layout=`, `layout-nrow`, `layout-align`, or `layout-valign`; those attrs would fall through to a generic div with the raw key as a bare class.
- **Proposed better:** Parse a `layout=` row-spec into CSS grid rows with fractional (fr) tracks derived from the relative weights, and support `layout-align`/`layout-valign` as justify/align-items. Keep `layout-ncol` as the equal-column shorthand. Decide whether the marginal expressiveness justifies the parser, or whether page-width columns (see wide-page-columns) plus nested layout-ncol divs already cover the real needs.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but correct and demote it. (a) Fix `taliesin_current`: `layout=`/`layout-nrow`/`layout-align`/`layout-valign` are parsed into DivAttrs.kv and silently dropped (no class, no warning), so panels stack in document order; this silent drop, not a bare class, is the real gap and it already dents the strict-validation story. (b) If implemented, reuse the existing `.tali-layout` class with an inline `grid-template-columns` built from `minmax(0,Wfr)` tracks so the base.css:757 narrow-width collapse and the intrinsic-image floor both apply unchanged. (c) Treat the validation path as a policy decision, not a one-off: a malformed nested array warning implies a stance on unknown div kv attrs generally, since none are validated today. (d) Reframe: nested equal-column divs cover the arrangement but not the asymmetric widths, so the honest residual is narrowly relative sizing. (e) Downgrade impact from medium to low-medium and explicitly sequence this behind subfigures and wide-page-columns, since the corpus uses layout-ncol in only two places and asymmetric sizing is a niche within a niche for a single-author math/ML blog.
- **Tradeoffs:** A small nested-array parser and its validation/error path (a malformed `layout=` should warn with click-to-source, per the strict-validation stance). More layout knobs to test responsively. Genuinely a judgment call: this may be lower value than subfigures and page-width columns. (skeptic-found downside: The entry misses four things. (1) Its premise is factually wrong: `layout=` and friends are `key=val` tokens routed to `DivAttrs.kv` (divs.rs:168), so they are silently dropped, not rendered as a bare class, and emit no warning. That silent drop is arguably worse than the entry claims and directly contradicts the project's strict-validation identity. (2) There is no div-attr validation surface today (validate.rs never checks div kv), so adding a warn-with-click-to-source path for malformed `layout=` establishes the FIRST such validator and forces the broader policy decision: should every unknown div kv attr now warn, or just this one? Warning only for `layout=` while `layout-nrow=99` and arbitrary keys stay silently ignored is inconsistent. (3) fr is not Quarto's percentage model: a naive `grid-template-columns:2fr 1fr` lets intrinsic-width images overflow the ratio, so the port must write `minmax(0,2fr) minmax(0,1fr)` to preserve the exact overflow-floor rationale already documented at base.css:755. (4) The "nested layout-ncol already covers it" fallback only half-holds: nesting covers the GROUPING (one big panel beside a stacked pair) but not the asymmetric SIZING (2:1 widths), which is the entire point of `layout=`, so the fallback does not actually close the gap. Point in the proposal's favor that the entry undersells: responsive collapse is class-keyed at base.css:757, so an asymmetric layout reusing `.tali-layout` inherits the narrow-width single-column collapse for free, making the "more responsive testing" cost smaller than feared.)
- **Invariant check:** Same Markdown `:::`-div attr syntax, server-rendered to CSS grid, so click-to-source and block-diff are preserved. HTML-only. Would be corpus-pinned. No write-back.

### D62. Server-rendered panel-tabset whose figures/refs resolve even inside hidden tabs (already better) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `.panel-tabset` becomes Bootstrap tabs; cross-references generally work but tab labels are headings, and figure numbering/linking into a tab that is hidden at load depends on client behavior and can be fragile.
- **Critique:** This is an area where Taliesin already wins, so the 'critique' is of Quarto: its tabset is a client-side Bootstrap component layered on the same heading stream, so a tab label is a real `<hN>` that can leak into the TOC and the numbering is a runtime concern.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto keeps tab titles as real headings in the Pandoc AST on purpose, because it renders one source to MANY formats. In PDF/LaTeX/docx there are no tabs, so a tabset must degrade to sequential subsections, and for that the tab title MUST survive as a genuine section heading with its figure inline and its crossref intact in print. Turning tab labels into non-heading buttons (Taliesin's choice) discards that information and is only affordable because Taliesin is HTML-only. Three of the critique's factual claims are also wrong: (a) Quarto builds the tab STRUCTURE server-side via a Lua filter, only the show/hide toggle is client-side, the same split as Taliesin's tabset.js, so it is not a fragile client-only Bootstrap component; (b) Quarto's Bootstrap tabs already carry ARIA roles (role=tab/tabpanel, aria-selected) and the tab-title headings are consumed into the nav rather than left to pollute the visible TOC; (c) Quarto's crossref numbering is a deterministic build-time Lua pass over the AST, so a figure in a hidden tab is numbered and linked correctly no matter the client state. Given its multi-format mandate, Quarto's design is the correct information-preserving tradeoff, not an oversight. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** divs.rs (lines 455-504) builds tabs server-side: the shallowest child headings become ARIA `role=tab` buttons (NOT `<hN>`, so they never pollute the TOC), panels get `role=tabpanel` + `hidden`, ids derive from the container block id. Crucially, figures inside a hidden tab are numbered and xref-registered at build time (corpus/layout/panels.qmd: `@fig-fit` lives in the third tab and still numbers/links). Each inner block keeps its own data-block-id/sourcepos, so click-to-source works inside a tab.
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line: keep tabs server-rendered with build-time numbering and ARIA semantics. Optional polish: deep-linking a `@fig-x` click could auto-activate the containing tab and scroll to it (client-side, read-only), which Quarto does not reliably do.
- **Revised recommendation:** Reframe the entry from "already better" to "parity on numbering, the differentiator is unbuilt." KEEP and pin the real, verified strengths: server-rendered tabs with labels as role=tab buttons (not headings, so no TOC leak), build-time figure numbering that resolves into hidden tabs, and per-block ids/sourcepos preserved by verbatim inner-block concat so click-to-source survives inside a tab. Then make the actual work a single generic reveal-ancestor primitive that, given a target element, opens every ancestor <details> and activates every ancestor tab before scrolling. Invoke it from (a) anchor navigation and hashchange, including the initial page-load hash, (b) Cmd-K search jump, and critically (c) client.js highlightAtLine, so reverse-sync click-to-source into a hidden tab reveals rather than silently scrolls to a hidden node. Register the hashchange listener once and guard it so it survives block swaps; keep it read-only (aria/hidden/open are view state, never a source write, consistent with the scrolly/lightbox/deck-slide precedent). Extend panels.qmd's assertions to the server-side preconditions and add a browser test for the reveal. Rewrite the critique to drop the inaccurate TOC-leak, numbering-is-runtime, and purely-client-side claims, and rest the Quarto contrast on the honest axis: Quarto keeps tab titles as AST headings because it must degrade to PDF/docx subsections, a correct tradeoff for its multi-format goal that Taliesin, being HTML-only, is free to trade away for a JS reveal layer.
- **Tradeoffs:** The optional auto-activate-tab-on-anchor behavior adds a small amount of client JS and must remain read-only (navigate/reveal only, never write source). Otherwise no cost; this is a strength to preserve. (skeptic-found downside: The entry conflates two things that split apart under scrutiny. Numbering/xref RESOLUTION into a hidden tab is build-time in BOTH tools, so Taliesin is at parity there, not ahead. The only genuine differentiator is the deep-link REVEAL (clicking @fig-x actually opening the tab that contains it), and that is currently UNBUILT: tabset.js has no hashchange/anchor handler and crossref links are plain in-page anchors to display:none panels, so today Taliesin reveals nothing on such a click, exactly like Quarto. Worse, the reveal gap is broader than crossref clicks and touches a load-bearing goal: client.js highlightAtLine (reverse-sync click-to-source) special-cases decks but for a normal block only scrollIntoViews, so an editor cursor whose block lives in a hidden tab is scrolled-to-but-not-revealed. A crossref-only patch would leave click-to-source, Cmd-K search jumps, and page-load-with-#hash all still broken into hidden tabs, and would not generalize to the same problem in collapsed callouts and collapsible-proof <details>. Nested tabsets need ancestor-chain activation, and the hashchange listener must be registered ONCE (guarded), not per-enhance, or block swaps double-bind it. Finally, the cargo corpus net can only pin the server-side preconditions (the link plus tab structure in panels.qmd); the actual JS reveal needs a browser test, a corpus-plus-roadmap wrinkle the entry ignores.)
- **Invariant check:** Already conforms: Markdown `:::` + `##` heading syntax, server-rendered HTML, per-block ids preserve click-to-source and block-diff. The optional enhancement is preview-read-only navigation, never a source write. HTML-only, corpus-pinned (panels.qmd).

### D63. Dual light/dark computational figures plus default lightbox gallery as first-class HTML floats (already better) (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A computational figure is captured as a single static raster (one theme). Lightbox is an opt-in extension; matching a plot to a dark page theme requires re-running with a dark style.
- **Critique:** Quarto's figure is a print-era artifact: one bitmap, one theme, static. It cannot follow an OS/reader theme switch and does not zoom without an add-on. That is the ceiling a PDF-first tool hits.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's single static raster is not a print-era accident; it is the only figure artifact that renders identically across every target Quarto commits to (HTML, PDF, docx, ePub, revealjs). A live CSS theme-swap is meaningless in PDF/docx, so a same-run light+dark pair would be dead weight in every non-HTML format. The single raster is also the reproducible, citable, archivable artifact: it is what gets committed and what every reader (and a screenshot in a paper) sees identically, whereas a figure that mutates with reader OS theme is by definition non-deterministic across viewers. Doubling rasters doubles page weight and capture time for a 50-figure document. Lightbox ships as an opt-in filter precisely so authors who do not want the JS/interaction pay nothing (pay-for-what-you-use). Taliesin only earns the dual-theme+always-on-lightbox win by abandoning all non-HTML targets, a cost Quarto deliberately refuses. The critique is accurate on the facts (default computational figures are one bitmap, one theme, no zoom without an add-on) but frames the rationale-free version; the real Quarto reason is multi-format determinism, not print nostalgia.
- **Taliesin today:** The kernel emits a light and a dark variant of each plot and CSS shows the one matching `data-theme` (base.css lines 614-621, `img.tali-fig-light`/`tali-fig-dark`), so plots track the live theme with no re-render. Every figure is click-to-zoom and a multi-image page becomes a keyboard-navigable gallery (corpus/media/gallery.qmd; image-lightbox feature). Computational figures are wrapped as numbered, anchored `<figure>` floats (exec.rs figure_wrap) that resolve `@fig-x` even when produced by the executor.
- **Proposed better:** Preserve and extend: ensure the dual-theme pair and lightbox interoperate with any new sizing (out-width must clamp both variants) and with subfigure grouping (a lightbox gallery over a subfigure set should step in sublabel order). This is a concrete 'wider than Quarto in a live HTML view' win to protect as other figure features land.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the direction but re-scope from 'preserve a shipped win' to 'fix a present, unpinned defect, then extend.' Order: (1) Fix the gallery double-count now: dedupe theme twins when building the gallery array, e.g. exclude offsetParent===null / the display:none variant so only the theme-visible raster enters the ArrowLeft/Right sequence and the (n / N) counter. (2) Add the missing corpus pin: a doc with several LABELED matplotlib figures plus a DOM/JS test asserting the lightbox gallery length equals the figure count (not double) and that navigation lands on the theme-visible src, since gallery.qmd (static PNGs) does not exercise this at all. (3) Correct the entry's copy: dual-theme is matplotlib/Python-specific, not 'each plot'; state that R/plotly/altair/static remain single-raster (parity with Quarto, not ahead). (4) Only then the forward guards the drafter named: when out-width lands it must set width on the <figure> or on BOTH imgs (an inline width on one img silently desyncs sizes across a theme switch since the twin is a sibling), and a subfigure lightbox set must step in sublabel order while still collapsing each figure's light/dark twin to one entry. Retain status as 'ahead of Quarto for matplotlib in a live HTML view', not 'already better for every figure'.
- **Tradeoffs:** Emitting two rasters per plot roughly doubles figure payload and doubles capture work; already accepted. Interactions with out-width/subfigures need test coverage so the pairing is not silently broken by new features. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter frames the pairing/lightbox interaction as a FUTURE risk to protect, but code reading shows it is already broken today. The lightbox gallery is built with querySelectorAll('figure img, img.lightbox') (11-lightbox.js:81) with no visibility filter, and a labeled computational figure wraps BOTH the light and dark img in one <figure> (exec.rs:961). So every labeled matplotlib figure is double-counted: on a real corpus page (pca-geometry, em-algorithm) opening the lightbox yields a gallery whose ArrowLeft/Right steps through the display:none theme-mismatched twin of each figure, and the (n / N) counter reads double. gallery.qmd cannot catch it (static PNGs only) and there is no JS/DOM test, so the interaction the entry claims is a shipped win is actually unpinned and latently defective. Second missed nuance: the dual-theme raster is matplotlib/Python-ONLY (kernel.rs:205-216 hooks matplotlib.figure.Figure); R/ggplot, plotly, altair, and static images emit a single raster exactly like Quarto, so 'the kernel emits a light and a dark variant of each plot' and 'every figure tracks the theme' are overstated. The doubled-payload tradeoff therefore only buys theme-follow for matplotlib users, not for the whole corpus.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only browser behavior (theme-follow + zoom), the exact meaning of 'wider than Quarto'. Read-only (zoom/gallery are reader interactions, never source writes). Server-rendered floats keep click-to-source. Corpus-pinned (gallery.qmd).

### D64. Wide tables scroll web-natively with a scroll-shadow, but relative column widths (tbl-colwidths) are unsupported (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Renders tables via Bootstrap; supports `tbl-colwidths` to set relative column widths, and df-print styles. Wide tables tend to overflow the page on narrow screens unless the theme intervenes.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's default is the better one for mobile (a wide table stays inside its own scrollable box with an edge shadow that signals more content, base.css lines 413-427, rather than blowing out the page width). The remaining gap is that `display:block; width:max-content` on the table means author-specified relative column widths (`tbl-colwidths`) have no effect, so a table that wants a wide first column and narrow numeric columns cannot express that.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto keeps tables as real display:table elements because it serializes ONE table model to LaTeX/PDF, Word, ePub, revealjs, and HTML at once. tbl-colwidths maps cleanly onto LaTeX p{width} column specs and Word column widths, expressions a display:block; width:max-content HTML hack could never carry. The choice is semantically faithful: a table stays a real table for assistive tech and for authors who style via table-layout or colgroup, and Bootstrap already ships .table-responsive as an opt-in scroll wrapper, so responsiveness is available without forcing every table (including ones that already fit) into a max-content scroll box. The mobile overflow is a deliberate multi-format-fidelity tradeoff, not an oversight, and it is exactly the constraint Taliesin only gets to drop because it is HTML-only. The critique is fair (it credits Quarto with tbl-colwidths and only claims the mobile default is better, which is accurate), its one under-credit being that it does not note display:table is what makes tbl-colwidths work at all and that Quarto's overflow is fixable per table.
- **Taliesin today:** base.css line 418: `table { display:block; width:max-content; max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto }` with a layered scroll-shadow background; `th,td` bordered; `caption-side: top`. Markdown pipe-table captions (`: cap {#tbl-x}`) fold into a numbered `<caption>` and register `@tbl-` (mod.rs apply_table_captions). No `tbl-colwidths` support; `display:block` also means the table does not participate in normal table column sizing.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the scroll-shadow overflow default (it is the right mobile behavior). Optionally add `tbl-colwidths` by switching a table that specifies it to `display:table; table-layout:fixed` with `<col>` widths, so authors who need proportional columns get them without losing the scroll fallback for the unspecified case.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry. (1) Ship and keep the taliesin-already-better half as-is: the scroll-shadow, max-content-clamped, no-mobile-page-overflow default (base.css 418-427) is genuinely better than Quarto's Bootstrap default and is already live, with the print path already overriding to display:table (base.css 815). Per-cell text-align from Markdown alignment already works (emit.rs 324-329); only column WIDTH is unexpressible. (2) Downgrade the tbl-colwidths addition from recommended-build to deferred low-priority maybe, because the honest cost exceeds the entry's estimate. If ever built, the correct shape is a real colgroup with per-column widths INSIDE an overflow-x:auto wrapper (never bare table-layout:fixed, which drops the mobile guarantee and imposes equal-share sizing on unsized columns); it also requires deciding the Markdown attachment point (a caption-line attribute, since #| reaches only executed-output tables), adding the key to the strict vocabulary, and shipping a NEW corpus doc that pins proportional columns rather than reusing the caption docs. Given impact is at best medium and the default already covers the common case, the sharpened call is: keep the default as the win, defer colwidths with these preconditions attached.
- **Tradeoffs:** Supporting tbl-colwidths means two table display modes (block-scroll default vs fixed-layout when colwidths are set), which is more CSS surface and more to test. Adding the key also means adding it to the strict vocabulary. Modest value; the default already covers most cases. (skeptic-found downside: The described mechanism (switch a colwidths table to display:table; table-layout:fixed) silently drops the very mobile protection that is the entry's headline win. A display:table element cannot be its own overflow-x scroll box the way the display:block one is, so on a narrow screen a wide colwidths table would once again blow out the page width. To keep the scroll fallback the fixed-layout table must ALSO be wrapped in a NEW overflow-x:auto container element inside emit_table, a bigger change than the CSS toggle the drafter assumed, so the promise of proportional columns without losing the scroll fallback is not automatically true. Two further costs go unmentioned: table-layout:fixed forces equal-share sizing on the columns you did NOT size and clips or wraps overflowing cell content rather than auto-fitting it (a behavioral cliff, not just more CSS), and the entry never resolves the attachment point for Markdown pipe tables, since #| cell options only reach executed-output tables, so a plain pipe table would need a caption-line attribute such as {#tbl-x tbl-colwidths=[75,25]}. The drafter also missed that base.css line 815 already overrides table to display:table !important under @media print, evidence the block-scroll model is a known screen-only hack the print path already undoes.)
- **Invariant check:** Markdown pipe-table + `: caption {#tbl-x}` syntax stays; server-rendered captions preserve `@tbl-` xref and click-to-source. HTML-only; the scroll container is browser-native layout. Corpus-pinned by the existing captioned-table docs. (possible violation flagged: Corpus-plus-roadmap discipline. The entry's invariant_check claims the addition is corpus-pinned by the existing captioned-table docs, but tbl-colwidths is a NEW capability; the rule (each new capability ships pinned by its own target corpus document added in the same change) requires a new corpus doc that exercises proportional columns. The existing caption docs pin only caption folding and @tbl- xref, not column widths, so leaning on them would ship the capability unpinned. No hard invariant among HTML-only, single read-only surface, Markdown-syntax, click-to-source, block-level, or warm-server is broken, but the mobile no-horizontal-page-scroll property base.css deliberately protects is undercut by the as-described implementation and must be preserved via the scroll wrapper.)

### D65. Emit probed intrinsic width/height plus loading/decoding on author images to prevent layout shift (CLS), not only an inline width/height style (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Pandoc's HTML writer (Quarto's rendering substrate) turns an image's width=/height= attributes into an inline CSS style="width:...;height:...", exactly as Taliesin does. It never reads the image file for intrinsic pixel dimensions, and it emits no HTML width/height attributes, no loading, and no decoding on content images. A percentage or absent dimension establishes no aspect ratio, so the image box reserves zero vertical space and reflows the page as it decodes. Quarto ships no CLS control for author images by default (its lightbox and figure numbering are orthogonal to this).
- **Critique:** A percentage width:50% in a style attribute does not tell the browser the image's shape, so the box has zero height until the bytes arrive and then snaps to full height, shoving everything below it down. On a slow connection or a cold cache this is exactly the jank Core Web Vitals penalizes, and it is precisely the kind of live-HTML-view quality a browser-first tool should own. Taliesin has the one thing Pandoc's pipeline lacks to fix it well: it renders server-side with filesystem access to the local image file, so it can know the true pixel dimensions instead of guessing.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto/Pandoc's HTML writer is deliberately a pure, hermetic source-to-HTML function inside a MULTI-format compiler, and its image handling is a principled delegation, not neglect. For a percentage width the author's intent is "fill half the column and reflow with it," and the modern answer to that is CSS (aspect-ratio, the img{height:auto} convention) plus the browser's own heuristics, not a build-time pixel probe. Declining to read content-image bytes keeps builds reproducible and side-effect-free (output cannot depend on which bytes happen to be on disk, and there is no new failure mode on a truncated or unreadable image), and keeps ONE image code path serving PDF/docx/HTML rather than an HTML-only special case; where a fixed-layout format actually needs pixels, Pandoc's ImageSize does probe. Omitting loading and decoding is the conservative correct-by-default choice: loading="lazy" on an above-the-fold or LCP image is a documented Core Web Vitals REGRESSION, and a stateless per-image writer cannot know which image is the LCP candidate, so emitting nothing is safer than emitting the wrong hint. The proposal's own admission that its "first image is eager" heuristic "is crude and can misfire" is exactly why Quarto declines to guess. One fairness caveat on the critique: "never emits HTML width/height attributes" and "never reads the image file" are overstated as blanket claims (Pandoc emits width=/height= attributes for absolute-unit dimensions and probes files for other writers). The non-strawman, and true, version is narrower: on the HTML path, for the common responsive case of a percentage or absent width, Quarto reserves no vertical space and does not probe intrinsic size. That narrower claim is real and is a genuine gap a browser-first tool can own.
- **Taliesin today:** Same gap as Pandoc, verified in code. figure.rs::emit_figure (crates/core/src/render/figure.rs:79-93) writes author width=/height= only into an inline style (e.g. style="width:50%") and emits no HTML width/height, no loading, no decoding. Inline images in emit.rs (crates/core/src/render/emit.rs:117-129) emit only src/alt/title, no dimensions at all. loading="lazy" appears in exactly two non-author spots: the iframe embed and the site listing card img (site/mod.rs:867); the about-page image (site/mod.rs:976) is not lazy, and the mermaid case lazy-loads the JS library, not an img. CSS gives img { max-width:100% } (base.css:408) and figure.tali-figure img { max-width:100%; height:auto } (base.css:657). No image-dimension crate is a dependency.
- **Proposed better:** At render, probe the intrinsic pixel dimensions of local raster images (a header-only read of PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP/AVIF) and emit them as unitless HTML width/height attributes on both figure and inline img, keeping the author's CSS width/height in the style unchanged. The browser derives aspect-ratio from the attributes; combined with height:auto this reserves the correct box even when the rendered width is 50%, eliminating CLS. Add decoding="async" to every author image, and loading="lazy" to all but the first image in the document (the likely LCP candidate stays eager), with an attribute escape hatch ({loading=eager} / {loading=lazy}) for override. Taliesin already reads local img targets from disk for existence checks (diagnostics/assets.rs), so the probe reuses an established file-access seam. Skip remote http(s) URLs and SVGs. Pin it with a corpus doc: a local raster image at width=50% whose emitted img must carry integer width/height plus decoding and loading, with a stable block-id.
- **Revised recommendation:** KEEP but split and correct. (a) Ship the intrinsic width/height probe plus decoding="async" as the unconditional pure-win core: this is the real CLS fix and Quarto's genuine gap. (b) Demote loading="lazy" from a crude "all but the first" default to opt-in ({loading=lazy}) or a conservative "first-viewport images stay eager" stance, because wrong-lazy regresses LCP, the same Core Web Vitals family the entry invokes; do not let the CLS win buy an LCP loss. (c) Make img{max-width:100%; height:auto} a REQUIRED global CSS change (prevents mobile distortion for every attributed image), not percentage-only polish. (d) Use the maintained zero-dependency imagesize crate instead of hand-rolling AVIF/WebP header parsing (ISOBMFF/ispe box parsing is genuinely error-prone and the crate fits the deliberate-vendoring constraint). (e) Implement as a post-render HTML pass keyed off the existing local-img walk with a process-global path+mtime memo, not by threading I/O into the pure emitters. (f) Correct the invariant note: data-block-id is fnv1a(block_src) (source-derived), so dims do NOT fold into the hash; the diff still ships dimension changes via its html!=html anchor check (diff.rs), so click-to-source and incremental updates are unaffected, but for that reason, not the stated one. (g) Explicitly skip data: URIs alongside http(s) and SVG, and fix the adjacent quirk that a unitless width=200 currently emits invalid style="width:200" (Pandoc emits width="200"); normalize it in the same emission the probe touches.
- **Tradeoffs:** Needs an intrinsic-dimension reader: either a small header-only crate (e.g. imagesize) or a hand-rolled parser for four or five formats, added to a project that vendors dependencies deliberately. The probe is a per-image file open at render and must be memoized by path plus mtime so it never re-costs the warm-preview loop (the _freeze cache is the existing precedent for that kind of memoization). Percentage-width inline images need the base img rule to also carry height:auto (figures already do), a one-line CSS change. The "first image is eager" lazy heuristic is crude and can misfire on a hero or multi-image masthead, hence the explicit override. Generated plots from code cells arrive as data URIs or _freeze files and would need dimensions read from the decoded bytes, a follow-on path that can ship later. Remote images stay uncontrolled, the same as today. (skeptic-found downside: Two the drafter missed or under-scoped. (1) The base rule img{max-width:100%} (base.css:408) MUST gain height:auto for EVERY attributed inline image, not just percentage-width ones. An img carrying width/height attributes gets a presentational-hint height that beats the initial auto value, so on any viewport where max-width:100% clamps the width (mobile), the height stays fixed and the image DISTORTS, arguably worse than the CLS being fixed. The drafter framed this as optional percentage-only one-line polish; it is a required correctness change scoped to all attributed images. (2) The change is not "purely additive to emit.rs/figure.rs": emit_figure and the inline Image arm have no doc-base-dir or memo-cache context today, so the feature must either thread base-dir plus a cache into the currently-pure emitters or (cleaner) run as an HTML post-pass over block.html reusing the local-img walk in diagnostics/assets.rs, which itself only stats (is_file()) rather than reading bytes, so even that seam is reuse of path-resolution, not of file reads.)
- **Invariant check:** Purely additive to the per-block img HTML in emit.rs/figure.rs. It does not touch data-sourcepos or the block wrapper's data-block-id; the new attributes fold into the img content hash deterministically, so block-level diff, incremental swap, and click-to-source are unaffected. HTML-only: no new output target. Read-only preview: the probe reads image files at render and never writes source. Warm-server: dimensions are cached by path+mtime so per-edit cost stays zero. Keep-Markdown: the ![alt](src){width=50%} syntax is unchanged; the improvement is entirely in emission. Corpus-plus-roadmap: shipped pinned by the raster-image corpus doc above.

### D66. Decide whether to expose caption-location (top/bottom/margin) or keep the fixed conventional placement (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `fig-cap-location` (default bottom), `tbl-cap-location` (default top), and per-element `cap-location`, including `cap-location: margin` which floats the caption into the page margin (Tufte style).
- **Critique:** Taliesin's fixed placement (figure caption below, table caption on top) matches the sensible defaults, so the everyday case is fine. The gap is only the margin-caption option, which is a genuinely web-native touch that pairs naturally with the existing .column-margin machinery and would be a nice differentiator, not a compatibility chore.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format compiler (HTML, PDF/LaTeX, docx, ePub, revealjs) and caption placement is not a universal convention: it varies by output engine, by discipline, and by publication venue. Many journals mandate a specific caption position and some invert the figure-below/table-above default; a docx house style may differ again. Because one source targets many formats, Quarto cannot hardcode a single convention without breaking someone's required output, so it exposes document-level `fig-cap-location`/`tbl-cap-location` plus a per-element `cap-location` escape hatch. `cap-location: margin` is not a bolt-on: it is one member of a coherent margin-layout system (`column: margin`, margin figures/tables, margin references and citations) that the Tufte and Distill HTML formats are built around, so exposing it uniformly alongside top/bottom keeps the whole margin vocabulary consistent. Given Quarto's multi-format plus academic-venue reality, the full knob is a correct, non-gratuitous design. Taliesin, being HTML-only and single-author with no venue-style obligations, faces none of that pressure and can legitimately hardcode the web convention, so the divergence is a consequence of scope, not Quarto over-engineering.
- **Taliesin today:** Hardcoded and conventional: emit_figure/figure_wrap always put `<figcaption>` after the image (below); table captions are a `<caption>` first-child with `caption-side: top` (base.css line 429). No cap-location key exists in the vocabulary, so `#| fig-cap-location:` is flagged as unknown.
- **Proposed better:** Keep top/bottom fixed at the conventional defaults (do not add a knob whose only settings are the defaults), but consider a single `cap-location: margin` variant that renders the caption into the margin column, reusing the .column-margin float and its responsive fallback. Add the key to the vocabulary only if margin captions ship, so the strict validator stays honest.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep top/bottom placement hardcoded at the web conventions (figure caption below, table caption above, listing caption above) and do NOT add a top/bottom knob: that is correct for HTML-only, single-author scope and already matches Quarto's own defaults. Treat margin captions as a FIGURES-ONLY, explicitly-deferred candidate. If it ships: scope it to `<figure>`-structured captions only (standalone-image + js/mermaid figures), reuse the existing `.sidenote`/`.column-margin` float with its clear:right stacking (so sidenote collision is handled by stacking, and accept the vertical-drift edge case rather than inventing a new rule), and in the SAME change add `cap-location` to BOTH the parse_attrs image-attr path and CELL_OPTION_KEYS so the strict validator stays honest across surfaces. Explicitly exclude tables and document that `<caption>` cannot float (a margin table is a separate, larger feature), or simpler, ship nothing and just document the fixed placement. Given low value versus subfigures/page-width plus the table asymmetry and dual-surface vocabulary cost, defer, and pin whatever ships with a corpus doc that exercises a margin figure caption on both a wide and a sub-73rem viewport.
- **Tradeoffs:** A margin caption competes for the same right-margin space as .sidenote blocks, so collision behavior needs a rule. Low overall value versus subfigures/page-width; may be worth deferring. If nothing ships, the decision is simply to keep placement fixed and document it. (skeptic-found downside: Tables are the missed case, and they break the core "reuse the .column-margin float" claim. A table caption is a `<caption>` table-model element (base.css:429), which cannot be reliably floated into the page margin; only `<figure>`-structured captions (standalone-image via emit_figure, js/mermaid via emit_js_figure) can reuse the float.
