Quarto's cap-location explicitly covers tbl-cap-location and Tufte margin tables, so a figures-only margin caption is an asymmetry: `cap-location: margin` would work on figures but silently no-op on tables. Worse, Taliesin markdown tables have no per-element attribute surface at all, and a code-cell `tbl-cap` table's caption is a `<caption>` child, so margin table captions need a structural rewrite (wrap the table so the caption becomes a floatable sibling), which is a separate, larger feature. Second missed cost: the vocabulary is not one surface. A `#|` cell-option `cap-location` is validated (must be added to CELL_OPTION_KEYS in validate.rs to avoid a false "unknown" warning), but a standalone-image `{... cap-location=margin}` lands in parse_attrs (divs.rs:162), which is NOT validated. "Add the key to the vocabulary" is under-scoped to one of three distinct paths (cell `#|`, image attr block, markdown table which has no slot). Minor third point: the drafter frames sidenote collision as needing a new "rule," but float:right + clear:right already makes margin items stack (queue) without overlap; the real residual is vertical drift, a margin caption may not sit beside its figure when sidenotes occupy the gutter above it.)
- **Invariant check:** Markdown/`#|` syntax unchanged; server-rendered, so click-to-source/block-diff hold. Margin captions are HTML-only browser layout. Corpus-pinned if built.

## Citations and bibliography

### D67. Whether to stay hardcoded IEEE-numeric or offer configurable citation styles (author-date), and stop silently ignoring csl: (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Runs a full CSL citeproc engine. `csl:` in front matter selects any of ~10,000 CSL styles (defaults to Chicago author-date); it renders numeric, author-date '(Bishop 2006)', and note/footnote styles, with year disambiguation (2006a/2006b), style-specific et-al rules, and author-suppression `-@key` producing '(2006)'.
- **Critique:** CSL XML plus a citeproc runtime is a heavy dependency at odds with Taliesin's lean native-engine philosophy (it already dropped reveal.js and the OJS runtime for the same reason), and most single authors only ever use one style. But hardcoding one style is not the real pain; the real pain is that `csl:` sits in the front-matter allowlist (frontmatter.rs:49) and is read NOWHERE, so a Quarto migrant who writes `csl: nature.csl` gets a silent IEEE render with no error. That directly breaks the clean-break strict-validation promise ('any non-Taliesin key is flagged'): the key is accepted and lies.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-FORMAT academic engine (one .qmd renders to HTML, PDF, Word, ePub), and citations must be identical across all of them. CSL is the only standard that expresses a venue's house style once and renders it to every format, including numeric, author-date, and note styles. Crucially, CSL is near-FREE for Quarto: it is built on Pandoc, which already bundles a mature citeproc, so supporting all ~10,000 community-maintained (Zotero) styles is close to zero marginal cost, not bloat. "One author uses one style" is false over a career: the style is a property of the SUBMISSION TARGET (Nature vs IEEE vs an APA journal vs a humanities notes style), and academics re-target constantly. Hand-coded per-type formatters, which is Taliesin's approach, cannot scale to that breadth or stay correct as house styles drift, and cannot serve non-HTML formats at all. So for Quarto's audience and Pandoc-based architecture, full CSL citeproc is the correct and economical choice, not a lean-philosophy violation. The entry's "heavy dependency at odds with lean philosophy" line judges Quarto by Taliesin's HTML-only, from-scratch constraints rather than Quarto's own, which is the one slightly uncharitable note; but the critique concedes exactly this ("hardcoding one style is not the real pain") and redirects to Taliesin's own verifiable honesty bug, so it is fundamentally fair rather than a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** One hardcoded style: IEEE numeric, implemented per BibTeX entry type in crates/core/src/cite/format.rs (fmt_article/fmt_book/fmt_inbook/fmt_misc). In-text cites render as bracketed numbers `[1]`. `-@key` is parsed in render.rs:319 then ignored ('n/a for numeric'). `csl:` is allowlisted but never consumed anywhere in the codebase.
- **Proposed better:** Two-part. (1) Cheap and immediate: make `csl:` honest. Since it is silently ignored, either emit a diagnostic ('csl: is not yet supported; Taliesin renders IEEE') or remove it from the allowlist so strict validation flags it, matching the clean-break ethos. (2) Judgment call for the owner: implement a SMALL curated set of native named styles via a new `citation-style:` key (e.g. ieee, vancouver, apa, chicago-author-date) rather than adopting CSL XML. Author-date is the highest-value addition because it makes `-@key` suppression meaningful and is what most scholarly blogs actually want. Keep it native and server-side, in the format.rs spirit.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split and ship part (1) NOW, decoupled from part (2): keep `csl:` recognized but attach a dedicated LOCATED diagnostic ("Taliesin renders IEEE numeric and does not read CSL files") via the existing diagnostics/ pattern, so Alt-click works, rather than a bare allowlist removal (which mis-suggests 'css'). Pin it with a corpus doc that asserts the warning fires. This closes the clean-break honesty hole at near-zero cost and is unconditionally correct. Part (2) is a genuine owner judgment call, not a slam dunk. If pursued: scope author-date ONLY first (the single highest-value style, and the one that makes `-@key` meaningful), and budget for BOTH the alphabetical-by-author reference-list REORDERING and robust family-name extraction, not just in-text formatting. Ship it as ONE key: either repurpose `csl:` to accept a small set of style NAMES (most migration-friendly, mirrors that Quarto's `csl:` also names a style) OR add `citation-style:` and remove `csl:` in the same commit, never both live; point the part-1 diagnostic at whichever key wins. Note (not a blocker): author-date year-disambiguation (2006a/2006b) is document-GLOBAL state, but this does not break block-level incremental updates because the existing `[1]` numbering is already global and cite::process already runs across all blocks after render, so author-date stays inside the established model. Do NOT adopt general CSL XML; that correctly stays out of scope and matches the syntect/KaTeX/deck native pattern and the reveal.js/OJS-removal precedent.
- **Tradeoffs:** Author-date is real work: author-year rendering, same-author-same-year disambiguation, style-specific et-al thresholds, and title handling all differ from the current numeric path. A curated style set is an ongoing maintenance surface and will never match CSL breadth, so a niche style request has no escape hatch. Part (1) alone is nearly free but only closes the honesty hole, not the capability gap. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter understated part (2)'s cost and glossed one part (1) trap. (a) Author-date is not just an in-text change; it is a SECOND full reference-list path. Author-date bibliographies sort ALPHABETICALLY by author (not by citation order), drop the [n] prefix, and lead with author+year, so it rewrites cite::render::process's whole ordering and emission, not merely format.rs's per-type body. (b) The sharp edge is family-name-only extraction for in-text "(Bishop 2006)" / "(Smith et al. 2006)" with von/Jr/corporate/{braced}/comma-form "Last, First" handling: exactly the problem CSL exists to solve, and harder than the initials+surname path author.rs already does for IEEE. (c) Part (1)'s "either diagnostic or remove from allowlist" are NOT equivalent: a bare removal makes did-you-mean suggest the nearest key by edit distance, which is 'css' (one substitution from 'csl'), actively misleading a migrant into thinking they meant a stylesheet. A dedicated "recognized-but-unsupported" diagnostic (the existing diagnostics/bibliography.rs pattern) is strictly better. (d) Adding a NEW `citation-style:` key while `csl:` stays allowlisted leaves two keys for one concept in a tool that prizes a tight vocabulary; the honest fix must remove or redirect `csl:` in the SAME change as any part (2), never leave both live.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only output, rendered server-side, no write-back to source, corpus-pinnable (add an author-date corpus doc). A native curated implementation matches the syntect/KaTeX/deck pattern and keeps Markdown/Pandoc `[@key]` syntax unchanged.

### D68. Whether to accept CSL-JSON and inline references: in addition to .bib-only (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Accepts many bibliography formats via pandoc: .bib/.bibtex, .json (CSL-JSON, the native Zotero/Better-BibTeX export), .yaml (CSL-YAML), .ris, .enl, and more. It also accepts an inline `references:` CSL-YAML block in the front matter, so a one-off document needs no separate file.
- **Critique:** The .bib-only stance is defensible (most authors have a .bib), but Zotero and many reference managers export CSL-JSON natively, and a short post often wants two or three references inline with no sidecar file. The current code does not just prefer .bib; it silently DROPS a `bibliography: refs.json` (load_bibliography skips any path not ending in .bib), so a CSL-JSON user gets an empty bibliography and every cite renders as a raw key with no clear cause.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto did not pick multi-format bibliography input as a feature; it inherited it for free by building on pandoc plus citeproc, a full CSL 1.0 processor. Pandoc normalizes .bib, .json (CSL-JSON), .yaml, .ris, and .enl into CSL-JSON internally, then renders with any of thousands of locale-aware CSL styles, with proper name disambiguation and et-al rules. So accepting whatever a reference manager exports is a one-line consequence of that architecture, not bespoke work, and rejecting a format you can already read would be user-hostile for a general tool whose users bring Zotero output (Zotero and Better-BibTeX default to CSL-JSON). The inline references: block is the same story: pandoc already parses CSL-YAML, so exposing it costs nothing and spares a one-off author a sidecar file. Set against that, Taliesin's entire citation stack (hardcoded IEEE, BibTeX-only) is strictly narrower, so multi-format input is just one small facet of a citation engine that is broadly more capable. If you accept Quarto's premise (any input, any output, any style), format tolerance is the correct default, not a compromise.
- **Taliesin today:** Only `.bib` is loaded: crates/core/src/render/mod.rs:757 does `if !path.ends_with(".bib") { continue; }` and the parser is BibTeX-only (cite/parse.rs). No inline `references:` support; that key is not in the allowlist. A declared-but-unreadable .bib warns, but a wrong-suffix path is skipped without a warning.
- **Proposed better:** Add a CSL-JSON reader: parse `.json` bibliography files with serde into the existing Entry model through a field-normalization layer (container-title to journal, issued.date-parts to year, structured author arrays to the author string). Optionally add an inline `references:` CSL-YAML front-matter block for file-free short docs. Both are additive and native, no citeproc runtime. At minimum, warn when a declared bibliography path has an unsupported suffix instead of silently skipping it.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry into three tiers by cost and confidence. (1) Ship the warn-on-unsupported-suffix NOW as a standalone bug fix, independent of the rest: a declared bibliography: refs.json currently yields an empty bibliography with ZERO diagnostics (render/mod.rs:757 skips it silently; diagnostics/bibliography.rs stays quiet because bibliography IS declared; the per-cite broken-citation warning fires only for a non-empty bib). That triple-silent failure is a real bug; make it a did-you-mean pointing at the front-matter line, matching the existing click-to-source diagnostic ethos. (2) Add the CSL-JSON reader as medium priority, but scope it honestly: it needs a CSL-type-to-BibTeX-kind map (not just field renames) and direct handling of structured/literal names into the existing author + double-brace conventions (not serialize-then-reparse). Pin it with a corpus doc built from a REAL Better-BibTeX/Zotero export (the drafter's own oracle) and assert the rendered IEEE strings, not merely a non-empty bib. Document that only IEEE is rendered and csl: is inert, so CSL-JSON changes input, never style. (3) Defer the inline references: block: highest schema cost, lowest payoff, and the only piece in tension with strict validation; if pursued later, validate CSL items against a real schema and reuse the same normalization rather than exempting the key.
- **Tradeoffs:** CSL-JSON field vocabulary differs from BibTeX (structured names and date-parts), so the normalization layer is real work and must be tested against a Zotero export. Inline `references:` adds front-matter schema surface that strict validation must cover. The warning-on-unsupported-suffix is trivial and worth doing regardless. (skeptic-found downside: The normalization is not field-renaming, and the drafter under-scoped it. CSL-JSON carries a different TYPE vocabulary (type: "article-journal" | "paper-conference" | "chapter" | "webpage") than the BibTeX kind (article/inproceedings/incollection/misc) that Taliesin's IEEE formatter dispatches on (cite/format.rs). The proposal lists field renames (container-title to journal, issued to year, author arrays to string) but omits the type-to-kind map, without which every Zotero entry parses successfully yet falls through to the misc/default formatter and renders wrong, a silent-looking-success that is worse than the current empty-bib failure. Second, the author step is a lossy round-trip: CSL structured names ({family, given, literal, "dropping-particle", suffix}) would be serialized to a string then re-split by format_one_author, dropping particles/suffixes and the literal-corporate distinction that the double-brace ({{Corp}}) convention depends on. Third, csl: is already accepted-but-inert (IEEE is hardcoded), so CSL-JSON input can never honor a user's requested CSL style; it only feeds the IEEE formatter, a partial-support footgun worth documenting. Fourth, the inline references: piece is the costliest and least valuable: a CSL item has ~50 valid optional fields, so strict validation must either allowlist all of them (large schema) or exempt references: entirely (a hole in the clean-break contract).)
- **Invariant check:** Additive, server-side parse, HTML-only, no write-back. New corpus doc pins a CSL-JSON bibliography. Leaves `[@key]` prose syntax untouched. (possible violation flagged: None is hard-violated: the change is additive, server-side, HTML-only, no write-back, leaves [@key] Markdown syntax untouched, and pins a new corpus doc, so it satisfies HTML-only, single-read-only-surface, keep-Markdown, click-to-source, block-incremental, warm-server, and corpus-plus-roadmap. The one point of friction is the inline references: sub-feature versus the strict clean-break front-matter validator (any unknown key is flagged): CSL items are a near-open schema, so honoring references: either bloats the allowlist or punches a validation-exempt hole. That is tension to resolve, not a broken invariant, and it disappears if the inline block is deferred or validated against a real CSL-item schema.)

### D69. Whether the reference list must always land at document end, or honor placement and a margin location (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Places the reference list where the author writes `::: {#refs} :::`, otherwise at the end. `reference-location` (document, section, block, or margin) controls placement, including per-section reference lists and margin-placed references next to their citation.
- **Critique:** End-of-document is the right default for a single long post, so this is not broken. But the current behavior is subtly wrong when the author's `# References` heading is NOT the last thing in the document (say an appendix follows): the heading stays put, yet the actual entries are appended after everything. And Taliesin already ships `.column-margin`/sidenote machinery, so `reference-location: margin` (each reference shown in the margin beside its first citation) would be a genuine browser-native win squarely inside the 'wider in the live view' mandate, which it currently forgoes.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's placement model is one mechanism serving every output format at once. The `#refs` div is Pandoc citeproc's own convention (not a Quarto invention): citeproc injects the bibliography into a div with id `refs` wherever it sits, working identically in HTML, PDF, and docx, so an author learns one portable rule. `reference-location` deliberately reuses the exact machinery that already places footnotes (block/section/margin), giving citations and footnotes a single uniform knob instead of two bespoke systems. The end-of-document default matches the academic References/Works Cited convention readers expect. Margin references are not a toy: Quarto tied them to its column/margin layout years ago and drops the end list so each reference lives beside its first mention, with a documented narrow-viewport collapse. Crucially, Quarto exposes placement DECLARATIVELY (an explicit `#refs` id) rather than inferring it from a heading's visible text, which is the more robust design: heading-text sniffing for "References"/"Bibliography" is locale-bound and brittle, whereas an explicit id is unambiguous.
- **Taliesin today:** The References `<section>` is always `blocks.push`ed as the final block (cite/render.rs:107); there is no splice or insert. A manual `# References`/`# Bibliography` heading only suppresses the duplicate auto `<h2>` (is_manual_references_heading), it does NOT move the entries. No `#refs` div mechanism, no `reference-location`, no margin references.
- **Proposed better:** (1) Honor explicit placement: if the author writes a `# References` heading (or a `::: {#refs}` div), splice the reference list THERE rather than pushing to the end. (2) Add `reference-location: margin`: render each reference as a margin note beside its first citation, reusing the existing sidenote/column-margin CSS, with a click/hover affordance and a graceful fallback to an end list on narrow (mobile) viewports.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry and ship the two parts at very different priorities. PART 1 (do now, near-zero cost, fixes a real correctness bug): when a manual `# References`/`# Bibliography` heading exists, INSERT the generated `qmd-references` section immediately after that heading block instead of `blocks.push` at the end (cite/render.rs:107). The heading index is already found by `is_manual_references_heading` (line 73); diff matches by stable id (diff.rs:37-39) and the `b.id == "qmd-references"` diagnostic consumer is position-independent, so the splice is diff-safe and invariant-safe. Pin it with a corpus doc where an appendix follows the References heading (today that yields an empty heading plus a headless trailing list). Treat `::: {#refs}` as an optional precise-placement override only if an author needs the list where no heading sits; it is legitimate Pandoc-familiar syntax so it is in-bounds, but it is not required by the bug fix. PART 2 (re-scope as a separate roadmap item, honestly costed as a NEW feature, not CSS reuse): margin references are a genuine "wider in the live view" win, but the spec must own inline injection at the citation site, collision-aware stacking for clustered cites, a dedicated mobile fallback (collapse margins to a single end list), and an explicit rule that margin mode SUPPRESSES the end list on wide viewports to avoid duplication. Injected margin content must carry no `data-sourcepos` (or a valid one) so it stays exempt from `reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total`, and it must not perturb the host paragraph's sourcepos.
- **Tradeoffs:** Placement-at-heading means splicing into the block vector instead of a simple push, and deciding behavior when multiple heading anchors exist. Margin references need per-citation anchoring, ordering, and a mobile fallback path (the margin collapses). The block-id/sourcepos invariant must hold for the spliced/margin blocks. (skeptic-found downside: Part (2)'s "reuse the existing sidenote/column-margin CSS" is materially wrong, and this is the biggest missed cost. The shipped `.sidenote` (base.css:598-610) is a BLOCK-level `::: div` that the author hand-places in the flow; the float aligns to the following block. But a citation is INLINE, mid-paragraph, mid-line, so a margin reference must be injected as a floated element at the citation's position INSIDE the paragraph block, not emitted as its own block. That is a new emission path (today the cite transform only rewrites plain-text runs and never touches tags, precisely to leave block sourcepos intact, cite/render.rs:3-4). Three further costs the "reuse" framing hides: (a) clustered citations `[@a; @b; @c]` need collision/stacking handling the naive `float: right; clear: right` model gives you as a vertical pile pushed far below the line; (b) the existing narrow-viewport fallback (base.css:606-609) inlines the note as an indented aside mid-prose, which is wrong for a reference entry, so margin mode needs a bespoke mobile path (hide margins, render an end list) rather than inheriting the sidenote fallback; (c) an unresolved duplication decision: keep the end list too (references appear twice) or suppress it (then the mobile fallback has no list on desktop). Separately, part (1) bundles two mechanisms; the `# References` heading-splice is nearly free because the heading block is ALREADY located (cite/render.rs:73, just insert-after instead of push-at-end), whereas the `::: {#refs}` magic-id is redundant extra surface for the same outcome.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, read-only preview, browser-behavior enrichment, corpus-pinnable. Margin mode reuses shipped sidenote machinery and adds no new output format.

### D70. Whether to add a citation: metadata block plus an interactive 'cite this' affordance (CFF/BibTeX/APA) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A `citation:` front-matter block (type, container-title, doi, issued, publisher, url, etc.) enriches Google Scholar/Highwire meta, generates a CITATION.cff, and renders a citation appendix so readers can cite the document, with copyable formats.
- **Critique:** Taliesin already emits partial Google Scholar `citation_*` meta from author/date/title, so it half-does this, but there is no structured `citation:` block (no DOI, no container-title) and no reader-facing 'how to cite this' affordance. For the actual target user (a scholarly single-author blog, per the shipped 'Scholar meta' work) a copyable 'cite this post' card is high value, and being interactive it fits the 'wider than Quarto in the browser' mandate better than Quarto's print-oriented appendix.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The `citation:` block is one declarative, CSL-grounded source of truth (a CSL-JSON item model: type, container-title, DOI, issued, volume, issue, page, ISSN, publisher, etc.) that simultaneously drives (a) academic-indexing meta (Highwire/Google Scholar plus Dublin Core), (b) a machine-readable CITATION.cff for repository/software citation, and (c) an in-HTML citation appendix that is ALREADY interactive: a formatted reference plus a copyable BibTeX block (rendered via Quarto's standard code-copy button), formatted with the document's own `csl:` so the self-citation matches the rest of the bibliography's style. The strength is the single source of truth plus style-consistency plus a standards-grounded, validated schema. The entry's 'print-oriented appendix' framing is a strawman: Quarto already delivers the copyable browser affordance the proposal treats as its differentiator, so the enrichment (structured venue fields feeding both meta and the appendix) is the actual design win, not print output. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** site/meta.rs emits `citation_title`/`citation_author`/`citation_publication_date`/`citation_journal_title`/`citation_public_url` meta tags from existing front matter. No `citation:` key (not in the allowlist), no DOI, no CFF, no rendered cite-this block, no BibTeX/APA export.
- **Proposed better:** Add a validated `citation:` front-matter block that (1) enriches the existing meta tags (DOI, container-title, issue/volume) and (2) renders an interactive 'Cite this' card at document end with tabs (BibTeX / APA / RIS) and a copy-to-clipboard button, generated server-side from the block. Optionally emit a CITATION.cff on build.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship the interactive 'Cite this' card, but tighten it. (1) MVP is opt-in via `citation: true`, generated server-side from EXISTING front matter (author, date, title, page url) with zero required new schema. (2) Offer BibTeX (@online/@misc) plus RIS as the copyable formats: both are style-independent and mechanically derivable from CSL-ish fields; for the single human-readable line reuse the existing IEEE formatter rather than adding APA, which dissolves the style-engine overlap the drafter flagged. (3) Make the fuller `citation:` block (DOI, container-title, volume/issue) an OPTIONAL enrichment added to KNOWN_KEYS + schema.rs with child-key did-you-mean validation, understanding those fields are a nice-to-have the target user rarely has. (4) Render the card as a first-class block (data-block-id + data-sourcepos) like References, wired into BOTH single-doc page assembly and site pages, not only site/meta.rs. (5) Drop CITATION.cff. Frame the win honestly as 'matches Quarto's copyable citation with less schema and strict validation,' not 'wider than Quarto,' since Quarto's HTML appendix is already interactive.
- **Tradeoffs:** New front-matter schema surface to add to the allowlist, schema.rs, and did-you-mean validation. Generating correct BibTeX/APA/RIS from the block is formatting work overlapping with the style-engine decision. CFF-on-build touches the build path, not just render. (skeptic-found downside: The genuinely valuable slice (a copyable 'cite this post' card) needs almost no new schema: it is derivable from the author/date/title/url that already exist in front matter (a `citation: true` opt-in suffices). The proposal's headline enrichment fields (DOI, container-title, volume, issue) are precisely what a single-author blog post normally LACKS, so the big `citation:` schema is over-engineered for the stated target user. Second, APA requires a specific style engine Taliesin does not have (it ships IEEE-only and is explicitly 'not a full CSL engine'), so an APA tab either forces a second style engine or produces a citation inconsistent with the document's own References section. Third, the feature today lives only in the site path (site/meta.rs fires citation_* meta only for site pages with date+author), so a document-end card must ALSO be wired into single-doc page assembly (render/page.rs), a second home the drafter did not name.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, read-only (clipboard copy is not a write-back to source), browser-behavior win, corpus-pinnable. No new document output format. (possible violation flagged: None hard. The one borderline element is CITATION.cff-on-build: a non-HTML, repo-root, project-scoped build artifact that is ambiguous for a multi-page site (which page's citation becomes the repo CFF?) and drifts from 'wider = richer browser behavior, never new output artifacts,' even though a .cff is metadata rather than a document format. It should be dropped or deferred. Separately, a requirement (not a violation): the generated card must carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos like the existing References block, or it breaks the block-model invariant.)

### D71. Whether in-text citations should show a hover/tap preview of the reference (Quarto choice stands)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** drop
- **Quarto does:** In HTML output `citations-hover: true` (default) shows a popup preview of the full reference when the reader hovers an in-text citation, so they need not jump to the reference list.
- **Critique:** This is a pure browser-behavior feature at the center of Taliesin's 'richer live HTML view' mandate, and Taliesin already built exactly this pattern for theorems (hover-preview) and cross-references, so its absence for citations is an internal inconsistency, not a missing capability class.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's citations-hover: true default is a well-reasoned progressive enhancement, and Taliesin actually agrees with it (it ships the same behavior). The reasoning: in a dense argument, a reader forced to jump to a reference list and back loses their place, so an inline popover that renders the full reference on hover preserves reading flow at zero navigation cost. It degrades gracefully: with JS off, or on a device that does not hover, the citation is still a plain in-page anchor that jumps to the reference list, the universal fallback. Making it a default rather than opt-in is correct because the reference HTML already exists in the DOM, so the popup costs the author nothing and asks nothing of the writer. Desktop-first hover is defensible precisely because that jump-to-list fallback already covers touch devices. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** An in-text citation renders as a bare `<a href="#ref-key">1</a>` (cite/render.rs:333) that only jumps to the reference list on click. No hover/tap preview. Contrast the shipped theorem hover-preview and the `data-qmd-xref` cross-ref infrastructure.
- **Proposed better:** Attach the formatted reference to each in-text citation for a hover (desktop) / tap (mobile) preview card, reusing the theorem hover-preview mechanism. The reference HTML is already generated for the list, so expose it via a data attribute or resolve it from the `#ref-` target on demand.
- **Revised recommendation:** Drop this as a build item and correct the catalog: the taliesin_current field is factually wrong. Taliesin already matches Quarto here and does it more elegantly than a citation-specific mechanism would, because one generic link-preview enhancer covers citations plus xrefs plus theorems plus sections plus footnotes with no per-citation data payload and no pipeline reorder (lazy resolution from the #ref- target). Do NOT add a data-attribute reference payload; that duplicates DOM content already present. Two genuine residuals survive, both small and separable from the false framing: (1) the enhancer is mouseover/mouseout only, so a touch/tap trigger for mobile is the one real capability gap, and even that is optional since tapping a citation already jumps to the reference list (Quarto's own fallback); (2) the corpus pin corpus/reader/hovercards.qmd exercises @fig-, @sec-, and footnotes but not a [@cite] plus bibliography case, so per the corpus-plus-roadmap invariant add a citation example there to lock the already-working behavior against regression. If anything is filed, it is a one-line touch-trigger enhancement to 12-link-preview.js plus a corpus pin, verified in-browser via chrome-devtools at mobile and desktop widths, not a new citation hover feature.
- **Tradeoffs:** The reference list is currently built AFTER the in-text pass, so either pre-compute the formatted entry before the prose pass or resolve lazily from the `#ref-` target in client JS. Adds a small client-JS surface and a mobile tap-dismiss interaction to get right. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter missed that the feature already ships, so the biggest downside is that the proposal is largely a no-op. Taliesin has one generic enhancer, taliInitLinkPreview (assets/js/code-enhance/12-link-preview.js), registered in 09-register.js and bundled at render/mod.rs:997, that binds via document-level delegation to every a[href^='#'] with length >= 2 that is not inside #TOC. An in-text citation is exactly a[href=#ref-key] (cite/render.rs:333) and the list entry is div id=ref-key class=csl-entry (cite/render.rs:100), so hovering a citation already resolves #ref-key and pops the reference card. There is no separate theorem hover mechanism to reuse: theorems, xrefs, sections, footnotes, and citations are all this same enhancer, so the entry's internal-inconsistency premise is false. Beyond redundancy, the proposal's own preferred implementation (attach the formatted reference to each in-text citation via a data attribute, or pre-compute the entry before the prose pass) is actively worse than what ships: it would duplicate the reference HTML into every citation anchor, fatten each block's payload, and force a needless pipeline reorder (the list is built after the prose pass), all to replace lazy DOM resolution that already works with no duplication.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, read-only, browser-behavior win, reuses an existing shipped pattern, corpus/browser-verifiable.

### D72. Whether to support the bare @key in-text citation form, not only bracketed [@key] (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Follows Pandoc: `[@smith2006]` is a parenthetical citation and bare `@smith2006` is an in-text citation ('Smith (2006)' in author-date, '[1]' in numeric). Both are first-class.
- **Critique:** The owner has decided to KEEP Markdown/Pandoc syntax as the substrate, and bare `@key` is standard Pandoc citation syntax, so silently dropping it is a fidelity gap against the stated substrate. Today a sentence like 'According to @smith2006, ...' leaves a literal '@smith2006' in the output with no diagnostic. It matters less under the current numeric style (bare and bracketed both read as [1]) but becomes important the moment author-date exists.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Pandoc's bare @key is not sugar, it is the grammatical backbone of author-date academic prose: "As @knuth1984 showed..." is meant to render "As Knuth (1984) showed...", where the citation is the sentence subject, not a parenthetical aside. One @key token, disambiguated purely by whether brackets surround it, is an elegant, decades-tested design, and Quarto inherits it correctly and for free via Pandoc/citeproc. Any tool claiming Markdown/Pandoc citation fidelity must honor both forms; supporting only the bracketed half silently discards standard syntax. Taliesin only got away with the gap because its IEEE-numeric style makes bare and bracketed render near-identically as [1], masking the omission, but it becomes glaring the moment author-date styling exists, and even under numeric the current fall-through to a raw literal is strictly a defect. Quarto is right here, and the owner directive ("keep Pandoc syntax, layer better above it") makes matching this the baseline, not the ceiling.
- **Taliesin today:** Only bracketed `[@key]` citations render. In rewrite_text (cite/render.rs) a bare `@` is routed exclusively through parse_xref, which only matches known cross-reference prefixes (fig/tbl/sec/eq/lst/thm/...). A bare `@smith2006` has no matching prefix, so it falls through and is emitted as literal text. The corpus only ever uses the bracketed form.
- **Proposed better:** Extend the bare-`@` path: when a word-boundary `@key` is NOT a cross-reference prefix but IS a key in the loaded bibliography, render it as an in-text citation (numeric today; author-date 'Smith (2006)' once a style engine exists). Keep the existing word-boundary guard so emails and @-handles are untouched, and warn on a bare `@key` that resolves to neither an xref nor a bib entry.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the core, drop the warn. Render a word-boundary bare @key as a citation ONLY when it is a member of the loaded bibliography (add Bibliography::contains, or reuse format(key).is_some(), and thread bib membership into transform_html/rewrite_text). Feed it through the same cite_key closure so numbering and the References list stay unified. Leave every non-matching @word literal exactly as today, and emit NO warning for the bare form: the bracketed [@key] stays the explicit-intent signal that already triggers the strict broken-citation warning (render.rs:80-98), so the clean-break strict philosophy keeps its teeth in the closed/explicit namespace without manufacturing false positives in open prose (that is how you beat Quarto here, not just match it). Pin it: add a corpus assertion that a-star's @russell2022artificial renders as an anchor to #ref-russell2022artificial, plus a corpus invariant that no raw @bibkey literal survives rendering (closing the regression-net hole that let the a-star defect ship). Priority is medium under numeric styling (visible payoff is small until author-date lands), but bumped because it fixes an existing live defect. Defer @key [locator] and -@key suppression to the author-date era.
- **Tradeoffs:** The bare-`@` scanner must consult the bibliography to disambiguate a citation key from stray text, adding a lookup to the prose pass. Risk of false positives on prose that happens to write `@word`; the existing at_word_boundary guard plus a bib-membership check contains this. Under numeric styling the visible payoff is small until author-date lands. (skeptic-found downside: The warn-on-unresolved-bare-@ sub-clause is unsound and self-contradicting: the bib-membership gate is exactly what contains false positives on the render path, and the warn clause throws that protection away, re-opening the same problem as warning noise. Because is_cite_key_char (mod.rs:69) includes / . : +, a word-boundary scanner greedily consumes @media, @import, @font-face, @staticmethod, @angular/core, @types/node, and email-like @example.com into "keys" that resolve to neither xref nor bib, each firing a "warning" in exactly the tech-blog prose this tool targets. That replicates Pandoc/citeproc's known "reference not found" footgun rather than beating it. Second missed item: the entry's premise "the corpus only ever uses the bracketed form" is false. corpus/tech-blog/posts/a-star/index.qmd:32 has bare "@russell2022artificial" whose key is in that post's references.bib, so it already renders as literal text: a live defect the corpus test does not catch. Third: plumbing cost is understated. Bibliography exposes is_empty() but no contains(), and bib membership is not currently threaded into transform_html/rewrite_text (they receive only the cite_key closure and xrefs). Fourth: the fix covers only the bare key, not Pandoc's fuller bare grammar (@key [p. 33] locator, -@key author-suppression), which stay unsupported.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, server-side, read-only, corpus-pinnable, and it makes the tool MORE faithful to the Markdown/Pandoc substrate the owner committed to keeping.

### D73. Located broken-citation, duplicate-key, and missing-bibliography diagnostics wired to click-to-source (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** pandoc/citeproc emits a plain console warning for an unresolved citation ('reference not found') with no source location, duplicate .bib keys silently last-write-win (biblatex warns at LaTeX time, the CSL path is quiet), and there is no 'you cited but declared no bibliography' hint.
- **Critique:** Quarto's citation diagnostics are console-only and unlocated, so tracking a bad key back to its line is manual, and a duplicate .bib key can render the wrong reference with no signal at all.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto/Pandoc is a multi-format batch compiler. Citation resolution runs as a citeproc pass over an AST after Markdown parsing, where reliable source positions back to the original .qmd line are largely gone (citations can also be injected by filters and includes). A precise, clickable "line N of file F" only has meaning in a live HTML view backed by a warm server and a block model that carries sourcepos, which is exactly the architecture Pandoc deliberately does not have. A format-neutral stderr warning is the correct lowest common denominator: it works identically whether the target is HTML, LaTeX, or docx, and it never claims a location the AST cannot honestly supply. Mirroring BibTeX's historical last-wins on duplicate keys is also defensible: the .bib is user-owned input with decades-old semantics, so inventing new validation risks diverging from every other BibTeX consumer. Quarto's choice is the price of generality, not laziness; Taliesin can beat it only because it gave up multi-format and batch rendering to gain the block model plus warm preview.
- **Taliesin today:** Already better. A cited key absent from a non-empty bib produces a located Warning ('broken citation: @key') carrying the block file and line via key_loc/sourcepos (cite/render.rs:84-95), so click-to-source can jump to it. Duplicate bib keys warn ('duplicate bibliography key ... using the last definition', parse.rs:96). A separate diagnostic fires when citations exist but no `bibliography:` is declared (diagnostics/bibliography.rs). The broken-cite warning is deliberately suppressed when no bib exists to avoid noise before setup, and a shared is_cite_key_char predicate keeps the .bib parser and prose scanner from disagreeing and false-warning on keys like smith.2020.
- **Proposed better:** Hold this lead and extend it: surface these located warnings as clickable in-preview markers (not just dev-console lines) so a broken cite is fixable in one Alt-click, and add the same located treatment to any new nocite/CSL-JSON paths so the diagnostic quality does not regress as the feature set grows.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the status as taliesin-already-better; that verdict and the critique of Quarto are fair. But rewrite the proposed_better, because its headline (surface located warnings in-preview, not just console) is already implemented for the located broken-cite path (serve/mod.rs:987-993 plus client.js setDiagnostics render it as a clickable jump-to-source row with a code frame). The real forward work is threefold: (1) locate the two currently-unlocated diagnostics: point citations-without-bibliography at the first citation's line (cheap), and give the duplicate-key warning a location, accepting that this needs new per-entry line tracking in the .bib parser and click-to-source into a .bib file (still read-only navigation, so invariant-safe, but genuine new cost, so pin it with a corpus doc); (2) keep the roadmap guard the drafter got right: any future nocite or CSL-JSON path must emit the same located Warning shape so diagnostic quality does not regress; (3) do NOT add inline gutter markers in the reading view: the existing dev-menu diagnostics panel is already the correct "toggle/affordance" the entry's own tradeoff asks for. Impact is really low-medium (mostly hardening plus two small localizations), not medium.
- **Tradeoffs:** Surfacing warnings in-preview is client-UI work and must not clutter the reading view (needs a toggle or a diagnostics affordance). Otherwise this is a lead to preserve, not new risk. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal's headline (surface located warnings as clickable in-preview markers, "not just dev-console lines") is already shipped, so its premise is wrong. serve/mod.rs:987-993 forwards located doc.warnings as Diagnostics preserving file+line, and client.js:97-123 (setDiagnostics) renders each located diagnostic as a clickable button (tali-diag-loc) with a code frame that calls gotoSource, posting qmd-goto to the editor. The located broken-cite warning is therefore ALREADY a clickable in-preview jump-to-source row in the dev-menu diagnostics panel, not a console-only line. The genuinely-new reading of the proposal (inline block-anchored gutter markers in the reading view) is what the entry's own tradeoff argues against, and would duplicate the existing panel. Separately, the drafter misses the real remaining gap: the two OTHER diagnostics are still unlocated. The duplicate-key warning is a plain Vec<String> in parse.rs:96 with no file/line and no click target, and citations-without-bibliography is Warning::new in diagnostics/bibliography.rs with no location. Locating the duplicate-key case is the hard, unbudgeted one: the location that matters is a line in the .bib FILE, which parse.rs does not source-map (no per-entry line tracking) and which lives outside the sourcepos-carrying .tmd block model, so "the same located treatment" is not free.)
- **Invariant check:** Built on data-sourcepos and click-to-source, the load-bearing invariants themselves; HTML-only, read-only navigation, corpus-enforced (cite tests already pin the located-warning behavior).

### D74. Where do footnotes render: one gathered end-of-document section vs pushed to the margin as sidenotes from ordinary [^x] syntax (Quarto's reference-location: margin)? (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto exposes one YAML knob, reference-location, with values document (default, gathered at the end), section, block, and margin; a sibling citation-location does the same for [@cite] content. With reference-location: margin, ordinary [^x] footnote syntax is relocated into the right margin beside its numbered reference in HTML output (Tufte/Distill style), reusing the SAME .column-margin grid machinery that .column-margin/.aside divs use, so in Quarto footnotes-in-the-margin and author-written margin divs are ONE unified mechanism. The setting is also scoped per section/div. footnotes-hover: true additionally gives a hover popover on the reference marker.
- **Critique:** In Taliesin the two are disjoint mechanisms with no bridge. Ordinary [^x] footnotes can only go one place, the gathered end section; a margin note can only be produced by hand-rewriting the prose as a ::: {.sidenote} div, which throws away the auto-numbered superscript marker, the reference/backlink pairing, and the [^x] authoring affordance. An author who wants Tufte-style margin footnotes (a signature web-native reading feature, exactly the richer-live-HTML-behavior Taliesin aims for) cannot get there from footnote syntax at all. Worse, the gathered section block is emitted with sourcepos: String::new() and its per-note <li>s carry no data-sourcepos, so click-to-source on an end-note does not even reach the [^x]: definition line, a reverse-sync hole the margin path would be a chance to close.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format compiler, the exact thing Taliesin rejects, and that mandate makes reference-location: document (gathered end-notes) the only correct default: end-notes are the single footnote placement that renders identically across HTML, PDF/LaTeX, docx, and epub, so the lowest-common-denominator default survives every target while margin stays an opt-in for the HTML/Tufte case. On top of that, unifying footnotes-in-margin and author-written margin divs onto ONE .column-margin mechanism, driven by a single knob with four values (document/section/block/margin) plus a sibling citation-location for [@cite] and a footnotes-hover popover, is a genuinely elegant, discoverable, and more granular API than the proposed Taliesin first cut, which offers only a document-level end-vs-margin switch. Quarto's design is coherent and, on breadth (per-section/per-div scoping, citation parity), currently ahead of the proposal.
- **Taliesin today:** Two unrelated mechanisms. (1) [^name] footnotes: comrak gathers all definitions and render/mod.rs (~lines 613-626) appends ONE synthetic block id "qmd-footnotes" = <section class="footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><hr><ol>...</ol></section> at document end, after any References; the in-text marker is <sup class="tali-fnref"> linking to #fn-name (emit.rs:94), each <li> gets a backlink (emit.rs:141). The gathered block has empty sourcepos and the <li>s no data-sourcepos. Footnote references do get the hover link-preview card (taliInitLinkPreview, tests.rs:1527). (2) Margin notes: ::: {.sidenote} (aliases .marginnote/.column-margin/.aside) is a normal authored div, CSS-floated right above 73rem and degrading to an indented left-border aside below (base.css:593-610); it is a real block so click-to-source works, but it is never produced from [^x] syntax. No reference-location or citation-location key is recognized anywhere in the codebase.
- **Proposed better:** Add a strict-validated front-matter key reference-location: end (default) | margin (schema.rs, so a typo gets the did-you-mean click-to-source on-ramp) that flips footnote emission: instead of pulling every definition into the end <section>, render each footnote body as a .sidenote-styled block anchored beside its reference, reusing the EXISTING margin float infrastructure and its 73rem fallback so no new layout code is needed, and unifying the two mechanisms the way Quarto does. Keep the numbered <sup> marker in the body (unchanged). Beat Quarto on the two things Taliesin already owns: give each margin footnote block a real data-block-id AND a data-sourcepos pointing at the [^x]: definition line (closing the current reverse-sync hole so click-to-source lands on the note's source), and keep the hover link-preview card. Below the margin breakpoint the notes fall back to the same indented aside the sidenote CSS already emits, so mobile stays clean. Pin it with a new corpus doc (e.g. corpus/layout/margin-footnotes.qmd) exercising a [^x] footnote under reference-location: margin, its data-sourcepos, and the narrow-screen fallback.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship it, but sharpen and unbundle. (1) Split the reverse-sync fix out and land it first, regardless of margin mode: emit data-sourcepos on each gathered end-note <li> from its definition node's sourcepos; client.js already honors nested sourcepos via .closest, so this closes the current end-section hole with a few lines and its own corpus assertion. (2) For margin mode, commit explicitly to the note-as-its-own-block approach (a first-class block inserted after the paragraph holding the reference) so it keeps data-block-id + data-sourcepos and rides the diff, and scope the claim honestly to block-adjacency (Quarto-parity placement), not a positioning win; call out the clear:right cascade and per-paragraph-multi-footnote drift as known limits. (3) Handle numbering: when a note leaves the shared <ol>, synthesize its numeral so the margin note reads "1. ..." matching the superscript. (4) Keep the first cut document-level end-vs-margin only, and name the key reference-location for Quarto familiarity but note in the schema that section/block scopes and the sibling citation-location for [@cite] are deferred follow-ups so users are not surprised by the missing parity. (5) Pin with the proposed corpus doc, exercising the [^x] footnote under reference-location: margin, its data-sourcepos landing on the [^x]: line, and the sub-73rem fallback; the current corpus is still .qmd (the .tmd rename is unpushed), so corpus/layout/margin-footnotes.qmd is the right path today.
- **Tradeoffs:** More emission complexity: today definitions are cleanly hoisted out of the flow into one appended block; margin rendering must anchor each note next to the block that holds its reference, which is fiddly when one paragraph has several footnotes (float stacking) or when the reference sits inside a table/figure/callout with no margin room. Long footnotes overflow the 12rem margin column, so margin mode is only good for short asides; the end section has no width ceiling. A future print/PDF-from-HTML track paginates end-notes more predictably than floated margin notes, though that is a later derived track and does not touch the HTML-only invariant now. Scope creep risk: Quarto also offers section/block scopes and per-div overrides; the honest first cut is a single document-level end-vs-margin switch, with per-scope override left as a follow-up rather than shipped up front. (skeptic-found downside: The headline "beat Quarto by giving each margin note a real data-sourcepos" is largely an ORTHOGONAL win the drafter mis-attributed to margin mode. client.js:157 resolves Alt-click via el.closest("[data-sourcepos], [data-block-id]"), so a nested footnote <li> that simply carries its own data-sourcepos (derivable now from the definition node's sourcepos at mod.rs:248) would already be honored. The end-section reverse-sync hole is therefore closeable today as a tiny standalone fix, without shipping margin mode at all, which inflates margin mode's apparent value. Second, "reuse the existing float so no new layout code" only yields BLOCK-adjacency, not marker-adjacency: a floated note-block placed after the referencing paragraph aligns beside the paragraph (roughly Quarto-parity), and multiple footnotes in one paragraph cascade downward via clear:right and drift away from their markers, so this is parity, not "beat." Third, there is an unacknowledged approach fork: a per-note first-class block (needed for the reverse-sync claim) forfeits precise marker-adjacent placement, while an inline Tufte-style span at the marker gets placement but lives inside the paragraph block and so lands click-to-source on the paragraph, not the [^x]: line; the drafter assumes both fall out of one float and they do not. Fourth, pulling each note out of the shared <ol> drops the automatic list numbering, so each standalone margin note must synthesize its own leading number (the <li> body carries none today); "keep the numbered <sup> unchanged" addresses only the in-text marker, not the note's own numeral.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: pure HTML/CSS layout reusing the existing float, no new output format. Single read-only surface: the note is still authored as [^x] in the .tmd source; preview never writes back. Keep-Markdown: no syntax divergence, ordinary [^x] footnotes plus one YAML key, exactly the layer-above-syntax mandate. Click-to-source: each margin footnote is a real block carrying data-block-id + data-sourcepos, and this path FIXES the current end-section reverse-sync gap by mapping the note to its [^x]: line. Block-level incremental: every margin note is a first-class block so the diff swaps it like any other. Warm server: a render-time placement change with zero added startup cost. Corpus-plus-roadmap: shipped pinned by a new corpus doc that is the arbiter of done.

### D75. Whether to support nocite / @* to include uncited entries in the reference list (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Supports `nocite:` in front matter to add references that appear in the bibliography WITHOUT an in-text citation, and `nocite: '@*'` to dump the entire bibliography. This is how you build a 'further reading' section or a whole-bibliography reading-list page.
- **Critique:** nocite is niche, but 'further reading' lists and whole-bibliography pages are real single-author blog patterns, and there is currently no way to surface an entry that is not cited in prose. It is also cheap to add.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** nocite/@* is not a Quarto invention or a niche indulgence: it is the one mechanism by which a citation pipeline decouples "what appears in the reference list" from "what is cited inline," and that decoupling is a genuine, long-standing genre need. LaTeX has had \nocite{*} for decades; Pandoc citeproc exposes the same via a `nocite` metadata field; Quarto simply inherits it for free (citeproc already runs). It unlocks three legitimate patterns at zero marginal engineering cost: (1) an annotated bibliography / reading-list page where nothing is cited inline yet everything must be listed, (2) a "works consulted / further reading" appendix, (3) building a whole-.bib index page from a shared library. Because it is a metadata key, it never touches prose syntax and it is a convention authors migrating from Pandoc/LaTeX already know. Removing it would silently break existing documents, and there is no cheaper alternative that produces an uncited entry in the list. For a general document compiler, keeping a standard, free, backward-compatible Pandoc affordance is unambiguously correct.
- **Taliesin today:** Not supported. The reference list is built strictly from keys encountered while transforming prose (the `order` vector in cite/render.rs); an entry never cited never appears. `nocite` appears nowhere in the codebase, and `@*` has no meaning.
- **Proposed better:** Add a `nocite:` front-matter key listing extra `@key`s (and `@*` meaning all entries) that get appended to the reference `order` after the cited keys, with no in-text marker emitted. Small, additive, native; pins a 'reading list' corpus doc.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature (Quarto is not right to leave Taliesin without any way to surface an uncited entry), but re-scope it in two tiers instead of shipping it as one "small additive key." Tier 1 (genuinely additive, ship first): support `nocite:` as a list of explicit `@key`s appended to `order` after the cited keys, with no in-text marker; route a nocite key missing from the .bib through the existing broken-citation warning; add `nocite` to KNOWN_KEYS + regen the schema via bless; thread the list into `cite::process`; pin a reading-list corpus doc. This is deterministic and clean. Tier 2 (gated on a real change): `@*` MUST first make the Bibliography preserve BibTeX source order (replace the HashMap ordering dependence with an insertion-ordered structure or a key-order sidecar) so output is reproducible and the corpus pin is stable. Separately, decide the numbering semantics deliberately: for a whole-bibliography / further-reading page, render nocite entries as an UNNUMBERED "Further reading" grouping rather than continuing the IEEE [N] sequence that has no in-text referent. Only after those two decisions is `@*` safe to enable.
- **Tradeoffs:** `@*` against a large shared .bib dumps everything, a deliberate but easy-to-misfire footgun. Adds a front-matter key that strict validation and schema.rs must cover with did-you-mean. Numbering semantics (nocite entries numbered after cited ones) must be specified. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal calls the whole thing "small, additive," but that is true only for the explicit-@key form. `@*` is the trap: it is the FIRST place in the codebase that would iterate `Bibliography.entries`, which is a std `HashMap<String, Entry>` with randomized (per-run, SipHash-seeded) iteration order. So a whole-bib reading list would reshuffle its reference order on every build. The References block's content-hash html changes each rebuild, forcing a spurious re-diff of that block, and, worse, a corpus doc pinned on `@*` would be FLAKY, undercutting the corpus-as-arbiter net. Making `@*` reproducible therefore requires preserving BibTeX source order in the Bibliography (HashMap -> insertion-ordered / a parallel key-order Vec), which is a parse-layer change, not a pure front-matter add. Second missed wrinkle: Taliesin's reference formatting is IEEE-NUMERIC ([N]). Appending uncited entries as [8], [9], [10] with no in-text [N] anchor pointing to them reads oddly (a numbered list whose tail numbers appear nowhere in prose). A "further reading" page really wants an UNNUMBERED rendering, a design decision the proposal leaves unspecified beyond "numbered after cited ones." Minor thirds: `process()` must be re-plumbed to receive the nocite list; nocite keys absent from the .bib should route through the existing broken-citation warning; and an unknown `nocite` value wants the strict did-you-mean/click-to-source treatment.)
- **Invariant check:** Additive, HTML-only, server-side, no write-back, corpus-pinnable. Prose syntax unchanged. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is broken (HTML-only, read-only single surface, prose syntax all untouched: `@*` lives in YAML front matter, not prose). But as-scoped there is a soft collision with the corpus-plus-roadmap invariant: `@*`'s nondeterministic HashMap iteration order makes any corpus doc that pins it flaky, so the corpus cannot cleanly arbitrate "done" until BibTeX source order is made deterministic. That determinism fix is thus a prerequisite, not an optional polish.)

## Math rendering

### D76. Render math to static HTML at build/parse time (server-side KaTeX) instead of shipping a client-side MathJax that runs in the browser (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's HTML default is html-math-method: mathjax, which injects a script tag pointing at MathJax v3 on cdn.jsdelivr.net (tex-mml-chtml.js). The browser downloads ~1 MB of JS plus CHTML fonts on demand, then walks the DOM and typesets every $...$/$$...$$ after the page has already painted. The alternative html-math-method: katex is still client-side: it loads KaTeX plus its auto-render extension from CDN and typesets in the browser.
- **Critique:** Client-side typesetting means a network round trip (broken offline and on file://), a flash of raw TeX source before MathJax runs, and a visible layout shift as boxed equations replace the placeholder. On a math-heavy page MathJax's DOM walk is the dominant cost of first paint, and it re-runs on every reload with nothing cached across edits.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general multi-format compiler facing an unbounded LaTeX input surface and an unknown reader/AT context, so defaulting to the most capable and most accessible renderer (with the author free to opt into faster, narrower ones) is a defensible, not naive, choice. MathJax v3 gives out of the box: full amsmath (align, gather, cases, multi-line) with automatic document-wide equation numbering plus \eqref cross-references, \require and custom macros loaded at runtime, mhchem chemistry, AsciiMath and MathML input, and a genuinely strong accessibility stack KaTeX does not match (the assistive-technology menu with on-demand speech, interactive subexpression exploration, collapsible math, and Braille). Client-side typeset also re-lays-out to the reader's zoom and container. For a tool that cannot predict what LaTeX authors will write or what AT context readers use, shipping the maximal standards-oriented engine and treating the CDN/FOUT/first-paint cost as an acceptable, opt-out-able default is a coherent bet, and browser caching historically amortized the CDN download across the many sites pinning the same jsdelivr MathJax URL (though cross-origin cache partitioning has since eroded that).
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/src/math.rs renders each fragment to static HTML+MathML with the `katex` crate 0.4.6 in an embedded JS engine (JS context reused per thread, ~1 ms/expr, no process spawn). emit.rs and render/mod.rs call crate::math::render at parse time so the emitted block already contains final .katex markup; no client JS ships. The only client-side asset is KaTeX's stylesheet for glyph fonts (page.rs).
- **Proposed better:** Keep the server-side static-render model as the permanent default; it is the correct answer for an HTML-only, offline-first, warm-server tool. No change needed beyond documenting it as a deliberate divergence in the corpus and roadmap.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep server-side static KaTeX as the permanent, non-negotiable default: it is the correct answer for an HTML-only, offline-first, warm-server tool and it is already load-bearing (render/mod.rs, emit.rs, page.rs verified; math blocks carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos, memoized so an edit is a hashmap hit on unchanged math). Sharpen the entry's tradeoffs rather than its recommendation: (a) fix the reflow claim, KaTeX scales with font-size, the real gap is mobile line-breaking of long display math, which is near-parity with MathJax; (b) state the a11y tradeoff honestly, MathML is emitted so screen readers still read the equation, only MathJax's interactive speech/exploration menu is not reproduced; (c) credit Taliesin's own `{#eq-x}`/`@eq-x` numbering as the equivalent of \eqref, narrowing the true coverage gap to intra-align per-line numbers plus a handful of macro packages (mhchem, physics). Optional consistency follow-up worth a backlog line: katex is configured throw_on_error=false, so a malformed expression renders in red inline; for a tool that otherwise flags unknown keys with did-you-mean, consider surfacing a math parse warning through check.rs so broken math is caught, not silently reddened. No new corpus doc is required (13 display-math docs already pin this); a doc explicitly exercising `@eq-x` would tighten the pin.
- **Tradeoffs:** KaTeX's macro/environment coverage is narrower than MathJax (see the align/eqref and macros entries), and static output cannot re-flow to a user font-size preference the way a client engine re-typesets. Both are acceptable given HTML-only scope. (skeptic-found downside: Two things the tradeoffs section gets wrong or omits. (1) The font-size claim is inaccurate: KaTeX is em-based, so its output DOES scale with the reader's font-size/zoom; the real residual is that KaTeX does not auto-linebreak long display equations for narrow (mobile) viewports, and MathJax barely does either, so this is close to a wash rather than a Quarto win. (2) The accessibility gap is understated: the entry only mentions reflow, but the actual loss is MathJax's interactive AT stack (on-demand speech, subexpression exploration, Braille). To keep the audit fair, note that KaTeX's default output is htmlAndMathml, so a screen reader still gets the equation via the emitted MathML; what is lost is the interactive exploration menu, not baseline AT access. Also, the entry lists \eqref/numbering as an open loss, but Taliesin already ships its own numbering layer: mod.rs labelled_display_eq/emit_equation turns `$$ ... $$ {#eq-x}` into a numbered equation and registers `@eq-x` cross-refs (pinned in corpus/posts/fourier-transform and Kruskal-Wallis-test), so document-wide numbering is solved the Taliesin way; the residual gap is only per-line numbering inside a single multi-line align block.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (renders to HTML markup, no parallel format); preview stays read-only (render is pure source->HTML); Markdown $/$$ syntax kept; each math block still carries data-block-id + data-sourcepos so click-to-source and block-level diff work; server-side render fits the warm-server model with zero per-edit browser typeset cost.

### D77. Memoize rendered math in a process-global cache so a live-preview save re-typesets only the edited expression, not the whole page (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** MathJax (or client KaTeX) re-scans and re-typesets the entire document on every reload; there is no cross-render cache. Quarto has no warm preview that preserves already-typeset equations, so each `quarto preview` refresh pays the full typeset cost again.
- **Critique:** For a doc with hundreds of expressions, re-rendering all of them on every keystroke-triggered save would cost hundreds of ms (KaTeX ~1 ms each), which directly fights the load-bearing 'no per-edit startup cost' goal.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a batch, multi-format compiler whose PRIMARY artifact is the final rendered document; `quarto preview` is a convenience wrapper around that same batch render, not a bespoke live-edit loop. Three defenses follow. (1) Statelessness is correctness-by-construction: rendering math from scratch every time means there is zero cache-coherence surface, no memory growth, no eviction policy, and none of the aliasing bugs a process-global memo invites (the very macro-aliasing hazard the entry itself has to guard against). Quarto trades a client-side cost it does not care about for the elimination of an entire bug class. (2) Format portability forces the choice: the same document renders to HTML, PDF (LaTeX), and more, so math must be produced per-backend; a memo keyed only on (latex, display) would be actively wrong the moment the same expression is emitted for two formats. A tool with Quarto's scope CANNOT safely share Taliesin's memo; Taliesin can only do this because it is HTML-only and KaTeX-only with fixed options. (3) The cost lands on the browser, off the server's critical path, and only on reload; and Quarto's DEFAULT is MathJax, chosen for coverage and robustness (full macro/extension support, right-click MathML/TeX, assistive-tech menu) rather than speed. Quarto also already caches the genuinely expensive work (computational cells via `freeze`); it declines to cache per-expression typesetting precisely because that work is cheap, client-side, and amortized. So Quarto's non-caching is a rational consequence of being a stateless multi-format compiler, not an oversight.
- **Taliesin today:** math.rs holds a bounded (8192-entry) FIFO cache keyed on (latex, display_mode), shared across a site's pages for the life of the process. After the first render, every unchanged expression on a save is a hashmap hit; only the block being edited re-renders. Eviction drops oldest-inserted entries one at a time rather than clearing the warm set. Verified by tests cache_evicts_oldest_first_and_stays_bounded and memoized_render_is_stable_and_mode_keyed.
- **Proposed better:** Keep as is. One guardrail for the future: if per-document math macros land (see user-macros entry), the cache key must gain the macro-set hash so two docs with different \newcommand definitions cannot alias the same (latex, display) entry.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the memo; the status "taliesin-already-better" is correct and sound as shipped (fixed KaTeX Opts make (latex, display) a complete key today, and the expensive eval stays outside the lock). Sharpen the forward guardrail from "add a macro-set hash" to a principle: the cache key must include a hash of the FULL effective KaTeX options set (macros are just one member), AND math rendering must stay a pure function of source, meaning any future macro support must resolve macros to a declared, order-independent, document-level set passed by value, never accumulated statefully across expressions. Also state the mechanism precisely: the memo makes the SERVER-side whole-document re-render cheap for math (every expression is re-rendered on each save, all but the edited one are hashmap hits); the block-level diff is a separate mechanism that limits what the BROWSER receives. Leave FIFO as-is (documented, intended). Note that correctness here is pinned by the two unit tests, not a corpus doc, which is appropriate because a cache is transparent to rendered output and cannot be regression-pinned by a corpus render; the user-visible math feature it accelerates is what the corpus pins.
- **Tradeoffs:** The cache is unbounded in identity but bounded in size, so a burst of >8192 distinct expressions evicts the oldest; that is the intended FIFO behavior. Adding macros to the key slightly lowers hit rate. (skeptic-found downside: The guardrail is under-specified in two ways the drafter missed. (1) Macros are only one of several KaTeX `Opts` that would alias if made configurable: `strict`, `trust`, `output` (html/mathml/both), `fleqn`, `leqno`, `min_rule_thickness`, `max_size`, `max_expand` all change output for the same latex. The key should hash the FULL effective options set, not just the macro set, so any future config toggle is covered by construction. (2) The deeper soundness risk: the memo is sound ONLY because KaTeX render is a PURE function of (latex, opts). A per-document macro-set hash does NOT rescue it if macros accumulate statefully across expressions (KaTeX mutates its `macros` map on `\gdef`/`\global\def`, so expression N can depend on 1..N-1). Under that model two identical `\x` fragments can mean different things, and a static per-doc hash would return a stale hit. The real invariant to preserve is: macros must be a declared, order-independent, document-level set fed as a value into every render, with stateful cross-expression `\gdef` forbidden (or the memo bypassed for such docs). Minor extras: FIFO (not LRU) evicts hot early-inserted expressions first past the cap, hurting hit rate for reused notation in >8192-expression docs (acceptable, not worth LRU's touch-on-hit complexity); and the stated "high" impact is density-conditional (near-zero benefit for a handful of equations).)
- **Invariant check:** Pure function of source, preview stays read-only; block-level incremental updates are exactly what the memo enables (only the diffed block re-renders); warm-server model preserved; HTML-only and Markdown syntax untouched.

### D78. Let the author define reusable math macros (\newcommand) once and have them apply to every expression in the document (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto (via MathJax or its KaTeX method) honors document-level \newcommand/\def and include-in-header macro blocks, and MathJax keeps those definitions in scope for every subsequent equation on the page. An author defines \R, \E, \argmax once and uses them everywhere.
- **Critique:** Taliesin renders each $...$ as an isolated katex::render call with a fixed Opts that sets only display_mode and throw_on_error. No macros dictionary is passed, so a \newcommand in one block does not persist to later blocks, and there is no front-matter macros: key. A math-heavy single author (the exact target user) currently repeats full expansions everywhere.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto renders HTML math CLIENT-SIDE (MathJax by default, KaTeX by option) in a single shared page context, so macro persistence is a free, zero-config emergent property, not a feature anyone had to build. The author defines \R once (in front matter via include-in-header, OR just inline in a $$ block) and every later equation on the page sees it, because one JS engine processes all the math with a shared macro table in document order. This exactly matches the LaTeX mental model (\newcommand where you like, in scope thereafter), needs no new config key to learn, and gives power users the full MathJax/KaTeX config surface through include-in-header. The costs Quarto pays (a client-side JS engine, a flash of unrendered TeX, HTML that is not offline-pure) are ones it accepts deliberately because it is a multi-format compiler where a per-page shared math engine is the norm. Within that architecture, Quarto's choice is coherent and arguably more author-friendly than any declarative map. The gap the entry names is not a Quarto defect: it is the price Taliesin pays for its own deliberate, better-for-HTML choice (server-side isolated KaTeX to static HTML+MathML, no client JS, memoized), and that isolation is precisely what drops the free persistence.
- **Taliesin today:** math.rs render_uncached builds katex::Opts::builder().display_mode(display).throw_on_error(false) with nothing else; the `macros` option of katex::Opts is never set. Front-matter parsing (frontmatter.rs) has no macros key, and the strict validator would flag one today.
- **Proposed better:** Add a front-matter macros: map (name -> LaTeX expansion), parse it in frontmatter.rs, register it in schema.rs so the strict validator accepts it, thread it into katex::Opts.macros, and fold a hash of the macro set into the memo cache key in math.rs so two docs with different macros never alias. This is a clean, KaTeX-native feature (Opts already supports macros) and a high-value quality-of-life win for the target user.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship it, high value and no invariant broken, but change the design and sharpen the plumbing. (a) Prefer a `macros:` block-literal scalar of raw LaTeX \newcommand/\def lines over a name-to-expansion YAML map: it matches the author's LaTeX muscle memory, dodges the YAML hash-comment and brace/backslash quoting traps, and keeps ONE schema key with a string value (no open-map child-key linting problem). Parse those lines into the katex Opts.macros HashMap. If the map form is kept instead, type it as an open string-to-string object in the schema and explicitly exempt it from child-key did-you-mean. (b) Mechanism precision: add "macros" to KNOWN_KEYS in frontmatter.rs (the load-bearing strict-warn path), update the schema.rs override, and regenerate the committed tali-frontmatter.schema.json so frontmatter_schema_matches_committed passes. (c) Thread the macro set to all three math::render sites and widen the memo Key to (latex, display, macros_hash) so cross-page renders of the same fragment under different macros never alias. (d) Make the block-id-stable-but-html-changed path explicit as a POINT IN FAVOR: because block id hashes only block source (mod.rs:1521) while diff.rs compares html, editing macros correctly re-renders unchanged-source math blocks via Update ops, so the incremental model already handles it. (e) Corpus pin must prove the two things that fail today: one macro DEFINED in front matter and USED across multiple separate blocks, plus an edit to the macro re-rendering downstream blocks. Frame the win honestly: not literal Quarto parity (in-body define-anywhere stays unsupported) but a cleaner, declarative, strict-validated, offline-static alternative that beats Quarto's order-dependent leak-prone in-body model.
- **Tradeoffs:** The memo key grows (latex, display, macros-hash), marginally lowering cross-doc hit rate. Macros defined inline in the body (a bare \newcommand in a $$ block) still would not persist unless separately harvested; the clean answer is front-matter-only macros, which slightly diverges from LaTeX authors' habit of defining in-body. (skeptic-found downside: Three edges the drafter missed. (1) YAML hostility: a front-matter name-to-expansion map collides with YAML syntax. A value like \left\lVert #1 \right\rVert silently truncates at the space-hash (YAML comment), and multi-arg macros need #1 forms that force the author to quote every expansion. Quarto sidesteps this because macros are written in raw LaTeX, not YAML. (2) Open-map linting trap: unlike every other nested Taliesin config key (theorems.*, etc.) which has a FIXED child-key allowlist run through did-you-mean, macros is an OPEN map whose children are arbitrary user names (\R, \E). The strict validator (validate_child_keys) must be explicitly EXEMPTED for this key, or it flags every macro name as an unknown child key. (3) Threading cost and an in-body asymmetry: macros must reach all THREE math::render call sites (emit.rs:92, mod.rs:428, mod.rs:1664) and be carried into the per-block emit context, not merely dropped into Opts, and the memo Key must widen from (String,bool). And the front-matter-only answer leaves a confusing asymmetry Quarto does not have: a bare \newcommand renders fine when USED inside its own $$ block (a self-contained fragment) but silently red-errors when reused in a LATER block, so authors will hit works-here-fails-there.)
