- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; front-matter is source the author edits, preview stays read-only; keeps Markdown + YAML front-matter substrate; math blocks keep data-block-id/sourcepos; warm-server memo preserved (key includes macro hash); corpus-plus-roadmap: pin a doc using macros:; strict validator stays strict once the key is schema-registered.

### D79. Inline KaTeX fonts as data URIs for a zero-network self-contained page, and decide whether to subset the 364 KB font payload per page (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's default MathJax loads fonts from CDN. embed-resources: true (self-contained) can bundle the math assets, but the MathJax bundle is large and the default posture is network-dependent. Quarto does not subset math fonts to the glyphs a given document uses.
- **Critique:** Taliesin already beats Quarto on offline (no CDN at all), but its own decision has a cost worth naming: the build inlines all 20 woff2 faces as base64 into one stylesheet (crates/core/build.rs produces a 364 KB katex-inlined.css), and page.rs ships that whole blob whenever body contains class="katex. A post with a single inline x^2 pays the full 364 KB of Caligraphic, Fraktur, AMS, etc. that it never renders.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The critique's facts are accurate and verified (ship gate is one boolean on class="katex" at page.rs:259, the whole ~361 KB const inlines at page.rs:104, so a lone x^2 really pays for Fraktur/AMS/Caligraphic it never renders), but it is not steelmanned. It frames Quarto as merely network-dependent-and-large and omits Quarto's real structural advantage. Strongest case FOR Quarto: its CDN MathJax fonts load from a stable shared URL, so a browser caches them ONCE and reuses that cache across every page of the site and across every other MathJax site the reader visits; on a returning reader or a multi-page math site Quarto's font byte cost amortizes toward zero, and MathJax lazily materializes only the glyphs it lays out. Taliesin made the opposite trade: it inlines ALL css (base, dark, site, katex) into every page (page.rs:157) with no external shared stylesheet, so a 5-page math book re-embeds the same ~361 KB five times with zero cross-page caching. Quarto keeps offline embed-resources opt-in precisely because most authors publishing online benefit from cache-once. Taliesin wins decisively on first-load-offline-single-file, but Quarto's posture is genuinely more byte-efficient on repeat views and multi-page sites. The per-page cost the entry laments is one Taliesin's own inline-everything choice created, not a Quarto failing. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** build.rs base64-inlines every assets/katex/fonts/*.woff2 (300 KB of fonts) into katex.min.css at build time, producing katex-inlined.css (KATEX_CSS in mod.rs). page.rs:259 gates shipping on `body.contains("class=\"katex")`, so math-free pages pay zero, but any math page gets the entire inlined stylesheet. woff2 only (no woff/ttf fallback shipped).
- **Proposed better:** Add a per-page glyph-subsetting pass: after render, scan the emitted KaTeX markup for which font-family classes actually appear (mathnormal, mathbf, AMS, Caligraphic, Fraktur, Script, etc.) and inline only those faces' data URIs, or better, subset each woff2 to the glyph coverage the page uses. A cheap first cut is family-level pruning (drop unused faces); a full cut is glyph-level subsetting. Gate it behind the existing ship_katex path so it stays a build-time, pure transform.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep a NARROWED version. Ship family-level face pruning as a BUILD-only, render-time transform: precompute the 20 data-URI @font-face blocks at build time, and per page emit base KaTeX CSS plus only the faces whose KaTeX classes appear in the body; keep preview shipping the full set so live editing never triggers head mutation or FOUT. Drop glyph-level subsetting entirely (dependency weight and PUA-mapping fragility outweigh the marginal win). Fix the entry's framing: it is render-time not build-time, and it does not touch _freeze (which caches cell outputs, not CSS). Guard against silent under-shipping with a corpus test that renders a page exercising every KaTeX face and asserts each required woff2 is present, in addition to the proposed light-math page asserting a reduced payload. Also evaluate the cheaper, composable lever the entry missed: for `build <dir>` and `_site/` modes, emit a single shared external katex.css cached once per site (still offline over file:// with a relative href) instead of re-inlining per page; for math-heavy multi-page sites that beats subsetting and carries no class-coupling fragility, though it forks the current inline-everything stance so it is a design call, not free, and the self-contained single-file `build <file>` must still inline. Net: family-prune the build, cache-once the site, leave preview and the single-file build inlining the full set.
- **Tradeoffs:** Family-level pruning is easy but coarse; true glyph subsetting needs a woff2 subsetter dependency and per-page work (though cacheable by content hash like _freeze). Subsetting slightly complicates the 'one inlined stylesheet' simplicity and must run before the ship decision. For a single small equation the win is large; for a heavy page it approaches zero. (skeptic-found downside: Four costs the drafter missed. (1) It is NOT a build-time pure transform: the needed face set depends on the rendered body, so it must run at RENDER time per page and cannot stay the compile-time const KATEX_CSS; the "_freeze-cacheable" claim is a category error (freeze.rs caches cell EXECUTION outputs keyed by cumulative code hash, not per-page CSS). The right architecture is to precompute the 20 individual data-URI @font-face blocks once at build time, then per page concatenate the base 23 KB CSS plus only the needed faces, which is cheap but still render-time. (2) Silent-breakage risk: family pruning requires a hardcoded map from KaTeX span classes (mathnormal to Math-Italic, mathfrak to Fraktur, delimsizing/sizing to Size1-4, amsrm to AMS, mathbf to Main-Bold, etc.) to the 9 font families. Ship too FEW faces and math renders in a fallback serif with broken metrics, a worse failure than shipping too much, and delimiters/radicals/big operators (Size fonts) and \\text runs are easy to miss. A KaTeX version bump can rename classes and silently break it, so it needs a corpus test that exercises every face. (3) Preview hot path: the font set is a page-global property, not a per-block one, but the incremental protocol swaps body blocks, not the head <style>. Dynamically subsetting as the author types math would force head mutation and a font-stylesheet swap/FOUT on relevant edits, fighting block-level incremental and no-per-edit-cost. The sane resolution is to subset only in `build` and keep the full set in preview, which the entry never states. (4) The single-author corpus already ships theorem environments, so math-heavy pages use AMS/Script/Caligraphic/Size/bold and see near-zero win; the payoff concentrates on math-LIGHT prose pages. Glyph-level subsetting (the "full cut") needs a woff2 subsetter dependency and must map KaTeX's PUA glyph slots, is fragile, and buys little over family pruning, so it should be dropped from scope.)
- **Invariant check:** Stays HTML-only and fully offline (still data URIs, no network); pure source->HTML transform so preview stays read-only; does not touch data-block-id/sourcepos on math blocks; subsetting is deterministic so it can be _freeze-cached in the warm-server model; corpus can pin it with a light-math page asserting a reduced payload.

### D80. Scope equation numbers to the chapter in book projects (Equation 2.1) rather than a flat per-page counter (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** In a Quarto book with number-sections/crossref chapter numbering, a labelled equation renders as 'Equation 2.1' (chapter.counter) and @eq-x resolves to that qualified number, matching how figures, tables, and theorems are numbered book-wide.
- **Critique:** Taliesin already gives theorems a number-within: chapter mode but does not extend it to equations, so a book with both would show 'Theorem 2.3' next to 'Equation 5', an inconsistency an author will notice immediately.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto exposes no per-type number-within at all, and that is the point. In a book, chapter-qualified crossref numbering (Figure 2.1, Table 2.3, Equation 2.4, Theorem 2.5) is a single automatic consequence of the book structure plus number-sections, applied uniformly to every crossreferenceable family at once. Chapter scoping is treated as a property of the document's PLACE in the book, not of any one family, so there is exactly one source of truth and the families can never drift out of sync. This also matches the reader's model (every '2.x' belongs to chapter 2) and the printed-book convention. Taliesin's per-family 'theorems: number-within: chapter' key is the anomaly; the thing worth copying is Quarto's uniform, structure-driven scoping, not a second per-family knob for equations.
- **Taliesin today:** render/mod.rs uses a flat `eq_count: usize` reset per page (line 235), incremented only for $$ ... $$ {#eq-x} blocks, emitting (N) via emit_equation. The theorems path honors NumberWithin::Chapter (fm_extract.rs parse_theorem_config), but there is no equivalent for equations; frontmatter THEOREM_KEYS covers number-within only for theorems.
- **Proposed better:** Reuse the existing chapter-scope machinery: when the book config sets number-within: chapter (or a new equations: number-within: chapter key), prefix eq_count with the chapter number so emit_equation renders (2.1) and register_xref stores '2.1', so @eq-x cross-refs and the site/xref.rs cross-page index show the qualified number.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the goal (chapter-qualified crossref numbers in books) but reframe the mechanism and scope. Do not add an 'equations:' key and do not overload 'theorems:'. Make chapter-scoping a single book-level switch, or derive it from 'this page is a numbered book chapter', that scopes ALL crossref families uniformly (figures, tables, equations, listings, theorems) in one pass, reading the same chapter number already threaded via site::chapter_for. The equation piece is genuinely trivial (chapter is already in scope at render/mod.rs:436, so emit_equation and its register_xref can prefix 'C.n'), but ship it as one family of the unified change, never alone. Migrate the existing 'theorems: number-within: chapter' onto the unified flag and keep it working as a back-compat alias so there stays exactly one source of truth for the scoping decision. Pin it with a two-chapter book corpus doc that contains a figure, table, equation, listing, AND theorem in a numbered chapter and asserts every one renders '2.x', plus a single-page doc asserting flat numbering is unchanged. The new key must be schema-registered so the strict validator still flags typos.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adds a config surface (either overload the existing number-within or add an equations: block, which the strict frontmatter validator must then whitelist). Standalone single-page docs are unaffected. Small risk of double-defining the chapter-scope source of truth if theorems and equations read it separately. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal fixes equations only, but figures, tables, and listings are ALSO flat per-page in Taliesin books (verified: fig_count/tbl_count/lst_count are per-page counters and register_xref stores the bare number; only section headings and opted-in theorems are chapter-scoped). So after this change a numbered chapter would render Theorem 2.3 and Equation 2.1 but Figure 5, Table 3, Listing 2. The inconsistency the entry names is moved, not removed. Worse, adding a separate 'equations: number-within: chapter' key entrenches the per-family fragmentation and is a footgun: an author must set N keys and gets a mismatched document if they set one family and forget another, which is the exact failure mode the entry is trying to eliminate. And note the inconsistency already exists WITHOUT equations, because theorem scoping is opt-in and off by default (NumberWithin defaults to None), so a default book today shows section 2.3 headings next to Figure 5 and Theorem 3.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; pure render-time numbering, preview read-only; Markdown $$ {#eq-x} syntax unchanged; equation block keeps data-block-id/sourcepos so click-to-source still lands on the source line; corpus-plus-roadmap: pin with a two-chapter book corpus doc; validator stays strict (new key must be schema-registered).

### D81. Support per-line numbering inside align environments and in-math \label/\eqref cross-references (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** With MathJax, Quarto can auto-number every line of a \begin{align} block and resolve \label{eq:x} plus \eqref{eq:x} inside the math itself, so a multi-line derivation gets (1),(2),(3) and prose can \eqref back to any line. This is a core MathJax capability Quarto inherits for math-heavy technical writing.
- **Critique:** KaTeX has no cross-expression equation registry: it cannot auto-number align lines and does not implement \eqref/\label. Taliesin's numbering lives entirely outside KaTeX (a wrapper (N) on the whole block), so a multi-line align renders as one un-numbered display block or, at most, one (N) for the entire block, and there is no way to reference an individual line.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's HTML default is MathJax, and MathJax maintains a page-global equation-label registry with a second typeset pass, so Quarto inherits LaTeX's exact AMS numbering semantics for free: `tags: ams` auto-numbers every non-starred display line, `\nonumber`/starred opts a line out, and `\label`/`\ref`/`\eqref` resolve anywhere in prose or even inside other math. Critically, the number gutter is laid out by the math engine itself in the same pass that computes the `&`-alignment columns, so the numbers and the alignment always agree and a 40-line derivation degrades uniformly. Zero custom code, full fidelity with a LaTeX author's muscle memory. For a math-heavy technical author this is a legitimately hard capability to give up, and it is the single strongest reason such an author stays on Quarto+MathJax.
- **Taliesin today:** bare_math_env (mod.rs:1634) renders \begin{env}...\end{env} as a single .tali-math-block with no number. labelled_display_eq only matches `$$ ... $$ {#eq-x}` and emits exactly one (N) for the whole block. KaTeX does support manual \tag{} inside, but there is no \eqref resolution and no automatic per-line numbering; the corpus (em-algorithm) uses starred align* precisely to stay unnumbered.
- **Proposed better:** Two-tier: (a) let an author put multiple $$ {#eq-a}, $$ {#eq-b} blocks and rely on the existing numbering (already works, just document it); (b) for genuine align numbering, post-process a labelled align block server-side, splitting on \\ to assign (N) per line and rewriting an in-prose {{< eqref eq-x >}} shortcode (or extend @eq-x) to the line number. Full LaTeX \eqref-inside-math is out of KaTeX's reach without a custom pre-pass, so scope it to a Taliesin-owned shortcode rather than emulating MathJax.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry (real gap, invariant-safe, medium impact) but revise the mechanism. Near-term, ship the zero-code answer and just document it: manual `\tag{}` inside a single `align`/`aligned` block gives numbered, aligned lines today, and `$$...$$ {#eq-x}` already numbers plus cross-references a whole display via `@eq-x`. For genuine per-line numbering, extend the EXISTING `@eq-x` two-pass registry rather than adding a `{{< eqref >}}` shortcode: a server-side pre-pass over a labelled align injects `\tag{N}` per numbered line (using a brace/environment-aware scan, never a raw `\\` split) and registers each line anchor into `xref_registry` so `@eq-a` resolves like any crossref. First verify KaTeX honors per-line `\tag` inside align; if it does not, scope this to whole-block `@eq-` numbering plus documented `\tag` and defer per-line auto-numbering, do not ship the fragile splitter. Do not emulate in-math `\eqref`: it is out of KaTeX's reach and the doc-level `@eq-` crossref is the invariant-respecting answer. Pin a new corpus doc; leave em-algorithm on `align*`. Note two accepted limitations: per-line refs still click-to-source at block granularity (sourcepos is block-level), and a global equation counter renumbers downstream blocks on edit exactly as `@fig-`/`@eq-` already do (consistent with existing behavior, not a new violation).
- **Tradeoffs:** Per-line align numbering by splitting on \\ is fragile (nested arrays, \\[2pt] spacing, \nonumber). A shortcode-based eqref diverges from the LaTeX \eqref an author may expect. Real risk of half-implementing a MathJax feature; may be better to accept manual \tag as the answer and just document it. (skeptic-found downside: Four things the drafter missed or understated. (1) KaTeX lays out an align's `&` columns and any number gutter internally as one unit, so "split on `\\` and assign (N) per line" either re-renders each line and loses cross-line alignment, or forces re-implementing column layout from outside KaTeX. The robust design the drafter never considered is to inject `\tag{N}` into each numbered line and let KaTeX place the numbers in-column (one block, alignment intact), pending verification KaTeX honors per-line `\tag` inside align. (2) The `{{< eqref >}}` shortcode cannot work as drafted and is redundant: shortcodes expand in a source pre-pass (`expand_shortcodes`) BEFORE equation numbers are assigned during block rendering (`eq_count`), so it could only emit a placeholder a later pass fills, which is exactly what the existing two-pass `@eq-x` registry (`register_xref` then `cite::process`) already does at the right time. Extend `@eq-x`; do not add a second crossref vocabulary. (3) Tier (a) is oversold: separate `$$ {#eq-a}` blocks cannot share `&` alignment, so they are a visually different result, not a numbered-align substitute. (4) `\\`-splitting is not merely "fragile at `\\[2pt]`" but semantically wrong whenever a line contains a nested `cases`/`pmatrix`/`array` `\\`, which is common in exactly this audience.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; server-side pre-pass keeps preview read-only; keeps Markdown/$$ syntax (a shortcode fits the kept {{< >}} layer); numbered lines still live in one block with data-block-id/sourcepos intact for click-to-source; corpus can pin an align-numbering doc; strict-validator-friendly since it is a shortcode not a new front-matter key.

### D82. Surface a malformed expression as a located build/preview diagnostic with click-to-source, not just a red box the reader sees (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** MathJax renders a parse error as red text inline in the browser at read time; there is no build-time or preview diagnostic channel that tells the author which source line is broken. The error is a runtime artifact for whoever opens the page.
- **Critique:** A reader-facing red box is a poor authoring signal: it does not point at the source line and it only appears once the page is loaded. For a fast edit loop the author wants the failure reported against the source immediately.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's pass-through of math to the render engine is a defensible multi-format decision, not negligence. (1) Renderer fidelity: the same $...$ source may target MathJax, KaTeX, or a LaTeX/PDF toolchain, each with its own macro set (\newcommand, physics, mhchem, per-format \def). If Quarto pre-parsed math with its own validator it would risk false positives/negatives that disagree with whatever engine actually renders the page; by deferring to the real engine at the real render site, the error the author sees is guaranteed to be the error the reader gets, with zero validator drift. (2) In-context locality: MathJax's red span is not truly unlocated. It appears exactly at the broken expression on the rendered page with a title/tooltip naming the cause, so for a human reading the page it is a precise, in-place signal. (3) It is the honest consequence of Quarto owning no math parser: Taliesin can afford a build-time located math diagnostic ONLY because it committed to a single engine (KaTeX) and HTML-only, i.e. it took exactly the format-agnosticism hit Quarto declined. Quarto's choice buys portability; Taliesin's buys authoring diagnostics. The critique that a reader-facing red box is a poor authoring channel (no source line, no machine-readable/CI channel, must visually scan the page) is fair and not a strawman; it only slightly understates that the red span is visually in-context.
- **Taliesin today:** math.rs runs KaTeX with throw_on_error=false (invalid expr becomes an inline red katex-error span; engine failure falls back to an escaped tali-math-error span). crates/core/src/diagnostics/math_render.rs then extracts each katex-error title= message from the block HTML and reports it as a located warning, and because the math sits in a block carrying data-sourcepos it is Alt-click navigable back to source. Verified by validate_math_flags_only_unparseable_katex_located.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Minor polish: the fallback tali-math-error span (engine-level failure) is not harvested by math_render.rs (which keys on the katex-error marker), so an engine failure shows to the reader but may not raise a located diagnostic; add a second marker scan so both failure classes surface in the dev-server diagnostics.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's core status (Taliesin genuinely beats Quarto here: check emits a located, file:line, sourcepos-anchored math diagnostic Quarto has no equivalent for in HTML), but fix two things before it goes in the catalog. (1) Correct the location claim: the located math diagnostic is a check / CI-gate artifact today, NOT a warm-preview overlay row, and Alt-click-a-rendered-block is the block-sourcepos property, not the channel that currently surfaces this warning. Drop the dev-server diagnostics / warm-server-dev-loop framing or make it true. (2) The real, higher-value decision is whether to run validate_math inside the live preview's compute_diagnostics so the warm loop gets the clickable jump-to-source math row the entry imagines. Present this as a genuine tradeoff, not a slam dunk: the deliberate design is cheap-warm-loop vs complete-check, and there is a strong noise argument for leaving it in check only, since while typing you transiently hold $\frac{ before finishing $\frac{a}{b}$, the inline red span is already the correct transient edit-time signal, and a per-keystroke jump-to-source row would flicker on every half-typed expression. If wired in, debounce to settle and dedupe. (3) Downgrade the second-marker polish sharply: the tali-math-error path is an engine-health failure, so if surfaced at all it should be ONE engine-failure diagnostic (KaTeX engine failed to render this page), never one contentless warning per block, and it should be flagged as unit-testable-only since no corpus .tmd can trigger it. As written, the polish is near-zero-value defensive code, so either cut it or reframe it as engine-health, not a symmetric second class of malformed-expression diagnostic.
- **Tradeoffs:** Harvesting the second marker is a tiny addition; risk is near zero. The diagnostic depends on KaTeX's error title text staying stable across crate upgrades (already noted as a documented coupling in math_render.rs). (skeptic-found downside: Two misses. First, the entry mislocates the whole benefit: validate_math is a check-only static validator (crates/server/src/check.rs lines 59/133). It is NOT run by either live server (serve/mod.rs and serve_site/mod.rs surface only front-matter errors, unresolved includes, kernel/executor diagnostics, doc.warnings, and validate_xrefs). So in the warm keystroke loop a broken $\frac{$ today produces exactly Quarto's outcome, a red katex-error span the reader sees and no clickable jump-to-source diagnostic row; the located math diagnostic exists only when you deliberately run check (a CI/pre-publish gate), not in the warm preview overlay the entry names. Second, the proposed second-marker harvest is weak on its own terms. The fallback tali-math-error span only fires when katex::render_with_opts returns Err, which with throw_on_error=false is an engine/environment failure (JS init/exception), not a per-expression syntax fault; those get caught and rendered as katex-error spans. So on a real engine failure EVERY math block emits a tali-math-error span, and a one-per-block harvest would misreport a single global engine failure as N separate this-line-is-broken warnings, each carrying only the contentless static title math render failed (yielding math failed to render: math render failed). The two markers are not the symmetric failure classes the drafter assumed: katex-error is per-expression and specific, tali-math-error is global-ish and detail-free, so they warrant different diagnostic UX, not the same block-loop scan.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; diagnostics are read-only reporting, preview never writes source; click-to-source is exactly the payoff (sourcepos-anchored math block); block-level model untouched; warm-server dev loop is where the diagnostic lands; corpus/tests already pin the located-warning behavior. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is breached (HTML-only, read-only preview, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, and block-level model are all untouched, and validate_math is a cheap string scan with no per-keystroke filesystem IO so warm-server latency is safe). Soft tension with corpus-plus-roadmap: the entry claims corpus/tests already pin the behavior, but the proposed tali-math-error branch cannot be pinned by any authorable .tmd, because an engine failure is environmental and not content-triggerable. Only a synthetic-HTML unit test can cover it, so this specific new branch lacks the corpus pin the invariant asks for, and it is near-dead defensive code for a path the corpus can never exercise.)

### D83. Decide whether to enable extended TeX packages (mhchem \ce{}, physics, cancel) that MathJax loads on demand (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's MathJax auto-loads extension packages such as mhchem (\ce{H2O}), physics, cancel, and color when the input uses them, so chemistry and physics notation just works without configuration.
- **Critique:** The vendored `katex` crate 0.4.6 does not enable KaTeX's mhchem or other contrib extensions, so \ce{} and similar commands fall through throw_on_error=false as a red katex-error span. An author writing chemistry or heavy physics macros hits a wall that Quarto does not have.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** MathJax v3 is a more complete TeX implementation than KaTeX, and its autoload extension turns that completeness into a zero-config guarantee: whatever command an author types, from any discipline (chemistry via mhchem, physics.sty operators, cancel, color, mathtools, bbox, and a long tail beyond), MathJax fetches and registers the needed package at render time. The tool author never has to anticipate a command set. A fixed server-side KaTeX build can only ever support what KaTeX itself implements plus whatever contrib extensions are compiled in, so it structurally trails MathJax on breadth forever. Taliesin's own live physics.sty gap (\dv, \pdv, \qty all render as a red error) is a concrete example of notation Quarto handles and Taliesin cannot. Quarto's choice buys universal coverage and future-proofing against unforeseen notation, a defensible default for a general multi-discipline tool.
- **Taliesin today:** math.rs sets no extension/trust options and the katex crate build does not bundle mhchem; \ce{...} renders as an error span. No corpus doc exercises chemistry notation, so this is currently an unpinned gap rather than a regression.
- **Proposed better:** Gauge real need first (the single author may never write \ce{}). If needed, either bundle KaTeX's mhchem extension into the embedded JS the katex crate runs, or pre-expand a small owned set of commands server-side. Do not add it speculatively; add it only when a corpus doc demands it, per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Revised recommendation:** Correct the entry's facts, then split it into three cases. (1) mhchem (\ce, \pu): already works server-side and offline via the katex 0.4.6 crate, which bundles and always loads mhchem.min.js. The correct corpus-plus-roadmap action is not "add if needed later" but "pin what already works now": add a tiny corpus doc exercising \ce{}/\pu{} so the accidental capability becomes a regression-protected one, guarding against a silent break on any future dependency bump or math-backend swap. This is cheap and net-positive regardless of how much chemistry the author writes. (2) \cancel, \textcolor, \braket/\ket/\bra: already work (KaTeX core), so basic quantum and colored notation is covered; drop these from the "gap" framing. (3) physics.sty operator macros (\dv, \pdv, \qty): the sole genuine gap versus Quarto's MathJax. Low value for this single author (the physics-adjacent corpus doc born-machines.qmd uses plain LaTeX plus core \ket, not physics.sty), so keep it an explicit open question and add support only if a physics-heavy corpus doc ever demands it. If it is ever needed, the katex crate cannot load physics.sty (KaTeX has no physics extension), so the realistic path is a small owned set of server-side macro pre-expansions, not a crate flag. Also remove the \trust attack-surface tradeoff, which does not apply to any of these extensions.
- **Tradeoffs:** mhchem adds JS weight to the embedded KaTeX and another surface to keep offline; enabling KaTeX \trust or extensions widens the attack surface for untrusted input (less relevant for a single-author tool). Low value unless the author actually writes chemistry. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal is built on a false premise and its main remedy is already shipped, so it inverts the real risk. Verified by rendering through the actual binary: the katex 0.4.6 crate unconditionally concatenates vendor/contrib/mhchem.min.js into the KaTeX engine (src/lib.rs JS_SRC, lines 47-63), so \ce{H2O}, \ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}, and \pu{123 kJ} already render correctly, server-side and offline, today. The drafter's option one (bundle mhchem into the embedded JS the crate runs) is therefore describing work the dependency already does. The genuine hidden problem is the opposite of the one stated: mhchem is an UNPINNED, undocumented, accidental capability. No corpus doc exercises it, so a future katex-crate bump, a backend swap, or a switch to a mhchem-less build would silently drop \ce{} with zero test failure. Deferring action until an author demands chemistry leaves a working feature exposed to silent regression. Two smaller misses: the entry lists \cancel and color as gaps, but \cancel, \textcolor, and \braket/\ket/\bra all render today because they are KaTeX core (the ONLY real gap is physics.sty macros like \dv/\pdv/\qty); and the tradeoffs note about widening attack surface via KaTeX \trust is a red herring, since mhchem registers ordinary math macros and needs no \trust at all.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (still server-side static render); offline preserved if the extension is bundled not CDN-loaded; preview read-only; Markdown/$ syntax unchanged; blocks keep data-block-id/sourcepos; explicitly gated on a pinning corpus doc so scope does not outrun the test net.

## Callouts, tabsets, and special content

### D84. Preserve active-tab / open-callout / within-panel reader state across incremental container Updates (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto has no incremental preview: every source change triggers a full page rebuild and browser reload, so there is no notion of preserving in-page UI state across an edit (it is simply lost on reload, which authors accept because a reload is expected).
- **Critique:** This is a Quarto non-feature, but it is exactly where Taliesin's live-loop goal creates a NEW bug that Quarto cannot have. Verified: a `.panel-tabset` container id is `make_id("div:.panel-tabset")`, hashed from the div ATTRS only (mod.rs make_id), so it is stable when you edit content inside a panel. The diff (diff.rs) then matches the container as an anchor whose html differs and emits a full `Update`; client.js applies it as `el.replaceWith(node)` (line 911), after which tabset.js re-inits and selects tab 0. So editing text inside panel 3 snaps the preview back to panel 1 on every save. The same replaceWith discards a reader-opened collapsible callout's `<details open>` state and any scroll position inside a panel.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's full-rebuild-plus-reload is the only preview contract that is simple, format-agnostic, and never wrong. Because the reloaded DOM is a pure function of source, an ENTIRE class of bugs (stale state, restored-the-wrong-tab, half-reconciled subtrees) cannot exist; there is nothing to key, clamp, or order. Quarto also compiles to many targets (PDF, docx, epub, revealjs, HTML), so a DOM-diff-plus-state-preservation layer would be an HTML-only investment that does not generalize, disproportionate for a multi-format Pandoc-lineage compiler whose author mental model is already save-equals-rebuild. Crucially, PARTIAL preservation is itself a leaky abstraction: a tool that keeps the active tab but silently drops a half-filled input, a video's playback position, or a spun-up WebGL scene is arguably more confusing than one that predictably keeps nothing, and browsers already restore window scroll on reload for free. So full reload is not laziness; it is the choice that refuses a whole bug class. Taliesin only earns the right to diverge because it is HTML-only (the multi-format objection evaporates) and its entire thesis is the sub-second incremental loop, which makes the leaky-abstraction cost worth paying if, and only if, the preserved-state surface is kept small and predictable.
- **Taliesin today:** No UI-state preservation on `Update`. `el.replaceWith(node)` is wholesale; tabset.js keys off `data-tabset-init` and always selects index 0; callout `<details>` open/closed is re-seeded from the server-side `collapse=` attribute, so a reader's manual toggle is dropped on any content Update to the enclosing container.
- **Proposed better:** In client.js, before `el.replaceWith(node)` for an Update whose target is (or contains) a stateful container, snapshot lightweight reader state keyed by the stable container `data-block-id`: active tab index (aria-selected), each `<details open>`, and panel scrollTop; after mounting `node`, restore it (clamped to what still exists). Because the tabset/callout container id is content-independent, this restoration is stable across edits. Optionally have tabset.js read a restored index instead of hardcoding 0.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but sharpen scope and keying. v1 preserves exactly two states across an incremental Update: active-tab index (read from aria-selected) and collapsible-callout open/closed (read from `<details open>`), each snapshotted from the live outgoing `el` before replaceWith and keyed by the stateful descendant's OWN stable data-block-id (query all `[data-block-id]` stateful containers inside the Update target, not just the target itself, since a parent Update, e.g. a callout wrapping a tabset, wipes nested containers too). After mounting the new node, match by data-block-id and restore, clamped to survivors (deleted tab falls back to index 0). Restore tab state by setting aria-selected/hidden/tabindex DIRECTLY on the new node synchronously right after replaceWith; drop the after-enhancers ordering assumption (tab state is pure DOM, independent of tabset.js listeners) and drop the optional tabset.js change (there is no index-0 hardcode to remove). Do NOT restore focus: in the single-editing-surface model the reader's focus is in the editor, so grabbing preview focus on every save would be wrong. Drop panel scrollTop from v1 (positional-key drift, low value, window scroll already handled by keepScroll). Pin it correctly: a static corpus tabset/collapsible doc can only fix the SERVER structure, so the actual behavior regression net must be a live-edit-harness (browser) assertion that edits inside tab 3 and asserts tab 3 stays selected, plus a callout-open assertion. Note the diff-level alternative (target the changed inner block instead of replacing the shell) as a later, cleaner optimization, not v1.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adds a small amount of client bookkeeping and an ordering assumption (restore must run after enhancers). Restoration can be wrong if the author deletes the tab/panel the reader was on (mitigated by clamping to first). Slightly complicates the otherwise-pure replaceWith path. (skeptic-found downside: data-block-id is a clean key only for CONTAINERS (each build_container call mints one, and collapsible callouts ARE containers, so their open-state keys cleanly). But reader state that lives on non-container DOM has no stable id: a panel's scrollTop and any nested non-container `<details>` can only be keyed by a POSITIONAL sub-key inside the container, which drifts the moment the author edits structure, reintroducing the exact restored-the-wrong-thing fragility the block-id keying was supposed to eliminate. So the honestly-preservable v1 is narrower than the entry implies: active-tab index (aria-selected) and collapsible-callout open-state, both of which key off a stateful descendant's OWN stable data-block-id; panel scrollTop should be dropped (speculative, low value, window scroll is already restored by keepScroll). Two smaller misses: (a) the entry's ordering assumption (restore must run after enhancers) is unnecessary for tab state, which is pure DOM attributes (aria-selected/hidden/tabindex) and can be restored synchronously right after replaceWith with no dependency on tabset.js re-init, so the self-flagged complication is avoidable; (b) the critique says tabset.js hardcodes index 0, but tabset.js never calls select() on init, the snap-to-first-tab comes from the server always emitting sel = i==0, so the fix must override server aria state on the new node, not patch a client hardcode that does not exist. A stronger architectural alternative the drafter did not raise: inner blocks inside a container already carry their own data-block-id/data-sourcepos (divs.rs:460), so the diff could descend into containers and emit an Update targeting the CHANGED INNER block rather than replacing the whole shell, which preserves ALL container state for free and shrinks the payload, at the cost of a bigger block-model change and still needing a whole-container Update for structural (heading-reclassification) edits.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; strictly read-only (it restores reader interaction state, never writes source and never touches the .tmd); keeps Markdown syntax; click-to-source preserved (container keeps its data-block-id/data-sourcepos through the Update); this DIRECTLY serves the block-level-incremental invariant by making incremental swaps non-destructive; warm server unaffected; pin with a corpus tabset doc plus a live-edit harness assertion.

### D85. Use native <details> for callout-collapse and code-fold instead of JS-driven Bootstrap collapse (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto renders collapsible callouts and `code-fold` blocks as Bootstrap components: a `.callout` with a `data-bs-toggle` header and a JS-managed `.collapse` region for callouts, and a `<details>` for code-fold. Callout collapse specifically depends on Bootstrap's collapse JavaScript and its `.collapsing` transition class.
- **Critique:** The callout collapse path needs the Bootstrap JS bundle loaded and initialized; with JS disabled or before hydration the callout body can be stuck hidden, and it does not expand naturally when the page is printed or saved to a single file. It also couples callout behavior to a large CSS/JS framework.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto already ships one Bootstrap bundle for its whole HTML widget family (navbars, tabsets, tooltips, accordions, offcanvas), so reusing Bootstrap `collapse` for callouts adds ZERO marginal payload and keeps callouts behaviorally and visually consistent with every other component on the page. In exchange it buys things native `<details>` does not give for free: a real animated height transition (the `.collapsing` class animates max-height, so open/close slides instead of snapping), automatic ARIA wiring (`aria-expanded`/`aria-controls`), programmatic control plus shown/hidden events, and `data-bs-parent` accordion grouping so opening one callout closes its siblings. It also sidesteps `<summary>` marker and phrasing-content quirks by not using disclosure semantics at all. And Quarto is a multi-format compiler: choosing a JS component for the interactive HTML target is deliberate, and the fact that Quarto DID pick native `<details>` for code-fold proves the choice is made per-feature, not out of Bootstrap dogma.
- **Taliesin today:** divs.rs emits `collapse=true` as `<div class="callout ... callout-collapse"><details><summary class="callout-title">...</summary><div class="callout-body">...</div></details></div>` (closed) and `collapse=false` as `<details open>`. code-fold (emit.rs, cell_numbered.rs) likewise emits `<details class="tali-code-fold">`. Both are pure native disclosure with zero JS; base.css only styles the summary cursor.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the native-<details> approach and make it a stated contract: every collapse affordance (callout, code-fold, collapsible proof) is a real `<details>`, so it works with JS off, expands for print via the existing `@media print { details { ... } }` hook, is keyboard/AT-native, and needs no framework. Add a corpus doc that renders a collapsed callout and a folded cell and asserts both are `<details>` (no `data-bs-*`).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the native-<details> contract as a genuine, catalog-worthy win over Quarto's Bootstrap callout-collapse (works JS-off, keyboard/AT-native, zero framework, zero marginal payload, click-to-source preserved because data-block-id/data-sourcepos ride the container). Sharpen three things. (1) Scope the win to CALLOUTS (and collapsible proofs); Quarto's code-fold is already native <details>, so present code-fold as parity, not a beat, and drop the title's implication that Quarto's code-fold is JS-Bootstrap. (2) Fix the print claim honestly: either delete "expands for print" or actually implement it, since no @media print details hook exists today and a closed <details> prints its body hidden; the robust fix is a tiny onbeforeprint pass that sets `open` on all <details> and restores on afterprint, which keeps interaction JS-free while making the print story true, pinned by a print-expand test. (3) Treat the corpus/test work as "add a NEGATIVE assertion that no data-bs-* is emitted" rather than net-new coverage, since the positive <details> tests already exist. Also note the residual tradeoffs the entry omits: no free height animation, find-in-page/deep-link into a collapsed region only auto-reveals on modern Chromium, and a block re-render resets reader-opened state.
- **Tradeoffs:** You inherit browser default disclosure-triangle quirks and cannot animate the open/close height without extra CSS (Quarto's Bootstrap gives a slide transition for free). Cross-browser summary styling needs a little CSS (already present). (skeptic-found downside: The headline "expands for print via the existing @media print { details {} } hook" is false: no such hook exists. base.css:799-819 (the only prose @media print block) contains no `details` rule, and there is none anywhere in the CSS. A closed `<details>` prints with its body hidden (browser-dependent), so Taliesin does NOT currently beat Quarto on "expands when printed"; both hide a collapsed body on paper. Forcing a `<details>` open is not reliably doable in pure CSS, so a real fix needs a small onbeforeprint/onafterprint handler (or an always-open + CSS display-toggle pattern), which reintroduces a sliver of JS for the print case. Two more edge cases the entry misses: deep-linking or Cmd-K search landing on text inside a collapsed callout will not reveal it except via modern-Chromium find-in-page auto-expand, and a block-level diff re-render of a collapsed block resets any reader-opened state back to the emitted default. Finally, the "add a corpus doc that asserts <details> with no data-bs-*" ask is largely redundant: callout_collapse_renders_as_details, code_fold_wraps_listing_in_details (asserts `<details data-block-id=`), and proof_collapse_folds_into_details already exist, plus corpus coverage in em-algorithm/evidence-lower-bound/Kruskal-Wallis/pca-geometry/theorems-interactive; only the negative data-bs assertion is genuinely new.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (no new format); read-only (toggling <details> is reader interaction, never a source write); keeps Markdown/::: syntax; click-to-source preserved because the container keeps data-block-id/data-sourcepos; block-level incremental unaffected; warm server unaffected; pinnable by a corpus doc.

### D86. Add cross-tabset group syncing (and optional persistence) for `::: {.panel-tabset group="..."}` (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto supports `::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}`: all tabsets sharing a group name switch together when the reader clicks a tab (choose Python once, every Python/R tabset on the page follows), and the selection persists in localStorage across navigation within a site.
- **Critique:** For a docs/blog author showing the same idea in two languages or two tools repeatedly, syncing is a real ergonomic win: the reader picks their language once instead of re-clicking every code block. Taliesin has strong tabset a11y but no grouping, so a language choice does not propagate.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's design is more considered than a naive read credits. (1) Matching tabs by TITLE text rather than by index is the only robust join when two tabsets list their tabs in a different order or a different subset; index-matching would silently pair Python-in-one with R-in-another. The shared-label collision the entry flags as a fragile heuristic is a cost Quarto knowingly accepts as the price of order-independence, not an oversight, so the proposal here replicates Quarto's join rather than improving on it. (2) Persist-by-default across a site is exactly what the target reader wants: on a bilingual docs site you re-meet the same Python-vs-R choice on every page, so remembering it site-wide is the whole ergonomic point, and localStorage (per-origin) is the natural scope for one-site-one-choice. (3) The feature is strictly opt-in via a named group=, so it is zero-cost and invisible for the vast majority of tabsets that never set it. Quarto shipped a small, correct, opt-in feature and this entry is right that Taliesin is simply behind on it.
- **Taliesin today:** Not yet built. divs.rs derives tab/panel ids from the container block id and emits ARIA tabs; tabset.js wires click/arrow/Home/End selection but has no concept of a group, no `group=` attribute is read, and there is no localStorage. Each tabset is independent and always opens on tab 0.
- **Proposed better:** Read a `group=` key in the `.panel-tabset` attrs (divs.rs), emit it as `data-tabset-group="..."`, and in tabset.js broadcast a selection to same-group tabsets by matching tab LABEL text (so tab order need not align). Persist the per-group choice in localStorage keyed by group name, restored on load. Add `group` to the tabset's recognized attribute vocabulary in validate.rs so a typo is flagged with did-you-mean.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship it, but flip the defaults and shrink the validator scope. Default to sync-WITHIN-page only, held as ephemeral in-memory per-group state, with persistence OFF by default and opt-in via an explicit persist=true on the tabset (or a site-config switch), because Taliesin values predictable clean loads and ships file:// portable builds where localStorage is flaky and cross-doc leaky. When persistence IS on, scope the storage key by document-or-site identity plus group name (never group name alone) so a shared origin and mounts: cannot clobber across projects. Keep Quarto's label-based join (it is the correct call for misaligned tab order, and it is a genuine Taliesin fit because labels survive block-id churn where id-based sync would not, so incremental re-render stays intact), but spec the no-match broadcast as a no-op and reject or flag duplicate labels within a single tabset. On validation, recognize group as a known tabset key but do NOT declare the tabset attr surface closed in this entry: either skip did-you-mean here (single key, negligible value) or split strict-div-attr-vocabulary into its own catalog entry with its own corpus pin, since it reaches well beyond group. Pin with a two-tabset same-group corpus doc PLUS a mismatched-labels three-way case, and add a note that persisted-restore must not regress first-paint.
- **Tradeoffs:** localStorage persistence is reader-state that survives reloads, which some authors may find surprising (mitigable: sync-within-page always, persist optionally). Label-matching across tabsets is a heuristic that breaks if two tabs share a label for different content. Adds a small cross-component event path to the otherwise self-contained tabset.js. (skeptic-found downside: Four misses. (1) Flash and reflow on every load: the server SSRs tab 0 as visible, so restoring a persisted non-default tab is a client-side switch after paint, giving a visible tab-0-then-tab-N flash plus a panel-height reflow on every page load, a per-load UX cost the drafter did not flag and one that cuts against Taliesin's care for clean loads. (2) Storage key collision: keying localStorage by group NAME alone means two unrelated documents that both use group=\"language\" clobber each other's choice on a shared origin, and this is acute under mounts: where the guide, internals, and marketing site all share one origin. Worse, Taliesin ships self-contained file:// portable builds where localStorage is browser-flaky and effectively a shared null-origin, so persistence is both unreliable and cross-doc leaky exactly in Taliesin's own distribution mode. (3) validate.rs scope is understated: there is currently NO closed vocabulary for div/tabset key=val attrs (they pass silently), so a single-key did-you-mean has nothing to disambiguate against, and to flag gruop= at all you must declare the tabset attr set CLOSED, which then also flags any legitimate styling attr an author puts on a tabset. That is a blast-radius decision, not the one-line vocab add it is framed as. (4) No specified fallback when a broadcast label has no match in a sibling tabset (choose R in {Python,R}, sync to {Python,Julia}); it should be an explicit no-op, and duplicate labels within one tabset should be rejected or flagged rather than left to silently mis-target.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only (writes only localStorage reader state, never the .tmd); keeps ::: syntax and adds only an attribute already expressible in Pandoc attrs; click-to-source unaffected (labels still emit as buttons, not headings, so they stay out of the TOC/xref); block-level incremental unaffected; warm server unaffected; pin with a two-tabset corpus doc sharing a group.

### D87. Support front-matter document-level defaults for code-fold, callout-appearance, and callout-icon (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto lets you set document- or project-level defaults under `format: html:` such as `code-fold: true`, `code-summary`, `code-tools`, `callout-appearance: simple`, and `callout-icon: false`, which cascade to every code cell and callout unless a local option overrides.
- **Critique:** Setting `appearance=simple` or `icon=false` on twenty callouts one by one, or `code-fold` on every listing, is exactly the repetition a document default removes. Taliesin cascades execute defaults (echo/include/cache) from front matter but NOT the presentation defaults, so an author cannot say once that this whole post uses simple callouts or folds all code.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's cascade is not three ad-hoc keys, it is one uniform inheritance model: every option can be set at project, then document, then element scope with local override, and the presentation defaults are nested under the specific `format:` (html/pdf/revealjs) they belong to. A multi-format compiler genuinely needs that format-scoping, because one source must be able to carry different code-fold and callout defaults per output target. Quarto also validates the full options schema, so an unknown key under `format: html:` is caught rather than silently ignored. Cherry-picking three high-value defaults, as this proposal does, reintroduces exactly the ad-hoc, per-option surface Quarto avoided by making inheritance universal and schema-backed: every future default becomes a bespoke thread through the render context rather than falling out of one general mechanism.
- **Taliesin today:** Partial. cell_extract.rs `detect_execute_defaults` reads front-matter `execute:`/top-level `echo|include|cache` and cascades them; render/mod.rs applies them per cell. But `code_fold` reads only the per-cell `#| code-fold`, and callout `appearance`/`icon` are read only from the per-div attrs in divs.rs. There is no document-level default for any of the three.
- **Proposed better:** Add front-matter keys `code-fold`, `code-summary`, `callout-appearance`, `callout-icon` (document scope), thread them into the render context, and have `code_fold` (cell_extract.rs) and the callout arm (divs.rs) fall back to the document default when the local option is absent, local always winning. Crucially, because Taliesin is a strict clean break, ADD these keys to the front-matter schema (schema.rs / frontmatter.rs) so they validate rather than trip the unknown-key warning.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature, sharpened. (1) Add the four keys at top level (matches Quarto spelling, per the keep-familiar directive) and register them in BOTH frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS (runtime warning) and schema.rs, which regenerates the committed JSON Schema from KNOWN_KEYS and is drift-locked by a bless test, so both must move together or CI fails. (2) Before wiring the cascade, refactor code_fold to a three-state result so `#| code-fold: false` can override a document `code-fold: true`; callouts need no parser change. (3) Pin a corpus doc that sets all four defaults AND includes one cell with `code-fold: false` plus one callout with appearance="default"/icon="true", proving local-overrides-global in the HARD direction (opting out of a default), not just the easy add-a-default case. (4) Since the natural Quarto `format: html:` placement silently no-ops, either document the top-level location prominently or extend validation to flag these keys if seen under `format:`. (5) Correct the entry's taliesin_current: detect_execute_defaults reads only the `execute:` mapping, not top-level echo/include/cache. Block-level incremental, click-to-source (fold already relocates data attrs to the <details>), HTML-only, read-only, and warm-server are all confirmed unaffected.
- **Tradeoffs:** Grows the recognized front-matter surface (each new default is a maintenance and documentation cost) and adds a cascade-resolution step that must be tested for local-overrides-global. Risk of scope creep toward re-implementing Quarto's full options cascade; keep it to these three high-value presentation defaults. (skeptic-found downside: Two costs the drafter missed. (1) The opt-out three-state gap: code_fold(literal) returns None for BOTH an absent option AND an explicit `#| code-fold: false` (cell_extract.rs:125 short-circuits unless the value is "true"/"show"). So once a document default `code-fold: true` exists, a cell cannot opt back out; "local always winning" is unimplementable until code_fold is refactored to distinguish present-false from absent. Callouts are fine (icon="true" and appearance="default" already fall through to the show/boxed arms in divs.rs), so only code-fold needs the parser change, but the drafter asserted a symmetric override that the current code cannot express. (2) The `format: html:` trap: Quarto authors habitually nest these under `format: html:`, but Taliesin only reads `format:` for deck detection and does NOT validate its children, so a doc that places the new keys there gets a silent no-op with zero warning. Minor: one front-matter default change re-renders every callout/cell (N Update ops via diff.rs); correct, but not free.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only; keeps YAML front-matter + ::: syntax; click-to-source unaffected; block-level incremental unaffected (defaults resolved at render time, not client); warm server unaffected; respects the clean-break invariant only if the keys are added to the schema so strict validation still passes; pin with a corpus doc that sets the defaults and a cell/callout that overrides locally.

### D88. Flag an unknown callout kind with did-you-mean and click-to-source, rather than silently rendering an inert callout (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto recognizes note/tip/warning/caution/important. A misspelled `.callout-notee` is not an error: Pandoc/Quarto emit a generic callout div with no accent, icon, or warning, so a typo silently produces a wrong-looking callout that the author may not notice.
- **Critique:** Silent degradation is the pain: the author sees a callout that renders but looks plain, with no signal that the kind was misspelled. There is no located feedback to fix it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The critique accurately describes real silent degradation, but Quarto's choice is principled, not lazy. Quarto is a multi-format Pandoc compiler and inherits Pandoc's open-world attribute model: unknown classes and key=value attributes on a fenced div MUST pass through untouched, because the same source targets HTML, LaTeX, docx, and revealjs, and a class or attribute is frequently meaningful to only one format or to a downstream Lua filter, custom CSS, or third-party extension. Turning an unrecognized callout class or attribute into an error would break every document that leans on that extensibility and would be format-hostile (a warning stream is noise in a batch compiler that emits PDF). Crucially, Quarto has no click-to-source reverse map, so even if it wanted to warn, it could not LOCATE the warning the way Taliesin can; an unlocated console warning is low-value. Given an open, filter-extensible, multi-format design with no source map, silent pass-through is the least-surprising, most-compatible default. Taliesin can do better only because it made three narrowing bets Quarto did not: HTML-only output, a closed owned vocabulary (clean break, no Quarto-tolerance tier), and a data-sourcepos reverse map that makes every warning a located, clickable diagnostic.
- **Taliesin today:** divs.rs calls validate.rs `validate_callout_kind`, which checks against Taliesin's own `CALLOUT_KINDS` and, on a miss, produces a located `Warning` with an edit-distance did-you-mean (`unknown callout kind ` importnat ` (did you mean ` important `?)`) carrying file+line, surfaced in the dev panel with click-to-source, while STILL rendering the callout with the given class. This is a deliberate clean break: no Quarto-tolerance tier.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it; close a small gap. Today only the callout KIND is validated. Extend the same did-you-mean vocabulary check to the callout ATTRIBUTE keys (appearance, icon, collapse, title) so `apearance=simple` or `collaspe=true` is flagged and located too, not silently ignored. Reuse `unknown_key_message` and a small `CALLOUT_ATTR_KEYS` set in validate.rs.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry: on the callout KIND, Taliesin is already better (located did-you-mean, still renders, corpus-pinned), and the steelman confirms Quarto's silence is a defensible open-world default that Taliesin's HTML-only + owned-vocabulary + sourcepos bets let it beat. Sharpen the extension three ways. (1) Validate BOTH the attribute keys and the enumerated `appearance` value: add `CALLOUT_ATTR_KEYS = {title, icon, appearance, collapse}` (exactly the four keys divs.rs reads) AND validate `appearance` against {simple, minimal} the way `validate_input` already validates INPUT_TYPES, so `appearance=simpel` is caught, not just `apearance=simple`. Leave `collapse`/`icon` as boolean-tolerant. (2) Land it as a shared `validate_div_attrs` helper keyed off a per-container known-key set so the same guard covers theorem/input/step/layout divs, and note in the entry that callouts are the first instance of a general div-attribute-typo gap, not a unique one. (3) State the `--strict` consequence explicitly (new warnings become CI failures under `--strict`; intended, aligned with the no-tolerance clean break). Pin all of it by extending corpus/diagnostics/typos.qmd with a callout that has both a misspelled attribute key (`apearance=simple`) and a misspelled attribute value (`appearance=simpel`), and keep the vocabulary comment in divs.rs pointing at the validator so the two do not drift.
- **Tradeoffs:** More validation surface to maintain and keep in sync with divs.rs (the vocabularies must not drift from what the code actually reads). A stricter attribute check risks false positives if a future feature adds an attribute without updating the set. (skeptic-found downside: A KEY-only check leaves the very bug the entry decries alive for attribute VALUES. `appearance` is a closed enum (only simple/minimal honored; divs.rs:372-376), so the more common typo `appearance=simpel` passes the key check yet silently falls back to the default boxed look with no signal, exactly the wrong-looking-callout-with-no-warning failure the entry attacks. Same for `collapse=ture` (anything but `false` is truthy). The input-type validator already validates the VALUE against a closed set (INPUT_TYPES), so validating only the key here is a regression in ambition relative to Taliesin's own precedent. Two more missed points: (1) the silent-drop of unknown attribute keys is not callout-specific, the theorem, input, step, and layout div arms read their own fixed kv keys and drop the rest just as silently, so a callout-only fix is inconsistent and the durable design is a shared `validate_div_attrs(known_keys, kv, line, file)` helper rather than a one-off `CALLOUT_ATTR_KEYS`; (2) because `--strict` promotes any located warning to a non-zero exit (build.rs:129, main.rs:140), adding attribute-key and value warnings will fail previously-passing `--strict`/CI builds for any author who had a tolerated typo. That is intended under the clean-break philosophy but must be named, not discovered.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only (diagnostics navigate, never write); keeps ::: syntax; click-to-source is the delivery mechanism (the warning IS located); block-level incremental unaffected; warm server unaffected; already pinned by validate.rs unit tests and extendable with a corpus typos doc (corpus/diagnostics/typos.qmd exists).

### D89. Replace Quarto's code-tools menu with a fold-all toggle, since view-source is already click-to-source (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `code-tools: true` adds a floating `</> Code` dropdown offering Show/Hide All Code, View Source (the full .qmd in a modal), and links to launch in Binder/Colab.
- **Critique:** Two of the three code-tools actions do not fit Taliesin. View Source (read the .qmd) is redundant with, and weaker than, Taliesin's Alt-click click-to-source that jumps to the exact editor line. Binder/Colab launchers are compute-provisioning features irrelevant to an HTML-only single-author tool. But the third action, Show/Hide All Code, has no Taliesin equivalent: a reader of a heavily code-folded post cannot expand everything at once.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** code-tools bundles two genuinely distinct reader affordances into one standardized, auto-placed control that appears ONLY when the document actually has foldable code: a single Show/Hide-All-Code toggle plus reader-facing View Source. View Source serves a PUBLISHED reader (someone with no editor and no Taliesin) who wants to inspect the literal source for reproducibility or transparency, which is core to Quarto's scientific-authoring audience. Taliesin's click-to-source cannot cover this: it is author-only and, verified in page.rs, exists only in the live preview (the static build ships no websocket client; Alt-click posts qmd-goto to the parent editor host), never in the deployed HTML a stranger reads. So Quarto is not being redundant; View Source reaches an audience (the published reader) that click-to-source structurally cannot. And Show/Hide-All is a legitimate, well-scoped default that ships with zero front-matter config the moment any cell is folded, whereas Taliesin's proposal gates the same capability behind an opt-in most posts never set. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. There is no code-tools menu. code-fold produces independent `<details>` elements with no global control; expanding a post means clicking each one. click-to-source (Alt-click) already covers the view-source intent for the author.
- **Proposed better:** Skip the Quarto code-tools menu wholesale (view-source is subsumed by click-to-source; Binder/Colab violate the HTML-only, no-compute-provisioning stance). Add ONLY a small, optional Expand/Collapse-all-code control (a reader-menu item or a header button) that toggles every `.tali-code-fold` and code-fold `<details open>` on the page. Gate it behind a document/front-matter opt-in so posts without folded code get no chrome.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the core: skip the code-tools menu, add no Binder/Colab (never in code-tools anyway) and no reader-facing View Source (correct reason: reader-facing source view is out of Taliesin's single-author, HTML-only scope, NOT that click-to-source subsumes it, since click-to-source is preview-and-author-only). Fix the entry's Quarto facts: the dropdown is exactly Show/Hide-All-Code + View Source. Treat Expand/Collapse-All as demand-driven per corpus-plus-roadmap: build it only when a real corpus post has enough folded cells to warrant it, not speculatively. When built: mount it as a reader-menu section via the existing window.taliReaderMenu.addSection API (reuse, do not add a bespoke header button), scope the toggle strictly to .tali-code-fold (never bare <details>, to spare collapsible callouts/proofs), register the opt-in key in the strict validator + JSON schema, and document that its stable value is the built static site (preview edits reset per-block fold state). Consider downgrading impact from medium to low.
- **Tradeoffs:** Yet another optional affordance and front-matter key to maintain and document. A global toggle interacts with the per-block reader state from the tab/collapse-preservation proposal (the two must agree on who owns `<details open>`). Low reader demand for many blog posts; easy to over-build. (skeptic-found downside: Four the drafter under-weighted. (1) Strict-validator cost: Taliesin is a clean break that flags ANY unknown front-matter key (validate.rs / schema.rs), so the new opt-in key must be registered there or it is reported as a did-you-mean typo; unstated implementation work. (2) Live-preview transience: editing a folded cell fires an Update op that does el.replaceWith(node), resetting the fresh <details> to its default state, so an in-preview Expand-All is clobbered per edit; the feature's stable value is the BUILT static site, not preview, which the entry never says. (3) Low corpus demand: corpus posts carry only 1-3 code-fold cells (pca-geometry has 2, em-algorithm 1), so Expand-All of two <details> is marginal, and gating it off-by-default means most posts never surface it; the feature may not earn its maintenance + docs + front-matter key + corpus doc. (4) Scope hazard: the entry says toggle every code-fold <details open>, but collapsible callouts (.callout-collapse) and theorem proofs (.tali-proof-collapse) ALSO emit <details>; the control must be scoped strictly to .tali-code-fold or it will blow open every collapsed callout and proof.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (explicitly rejects Binder/Colab which would break it); read-only (toggling <details> is reader interaction); keeps Markdown/cell-option syntax; click-to-source PRESERVED and in fact positioned as the superior replacement for View Source; block-level incremental unaffected; warm server unaffected; pin with a corpus doc containing several code-fold cells.

### D90. Ship native inline code annotations (# &lt;1&gt; markers) as a capability distinct from the narrated walkthrough, instead of letting the walkthrough silently stand in for them (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto reads trailing comment markers in a code block (`x = 1  # &lt;1&gt;`, `// &lt;2&gt;`, etc.), strips them from the displayed code, and turns each into a numbered circle anchored to that exact line. An ordered list placed immediately after the block supplies the descriptions (`1. explanation`, `2. ...`), matched positionally to the markers. A `code-annotations` option picks the display mode: `select` (default: click a number to reveal its note), `hover`, `below` (static list under the code), or `none`. It works on both static and executable cells (markers are real comments, so the kernel ignores them) and is the standard way Quarto tutorials and books explain a snippet line by line in flowing prose. It ships a small client runtime (tippy-based) to drive the hover/select popovers.
- **Critique:** Code annotations and the narrated walkthrough address different authoring jobs, so shipping only the walkthrough leaves a real, heavily-used Quarto affordance uncovered; the catalog listed the walkthrough but never resolved whether it replaces annotations, and the code shows it does not.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The critique is fair and the quarto_does description is accurate, so the steelman is FOR the design, not against a strawman. Quarto's comment-marker-plus-following-ordered-list is the minimal, kernel-safe, format-portable way to bind prose to specific code lines. Because the markers are real comments the kernel ignores them, so the executed code is byte-identical to source and annotations work uniformly on static AND executable cells with no special fenced syntax to learn (plain code plus a normal ordered list). The decisive justification is multi-format: the SAME source must degrade to a static numbered list in PDF/LaTeX/docx (where popovers cannot exist) and enhance to interactive popovers in HTML, which is exactly why the select/hover/below/none modes exist. A general mechanism with modes is the correct response to that cross-format constraint, and shipping a small tippy runtime is a pragmatic way to get consistent hover/select across every theme in a purely static build with no dev server. For Quarto's actual design space (many targets, static hosting, no click-to-source, no server-side line addressing) this is close to optimal, and it is genuinely a heavily-used, distinct affordance, so declining to cover it because the walkthrough exists would be a real gap.
- **Taliesin today:** No `# &lt;1&gt;` marker parsing exists anywhere (verified by grepping crates/, assets/, web-client/, docs/, corpus/; the only "annotation" hits are KaTeX MathML tags and deck drawing). What ships instead is the narrated walkthrough: `::: {.code-walkthrough}` emits a sticky `.cw-code` panel plus one `.step` div per narration step carrying `data-cw-lines` (divs.rs:404-454), and walkthrough.js focuses the active step's line range by toggling `.tali-hl-ln-hl` on the syntect line spans. Its own design spec (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-24-code-walkthrough-design.md) claims to unify "what Quarto splits across code-annotation and magic-move," but only the scrollytelling half was built; the inline-annotation half was never implemented and the fork was left unresolved.
- **Proposed better:** Add inline code annotations as a first-class, separate capability, reasoned from Taliesin's seams rather than ported from Quarto's runtime. Keep Quarto's exact author syntax (trailing `# &lt;n&gt;` comment markers plus a following ordered list), since both are CommonMark-legal and the owner decision is to keep the Markdown substrate familiar. Improve every layer above it: (1) parse markers during emission and anchor each to the already-existing `.tali-hl-ln` ordinal spans that line-wrapping produces, so no separate anchoring runtime is needed; (2) emit each annotation's prose as its own block with `data-block-id` + `data-sourcepos`, so Alt-clicking a note jumps to the list item in source, a click-to-source affordance Quarto lacks; (3) default to a static `below` rendering that needs zero JS, and progressively enhance hover/select through a `taliEnhancers`-registered enhancer (like walkthrough.js) that is idempotent and survives block-swap; (4) apply Taliesin's strict-validation ethos: when marker count and list-item count disagree, or a marker points past the code, emit a located, did-you-mean warning instead of Quarto's silent mismatch. Document the division of labor explicitly: annotations for inline footnotes on a few lines, walkthrough for a full guided tour.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship inline code annotations as a distinct, corpus-pinned capability at corpus/narrate/annotations.tmd (sibling to the existing corpus/narrate/walkthrough.qmd), and document the division of labor: annotations for a few line-anchored footnotes, walkthrough for a full guided scroll tour, footnotes/sidenotes for non-line-anchored asides. Fold in three corrections the draft missed: (1) render the numbered gutter markers OUTSIDE the code text flow (aria-hidden absolute overlay or CSS counter pseudo-element) so code.innerText copy stays clean and the deck/line-numbers enhancers do not collide on .tali-hl-ln, and decide that copy yields the marker-stripped clean source; (2) restate layer-1 as force the existing idempotent wrap_pre_lines on annotated blocks rather than reuse already-existing spans, and let the zero-JS below default skip line-wrapping entirely; (3) scope to page context first, defer deck annotations like theorem Phase 4. Keep the two real edges over Quarto (strict located did-you-mean validation on marker/list count mismatch, and per-note click-to-source via data-block-id) and do NOT reimplement Quarto's tippy runtime, progressively enhance through the taliEnhancers registry.
- **Tradeoffs:** Introduces a second code-explanation mechanism alongside the walkthrough, so docs must clearly draw the line or authors will not know which to reach for. Stripping the markers from displayed code has to happen without corrupting the syntect-highlighted comment spans they sit inside, which means a careful post-highlight strip rather than a naive pre-parse. For executable cells the displayed code will differ from the executed code (markers are comments, so exec is unaffected, but the two texts diverge, a subtlety to keep in mind for the freeze hash and any "copy code" affordance). The positional marker-to-list binding is inherently fragile; the validation layer mitigates but does not eliminate the ergonomics cost of keeping list and markers in sync. It is additive surface, not load-bearing, so it competes for effort against higher-leverage roadmap items. (skeptic-found downside: The sharpest miss is a copy/enhancer collision the drafter did not surface. Taliesin's copy button reads code.innerText (crates/core/assets/js/code-enhance/08-copy-buttons.js:20), and the deck/code-line-numbers path toggles classes on the same .tali-hl-ln spans. If the numbered circle markers are rendered as real text nodes inside the code element, copied snippets carry stray glyphs, and if annotations coexist with code-line-numbers or deck line-stepping on one block, two enhancers fight over the same spans. The draft flagged stripping markers for display and the freeze/copy divergence of the stripped text, but missed that the INJECTED marker gutter must live outside the copyable/highlightable text flow (aria-hidden absolute overlay or a CSS counter pseudo-element). Second, ordinary static code blocks are NOT line-wrapped by default (emit.rs wraps only for code-line-numbers, magic-move, and the walkthrough panel), so anchor to the already-existing .tali-hl-ln spans overstates it: annotated blocks must force the existing idempotent wrap, and the zero-JS below default needs no line spans at all. Third, deck context is unaddressed and, like theorem Phase 4, will likely lag.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: annotations are a pure in-browser affordance, no new output format. Single read-only surface: markers strip at render time, the enhancer only reads DOM and toggles classes, and click-to-source on annotation prose navigates to source without ever writing. Keep-Markdown: reuses Quarto's `# &lt;n&gt;` comment markers plus a standard ordered list, both plain CommonMark, no syntax divergence. Click-to-source: strengthened, since each annotation note becomes a block with data-block-id + data-sourcepos and the annotated code line is addressable by ordinal. Block-level incremental: the code block and each note are ordinary blocks, and the enhancer re-runs idempotently after a diff swap. Warm-server: no per-edit startup cost; the static default needs no JS and parsing rides the existing emit pass. Corpus-plus-roadmap: ship pinned by a new corpus doc (for example corpus/narrate/annotations.tmd) so done is defined and regression-netted.

### D91. Decide whether code-line-numbers should render a line-number gutter on articles, not only drive deck stepping (Open question)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** keep
- **Quarto does:** In Quarto HTML (non-reveal), `code-line-numbers: true` renders a real line-number gutter beside the code (Pandoc numberLines), useful for referencing `line 12` in prose. The `"1|3-5"` progressive-highlight form is a revealjs-only behavior.
- **Critique:** Taliesin repurposes `code-line-numbers` entirely as a deck-only stepping spec. Verified: emit.rs `code_line_numbers` emits `data-code-lines` and wraps each line, but only deck.js consumes `data-code-lines`; on a normal article page nothing highlights and there is NO numeric gutter at all.
