So a code-heavy blog post cannot show line numbers, and an author who writes `#| code-line-numbers: true` expecting a gutter gets nothing visible.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's design is coherent and well-motivated, and Taliesin, not Quarto, is the one that broke the contract. Quarto gives `code-line-numbers` one author-facing name with format-appropriate semantics: in HTML output `true` renders a real line-number gutter (verified on quarto.org, both document-level YAML and per-block attribute), which serves a genuine need in tutorials, books, and reference docs where prose says "see line 12"; in revealjs the same key additionally accepts a `"1|3-5"` string to highlight and animate line sets, because stepping only makes sense in a paged, incremental medium. Reserving the animated string form to reveal while keeping the plain gutter everywhere is the right split, and it inherits Pandoc's `.numberLines` lineage so the mental model is single. Taliesin took the option name but implemented only the reveal-stepping half, so on an article the key is accepted by the strict validator yet drops the gutter contract entirely, which is a worse outcome than either matching Quarto or rejecting the key.
- **Taliesin today:** emit.rs treats `code-line-numbers` as a highlight/step spec parsed from the cell option or fenced attr, wraps lines with `wrap_code_lines`, and sets `data-code-lines`; deck.js steps through it on slides. No gutter CSS or article-side rendering exists. `true` (the plain gutter case) is effectively a no-op on articles.
- **Proposed better:** Split the semantics cleanly. Treat `code-line-numbers: true` (bare) as an article gutter: emit `<pre>` with a numbered-line presentation (CSS counters on the already-wrapped `.tali-hl-ln` spans, no layout-shifting markup), and reserve the `"1|3-5"` step-spec for decks/walkthroughs as today. Alternatively, if the single-author judgment is that blog code rarely needs gutters, document `code-line-numbers` as a deck/walkthrough-only feature so the article no-op is intentional rather than surprising.
- **Tradeoffs:** A gutter adds visual noise and horizontal space to every numbered listing and needs careful copy-button and wrap interaction (the copy button must not copy line numbers; innerText already excludes CSS counters, so this is safe). It is arguably low value for a single author who can reference code by content. Doing nothing but documenting is cheaper but leaves `true` inert. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's severity is understated and its cheap alternative is unsound. Current behavior on an article is not a benign inert no-op: because `wrap_code_lines` strips the newlines and the only `.tali-hl-ln { display:block }` rules are scoped to `.tali-deck` and `.code-walkthrough`, a plain article `<pre data-code-lines>` collapses the whole listing onto one visual line (rendered proof: three lines came back as `def foo():    x = 1    return x`, zero newlines in the pre), and since the copy button reads innerText it also copies that single mangled line. So the proposed "do nothing but document code-line-numbers as deck-only" path does NOT hold: documentation cannot un-break an already-broken render, and the validator still green-lights the key. The true minimum fix is a one-line unscoped rule `pre[data-code-lines] .tali-hl-ln { display:block }` (or not stripping newlines in the article path), which alone stops the collapse and restores copy line breaks; the gutter is then additive. Two more edge cases the drafter missed: (1) `code-fold` takes a different emit branch that never calls `code_line_numbers`, so `code-fold: true` + `code-line-numbers` silently drops numbers; (2) the drafter's split leaves `code-line-numbers: "1-3"` (a single non-piped range) on an article still inert, when a static line-range highlight there is exactly the richer-than-Quarto behavior worth reaching for since Quarto's string form is reveal-only.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only; keeps Markdown/cell-option syntax (no new syntax, only a clarified meaning); click-to-source unaffected (the <pre> keeps its data-block-id/data-sourcepos); block-level incremental unaffected; warm server unaffected; pin with a corpus listing using code-line-numbers: true.

### D92. Ship an always-on copy button with a file:// / LAN fallback and scroll-pinning, versus Quarto's configurable code-copy (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto exposes `code-copy: true|false|hover` (default: show on hover) using clipboard.js; the button uses the async Clipboard API, which silently fails in insecure contexts (file:// or plain-http LAN preview), and can be turned off per document.
- **Critique:** The Clipboard API path is the pain: opening a built HTML file directly (file://) or previewing over a phone on the LAN (http, non-secure-context) makes Quarto's copy button click with no effect. The configurability (`hover`/`false`) is a genuine nicety Taliesin lacks.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto deliberately copies through clipboard.js (bundled v2.0.11), whose primary path is document.execCommand('copy'), NOT the async Clipboard API. execCommand has no secure-context gate, so Quarto's button works uniformly in every context: file://, plain-http LAN, and HTTPS. That is by design, and it already covers the very file:// and phone-preview cases the entry claims as a Taliesin exclusive. Quarto defaults to `hover` to keep code blocks visually clean (button revealed on interaction) while force-showing on touch devices where hover is unavailable, and exposes `true|false|hover` for per-document control of the printed/clean look. It also fixed horizontal-scroll pinning (issue #5538 closed via PR #12787). So current Quarto already ships robust cross-context copy, a clean configurable default, and correct touch handling: the exact bundle the entry claims Taliesin uniquely provides. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** code-enhance/08-copy-buttons.js always adds a `.tali-copy` button to every `<pre> > <code>`, uses `taliCopyText` which falls back to `execCommand` for file:// and LAN, swaps a check icon on success, and counter-translates the button by `pre.scrollLeft` so it stays pinned to the visible corner on horizontally scrolling code. There is no way to disable it or make it hover-only.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the robust always-on button (the fallback and scroll-pin are genuinely better than Quarto for this tool's file:// and --host phone-preview workflows). Add only the small missing knob: honor a document-level `code-copy: false` / `hover` front-matter default (tie into the document-defaults cascade above) so an author who wants a clean printed look or hover-only reveal can opt out, defaulting to always-visible.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature (add `code-copy: true|false|hover`) but correct the framing and the plan. Change status from \"taliesin-already-better\" to \"near-parity; Quarto is ahead on the one thing that matters here (the toggle).\" Drop the fallback and scroll-pin as differentiators: Quarto's execCommand path already works on file://+LAN, and PR #12787 already pins its button. Retain the honest, narrow Taliesin edge: preferring navigator.clipboard in secure contexts is marginally more future-proof than Quarto's deprecated-execCommand-only path. Implementation: register `code-copy` as a top-level key in frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS plus schema.rs (else strict validation flags it), with value-validation to false|true|hover; propagate the doc-level value to a `<body>` class/data-attribute in page.rs; drive `hover`/hide with CSS and have taliCopyButtons early-return on `false` so no listeners attach; keep force-show on touch for `hover`; keep always-on as the default (a defensible better default for this tool's file:// and --host phone workflows). Because Quarto authors put this under `format: html:` (which Taliesin does not lint), either read it there too or add a targeted lint so `format: html: code-copy` is not a silent no-op. Pin with a render test asserting the body class/attribute per value; treat the insecure-context copy itself as a manual browser smoke check, not a cargo corpus invariant.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adding the toggle expands the front-matter surface (and must be schema-registered to survive strict validation). Hover-only reveal hurts touch devices (no hover), so the default should stay always-on. Minimal engineering, mostly a CSS class plus a default read. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's two claimed Taliesin advantages both evaporate under scrutiny, leaving only a gap that runs in Quarto's favor. (1) Quarto's copy already works in insecure contexts: it uses clipboard.js/execCommand (verified: `new window.ClipboardJS(...)` in quarto-html-after-body.ejs; zero `navigator.clipboard.writeText` in the repo), so Taliesin's fallback is PARITY, not superiority. Taliesin's only residual edge is marginal future-proofing (it prefers navigator.clipboard in secure contexts, so it survives if browsers ever drop the deprecated execCommand). (2) Quarto fixed scroll-pin in PR #12787, so that is parity too. (3) Implementation gaps the drafter glossed: the button is built client-side by taliCopyButtons with no front-matter knowledge, so `false`/`hover` must reach the DOM via a server-emitted body class/data-attribute and the enhancer/CSS must read it; a live front-matter-only edit may not re-emit that body class, so toggling code-copy in preview could need a reload (SetMeta/shell-update edge). (4) Quarto's `code-copy` lives under `format: html:`, where Taliesin explicitly does NOT lint subkeys, so a migrating author who writes `format: html: code-copy: false` gets a silent no-op with no did-you-mean warning. (5) The promised \"corpus doc under a --host/file:// smoke check\" cannot be a deterministic cargo invariant: a render test can only assert the body class/attribute is emitted per value; insecure-context copy behavior stays a manual browser check.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only (copy reads the DOM, never writes source); keeps Markdown syntax; click-to-source unaffected; block-level incremental unaffected (the enhancer re-runs idempotently after swaps via the taliEnhancers registry); warm server unaffected; pin with a corpus doc under a --host/file:// smoke check.

## Theming and appearance

### D93. Add a small native accent/font config that maps onto --tali-* tokens (a lite brand knob) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Supports _brand.yml (Posit's cross-tool brand.yml spec, Quarto 1.6+): color.palette + color.primary/secondary, typography.fonts/base/headings, and a logo, applied consistently across Quarto, Shiny, and other Posit tools from one file.
- **Critique:** brand.yml is genuinely good for organizational consistency, but it is a whole external spec plus an extra config file, and it is overkill for a single author who just wants 'my accent is #6b46c1' without dropping into raw CSS.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** brand.yml's "heaviness" is not gratuitous, it is the deliberate solution to the exact problem Taliesin's lite proposal is about to walk into. Setting an accent is never a single-token edit: a primary color has to propagate to links, buttons, focus rings, filled/active surfaces, and their on-color text, and each of those must stay WCAG-AA in every theme. Quarto runs that propagation through Bootstrap Sass so the author writes one value ($primary, or brand.yml color.primary) and the framework derives the rest across light and dark. brand.yml also intentionally lives in a file precisely because its payoff is one source of truth reused across many documents and even other tools (Shiny, dashboards, Typst), which is real value the moment an author has more than one project. And the critique sets up a false dichotomy: Quarto does NOT force brand.yml on the single author. The one-line path already exists (a theme scss :defaults block setting $primary, no raw CSS, no brand.yml), so the "whole external spec plus extra file, overkill for a single author" framing understates Quarto by omitting its lighter tier and by reading the file/cross-tool nature as bloat rather than as the point. Steelmanned, Quarto's stance is: the naive single knob is a trap, so we ship both a light Sass-variable path and a heavier centralized brand spec, and both do the cross-token, cross-theme derivation for you. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. No `brand` key exists in front-matter KNOWN_KEYS (schema.rs) or in _site.yml NATIVE_KEYS (site/config/mod.rs). The single accent knob is the --tali-accent CSS variable (plus the derived --tali-accent-fill/--tali-on-accent for WCAG-AA fills), and the ONLY way to set it is to hand-write css: overriding the token.
- **Proposed better:** Add a small, strictly-validated native theming block (e.g. top-level accent:/font:/max-width:, or a compact brand: map) that maps a handful of high-value values onto the existing --tali-* tokens (accent sets --tali-accent and its derived fill/link, font sets --tali-font-*, max-width sets --tali-maxw), emitted as one :root override before the theme layer. Do NOT adopt the full brand.yml spec, just the 4-5 knobs that matter.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature, fix the sketch, and stop treating the knobs as one uniform batch. (a) Do NOT name it brand:. A brand: map re-imports the exact Quarto concept the project is shedding AND signals the full brand.yml surface (logo, secondary, palette), inviting the scope creep the entry wants to avoid. Use flat, self-limiting top-level keys: accent:, font:, max-width:. (b) Ship the cheap correct win first: max-width: maps 1:1 to --tali-maxw, theme-invariant, no derivation, no asset story, land it now with a corpus doc. (c) Treat accent: as the real work: emit the override at every theme scope (:root, html[data-theme="dark"], html[data-theme="sepia"]) so it beats the existing per-theme redefinitions, and recolor the full correlated set (--tali-accent, --tali-accent-fill, --tali-on-accent, --tali-link, and --tali-flash) not just --tali-accent. Derive fill/on-accent/flash with a small tested sRGB-luminance contrast step (darken until 4.5:1 vs the theme bg, pick on-color by contrast), and pin a corpus doc whose test asserts the derived fill clears AA in all three themes so the accent knob can never silently regress the a11y invariant. If the solver is deemed too much for v1, ship accent: requiring the author to supply accent plus its AA fill explicitly, and say so, rather than pretending one hex is enough. (d) Defer font: until there is a font-embedding path, or scope it explicitly to "system font stacks only" so it is not a silent offline footgun. Invariant-wise the proposal is clean and even invariant-positive: build-time config, no preview write-back, HTML-only, Markdown/YAML surface unchanged, and it routes through the same did-you-mean strict-validation path as every other key.
- **Tradeoffs:** A new validated key surface to maintain, and deriving an AA-compliant --tali-accent-fill from an arbitrary accent needs a contrast-adjust step (or the author supplies both the accent and its fill). Naming it brand: buys Quarto familiarity but re-imports a Quarto concept the project is otherwise shedding. (skeptic-found downside: Three concrete misses. (1) Cascade defeat: the proposal emits "one :root override before the theme layer," but --tali-accent is redefined in html[data-theme="dark"] (dark.css) and html[data-theme="sepia"] (base.css), and those attribute selectors out-specify a bare :root, so the author's accent would silently apply in light mode only and revert to stock blue in dark/sepia. To actually work the override must be re-emitted at each theme scope (or match that specificity), not a single :root block. (2) "The accent" is not 1 token, it is a 4-token by 3-theme matrix. Verified in code: --tali-accent, --tali-accent-fill, --tali-on-accent, and --tali-link are each hand-tuned per theme for AA (light/sepia/dark), and none of the fill/on-accent/link values are color-mix-derived today. Additionally --tali-flash (the click-to-source block-highlight animation, a load-bearing feature) is a hardcoded rgba of the default blue with alpha, not var(--tali-accent), so a brand accent leaves the click-to-source flash still blue and cannot be fixed by a simple color-mix. So a single input either needs a real build-time sRGB-luminance contrast solver (new color math plus tests, and if it ships a sub-AA fill it regresses the project's own AA guarantee) or forces the author to supply the whole matrix, which erodes the one-knob ergonomics that justified the feature. (3) The knobs are not uniformly cheap, which the "just 4-5 knobs" batching hides. max-width maps to --tali-maxw which is theme-invariant (only in base :root, absent from dark.css), so it is genuinely trivial and correct. But font: is a footgun under Taliesin's offline/self-contained posture: --tali-font-* are system font stacks, so font: "Inter" renders as a fallback unless the author also bundles an @font-face, which the knob has no asset-embedding story for.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time config only, no preview write-back; HTML-only; validated through the same did-you-mean path as every other key; pin a corpus doc that sets the accent key.

### D94. One stylesheet with data-theme + pre-paint bootstrap beats dual Bootstrap builds (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** theme: {light: cosmo, dark: darkly} builds two separate Bootstrap stylesheets and a navbar toggle swaps them at runtime; a single-theme doc has no dark mode at all. The two themes are defined independently and the swap can flash.
- **Critique:** Two full stylesheets ship, the light and dark designs are defined separately and can drift apart, and toggling or first paint can show a flash of the wrong theme (FOUC), especially on navigation.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's dual-Bootstrap-theme model is a deliberate consequence of two commitments Taliesin does not make. First, multi-format output: the same source renders to HTML, PDF/LaTeX, Word, revealjs, and ePub, and a runtime data-theme JS toggle is meaningless for PDF or Word, so theming must resolve at build time per format via SASS/Bootstrap variable compilation. The two-theme model (a light Bootswatch theme plus a dark one) is the build-time-portable way to offer dark. Taliesin can afford a single-sheet runtime JS toggle precisely because it is HTML-only. Second, the Bootswatch ecosystem: theme: {light: cosmo, dark: darkly} hands the author 25+ professionally designed, mutually independent themes for two words of config. The 'drift' the critique treats as a defect is the intended feature: darkly is not a mechanical inversion of cosmo, it is a separately designed dark aesthetic (different type scale, accent, component styling), which Taliesin's token-override model forecloses in exchange for guaranteed consistency and which forces the Taliesin maintainer to hand-author every dark token. Shipping two bundles can also cache across sites using the same Bootswatch theme, and Quarto does ship an inline color-scheme script, so the critique's careful 'can flash' (not 'always flashes') is fair rather than a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** One base sheet; dark and sepia are --tali-* overrides keyed by html[data-theme] (dark.css, base.css). theme_head (theme.rs) injects a pre-paint <script> that sets data-theme + el.style.colorScheme + el.style.background BEFORE first paint, explicitly to kill the cross-page white flash; it follows OS prefers-color-scheme with a saved-choice (localStorage qmd-theme) precedence and a live OS-change listener, and dispatches qmd:themechange so mermaid SVGs and theme-matched {{< video >}} clips re-sync. Default mode is auto (OS-follow, light fallback).
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line. The only worthwhile additions: expose the pre-paint bootstrap and token contract for the eventual print/PDF-from-HTML track, and document the --tali-* dark/sepia override contract so custom themes inherit a matching dark mode instead of only styling light.
- **Revised recommendation:** Hold the line on the core: the single base sheet plus data-theme token overrides plus a pre-paint bootstrap genuinely beats Quarto's dual-Bootstrap build for the live-HTML target, so status taliesin-already-better stands. But revise the additions. DROP 'expose the pre-paint bootstrap for the print/PDF track': base.css already forces a light palette via @media print regardless of data-theme and strips chrome, so print theming is solved and the JS bootstrap has no role on paper (and the addition pins to no corpus doc). KEEP and sharpen 'document the --tali-* dark/sepia override contract', pinned by a docs/corpus example that supplies an html[data-theme="dark"] block, since a custom light-only theme silently having no dark mode is the one real user gap. ADD to the honesty/tradeoffs line: OS-follow is JS-gated in the non-bare deployed build (JS-off renders light even on an OS-dark machine because only --bare emits an @media prefers-color-scheme fallback), and no <meta name="theme-color"> is set so mobile chrome does not re-tint. Optional 'wider than Quarto' win worth flagging: an opt-in color-mix-derived dark fallback for custom light-only themes, giving them a free matching dark mode Quarto cannot, rather than only documenting the contract.
- **Tradeoffs:** Dark and sepia must be maintained as token overrides in one place, and a custom-CSS theme author who only sets light values gets no matching dark mode unless they also supply html[data-theme="dark"] overrides. (skeptic-found downside: Two gaps. (1) The 'follows OS prefers-color-scheme' behavior is JS-gated in the deployed non-bare build: dark.css keys only on the JS-set html[data-theme="dark"], and base.css emits no screen-level @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) (only the --bare path does), so a reader with JS disabled on an OS-dark machine gets a white page, and no <meta name="theme-color"> is emitted so mobile browser chrome never matches dark. This is a defensible tradeoff (a clean saved-choice override is why they went JS-only, and flash-kill needs JS anyway) but the entry's flash-kill/OS-follow framing hides it. (2) The print/PDF-from-HTML addition is redundant: base.css already has an @media print block that forces a light palette regardless of data-theme and strips live chrome, so print theming is solved in CSS; the pre-paint JS bootstrap is a live-view flash-killer and paper does not flash, so 'expose it for the print track' is a category error.)
- **Invariant check:** The reader toggle is reader-local (localStorage), never writes .tmd, honoring the single-editing-surface invariant; HTML-only; block-ids/sourcepos untouched; pre-paint script is inert in bare/script-free build output (page.rs drops it). (possible violation flagged: Soft corpus-plus-roadmap tension, not a hard breach: the 'expose the pre-paint bootstrap and token contract for the eventual print/PDF track' addition names no corpus document and is not buildable now (the print track does not exist and print already forces light via @media print), so it cannot be pinned and should be dropped from this entry rather than carried as roadmap vapor. The 'document the --tali-* override contract' addition is pinnable via a docs/corpus custom-theme page. No violation of HTML-only, single-editing-surface (toggle writes localStorage not .tmd), Markdown-syntax, click-to-source, block-level incremental, or warm-server invariants.)

### D95. Reader-side Display panel (size/measure/spacing) that Quarto's author-only knobs cannot match (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** fontsize, linestretch, and max-width are AUTHOR build-time settings baked into the page. The rendered Bootstrap page gives the READER no controls to change text size, reading measure, or spacing; the reader falls back to browser zoom.
- **Critique:** The reader is stuck with the author's sizing and measure; accessibility needs (large text, wider line/letter/word spacing) depend on the blunt instrument of browser zoom, and there is no persisted reading-comfort UI.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format compiler (one source to PDF, docx, ePub, revealjs, HTML). fontsize, linestretch, mainfont, and max-width are format-agnostic authoring knobs that must also map onto LaTeX and Word, so a browser-runtime reader panel structurally cannot be Quarto's primary mechanism without becoming HTML-only, which contradicts its write-once-render-many premise. Taliesin can afford the panel precisely because it dropped every non-HTML target. Second and stronger: reader-side text size, measure, and spacing are arguably the browser's and OS's job. Browser zoom (the WCAG 1.4.4 path), Reader View, OS text scaling, forced-colors, prefers-contrast, and user stylesheets already give the reader size/measure/spacing/contrast overrides that persist, apply to EVERY site, travel across devices, and honor the accessibility profile the reader configured once. Quarto's clean semantic Bootstrap output is built to reflow under those global mechanisms and to survive a 1.4.12 text-spacing bookmarklet without clipping, which is the standards-blessed conformance path, not a deficiency. A per-document panel only works on that one site, does not sync across devices, can fight Reader View, and lets readers break the author's tuned layout (figure widths, margin notes, code blocks). Keeping typography author-controlled yields one coherent, designed reading experience that is identical across all output formats. (Fairness nuance: Quarto DOES ship a reader light/dark toggle when two themes are configured, so it is not literally zero reader controls; the critique is accurate only because it scopes itself to size/measure/spacing.)
- **Taliesin today:** 14-reader-prefs.js mounts a 'Display' section in the reader menu with segmented controls: Theme (light/dark/sepia), Text size (0.9/1/1.15/1.3 via --tali-reader-scale), Width (Narrow 38rem / Normal / Wide 58rem via --tali-maxw), Line spacing, Letter spacing, and Word spacing where the 'Wider' steps hit WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing minimums. All are persisted per-reader in localStorage and applied PRE-PAINT by theme_head's applyReader (no flash), reader-local, and skipped on decks.
- **Proposed better:** Keep and extend along the read-only-view thesis (e.g. an optional serif/sans body toggle, hyphenation, a dyslexia-friendly stack the reader opts into), always reader-local and never a source write. This is the concrete meaning of 'wider than Quarto = richer browser behavior in a live HTML view.'
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the Display panel: it is a real, code-verified win over Quarto and squarely honors the single-editing-surface invariant (14-reader-prefs.js writes only localStorage; theme.rs applyReader applies CSS vars pre-paint so there is no flash; never touches .tmd; skipped on decks; block-ids/sourcepos untouched). It is also already corpus-pinned by corpus/reader/preferences.qmd, so corpus-plus-roadmap is satisfied for the current panel. Sharpen the entry on four points. (a) Position the panel as ADDITIVE comfort, and add the standard the entry currently omits: the BUILT page must independently satisfy WCAG 1.4.4 (survive 200% browser zoom without clipping) and 1.4.12 (survive a reader-applied text-spacing stylesheet), because the panel is not a substitute for a page that is robust under the reader's own browser/OS overrides, which is the real accessibility baseline. (b) Prefer CSS-variable-only knobs; gate any font-family extension (serif/dyslexia) on the offline-payload cost and the silent-no-op-when-font-absent risk, and if shipped, embed the face or fall back explicitly and extend preferences.qmd to pin it. (c) Make theme/contrast knobs DEFER to forced-colors, prefers-contrast, and prefers-reduced-motion rather than override them, so the panel augments the reader's global settings instead of fighting them. (d) Fix the one loaded detail: scope the "no reader controls" claim to size/measure/spacing (the critique text already does), since Quarto does ship a reader light/dark toggle with two themes configured.
- **Tradeoffs:** More reader-side UI and localStorage keys to maintain, and by design the author cannot force these preferences off. Broad prose-scoped spacing rules must stay careful not to distort code/math (already handled by the code/pre/.katex letter-spacing reset in base.css). (skeptic-found downside: The current panel is verified-correct and genuinely beats Quarto; the hidden costs live in the "extend" arm. (1) A serif/dyslexia-friendly (e.g. OpenDyslexic) font toggle breaks the self-contained/offline build ethos: it either relies on a system font that may be absent (so the opt-in silently does nothing, a worse-than-no-feature outcome for the reader who needs it most) or embeds a webfont that bloats every built page. The present panel is pure CSS-variables with zero font payload; font-family knobs forfeit that cleanliness. (2) Hyphenation needs a correct `lang` plus browser dictionaries and must be scoped away from code/inline literals and justified text, or it distorts them. (3) The panel duplicates browser/OS mechanisms, so every added knob risks FIGHTING them: the sepia/theme toggle and any contrast control must defer to forced-colors (Windows High Contrast) and prefers-contrast, and the broader thesis should honor OS signals (prefers-reduced-motion) rather than reinvent them. (4) localStorage prefs do not travel across sites or devices, so this is a reading-COMFORT affordance for THIS site, not the accessibility substitute the "accessibility needs" framing implies; a reader with a real vision need is better served by the global browser/OS path.)
- **Invariant check:** Squarely honors single-editing-surface: 100% reader-local, applied via CSS variables in localStorage, never writes .tmd and never mutates the source; HTML-only; block-ids/sourcepos untouched.

### D96. Do not silently accept .scss: either compile it or reject it with a diagnostic (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** theme: accepts a .scss file carrying `/*-- scss:defaults --*/` and `/*-- scss:rules --*/` layers, compiled by an embedded dart-sass and layered over Bootstrap 5. You customize appearance by setting Bootstrap Sass variables ($primary, $body-bg, $font-family-sans-serif, etc.) in the defaults layer and writing rules in the rules layer.
- **Critique:** You must learn Bootstrap's large Sass variable surface (hundreds of $vars) and the non-obvious two-phase defaults/rules split, and a whole Sass toolchain ships to compile it. It is heavyweight for a single author who wants a few color/font tweaks.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's defaults/rules SCSS system is a principled, high-leverage design, not arbitrary complexity. The two-phase split is forced by how Sass !default works: the defaults layer must load BEFORE Bootstrap so your $primary/$body-bg override Bootstrap's !default values, and the rules layer must load AFTER so your literal CSS wins the cascade. That ordering is the minimum needed to reparametrize a variable-based framework, not gratuitous ceremony. The payoff is a coherent design system: setting $primary once cascades through buttons, links, navbars, alerts, form focus rings, and active states with tested internal consistency, which a flat CSS-custom-property set only matches if the token surface is exhaustively hand-wired. Sass also brings functions (lighten/darken/color-mix), mixins, nesting, and loops, giving durable authoring power the same author reaches for six months later when a few tweaks become a palette shift. The critique's "hundreds of $vars" is a red herring: you override the handful you care about ($primary alone themes a whole site) and ignore the rest. And the toolchain cost is build-time only: dart-sass is bundled and fast, compiled CSS ships, runtime cost is zero. For a multi-format, Bootstrap-based publishing system serving thousands of authors, Sass-over-Bootstrap is the correct, well-engineered choice.
- **Taliesin today:** resolve_theme (crates/core/src/render/theme.rs) matches a `.scss` path in the SAME arm as `.css` and inlines it raw via std::fs::read_to_string; there is NO Sass compiler (no sass/grass dependency in any Cargo.toml). A real Sass file (e.g. corpus/tech-blog/theme.scss, full of $vars, nesting, &:hover, and scss:defaults markers) is emitted verbatim into a <style>, which the browser parses as invalid CSS and largely discards. So `.scss` support is silently broken.
- **Proposed better:** Keep no Sass compiler (the --tali-* CSS-custom-property layer is the intended customization surface and is far smaller than Bootstrap's Sass vars), but change the `.scss` branch from silent raw-inline to a hard, click-to-source diagnostic: 'Taliesin does not compile Sass; use a plain .css that overrides --tali-* tokens, or ship an _extensions/<name>/theme.css bundle.' A Sass file then fails loudly instead of emitting dead CSS.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the core direction (ship no Sass compiler; reject .scss instead of raw-inlining dead CSS) because it is sound and even stronger than the entry argues: Taliesin ships NO Bootstrap, so a Sass layer would buy it almost nothing (there is no framework variable surface to reparametrize), which is the real reason to decline it, more than "heavyweight for a few tweaks." But revise the entry on five points before cataloguing it. (a) Fix the false evidence: corpus/tech-blog/theme.scss is orphaned and never emitted; delete it as part of this change and stop citing it as proof of a live bug. State the actual reachable trigger precisely: a single-doc scalar `theme: x.scss`. (b) Extend the diagnostic to where the silent failures really are: route ANY `.scss`/`.sass` entry to the diagnostic in detect_theme (so the list form `theme: [base, layer.scss]` fails loudly instead of dropping the layer), not just the scalar resolve_theme arm. Cover `.sass` alongside `.scss`. (c) Describe the mechanism honestly as a Warning (logged + shown, build-failing under --strict), not a "hard stop"; if click-to-source is wanted, budget the small work to thread the front-matter theme: line into Warning::at, since resolve_theme currently has no sourcepos. (d) Point the message at the correct customization surface: plain .css overriding --tali-* tokens, or an _extensions/<name>/theme.css bundle. (e) Pin a corpus doc that exercises BOTH the scalar and list-form scss diagnostics so the regression net covers the real trigger paths. No invariant is violated; this is a scope-tightening and accuracy fix, not a redesign.
- **Tradeoffs:** Authors porting a Quarto Sass theme get a hard stop rather than an automatic conversion, and the (illusory) appearance of .scss acceptance is removed. Loses nothing real because the current behavior already does not work. (skeptic-found downside: The entry rests on a false example and misses the most common porting case. (1) The cited corpus/tech-blog/theme.scss is ORPHANED, not "emitted verbatim": _site.yml loads css: custom.css, SiteConfig has no theme field, and `theme` is not in NATIVE_KEYS, so a site project cannot reach the raw-inline path at all (a site `theme:` key would be flagged as unknown). That scss file is dead Quarto-era residue that no path renders. (2) The raw-inline bug is reachable ONLY via a single-doc .qmd with a SCALAR `theme: x.scss` front-matter value, far narrower than implied. (3) Biggest hole: the Quarto list form `theme: [base, layer.scss]`, the exact shape that scss file documents, is handled by detect_theme taking the FIRST entry, so the .scss layer is silently DROPPED (base name falls back harmlessly, no warning; test theme_list_takes_first_entry confirms). The proposal's diagnostic never fires for the most common ported-Quarto-theme pattern, so it fails to deliver its own promise of "fail loudly." (4) `.sass` is uncovered: resolve_theme matches only `.scss`; `theme: x.sass` falls to the ext arm and silently returns empty. (5) "hard stop / fails loudly" is overstated: the natural implementation is another Warning at the same soft severity as the sibling "theme file not found" arm, which only truly fails the build under --strict; in preview the page renders with no theme. (6) "click-to-source diagnostic" is not free: Warning supports .at(file, line), but resolve_theme is passed only theme: Option<&str> with no front-matter line, so making it clickable needs new sourcepos plumbing to the theme: key.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only preserved; no preview write-back; the --tali-* token layer keeps data-block-id/data-sourcepos and click-to-source intact; pin a corpus doc that exercises the .scss diagnostic so the regression net covers it.

### D97. Warn on an unknown named theme instead of silently falling back to default (Proposed change)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** keep
- **Quarto does:** Ships 25 built-in Bootswatch themes selectable by bare name (theme: darkly | cosmo | flatly | ...), plus theme: default = plain Bootstrap. A named theme is a one-word discovery-friendly consistency win.
- **Critique:** The 25 named themes are a genuine discovery and consistency benefit, but they ship the full Bootstrap CSS and lock the page's whole design language to Bootstrap, most of which a prose author never uses.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A bare Bootswatch name is not "prose color" that a prose author wastes; it is a complete, professionally curated design system covering everything Quarto's actual target (scientific/technical publishing) uses: nav, sidebar TOC, tables, cross-refs, callouts, figures, code blocks, listing pages, pagination, forms. `theme: darkly` yields a fully coherent, contrast-checked, cross-browser-tested surface from one recognizable word (the 25 names come from the well-known bootswatch.com set, so they are discoverable and portable). Crucially, Quarto is NOT hard-locked to Bootstrap the way the critique implies: its theming is SCSS-variable-driven (`theme: [darkly, brand.scss]` overrides `$primary`, `$body-bg`, etc. without touching Bootstrap internals), which is the exact same override-token model as Taliesin's `--tali-*`, just via Sass. The full-CSS-weight cost is real but modest, cacheable, and gzips well, and Quarto compiles only referenced Sass. So "locks the whole design language to Bootstrap" overstates it (SCSS layering is the escape hatch the critique omits), and "most of which a prose author never uses" is true only for Taliesin's narrow single-author-prose scope, not for Quarto's multi-format audience where that breadth is load-bearing.
- **Taliesin today:** resolve_theme handles only "light"/"default"/"dark" as built-in modes (plus reader-side sepia). ANY other bare name (e.g. darkly) falls to the extension arm, tries _extensions/<name>/theme.css, and on a miss returns unwrap_or_default() = empty string with NO warning. The code comment is explicit: a bare name is not warned so a Quarto built-in like `darkly` 'harmlessly falls back to the default'.
- **Proposed better:** Now that Taliesin is a clean break from Quarto (the front-matter validator already flags every unknown key with did-you-mean + click-to-source), drop the silent-fallback special case: warn on an unknown bare theme name the same way, so `theme: darkly` says 'no built-in theme "darkly"; ship _extensions/darkly/theme.css or override --tali-* tokens.' Optionally ship a tiny curated set of named tone/accent presets that only set --tali-* tokens (no Bootstrap).
- **Tradeoffs:** A doc copied from Quarto with `theme: darkly` now warns instead of quietly rendering the default, which is the intended clean-break behavior but a migration friction. Any curated preset set must be named and maintained. (skeptic-found downside: The bare-name arm is the SAME code path that legitimate installed extension themes use (`theme: mytheme` reading `_extensions/mytheme/theme.css`), so the warning must be gated strictly on the read MISS, not on "any non-built-in name," or it breaks working extension themes. The entry's phrasing "warn on an unknown bare theme name" is looser than the safe implementation ("warn only when `_extensions/<name>/theme.css` is unreadable"). Two more the drafter missed: (a) list-form `theme: [cosmo, brand.scss]` has detect_theme take only the first entry, so beyond warning on `cosmo` it ALSO silently drops the `brand.scss` layer, meaning the warning is not the full honesty story; (b) the "curated --tali-* presets" half is an unbounded naming/maintenance surface that must also be registered in resolve_theme's built-in arm so the warning does not fire for them, and it should not gate or muddy the pure-honesty warning change.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; no write-back; consistent with the existing strict-validation stance (schema.rs); pin a corpus doc with an unknown theme name to lock the new warning.

### D98. Keep SSR scope-class highlighting, but promote the code palette to --tali-hl-* tokens (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** highlight-style: picks one of ~20 Pandoc/skylighting themes (arrow, github, monokai, ...), some with paired light/dark files; highlighting is baked by Pandoc at build into inline-colored spans.
- **Critique:** The skylighting palette is chosen independently of the page theme, so it can clash with the site colors, and supporting light/dark needs two token files or a re-highlight; the colors are also locked to skylighting's named themes.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's highlight-style is format-agnostic by necessity, and that is the real justification the critique never engages. highlight-style must also color LaTeX/PDF listings and other Pandoc targets from ONE definition, and CSS custom properties do not exist outside HTML, so a portable named-theme abstraction is the correct choice for a multi-format compiler. Skylighting/KDE themes are a shared, cross-editor standard with dozens of curated, often colorblind-tested palettes (github, monokai, solarized) that authors already recognize, and decoupling code color from the page's Bootstrap theme is deliberate: code reads consistently across sites and the code theme can be swapped without touching the site theme. Two accuracy points cut against the critique itself: Pandoc HTML emits scope CLASSES plus a header style block, not "inline-colored spans" (only fragment/edge modes inline), and Quarto already supports highlight-style light/dark PAIRS that it ships together and swaps by CSS class with no re-highlight, so Quarto is not as rigid as "needs two token files or a re-highlight" implies. Taliesin can afford CSS tokens precisely because it discarded every non-HTML target: that is a consequence of the HTML-only invariant, not a Quarto mistake. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** highlight.rs runs syntect server-side and emits SCOPE CLASSES (tali-hl-comment/string/keyword/entity/...), and base.css/dark.css/sepia map those classes to colors, so a theme toggle recolors code purely in CSS with NO re-highlight and no client JS. This is already better on the SSR/one-highlight/offline axis. But the per-scope colors are HARDCODED literals (e.g. .tali-hl-keyword { color: #cf222e } light, #ff7b72 dark, #9a3b28 sepia), not variables, so there is no knob to retune the code palette short of editing bundled CSS or re-overriding each class.
- **Proposed better:** Promote the per-scope colors to --tali-hl-comment/string/keyword/... custom properties defined per theme (:root / [data-theme]) and referenced by the .tali-hl-* rules, so a theme, the proposed brand block, or a css: file can retune the whole code palette in one place per theme, matching how every other color is already a token. The existing literals become the default token values.
- **Revised recommendation:** Do the tokenization: it is directionally correct and makes the code palette consistent with how every other color in the system is already a token. But sharpen it: (a) downgrade impact from medium to LOW, because a theme file can already override the six classes by source order, so this is consistency polish, not a new capability; (b) define default (light) tokens on :root and sepia tokens in base.css, and dark tokens in dark.css under html[data-theme="dark"], then verify the bare-output rewrite (dark prefix -> :root) still resolves them (it does, checked); keep the existing literals as the :root defaults and use var() with those defaults so a partial custom theme never blanks a scope; (c) confirm the token names pair 1:1 with only the syntect scope classes and note the `.tali-hl` UI-highlight overload so syntax color is never conflated with cursor/line highlight; (d) add a lightweight regression since the corpus HTML net will not catch a token break: assert base.css references var(--tali-hl-keyword) and that :root/dark/sepia each define it, or a per-theme browser computed-color check; (e) drop the "brand block" from the justification until that block actually exists, and re-scope the pitch to "retune the mapped scopes" rather than "the whole code palette."
- **Tradeoffs:** A bit more CSS indirection and the token set must be defined across light/dark/sepia. No behavior change for existing docs (defaults preserved). (skeptic-found downside: The realized benefit is much thinner than "medium impact" implies. (1) A css:/theme: file can ALREADY retune the palette today by re-declaring the six mapped class rules: they layer after base.css and dark.css and win by source order (verified in page.rs), so tokens save ~6 override lines, they do not unlock a capability. (2) One of the two cited beneficiaries, the "proposed brand block," does not exist in the codebase (grep: brand = navbar title only), so it is vaporware motivation. (3) Only ~6 to 8 syntect scopes are mapped; the code comment says unmapped scopes inherit the default code color, so tokens retune the MAPPED scopes, not "the whole code palette" as claimed. (4) The `--tali-hl-*` token names collide semantically with the overloaded `.tali-hl` family, which is NOT syntax color: `.tali-hl`/`.tali-hl-flash` are the editor cursor-sync outline and `.tali-hl-ln`/`.tali-hl-lines-active`/`.tali-hl-ln-hl` are code-walkthrough line highlighting; a reader could conflate the two namespaces. (5) There is no natural corpus pin: the corpus tests assert emitted HTML and the block model, not computed CSS colors, so a token regression would sail through the regression net.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure CSS/token change; no write-back; HTML-only; highlighting stays server-side so first paint and incremental block swaps are unaffected; data-block-id/sourcepos untouched. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation. HTML-only is reinforced (CSS custom properties are an HTML-only affordance); no write-back to source; Markdown/Pandoc syntax untouched; data-sourcepos, data-block-id, SSR highlighting and block-level diffing are all unaffected, so click-to-source, incremental swaps, and the warm server are untouched; the entry's invariant_check is accurate. The only soft friction is with corpus-plus-roadmap: a CSS-only token change sits below the corpus's HTML-level resolution, so "each capability is pinned by a corpus document" is only weakly satisfied and needs a css-presence or browser computed-color assertion to stay honest.)

### D99. System-font-first (no third-party font requests) with a self-hosted on-ramp (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Exposes mainfont/monofont/sansfont/fontsize knobs, and Bootswatch themes import Google Fonts by default (darkly pulls Lato); $web-font-path controls or disables the import in a Sass theme.
- **Critique:** Google Fonts is a third-party network dependency: privacy exposure, offline/self-hosted breakage, and FOUT/CLS as the webfont swaps in. The font knobs are also build-time-only.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The core critique is fair for Quarto's DEFAULT web output: a non-self-contained `quarto render` with a Google-Fonts-importing Bootswatch theme (darkly=Lato) ships an `@import url(fonts.googleapis.com...)` that is a third-party request, fails offline, and produces a swap-in FOUT/CLS. Those claims are accurate and not a strawman. But two sub-claims are overstated and must be steelmanned: (1) The strongest case FOR Quarto is that `mainfont`/`fontsize` are CROSS-FORMAT typographic keys. Quarto is a multi-format compiler (HTML, PDF/LaTeX, Typst, docx, epub, beamer); one `mainfont: Palatino` maps consistently into fontspec, Typst, and docx styles as well as CSS. Taliesin sidesteps this only because it is HTML-only, so 'just override a CSS variable' is not a like-for-like replacement for what Quarto's key buys a print-oriented author, and FOUT/CLS/privacy simply do not exist for the PDF/docx targets at all. (2) The 'offline/self-hosted breakage' claim ignores Quarto's real escape hatches: `$web-font-path` disables or self-hosts the import in a Sass theme, and `embed-resources`/self-contained fetches and inlines even remote fonts at build time, so an offline single-file Quarto HTML is achievable. The weakest link in the critique is 'build-time-only', which is nearly a non-differentiator: Taliesin's own font selection (a `--tali-font-*` CSS variable resolved at render) is equally build-time, so the meaningful gap is the third-party network default plus Sass-rebuild friction, not the timing.
- **Taliesin today:** Ships ZERO prose web fonts. --tali-font-body/head/mono (base.css) are system stacks (ui-serif/Georgia, ui-sans-serif/system-ui, ui-monospace); the only bundled font is KaTeX's self-hosted woff2 set for math. There is no mainfont/fontsize key; changing the typeface means overriding --tali-font-* via css:.
- **Proposed better:** Keep system-first as the default (offline, private, no FOUT), but close the on-ramp gap two ways: (a) let the proposed brand/font config set --tali-font-* without hand-written CSS, and (b) document and support a self-hosted @font-face recipe (drop a woff2 next to the doc, reference it in css:) so a custom typeface never reintroduces a third-party request. The portable build already copies local assets.
- **Revised recommendation:** KEEP the default verdict (system-first is genuinely already-better: base.css:18-20 ships zero prose web fonts as system stacks, only KaTeX woff2 is self-hosted, no FOUT, no third-party request), but REVISE the on-ramp before cataloguing it. (1) Fix recipe (b): the documented self-hosted recipe must base64 data-URI the woff2 into `@font-face src` within the css: file (survives both the portable folder and the single-file self-contained build); a bare `url('myfont.woff2')` is broken because the asset copier never scans CSS url(). Optionally extend copy_local_assets (build.rs:397) to bundle url()-referenced assets from inlined CSS so a bare-url recipe also travels, and add a corpus doc that portable-builds a custom-font page to pin it. (2) Delete the 'the portable build already copies local assets' justification for fonts, it is false as stated. (3) For config (a): a new brand/font key that sets `--tali-font-*` must be registered in the STRICT schema (schema.rs / frontmatter allow-list) or strict validation will flag it as unknown, and per corpus-plus-roadmap it must ship pinned by a corpus doc in the same change. (4) In the tradeoffs, reframe the Quarto contrast honestly: Quarto's `mainfont` is a cross-format key (not just an HTML convenience), and Quarto CAN go offline via `$web-font-path` + embed-resources, so the real Taliesin win is 'private/offline BY DEFAULT with no opt-in step', not 'Quarto cannot do offline'.
- **Tradeoffs:** Self-hosting a custom face is more author effort than Quarto's one-line mainfont:, and there is deliberately no Google-Fonts convenience path. That is the intended offline/privacy stance, not an oversight. (skeptic-found downside: The on-ramp recipe (b) does not survive either build target, and its own justification is false. The proposal says 'reference [a woff2] in css: ... the portable build already copies local assets.' But css: files are inlined as `<style>` blocks (doc_includes.rs:107-116), not emitted as `<link>`, and the asset copier (build.rs local_refs:1135 / copy_local_assets:397) scans ONLY `src=`/`href=` HTML attributes plus `{js}` ESM imports (copy_js_imports:581). There is zero CSS `url()` scanning. So a `@font-face { src: url('myfont.woff2') }` inside a css: file is silently dropped from the portable `--out` folder, AND the single-file `build doc.qmd out.html` never data-URI-inlines it either, leaving a dangling relative url() next to a lone .html. Result: the custom typeface falls back to system in exactly the offline/portable scenario the entry is selling. The robust recipe the drafter missed is to base64 data-URI the woff2 INTO the `@font-face src` inside the css: file (the only form that survives both the portable folder and the single-file self-contained build), or to extend copy_local_assets to also bundle `url(...)` refs from inlined CSS.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time/asset-only; HTML-only; the portable offline build copies referenced local assets; no preview write-back.

### D100. Honor prefers-reduced-motion consistently across CSS, the deck runtime, and (next) author {js} animations, as one owned invariant (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto has no single owned motion policy: it inherits two disjoint stacks. Website/book chrome rides Bootstrap 5, whose reboot ships a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block that neutralizes transitions, animations, and smooth-scroll globally, so that surface is broadly covered. But slide decks run on reveal.js, whose CSS slide transitions and JS-driven zoom/auto-animate are not gated on the preference and animate regardless of the OS setting; OJS/Observable animations, mermaid, and any custom JS are likewise ungated. The result is inconsistent: motion-sensitivity is respected in the article chrome but ignored the moment you present a deck or run an interactive cell, and Quarto never exposes the resolved preference to author code.
- **Critique:** Because Quarto stitches together Bootstrap plus reveal.js plus Observable, no one owns the reduced-motion contract end to end. A blanket Bootstrap reset only catches CSS on the pages Bootstrap styles; it cannot reach reveal's JS zoom fly or a `requestAnimationFrame` loop in an OJS cell, and there is no seam where an author can ask "did the reader opt out of motion?" So the same document is accessible in one view and vestibular-hostile in another, and the author has no lever to fix it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format document compiler whose job is orchestration, not owning a motion runtime. It deliberately delegates each surface to a best-in-class upstream: Bootstrap 5 for HTML/book chrome (whose reboot ships a real prefers-reduced-motion block plus a reduced-motion mixin used per component), reveal.js for slides, Observable for reactive cells. That delegation is a feature, not negligence: when any of those projects improves its reduced-motion posture upstream, Quarto inherits it for free with zero maintenance and zero divergence from the vendor. Re-implementing a single cross-cutting motion invariant over three independently-versioned engines would be a standing liability that fights its own upstreams on every release. Moreover, a single owned motion policy is not even a coherent concept across Quarto's actual scope: most of its output targets (PDF, LaTeX, Word, ePub) have no notion of motion at all, so the policy would only apply to the HTML/JS slice, which is precisely the slice Quarto chose to hand to specialists. And the seam Taliesin proposes (a runtime that exposes the resolved preference to author code) only exists because Taliesin threw away reveal.js and Observable and rebuilt them; Quarto cannot offer that seam without paying the same reconstruction cost, and an author in Quarto's OJS or raw-JS cells can already call matchMedia directly. Quarto's non-ownership is the rational consequence of being multi-format and vendor-delegating.
- **Taliesin today:** Taliesin owns every surface, so the policy is one coherent thing, verified in code. base.css:766-769 is a universal reset (`*, *::before, *::after` collapse animation/transition durations to .001ms and force `scroll-behavior: auto` under `reduce`). New motion is authored as progressive enhancement inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` wrappers (skip link base.css:199; code walkthrough 528-531; scrolly 552-554; tabset 578-580; deck fragments deck.css:384-388; code-line stepping 405-407; preview progress-dot + running-cell badge pulse serve/mod.rs:501,518), so the default and reduced states are already motionless. The one case CSS cannot reach, the deck's van Wijk rAF camera zoom, is gated in the runtime: deck.js:203-234 `reducedMotion()` reads `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` and `setCamera` snaps instead of flying. Component-level `reduce` blocks back this up (deck.css:250-253 LOD, 285 minimap, 586-590 camera layer !important; site.css:227 book-drawer slide-in animation:none). Verified gap: qmd-js.js, the native {js} reactive runtime, contains no prefers-reduced-motion or matchMedia handling, so author {js} cells (d3/Plot/canvas rAF) animate regardless of the preference.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the current design (it is already more consistent than Quarto) and close the one verified gap plus lock the whole thing against regression. (1) Expose the resolved preference to author code: add a reactive builtin to qmd-js.js, e.g. a `reducedMotion` value plus a `Taliesin.reducedMotion` boolean, updated from a `matchMedia` change listener so a `{js}` cell can branch (skip a d3 transition, jump to the final frame) and re-run reactively when the reader toggles the OS setting. Document it in the {js} reference and pin it with a corpus doc whose cell reads the flag. (2) Make the cross-cutting decision a tested invariant, mirroring the existing reverse-sync sourcepos totality test: a corpus/render test asserting the universal reset is emitted and that the deck runtime gates its fly, so the policy cannot silently rot when someone adds a new animated component. This turns an implicit convention into a corpus-arbitrated contract.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the framing "Taliesin already beats Quarto here" (verified: universal * reset at base.css:766 backstops ALL CSS motion under reduce, so any ungated CSS animation is already neutralized by construction; the deck rAF fly is gated at deck.js:229). That fact narrows the real gap to exactly one surface, the {js} runtime, which the entry correctly identifies. Sharpen the fix on four points. (1) Reframe from "close the gap" to "provide the idiomatic lever AND make Taliesin's own animated corpus cells honor it": in the same change, update three-scene.qmd (and any d3/Plot transition cell) to branch on the flag (skip the rAF loop or jump to the final frame under reduce), so the corpus demonstrates the policy instead of a synthetic new doc alone. This is the strongest reader-facing justification and the entry undersells it. (2) Expose ONE name, hung off the existing global, taliJs.reducedMotion, as a live-reading reactive input, not a separate Taliesin.* namespace (no window.Taliesin exists today) and not a duplicate static snapshot. (3) Register the matchMedia change listener inside enhance() idempotently and remove it in resetRuntime/teardownIn so it does not leak or double-fire across warm-preview hot reloads; confirm the toggle-driven re-run flows through the same reactive path that already preserves the output block's data-block-id and data-sourcepos wrapper. (4) Right-size the regression test: the CSS-reset assertion is near-redundant because the universal * reset is already a catch-all, so pin the two things the reset cannot reach, the deck runtime gate (deck.js) and the new qmd-js flag plumbing, asserting intent (a gate on the media query exists) rather than exact strings, mirroring reverse_sync_sourcepos_is_total. Note one honesty caveat in the entry: Quarto's "author has no lever" is slightly overstated (raw matchMedia is always available); the true Taliesin advantage is reactive, idiomatic, and enforced-by-corpus, not that honoring the preference is otherwise impossible.
- **Tradeoffs:** Exposing a `reducedMotion` builtin widens the {js} runtime API surface (one more name authors can depend on, so it must stay stable) and shifts responsibility for honoring the preference onto author code for animations Taliesin cannot see inside, meaning a careless cell can still animate; the builtin makes the right thing possible and idiomatic, not automatic. The regression test couples a test to specific CSS/JS text, so it needs to assert intent (a reduce block exists and neuters durations; the deck gates on the media query) rather than brittle exact strings. Both are small, additive, and carry no runtime cost on the warm path. (skeptic-found downside: The builtin does not actually "close the gap," it only offers an opt-in lever, so the headline overclaims. Taliesin already lets a {js} cell call matchMedia today; adding taliJs.reducedMotion buys ergonomics and reactive re-run on toggle, not a new capability. Crucially, every animation Taliesin cannot see inside still runs unless its author opts in, including Taliesin's OWN corpus cell (corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd runs a continuous requestAnimationFrame Three.js rotation that ignores the preference right now). So to genuinely close the gap the change must also rewrite the existing animated corpus cells to consume the flag, not merely add a new synthetic corpus doc that reads it, otherwise the dogfood keeps violating the very invariant the entry claims to enforce. Secondary missed costs: (a) the proposed reactive-re-run-on-toggle must tear down and rebuild a cell's DOM, which for a WebGL/Three.js cell risks leaking GL contexts or flashing, and the global matchMedia change listener must be registered and torn down with the warm runtime (resetRuntime) or it stacks and leaks across preview hot reloads; (b) exposing BOTH a reactive value and a static Taliesin.reducedMotion boolean is a redundant dual API where the snapshot boolean invites a stale read that never re-runs.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: pure browser-view CSS/JS, touches no output format and adds none. Single read-only surface: reduced-motion is a display/render concern with zero write-back; the {js} builtin only reads a media query and feeds the reactive graph. Keep-Markdown: no syntax change; the builtin rides existing `{js}` cell syntax. Click-to-source: untouched, blocks keep data-block-id + data-sourcepos. Block-level incremental: the reset is document-global CSS and a runtime check, orthogonal to diffing; a change to the OS preference re-runs only the consuming cell via the existing reactive scheduler. Warm-server: no per-edit startup cost. Corpus-plus-roadmap: the proposal ships pinned by a new corpus doc plus an invariant test, exactly the corpus-leads discipline.

### D101. Default the color scheme to OS-follow with an always-present persisted reader toggle, not a fixed light theme (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's HTML default is a single fixed light Bootstrap theme (cosmo). Dark mode and a scheme toggle are strictly opt-in: the author must set a `theme:` map with both `light:` and `dark:` sub-keys. Only then does Quarto render a `.quarto-color-scheme-toggle`, honor `prefers-color-scheme` for the initial pick, and persist the choice (localStorage `quarto-color-scheme`). Out of the box (a scalar `theme:`), the page is fixed light: it does not follow the OS and gives the reader no switch. The catalog captured Quarto's one-stylesheet-plus-runtime-swap MECHANISM but never recorded the default-scheme POLICY.
- **Critique:** The default punishes the common case. A reader whose OS is in dark mode lands on a glaring light page and, unless the author configured a dual theme, has no control at all. Getting OS-follow plus a toggle requires the author to know about the `light:`/`dark:` map form and to supply a second theme, so most Quarto sites ship fixed-light. It treats "respect the reader's system preference" and "let the reader choose" as advanced opt-ins rather than the baseline a live HTML reading surface should give for free.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's fixed-light default is a defensible policy for what Quarto is, not negligence. (1) Quarto is a MULTI-format, MULTI-author publishing system; a light default keeps HTML visually aligned with its PDF/print default (paper is white), preserving the one-source-many-formats parity that is its whole ethos. (2) Correctness under arbitrary content: auto-dark-by-default breaks author-supplied assets that assume a light canvas (matplotlib/ggplot figures with baked white backgrounds, screenshots, embedded HTML widgets, third-party iframes). Quarto cannot guarantee every author's content is dark-safe, so gating dark behind an explicit opt-in (author picks a dark theme AND implicitly audits their figures) is the conservative choice that avoids a flood of "my plots look wrong in dark mode" reports. (3) Determinism/brand: institutional, journal, and book publishers want a page that looks identical for every visitor and every screenshot; OS-follow makes appearance visitor-dependent, complicating QA and brand control. (4) Stability: flipping the default to OS-follow would silently change the rendered appearance of thousands of already-deployed sites on their next rebuild, a breaking change a widely-installed tool avoids. (5) Cost: the dual-theme machinery compiles two SCSS bundles plus a runtime swap; keeping it opt-in keeps the default build lighter. Taliesin can override all five because it is single-author (no brand-lock need), HTML-only (no PDF-parity constraint), an explicit reading tool that elevates reader autonomy as a design value, and owns its content conventions. So the catalog should record this as a scope/values divergence, not as Quarto being dumb.
- **Taliesin today:** Already OS-follow by default. `theme_default_mode()` (theme.rs:55) returns `"auto"` for every doc except one with an explicit front-matter `theme: dark`/`light`. `theme_head()` emits a pre-paint `<head>` script that, before first paint, sets `<html data-theme>`, `el.style.colorScheme`, and an inline background, so there is no flash of the wrong theme even on cross-page navigation. Active-mode resolution: saved reader choice `qmd-theme` (light/dark/sepia) wins, else forced front-matter mode, else OS `prefers-color-scheme`, else light. An OS-change listener re-applies only when mode is auto AND no saved choice exists, so an explicit reader toggle is never clobbered by an OS flip. The toggle ships in the site navbar (chrome.rs:115/265) and is injected into the single-doc preview control bar (client.js:423); it persists to localStorage and fires `qmd:themechange` so mermaid and theme-matched videos re-render. `--bare` output degrades to CSS-only OS-follow via `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` (page.rs:199), pinned by `bare_theming_resolves_per_theme_default`.
- **Proposed better:** Keep OS-follow ("auto") as the shipped default with an always-present persisted reader toggle and the pre-paint `data-theme` bootstrap: this is already strictly better than Quarto's opt-in dual-theme. Harden it in two verified-gap places. (1) Also emit a static `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` (or the single forced value when front matter forces one) in the standalone page head, so native UI (scrollbars, form controls, the default canvas) themes correctly even in the pre-script frame and when JS is disabled, complementing the inline `colorScheme` the script sets once JS runs. (2) Add a corpus document that pins the INTERACTIVE precedence (saved > forced > OS > light) and the "an OS flip never overrides an explicit reader toggle" rule with a browser test; today the corpus test only covers the bare CSS-only path, leaving the load-bearing `hasSaved()` logic unpinned.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship the entry, but split its two hardening items on their merits. KEEP the core, which is already shipped and verified strictly better than Quarto: OS-follow (\"auto\") default, an always-present persisted reader toggle, the pre-paint `data-theme`/`colorScheme`/background bootstrap, and the `hasSaved()`-guarded OS listener so an OS flip never clobbers an explicit toggle. DROP item (1), the color-scheme meta, from the non-bare page: it is redundant when JS is on and actively mismatches (light content, dark chrome) when JS is off, because non-bare content only follows the OS through JS-set `data-theme`. If any meta is wanted at all, restrict it to the `--bare` path and only there, where content truly follows the OS without JS, and even then note it is near-redundant with the `color-scheme: dark` already emitted inside bare's `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` block. KEEP and prioritize item (2): the interactive precedence (saved > forced > OS > light) and the OS-flip-vs-saved rule live entirely in the untested `pref()`/`hasSaved()`/`apply()` JS; the corpus only pins the bare CSS path. Pin it two ways, since the corpus net is Rust render tests: (a) a render-level string assertion that the emitted `theme_head` script contains the precedence + `hasSaved` guard, runnable in `cargo test -p taliesin-core`; and (b) a browser test (chrome-devtools MCP) driving localStorage + `matchMedia` to prove a saved choice survives an OS flip. Flag in the entry that (b) is not a pure corpus render test and needs its own harness. Finally, document the deliberate stance precisely: a per-origin saved reader choice (including sepia) intentionally overrides an author's per-document forced `theme:`, reader autonomy wins by design; this is a stance to state, not a bug to fix.
- **Tradeoffs:** The `color-scheme` meta is redundant with the inline `el.style.colorScheme` the bootstrap already sets when JS runs, so its only marginal value is the JS-disabled and pre-script-frame cases: small, honest hardening, not a fix for a live flash. Shipping both light and dark CSS layers on every page (the existing status quo) has a minor payload cost versus a single-theme build. The always-on reader toggle deliberately lets a returning reader's saved `light` override an author's `theme: dark`: reader autonomy wins by design, which an author who wants a locked brand scheme cannot defeat. That is a deliberate stance (single-author reading tool), and it should be documented as such rather than treated as configurable. (skeptic-found downside: Proposal item (1), the `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` in the standalone (non-bare) page head, backfires in exactly the JS-disabled case it claims to serve. Verified in code: the non-bare page's dark styling is gated solely on `html[data-theme="dark"]` (dark.css) with NO `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` fallback, and `data-theme` is only ever set by the head JS. So with JS disabled on a non-bare page whose reader's OS is dark, the CONTENT stays light (base `:root`), but the meta tells the browser the page supports dark, so the UA canvas, scrollbars, and default form controls render dark: a light-content / dark-chrome mismatch that is worse than today's consistent all-light JS-disabled render. Same failure for a forced `theme: dark` doc (content is still light without JS, so `content=\"dark\"` mismatches). With JS ENABLED the meta is fully redundant: the head script sets an inline `el.style.colorScheme` on the root, and inline style overrides the meta. And the drafter's own concession kills the \"pre-script frame\" rationale: the theme script is a synchronous `<head>` script that runs before the first paint, so there is no observable pre-script frame to protect. On the bare path, where content genuinely follows the OS via the media query, the meta is also redundant because bare's rewritten dark layer already carries `color-scheme: dark` inside that `@media` block (page.rs:199 + dark.css). So item (1) is either harmful (non-bare, JS off) or redundant (JS on, or bare), never a net win. Secondary edge the tradeoffs half-acknowledge but underspecify: `qmd-theme` is a per-ORIGIN localStorage key, not per-document, so a reader who once toggled `light` (or `sepia`, a reader-only mode) silently overrides a specific page authored `theme: dark` site-wide, which can break a deliberately dark-designed page, not just a global brand preference.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: theming is pure CSS variables plus a `data-theme` attribute in the one HTML output, no new format. Single read-only surface: the toggle writes only to the reader's localStorage (client state), never to the .tmd source, so click-to-source and the one-way edit flow are untouched. Keep-Markdown: the author-facing control is the unchanged front-matter `theme:` YAML key. Block-level incremental: a theme switch is a runtime attribute/CSS-var swap with no re-render, so every block keeps its data-block-id and data-sourcepos. Warm-server: the toggle is entirely client-side with no server round-trip. Corpus-plus-roadmap: the proposal ships pinned by a new corpus doc plus browser test for the interactive precedence and the meta tag.

## Slides and presentations

### D102. Own a native slide engine instead of coupling to reveal.js (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** format: revealjs bundles reveal.js (roughly 400KB+ of JS/CSS plus its plugins) and emits the reveal DOM; all of navigation, fragments, PDF, speaker view and chalkboard are reveal or reveal plugins.
- **Critique:** reveal.js owns the entire slide DOM and reflows/rebuilds on init, wrapping and re-transforming your nodes, so you cannot cleanly diff-patch a single changed block into a live deck and click-to-source has nowhere stable to attach. It is also a heavy dependency to keep vendored and offline.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general multi-format document compiler, and for HTML slides reusing reveal.js is the rational, risk-minimizing choice. Reveal is a decade-hardened, widely adopted engine with an enormous shipped feature set: a transition catalog, fragments, speaker notes, tested print-to-PDF pagination, menu, search, chalkboard, multiplex, RTL, touch, embedded-media handling, plus a large ecosystem of themes and third-party plugins users can extend without touching Quarto internals. By delegating the slide runtime, Quarto spends its effort only on the Pandoc-to-reveal translation and ships a single portable self-contained HTML deck that also exports to PDF and works offline. Reveal's init-time DOM reflow is not a bug: it is a documented contract tuned for a static present-mode deck, and it is a non-issue for Quarto because Quarto's preview is full-page reload, not live block diffing. So reveal is only a liability under a requirement Quarto never adopted (block-level diff-patch plus click-to-source). Given Quarto's actual design center, delegating to a mature engine rather than authoring and maintaining a bespoke one is the disciplined call.
- **Taliesin today:** reveal.js is removed. assets/js/deck.js (~1687 lines) drives the native .tali-deck > .tali-slides > section contract via window.TaliesinDeck; each slide's inner blocks keep their own data-block-id/data-sourcepos, so block-swap and Alt-click work on slides exactly as on a page. Pinned by corpus/deck.tali.
- **Proposed better:** Keep owning it. The structural win is that a deck is just another view over the same block model, which is what makes incremental updates and click-to-source free on slides. Continue pinning capabilities with corpus deck documents.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep owning the engine: the core recommendation is correct and already shipped. A deck is genuinely just another view over the same block model (verified: section-level ARIA/id/bg attrs are additive, inner blocks keep byte-stable data-block-id/data-sourcepos, live edits apply block ops then TaliesinDeck.sync() re-scans while preserving the current index, and Alt-click maps to TaliesinDeck.slide(i)), which is exactly what makes incremental updates and click-to-source free on slides in a way a re-initializing reveal DOM cannot cleanly offer. Sharpen the entry on two points rather than accept it as written. First, rewrite the critique framing to concede reveal's reflow is a liability only under Taliesin's live-diff plus click-to-source invariant, not a defect for Quarto's full-reload batch model. Second, rewrite the tradeoffs: stop claiming reveal's feature set is still owed (speaker/chalkboard/overview/fragments/print already ship) and instead name the true residual costs, the permanent loss of the reveal theme and plugin ecosystem as an escape hatch and a standing cross-browser, print-pagination, and a11y hardening tax borne alone. Continue pinning each deck capability with a corpus deck document (corpus/deck.qmd), and add corpus coverage specifically for slide print/PDF pagination since that surface is now owned end to end.
- **Tradeoffs:** You re-implement everything reveal gave for free (the transition catalog, the third-party plugin ecosystem, multiplex, established chalkboard) and carry that maintenance yourself with no plugin market to lean on. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's own tradeoff list is partly wrong, which understates one cost and overstates another. Overstated: "re-implement everything reveal gave for free" is largely already paid down. deck.js already ships speaker view (openSpeaker), chalkboard/draw, overview, fragments, print/PDF via beforeprint+enterPrint, cross-window postMessage sync, and reduced-motion, so the expensive core is done, not pending. Understated (the real missed cost): a permanent forfeit of reveal's theme and plugin ecosystem as an escape hatch. There is no drop-in market for a menu, a networked multiplex, a search plugin, or hundreds of community themes, so any such capability must be authored in-house or foregone, and a departing author cannot carry a Taliesin deck into the reveal world. Plus a standing long-tail hardening tax that a solo 1686-line engine keeps paying alone: touch, RTL, projector aspect ratios, Safari scaling, embedded-video autoplay, and especially slide PDF pagination, which now rests entirely on Taliesin's own print CSS (the invariant "print renders FROM the built HTML" makes deck print-CSS a load-bearing surface Taliesin owns outright, where reveal shipped a tested print-pdf mode).)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (slides are HTML sections in the one build target); block-level incremental preserved because per-block ids survive inside sections; click-to-source works on slides; warm-server unaffected; ## = slide keeps the Markdown substrate; corpus-pinned.

### D103. Navigate with a spatial camera and a pannable overview map, not a linear filmstrip (Taliesin already better)
