- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** reveal is a linear filmstrip with optional vertical stacks; the overview (press O) is a static zoomed-out tile grid; navigation is strictly horizontal/vertical arrows through that filmstrip.
- **Critique:** reveal's overview is a flat tile grid that turns into a field of specks past roughly 30 slides, with no pan, zoom, or filter, so it stops working as a 'where am I' map and offers no spatial memory of topic structure. (Its linearity is, however, dead simple and predictable.)
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A strict linear filmstrip is a mental model that survives ANY authoring style: every deck navigates identically (space, arrows, clicker) with zero per-deck learning cost and nothing to mis-group, whereas Taliesin's "rows = topics" is inferred from heading structure and can guess wrong. Reveal's vertical stacks give authors EXPLICIT, author-controlled 2-D structure (main line horizontal, detail vertical) without a heuristic. The static overview needs no pointer: at a podium with only a clicker, "press O, glance, press a number" is more robust than a pannable map that needs a mouse or trackpad to drive and can be dragged off into empty space. Up and down equals within-stack is a decade-old convention a large existing audience already knows, so re-binding it is a switching cost reveal never imposes on its own users. And the camera plus map is materially more code and failure surface (pinch vs pan vs wheel disambiguation, drag vs click, clamp math, touch) for a payoff that mostly appears past roughly 30 to 50 slides, a size most talks never reach.
- **Taliesin today:** deck.js lays every slide into a 2-D grid where each #-stack or run of top-level slides is one ROW (a topic), and a single transform on .tali-slides is the camera; big moves use a van Wijk and Nuij smooth zoom. The overview is a pannable/zoomable MAP with a corner minimap, semantic-zoom level-of-detail title cards (.tali-lod-far), and a '/' filter box. Arrows: left/right step linearly, up/down jump between topics.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it; it is a real richer-browser-behavior win that scales to 100+ slides. Add a one-time onboarding hint because up/down = topic-jump diverges from reveal's up/down = within-stack.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the spatial camera and pannable map: verified in code, it is a real richer-browser-behavior win that scales past reveal's speck-grid, preserves block-id/sourcepos and click-to-source under the camera transform, stays HTML-only, and never writes source. But sharpen the "add onboarding" step: (1) First fix the existing in-product keyboard legend (deck.js:1411-1415), which currently says "up/down = Vertical slides" and misdescribes the engine; relabel to "up/down = Jump topic" and clarify "left/right" is the linear step through every slide. That is the cheapest, most discoverable fix and it must precede any new overlay. (2) Reframe the divergence honestly: a reveal vertical stack becomes a horizontal row, so within-stack stepping moved from up/down to left/right; the onboarding text must state that and must also cover touch (a vertical swipe = topic jump via onTouchEnd), not just keyboard. (3) Handle the default all-## deck where the map is a single row: gate the topic-jump affordance and legend on rows > 1 (do not advertise dead keys), or document that topic rows require # section headers, so the headline benefit is not silently absent for the common authoring style. Prefer correcting the persistent legend over a one-time overlay that adds first-run state and is routinely dismissed unread; if an overlay is added, pin it with a corpus deck that has both # stacks and an all-## case.
- **Tradeoffs:** The spatial reinterpretation can surprise reveal users; up/down semantics differ; the 'rows = topics' heuristic can mis-group an author who never uses #-stacks; more code to maintain than a filmstrip. (skeptic-found downside: Two missed items. (1) The product ALREADY ships a keyboard legend that lies about the very divergence the proposal wants to onboard: deck.js:1412 renders "up/down = Vertical slides" (reveal vocabulary), but up/down actually jump topic ROWS (moveTopic at :618), and a reveal vertical stack is rotated into a horizontal row so within-stack stepping moved to left/right; "left/right = Navigate" also undersells that it is the linear all-slides path. Correcting that discoverable legend is cheaper and higher-value than adding a new one-time overlay, and the proposal did not spot that the divergence is a 90-degree rotation of stack semantics, not merely "up/down = topic jump." (2) The headline 2-D topic-map benefit is OPT-IN on authoring style: with only ## slides and no # section headers (the reveal/Quarto default slide-level), gridRows folds every slide into a single row, so the map collapses to a 1-D strip and up/down become dead keys while the legend still advertises them. The pannable overview, minimap, and filter still beat reveal's static grid even for that 1-D deck, but the "spatial memory of topic structure" that answers the critique only materializes when the author uses # stacks.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; the preview stays read-only (navigating never writes source); block ids stay intact under the camera transforms; the ## and # heading structure is unchanged Markdown; corpus-pinned.

### D104. Presenter/speaker view as a postMessage window that works from file:// (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** The reveal notes plugin: S opens a speaker window, notes come from ::: {.notes}, and sync uses localStorage / BroadcastChannel, which requires a same-origin http server and generally does not work when the deck is opened as a file:// document.
- **Critique:** Because sync depends on localStorage/same-origin, a built and emailed .html deck opened via file:// often cannot drive its own speaker window, and the setup is fragile in exactly the offline-handout case a single author cares about.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Reveal's notes plugin does NOT sync via localStorage/BroadcastChannel; it uses postMessage with a connect/connected handshake and a '*' targetOrigin, and its own source explicitly claims it "enables us to work in situations where the origins differ, such as a presentation being opened from the file system." So reveal's sync design is the same family as Taliesin's, not the inferior mechanism the critique implies. Reveal's Upcoming pane is also step-aware (it advances one step, fragment or slide), which is finer-grained than Taliesin's Next pane. And reveal only asks for a local web server, a near-zero cost for its actual users: Quarto ALWAYS serves the deck (quarto preview), and a shared deck is normally hosted, so "email a self-contained .html and present it from file://" is a scenario reveal/Quarto never targeted, not a failure of their design. Reveal's separate notes.html also keeps all speaker chrome out of the audience DOM. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** s / openSpeaker opens a popup at ?qmd=speaker showing current + next as live ?qmd=embed iframes, the current slide's .notes, and a timer + clock; audience and speaker stay in sync (including fragment steps) via opener/popup postMessage. sameOrigin()/targetOrigin() explicitly allow the empty/null origin only when the deck itself is on file://, so presenting from a built file works. ::: {.notes} is pinned in corpus/deck.tali.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Optionally add a configurable notes font-size and a preview of the next fragment. It already covers the load-bearing case reveal misses (offline file:// presenting).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the speaker view: it genuinely wins the load-bearing offline case (verified in deck.js: same-file ?qmd=speaker mode with sameOrigin/targetOrigin at 922-923 allowing the empty/null origin ONLY when the deck itself is on file://), which reveal's own docs say needs a local web server. But sharpen the entry so it is not a strawman: (1) State the real contrast: reveal ALSO syncs via postMessage, so Taliesin's edge is a self-contained single-file deck plus explicit file:// null-origin handling, versus reveal's web-server-mandated, iframe-and-module-based separate notes.html, not "postMessage vs localStorage." (2) Reclassify "next-fragment preview" from optional nicety to a genuine gap-closer and make Next step-aware (current-slide frag+1 until fragments exhaust, then next slide), because reveal's Upcoming is finer-grained than the current slide-only Next. (3) Record the missed tradeoffs: two embed iframes reload the full deck (about 3x load on file://) and the timer resets on a bfcache restore. (4) Note the coverage gap: today only the ::: {.notes} MARKUP is corpus-pinned, while the load-bearing file:// postMessage round-trip is browser-only and has no regression net, so add a chrome-devtools/e2e test that drives the opener<->popup sync (including a fragment step) from a file:// build before calling this "done."
- **Tradeoffs:** Popup blockers can suppress the speaker window; a two-window postMessage bridge is more moving parts than one in-page reveal plugin. (skeptic-found downside: The "next-fragment preview" is framed as optional polish but is actually a real gap-closer: Taliesin's Next pane is slide-only (nextIndex skips remaining fragments on the current slide and posts frag:null = fully shown), so on a fragmented slide it already jumps to the whole next slide, which is COARSER than reveal's step-aware Upcoming. Adding it also collides with the current "Next slide" semantics and needs a real decision (show current-slide frag+1 until fragments exhaust, THEN the next slide). Also missed: the speaker window loads the full deck TWICE as ?qmd=embed iframes on top of the audience window (roughly 3x the deck, including any {js} reactive runtime / KaTeX / mermaid), so a heavy self-contained file:// deck can be slow to spin up the speaker window; and the presentation timer silently resets to 0:00 on a bfcache restore of the speaker window, because initSpeaker re-inits spStart = Date.now() and the pagehide/bfcache path re-runs it.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; preview stays read-only (notes are shown, source is never touched); works offline/file:// which aligns with the static-build target; ::: {.notes} keeps the Markdown substrate; corpus-pinned.

### D105. PDF via native browser print, not decktape or a print-pdf stylesheet (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** revealjs PDF requires either decktape (a separate Node plus headless-Chromium tool) or reveal's ?print-pdf stylesheet followed by the browser's Save as PDF; Quarto documents decktape as the path.
- **Critique:** decktape is an extra toolchain to install and keep working; ?print-pdf is a hidden query flag; either way PDF export is a second rendering path bolted on outside the normal flow.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's revealjs PDF story is stronger than the entry implies, on one axis Taliesin does not yet cover: unattended, deterministic, file-on-disk output. decktape is a headless Chromium driven programmatically, so `quarto render` (or a CI job) emits a real .pdf with zero human interaction and byte-stable results. Taliesin's path requires a person to open the browser print dialog, pick "Save as PDF", and (depending on browser) fuss with margins, headers/footers, and the "Background graphics" toggle; fidelity then varies by print engine (Chrome honors @page `size`, Firefox/Safari support it weakly). decktape sidesteps all of that and, crucially, captures the deck AS PRESENTED, backgrounds and per-slide imagery included, because it screenshots the real rendered slides rather than reflowing to a stripped light handout. The `?print-pdf` route is also not really a "second rendering path": it is the same single HTML reflowed by a print stylesheet, functionally identical to Taliesin's enterPrint, so a transform-based single-viewport engine genuinely NEEDS such a mechanism, and gating it behind a query flag is a defensible way to avoid loading print CSS during normal presentation. So Quarto's choice is right for the batch/CI/faithful-artifact use case decktape exists to serve.
- **Taliesin today:** Native beforeprint/afterprint hooks plus ?qmd=print flatten the deck to one slide per page (enterPrint): every slide shown, transforms dropped, all fragments revealed, code un-dimmed, magic-move set to its final block, @page set to the deck aspect, and inert cleared so all pages are readable. Cmd/Ctrl+P just works, and the menu already has an Export PDF item.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it; this is exactly the 'PDF rendered FROM the built HTML' model the invariants mandate. If a fully headless artifact is wanted later, a build-time --pdf could drive a headless browser over the same print layout rather than a parallel format.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the native browser-print approach, but narrow and sharpen the claim. The verified, defensible win is ERGONOMIC and zero-dependency: Taliesin auto-wires beforeprint/afterprint so vanilla Cmd/Ctrl+P produces the flattened handout with no `?print-pdf` flag to remember and no decktape to install, plus an explicit Export PDF menu item. That is genuinely better than Quarto's reveal.js default, which prints garbage unless you first append `?print-pdf`. Do NOT frame it as full parity with decktape: explicitly concede that decktape still wins for unattended/CI/deterministic file-on-disk output and for faithful capture of per-slide backgrounds, since Taliesin currently drops backgrounds for a light handout and has no headless file export. Fix the "@page = deck aspect" wording to "hardcoded to the 16:9 default" (or make @page actually derive from deck.config.width/height so the claim becomes true and custom-aspect decks print correctly). Reframe the future `--pdf` honestly as reintroducing a headless-browser dependency (the same class of tool the critique criticizes), justified only by it rendering FROM the built HTML print layout rather than as a parallel format. Corpus-pin what is pinnable (print CSS/JS emitted, magic-move-final, fragments expanded) and label PDF fidelity as browser-verified, not cargo-tested.
- **Tradeoffs:** Depends on the browser's print engine, so page-break fidelity varies by browser; no server-side PDF without shelling a headless browser. (skeptic-found downside: Three things the drafter missed. (1) There is no unattended/deterministic PDF today: the exact job decktape exists for (scripted, CI, file-on-disk, no human clicking through the print dialog) is unserved, and the tradeoffs field only mentions page-break fidelity, not this capability gap. Worse, the proposed future `taliesin build --pdf` would reintroduce the very headless-Chromium toolchain dependency the critique dinged Quarto's decktape for, so the entry should own that irony rather than present it as a clean win. (2) Fidelity loss by design: per-slide backgrounds/images are dropped in print (deck.css:373 hides .tali-slide-bg, deck.js:1025 drops tali-dark-bg), so the PDF is a readable light handout, NOT a faithful capture of the designed deck. decktape's ability to reproduce the real slides is a genuine advantage for anyone sharing the deck as-presented. (3) The "@page set to the deck aspect" claim is overstated: @page is hardcoded to `960px 540px` (deck.css:529) and nothing rewrites it from deck.config.width/height; it works only because initialize never overrides the 16:9 default, but the engine accepts config overrides (deck.js:1565/1667), so a custom-aspect deck would print letterboxed/cropped. Also, "corpus-pinnable" is limited: print is runtime JS with no cargo/corpus coverage, so a corpus doc can only assert the print CSS/JS is emitted, not verify actual PDF fidelity.)
- **Invariant check:** Perfect fit with 'a print/PDF track renders FROM the built HTML, never as a parallel format'; HTML stays the only output; read-only; corpus-pinnable.

### D106. Give decks a small deliberate front-matter config surface (resolution, footer, logo, slide-number) instead of hardcoding and rejecting (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** revealjs exposes a large front-matter surface: width/height (the design resolution and thus aspect), slide-number format, footer, logo, transition/background-transition, controls, progress, center, menu, navigation-mode, theme, and more.
- **Critique:** Many of those are reveal-specific knobs, but width/height (aspect ratio), footer, logo, and slide-number format are legitimate branding and layout wants for any deck, and an author reaches for them first.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Reveal.js is the ACTUAL rendering engine in Quarto revealjs, so exposing its config surface is honest passthrough, not an invented API: Quarto's job as a multi-engine compiler is to surface the engine faithfully, and width/height (the design resolution and thus aspect), slide-number, footer, and logo are documented reveal capabilities with years of author muscle memory. Migrating a real deck depends on them; hardcoding or hiding them would be paternalistic and would silently break decks. Crucially, transition and background-transition are NOT meaningless knobs in reveal's world: they are core to its discrete-slide model. They only became meaningless once Taliesin unilaterally swapped reveal for a continuous-camera engine, so Quarto exposing them is correct FOR its engine. Quarto is also honest here (an unknown reveal key is passed through), whereas the branding wants are exactly the keys a deck author reaches for first.
- **Taliesin today:** None are read. deck.config hardcodes width:960/height:540 (16:9), and initialize() is called with a fixed {hash:true, slideNumber:'c/t', center:false} in both deck.rs:103 and client.js:646. frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS has zero deck keys, so the strict validator actively FLAGS footer:/logo:/width:/slide-number:/transition: as unknown-key errors with did-you-mean. Only per-slide heading attributes (background-*, auto-animate) and theme: are honored.
- **Proposed better:** Add a small opinionated deck config (a deck: block or a few top-level keys) to KNOWN_KEYS and the JSON schema, wiring width/height (aspect), slide-number (on/off plus format), footer, and logo through to deck.config and emit. Keep keys that are meaningless under the continuous-camera model (transition, background-transition) explicitly unsupported with a clear validator message rather than a generic typo guess.
- **Revised recommendation:** Revise, do not keep as written. Adopt a top-level deck: block (sibling to theorems:), with validated children and schema drift-lock; do NOT scatter width/footer/logo/slide-number into the global KNOWN_KEYS (that creates silent no-ops on non-deck docs). Phase 1 (cheap, already plumbed, one corpus pin): deck aspect via width/height and slide-number on/off, threaded to BOTH deck.rs and client.js via a new window global. Phase 2 (separate corpus pins, costed as real engine work): footer, logo, and slide-number format, since none exist in deck.js/deck.css today and each needs stage-relative placement plus print/scroll/overview/embedded and a11y handling. Keep transition/background-transition explicitly unsupported with a specific validator message (agree with the entry). Finally, close the strict-validation blind spot: since format: sub-keys are unlinted, add a deck-specific nudge so a format: deck: width: misplacement produces a did-you-mean pointing at the deck: block instead of a silent no-op, so the strict-validation promise actually holds for decks.
- **Tradeoffs:** Grows the config surface the clean break deliberately shed, and invites reveal-option creep; each key needs its own corpus pin and schema drift-lock. (skeptic-found downside: The entry bundles width/height/footer/logo/slide-number as one uniform wire-through, but their costs are wildly unequal and the drafter mis-costs the expensive half. width/height already live in deck.config and drive --tali-deck-w/h, so aspect is nearly free; slideNumber is already truthiness-gated so on/off is free. But deck.js/deck.css have NO footer or logo rendering at all, and updateNumber() ignores any format string (it always prints 'N / M'), so footer, logo, and slide-number FORMAT are net-new rendering features (DOM plus placement inside the letterboxed, scaled stage, plus the print/scroll/overview/embedded modes and a11y), not config plumbing. Two coupled edit sites (deck.rs:103 static tail and client.js:646 live client) must change together, and since the live client cannot read front matter it needs a new window handshake (like the existing TALIESIN_FORMAT/TALIESIN_TOC globals). Placement is also under-decided: dropping these into the global KNOWN_KEYS would make slide-number: true validate clean but do nothing on a non-deck article, the exact silent no-op the strict validator exists to kill. And the strict-validation promise has a blind spot: because format: sub-keys are deliberately unlinted, a Quarto-muscle-memory format: deck: width: 1280 is a silent no-op with NO did-you-mean, so the philosophy is not as preserved as invariant_check claims.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; read-only; keeps YAML/Markdown front matter; the strict-validation philosophy is preserved (keys are added deliberately, everything else still flagged); block model and click-to-source untouched; corpus-plus-roadmap because each new key ships with a pinning document.

### D107. Add a global incremental toggle and a minimal set of fragment effects (fade-out, highlight, index ordering) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** incremental: true makes ALL lists reveal item-by-item (.nonincremental opts out); .fragment supports a catalog of effects (fade-in/out, fade-up/down/left/right, grow, shrink, strike, highlight-red/green/blue, semi-fade-out) plus data-fragment-index to reorder or pair steps.
- **Critique:** The effect catalog is mostly ornamental, but three behaviors are genuinely useful and Taliesin lacks all three: a fragment that REMOVES content on its step (fade-out), a highlight-on-step, and out-of-document-order stepping (data-fragment-index). The global incremental: toggle is also a real ergonomic saver for bullet-heavy decks.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto did not author the effect catalog: it inherited the whole thing from reveal.js at zero marginal cost, so pruning would mean deliberately deleting working capability some presenters depend on, and a broad-audience tool has no business adjudicating which effects a given speaker finds ornamental. Two of the "ornamental" items are actually load-bearing. semi-fade-out (dim the earlier bullets as you advance) is a real attention-focusing device, not decoration, and the critique wrongly lumps it in with grow/shrink. More importantly data-fragment-index is the ONLY mechanism for non-linear reveal choreography: reveal a bullet while simultaneously highlighting a diagram region, pair a fade-out of one element with the reveal of another, or sync two separate elements onto one step. That is precisely what separates a built presentation from a scrolling document, so calling it merely "out-of-order stepping" undersells it. Finally, incremental: true with a .nonincremental opt-out is the correct default polarity for bullet-heavy talks and costs Quarto nothing. The full package is justified for a general tool; the pruning only becomes the right call for Taliesin because Taliesin removed reveal.js and now pays re-implementation cost for every effect it keeps.
- **Taliesin today:** Only explicit ::: {.incremental} lists and .fragment blocks step, and always by revealing (visibility) in document order, plus . . . pauses (deck.rs is_pause), code-line steps (data-code-lines segments in fragsOf), and magic-move. There is no global incremental, no fade-out/removal, and no data-fragment-index ordering. The incremental: key is currently validator-rejected.
- **Proposed better:** Add front-matter incremental: true (plus a .nonincremental escape) wired into deck.rs where .incremental is already understood, and support a minimal effect set as extra classes on the existing .fragment syntax: .fade-out (hide on its step), .highlight, and honor data-fragment-index in fragsOf ordering. Leave the ornamental effects out.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship the high-value, bounded subset and defer the risky piece. (1) Add incremental: true + .nonincremental and the .fade-out + .highlight effects; all are invariant-safe (HTML/CSS/JS only, no write-back, substrate kept, source-hashed block ids stay stable, no startup/diff impact). (2) Stop calling fade-out/highlight a class add: they are a NEW visible-at-base, mutate-on-step fragment category needing a deck.css carve-out over the blanket .fragment hidden rule, a second branch in applyFragments, and correct backward-step restore, so corpus-pin each with a deck that steps forward AND back. (3) Make .highlight use a --tali-* theme token so it reads in light and dark decks. (4) Scope global-incremental's selector to top-level content lists only, excluding .nonincremental subtrees and the deck's own chrome/menu lists; prefer a runtime data-incremental on .tali-slides that broadens FRAG_SEL over adding classes server-side. (5) Note incremental is deck-only while KNOWN_KEYS is format-blind (it will be inertly accepted elsewhere); consider format-scoped validation. (6) DEFER or tightly scope data-fragment-index: ship it first only for .fragment elements with reorder-only semantics (no same-index grouping, no interaction with code-line or magic-move steps), or split it into its own later corpus-pinned entry, because it is the one part that reintroduces disproportionate step-machine complexity for limited Markdown reach, exactly the reveal.js baggage the clean break shed.
- **Tradeoffs:** Enlarges the fragment engine (fragsOf/applyFragments) and the step-ordering logic, adds classes to document and pin, and risks reintroducing some of the complexity the clean break shed. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's "purely additive Markdown classes" framing is too rosy for .fade-out and .highlight. Both invert the fragment engine's core assumption. A .fragment today is hidden-at-base (deck.css: .tali-deck .fragment { visibility: hidden }) and revealed monotonically. fade-out and highlight need the element VISIBLE at base and MUTATED on its step, plus correct restore on backward stepping. That means (a) a CSS carve-out overriding the blanket hidden rule, (b) a second base-state category in applyFragments (which currently just strips tali-frag-visible from all FRAG_SEL and re-adds for taken steps), and (c) highlight must use a --tali-* token, not a fixed color, to read in both light and dark decks. Separately, data-fragment-index is the real trap the drafter glossed: fragsOf yields heterogeneous steps (fragment nodes, .incremental list items, code-line segments, magic-move morphs) from one document-order walk, so an index forces a definition of ordering BETWEEN indexed fragments and un-indexed non-fragment steps, and same-index means two nodes reveal on ONE step, turning each step from a single node into a set (a structural change to fragsOf, not a sort). Meanwhile Markdown has no clean per-<li> attribute syntax, so fragment-index only reaches .fragment spans/divs, never the list-item incremental case, narrowing its payoff. One more wart: incremental is a deck-only concept but KNOWN_KEYS is format-blind, so adding it there silently accepts an inert incremental: on a blog post, denting the strict-validation ethos.)
- **Invariant check:** Purely additive Markdown classes and one YAML key, so the substrate is kept; HTML-only; read-only; each fragment's block id stays stable; corpus-pin each effect.

### D108. Default a standalone deck to reader/scroll, put step-mode behind an opt-in, but make presenting discoverable (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A revealjs deck always opens in stepped presentation mode (the 16:9 filmstrip), regardless of how it is reached.
- **Critique:** A deck link shared on the web is often READ, not presented, and a stepped 16:9 filmstrip letterboxes on a phone and forces click-through just to read, which is poor web-native behavior. Conversely, Quarto's always-present behavior is predictable and matches the expectation of 'slides'.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Stepped-by-default is the least-surprise contract: a link labeled "slides" that opens as a long scrolling page reads as broken ("where did my slides go?"). Presenting is the PRIMARY purpose of a deck and reading is secondary, so optimizing the default for the secondary use is a genuine tradeoff, not a free win. Stepping also preserves authored rhetoric: fragments, staged builds, a hidden punchline or quiz answer are meant to reveal on cue, and a scroll/reader default that shows every fragment at once (which Taliesin's reader does) spoils that sequencing on the very first view. Finally, reveal.js 5 (in current Quarto) already serves every audience without moving the default: the desktop presenter gets stepped, a phone reader gets Scroll View auto-activated at narrow widths, any reader can force ?view=scroll, and an author who wants reading-first sets view: scroll. That is arguably more complete than flipping the default and then having to re-teach how to present. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** A standalone deck page defaults to scroll/reader mode (every slide stacked, full-width, all fragments shown); step mode is opt-in via ?qmd=present or ?qmd=slides; a narrow/portrait screen always forces scroll; an EMBEDDED deck ({{< embed >}}, detected via window.taliDeckEmbedded) keeps step mode. This lives in deck.js initialize's syncScroll logic.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the reader default (it is the better web-native read), but make presenting discoverable: a visible 'Present' affordance on the standalone reader instead of a hidden query flag, and consider a front-matter default so an author can force step-mode for a deck that is meant to be presented.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep scroll/reader as the standalone default (the genuine web-native win is inverting Quarto's stepped-by-default for a shared read-link). First reframe the entry to the accurate contrast: Quarto/reveal 5 already auto-scrolls on narrow phones and offers view:scroll (author) and ?view=scroll (reader), so this is "better default plus better discoverability," not "Quarto can only step." For discoverability, do NOT add a parallel affordance: the corner menu already survives in scroll mode and already has a reader/scroll toggle, so give the reader view one prominent, positively-labeled "Present" entry that calls the existing exitScroll/toggleScroll plumbing, and keep ?qmd=present as the shareable URL form for deep-link parity. Add the optional front-matter default under the already-permissive format: deck key (schema.rs:108-109 will not flag it), plumbed YAML -> deck.rs -> deck.js initialize opts -> syncScroll, with an explicit precedence so it is unambiguous: URL ?qmd wins, then the narrow-screen force (must beat an author "present" default so phones never letterbox), then the front-matter default, then the built-in standalone-scroll default. Because scroll shows all fragments, treat the front-matter present default as the real fix for reveal-dependent decks and document the fragment caveat. Pin BOTH the Present affordance and the front-matter flip with a corpus doc plus test (extend corpus/deck.qmd) per corpus-plus-roadmap; verify in that test that data-block-id/data-sourcepos still emit in scroll mode (they do today: enterScroll only toggles classes) so click-to-source stays intact.
- **Tradeoffs:** The reader default surprises users who expect a deck link to present; ?qmd=present is undiscoverable today; a visible Present button adds chrome to the reader view. (skeptic-found downside: Two things the drafter missed. (1) The premise "presenting is only reachable via a hidden query flag" is factually wrong: in reader mode the corner control menu is still visible (deck.css:662 hides only the progress bar and prev/next arrows in .tali-scroll, NOT .tali-ctl-menu), and that menu already carries a "Reader mode" toggle (deck.js:1454/1491/1506 -> toggleScroll/exitScroll) that switches a standalone deck into step mode. So a brand-new "Present" button is redundant chrome layered over an existing path; the real defect is that the entry point is labeled as a reader toggle-off rather than a positive "Present" call-to-action and is buried in a hamburger menu. (2) Scroll/reader default shows ALL fragments at once, so any deck authored around progressive reveal is spoiled the instant a shared link is opened, with the author powerless unless they know ?qmd=present, which is exactly why the proposed front-matter default matters more than the button. And that front-matter present default must still yield to the narrow-screen force (matchMedia max-width:600px), otherwise it reintroduces the exact phone-letterbox problem the entry critiques.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (both reader and step are the same HTML); read-only; Markdown unchanged; block ids intact in both modes; corpus-pinnable.

### D109. Make slide-level configurable rather than fixing it at heading level 2 (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** slide-level (default 2) sets which heading level starts a new slide; headings above it become section/stack dividers, letting an author structure at h1 or h3.
- **Critique:** Hardcoding level 2 forces one structuring convention. An author who writes # sections with ## slides, or who wants ### not to break a slide, has no lever, and the natural key would currently be rejected by the validator.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** slide-level is not a Quarto invention, it is a Pandoc structural primitive Quarto passes through. Pandoc's section model is arbitrarily deep, and slide-level feeds not just reveal.js but beamer and pptx, where multi-level section nesting is real and needed. Exposing the knob costs Quarto almost nothing (it forwards an existing Pandoc option) while giving authors genuine structural control across several output formats: slide-level=1 for a flat deck, or a higher level for section-heavy academic decks where h1/h2 are dividers and h3 starts slides. It is well documented and well understood. Taliesin, by contrast, is HTML-only with a deliberately 2-deep camera model, so the same knob that is nearly free for Quarto is expensive to honor faithfully here. Quarto keeping a configurable pass-through of a primitive it did not have to design is the low-cost, correct move for a multi-format compiler. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** SLIDE_LEVEL is a hardcoded const = 2 in deck.rs; h1 opens a vertical stack, h2 opens a slide, deeper headings accrete onto the current slide, and --- also breaks. There is no front-matter override.
- **Proposed better:** Read an optional slide-level (through the same deck config work above) and thread it into split_slides/group_slides in place of the const, defaulting to 2.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature but constrain and re-frame it. (1) Scope the accepted values to slide-level in {1, 2}, the only structures the 2-deep camera can represent; if a higher value is ever allowed, the validator must reject or explain it (or the camera must first be extended to N-deep, a much larger, separate change). Do not ship a bare const-swap. (2) Rewrite the catalog entry's critique: drop both stated examples (# sections with ## slides, and ### not breaking a slide) because both are already the default today, and lead instead with the one genuine gap, slide-level=1, where an author wants h2 to be an in-slide subheading rather than its own slide. (3) Correct the validator claim: place the key under the deck's format block, where sub-keys are not linted, rather than at top level. (4) Confirm it stays low priority: for a single author the existing h1-stack / h2-slide convention already covers the common cases, so the real value is the narrow flat-deck (slide-level=1) affordance. Block-id, sourcepos, HTML-only, read-only, and corpus-pinning are all unaffected (slide grouping wraps blocks in sections and never touches inner data-block-id, per the deck.rs byte-stable comment), so the invariants are safe; the fix is scope and framing, not architecture.
- **Tradeoffs:** It interacts with the camera's rows=topics heuristic (changing slide-level reshapes the overview map), adds a little parsing complexity, and is another key to pin; the payoff is modest for a single author who can adopt the level-2 convention. (skeptic-found downside: The 2-deep camera model cannot faithfully represent slide-level 3 or higher, and the naive const-swap would silently produce a structurally wrong deck rather than error. Verified in deck.rs: the model is only Top::Slide or Top::Stack{lead, children}, a single vertical nesting level. With slide_level=3, split_slides makes h1/h2/h3 all start slides, and group_slides opens_stack for any level < 3, so both h1 and h2 qualify. But when it hits an h1 it gathers children until the next level < 3, and the immediately following h2 also satisfies level < 3, so it breaks the h1 stack instantly: h1 becomes a childless Top::Slide and h2 becomes a separate Top::Stack. The h1-contains-h2 section hierarchy Quarto would nest is lost, flattened into two adjacent horizontal tops, with no diagnostic. So slide-level 1 and 2 substitute cleanly, but 3+ is unrepresentable, and the proposal's phrasing (thread the value in place of the const, defaulting to 2) implies any value works. Secondary misses: the entry lists the camera rows=topics interaction as an added cost, but gridRows() in deck.js reads DOM structure with zero slide-level awareness, so it needs no change and the reshaped map is a free, benign consequence, not complexity to build. And the entry undersells the only real payoff: slide-level=1 (h1 opens slides, h2 accretes as an in-slide subheading) is the single behavior the current default genuinely cannot express.)
- **Invariant check:** Keeps Markdown heading semantics; HTML-only; read-only; block ids intact; corpus-pinned.

### D110. Persist pen annotations across reload (localStorage/export), not in-memory only (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** chalkboard: true loads reveal.js-chalkboard: a pen plus a separate chalkboard canvas, colors, and persistence, where annotations can be saved to and reloaded from a JSON file (src), so a marked-up deck survives a reload or a later session.
- **Critique:** reveal-chalkboard is heavy and its file-based save is clunky, but the core value (annotations that survive a reload) is real for teaching, and Taliesin's pen loses everything on refresh or a live re-render.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's chalkboard is not just a pen, it is a portability-and-reproducibility model that localStorage cannot match. reveal.js-chalkboard actually persists in TWO layers: it auto-saves to localStorage (so a same-browser reload already survives, exactly what this proposal wants to add), AND it can download annotations to a JSON file that a deck reloads via `src:`. That file layer buys three things localStorage structurally cannot: (1) portability across machines and browsers, which is the real teaching case (you annotate on your prep laptop, then present from the lecture-hall machine; localStorage is per-origin-per-browser and does not travel); (2) reproducibility, the annotated file can be committed next to the deck, versioned, and reopened identically by anyone; (3) durability against a cache clear, which silently wipes localStorage but not a saved file. Quarto also offers a genuinely separate second canvas (a blackboard, not just a transparent pen-over-slides overlay), giving a presenter room to work off the slide. So Quarto's choice is defensible: a file keyed by slide index is the one persistence format that is stable, shareable, and reproducible across the presenting environments teachers actually use, and the localStorage layer already covers the cheap same-browser reload case. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** A built-in pen via d (toggleDraw/ensureDraw): three colors, eraser, clear, per-slide strokes redrawn on navigation, on a canvas inside .tali-slides so it scales with the deck. But deck.draw.strokes is in-memory only (no localStorage or file persistence), so a reload or an incremental block-swap loses all annotations.
- **Proposed better:** Persist strokes to localStorage keyed by deck path plus slide id (surviving reload and the preview's block-swap), with a menu 'Clear all' and an optional JSON export/import. Never write annotations back to the .tmd source.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature, it is invariant-clean (verified: writes go to localStorage or a download, never to source, so the single read-only editing surface holds; HTML-only; the idle canvas is pointer-events:none so click-to-source is unaffected). Revise the mechanism: (1) Persist strokes to localStorage ONLY for slides carrying an explicit `{#id}`; keep positionally-keyed (id-less) slides in-memory so an edit can never silently reattach old marks to new content. Document "give a slide an id to keep its annotations across reloads," which reuses the anchor authors already set for deep-links and click-to-source. (2) Derive the storage key from the deck's source-relative path baked into the page (not `location.href`), so preview and the built file:// deck key deliberately, and treat preview annotations as scratch that need not survive into the delivered build. (3) Make JSON export/import first-class, not optional: it is the layer that actually serves cross-machine teaching, the thing localStorage cannot do and Quarto's `src` file can. (4) Wire a redraw on `sync()` and eagerly recreate/replay the canvas at init so annotations survive block-swaps and reloads; guard every setItem in try/catch with a quota fallback; write on stroke-end and slide-change only. (5) Correct the catalog critique text: Quarto's chalkboard already auto-persists to localStorage, so this reaches parity plus the portable file layer, rather than fixing a gap Quarto left open. Corpus pins the pen's presence and the restore hook's existence only; the stroke round-trip is browser-verified, consistent with other reader-side JS features but a weaker-than-usual corpus pin worth noting.
- **Tradeoffs:** The localStorage key must stay stable across edits even though a slide id can change; export/import adds UI; annotations remain ephemeral relative to source, which is intended. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter named "slide id can change" but understated the real landmine: `drawKey()` defaults to a POSITIONAL key (`i<h>-<v>`) whenever a slide lacks an explicit id, which is the common case. In a live-edit tool, persisting a positional key means that after you insert or reorder a slide, restored strokes silently reattach to WHATEVER content now sits at that index. That is worse than a clean loss: stale annotations landing on the wrong slide mid-lecture. Persistence must therefore be gated to slides with a stable author-assigned `{#id}`, keeping id-less slides in-memory only. Second missed cost: export/import is framed as "optional," but it is the ONLY piece that delivers the stated teaching use case, since localStorage does not travel to a different machine or browser (the exact portability Quarto's file layer provides); it should be first-class, not optional. Third: restore-on-load forces EAGER canvas creation plus a redraw-on-`sync()` hook (today `ensureDraw` is lazy and `sync()` never touches the canvas), or block-swaps will visually drop annotations even with data persisted. Fourth: on portable file:// builds localStorage is origin-quirky and may be disabled, so writes need the same try/catch degrade-silently guard the reading-progress code already uses, plus a quota guard since dense point arrays serialize large. Fifth: writes must fire on stroke-end and slide-change only, never per pointermove.)
- **Invariant check:** Critical: annotations persist to localStorage or a downloaded file, NEVER to source, so the single read-only editing surface holds; HTML-only; block ids untouched; compatible with warm-server live edits; the corpus can pin the pen's presence, not the strokes.

## Website and multi-page site

### D111. Config model: one flat, strict `_site.yml` vs Quarto's `_quarto.yml` + `_metadata.yml` cascade (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto layers config across `_quarto.yml`, optional per-directory `_metadata.yml` files that cascade down the tree, and per-file front matter, merged by a precedence chain. Navbar/sidebar/about/listing sit nested under `website:` and `format: html:`. Unknown keys are silently ignored.
- **Critique:** The cascade is powerful but its merge order is invisible: a stray `_metadata.yml` or a typo'd key silently changes or drops behavior with no error, and you cannot tell from one file what a given page will actually receive. The nested `website:`/`format: html:` scaffolding is ceremony for a tool that only emits HTML.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Within Quarto's own design space the cascade is not ceremony, it is load-bearing. Quarto targets many output formats (HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs, books, manuscripts) across multi-directory projects, and three things earn their keep there: (1) the `_metadata.yml` directory cascade is a real DRY win, letting you set author, license, bibliography, freeze, or code-fold once for a whole `posts/` subtree instead of repeating it in 200 files; (2) `format: html:` vs `format: pdf:` namespacing is required precisely because one source emits multiple formats, so per-format options must be scoped somewhere; (3) silently ignoring unknown keys is a deliberate multi-format affordance, it lets one source doc carry a `pdf:` block or an extension key that the current render does not consume, so a shared corpus renders across targets without erroring. For a general multi-format, multi-author compiler these are coherent, defensible choices. The cost only materializes when you collapse to Taliesin's design point: single author, HTML only, one project. The critique is fair for THAT point, but it slightly overreaches when it calls the cascade purely invisible (every cascade, CSS/editorconfig/gitignore, makes the same DRY-vs-locality trade) and when it treats silent-ignore as pure negligence rather than a multi-format necessity.
- **Taliesin today:** `crates/core/src/site/config/mod.rs`: a single flat `_site.yml` parsed into `SiteConfig`, with NO `_metadata.yml` cascade (root config is the sole project default; a page's own front matter overrides it). A closed `NATIVE_KEYS` set is enforced by `validate_keys`, warning on any unknown key with a `frontmatter::closest()` did-you-mean; malformed YAML is tagged via `MALFORMED_CONFIG_PREFIX` so build `--strict` fails and the preview watcher keeps its last-good config. `about:`/`hero:`/`listing:` are flat top-level or front-matter blocks (`AboutSpec`/`HeroSpec`/`ListingSpec` in mod.rs).
- **Proposed better:** Keep the flat strict model. Document the one precedence rule (page overrides site, no cascade) in the config reference so migrants stop hunting for `_metadata.yml`. Optionally extend the strict-key + did-you-mean discipline into nested `nav`/`footer` item keys, since `NavItem` currently deserialize-drops unknown sub-keys silently (config/mod.rs `nav_item`).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry as taliesin-already-better: the flat single `_site.yml` + closed `NATIVE_KEYS` + `closest()` did-you-mean + `MALFORMED_CONFIG_PREFIX` (`--strict` fail plus last-good preview) is the correct, already-shipped, clearly-better decision for an HTML-only single-author tool, and no invariant is touched (config is read, never written). But sharpen `proposed_better`: (a) DROP the "document the precedence rule" item, it is already shipped in configuration.qmd and migrating-from-quarto.tali. (b) Reframe the only real action, nav/footer sub-key validation, correctly: add a `NAV_ITEM_KEYS` closed set {text, href, icon} and validate item sub-keys with a manual loop + `closest()` that pushes a warning, explicitly NOT `deny_unknown_fields` (which would silently drop the item). Flag that this will also warn on legitimate-but-unsupported nav features (dropdown menus, target/rel/aria-label), so either widen the native nav vocabulary first or accept the warning as an honest feature-gap signal. Note the warning is console-only, not click-to-source. (c) Per corpus-plus-roadmap, pin the new validation with a corpus test (a typo'd nav key in a test `_site.yml` asserting the warning). Downgrade the marginal work from high to low-impact polish: the config MODEL is the high-impact win and it is already done; the nav-item lint is a small consistency patch, not a headline capability.
- **Tradeoffs:** No cascade means a large multi-section site cannot set a per-directory default (e.g. every `posts/` page inherits an author) in one place; each page repeats it or leans on listing-level defaults. For a single-author tool this is an acceptable, even clarifying, loss. (skeptic-found downside: Two the drafter missed. (1) The "document the precedence rule" item is already shipped: `docs/guide/reference/configuration.qmd:59-60` and `docs/guide/using/migrating-from-quarto.qmd:78,207-212` already state "no `_metadata.yml` cascade, root `_site.yml` sets defaults, a page's front matter overrides them," complete with the did-you-mean note. So that half is a no-op, not a recommendation. (2) The nav/footer strict-key extension is NOT a simple `deny_unknown_fields` flip: `nav_item` does `serde_yaml::from_value(...).ok()`, so a typo'd sub-key currently yields a label-less-but-rendered NavItem, and adding `deny_unknown_fields` would turn that into `None` and silently DROP the whole item, which is worse than today, not a warning. To actually warn you must add a manual `NAV_ITEM_KEYS` closed set and a `closest()` check that PUSHES a warning, mirroring `validate_keys`. Furthermore, enforcing it converts genuine unsupported-nav needs (Quarto `menu:` dropdowns, `target: _blank`, `rel`, `aria-label`, `id`) into config warnings, because the native nav vocabulary is a minimal {text, href, icon}, so the strict door flags real feature gaps, not just typos. Finally, unlike front-matter warnings these `_site.yml` warnings are console-only, not click-to-source (a config key has no rendered block to Alt-click from), so the "did-you-mean click-to-source" framing the entry leans on does not carry over to config.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only by construction (no `format:` nesting); single editing surface intact (config is read, never written by preview); the strict closed-set validation is the same clean-break stance already chosen for front matter. No invariant touched.

### D112. Search: a self-built offline JSON index vs Quarto's lunr.js / Algolia (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto builds a lunr.js index at render and ships lunr plus the index JSON to the browser, or integrates hosted Algolia for large sites. Ranking is lunr's TF-IDF over titles and body text.
- **Critique:** lunr adds a vendored runtime plus a prebuilt index to fetch; Algolia is a paid hosted third party (network + account) that is off the table for an offline single-author tool. Neither loads cleanly from `file://`, so a book opened from disk has no search.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Fuse.js plus a prebuilt search.json, with Algolia as an escape hatch, is defensible for Quarto's actual target: thousands of third-party, web-server-hosted sites across many themes, locales, and RTL. Fuse.js is a mature, community-known, zero-dependency library that hands authors a documented, tunable search surface (weighted title-vs-body keys, a fuzziness threshold, and extended operators like exact-quote, prefix, suffix, negation, and OR) with no code, and its fuzzy bitap matching is corpus- and language-agnostic, giving reasonable typo tolerance without any per-language stemming config. The prebuilt search.json is generated once at render and can ship as a pre-serialized Fuse index so the client skips re-indexing, keeping ranking consistent across pages. Crucially, Algolia is a real capability Taliesin has deliberately surrendered: for a genuinely large corpus (thousands of pages) where a shipped client index becomes too big to load, Algolia offloads indexing, typo-tolerance, sub-50ms ranked queries, and analytics to a hosted backend with server-side relevance tuning. Quarto's file:// weakness is also a non-issue for its audience, which deploys to GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Quarto Pub, so fetch() of search.json is fine with normal caching. In short, Quarto optimizes for a huge, hosted, multi-locale install base with a battle-tested library and a paid scale path, which is exactly the right call for Quarto even though it is the wrong call for a single-author offline-first tool. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `crates/core/src/site/search.rs` builds a compact `{u,p,i,l,t,b}` object per page-title and per anchored heading, each carrying the section's plain-text body capped at `BODY_CAP` (1500), written to `search-index.js` and lazy-loaded on first Cmd-K open via a `<script>` element (CORS-free, works under `file://`). `web-client/search.js` does multi-term AND matching, field-boosted scoring, edit-distance-1 fuzzy for terms >=4 chars, snippet windowing, cross-page navigation, and a Custom-Highlight-API search-hit flash on arrival. Single docs build the index from the live DOM so it tracks edits.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Add a size budget: the whole index is one JS file loaded on first open, fine for a single-author corpus but worth a build warning if it ever passes a few hundred KB (shard by section then). Consider light stemming/prefix matching if the fixed edit-distance-1 fuzzy proves too narrow for recall.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the implementation: it genuinely beats Quarto for the offline single-author file:// case, and the code claims in the entry all verify. But fix the entry's facts and sharpen the follow-ups. (1) Correct the Quarto description: it uses Fuse.js (fuzzy bitap over weighted title/body keys, plus extended-search operators) writing search.json, NOT lunr.js/TF-IDF. Delete the "no lunr-grade TF-IDF ranking" tradeoff (a phantom) and replace it with the true concessions: no extended-search operators and no hosted-Algolia scale/analytics path, both deliberately out of scope. (2) Make the size budget a build WARNING only; do not promise sharding, since it regresses file://. Treat exceeding the budget as a signal the corpus is outside single-author scope, not a trigger to build shard loading. (3) Raise recall the honest way first: index beyond BODY_CAP (or make the cap configurable) and consider including h5/h6, before reaching for stemming. If stemming is ever added, it must preserve the existing no-false-mark discipline (stem to ACCEPT a match, but still only <mark> exact substrings, never an unanchorable run). (4) Pin any new behavior with a corpus/check test per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Tradeoffs:** No lunr-grade TF-IDF ranking; the client matcher is a linear `indexOf` scan per keystroke (O(index)), fine for one author's pages but not for thousands. Fuzzy tolerance is fixed at one edit. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter missed. (1) The "shard by section" remedy would REGRESS the very file:// property the entry praises: on-demand shard loading needs fetch() (CORS-blocked from disk) or a query-to-shard map you cannot build without already having the index, so sharding trades away works-from-disk to solve a size problem a single author will never hit. (2) Stemming collides with a deliberate invariant in the same file: search.js goes out of its way (termRanges/firstTermRange, "Fuzzy-only terms yield no span, honest, never the wrong run") to only <mark> exact substring occurrences, so a stemmed match ("run" hitting "running") would be a hit with no anchorable substring, forcing the snippet/flash to either mark nothing or mark the wrong run. (3) The real recall ceiling today is not fuzzy narrowness or total size, it is BODY_CAP=1500: each section body is truncated, so a long section's later prose is silently unindexed, and single docs additionally index only h1-h4 WITH ids (h5/h6 and id-less headings are unfindable). The proposal aims at scaling concerns the author will not reach while ignoring the truncation that actually drops content now.)
- **Invariant check:** Fully offline and self-contained (no CDN, no hosted service); read-only navigation; the `<script>` load path preserves the works-from-disk property. All invariants held. (possible violation flagged: The proposed shard-on-budget follow-up would violate the works-from-disk (file://) invariant that the entry itself lists as held: sharding implies loading a subset on demand, which under file:// requires a CORS-blocked fetch(), breaking the single-<script>-tag load path that makes Cmd-K work from disk. Also, corpus-plus-roadmap: the new build-warning capability (and any stemming) must ship pinned by a corpus/check.rs test, which the proposal does not mention. The CORE recommendation (keep the current implementation) violates nothing: go() only navigates (location.href / scrollIntoView / history.replaceState hash) and the flash uses the Custom Highlight API specifically to avoid DOM mutation, so the read-only-preview and single-editing-surface invariants are honored.)

### D113. Intra-site links: `.qmd`/`.tmd`→`.html` rewrite plus offline cross-page link and anchor validation (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto rewrites `.qmd` links to `.html`, and `quarto check` does some validation, but cross-page anchor/link checking is limited; a broken relative link or a dead `#fragment` usually surfaces only at runtime (a 404 or a scroll that does nothing).
- **Critique:** A renamed section or moved page leaves dead internal links that ship silently; without a build-time check you discover them in production.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-target compiler (HTML, PDF/LaTeX, docx, ePub, revealjs, books), and link/anchor semantics differ per target: `.qmd#sec` becomes `.html#sec` in a website, an internal `\ref` in a single-file LaTeX book, and something else again in a deck. A build-time cross-page anchor validator that is correct across ALL of those is far harder and more error-prone than one that only has to be right for a single HTML target. More decisively, Quarto's rendering is an extensible Pandoc + Lua-filter pipeline: shortcodes, filters, and computed cell output can inject ids Quarto cannot see statically, and projects legitimately link into generated or cross-project content whose resolution is undecidable offline. A validator that false-flags a legitimate anchor (or misses a filter-injected one) is arguably worse than none, so Quarto punts to runtime, where a 404 is at least honest, and leaves link-checking to the industry-standard division of labor: a dedicated checker (lychee, htmltest) run over the built output. Taliesin can afford a precise, no-false-positive validator PRECISELY because it dropped every non-HTML format and every third-party filter, collapsing the problem to one deterministic target. That is a scope dividend, not a smarter algorithm, and it is honest to say so. (Note: the entry's `quarto_does` line overcredits `quarto check`, which validates the toolchain/environment, not a project's links.)
- **Taliesin today:** `site/links.rs` rewrites every intra-site `.qmd`/`.tmd` href (prefix + `#fragment` preserved; external/`data:`/`mailto:`/`tel:`/`vscode:` skipped). `mod.rs::validate_cross_page_links` renders each page ONCE, building an id registry and capturing outgoing local links in the same pass, then resolves each link against the page registry and flags (a) a target that is no page and (b) a `page.html#frag` whose frag is no element id on that page. It is deliberately false-positive-averse: `join_rel_in_root` returns None for root-escaping cross-book/mount links (skipped), the anchor check is suppressed for target pages that run cells (a cell may emit an id at runtime), `?query` is stripped, and `mounts:`/decks/on-disk-backed targets are honored. Each warning is source-mapped (source_file + line).
- **Proposed better:** Keep. The single-render-pass-per-page reuse is already efficient. Surface these warnings inline in the live preview as a first-class diagnostic with click-to-source to the offending link line (the `Warning` already carries the location), rather than only on build stderr.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the validator (it is genuinely better than Quarto for Taliesin's single HTML target, and every no-false-positive guard is confirmed in code). But re-order the enhancements and fix the framing. (1) Highest leverage, closest to the critique: run validate_cross_page_links inside the static BUILD, not only the `check` subcommand, and let `--strict` fail on it, so a renamed section cannot silently deploy a dead internal link. Today it is `check`-only and build never invokes it. (2) Only then consider preview surfacing, and scope it honestly: build the site id registry once, keep it fresh off the existing site file-watcher (never re-render the world per edit), and present cross-page link problems in a site-wide diagnostics panel, not just a per-page inline row, since the incoming-link-break case cannot appear on the page you are editing. Reuse already-rendered per-page docs where the session has them. (3) Correct the entry text: warnings surface via `qmd-fast check`, not "build stderr," and `quarto check` validates the toolchain, not links. (4) State the anchor-suppression tradeoff at its true breadth: one cell anywhere on a target page disables anchor validation for that ENTIRE page, not just the one runtime-emitted id, still the right no-cry-wolf call, but broader than "a cell may emit an id.")
- **Tradeoffs:** The cell-emits-id suppression trades a possibly missed dead anchor for zero false positives (the right call for a warning that must not cry wolf). External URLs are never fetched (offline, so `check` stays deterministic), so a dead external link is not caught. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal defeats its own motivating scenario. The critique's headline case is "rename a section HERE, break an incoming link OVER THERE." Taliesin's preview diagnostics channel is per-page (serve_site sends only the currently-viewed page's warnings via protocol::diagnostics). A broken cross-page link is located to its SOURCE page, so surfacing it inline can only show the current page's OUTGOING broken links, exactly the direction the author is least likely to break by accident. The edit-here-breaks-there direction is structurally unshowable in a per-page inline channel; catching it needs a whole-site diagnostics surface, not an inline row. Second, the entry frames this as free ("the Warning already carries the location"), but validate_cross_page_links renders EVERY page once to build the id registry; that is fine as a one-shot `check`, but to live in the warm incremental preview it must be built once and kept fresh as any page changes on disk (the watcher spans the whole site), then re-emitted for the current page. That is real machinery, not piping an existing Warning. Third, a factual slip the drafter missed: these warnings do not surface "on build stderr" at all; build.rs never calls the validator. A user who only runs `build` (not `check`) ships broken internal links silently today, which is the higher-leverage gap than preview-inline.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time and offline (no network probes, deterministic); read-only; every finding is source-mapped so click-to-source is honored. Invariants held. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation, but a real tension: putting a whole-site render pass on the per-edit preview hot path would fight the "no per-edit startup cost" + block-level-incremental invariants. It is only safe if the id registry is computed once and incrementally patched on file-change events rather than rebuilt per keystroke. Click-to-source is honored (the diagnostic navigates, never writes), and HTML-only / read-only-surface / Markdown-syntax are untouched.)

### D114. Site navigation chrome: navbar-only websites + off-canvas book drawer, with no nested sidebar, breadcrumbs, or website prev/next (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto websites offer a top navbar AND a multi-level collapsible left `sidebar:` (sections, auto-expanding the active branch), breadcrumbs on deep pages, and automatic prev/next page links threaded through sidebar order. A docs-style site typically leans on the nested sidebar.
- **Critique:** For a large hierarchical docs site that is not a linear book, a flat top navbar alone loses the section tree: a reader cannot see where they are (no breadcrumb) or move linearly through pages (no prev/next). Taliesin gives prev/next only to books.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A persistent, multi-level collapsible sidebar is the recognized best-in-class docs UX, not config bloat for its own sake: Docusaurus, GitBook, MkDocs Material, Sphinx/ReadTheDocs, VitePress, and Mintlify all converge on it. It solves three things a flat navbar cannot for a large reference set: (1) it shows the whole information architecture at a glance so a reader can jump between siblings and cousins without going home first; (2) breadcrumbs answer "where am I in the tree" on deep pages; (3) prev/next threads a defined reading order. Crucially Quarto's sidebar auto-expands the active branch, so it is declared ONCE in _quarto.yml, not maintained per page, and it serves the genuine middle ground between a flat blog and a strictly linear book: a hierarchy that is meant to be browsed non-linearly but still needs a spine. This entry honestly concedes that (status is open-question, proposed option (a) defers to Taliesin's book model), so it does not strawman Quarto.
- **Taliesin today:** `site/chrome.rs`: a website renders ONLY a flat top navbar (`nav: left/right` groups, active-item marking, a keyboard/SR-operable mobile burger). A book renders a slim sticky topbar + off-canvas chapter drawer + bottom-of-chapter prev/next (`book_nav_html`). `mod.rs::page_chrome` sets `post_nav_html` to `String::new()` for websites, so a website page has NO prev/next. There is no website `sidebar:` (none in `NATIVE_KEYS`) and no breadcrumb component (the only `breadcrumb` in the tree is an unrelated Quarto-migration message).
- **Proposed better:** Decide the docs-site story: (a) tell authors to model a hierarchical doc set as a book (drawer + prev/next), which the owner already does by mounting docs as sibling books, or (b) add an optional nested website `sidebar:` reusing the book drawer's a11y wiring. Given the mount-as-books practice, (a) may be enough. A lightweight breadcrumb derived from URL depth + page titles is cheap and helps deep sites regardless.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the core of (a) but reframe it as the blessed answer, not a fallback: docs-as-book plus mount is already the owner's shipped practice (docs/guide is a book) and is genuinely sufficient for a hierarchical doc set, at zero new config surface. Explicitly REJECT option (b) as written: a standalone website sidebar: tree re-imports the exact nested-config surface Quarto is criticized for, creates a second source of truth for page order (colliding with path order, listing order, and the reference graph), and largely reinvents the book. If a hierarchy truly needs a top navbar AND a section tree on the same page (the one thing the book model cannot do, since a book suppresses navbar_html), the sharp move is a small contained extension, let a book also render the site navbar (or let a mounted book inherit the parent navbar), NOT a parallel website sidebar. Downgrade the breadcrumb from "cheap URL-depth" to "defer, or derive from the book's real part/chapter hierarchy", pinned by a corpus doc and weighed against the reading-first redesign that removed chrome. Website prev/next is correctly left off: a blog navigates by listings, and path order is arbitrary.
- **Tradeoffs:** A second website nav system (sidebar) re-introduces exactly the config surface Quarto is criticized for, and can visually collide with the navbar. A website prev/next needs a meaningful page order (path order exists but is arbitrary for a blog). (skeptic-found downside: The book model option (a) leans on suppresses the site navbar entirely (navbar_html = String::new() for books, mod.rs:386-390), so a single page cannot show a global top navbar AND a docs section tree at once. That is precisely why the owner mounts docs as SEPARATE book projects under /docs rather than nesting them as a section of one site, an indirection the proposal presents as frictionless without naming it. Two more unmissed costs: a book is one linear order rendered as a FLAT parts+chapters list in the drawer (chrome.rs:292-315), so it does not represent 3+-level nesting or a many-sibling reference set that is not meant to be read start to finish; and the "cheap" URL-depth breadcrumb is not cheap: correct crumbs need each path segment to resolve to a real, titled, linkable parent (a per-directory index page), which flat website discovery does not create, so segments like using/ would produce broken or non-clickable crumbs, and any breadcrumb re-adds exactly the chrome the reading-first redesign deliberately stripped.)
- **Invariant check:** All chrome is server-rendered, read-only navigation; a sidebar or breadcrumb touches no output-format or single-surface invariant. In scope. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is broken: all proposed chrome is server-rendered, read-only navigation (never writes source), a sidebar:/breadcrumb is YAML config not prose-syntax divergence, and none of it touches block-level data-block-id/sourcepos. Two soft, in-scope requirements the proposal omits: (1) corpus-plus-roadmap means options (b) and the breadcrumb are NEW capabilities that must each ship pinned by a corpus site document, which the entry does not mention (option (a) alone adds no capability and needs no new pin, another point in its favor); (2) any new nav chrome must carry data-qmd-src="_site.yml" to keep Alt-click-to-config parity with the existing navbar and drawer.)

### D115. Listings and taxonomy: client-side category chips vs Quarto pagination, listing types, and tag pages (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto `listing:` supports `type: default|table|grid`, `page-size` pagination, `sort`/`sort-ui`/`filter-ui` controls, a category sidebar/cloud with client-side filtering, custom `fields`/EJS templates, and `feed: true` RSS.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's listing is leaner: a long blog index shows every card (no pagination), offers only grid or stacked list, and has no cross-listing tag index (no site-wide `tags:`/category browse). A migrant with a big archive and a category cloud loses those.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto deliberately makes taxonomy browse ONE mechanism instead of a generated per-tag page tree, and that is a defensible, arguably better call for its constraints. A single listing whose categories filter client-side via a URL hash (listing.html#category=ml) gives every category "view" a shareable, deep-linkable URL with zero extra build output and no parallel /tags/ tree to keep in sync. Crucially it COMPOSES: filter to "ml" AND sort by date AND typeahead "vae" all at once, which N static category pages cannot do. Layered on top, page-size pagination keeps a 500-post archive usable without shipping 500 cards or 500 static pages; sort-ui/filter-ui give readers control; EJS templates let institutional users match a house style; and feed:true RSS is the actual cross-site syndication primitive readers subscribe to, not per-tag pages. A post's category badge already links back to the filtered listing, delivering cross-page browse without a separate page. So Quarto is not "missing" tag pages: it decided one composable, deep-linkable, paginated listing beats a multiplied static page tree, which is the right tradeoff for a large-archive, multi-author, multi-format tool. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `mod.rs`: `ListingSpec` = grid|default, `sort` desc/asc by ISO date, `max-items` cap, and `categories: true` renders a client-side filter chip row (per-category counts, multi-select, an All chip). Each card carries `.tali-cat[data-cat]` badges read by the filter (comma-safe category names). No pagination, no table type, no sort/filter dropdowns, no dedicated tag/category pages, no RSS. Cards are real blocks (diffed like any other content).
- **Proposed better:** Ship build-time tag-index pages (FEATURE-IDEAS #35): front-matter `tags:` generate read-only `/tags/foo.html` pages riding the existing listing machinery and the `_`/`.`/`draft:` exclusion. That is the genuinely missing navigational primitive (cross-page browse), since in-page filtering is already covered by chips. Add `page-size` pagination only if a real corpus index grows long. Skip `type: table` and template DSLs until demanded.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the direction (cross-page taxonomy index is the one genuinely missing navigational primitive, and it is HTML-only, read-only, corpus-pinnable, in scope) but revise the mechanism. Generate category-index pages from the EXISTING categories: field, not a new tags: field, so there is ONE taxonomy powering both the chips and the index pages, zero new front-matter surface, and a Quarto migrant's categories: carries straight over (matching the owner's keep-familiarity, shed-Quarto-identity direction). Specify the parts the entry left implicit: a config-named reserved output prefix (default categories/) with a warning on collision against real page slugs; an explicit slugification + case-fold rule with a warning on slug collisions between distinct category names; cards on the generated page that click-to-source to each post, and no phantom data-source-file/sourcepos on the synthetic page; and a serve_site dependency edge so a warm-preview edit to any post's categories: re-renders the affected index pages. Also correct the framing: these pages are a wider-than-Quarto ADDITION (Quarto has no per-category pages), not a recovered migration loss, so market them as such and let a category page's URL reflect chip state so it delivers BOTH the static deep-link Quarto lacks and the composable in-page filter Quarto has. Defer page-size pagination until a real corpus index crosses a length threshold; skip type: table and EJS templates until demanded; RSS stays in the reader-engagement entry. Do NOT count a "category cloud" as a Quarto loss: Taliesin's counted, multi-select chips already match Quarto's numbered category cloud.
- **Tradeoffs:** Tag pages add build output plus a taxonomy config surface; static pagination multiplies files while a client show-more adds JS. Because category chips already handle in-page filtering, the marginal value of tag pages is specifically cross-listing browse. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal invents a SECOND taxonomy field (tags:) alongside Taliesin's existing categories:, which is already in KNOWN_KEYS, used across the whole corpus, and read by the chip filter. That splits taxonomy into two disjoint vocabularies: chips would filter on categories while index pages build on tags, and the two axes never compose. It also adds a new strict-validation surface (tags must be added to KNOWN_KEYS or every post using it warns), when reusing categories: adds ZERO new front-matter surface and carries a Quarto migrant's categories: straight over. Beyond that, the entry underweights three costs that in-page exact-match chips entirely avoided: (1) slugification/case-fold: "Machine Learning" and "machine-learning" and "I/O" must become URL-safe /tags/*.html slugs, so distinct categories can collide into one slug or a slash can break the path (chips dodged this by matching exact strings and never minting a URL); (2) output-namespace collision: /tags/foo.html claims a top-level URL prefix that can clobber a real page slug or a content dir, and the cited _/./draft: rule governs source exclusion, not output collision; (3) incremental correctness: "rides the existing listing machinery" is optimistic, because listings live ON the host page you are viewing while tag pages are standalone DERIVED pages with a fan-in dependency (editing any one post's categories: must re-render every affected index page under the warm dev server), a new derived-page class serve_site does not yet track.)
- **Invariant check:** Tag pages are build-time HTML (HTML-only intact); filter chips are read-only client enhancement with no write-back. In scope. RSS is handled separately (see reader-engagement entry). (possible violation flagged: No invariant is violated outright, but two obligations the entry glosses must be met or click-to-source and warm-incremental degrade. Click-to-source: a generated /tags/foo.html (or /categories/foo.html) has no .tmd source, so its cards must click-to-source to each POST's source and the synthetic page must emit NO phantom data-source-file/data-sourcepos into a nonexistent file (same pattern as about:/hero: synthetic blocks, must be pinned). Warm server / block-level incremental: the derived index pages must be invalidated and re-rendered when any contributing page's front-matter taxonomy changes, which is a new cross-cutting dependency in serve_site, not a free ride on the host-page listing path.)

### D116. SEO output: sitemap.xml, robots.txt, and JSON-LD structured data at publish (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto emits `sitemap.xml` (honoring `site-url`), and authors routinely add robots.txt and structured data, so search engines get a crawl map and rich-result-eligible metadata.
- **Critique:** Taliesin ships og/twitter/canonical `<meta>` (good) but no sitemap, no robots.txt, and no `Article`/`WebSite` JSON-LD, so a published Taliesin site is less crawlable and less rich-result-eligible than the equivalent Quarto site.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto automates exactly one SEO artifact, sitemap.xml, and deliberately declines the other two, and that split is principled, not lazy. A sitemap is mechanically derivable (page list plus site-url), schema-frozen since 2008, and universally safe: it can only help crawlers, never de-index.
