So Quarto generates it. robots.txt is a crawl-POLICY file, not a derivation: a single wrong line (Disallow: /) de-indexes the whole site, hosts like GitHub Pages / Netlify may supply their own, and authors routinely hand-write it once. A document compiler that presumes your crawl policy is overreaching, so Quarto (correctly) leaves it to the author. JSON-LD is a semantic contract with Google's rich-results validator: a valid Article needs a structured publisher plus a logo ImageObject, headline, datePublished, and author as a Person/Organization, and emitting Article for a page that is not really an article can be ignored or penalized. Quarto ships Open Graph and Twitter cards (the same tier Taliesin already ships) and stops short of asserting schema.org content types on the author's behalf, because guessing that type is a correctness risk it declines to take. Automate the safe mechanical one, refuse to guess the two that encode author policy and semantics: that is a defensible line, not a gap.
- **Taliesin today:** `site/meta.rs::social_head` emits per-page description, og:*, twitter:*, canonical, and Google-Scholar `citation_*` (for dated authored posts), all gated on a configured `url:`. Sitemap/robots/JSON-LD are NOT built; they are roadmapped as `build-seo-completeness` (BEYOND-QUARTO.md ~308-312, backlog Wave 5).
- **Proposed better:** Implement `build-seo-completeness` as specced: at build, when `url:` is set, emit `sitemap.xml` (reusing the nav `_`/`.`/`draft:` exclusion so drafts stay out), a `robots.txt` pointing at it, and per-page `Article`/`WebSite` JSON-LD reusing the `social_head` fields. Build-time metadata files only.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature, but split it and sharpen the framing. Reframe against Quarto honestly: sitemap.xml is genuine catch-up (Quarto auto-generates it, Taliesin does not, real gap); robots.txt is NOT something Quarto auto-generates either (their authors hand-write it), so this is a convenience add, not closing a Quarto gap; JSON-LD is a beyond-Quarto move (default Quarto ships no JSON-LD, so out-of-the-box the two are at PARITY on structured data). Drop the critique's implication that an out-of-the-box Quarto site is "more rich-result-eligible." Implementation: ship sitemap.xml first (truly small, reuses self.pages minus drafts/_/., and MUST reuse meta.rs clean_url normalization so <loc> matches canonical). Ship robots.txt with a strict "never overwrite an existing robots.txt in the tree" guard, defaulting to just Allow plus a Sitemap: line. Treat JSON-LD as a separate medium item, and do it right or not at all: add optional publisher/logo config so the emitted Article/WebSite actually validates, gate Article on the same page.date.is_some() rule already used for og:type, and skip JSON-LD when the needed fields are absent rather than emit an invalid stub. Pin with a site-level corpus fixture that builds a full _site/ and asserts on sitemap.xml, robots.txt, and the ld+json script (a build assertion, heavier than the render-only corpus tests, consistent with the corpus.rs:470 pattern that already asserts on emitted .xml). All build-time only, gated on url:, no source write-back, HTML-only intact.
- **Tradeoffs:** More build outputs to keep correct, and JSON-LD duplicates the og/meta data so it must stay in sync with `meta.rs`. Only meaningful once `url:` is set (a personal domain), which the tool already nudges via the `image:`-without-`url:` warning. (skeptic-found downside: Three costs the drafter under-weighted. (1) JSON-LD built from only the social_head fields is INCOMPLETE for its own stated goal: a Google Article rich result requires a structured publisher plus a logo ImageObject (with dimensions), headline, and author as a Person/Organization, none of which social_head carries, so "rich-result-eligible" is only half-delivered unless new publisher/logo config is added, which pushes the JSON-LD piece from "small" to "medium." (2) robots.txt clobbering: the build copies local assets into _site/, so a build-generated robots.txt can overwrite an author's hand-written robots.txt (or collide with a host default like GitHub Pages), and the spec has no "do not overwrite an existing robots.txt" guard. (3) Clean-URL desync: the sitemap <loc> must reuse the exact same index.html to trailing-slash normalization that meta.rs already applies to canonical (clean_url), or the sitemap lists /posts/x/index.html while canonical says /posts/x/, splitting the crawl signal. The drafter flagged only the JSON-LD/meta duplication, not the publisher-completeness gap, the overwrite guard, or the URL-normalization coupling.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time metadata (sitemap/robots are crawl metadata, not document formats, consistent with the roadmap's own HTML-only reading); read-only; no per-edit cost. In scope.

### D117. URL stability: front-matter `aliases:` generating redirect stubs on rename/move (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto supports `aliases:` in a page's front matter and generates redirect stub HTML (`<meta http-equiv=refresh>` + canonical) at each old URL, so renaming a post does not break inbound links or bookmarks.
- **Critique:** Taliesin has no alias/redirect mechanism. Rename `posts/old.qmd` to `posts/new.qmd` and every external link, bookmark, and search-engine result to the old URL 404s. The cross-page checker catches internal breakage, but nothing external survives the rename.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** URL permanence is a genuine, load-bearing weakness of every static-site generator: rename a source file and its output URL changes, so every inbound link, bookmark, RSS entry, and search-engine result silently 404s. Quarto's design is close to ideal for the problem. It puts the redirect declaration IN the moved page's own front matter, so it is co-located with the thing that moved, travels with the file in version control, and is reviewable in the SAME diff as the rename. It emits a portable `meta http-equiv=refresh` + `rel=canonical` stub that works on EVERY static host, including GitHub Pages, which cannot issue server-side 301s at all, so a host-native `_redirects` file would not help there. It is opt-in and costs nothing when unused. The entry's `critique` is not adversarial to Quarto: it credits Quarto's capability and faults Taliesin's gap, and the proposal essentially copies Quarto. Verified against code: Taliesin genuinely has no alias/redirect mechanism (no `aliases`/`redirects`/`http-equiv`/`canonical` anywhere; `discovery.rs` maps one source path to exactly one `.html`; `render_404_page` exists but offers no redirect path), so the critique is accurate and steelmanned, not a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. No `aliases`/`redirects` key; `discovery.rs` and `links.rs` map one source path to exactly one `.html` URL. `render_404_page` provides a themed 404 but no redirect path.
- **Proposed better:** Add a page front-matter `aliases: [old/url, ...]` that, at build, writes a minimal stub HTML at each alias URL (meta-refresh + `rel=canonical` + a one-line 'moved' link), and in preview serves the same redirect. It reuses the URL mapping already on `Page` and is pure build-time HTML.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature, revise for the Taliesin-specific integration the draft glossed. (1) Wire `aliases` into `frontmatter::KNOWN_KEYS` plus an array-of-strings schema override, or strict validation flags it as unknown on every use. (2) Add a build-time collision check that warns (Taliesin-style, loud) when an alias equals any real page URL or another page's alias, and never let a stub overwrite a real page. (3) Pin the URL form: treat each alias as a literal output path and always emit the stub at the exact `.html` target (mirroring `qmd_to_html`), documenting that aliases are output URLs, so redirects hit the actually-bookmarked links. (4) In preview, prefer a real HTTP redirect (axum `Redirect`, 301/302) slotted before the 404 fallback in `serve_site`, while the static build emits the `meta-refresh` + `rel=canonical` stub; say this explicitly rather than claiming preview "serves the same redirect." (5) Ship pinned by a corpus doc that asserts the stub exists at the alias URL with the refresh + canonical, since corpus-plus-roadmap is the arbiter of done and the draft did not mention it. (6) Optional: also emit a host-native `_redirects` file so Netlify/Cloudflare Pages get real 301s while GitHub Pages falls back to the stub. Lean into the migration angle: an author moving a live Quarto blog to Taliesin is the prime beneficiary (existing public URLs, real SEO exposure), which fully justifies the medium impact rating.
- **Tradeoffs:** Stub pages are extra build outputs; meta-refresh is a client-side redirect (no HTTP 301, since the static host owns real redirects). Authors must remember to add the alias when renaming, though a future editor command could suggest it. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's `invariant_check` misses the single biggest integration cost in THIS codebase: Taliesin's front-matter validator is a closed set (`frontmatter::KNOWN_KEYS` plus `schema.rs` with `additionalProperties: false`, generated from the same const). `aliases` is not in that list, so as written the strict validator would flag `aliases:` as an unknown key with a did-you-mean warning on every page that uses the feature. Shipping it REQUIRES a coupled edit: add `aliases` to `KNOWN_KEYS` and a schema override typing it as an array of strings (exactly the `theorems.shared` pattern already in schema.rs). That is mandatory, not optional. Two more gaps the tradeoffs skip: (1) No collision guard. An alias equal to a real page URL, or two pages claiming the same alias, would have the stub write (`fs::write(out.join(alias))`) clobber real output, or be clobbered, in nondeterministic order and silently, which is exactly the failure class Taliesin's strict-warn ethos exists to catch. (2) URL-form ambiguity: the example `aliases: [old/url, ...]` never says whether the stub lands at `old/url`, `old/url.html`, or `old/url/index.html`, yet real inbound links from a prior Quarto site are `.html`, so a normalization convention is needed or the redirect misses the actual bookmarked URL.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time HTML stubs (HTML-only); read-only (no source write-back); trivial per-edit cost. In scope.

### D118. Subpath deploys: modeling a base path so root-absolute links survive `user.github.io/repo/` (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `site-url`/site-path handling lets a project deploy under a subpath, resolving resource and absolute links against the configured base.
- **Critique:** Taliesin is mostly subpath-safe because chrome links and the favicon are depth-relative, but the built-in 404 page is necessarily root-absolute (a static host serves that one file for any bad path while keeping the URL in the bar, so its links must be `/...`). On a project-subpath deploy its 'Back to site' link and any `/`-absolute link point at the domain root, not the repo subpath. The code comment flags this as unmodeled.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's choice is defensible and, for Quarto, correct. Quarto models a single site base (`site-url` with a derived `site-path`) that solves an entire class of absolute-URL cases at once: the sitemap.xml, RSS feeds, redirect stubs, social/canonical tags, AND the 404 page all need the deploy base, so one config knob is the clean general answer rather than N one-off patches. Note the fair nuance: Quarto does NOT actually resolve ordinary resource/page links against `site-path`; like Taliesin, it uses depth-relative (offset) links for those, so they survive any subpath for free. `site-path` earns its keep precisely on the links that CANNOT be relative (the 404 served at arbitrary depth, sitemap/feed absolutes). Because Quarto emits sitemaps and feeds and multi-format output, a full base-path model pays for itself. Taliesin emits none of those (HTML-only, feed.rs removed) and its only non-relative link in the entire generated site is the 404's one home link, so copying Quarto's whole `site-path` machinery would be over-engineering. Quarto is right for Quarto's surface; Taliesin needs the same insight applied to a surface of exactly one link.
- **Taliesin today:** `mod.rs::render_404_page` hardcodes `/` links and documents: 'a project-subpath deploy (`user.github.io/repo/`) would need a base path the config doesn't model yet.' `url:` drives absolute og:url/canonical (which DO work if `url:` already includes the subpath). `site-url` is not in `NATIVE_KEYS` (it would warn as unknown) and is a known dead/tolerated key elsewhere in the tree.
- **Proposed better:** Either (a) derive a base path from the existing `url:` (its path component) and use it for the 404 page's absolute links and any absolute asset, so a subpath 404 works; or (b) declare root-deploy the supported target and make the 404 home link origin-relative via a tiny inline `location.origin`+base script. Option (a) reuses config already present and is the smaller change.
- **Revised recommendation:** Revise and keep, scoped tighter than drafted. Take option (a): derive the base from the path component of the existing `url:` (consistent with how meta.rs already treats `url:` as including the subpath for canonical/og:url), and use it ONLY for the 404 home link. But make render_404_page take an explicit base argument: build.rs passes the normalized `url:` path (leading slash, single trailing slash, empty when `url:` is unset or root), and serve_site's preview fallback passes an empty base so the preview link stays `/`. This is the only way to satisfy the code's own "preview mirrors production" goal, which the drafter's version would break. Drop the "any absolute asset" language: the favicon and CSS are inlined, so the fix is a single href. Do NOT add a separate `site-path` config key (it could disagree with `url:`'s path and fights the closed-vocabulary clean break); reuse `url:`. Pin it with a new corpus site whose `_site.yml` sets `url: https://user.github.io/repo` and a test asserting the built 404's home link is `/repo/` while a root-`url:` site (and preview) stays `/`. Re-rate impact as low-to-medium: it fixes one genuinely-wrong link on GitHub project-page deploys, which this author has used historically (the purged bayesian-book `site-url` was a project subpath), so it is not hypothetical, just narrow.
- **Tradeoffs:** A base path threads through the one place (the 404) that cannot be depth-relative; small surface but easy to get subtly wrong (trailing slash, empty base). Most single-author deploys use a custom domain (root), so real-world impact is limited to GitHub project pages. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter missed that render_404_page is shared by BOTH the static build (build.rs:1023) and the live-preview fallback (serve_site/mod.rs:330), and the preview serves the site at localhost ROOT, not under the subpath. So deriving the base from `url:` and baking it into the home link makes production correct but breaks the PREVIEW 404 link (it would point at localhost/repo/, which does not exist in preview), directly violating the "preview mirrors production 404" property the code deliberately maintains. The real fix must thread the base as a build-vs-preview parameter (url-path for build, empty for preview), which turns "the smaller change" into a two-call-site change with exactly the trailing-slash/empty-base pitfalls flagged, plus a mode dimension. Two smaller misses: (1) "use it for the 404's absolute links and any absolute asset" overstates the surface: the favicon is an inlined data URI and CSS is inline, so there is exactly ONE absolute link to fix, not a class of assets. (2) The fix only helps authors who set `url:` to include the subpath (it is optional), so it degrades gracefully to `/` but does nothing for a subpath deploy with no `url:` set. Impact is therefore narrower than "medium": one link, on one page, in one deploy topology (GitHub project pages), for authors who set a subpath `url:`.)
- **Invariant check:** Build-time link resolution; read-only; HTML-only. The narrow surface (404 only) keeps it low-risk and in scope. (possible violation flagged: Corpus-plus-roadmap: no corpus document currently exercises a subpath deploy (the only corpus `url:` is tech-blog's root custom domain `https://andreasbogossian.com`). A base-path capability is exactly the kind of new behavior CLAUDE.md requires to ship "pinned by a target corpus document added in the same change." As written the proposal adds a code path with no regression net, so it would land un-pinned. Not a hard violation of HTML-only / read-only / warm-server / click-to-source (it is build-time, read-only, HTML-only, and touches only generated chrome), but it is out of compliance with the corpus-plus-roadmap discipline until a subpath-404 corpus doc is added.)

### D119. Reader engagement and distribution: comments (giscus) and RSS feeds, both deliberately absent (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto ships built-in `comments:` (giscus, utterances, hypothesis) that inject a third-party comment widget, and `feed: true` on a listing generates an RSS/Atom feed for subscribers.
- **Critique:** A personal tech blog often wants both: readers subscribe via RSS and discuss via giscus. Taliesin offers neither, and it actively DROPS a configured local `.xml` footer link, so an author's habitual `/blog.xml` link silently vanishes with no warning, which surprises a Quarto migrant (the tech-blog corpus config even still lists `/blog.xml`).
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** A publishing tool's remit includes distribution and engagement, not only rendering. RSS is the strongest case: it is a plain XML file, no JavaScript, no third party, no tracking, the reader owns the subscription, and it keeps working offline forever. It is arguably the MOST self-contained, lock-in-free distribution primitive that exists, more aligned with Taliesin's own offline ethos than almost any alternative, so Quarto emitting `feed: true` is principled, not a compromise. For a blog engine, syndication is table stakes: omit it and you are a worse blog tool than Hugo or Jekyll. giscus is the weaker but still reasonable half: it lets a static site gain comments with no backend to run, is opt-in, and rides GitHub Discussions (no ads or data-broker tracking, unlike Disqus). Quarto makes both one line because its broad audience of academics and bloggers publishes to be read and discussed, and the marginal author cannot hand-build either. The critique is accurate and steelmanned, not a strawman: Quarto genuinely ships both, a personal tech blog commonly wants both, and the silent-drop papercut is real and verified in code.
- **Taliesin today:** No comments feature. RSS was deliberately removed (`feed.rs` deleted; nothing generates a feed); `chrome.rs::footer_html` silently drops a local `.xml` href (external `.xml` URLs are kept). Owner framing in FEATURE-IDEAS: `categories`/RSS is a non-goal, tags are a navigational index, not a feed.
- **Proposed better:** Two separable calls. Comments: a thin opt-in `comments: giscus: {repo, ...}` injecting the giscus `<script>` at the article foot, anchored to a `data-block-id` so it survives the diff; it never writes source, and built sites already load some CDN JS (mermaid). RSS: reconsider only as build-time XML *navigation metadata* (the same category as the roadmapped sitemap.xml), generated from a listing's collection, and restore the `.xml` footer link when present. If RSS stays a non-goal, at minimum WARN on (not silently drop) the local `.xml` footer link so the author knows it was removed.
- **Revised recommendation:** Reframe the entry from "reconsider both" to "both stay absent by design; fix one real papercut." (a) Do NOT add giscus: it breaks the certified 0-CDN self-contained build, a solo author has near-zero comment demand, and the owner's own roadmap points at NATIVE block-anchored comments if comments ever ship, so a third-party bolt-on is the wrong architecture. (b) Do NOT restore RSS: it reverses a twice-documented non-goal, and the sitemap.xml precedent does not transfer (SEO crawler metadata is a different category from a reader subscription/distribution feed, which is exactly what the non-goal rejects). (c) The ONLY actionable change is the drafter's fallback, and it is a good one: make Taliesin WARN through the check/lint path (consistent with its strict-validation identity, matching how it already flags unknown config keys with click-to-source) when it drops a configured LOCAL .xml footer link, so a Quarto migrant learns the /blog.xml link was intentionally removed instead of it vanishing silently; AND purge the dead /blog.xml RSS item from corpus/tech-blog/_site.yml so the corpus stops shipping a link to a deliberately-removed feature. Pin the warn with a corpus/check test.
- **Tradeoffs:** Comments pull in a third party (external script + a GitHub Discussions account + a privacy footprint), against the offline/self-contained grain. RSS-as-XML sits in the same gray zone as sitemap.xml: defensible as metadata, but a strict reading of HTML-only could reject a feed as a format. Both add config surface for a single-author tool. (skeptic-found downside: The comments half rests on a FALSE precedent: a static Build inlines mermaid and is certified 0 CDN refs (AUDITS.md:259); the CDN is touched only in dev preview, so a giscus script at the article foot of a BUILD would be the first external RUNTIME dependency in a published Taliesin site, a net-new offline regression rather than a continuation. The "anchored to a data-block-id so it survives the diff" framing is confused: giscus maps a whole PAGE to a discussion (data-mapping pathname/url/title), never a block, and comments should be Build-only anyway (a live GitHub thread injected in the warm dev loop would fire network on every save, keyed to a localhost preview URL that will not match the production discussion), and in a Build there is no live diff to survive, so the whole diff-survival concern is moot and hides an unresolved gating question. Worse, giscus's per-URL mapping would hit the exact clean-directory-URL vs index.html mismatch already documented as a bug for the OLD RSS feed (AUDITS.md:213), mis-keying or splitting threads. And the owner's own STARTUP-PLAN frames future comments as NATIVE block-anchored (the intended differentiator), so a thin third-party giscus bolt-on is the wrong shape even if comments are ever wanted. Finally the stale /blog.xml line is itself corpus-hygiene debt: the corpus is the arbiter of done, so a dead RSS footer item should be purged, not preserved as evidence.)
- **Invariant check:** Comments live on the third party and never write `.tmd` (single surface intact) but are an external-script dependency (weakens self-contained/offline). RSS is XML: arguably metadata (sitemap precedent) but a strict reading of 'HTML is the ONLY output target' would flag a feed as a parallel format, so it is flagged here for the owner. Neither adds per-edit cost. (possible violation flagged: No hard enumerated invariant is strictly broken. giscus never writes .tmd (single read-only surface intact) and a script embedded in HTML is still HTML output (HTML-only intact). RSS-as-XML also does not cleanly break HTML-only, because sitemap.xml/robots.txt are already roadmapped, so XML metadata coexists with the identity: the drafter's HTML-only framing for RSS is a red herring. The REAL conflicts are (1) a values violation for giscus: it erodes the self-contained/offline property the architecture defends and certifies (0 CDN refs); (2) a stated NON-GOAL violation for RSS: BEYOND-QUARTO.md:464 and FEATURE-IDEAS.md:274 list RSS/categories as explicitly out; (3) a corpus-plus-roadmap tension: restoring RSS would require pinning a corpus doc for a capability that is a declared non-goal, which inverts the discipline.)

### D120. Output URL convention: keep the flat, visible-extension source mirror (page.tmd -> page.html) and decline pretty-URL rewriting (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's default is the same base shape: each input renders to a sibling output with the extension swapped (`page.qmd` -> `page.html`), extension visible in the URL, output tree mirroring the source tree. Quarto has no project-level pretty/clean-URL toggle that auto-rewrites `page.qmd` into `page/index.html`; the only way to get a slash-terminated directory URL is the same opt-in idiom Taliesin uses, authoring `folder/index.qmd`. On top of that base Quarto layers two things Taliesin does not: `aliases:` front matter that emits meta-refresh redirect stub pages (rename/link-rot mitigation), and `site-url`/`site-path` for absolute-URL and base-path resolution. So the framing of Quarto having distinctive clean/pretty directory-index URLs is generous: concretely, both tools share the visible-extension mirror, and Quarto's clean URLs are the identical `index.*` convention plus redirect stubs.
- **Critique:** The genuine design tension, stated without strawman: an extensionless "pretty" scheme that rewrites `page.tmd` into `page/index.html` reads cleaner in a browser bar and survives a future move to a different renderer, but it sacrifices a reversible source<->URL mapping and introduces real ambiguity (a `page.tmd` and a `page/index.tmd` would both claim `/page/`, and asset/relative-link depth silently shifts by one level for every page). The visible-extension mirror is the opposite trade: fully transparent and collision-free, but it leaks `.html` into shared links and gives no built-in safety net when a page is renamed (a deep link 404s with nothing to redirect it). Quarto lands on the same visible-extension default but never states the reversibility rationale, and patches the rename gap with redirect stubs rather than a stable, predictable convention.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is not naive here. It deliberately kept the same transparent visible-extension mirror as its default (source-to-URL stays legible and collision-resistant), then layered on exactly the two safety nets this scheme structurally lacks, without ever resorting to a lossy pretty-rewrite. (1) aliases: emits redirect-stub pages, so renaming intro.qmd to getting-started.qmd does not 404 every external deep link, which is the one genuine weakness of a path-mirror scheme. (2) site-url plus site-path support hosting under a base path (GitHub project pages at /repo/, a reverse-proxied subdirectory) and emit correct absolute canonical/sitemap URLs. So Quarto arguably ships the STRONGER version of the very convention the entry praises: same good default, plus a rename net, plus subdirectory deployability. Taliesin matches only the default and declines two of Quarto's add-ons, so "already better" is really "matches Quarto's default while lacking base-path portability."
- **Taliesin today:** A pure, reversible bijection between source path and URL. `qmd_to_html` (crates/core/src/site/links.rs:10) strips the source extension and appends `.html`; `html_to_qmd` (links.rs:166) is its exact inverse. `page.url` is just `qmd_to_html(rel)` of the source-tree-relative path (discovery.rs:17), so the URL is the source path with the extension swapped: `page.tmd`->`page.html`, `posts/em/index.tmd`->`posts/em/index.html`. Build writes `out.join(&page.url)` with parents created (build.rs:740), a 1:1 on-disk mirror; the dev router matches a request path straight against `page.url` with only empty-path -> `index.html` (serve_site/mod.rs:249, page() at mod.rs:333). No pretty-URL toggle, no extension stripping, no aliases feature. Clean directory URLs are available purely by authoring `folder/index.tmd`; the cross-page checker already resolves `dir/` links to `dir/index.html` (mod.rs:514).
- **Proposed better:** Keep the flat, visible-extension source mirror and elevate it from accidental behavior to a stated invariant: the URL is the source path with `.tmd` swapped for `.html`, a lossless reversible bijection (`qmd_to_html` / `html_to_qmd`). Treat `folder/index.tmd` -> `/folder/` as the one, documented, first-class way to get a clean directory URL (it already resolves in both preview and static host), rather than adding a project-wide pretty-URL rewrite. Explicitly decline extensionless auto-rewriting, and record why: it would break the reversible mapping that three load-bearing systems depend on and would create the `page.tmd` vs `page/index.tmd` collision that the flat scheme is immune to. Leave rename link-rot to the separate aliases catalog entry, which is the right layer for redirect stubs. This is better than Quarto not because the default shape differs but because the mapping is a deliberate, reversible contract instead of an unstated pipeline side effect.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the decision but fix its framing. The DIRECTION is right and Taliesin already does it: keep the flat visible-extension mirror, keep declining a project-wide pretty-URL rewrite, and document folder/index.tmd as the one clean-directory-URL idiom. But the central "lossless reversible bijection / exact inverse" justification is factually wrong and must not be codified as an invariant. ACCEPTED_SOURCE_EXTS = ["tmd","qmd"] (ext.rs:13), so qmd_to_html is 2-to-1 (page.tmd and page.qmd both map to page.html), and html_to_qmd (links.rs:166) hardcodes .html to .qmd so it never recovers a .tmd source. State the contract honestly instead: a deterministic FORWARD map (source stem + .html), with URL-to-source recovered by a registry lookup on page.rel/page.url, not a pure inverse function. Either narrow the accepted extension to one per project or make html_to_qmd return the bare stem, and drop "collision-free" (page.tmd vs page.qmd, and a page.tmd vs a literal page.html asset, are real collision classes the flat scheme is not immune to). Decouple the click-to-source rationale from the URL scheme: click-to-source rides on per-block data-sourcepos/data-source-file, not on URL inversion, so the invariant_check's claim that the qmd_to_html/html_to_qmd pair is "precisely what lets a rendered page map back to one source file" overstates the coupling. Finally, add two acknowledged tradeoffs the draft omits: domain-root-only deployment (no site-path base-path, unlike Quarto) and the bare-/folder/ preview 404. Then the entry is a defensible "right direction, two named gaps" rather than "better via a bijection that does not exist."
- **Tradeoffs:** Visible `.html` in URLs is marginally less marketing-clean than the extensionless URLs some static-site generators emit, and it couples the public URL to the current renderer's output extension. Authors who want `/about/` must remember the `about/index.tmd` idiom rather than getting a slash URL for free from `about.tmd`. And on its own the convention offers no rename safety net: moving `intro.tmd` to `getting-started.tmd` silently breaks every external deep link, which only the (separately cataloged) aliases redirect feature can soften. None of these outweigh the reversibility win, but they are real ergonomic costs the flat scheme pays. (skeptic-found downside: No base-path support, the exact gap Quarto's site-path fills, and the entry dismisses it. Taliesin's url: yields an absolute canonical/og URL but there is no base-path config; resolve_href (links.rs:30-31) emits every site-absolute link as /blog.html with no prefix. Deploying under a subdirectory (user.github.io/repo/) silently breaks every site-absolute link plus the canonical/og:url, which is precisely what site-path exists to solve. Second, smaller miss: the preview server does NOT resolve the trailing-slash clean URL /folder/ that meta.rs:23 advertises as canonical. page() (mod.rs:329-334) matches only exact url or rel, and the router (serve_site/mod.rs:243-249) maps only empty-path to index.html, so a bare /folder/ 404s in preview while the checker (mod.rs:514) and a real static host both serve folder/index.html: a preview-vs-production divergence for the very clean-URL idiom the proposal elevates to first-class.)
- **Invariant check:** Respects every invariant. HTML-only: this governs URL shape, not output format, so no new target is introduced. Single read-only surface: the URL derives from the file path plus front matter, never from a preview gesture; nothing writes back. Click-to-source: the reversible `qmd_to_html`/`html_to_qmd` pair is precisely what lets a rendered page map back to one source file. Block-level incremental / warm server: a stable per-page URL is the identity key live-reload uses to target a page. Keep-Markdown: the convention layers above the existing syntax (path plus YAML front matter drive the URL), diverging no Markdown. Corpus-plus-roadmap: already pinned by the multi-page corpus sites (tech-blog, bayesian-website, demo-book), whose build and cross-page link tests assert `.tmd`->`.html` and `dir/index` resolution; making the invariant explicit adds an assertion, not a new capability that could outrun the net.

### D121. Ship no first-class analytics, telemetry, or cookie-consent wiring: privacy-by-default is the only default (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's HTML format exposes first-class `google-analytics:` (a bare `G-`/`UA-` tracking id, or an object with `anonymize-ip`, `storage`, `version`) that auto-injects Google's gtag.js loader, plus `cookie-consent:` (`implied`/`express`, palette, policy-url) that bundles the third-party Osano cookieconsent library from a CDN and gates GA on it. It also ships `feed:`/RSS for listing pages. The web default is a tracker-ready surface: one config line turns a page into a Google CDN request plus (with consent) a second third-party script.
- **Critique:** Quarto's convenience keys make the easy path a privacy-hostile one. Adding `google-analytics:` ships gtag.js (an outbound Google request on every visit) and defeats any offline or self-contained guarantee; enabling consent bundles a second CDN-hosted library and quietly pushes GDPR/ePrivacy liability onto a single-author blogger who just wanted a visitor count. There is no cookieless or self-hosted first-class option, so the genuinely privacy-respecting configuration is "add nothing," which is exactly the state Quarto treats as the feature-poor default rather than the intended one.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general, multi-format, multi-audience publisher whose users include institutional and academic authors who are organizationally required to run analytics and legally required (GDPR/ePrivacy) to show a consent banner. For that audience, first-class google-analytics: plus cookie-consent: is a safety rail, not a hazard: two config lines produce a defensible setup (IP anonymization, GA gated behind consent, session vs persistent storage selectable) that a non-expert would otherwise hand-roll incorrectly by pasting a raw gtag snippet with no consent gate and no anonymization, which is strictly worse for the end user. The keys default OFF, so shipping them makes nobody's site track; it makes the authors who WILL add analytics do it more safely and uniformly. Refusing analytics entirely does not stop those authors, it just pushes them to unsafe hand-wired snippets. Given Quarto's breadth mandate, "provide the affordance, default it off, wire the safety rails" is the correct call for its scope. Taliesin can decline only because it deliberately serves one privacy-minded author who can hand-write the two lines when needed, so the safety-rail argument that justifies Quarto simply does not apply to Taliesin's scope. Critique fairness caveat: the entry's "web default is a tracker-ready surface" phrasing overstates, since the default ships no tracker, and the critique omits Quarto's genuine consent-plus-anonymize rationale.
- **Taliesin today:** Verified in code. `NATIVE_KEYS` (crates/core/src/site/config/mod.rs:96-113) is a closed 16-key set (title, author, description, url, favicon, image, output, toc, css, head, body-start, body-end, nav, footer, chapters, mounts) with no analytics/consent key; `validate_keys` (config/mod.rs:210-218) flags an `analytics:`/`google-analytics:`/`cookie-consent:` key as `unknown config key` with a did-you-mean. The page head hard-codes `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer" />` (crates/core/src/render/page.rs:153); assets carry zero CDN references and the binary makes no outbound network calls (only a localhost `TcpStream::connect` to the Jupyter kernel, kernel.rs:504); `--bare` emits zero `<script>`. RSS is already the recorded deliberate omission (corpus.rs:470-480). The sole way to add a tracker is hand-writing it into the raw `head:`/`body-end:` include (config/mod.rs:106-108, site/mod.rs:270-275).
- **Proposed better:** Record analytics/telemetry/cookie-consent in the catalog as a first-class deliberate omission, sibling to the already-recorded RSS omission, and lock the current stance rather than adding a feature. Keep zero `analytics:`/`cookie-consent:` config keys so the closed `NATIVE_KEYS` set turns a pasted Quarto key into an honest `unknown config key` error (migration signal, not a silent no-op). Keep the `no-referrer` head default, the zero-CDN offline guarantee, and the no-phone-home posture as the load-bearing privacy properties. Leave the raw `head:`/`body-end:` include as the ONLY analytics path (author's choice, author's privacy cost, and Taliesin never generates a tracker snippet or a third-party consent-library dependency on the author's behalf). Do NOT build even a cookieless self-hosted counter: it would add an output-time network dependency and contradict the no-phone-home ethos. Pin the stance with a corpus assertion that a built page contains no `gtag`/`google-analytics`/`cookieconsent` string and retains the `no-referrer` meta, mirroring the existing no-`feed.xml` assertions.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the stance (taliesin-already-better): ship no analytics/consent config keys, keep the closed NATIVE_KEYS set so a pasted Quarto key stays an honest unknown-key click-to-source diagnostic, keep no-referrer, and leave head:/body-end: as the only, author-owned tracker path. Do not build a counter (correct, but justify it by "static HTML with no backend, out of scope," not "phone-home"). Before publishing, correct three things: (1) Replace the absolute "zero-CDN offline guarantee" with the accurate split: the static Build and --bare are zero-network, but the live Preview lazy-loads mermaid from jsdelivr unless QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL is set, so the offline guarantee is a Build property, not a global one. (2) Split the two promises the title conflates: (a) the generated SITE injects no tracker (lock with a corpus assertion, scoped to "no auto-generated gtag/cookieconsent AND no-referrer meta present," patterned on the RSS test) and (b) the TOOL itself has no telemetry phone-home (either add a lightweight guard such as a cargo-deny/audit against known telemetry crates or a socket assertion, or drop "telemetry" from the title and claim only what is tested). (3) In the steelman column, credit Quarto's opt-in-plus-consent-plus-anonymize design and note the keys default off, so the entry reads as a scope contrast (one privacy-minded author vs a broad institutional audience) rather than a strawman.
- **Tradeoffs:** A single-author blog gets no built-in traffic numbers: the author forgoes Quarto's one-line `google-analytics: G-xxxx` convenience and must self-host or hand-wire a snippet. No consent scaffolding means an author who DOES add a tracker via a head include must supply their own GDPR/ePrivacy banner; Taliesin will not generate one. The escape hatch is unenforced, so a head-include tracker can still defeat the `no-referrer`/offline guarantees at the author's discretion (privacy is default, not sandboxed). Recording a non-feature as a decision also risks reading as scope-avoidance rather than a stance, so the catalog entry must state the reasoning, not just the absence. (skeptic-found downside: Two supporting claims in the entry are overstated and would make the catalog naive if copied verbatim. (1) "Assets carry zero CDN references / zero-CDN offline guarantee" is FALSE for the live Preview: when a {mermaid} block is present the preview lazy-loads mermaid from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@11.4.1/... (render/mod.rs:859), which leaks the visitor IP to jsdelivr; only the static Build inlines the vendored copy for true zero-network, and QMD_FAST_MERMAID_URL exists precisely to redirect that CDN. And note no-referrer hides the URL, not the IP, so it does not neutralize that leak. So "zero-CDN" holds for Build/--bare, not as an unqualified load-bearing property. (2) The title promises "no telemetry," but only the site-tracker half is pinnable by the proposed corpus assertion; the CLI-makes-no-phone-home half rests solely on the kernel.rs:504 localhost-only read with no test lock, so nothing regression-guards a future crate quietly adding usage reporting. Minor: the proposed blanket assertion that a built page contains no gtag/google-analytics/cookieconsent substring would false-fail if the author ever uses the sanctioned head:/body-end: escape hatch to add a tracker inside a corpus doc; scope it to "no AUTO-injected tracker plus no-referrer meta present" instead. Also the "don't build a counter because it phones home" reasoning is muddled: a self-hosted counter reports to the author's own endpoint, not to Taliesin; the real reason is scope (static HTML, no backend, out of the browser-behavior wheelhouse).)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only is untouched (this removes output surface area, never adds a format). Single editing surface is untouched: analytics is a build-config concern and would never be a preview write-back; click-to-source, the block model (data-block-id/data-sourcepos), and the warm-server/warm-kernel path are unaffected. Markdown/Pandoc substrate is unaffected (no syntax change). It reinforces the clean-break, no-Quarto-tolerance decision: the Quarto keys stay flagged as unknown, not quietly accepted. Corpus-plus-roadmap is honored by pinning the stance with a no-tracker/`no-referrer` corpus assertion patterned on the existing no-RSS test.

## Books

### D122. Chapter-scope figure/table/equation numbering ('Figure 2.3'), not just theorems (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** In a book, cross-referenceable floats number as chapter.n: 'Figure 2.3', 'Table 4.1', 'Equation 3.2', and a cross-chapter `@fig-x` renders that full 'Figure 2.3' label.
- **Critique:** Taliesin already chapter-scopes theorems (`number-within: chapter`) but NOT figures/tables/equations/listings, so the same book numbers a theorem 'Theorem 2.3' while its figures are just 'Figure 1', 'Figure 2' restarting each chapter, and a cross-chapter figure reference shows no number at all. That inconsistency is more jarring than either rule applied uniformly.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's design is internally UNIFORM, and that uniformity is the whole value. In a book every cross-referenceable float (figure, table, equation, listing, and theorem-like environment) numbers chapter.n, and every cross-reference, same-chapter or cross-chapter, renders the full label ("Figure 2.3"). The number is navigation, not decoration: "2.3" tells the reader the target lives in Chapter 2, which is actionable in a paginated or printed book where you cannot click. It matches the LaTeX book/report convention readers of academic books already expect. Quarto never numbers one float class chapter.n and another flat, and never silently drops the number on a cross-chapter link, so there is no jarring seam anywhere. The entry is, in effect, asking Taliesin to adopt exactly this end-state. Taliesin today sits in the inverse partial state (theorems chapter.n within a page, nothing numbered cross-page for any float), so Quarto's choice is the consistent target the proposal is chasing.
- **Taliesin today:** `emit_figure` (figure.rs:70) emits a plain `Figure&nbsp;{num}` counted per page; there is no chapter prefix. `number-within: chapter` exists only for theorems (fm_extract.rs:189, render/mod.rs:1327). In the cross-page xref scan, figure/equation anchors are recorded with an EMPTY number (`String::new()`, xref.rs:109), so a cross-chapter `@fig-x` link carries the label but no '2.3'.
- **Proposed better:** Extend the existing theorem `number-within: chapter` machinery to figures, tables, equations and listings when the page is a book chapter: prefix the chapter number at emission (the chapter is already available via `render_document_with_includes_scoped` + `Site::chapter_for`), and record the composed number in the xref registry so cross-page `@fig-`/`@tbl-` render 'Figure 2.3'.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry in two and ship only the sound half now. (1) KEEP: chapter-prefix figure, table, equation, and listing captions AND same-page refs when chapter is Some, reusing the chapter already threaded into render_internal_impl plus the existing fig_count/eq_count/tbl_count/listing counters; websites (chapter None) stay flat. Pin with demo-book (methods.qmd is already chapter 2). This alone fixes the real within-chapter theorem-vs-figure inconsistency, which is the strongest part of the critique. (2) For cross-page, do NOT ship figures-only. Either defer it, or do it UNIFORMLY across every float kind including theorems, and source the numbers from the real per-page render (each page's own xref_registry already holds the true fig/eq/tbl/thm numbers) rather than a parallel non-rendering re-count in scan_page_anchors, which means a two-pass site build or caching each page's registry. When shipped, deliberately update corpus.rs:804-810 to assert cross-page refs now carry chapter.n for ALL float kinds, so the fix removes the inconsistency instead of moving it. Net: within-page is a clean keep; cross-page needs re-architecting to avoid drift and to stay uniform.
- **Tradeoffs:** The float counter must be seeded with the chapter number and the xref scan (scan_page_anchors) must compute float numbers, not just section numbers; a website (non-book) must keep flat numbering. More state threaded through figure emission, but it reuses a mechanism that already exists for theorems. (skeptic-found downside: The within-page half holds and is cheap, but the cross-page half is unsound as written and the drafter missed why. Cross-page numberlessness is NOT a figure-specific gap: corpus.rs:804-810 explicitly pins cross-page theorem refs to render just "Theorem" with no number, with the comment "(no number cross-page, consistent with figures/equations)." It is a deliberate, uniform, corpus-pinned contract. So making cross-page @fig-/@tbl- render "Figure 2.3" while leaving cross-page theorems numberless would CREATE a new figure-vs-theorem inconsistency, the exact jarring seam the entry claims to remove, just relocated to the cross-page axis. Second, the mechanism "make scan_page_anchors compute float numbers" is worse than it sounds: scan_page_anchors (xref.rs:77) is a lightweight NON-RENDERING source pass. Section numbers are cheap (count heading hashes), but float numbers require re-deriving figure-paragraph detection, mermaid figures, executed-cell tables, listings, and labelled display-equation detection from raw source, which will drift from the real render (the precise drift the section-scan comment at xref.rs:31-39 warns about). And scan_xref_targets runs BEFORE any page renders (site/mod.rs:280), so it cannot borrow the real per-page fig_count/eq_count/tbl_count without a two-pass build. The "tradeoffs" note ("must compute float numbers, not just section numbers") badly understates this duplication, the drift risk, and the corpus contract it silently rewrites.)
- **Invariant check:** Render-only; blocks keep data-block-id/data-sourcepos. HTML-only, no new output format. Consistent with the already-shipped theorem chapter-scoping. (possible violation flagged: No HARD invariant is broken: it is render-only, HTML-only, keeps Markdown syntax, and blocks retain data-block-id/data-sourcepos so click-to-source and block-level incremental are untouched (a warm server re-renders as today; renumbering already cascades downstream for plain figures, so no new behavior). The one discipline it steps on is corpus-plus-roadmap: as written it would flip a corpus-pinned assertion (corpus.rs:804-810, cross-page refs carry no number) without acknowledging that as a deliberate contract change and without shipping its own pinning corpus doc. That is a process concern, not a hard-invariant break.)

### D123. Infer book-ness from `chapters:` presence instead of `project: type: book` + a `book:` wrapper (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A Quarto book needs `project: type: book` AND a top-level `book:` mapping that nests title, author, chapters, part, appendices, references, downloads, cover-image, sidebar, page-navigation and search. Book config is a second namespace layered over the site's `_quarto.yml`, and the format lives under `format: html:`.
- **Critique:** Two levels of ceremony (`project:` + `book:` + `format: html:`) for what is, for a single author, one decision: 'this directory is a book'. Keys are split across three maps and it is easy to put a book key at the wrong level.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's three-namespace split is load-bearing precisely because Quarto is multi-format and multi-project-type, the two things Taliesin gives up by invariant. `project: type:` selects the render PIPELINE (default, website, book, manuscript), controlling pre/post-render, output layout, and cross-page numbering. `book:` holds FORMAT-INDEPENDENT structure (chapter/part/appendix ordering) that must feed the HTML book, the PDF/LaTeX book, the ePub, and the Docx from one source, so it cannot live under any single `format:`. `format: html:` holds only per-format options. The `book:` vs `website:` split also disambiguates two schemas that share one `_quarto.yml`. So the "second namespace" is not ceremony in Quarto's world: it is the seam that lets one chapter list drive four output formats and keeps structure orthogonal to presentation. A presence-based inference could not express "a book that also targets PDF with different chapter options," which Quarto must support. Taliesin is HTML-only and single-author, so every one of those justifications collapses and the inference is genuinely the right call. The critique is fair for Taliesin, not a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** Flat `_site.yml`: `is_book: !chapters.is_empty()` (config/mod.rs:159). Presence of `chapters:` alone makes the directory a book, no `type:` and no `book:` wrapper; every key (title, author, toc, chapters, mounts, nav, footer) sits at top level. Unknown keys are flagged against the closed `NATIVE_KEYS` set with a did-you-mean (config/mod.rs:206).
- **Proposed better:** Keep the flat inference and strict closed-set validation. It is the right call for a single-surface tool.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the flat `chapters:`-implies-book inference and the closed-set strict validation: it is correct for a single-author, HTML-only tool and beats Quarto's three-namespace ceremony, whose justification (multi-format, multi-project-type) does not exist in Taliesin. But close the one gap so the inference gets the same strict treatment as the rest of the config: when `chapters:` is present but not a non-empty sequence (empty, null, scalar, or mapping), emit a warning (e.g. "`chapters:` must be a non-empty list of pages; treating this as a website") instead of silently dropping book-ness. That preserves presence-based inference while removing the only silent-degradation path, keeping the entry honest about the clean-break strict-validation stance it cites. Also correct the tradeoffs text: parts are already nested inside `chapters:`, so only genuinely new top-level book keys (appendices, references, cover-image) would crowd the flat namespace, and if that ever happens a `book:` sub-map can be added without breaking the inference rule. Status stays taliesin-already-better; impact medium is right.
- **Tradeoffs:** As book-only features grow (a references chapter, a cover, part pages), their keys land at top level next to website keys, so the flat namespace gets busier and slightly less self-documenting than Quarto's isolated `book:` block. Strict validation plus a single author keeps that manageable; if it ever gets crowded, a `book:` sub-map could be added without breaking the inference rule. (skeptic-found downside: The inference itself is NOT strictly validated, which is a tension with the very stance the entry leans on. `is_book` is `!chapters.is_empty()` where `chapters` comes only from `value.get("chapters").and_then(|v| v.as_sequence())` (config/mod.rs:153-159), and validate_keys (line 206) only checks unknown KEYS, never a known key's shape. So a `chapters:` that is present but wrong-shaped (an empty list `chapters: []`, a null, a bare scalar `chapters: index.qmd` with a forgotten list, or a mapping typo) silently yields `is_book: false`: the author gets website chrome (navbar) instead of book chrome (reading column + drawer, `_book` output, chapter numbering) with NO diagnostic. Everywhere else Taliesin's config refuses silent fallback and emits did-you-mean; the single book-triggering decision is the one place it degrades silently. It is low-severity in practice (you see the wrong chrome instantly in live preview) but it is exactly the class of silent config failure the strict-validation brand exists to eliminate. Secondary miss: the tradeoffs' "part pages land at top level" example is factually wrong (parts are nested inside `chapters:` as `{ part:, chapters: }`, book.rs:39-56), so the flat-crowding worry is smaller than stated and applies only to future keys like appendices/references/cover-image.)
- **Invariant check:** Config-only; preserves the clean-break strict-validation stance (any unknown key flagged, no Quarto-tolerance tier). No effect on click-to-source, block model, or HTML-only output.

### D124. Give the book a numbering-depth cap instead of numbering every heading level unconditionally (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Books default to `number-sections: true` and expose `number-depth: N` to cap how deep numbering goes (e.g. number H1/H2 only, leave H3+ unnumbered), plus `number-sections: false` to turn it off wholesale.
- **Critique:** Numbering every level down to H5/H6 produces noisy labels like '2.4.3.2.1' in deep reference books, and there is no single knob to dial it back or off.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's design is coherent and is actually AHEAD of Taliesin on this exact point. For a book, numbered sections are the sensible default (readers expect "Chapter 2, Section 2.1"), so number-sections defaults on. Quarto then exposes ONE documented knob, number-depth: N, to cap how deep numbering goes, plus a single bool, number-sections: false, to disable it wholesale. Because Quarto computes both the printed heading number and the cross-reference number from one numbering pass, capping depth keeps @sec- refs consistent with printed labels for free. That is precisely the layered, discoverable configuration Taliesin currently lacks: Taliesin numbers every level unconditionally (counters is [u32;5] over h2..h6 with no cap in chapter.rs) and offers only a per-heading .unnumbered/{-} escape, with no book-level cap and no off switch. On this feature, Quarto's choice is the one to match, not beat. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `number_chapter_headings` (chapter.rs:10) numbers ALL heading levels in a numbered chapter unconditionally: `counters` is `[u32;5]` covering h2..h6 with no cap. The only escape is a per-heading `.unnumbered`/`{-}` (chapter_heading in book.rs:164). No book-level depth cap and no whole-book 'off' switch.
- **Proposed better:** Add a native `number-depth:` (and optionally `number-sections: false`) to `_site.yml`, threaded into `section_number` (chapter.rs:28) so deeper headings stop receiving a number. Because `section_number` is shared by both render-time numbering and the xref registry scan (xref.rs:102), one change point keeps the printed numbers and the cross-ref numbers in lockstep.
- **Revised recommendation:** Adopt number-depth: as the primary, low-risk change and thread the cap through BOTH call sites of section_number (chapter.rs render + xref.rs:103 scan) so printed and cross-ref numbers stay in lockstep. Define depth with H1 = level 1 (depth 1 = chapter number only, depth 2 = through N.1) to match Quarto, and leave counter advancement intact for capped levels so a capped H3 between two H2s does not misnumber the second H2. Verify @sec- to a now-capped heading falls back to a bare label, as unnumbered sections already do. Pin it with a corpus reference book that sets number-depth and asserts deep headings are unnumbered while shallow ones are numbered (corpus-plus-roadmap). Treat number-sections: false as a SEPARATE, larger item because it also touches chrome.rs sidebar labels and the Chapter/Section xref label; scope it explicitly (does it drop chapter numbers too, or only within-chapter sub-numbers?). Reframe the entry: Quarto is ahead here, so this is parity, not a Taliesin advantage; downgrade impact to low-medium since the per-heading .unnumbered escape already exists.
- **Tradeoffs:** One more config key; must decide whether depth also affects TOC/sidebar. Small surface, but it does add a mode where a heading has no number that a `@sec-` might still want to reference (fall back to a bare label, as unnumbered sections already do). (skeptic-found downside: Two costs the drafter understated. (1) "One change point" is optimistic: section_number (chapter.rs:28) is called from BOTH the render path (number_chapter_headings) AND the source scan that builds the xref registry (scan_page_anchors, xref.rs:103). The cap and its config value must be threaded into BOTH, or the printed heading loses its number while @sec- still shows a stale one, which is exactly the divergence the design claims to prevent. (2) number-sections: false is not a free add-on: it must also suppress the sidebar chapter-number labels (chrome.rs:332 reads e.number) and the "Chapter N" vs "Section" xref label logic (xref.rs:215), or the sidebar and cross-refs contradict the now-unnumbered headings. Minor third cost: NATIVE_KEYS (config/mod.rs:96) is a closed set and validate_keys warns on anything outside it, so the new keys must be added there plus the schema JSON, or the strict validator flags them.)
- **Invariant check:** Render-only surgery on block HTML; every block keeps its data-block-id and data-sourcepos, so click-to-source and incremental diff are untouched. HTML-only.

### D125. Project-wide cross-chapter references resolved by a lightweight source scan, with duplicate-label warnings (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Cross-references resolve across chapters and render 'Chapter 2' / 'Section 2.1'. Resolution rides Quarto's full multi-pass Pandoc render, and a duplicate label is handled quietly (first/last wins) rather than surfaced.
- **Critique:** Quarto's cross-book resolution is correct but expensive (it is part of the whole render) and it does not proactively warn you that two chapters defined the same `#sec-intro`, so a stale `@sec-intro` can silently point at the wrong chapter.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto resolves cross-references off the actual rendered Pandoc AST via its crossref filter, so a printed "Figure 2.3" / "Chapter 2" / "Section 2.1" is GUARANTEED to equal what the reader sees: the number and the render come from one pass, so they can never drift. That single path handles full generality Taliesin's scanner does not: chapter-scoped numbers for every crossref type (figures, tables, equations, listings, theorems), subfigure refs like @fig-panel-1, custom crossref definitions, and arbitrary label namespaces. The "expensive, it is part of the whole render" framing undersells the payoff: for a batch book build you render once regardless, so resolving during that render costs essentially nothing extra while eliminating an entire class of scanner-vs-renderer drift bugs. Taliesin's separate lightweight source scan spends effort to reintroduce exactly the drift surface Quarto's architecture rules out. On warnings, Pandoc DOES emit within-document "Duplicate identifier" warnings, so Quarto is silent only in the specific multi-file case where identifiers are per-chapter namespaces, which is a narrower gap than "does not proactively warn" implies.
- **Taliesin today:** `scan_xref_targets` (xref.rs:20) builds a project-wide anchor->{url, number} map with a lightweight source pass (includes resolved, NO second execution), first-definition-wins, and pushes 'duplicate cross-reference label ... defined on multiple pages (using ...)' once per clashing label (xref.rs:55). A whole-chapter `@sec-` renders 'Chapter N', a subsection keeps 'Section N.1' (xref.rs:215). Rewrites only `data-qmd-xref`-marked links, preserving each block's sourcepos.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. The no-second-execution scan and the explicit duplicate warning are both wins. The one adjacent gap is that figure numbers are empty here (see chapter-scoped-figure-numbering); fixing that entry closes the remaining difference from Quarto's 'Figure 2.3' cross-chapter labels.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the architecture (source-scan resolution with no second execution is genuinely right, and proactive cross-chapter duplicate warnings are a real Quarto-beating win), but revise the entry and harden two things before calling it "already-better". (1) Convert drift from a footnote into a guarded invariant: either derive the cross-ref registry from the SAME numbering pass the renderer runs (chapter.rs::section_number over rendered heading blocks) instead of a parallel line-scanner, or add a corpus regression that asserts, for a numbered book, that each anchor's scanned number equals its render-time number, and harden or explicitly document setext-heading and indented-code handling. (2) Wire the duplicate-label warning into --strict so the differentiator has teeth. (3) State the status honestly: better than Quarto on cost and on proactive cross-chapter duplicate detection, but currently BEHIND Quarto on cross-page numbered references for EVERY non-section crossref type (not just figures) until chapter-scoped numbering lands, and widen the referenced follow-up entry accordingly. The critique of Quarto is fair but should drop the unqualified "expensive" (that cost buys a drift-proof correctness guarantee) and scope "does not warn" to the multi-file case (Pandoc does warn on within-document duplicate identifiers).
- **Tradeoffs:** First-definition-wins is a heuristic and the duplicate warning is non-fatal by default (does not fail `--strict` unless wired to). The scan re-reads sources rather than reusing rendered blocks, so it can in principle drift from render; it mitigates this by sharing `section_number` and the renderer's own `parse_attrs`. (skeptic-found downside: Three things the "keep it" writeup missed. (1) Drift is not merely "in principle": scan_page_anchors is a hand-rolled parser that reimplements only a SUBSET of comrak block parsing (ATX headings, ```/~~~ fences, front matter). It misses setext (underline) headings entirely, treats a `#` line inside a 4-space indented code block as a real heading (trim_start strips the indent), and toggles `in_code` on any fence-length line. Any of these makes its section counters diverge from the render-time counters, so a cross-page ref can read "Section 2.4" while the target page shows "2.5", the exact stale-mispointing failure the entry pins on Quarto, reintroduced through a different door. (2) The numberless-cross-page gap is broader than "figure numbers are empty here": ONLY sec- gets a number, so every other type (tbl/eq/lst/thm/lem/cor/prp/def/exm/rem) renders cross-page as a bare label with no number. corpus.rs:806 literally pins `@thm-kl` cross-page as "Theorem" (no number), so on cross-page numbered references Taliesin is currently WORSE than Quarto's "Theorem 2.1"/"Figure 2.3" across the board, not just for figures. (3) The duplicate warning is non-fatal and not wired to --strict, so the "we warn where Quarto is silent" differentiator is soft: in a plain build the warning scrolls past and CI does not fail, so a stale @sec- can still ship.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure source scan plus link rewrite; every block keeps data-block-id/data-sourcepos so Alt-click-to-source still lands on the anchor line. HTML-only.

### D126. Offer one book-wide References chapter, not a separate reference list stapled to every chapter (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A book typically ends with a single References chapter (a `references.qmd` holding `# References` and a `::: {#refs}` div); Quarto aggregates the works cited across ALL chapters into that one consolidated bibliography.
- **Critique:** For a scholarly book, one consolidated bibliography at the end is the expected shape; scattering a per-chapter reference list under every chapter duplicates entries and gives no single place to find a citation.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** For a scholarly monograph or thesis, a single end-of-book References chapter is the academic convention, and Quarto's `#refs` + project-level citation processing delivers it correctly: every work is listed once (de-duplicated across chapters), the bibliography is one canonical, consistently-ordered list, and for a numeric style the in-text markers are numbered GLOBALLY across the whole book so `[37]` in chapter 5 unambiguously points to the same entry the back matter shows. This is not laziness; it is the only shape that keeps numeric citations coherent across a multi-chapter document, and Quarto pays the cost of a project-aware render to achieve it. Quarto is also not dogmatic: authors who want per-chapter reference lists (edited volumes, textbooks with per-chapter "Further Reading") can place a `#refs` div per chapter. So Quarto's default is the right default for the common book case, with an escape hatch for the rest.
- **Taliesin today:** `cite::process` (cite/render.rs:36) runs per page and appends a `qmd-references` section containing only THAT page's citations; a manual `# References` heading suppresses the auto one on the same page (cite/render.rs:71). There is no cross-page aggregation, so a Taliesin book gets N separate 'References' sections, one per chapter that cites anything, and no book-level References chapter.
- **Proposed better:** Add a book-level opt to harvest every chapter's citations (reusing the existing project-wide discovery pass) into a single References chapter: either an author-provided `references.tmd` chapter whose `# References` div is filled with the union of all cited keys, or an auto-appended final chapter. Keep the current per-chapter behavior available as an explicit mode for authors who want it.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but sharpen it from "medium/easy aggregation" to "a real, deliberately-scoped feature." (1) Correct the cost line: with IEEE numeric in-text citations, a single consolidated list forces GLOBAL cross-chapter numbering, making every chapter's citation markers downstream of all upstream chapters, a material hit to block-level incremental, not a slight one. (2) Add the missing implementation surface: a cross-page citation-link path (citations must gain a marker analogous to `data-qmd-xref` so `#ref-key` rewrites to `references.html#ref-key`), and an explicit preview-freshness decision mirroring the build-only `harvest_xref_numbers` (accept a possibly-stale consolidated chapter in live preview, refreshed on build). (3) Keep per-chapter as the DEFAULT (it matches the single-author technical-book case, preserves locality, and is legitimate for edited volumes/textbooks); make the consolidated chapter opt-in. (4) Decide the numbering contract deliberately: a strict single numeric bibliography should be an explicit build-oriented "monograph mode" that accepts the cascade; note that an author-date rendering (no in-text numbers) would let a consolidated list sidestep the numbering coupling entirely, but that is a separate citation-style feature, not free. (5) Pin with a corpus book that cites one key from at least two chapters and asserts: exactly one de-duplicated entry, an in-text link that resolves cross-page to the consolidated chapter, and correct numbering under the chosen contract.
- **Tradeoffs:** Requires collecting cited keys across pages during discovery and re-rendering the References chapter whenever ANY chapter's citation set changes, which slightly complicates the block-level incremental story (the references chapter is downstream of every chapter). The .bib parsing and CSL-lite formatting already exist, so the new work is aggregation and invalidation, not formatting. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal treats the cost as "aggregation and invalidation, not formatting," but it misses two load-bearing pieces. (1) Because Taliesin's in-text style is IEEE NUMERIC ([n]), a single consolidated list is only coherent under GLOBAL cross-chapter numbering: `[37]` in chapter 5 must equal the 37th unique work cited across the whole book. That makes every chapter's in-text citation markers downstream of every EARLIER chapter's citation set, so inserting one citation in chapter 1 renumbers markers in every later chapter. This is far more than "the references chapter is downstream of every chapter"; it is the whole book's citation blocks becoming downstream. (2) There is no cross-page citation-link mechanism today: citations emit a same-page `#ref-key` anchor only, with none of the `data-qmd-xref` marker/`resolve_cross_refs` machinery xrefs use. A consolidated chapter forces every in-text link to become `references.html#ref-key`, i.e. a new cross-page rewrite path plus a preview-freshness decision (the analogous cross-page-number harvest, `harvest_xref_numbers`, was deliberately made build-only so preview stays cheap).)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only; the consolidated chapter is just another page in the block model with normal data-block-id/data-sourcepos. Single editing surface preserved (author still edits the .tmd; the aggregation is a build/preview computation, never a write-back). (possible violation flagged: No hard break, but a real erosion of a load-bearing goal (block-level incremental updates + no per-edit startup cost). Under numeric in-text citations, a single consolidated list requires global numbering, which couples every chapter's citation-bearing blocks to all upstream chapters' cited-key sets; a citation edited early can cascade re-renders of markers throughout the book, exactly the locality the block model is meant to preserve. Keeping the consolidated chapter fresh in live preview also forces either a project-wide render pass in preview (violates the cheap-warm-preview principle the build-only `harvest_xref_numbers` was designed to protect) or a knowingly-stale preview. HTML-only, single read-only editing surface, Markdown syntax, and click-to-source are all preserved (the generated chapter carries empty sourcepos, consistent with today's auto References block).)

### D127. Add an opt-in single-page whole-book HTML build as the invariant-respecting answer to downloads (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A Quarto HTML book is always multi-page (one page per chapter); the 'whole book as one artifact' need is met by `downloads: [pdf, epub, docx]`, which renders parallel formats and shows download buttons in the sidebar.
- **Critique:** Multi-page-only HTML gives no artifact that supports find-in-page across the entire book, no single self-contained file to hand someone offline, and no obvious source document for a future print/PDF track. Quarto answers this only by leaving HTML and rendering PDF/ePub, which Taliesin has deliberately ruled out.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's multi-page-only HTML book is a deliberate, correct web-native default, not a limitation it papers over with `downloads`. Per-chapter pages give stable shareable/bookmarkable URLs, per-chapter analytics and SEO, browser-native back/forward, and incremental loading that keeps first paint fast and the DOM small on mobile. Crucially, Quarto treats "a whole book as one artifact" as a fundamentally DIFFERENT job from online reading, and picks formats purpose-built for it: ePub is reflowable and belongs on an e-reader shelf, PDF is fixed-layout, page-numbered, citable and prints predictably. A single giant self-contained HTML is a jack-of-two-trades: a worse online reader than multi-page (huge DOM, slow paint, janky mobile scroll) and a worse offline/print/handoff artifact than PDF/ePub (no pagination, unreliable browser print across page breaks, no e-reader format). Quarto also already answers "find across the whole book" with ranked full-text book search spanning all chapters, so the critique's "no find-in-page across the entire book" overstates the gap (native Ctrl-F over one page is the only thing actually missing, and Taliesin already has Cmd-K). The honest framing: Quarto's split (multi-page HTML for online + real paginated formats for offline) is cleaner engineering; Taliesin's single-page HTML is the best move available only because Taliesin chose the HTML-only constraint, not because it is a better artifact.
- **Taliesin today:** A book builds to `_book/` (output_dir default, site/mod.rs:312) as one `.html` per chapter via `build_one_page` (server/build.rs:686); multi-page is the only book output. Downloads (pdf/epub/docx) are intentionally absent: HTML is the only target and the print/PDF track is deferred, to be derived FROM the built HTML.
- **Proposed better:** Add an opt-in single-page build that concatenates all chapters into one scrollable self-contained HTML (chapter drawer links become in-page anchors). This is the HTML-native substitute for Quarto's downloads AND the natural source document for the deferred print/PDF track, so it advances two goals at once.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry, sharpened. It is genuinely the ONLY invariant-respecting answer to a real need (offline hand-off + a source document for the deferred print/PDF track), and no Taliesin invariant is broken: HTML-only holds, it is a read-only build artifact (no write-back), and click-to-source simply not being offered on a static export is fine. Refine the spec: (a) scope it BUILD-ONLY at first, never a second live preview view, because a single giant page strains the block-level incremental diff and warm-server goals and duplicate block-ids would break live-state preservation. (b) Implement by ASSEMBLING already-rendered per-chapter HTML (each chapter keeps its private kernel/cwd/freeze), not by re-parsing concatenated source, and strip per-page chrome into one book shell with a single running TOC. (c) Namespace BOTH data-block-id dedup AND heading autoslugs per chapter (e.g. chapter-slug prefix), and rewrite cross-chapter `@ref`/figure numbers to those namespaced in-page anchors. (d) State plainly that this is a heavy export artifact whose primary justification is the print/PDF source, not day-to-day reading, and lean on Cmd-K rather than claiming Ctrl-F parity. (e) Pin it with a dedicated corpus book document per corpus-plus-roadmap. Do not claim it beats multi-page for online reading; claim only that it closes the HTML-only gap Quarto fills with PDF/ePub.
- **Tradeoffs:** Block-id uniqueness must be namespaced across concatenated chapters (two chapters can hash-collide on identical blocks), page weight grows large, and the reading model differs from the per-chapter drawer view (decide whether preview offers it or only `build`). Cross-chapter `@ref` and figure numbers must resolve to in-page anchors rather than cross-file URLs. (skeptic-found downside: The entry under-specifies the two hardest parts. (1) It flags block-id namespacing but misses the sharper, human-facing collision: plain heading autoslugs dedup only per-document, so every chapter's `## Summary`/`## Introduction` wants `id="summary"`, and concatenation makes the drawer-turned-anchor links and plain `#heading` fragments land on the wrong chapter. `{#sec-}` labels are already project-unique (xref.rs warns), but bare headings are not, so per-chapter slug namespacing is mandatory and it changes the anchor URL contract versus the multi-page build. (2) It never addresses the execution model. Chapters today run on page-PRIVATE kernels with per-chapter cwd and `_freeze/<rel>.json` (build.rs:686). Re-parsing one concatenated source would leak kernel variable state across chapters and break relative `{{< include >}}`/asset paths, so the design is effectively forced to ASSEMBLE already-rendered per-page HTML (strip each page's navbar/footer/prev-next chrome, emit one book shell + one running TOC), not re-render concatenated markdown. That constraint is load-bearing and unstated. (3) Self-contained weight is worse than "large": inlining every image as a data URI plus KaTeX fonts plus all JS across a whole book can reach tens of MB with a massive DOM, which is exactly the mobile cost that justifies Quarto's multi-page default, so this artifact is honestly a heavy export, not a daily reading view.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, so it is squarely in scope and is explicitly the sanctioned path to a future print/PDF (rendered from this HTML, never a parallel format). Preview stays read-only; this is a build artifact, not a second edit surface.

### D128. Make a book's reading-progress affordances book-scoped (chapter N of M + whole-book percent + cross-chapter resume), not just the per-chapter prev/next and per-page progress bar that already ship (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A Quarto book renders automatic bottom-of-page previous/next chapter links as part of the book layout, and the left sidebar highlights the active chapter. That is the entire navigation story: there is no reading-progress bar, no "N min left" estimate, no resume-where-you-left-off, and nothing that tells the reader how far through the whole book they are. Tracking position across a multi-chapter linear read is left entirely to the reader; the sidebar's active-chapter highlight is spatial ("you are on this page"), not progress ("you are 40% through the book").
- **Critique:** For an artifact whose defining property is that it is read start to finish, Quarto gives no sense of overall progress. Prev/next only asserts "a next chapter exists," never "you are 3 of 12" or "40% through." The reader cannot see at a glance which chapters they have finished, and closing the tab mid-book loses their place completely (no resume of any kind).
