The book is treated as a bag of independently-navigable pages that happen to have neighbor links, not as one continuous read with a measurable position.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto keeps book navigation deliberately minimal and format-agnostic because a Quarto book is one source rendered to HTML AND PDF AND ePub: a live scroll-driven progress bar, a "% through the book", and a localStorage resume have no analog in print and would be HTML-only chrome Quarto refuses to special-case. The deeper, honest objection is metric integrity: scroll fraction is not reading fraction. A chapter that is 60% code, figures, and math reads "40% done" when the reader has finished all the prose, so Quarto declines to ship a progress number it cannot make truthful. Books are also frequently consumed non-linearly (cross-ref jumps, Cmd-K search, reference lookup), so a prominent "you are 40% through" assumes a cover-to-cover read many technical books never get and can actively mislead. Resume-where-you-left-off is per-browser, non-portable across devices, privacy-touchy, and silently wrong; Quarto defers to platform features (browser scroll restoration, bookmarks, Reader/Pocket) rather than reinventing a worse one. Its per-page static `reading-time: true` badge (which the critique omits) is the maximal honest, format-portable statement Quarto is willing to make.
- **Taliesin today:** Verified from code. A book ALREADY ships bottom-of-chapter prev/next: book_nav_html (crates/core/src/site/chrome.rs:322) emits a `<nav class="tali-postnav tali-book-postnav" aria-label="Pagination">` with a left ← link and a right → link, each labeled "N  Title", and mod.rs:392 wires `post_nav_html: if book { self.book_nav_html(...) } else { String::new() }`, so websites get an empty post-nav (confirming the deliberate website-vs-book prev/next split). The off-canvas chapter drawer (sidebar_html) marks the current chapter with `aria-current="page"` + `.tali-book-active` and shows chapter numbers. Separately, every non-deck page ships the reading-progress enhancer taliInitReadingProgress (assets/js/code-enhance/15-reading-progress.js): a top `.tali-readbar` bar tied to scroll fraction, a "~N min left · X% read" readout registered into the reader menu's Reading section, and a block-id-anchored resume pill. BUT all of that is per-PAGE: the word count comes from the current document's DOM, the fraction from this chapter's scrollHeight, and the resume position is keyed by `KEY = 'tali-pos:' + location.pathname`. The bar refills from zero at the top of each chapter, and nothing aggregates across the book. `book.chapters()` already holds the ordered chapter list and the current index, yet "chapter N of M", a whole-book percent, and a cross-chapter resume are never surfaced. So Taliesin already beats Quarto on both prev/next and on having any progress bar/resume at all; the unmade decision is whether that progress should be book-aware.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the per-chapter prev/next and per-page bar (they already beat Quarto) and add a book-scoped progress layer on top, entirely reader-side and read-only. (1) Server-side, free: surface "Chapter N of M" in the prev/next nav and/or drawer header from `book.chapters()` index + len, pure HTML, no JS, no source write. (2) Reader-side aggregation: when the enhancer detects a book (the existing `.tali-book-topbar` plus a one-time chapter manifest emitted from `book.chapters()` carrying each chapter's url + word count), it reads the per-chapter `tali-pos:<path>` entries it already writes and computes a whole-book percent (finished chapters + current fraction, word-count-weighted) shown beside the per-chapter bar. (3) Book-wide resume: on the book index/landing (and optionally the topbar), a "Resume · Chapter 5, 40% →" affordance rendered as a plain `<a href>` to that chapter's URL, derived from the newest reader-local position. (4) Drawer read-state: mark each drawer chapter visited/finished from the same reader-local store (a check or a thin ring) so the chapter list doubles as a progress map.
- **Revised recommendation:** Revise and stage it. (A) Ship item 1 ("Chapter N of M") first as the highest-value, genuinely-free, no-JS piece, but derive N and M from the NUMBERED-chapter sequence (`e.number` / count of numbered entries), not raw index into `chapters()`, so it matches the visible chapter numbers; for an unnumbered preface show "Preface" or nothing, never "Chapter 1 of M". (B) For the whole-book percent, do NOT ship a word-weighted number on top of the current scroll-fraction store. The honest v1 is a chapter-count progress ("3 of 12 chapters started" plus the current chapter's own bar), which needs no word counts, no manifest weights, and no second word-count implementation. Only pursue a weighted percent after fixing the existing per-page bug so remaining-time and read-percent use a consistent prose-read denominator. (C) Book-wide resume: add a timestamp to the stored value (`f|id|ts`), tolerate legacy 2-field entries, keep it a plain `<a href>` to the chapter URL so it navigates like click-to-source. (D) Drawer read-state: mark "visited" (on page load), not "finished" (undetectable), and explicitly handle single-screen chapters that never write a store entry. (E) Emit any manifest in page chrome (`data-qmd-src`, outside the block model) so it never enters the diff; prefer per-chapter self-report into localStorage over a server-side word counter to avoid a second, drift-prone implementation. (F) Hard scope floor, resisted in the corpus test: chapter N of M + one book progress figure + one resume link + visited rings, no streaks, timers, or sync. Pin on `corpus/demo-book/` with an assertion that the nav/manifest stays out of the block model.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adds reader-side state plus a new once-per-book manifest emission (chapter order + word counts). The whole-book percent is necessarily an estimate: word counts are per-page, so until the manifest carries them (or the reader has visited a chapter) the total length is approximate, making early-book percentages rough. Cross-chapter resume rides localStorage, so it is per-browser and silently absent in private windows or after a clear, acceptable because it is an affordance, not state of record, but it must degrade gracefully rather than error. The drawer read-state UI adds surface that has to stay legible on mobile, and this whole area invites scope creep (streaks, per-chapter timers, sync) that must be resisted; the floor is "chapter N of M + one book percent + one resume link." None of it changes what "done" means for a chapter's content, so it is purely additive polish. (skeptic-found downside: The direction is right but the drafter missed real flaws, verified against the code. (1) Dimensional mismatch: the whole-book percent is specced as "finished chapters + current fraction, word-count-weighted", but the per-chapter fraction stored in `tali-pos:<path>` is a SCROLL fraction from `frac()` (scrollY / (scrollHeight - innerHeight)), while the weights are word counts. Multiplying a scroll fraction by a word-count weight mixes two denominators and yields a misleading book percent. This inherits an existing bug: `updateReadout` already computes `left = totalMin * (1 - frac())`, so even the per-page "N min left" multiplies a prose word count by a scroll fraction. Building a book number on top of that compounds a metric that is already not honest for code/math-heavy chapters (exactly Quarto's objection). (2) "Chapter N of M" off-by-one: `book.chapters()` filters only `part.is_none() && !url.is_empty()`, so an unnumbered preface (index.qmd, `.unnumbered`) IS in that list with `number: None`. Deriving N from raw index would count the preface as "1 of M", disagreeing with the visible chapter numbers (prev/next `label()` already uses `e.number`, which skips prefaces), so the two numbers would clash. (3) "Finished/visited" is undetectable and short chapters are invisible: a single-screen chapter has `max <= 0`, so `frac()` returns 0 and NO store entry is ever written; and the `f <= 0.02` branch actively deletes an entry when the reader scrolls back to top. So the drawer read-state map (item 4) silently misses short chapters and cannot distinguish "read to end" from "left at 95%". (4) Book-wide resume needs recency the store does not carry: the value is `f.toFixed(3) + '|' + id` with no timestamp, so "resume the chapter you were most recently reading" cannot pick a winner among several visited chapters without a storage-format change (add a timestamp, tolerate old 2-field values). (5) The manifest is not "free": `book.chapters()` gives order + url but NO word count (BookEntry has none), so a word-weighted percent needs a server-side prose word counter that reproduces the client's `pre, code, .katex` exclusions or the two denominators diverge, a second implementation to keep in sync, or a per-chapter self-report into localStorage on first visit instead.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only: a progress bar plus a resume link, no new output target. Single editing surface preserved: everything derives from the live DOM and the reader's own localStorage and never writes the .tmd; the resume affordance is a plain `<a href>` to a chapter URL, so it NAVIGATES like click-to-source and never mutates source. Block model reused: resume is already `data-block-id`-anchored, so it survives block-level incremental re-render. Warm-server / no-per-edit-startup-cost untouched (client-side only, no extra kernel or build work). Corpus-plus-roadmap: pin it on the existing `corpus/demo-book/`, which becomes the regression net and arbiter of done. "Wider than Quarto" is satisfied in the intended sense, richer BROWSER behavior in a live HTML view (a book-scoped progress/resume UI), not a new format and not at the cost of any invariant.

### D129. Let a `part:` point at a .tmd page, not only a bare string label (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A part can be a bare label (`- part: 'Core'`) OR a part with its own intro page (`- part: intro.qmd` with a nested `chapters:` list), so the part gets a real landing page that sits at the part boundary in the reading flow and prev/next.
- **Critique:** Without part pages, there is no place to introduce a part ('Part II covers ...'); the author has to fake it with a spurious unnumbered chapter, which then clutters the chapter count and sidebar.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's `part: intro.qmd` collapses "section divider" and "section intro" into one node: the part header in the sidebar becomes the clickable landing page, so a reader gets a real "Part II: Foundations" opener with prose that sits exactly at the part boundary in prev/next, rendered as an unnumbered preface (no chapter number consumed, running count uninterrupted), with zero redundant rows. It is a strict superset of the bare-label form (a plain string still works), it is the natural home for part-level overview content, and it is one model that scales from a bare divider to a full section opener without the author inventing a fake chapter. The same source node also maps cleanly onto an eventual print/PDF part-page, so one construct serves both the live HTML view and a future derived print track. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `build_book` reads `part` only as a string: `map.get("part").and_then(|v| v.as_str())` (book.rs:50), producing a `BookEntry { part: Some(..), url: "" }` that renders as a non-navigable sidebar header (chrome.rs:294). Its inner `chapters:` are pushed as normal chapters, but the part itself has no page and is not a prev/next stop.
- **Proposed better:** Accept `part:` pointing at a `.tmd` file (detect a string ending in the source extension, or a `{ part:, file: }` shape) and, when present, render it as a page that occupies the part boundary in `chapters()` prev/next while still emitting the sidebar part header. Keep the bare-string form for label-only parts.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the feature but sharpen it. (a) Support ONLY the bare-string form `- part: page.tmd`, detected via strip_source_ext (ext.rs:31); it matches Quarto exactly and stays schema-valid. Drop the invented `{ part:, file: }` shape, or if retained, update schema.rs and its drift pin in the same commit. (b) Model it as a single BookEntry with part:Some(title from the page's H1 via chapter_heading) plus url/rel set; change `chapters()` from `part.is_none() && !url.is_empty()` to just `!url.is_empty()` (label-only parts keep an empty url so they stay excluded), make the sidebar part `<li>` a link and active-aware when it has a url, and let book_pages generate its Page. (c) Number it unnumbered like the index preface (no chapter number consumed; the running count is already continuous across parts, so numbering logic needs no other change). (d) Pin it by adding a part landing page to demo-book in the same change. Also correct the entry's critique: the fake-chapter workaround does NOT inflate the chapter count (unnumbered chapters are skipped in book.rs:120-125), so the real motivation is the inert part header plus presentational grouping, not count clutter.
- **Tradeoffs:** Needs a numbering decision for a part page (likely unnumbered, like the index preface), a clickable sidebar part header (currently a plain `<li>`), and another shape in `push_chapter_entry`/`build_book`. Modest added branching in an otherwise small module. (skeptic-found downside: Two costs the drafter missed. (1) Schema drift: the `{ part:, file: }` alternative shape violates the drift-locked _site.yml JSON Schema (schema.rs:141-149 pins the part-group with additionalProperties:false, required:[part], properties only part+chapters), so the editor `$schema` on-ramp would flag a valid config unless schema.rs is edited in lockstep. The bare string form `- part: intro.tmd` is BOTH schema-valid (part is `{type:string}`, a filename is a string, detected at runtime via strip_source_ext) AND byte-identical to Quarto's real syntax, so it is strictly better and the mapping shape should be dropped, not offered as an equal option. (2) Cost is undersold as `modest added branching`: a part-with-page is a third BookEntry state (a header that is ALSO a page), which breaks the header-XOR-page binary and forces a change to the load-bearing `chapters()` predicate (book.rs:27, `part.is_none() && !url.is_empty()`), because that predicate drives prev/next AND page generation in book_pages (book.rs:173) AND the chapter-not-found check (mod.rs:247); leave it unchanged and a part-page never gets a Page rendered and 404s. It also needs the sidebar `<li>` to become conditionally a link and active-state-aware (chrome.rs:293-314). Not huge, but it touches the model's core, not just build_book.)
- **Invariant check:** Config + render only; the part page is an ordinary Page in the block model with data-block-id/data-sourcepos. HTML-only, single editing surface preserved. (possible violation flagged: None of the fixed invariants is violated: HTML-only, read-only single editing surface, Markdown syntax, click-to-source (the part page is an ordinary Page carrying data-block-id/data-sourcepos), block-level incremental, and warm server are all preserved. One process caveat on corpus-plus-roadmap: the written tradeoffs omit the required corpus pin. demo-book currently exercises only a label-only part, so shipping this must extend demo-book (or add a corpus doc) with an actual part landing page in the same change, plus a schema.rs edit if the mapping form is kept.)

### D130. Whether a dedicated `cover-image:` earns its place when `index.tmd` + `hero:` already own the landing (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `cover-image:` sets a book cover shown on the HTML landing and embedded as the ePub cover.
- **Critique:** In HTML the cover is mostly a landing-page decoration, and a dedicated key partly duplicates what a normal landing page already does; the strongest reason to have it (ePub) is a format Taliesin does not target.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** cover-image is a single format-polymorphic declaration of intent ("this document's cover is X"). From one key Quarto emits the correct artifact in every target: an on-page image at the top of the HTML landing, the actual cover page in ePub, and a title-page image in PDF. A hand-placed Markdown image in index.qmd does NOT propagate to ePub/PDF, so cover-image is the only DRY, format-agnostic way to say "cover once, correct everywhere." It also decouples cover intent from presentation (the whole premise of Quarto's multi-format model), gives an accessible, theme-consistent cover slot via cover-image-alt instead of author-rolled HTML, and is a shared source of truth a parent listing or thumbnail can reuse. In a many-format tool it is not redundant with the landing page; it is the cross-format anchor a per-page index cannot be.
- **Taliesin today:** No `cover-image` key exists (absent from `NATIVE_KEYS`, config/mod.rs:96; grep finds none). The book landing is the unnumbered `index.tmd` preface (book.rs:120), which can already carry any image, a `hero:` block, or an `about:` block via the existing front-matter machinery.
- **Proposed better:** Likely leave it out: the HTML landing is already fully author-controlled through `index.tmd` + `hero:`, so a `cover-image:` mostly re-implements that. If a one-line cover is wanted for ergonomics, add a thin `cover-image:` that renders a standard banner atop the index page only (never as a separate format artifact). Owner's call.
- **Revised recommendation:** Leave cover-image out, and say so decisively rather than "owner's call." Do NOT add a thin cover-image clone: it collides with the existing image: (og/social-card) key and re-implements the author-controlled landing. Correct the entry's framing first, hero: has no image today, so the real fallbacks are an inline Markdown image (unstyled) or about:'s avatar. The load-bearing reason is that HTML-only removes cover-image's entire justification (a cross-format cover artifact), so nothing of substance is missing. If a themed wide-cover treatment is ever genuinely wanted, the better-for-Taliesin move is to add an optional image/background sub-key to the EXISTING hero: primitive (one landing-header primitive, DRY, no competing config key, composes cleanly since hero already replaces the title block), pinned by a corpus book-index doc, rather than importing a second overlapping cover-image key.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adding it introduces a second, overlapping way to set the landing visual (config key vs `index.tmd`/`hero:`), which cuts against the flat single-way-to-do-it schema. Not adding it means no terse one-key cover, but nothing is actually missing in HTML terms. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's premise that "index.tmd + hero: already own the landing visual" is overstated. hero: carries NO image (HERO_KEYS = eyebrow/headline/lead/actions only, frontmatter.rs:74); it is a text-plus-CTA band. The only landing image paths today are a raw Markdown image in the index body (unstyled, no themed cover framing) or about:'s round avatar (a jolla-style profile photo, not a wide cover banner), so there is a small genuine gap: no themed wide-cover primitive. Second, a new cover-image: would sit right beside the EXISTING image: key (the og/social-card image, NATIVE_KEYS at config/mod.rs:102), importing exactly Quarto's own image-vs-cover-image ambiguity into a schema that deliberately kept ONE image key. Third, placement is unclear and the entry hand-waves it: a site-wide _site.yml key that affects only the index page's body is an odd fit, and an index-only front-matter key barely beats writing the image inline. Fourth, a cover banner must compose with hero:/about:, which REPLACE the title block (mod.rs:747), so it is a real render-ordering change, not the "config/render only, block model preserved" the entry implies.)
- **Invariant check:** Any cover would be an HTML-landing element only; an ePub/print cover artifact would violate the HTML-only invariant and is out of scope. Config/render only, block model preserved. (possible violation flagged: None for the "leave it out" recommendation, and none for the guarded "HTML-landing banner only" variant, which respects HTML-only, the single read-only editing surface, Markdown syntax, click-to-source, and the block model. One flag the entry omits: corpus-plus-roadmap means IF any cover treatment were ever added it must ship pinned by a corpus book-index document; the entry does not name that gate. No hard invariant is broken.)

## Publishing and output artifacts

### D131. Committed _freeze/ so CI can build without a kernel vs. gitignored local-only cumulative-hash cache (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `freeze: true`/`auto` writes per-cell results into `_freeze/` that you COMMIT to the repo, so a deploy machine (Netlify build image, CI runner) with no R/Python installed restores the frozen outputs and never boots a kernel. Freeze is explicitly a deploy mechanism, not just a local cache.
- **Critique:** Quarto's per-cell freeze is fragile: kernel VARIABLE state is not captured, and `freeze: auto` can silently serve a stale result when it mis-decides a cell is unchanged. But the committed-artifact idea is real and load-bearing: it is what lets a docs site build on a runner with no scientific stack.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The critique commits a category error: it attacks Quarto's `freeze`/`_freeze/` using fragilities that actually belong to Quarto's separate per-cell `cache: true` (knitr / jupyter-cache) mechanism. Quarto's freeze is DOCUMENT-granular, not per-cell. `freeze: auto` re-renders the whole document whenever the .qmd source changes and reuses `_freeze/` otherwise, so it never mis-decides a single cell is unchanged, and it never needs to capture kernel variable state because it restores or recomputes an entire document at once (there is no resume-from-cell-N-with-variables scenario). The famous variable-state and downstream-stale-hit problems are `cache: true`'s, not freeze's. Freeze's one genuine blind spot, staleness when an external input the source hash cannot see (a CSV a cell reads, an imported module) changes, is inherent to any hash-of-source scheme and is shared verbatim by Taliesin's own cumulative hash, which likewise keys only on interpreter + code + upstream code and never on the data a cell reads. So on the very axis the entry claims superiority (stale hits), Quarto freeze and Taliesin's cache are equivalent. Committing `_freeze/` is a deliberate, documented deploy contract: it is precisely what lets a Netlify build image or CI runner with zero R/Python stack publish a fully computational site, the load-bearing capability the entry correctly credits. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `_freeze/<page>.json` is keyed by a cumulative content hash (this cell's code + all upstream same-language code + interpreter id), so a change anywhere upstream busts everything downstream with no stale hits. But `.gitignore` line 17 ignores `_freeze/`, framing it as a private local cache. Consequence: a fresh CI checkout has no cache, so it MUST have QMD_FAST_PYTHON/R available or cells silently fall back to source (build.rs logs 'kernel unavailable; code cells were emitted as source').
- **Proposed better:** Make freeze-as-deploy an explicit, opt-in mode. Document that committing `_freeze/` is supported, and add a `build --frozen` that trusts the cache and ERRORS on any cell missing from it (instead of the silent source-fallback), so a kernel-less CI build is honest: it either fully restores or fails loudly. Taliesin's cumulative-hash keying makes this safer than Quarto's per-cell version (no stale hits).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the load-bearing core, drop the overclaim, and name the redesign honestly. (1) The real, cheap win Taliesin genuinely lacks: today build.rs:995 only warns and emits cells as source when the kernel is unavailable. Add a `--frozen`/`--require-frozen` build mode that exits non-zero on any cell with no cached output, so a kernel-less CI build either fully restores or fails loudly. (2) Portability is a deliberate design decision, not a tweak: the frozen-deploy key must be interpreter-INDEPENDENT (code-chain only), with the producing interpreter recorded alongside for provenance. Frame it as an explicit 'these outputs are canonical' contract (the same bet Quarto freeze makes); do NOT weaken the live preview/build key, which keeps interpreter identity. (3) Do not flip the `.gitignore` default. Keep `_freeze/` ignored and support committing via an explicit opt-in, ideally a separate `freeze export`/portable-artifact path so the throwaway cache and the committed artifact are not the same directory (removes the dual-use footgun the drafter named); consider a per-cell on-disk layout if committing becomes first-class, since the current one-JSON-per-page format bloats history. (4) Reframe the catalog comparison to Quarto's FREEZE (document-granular deploy), not its cache: Taliesin's real edge is finer-grained code/interpreter invalidation on the LIVE path; concede the external-input-drift blind spot is shared and drop 'no stale hits, safer.' (5) Pin the capability with a corpus document plus a CI job that builds it with no kernel from committed frozen outputs, the regression net the whole claim rests on.
- **Tradeoffs:** Committing computed outputs (base64 PNGs inline) bloats the git history. Two use-modes for one directory (throwaway cache vs. committed artifact) needs clear docs so people don't accidentally commit a huge `_freeze/`. The `--frozen` error path needs the cumulative-hash to be stable across machines (it is content-based, but the interpreter id component must be normalized or it will miss across CI vs. laptop). (skeptic-found downside: The drafter treats interpreter-id portability as a minor normalization, but it is the crux and it inverts a correctness property. `interp_id` = `format!("{lang}::{}::{version}", program.display())` (exec.rs:929): absolute interpreter PATH plus full version string, deliberately in the key so a different or upgraded interpreter cannot serve another's outputs. A kernel-less CI machine has NO interpreter to identify: `interp_id` falls back to the bare program path with an empty version, which can never match a laptop-computed key, so a literal `--frozen` build would error on every single cell. Making it restore is therefore not normalizing an id; it requires a SECOND, interpreter-independent key for the frozen path that knowingly discards the safety the cumulative hash was built to provide (exactly the bet Quarto freeze makes, which the drafter is unaware they are re-deriving). Two further missed costs: (a) the on-disk format is one JSON blob per page holding every cell's output in an order-preserving array (freeze.rs OnDisk/Entry), so any single cell change rewrites the whole page file, giving coarser diffs and worse git bloat and merge conflicts than Quarto's per-cell `_freeze/` files; (b) inline base64 PNGs plus non-deterministic plot metadata make committed outputs churn in history even when visually identical. The 'safer than Quarto, no stale hits' line also overclaims: it compares Taliesin's freeze to Quarto's CACHE, not to Quarto's FREEZE, which shares the same external-input-drift blind spot.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only and single-surface untouched. This strengthens the 'no per-edit startup cost' goal into 'no kernel needed at deploy time' without weakening the warm-server preview path (which still runs cells live).

### D132. Own deployment (quarto publish gh-pages/netlify/connect) vs. produce a host-agnostic artifact and stop (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `quarto publish gh-pages|netlify|connect|confluence` re-renders locally, then pushes the output: for gh-pages it force-pushes the built site to a `gh-pages` branch via ghp-import; it stores provider/account state in `_publish.yml`, prompts for and caches API tokens, and manages the branch lifecycle. The tool itself performs the network deploy.
- **Critique:** Baking provider coupling and credentials into the renderer makes it stateful and account-aware: `_publish.yml` drifts, the force-push to a `gh-pages` branch fights a normal CI pipeline, and 'publish re-renders on my laptop' is exactly the non-reproducible path CI exists to kill. It also grows the tool's surface with Netlify/Connect/Confluence adapters that have nothing to do with rendering.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's publish command is not renderer bloat; it is the correct design for two user classes that a "produce a folder and stop" stance cannot serve. First, the no-CI solo author: `quarto publish gh-pages` genuinely is one command that creates the orphan gh-pages branch, writes .nojekyll, commits and pushes. The Actions equivalent requires enabling Pages in the repo UI, granting pages:write/id-token:write, and pinning action versions, which is objectively more steps for someone who just wants their site live. Second, and decisively, Quarto targets Posit Connect and Confluence, which are stateful application servers, not static hosts. There is no "rsync the folder" equivalent for them, so an in-tool API push is the only option and the adapter surface is intrinsic to serving those targets, not gratuitous. Quarto also already answers the reproducibility critique: it documents `--no-render` plus an official `quarto-actions/publish` GitHub Actions workflow, so "publish re-renders on my laptop" is a default you can opt out of, not a trap the tool forces. And `_publish.yml` stores the destination record (provider id and url), not the secret; cached tokens live in a separate account store, so "credentials committed to the repo" overstates the exposure. For a general multi-format tool serving many host types and many skill levels, owning publish is a defensible convenience-plus-necessity, not a category error.
- **Taliesin today:** No publish/deploy subcommand exists (main.rs dispatches only render/build/blocks/schema/check/init/serve/preview/dev/help). `build <dir>` writes a self-contained static `_site/` (or `_book/`); deploying it is left entirely to the user (git push, rsync, any static host). An `init` scaffolder already exists.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the tool a pure artifact producer (this stance is already the Unix-correct one). Instead of an interactive publish command that holds tokens, extend `taliesin init` with an optional CI recipe (`init --ci github`) that drops a GitHub Actions workflow running `taliesin build <dir> --strict` then `actions/deploy-pages`. The tool never holds credentials; the host's own OIDC/deploy step does. Optionally emit a one-line `taliesin build` + host hint in the build summary.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry's thesis (do NOT build a `quarto publish`; stay a pure host-agnostic artifact producer) because it is a real, sound Quarto divergence, but note that this half is already the shipped status quo, so it needs no code, only documentation as a deliberate stance. Drop `init --ci github` as the concrete recommendation for now; replace it with a docs page of copy-paste deploy recipes (gh-pages via Actions, rsync/scp, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify drop) plus an optional one-line "built _site/, deploy hint: <docs URL>" in the build summary. Documentation owns zero drift-carrying code, adds zero adapter surface to the binary, and creates no CI-install obligation. Gate any future CI generator behind a prerequisite that does not exist yet: a supported CI-install path (a published release binary plus a `setup-taliesin` action or a `cargo install`), and pin it with a golden-string test, not a corpus doc. Also fix the entry's `taliesin_current` nit: the `_book/` output name comes from `_site.yml` output-dir config, the hardcoded default is `_site`.
- **Tradeoffs:** Users who wanted a one-command `publish` still have a two-step setup the first time. A generated workflow can go stale against a provider's action versions. Choosing to generate only a GitHub recipe (not Netlify/Cloudflare/etc.) leaves other hosts to hand-write a two-line build+deploy step. (skeptic-found downside: The net-new `init --ci github` is broken on arrival. A generated workflow that runs `taliesin build` needs the taliesin binary ON the runner, but Taliesin ships no CI-installable path today (no crates.io release because the name collided, no apt/brew, no setup-action; the binary is built from source via a local launcher). Quarto had to ship `quarto-actions/setup` for exactly this reason. So the recipe fails on a fresh runner and silently creates a new maintenance obligation: publish and version a release binary or a setup action. Second, the generator does NOT deliver the one-command deploy it implies: `actions/deploy-pages` still requires the repo owner to toggle Settings > Pages > Source: GitHub Actions in the web UI and grant pages:write/id-token:write, a manual step no emitted file can perform, so first-time setup stays multi-step and is not clearly better than `quarto publish gh-pages`. Third, a generated `.github/workflows/*.yml` is exactly the "emit once, then drift" state the critique attacks in `_publish.yml`: it pins provider action versions and the output-dir name, then diverges from the tool silently, and a stale generated file fails quietly, which is worse than a publish adapter that fails loudly at publish time. Fourth, shipping `--ci github` invites `--ci gitlab/cloudflare/netlify`, relocating Quarto's adapter zoo into the scaffolder rather than eliminating it.)
- **Invariant check:** Respects HTML-only (produces the same static HTML tree), the single read-only surface (no source writes), and warm-server/incremental (unaffected; this is the cold `build` path). A CI recipe is deploy plumbing, not a new output format. (possible violation flagged: No hard invariant is broken. HTML-only holds (same static tree, no new format), the single read-only editing surface holds (`init` writes at scaffold time from the CLI, not from the preview, so the "preview never writes source" rule is intact), and warm-server/block-incremental are on the cold build path and unaffected. The one soft mismatch to flag: a generated CI YAML cannot be pinned by a corpus `.tmd` document rendering correctly, so `init --ci github` falls outside "the corpus is the arbiter of done." It would need a golden-string unit test plus a real green run on GitHub, which the `cargo test` corpus harness cannot provide.)

### D133. Truly self-contained single file (base64-inline everything) vs. inline framework assets but copy author images alongside (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `embed-resources: true` (the successor to the deprecated `self-contained: true`) base64-inlines EVERYTHING into one `.html`: CSS, JS, fonts, and every referenced image/media, producing a single file you can email with no sidecar directory.
- **Critique:** Inlining every asset bloats the file (base64 is roughly +33%), makes large images/video impractical, and still cannot inline genuinely cross-origin resources. It is one coarse switch: you either get a fat single file or a loose folder, with nothing in between.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's embed-resources sells one unambiguous, archival promise: a .html with ZERO external dependencies you can email, drop in a journal's supplementary-materials zip, or open in ten years offline. For that use case, inlining EVERYTHING (images included) is exactly correct: a half-measure that inlines the framework but leaves images as sidecars would defeat the entire 'email one file' guarantee, and 'is this actually self-contained?' would become ambiguous. The boolean switch is a feature, not a flaw: it is a single, predictable, well-documented contract rather than a matrix of 'which assets got inlined.' Quarto also inherits this from Pandoc's battle-tested asset resolver, which uniformly handles CSS url(), fonts, video/audio, srcset, and even fetches and inlines statically-linked REMOTE resources, so the critique's 'cannot inline cross-origin resources' is inaccurate (only assets loaded dynamically by client JS at runtime genuinely cannot be inlined). The +33% base64 bloat is a known, accepted cost of guaranteed portability, and Quarto separately offers resource-path / project _files output for the web-serving path, so it is not truly 'single file or nothing.' (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `build doc.qmd` inlines the framework's own assets (base CSS, client JS, KaTeX CSS with fonts as data URIs, the favicon SVG) and executed matplotlib figures come back as base64 data URIs from the kernel. But author `![](img.png)` images stay as `<img src="img.png">` and are COPIED next to the output by `copy_local_assets` (build.rs:211). So `build doc.qmd out.html` into another folder is portable-as-a-folder, not a single emailable file.
- **Proposed better:** Add an opt-in single-file mode (`--embed`, or front-matter `embed-resources: true`) that data-URI-inlines in-tree images/audio for the single-file target, while keeping copy-alongside as the sensible default. This makes the tradeoff a per-build choice (folder vs. one file) instead of forcing one.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep it opt-in via --embed (copy-alongside stays the default so the author's existing portable-folder workflow is untouched), but sharpen four things the draft skipped. (1) Before trusting the single-file guarantee, either EXTEND local_refs to cover srcset, <source>, poster, and CSS url(), or make --embed loudly warn on any reference it cannot inline (including remote and JS-loaded ones) so 'self-contained' never silently ships a broken asset; matching Quarto/Pandoc's uniform coverage is the actual bar here, not just reusing the src=/href= scanner. (2) Inline in-tree images and audio only, never video, with a per-asset size cap in addition to a total warn-above-N-MB. (3) Register the front-matter key in schema.rs (a familiar name like embed-resources is fine: that is Markdown/Pandoc familiarity, not Quarto identity). (4) Pin with a corpus doc that has a static author image and assert the built HTML has zero sidecar files and no un-inlined local refs. Also flag, secondarily, that Taliesin's own positional form build doc.qmd out.html already under-delivers on 'one file' by scattering images, so the doc for --embed should point users there.
- **Tradeoffs:** The inlined file is large; needs a size cap or a warn-above-N-MB guard to avoid a surprise 40 MB HTML. Adds a code path that must resolve+read+encode referenced assets (already have the local_refs scanner to build on). Cross-origin/remote images still cannot be inlined and must be flagged. (skeptic-found downside: The scanner is not a free foundation: local_refs matches only src=/href= (build.rs:1135), so it silently misses srcset, <picture>/<video>/<audio> <source>, poster=, and CSS url() references. For copy-alongside that is a tolerable gap (a missed asset just isn't copied); for INLINE it is a correctness trap: the resulting 'self-contained' file ships a broken image with no sidecar folder the recipient could ever repair, so the single-file promise silently lies. Inlining thus raises the scanner's correctness bar well above what copy-alongside needs. Secondary: data-URI images defeat browser lazy-loading and per-asset caching and force the whole HTML to parse before first paint, so this output is strictly an archival/email path, never the web-serving path (fine, because it is opt-in). Video must stay excluded (base64 kills seeking/streaming); audio and even large PNGs need a PER-ASSET cap, not only the global warn-above-N-MB the drafter noted.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (still one HTML file, no new format). Read-only preview and click-to-source untouched (this is the build path). Data-URI inlining is exactly what Taliesin already does for KaTeX/figures, so it is inside the existing model. (possible violation flagged: No invariant is broken (HTML-only, read-only preview, click-to-source, block-level, warm server, Markdown syntax all untouched; it is a build-path flag). But two invariants impose unmentioned obligations: (1) the clean-break STRICT front-matter validator flags any unknown key, so an embed-resources: front-matter key must be registered in schema.rs or every doc using it fails validation; (2) corpus-plus-roadmap requires a pinning corpus doc containing a real author image whose build asserts zero sidecar files. Neither is in the proposal.)

### D134. Auto-build mounted sub-projects into the deploy vs. warn and make the author run N extra builds (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto has no direct mounts concept; the closest is a single project rendering all its subdirectories. There is no per-subproject nested-build story.
- **Critique:** This is a self-imposed Taliesin gap, not a Quarto one. `preview` serves mounted sub-projects (the docs book at `/docs/guide`) live and complete, so a previewed site looks fully deployable, but `build <dir>` skips every mount and only prints a per-mount warning with a manual `taliesin build <path> --out <out>/<at>` command. An author who trusts the preview ships a site whose `/docs/...` links 404.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto never has this footgun precisely because it has no mounts: a Quarto project is a single tree, and one `quarto render` builds every subdirectory into one output, so preview and render see the same page set by construction. Mounts are a NEW Taliesin capability (URL-space composition of independent projects) that Quarto lacks, and the preview/build divergence is the cost of inventing it. The current warn-only choice is the conservative form of that capability, and it is defensible: a mount is by design a separate project that may be un-rebuildable in the parent's build host (a different or absent Jupyter kernel, a different toolchain version, a project the author does not own, or one that is independently deployed to its own domain). Warning and handing over the exact `build ... --out <out>/<at>` command keeps `build` fast, hermetic, and structurally unable to fail because of a sub-project outside the author's control, instead of coupling the whole deploy's success to every mount.
- **Taliesin today:** In build_site_async, `mount_warnings` emits one 'mount is preview-only and not in the static build (its links will 404)' line per `mounts:` entry, each with the exact secondary build command. The code comment states 'Auto-building mounts is a deferred follow-up.' The machinery to recurse (build_site_async itself) already exists.
- **Proposed better:** During the site build, recursively build each `mounts:` entry into `<out>/<at>/` (reuse build_site_async with the mount's root and an `--out` of the subdirectory), so the deployed tree matches what `preview` showed. Keep the current warning only as a fallback when a mount fails to build.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the direction (close the preview/build 404 gap so the static artifact matches the read-only preview) but ship it hardened: (1) Auto-build mounts the author can build, with a per-mount opt-out (e.g. `build: false`) for separately-deployed sub-projects, so the deploy topology stays the author's choice; the warn-with-command survives for opt-out mounts and for build failures. (2) Add cycle/nesting safety: track visited roots, refuse a mount path that resolves to the parent root, and build each mount's own pages without transitively recursing into the mount's own mounts (or detect and refuse a cycle). (3) Aggregate problems and ExitCode upward: under `--strict` a broken mount FAILS the parent build (do not downgrade to a warning), and reuse the parent's concurrency/kernel budget instead of letting each nested build spin its own. (4) Extend link validation to cross-mount climbing links now that they are load-bearing in the deploy, or at minimum warn when a `../<other-at>/…` link has no on-disk target after all mounts are built, so parity is real rather than page-local. (5) Pin it with a corpus site that mounts a small sub-project and asserts the mounted HTML plus a cross-mount link land in `_site/`.
- **Tradeoffs:** Recursive builds multiply build time and kernel usage for a large mounted book; needs the same memory/concurrency budget accounting the top-level build uses. A mount that shares a `_freeze/` or output path with the parent must stay isolated (per-mount output dir). Cross-mount link rewriting (relative `../guide/x.html`) must resolve correctly in the nested output, which the preview already handles. (skeptic-found downside: Three misses. (1) The biggest: auto-building makes cross-mount relative `../<other-at>/x.html` links load-bearing in the DEPLOY, but nothing validates them. Link-validation deliberately skips climbing `../` links as "unresolvable offline" (site/mod.rs:505-509), so a mis-aimed cross-mount link builds green and 404s in the deploy just as quietly as today, only now the author trusts the artifact more. The docs case (guide + internals as siblings under /docs/) resolves by construction, but that is layout luck, not a guarantee the build enforces. (2) Recursion/cycle safety is unhandled: build_site_async re-discovers each Site including ITS OWN `mounts:`, so naive reuse can infinite-loop on a mount that declares mounts, or rebuild the parent if a mount path resolves back to root; needs a visited-roots set and a refuse-self-mount guard. (3) The proposal inverts `--strict` semantics: it says "keep the warning only as a fallback when a mount fails to build," which downgrades a hard failure to a soft warning, but under `--strict` a broken mount book must FAIL the parent build. The mount's problem count and ExitCode need to aggregate up, and the nested build must reuse the parent's concurrency/kernel budget rather than spin its own and blow past it.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only (mounts are just more HTML pages). Preview/build parity is the point: it makes the static artifact match the read-only preview instead of diverging from it. No new write path to source. (possible violation flagged: None strictly. HTML-only holds (mounts are HTML pages), no source write path is added, and click-to-source, block-level diff, and warm-server are untouched. One process obligation, not a violation: corpus-plus-roadmap requires the change ship pinned by a corpus site that mounts a sub-project and asserts the mounted pages (and a cross-mount link) land in the build output. Today the only mounted site lives in `site/`, not `corpus/`, and the corpus sites carry empty mounts, so this capability is currently unpinned by the regression net and must be pinned in the same change.)

### D135. Generate sitemap.xml / robots.txt / RSS feed for a deployed site vs. emit none (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** With `site-url` set, Quarto generates `sitemap.xml` (and honors robots), and for listing pages it can generate an RSS/Atom feed (`feed: true`) so readers subscribe and search engines crawl.
- **Critique:** For a public blog or docs site (in Taliesin's scope: 'multi-page sites'), no sitemap means weaker crawl/discovery and no RSS means readers cannot subscribe to a blog. Taliesin already sets `url:` and emits canonical/og:url from it (site/meta.rs), so it has the one input a sitemap needs, but produces no crawl/subscribe artifacts. It even actively DROPS a `.xml` footer link because 'this build generates no RSS feed' (chrome.rs:170), which is a visible papered-over gap.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general publishing system that must serve thousands of public blogs and docs sites it will never see, so it cannot assume the solo-author-with-no-subscribers case. Sitemap and RSS are the open web's decentralized discovery and subscribe primitives, and Quarto derives both almost for free from metadata it already holds: sitemap.xml from `site-url` plus the page set, an Atom/RSS feed from the listing's dates/titles/descriptions/permalinks it already computed for the cards. Emitting them by default is exactly the derived-artifact win a publishing tool should give: crawlers get an authoritative URL list, readers get a subscribe endpoint, and the author writes nothing. For a tool whose job is to get people published, discovery and subscription are table stakes, not scope creep, and defaulting them on is the correct posture for an audience whose needs Quarto cannot enumerate. (Two nits in the entry, not in Quarto's favor or against it: Quarto does NOT auto-generate robots.txt, it generates sitemap.xml, so "honors robots" overstates Quarto; and the entry calls Taliesin's dropped `.xml` link a "papered-over gap" when it is the deliberate residue of a removal, which is unfair to Taliesin, not to Quarto.)
- **Taliesin today:** No sitemap.xml, no robots.txt, no RSS/Atom feed are generated. `url:` in `_site.yml` feeds only the per-page og:url/canonical/og:image absolute tags (site/meta.rs). The footer explicitly discards a local `.xml` link because there is no feed to point at.
- **Proposed better:** When `url:` is set, emit `sitemap.xml` (all built page URLs) and a minimal `robots.txt` pointing at it, alongside the search-index.js/404.html the build already writes. For listing/blog pages, generate an RSS or Atom feed and stop dropping the footer `.xml` link. These are derived deploy-metadata artifacts, computed from the already-built HTML.
- **Revised recommendation:** Split the entry and downgrade it from "proposed-change" to "already-planned, partly non-goal." KEEP the sitemap/robots recommendation but reframe it as adopting the existing `build-seo-completeness` roadmap item (Wave 5, low priority): when `url:` is set, emit sitemap.xml over the built non-draft page set, a minimal robots.txt pointing at it, and the Article/WebSite JSON-LD the roadmap already specs (the entry drops JSON-LD and should not), reusing the nav `_`/`.`/`draft:` exclusion, all as build-time metadata files. Note explicitly that Taliesin already agrees this is invariant-safe and merely deprioritized it, so the catalog value is "planned, not missing." DROP the RSS/Atom half entirely: it was built and deliberately removed, it is a documented non-goal for a solo author, and it silently re-imports the deleted post/category machinery. Also correct two framings: stop calling the dropped `.xml` footer link a "papered-over gap" (it is the correct residue of a deliberate decision, not a bug), and stop implying Quarto auto-generates robots.txt (it does not; robots.txt would be a small step past Quarto, not parity).
- **Tradeoffs:** Judgment call on the invariant: XML is not HTML. But a sitemap/feed is site plumbing (like the 404.html and search-index.js already emitted), not an alternate READING format competing with HTML, so it is arguably inside 'HTML is the only output target'. If the owner reads the invariant strictly, RSS could be deferred while sitemap/robots (pure URL lists) ship first. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal bundles two asks with opposite standing and the drafter missed both seams. (1) Sitemap.xml + robots.txt is NOT a novel change: it is already specced as `build-seo-completeness` (BEYOND-QUARTO.md:308-312, backlog.md:90-91,321), tagged low/small with no invariant concern, and the roadmap version also emits Article/WebSite JSON-LD, which the proposal omits, so the roadmap is strictly more complete than the entry. Framing it as a fresh "proposed-change" understates that Taliesin already agrees and just deprioritized it. (2) RSS is not a free derived artifact. It was built (commit 3c5e497) then deliberately ripped out end-to-end (a8e5e7f) together with the whole `posts/` special directory, category/tag archive pages, and the `is_post` field, precisely to make every page uniform. A correct feed needs a defined post-set, stable GUIDs, pubDate, author, and body/summary encoding, so "generate an RSS or Atom feed" quietly re-imports the deleted blog/post distinction (`og:type=article` now keys only on `date.is_some()`, there is no "post" anymore). The old feed.rs also carried audited XML-escaping bugs (AUDITS.md:215, invalid feed on C0 control chars), so re-adding it reopens that surface. And for a solo English author with no subscriber base, the feed is dead plumbing, which is exactly why it is a documented non-goal.)
- **Invariant check:** Flag: sitemap.xml/RSS are XML, so this is the one entry that brushes the HTML-only line. It respects it in spirit: the reader still consumes HTML; these are crawler/subscriber metadata derived from the build, not a parallel document format like PDF/ePub. No source writes, no preview mutation. (possible violation flagged: The RSS half violates corpus-plus-roadmap governance: "RSS / categories" is an EXPLICIT non-goal in BEYOND-QUARTO.md:464 ("deliberate non-gaps for a solo English author with this corpus; not to be re-filed as breadth"), and the entry re-files it as breadth without engaging the recorded removal decision, which BEYOND-QUARTO.md:465 specifically warns against. It also arguably brushes HTML-only more than the entry admits, because a feed's description/content:encoded carries the article body, which a feed reader renders as an alternate reading surface, unlike a sitemap URL list. The sitemap.xml + robots.txt + JSON-LD half violates NOTHING: Taliesin's own roadmap classifies it "build-time only; HTML-only," the reader still consumes HTML, and there is no source write or preview mutation.)

### D136. Support a base-path for subdirectory deploys (project pages at user.github.io/repo/) vs. rely on relative links and break root-absolute ones (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** medium, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto emits relative links that work under a subpath and uses `site-url` for sitemap/canonical; deploying under `/repo/` generally works because links are relative.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's per-page links are relative-with-depth (`../x.html`) and DO survive a subdirectory deploy, but two things break: the generated 404.html uses ROOT-ABSOLUTE `/` links (site/mod.rs:594 'every link must be root-absolute'), and any author-written site-absolute href (`/blog.qmd`) is emitted as `/blog.html` (links.rs resolve_href). Deployed at `user.github.io/repo/`, the 404 'back home' link and every `/absolute` link point above the project root and 404. There is no `path-prefix`/base config to correct this.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto deliberately avoids a base-path/path-prefix key by making the entire website relative-linked, so the built artifact is location-independent: it works at the domain root, under any subdirectory (user.github.io/repo/), from file://, and offline, with zero routing config to forget or double-prefix. A base-path key is a classic footgun (double-prefixing, preview-vs-build divergence, stale value after a repo rename). Quarto confines absolute URLs to the two artifacts that genuinely require them, sitemap.xml and rel=canonical, and derives those from site-url, which already carries the full path, so even those are correct under a subpath. In effect Quarto makes the base-path problem vanish for navigation and quarantines it to SEO metadata where an absolute URL is mandatory anyway. Taliesin already adopts the good half of this (depth-relative chrome, cards, brand via `up`); the only gap is that two link paths escaped the relative discipline (author `/absolute` hrefs and the 404), not that Quarto solved something Taliesin cannot.
- **Taliesin today:** No base-path/path-prefix key. resolve_href keeps site-absolute hrefs rooted at `/`; render_404_page hard-codes root-absolute links (correct only when the site is at the domain root). Relative in-tree links work at any depth.
- **Proposed better:** Either derive a base path from the `url:` path component (e.g. `https://x.github.io/repo/` -> prefix `/repo`) and prepend it to root-absolute links + the 404, or add an explicit `base-path:` config, OR (cheapest) document 'deploy at the domain root, or use only relative links and a custom 404.qmd'. Given the single-author scope, documenting the root-deploy assumption plus a relative-404 option may beat adding a config key.
- **Revised recommendation:** Revise, do not add a `base-path:` key (redundant with `url:` and a second footgun). Ship a two-part fix that stays true to the all-relative discipline Quarto is right about. (1) Author intra-site `/absolute` links: resolve them to depth-relative at build in resolve_href/rewrite_one_href (the page depth `up` is already known), so they become location-independent like the rest of the chrome. Guard: only rewrite paths that resolve to a known in-site page; leave an unknown `/absolute` path untouched so a deliberate domain-absolute link to a non-Taliesin resource (`/other-app/`) is not wrongly pulled into the site subtree. (2) The 404, the one page that genuinely needs a base: derive its home-link base from the existing `url:` path component (already the canonical base in meta.rs); when `url:` is unset, keep `/` and document the root-deploy default. Document that the 404 home link is the single spot where preview-at-localhost-root may differ from a subpath production deploy, or optionally have preview serve under the derived prefix to preserve parity. Pin with a corpus site whose `url:` sets a `/repo/` subpath and assert: no root-absolute intra-site link leaks into any built page, and the 404 home base equals the url path (corpus-plus-roadmap requirement, not optional).
- **Tradeoffs:** A base-path key is another config surface and another thing to get wrong (double-prefixing, preview vs. build divergence). Deriving from `url:` couples two concerns. Doing nothing leaves project-pages deploys with a broken 404 and broken author `/absolute` links, which is a real papered-over case today. (skeptic-found downside: Three misses. (1) Option 3 (document root-deploy + author a relative custom 404.qmd) does NOT actually close the 404 hole it names: a static host serves the same 404.html for a wrong URL at arbitrary depth while the browser keeps the bad URL in the address bar, so relative links resolve against the wrong directory and root-absolute `/` points above /repo. A hand-authored 404 hits the identical wall unless it is given the base path, so the cheapest option leaves the exact case it flags still broken. (2) The 'deriving from url couples two concerns' worry is overstated: meta.rs:20-24 ALREADY uses the full `url:` (path component included) as the canonical/og:url base, so the url path is already the de-facto base path. Deriving routing from it is consistent with existing behavior, not a new coupling, which strengthens the derive-from-url option the drafter treated as merely tied. (3) A base path applied at build time silently breaks the documented 'the 404 preview matches production' guarantee (mod.rs:603): in preview served at localhost root, a `/repo`-prefixed home link 404s, so parity flips (preview breaks while production works). The drafter names preview/build divergence generically but not that it violates this stated invariant of the 404 page specifically.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only and read-only surface untouched. This is purely about link correctness in the built artifact; no new output format, no write-back.

### D137. Derive per-page asset inclusion from the typed block model, not from a substring scan of the emitted HTML string (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto builds on Pandoc and attaches a fixed set of format dependencies to `format: html`: on the default (Bootstrap) theme every page ships the compiled Bootstrap CSS bundle plus quarto.js, popper, tippy, anchor.js and clipboard.js, whether or not the page uses tooltips, anchors or code-copy. On top of that baseline Quarto does some conditional injection, but through several different mechanisms: MathJax/KaTeX is added only when the Pandoc AST contains math (and MathJax loads from a CDN by default), the mermaid runtime is added by a diagram post-process only when a mermaid cell is present, and code-copy/code-tools/line-numbers are toggled by config flags. So Quarto's gating is real but coarse (a large Bootstrap + quarto.js floor ships regardless), scattered across Lua filters, format definitions, HTML post-processors and config so no single place states a page's exact asset set, and several defaults reach a CDN rather than being inlined offline.
- **Critique:** The gate is stringly-typed and decoupled from the block model that is otherwise Taliesin's single source of truth (data-block-id/data-sourcepos key off it per CLAUDE.md). Because it scans the emitted HTML for literal class-name substrings, it produces verified false positives: a page that merely MENTIONS a marker in prose or a code sample ships that feature's asset even though nothing on the page uses it. The worst case is measured, not hypothetical: 512 KB of d3+Plot inlined into a build with no `{js}` cell because a JS code block contained the text `application/qmd-js`. This is exactly the shape of Taliesin's own dogfooded docs book, which documents `{js}` cells, `.panel-tabset` and `.code-walkthrough` and so trips the very gates it describes. The gate family is also inconsistent (quoted markers get accidental escape protection, bare ones do not) and hand-maintained: every new browser feature on the roadmap must remember to add a marker plus a gate line, and a forgotten arm silently either always-ships (weight regression) or never-ships (feature dead in Build) with nothing in the type system to catch it.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's floor is a deliberate consequence of being a batteries-included, multi-format system, not laziness. (1) Shipping a full design system means any page gets consistent, themeable, responsive, accessible chrome (grid, typography, dark toggle, TOC, footnote popovers, margin content) with zero per-feature opt-in, across thousands of user themes and 40-plus output targets where per-page byte-optimality is explicitly not the goal; predictable uniform output across a huge matrix is. (2) The strongest point: on a static multi-page site served over HTTP, Bootstrap and quarto.js are ONE shared file the browser caches once and reuses across every page, so the floor is amortized site-wide. Taliesin's inline-everything model has no cross-page cache: its own Build inlines d3+Plot (about 487 KB, verified) into every js-using page rather than sharing one cached asset, so over a large site Quarto's shared bundle can win in aggregate even though it looks heavier per isolated page. (3) The CDN defaults (MathJax, mermaid) are a real tradeoff (smaller output, always-current library) with embed-resources as the offline opt-in, so Quarto serves both audiences. (4) For conditional injection Quarto actually exposes a typed quarto.doc.add_html_dependency registration API that dedupes and injects at finalize, so its extension gating is structured, not a substring scan. The critique is right that the baseline floor is coarse and some defaults reach a CDN, but Quarto's choice is coherent given its scope.
- **Taliesin today:** One function, `code_scripts_for(body, mode)` (crates/core/src/render/mod.rs:888), plus sibling gates `ship_katex` (page.rs:259, deck.rs:117), `has_js_cells`->`js_cell_head` (mod.rs:974, wired at page.rs:126), and the Build-only inline of the 2.5 MB mermaid lib (mod.rs:899), decide per page which script/style ships. `code-enhance.js` (copy/lightbox/reader-menu/skip-link/keyboard) rides every non-bare page; each feature asset (KaTeX CSS, d3+Plot, mermaid lib, walkthrough, tabset, scrolly, qmd-js) ships only when a marker is present. Detection is a substring scan of the ALREADY-EMITTED HTML body: `body.contains("class=\"mermaid\"")`, `contains("application/qmd-js")`, `contains("panel-tabset")`, `contains("code-walkthrough")`, `contains("tali-scrolly")`, `contains("class=\"katex")`. Mode is asymmetric: Preview opens every light-enhancer gate unconditionally (an edit can add any construct to a warm session), Build gates strictly on the marker. Everything is inlined offline (mermaid inlined in Build); Bare ships zero scripts. Verified: a static Build of a doc whose only feature is a JS CODE SAMPLE containing the literal `application/qmd-js` ships 512,687 extra bytes (d3 280 KB + Observable Plot 207 KB + enhancer) with zero real cells; clean build 126,176 B vs 638,863 B. Quoted markers (`class="mermaid"`, `class="katex`) are incidentally shielded by quote-escaping in highlighted code; the bare markers are not.
- **Proposed better:** Accumulate a typed `FeatureSet` (bitflags/enum) during block emission: the mermaid emitter, the `{js}` cell emitter, the `.panel-tabset`/`.code-walkthrough`/`.tali-scrolly` div emitters and the math emitter each set their own flag as they run, so the flag comes from the construct that was actually rendered, not from text that happens to appear. Store it on `RenderedDoc.features` and have `code_scripts_for`/`js_cell_head`/`ship_katex` consume the set instead of `body.contains(...)`. Back it with a single registry mapping each `Feature` variant to `{ head_asset, body_script, open_in_preview }` so an exhaustive `match` (and one corpus test) makes a forgotten feature a compile error rather than a silent weight or coverage bug. This keeps the headline win Taliesin already has over Quarto (a tiny idle floor: one inlined enhancer + base CSS, verified 126 KB, versus Quarto's Bootstrap+quarto.js baseline; offline-total; one legible decision point) while removing the false positives and the stringly-typed coupling. The deliberate "Preview opens all light gates" policy can stay as a per-feature `open_in_preview` flag rather than an artifact of scanning.
- **Revised recommendation:** Reframe the entry from replace-the-scan to two layered moves. (1) Immediate correctness patch, no refactor: tighten the four bare markers (application/qmd-js, panel-tabset, code-walkthrough, tali-scrolly) to match with their surrounding quotes/angle brackets so highlighted code samples stop tripping them, mirroring the escape-shielding that already protects the mermaid/katex gates. Pin it with the mention-but-don't-use corpus doc the entry proposes; this is the highest-value part and I confirmed the current test build_mode_content_gates_separate_enhancers uses only innocuous prose and therefore does NOT cover the false positive. (2) Optional robustness layer: add the typed FeatureSet for the compile-time exhaustiveness win (a forgotten first-party feature becomes a compile error), but scope it honestly: it touches every emitter plus the separate deck path (deck.rs currently ships light enhancers unconditionally even in build), and it MUST NOT under-ship for raw-HTML / {{< include >}} / include-* / extension-injected DOM, so keep a final-HTML scan as a backstop for passthrough content rather than deleting it. Keep the FeatureSet strictly out of the block-id content hash and sourcepos so click-to-source and block-diff are untouched. Separately, flag in the catalog that the tiny-idle-floor-beats-Quarto headline should not obscure that Taliesin's per-page inlining of d3+Plot forfeits the cross-page HTTP cache that Quarto's shared bundle keeps; revisit shared vs inlined for large sites as its own item.
- **Tradeoffs:** Threading a FeatureSet through emission touches many emitters (the mod.rs orchestrator, divs.rs, figure.rs, the cell emitters, deck.rs, math) versus today's six-line substring gate, which is dead simple and centralized. The win is Build-only: Preview already ships the light enhancers regardless, so nothing changes there except the heavy libs that were already content-gated. False positives today cost page weight, not correctness (an inlined script no-ops without its DOM), and the corpus already catches marker drift feature by feature, so this is a robustness/weight improvement, not a correctness emergency. A registry adds one layer of indirection over a very readable inline `format!`. The 512 KB case is real but bounded to pages that textually mention feature markers, chiefly the docs book. (skeptic-found downside: The proposal trades a HARMLESS false-positive (extra inlined weight that no-ops) for a CORRECTNESS false-NEGATIVE it never reckons with. Emitter-set flags only fire when a construct flows through a first-party emitter (divs.rs, the cell emitters, math). But real feature DOM can arrive as raw HTML passthrough, via {{< include >}}, or via the unescaped include-in-header/before-body/after-body strings (model.rs:229 injects them verbatim). A literal <div class=panel-tabset> or a mermaid/scrolly block injected that way never runs the emitter, so the FeatureSet MISSES it and Build silently UNDER-ships the script, killing the feature. The current final-HTML substring scan catches those passthrough constructs for free precisely because it scans the emitted body. So the fix must keep a scan backstop for raw-HTML/include blocks or the win becomes a dead-feature regression. Second missed point: a much cheaper fix resolves the sole MEASURED bug. The four vulnerable markers are exactly the bare ones (application/qmd-js, panel-tabset, code-walkthrough, tali-scrolly); the mermaid/katex gates are already immune only because their quotes escape to &quot; inside highlighted code. Tightening the four gates to include their surrounding quotes/angle brackets (type=\"application/qmd-js\", class=\"panel-tabset\") makes highlighted code samples stop matching for the same escape reason, closing the 512 KB false positive in a six-line edit with zero emitter refactor and zero passthrough risk. Third: deck.rs:107 ships all light enhancers via code_scripts() in Preview mode even in a static deck build, a separate path the FeatureSet must also govern but the tradeoffs section ignores. Fourth: in the load-bearing live Preview the set is bypassed entirely (open_in_preview keeps everything on), so the whole value is Build-only and the strengthens-the-block-model framing is rhetorical: gate and block model stay decoupled in the warm path by design.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML stays the only output target; nothing here adds a format. The preview stays read-only: the FeatureSet is computed server-side during render, never written back to source, so click-to-source is untouched (sourcepos/data-block-id emission is not modified). It strengthens rather than fights the load-bearing block model, since asset gating would now key off the same block model as incremental swap and source mapping instead of a parallel string scan. No per-edit startup cost is added: the set is built inline during emission, and Preview keeps its warm-session policy of opening light gates so scripts are never re-injected mid-edit. Markdown/Pandoc syntax is unchanged (this is purely internal to the render pipeline). Corpus-plus-roadmap is respected and in fact tightened: pin it with a corpus doc that mentions every marker string in prose and code but uses none of the features, asserting the strict Build ships none of those scripts, a direct regression test for the verified false positive.

### D138. Ship the search index as a window-global .js so Cmd-K works under file:// vs. a fetched .json that needs a server (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's full-text search ships a JSON index that the client fetches over XHR/fetch at page load; opening the built HTML directly from disk (file://) hits CORS/same-origin restrictions and search silently fails without a local web server.
- **Critique:** A fetched `.json` index means 'just open the file' does not work: you must run a static server to get search. For a single-author who often double-clicks a built page or shares a folder, that is an avoidable friction.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto optimizes for its real primary target: sites deployed to a web server (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Quarto Pub), not double-clicked from disk. For that target, fetching a pure .json index is defensible, even superior, on several axes. (1) Code/data separation: search.json is inert data with a correct content-type, so a hardened deployment can run a strict script-src / nonce CSP and still load the index via connect-src, whereas a window.X=[...] file is an executable script subresource. (2) Composability: a plain-JSON index can be consumed by other tooling (a custom search UI, an external indexer, analytics) without executing browser code; a global-assign .js is coupled to being run in a page. (3) Pluggable backends and scale-out: the fetch-an-index architecture is the same substrate that lets Quarto swap in hosted Algolia for large docs sites where shipping a multi-megabyte index to every visitor is untenable. (4) HTTP-cache friendliness on a server: a separate .json is cached, revalidated, and compressed independently of page HTML. Given Quarto's assumption that you publish to a server, fetch(json) is a reasonable default, and the file:// failure is the accepted cost of that assumption, not a naive mistake.
- **Taliesin today:** The site build writes `search-index.js` that assigns `window.TALIESIN_SEARCH_INDEX = [...]` and pages load it via a `<script>` tag with `window.TALIESIN_SEARCH_URL` (build.rs:1001-1012). A `<script>` load works under file://, so Cmd-K search works from disk with no server. The 404.html and all framework assets are likewise self-contained/offline.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it. Optionally document this as an explicit portability guarantee ('the built folder works by double-clicking index.html, no server needed') and add a corpus/tech-blog assertion that pins the window-global (not fetch) shape so a future refactor cannot regress file:// search.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the design: verified in code it is genuinely already better than Quarto for Taliesin's offline, self-contained, single-author workflow (build.rs:1006-1012 writes the global-assign .js; search.js:113-134 loads it via a lazy <script>, which works under file:// where fetch is CORS-blocked; and it surfaces load failure via TALIESIN_SEARCH_LOAD_FAILED instead of failing silently like Quarto, a point the entry should add to its favor). Sharpen three things. (1) Note the regression net mostly EXISTS (crates/core/tests/search.rs) so do not re-propose it wholesale; the one worthwhile new pin is a build-level assertion that the emitted search-index.js body is a window-global assignment, not raw JSON, since that build path is currently untested. (2) Add the honest cost to tradeoffs: the dynamic-script-injection index is incompatible with a nonce-based CSP, a case Quarto's fetch(json) handles, so the win is scoped to file:// / non-nonce deployments (which is exactly Taliesin's target, but say so). (3) Reframe the critique to acknowledge Quarto's fetch(json) is the correct substrate for server deployment, hosted Algolia scale-out, and code/data separation; Taliesin is right to trade that composability away because it is HTML-only and offline-portable by charter, not because Quarto blundered.
- **Tradeoffs:** A window-global index is loaded eagerly as a script rather than lazily fetched, so a very large index is parsed up front; but it is already gated (only written when non-empty) and lazy-loaded via the palette, so the cost is bounded. Slightly larger inline surface than a streamed JSON. (skeptic-found downside: Two costs the entry understates. (1) The script-injection approach is LESS friendly than fetch(json) to a hardened server deployment: search.js dynamically injects <script src=search-index.js> (web-client/search.js:123-133), which a nonce-based CSP (script-src 'nonce-...') would block because the injected element carries no nonce, whereas Quarto's fetch(json) works under connect-src 'self'. For Taliesin's offline single-author workflow this rarely bites, but it is a real regression on the deployed-to-a-locked-down-host case, so the tradeoffs field should not read as pure upside. (2) The proposed 'add a corpus/tech-blog assertion' is largely already implemented: crates/core/tests/search.rs:13 (cross_page_search_wires_a_script_loadable_index_not_a_raw_fetch) already pins that pages wire search-index.js and never reference a fetched search.json. The only genuinely un-pinned surface is the BUILT artifact's body: no test asserts build.rs emits window.TALIESIN_SEARCH_INDEX=... (a global assignment) rather than raw JSON.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only and offline-portable, which is the strongest form of the 'self-contained artifact' goal. No source writes; the preview stays read-only.

### D139. Output-dir convention and in-place-build safety vs. Quarto's output-dir footguns (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `output-dir` defaults to `_site` for a website and `_book` for a book, but a common gh-pages recipe sets `output-dir: docs` so GitHub Pages can 'serve from /docs', mixing built output into a source-tracked folder. Quarto does not hard-refuse an output dir that overlaps the source.
- **Critique:** The `output-dir: docs` gh-pages convention interleaves generated files with source in a committed directory, which is easy to mis-clean and easy to accidentally edit a generated file. And nothing stops a config that writes output back over inputs.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** GitHub Pages' classic "Deploy from a branch" mode can only serve from the repo root or a /docs folder, with no CI in the loop. For a user who wants zero-Actions, zero-secrets publishing (git commit and it is live), output-dir: docs plus a commit is genuinely the simplest possible deploy: no workflow YAML, no Actions minutes, no personal access token. Quarto is a general multi-format tool serving a heterogeneous base, so offering that escape hatch meets users constrained by their host rather than forcing a CI pipeline they may not want. And Quarto does not strand them there: its recommended path, `quarto publish gh-pages`, pushes built output to a dedicated gh-pages branch (with .nojekyll), keeping source and output on separate branches, so the clean solution exists and output-dir: docs is a deliberate convenience for the CI-averse, not carelessness. Hard-refusing an in-tree output dir outright would break these real, low-friction workflows.
- **Taliesin today:** The `output:` key (default `_site`, `_book` for a book) is honored; `_site/`/`_book/`/`_freeze/` are gitignored. build_site_async canonicalizes the output dir and REFUSES to build when it equals the source directory ('refusing to build in place (it would overwrite/truncate your source files)'), because fs::copy truncates the destination first. It also skips recursing into the output dir and skips `*_cache`/`*_files` build residue.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the defaults and the in-place guard. Do NOT add a `docs/` gh-pages convenience (it is the footgun above); instead, if a docs-branch deploy is wanted, cover it with the CI recipe from the publish entry (build to `_site/`, deploy-pages from there), keeping source and output cleanly separated.
