- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the _site/_book defaults and the truncation guard, and keep steering docs-branch deploys to the CI recipe (build to _site/, deploy-pages from there): that is the right opinion and is invariant-safe (it actively protects source, no write-back, HTML-only). But sharpen three things. (1) Correct the framing: `output: docs` is unblessed, not blocked; Taliesin will build it. State that explicitly so the entry does not overclaim prevention. (2) Steelman-correctly: note Quarto's own clean path is `quarto publish gh-pages` (separate branch), not `output-dir: docs`, so the fair comparison is against Quarto's recommended path, which is also clean; Taliesin's edge is the hard in-place refusal Quarto lacks, plus gitignored defaults, plus residue-skip. (3) Close the two real gaps per corpus-plus-roadmap: add a test/corpus pin for the in-place refusal (currently untested), and OPTIONALLY emit a soft warning (not a refusal) when the resolved output dir is in-tree and not one of the gitignored defaults, nudging toward _site + CI. The soft warning is a new capability, so pin it with a corpus doc or leave it as documented guidance rather than shipping it silently. Also cite stale-committed-output as the extra argument the drafter did not make: gitignored _site/ discards stale files for free, a committed docs/ accumulates them, which independently justifies not blessing docs.
- **Tradeoffs:** Not offering an `output-dir: docs` path means a user wanting the old 'serve from /docs' GitHub Pages setting has to use the Actions-based Pages deploy instead. That is a deliberate opinion, not a capability loss, but it is one migrating Quarto users will notice. (skeptic-found downside: The entry reads as if Taliesin blocks the docs footgun, but the guard is equality-only (build.rs:829, `r == out`): it refuses ONLY when the output dir canonicalizes to the source ROOT. An output dir NESTED in source is not refused, so `output: docs` still builds fine today (mirror_assets skips the output dir at build.rs:1094, discovery ignores generated .html at discovery.rs:94). So a Quarto user who ports `output-dir: docs` gets the exact interleaving-hygiene footgun the critique names: generated files committed in-tree, easy to mis-edit, and (because neither tool cleans the output dir before building) stale .html from renamed/deleted pages lingers in git. Taliesin is better only on the narrow data-loss axis (exact in-place truncation), not on the interleaving hazard the critique leads with. Second miss: no test pins the in-place guard (only mirror_assets_skips_build_residue exists), so under corpus-plus-roadmap a refactor could silently drop the refusal.)
- **Invariant check:** HTML-only, read-only surface, no write-back to source (in fact it actively prevents the output path from clobbering source). No new format.

## Interactivity and computed output

### D140. Explicit //| input dependency annotations plus a compile-time reactive validator, instead of implicit free-variable reactivity (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** OJS derives the dataflow graph automatically by parsing each cell for the free variables it references; cell order in the document is irrelevant, and moving an input re-runs exactly the transitive dependents. There is no author annotation and no build-time check: a typo'd variable name or a dependency cycle only surfaces at runtime in the browser.
- **Critique:** Implicit reactivity is convenient but is 'magic': the graph is invisible in the source, it requires a full JS parser/interpreter to extract free variables, and mistakes (a reference to an undefined name, an accidental cycle) fail silently or at runtime with an obscure Observable error. It is hard to reason about which cells re-run.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** OJS's dependency graph is EXTRACTED FROM the code, so it can never disagree with what a cell actually reads: reference a name in the body and the edge is tracked automatically; there is no parallel `//| input:` list to maintain or desync. That is the decisive advantage the entry inverts. Taliesin's explicit annotations are a SECOND source of truth that can drift silently, a cell body that reads `tali.get('foo')` without declaring `//| input: foo` simply never re-runs, and the deliberately parser-free validator (reactive.rs reads only cell.js.inputs, never the body) cannot catch it. OJS is structurally immune to exactly that. OJS also fails LOUDLY and located: an undefined reference renders an inline `x is not defined` at that cell and a cycle renders `circular definition`, so the entry's `fail silently ... obscure Observable error` is misdirected (Taliesin is the one with a silent failure mode here). Finally, order-independence is a genuine authoring ergonomic (put the input control anywhere), which Taliesin only partially matches, its first paint is still document-order-dependent, the very defect this entry proposes to fix. For rapid exploratory reactive notebooks the zero-bookkeeping model is faster to write and impossible to desync. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** Cells declare wiring explicitly via `//| name:` (publish), `//| viewof:` (publish an input control), `//| input: a, b` (consume). qmd-js.js buildGraph runs Kahn's topo-sort over define->consumer edges; scheduleFrom re-runs the transitive downstream closure in topo order; cycles are diagnosed and excluded. Crucially, crates/core/src/diagnostics/reactive.rs is a static mirror that flags dangling inputs (with a levenshtein did-you-mean) AND cycles at render/check time, located to the source line for click-to-source. The INITIAL run, however, is document order (qmd-js.js line 332), so a consumer placed above its producer reads undefined on first paint.
- **Proposed better:** Keep explicit annotations (they are the substrate-honest, debuggable, parser-free choice and the static validator is a genuine advantage Quarto lacks). Two concrete improvements: (1) make the INITIAL run use the computed topo order `r.graph.order` instead of document order, so first paint is order-independent like OJS; (2) when a `//| input:` name resolves to neither a define nor an `{{< input >}}` nor a runtime `ojs_define`, keep the located warning but also render an inline placeholder so the reader sees the gap.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the explicit-annotation plus render/check-time static-validator architecture: it is genuinely shipped (reactive.rs wired into check.rs with located did-you-mean and cycle diagnostics) and is a real edge over OJS's runtime-only errors. Reframe the entry as already-won-plus-polish and downgrade impact from high to MEDIUM (the load-bearing win is shipped; the delta is first-paint ordering). Adopt fix (1) but sharpen it: run the FRESH cells in the global topo order, r.graph.order.filter(c => fresh.indexOf(c) >= 0 && r.graph.cyclic.indexOf(c) < 0), never the whole graph, so block-level-incremental holds and independent cells keep document order (Kahn seeds in doc order); pin with a corpus doc that puts a consumer above its producer and asserts correct first paint. Narrow fix (2): render an inline gap placeholder only under the SAME no-non-js-executable-cell condition reactive.rs uses, so a runtime `ojs_define` name is never falsely flagged; treat it as low-value optional polish. Most importantly, close the silent failure the entry glosses: add a cheap substring/regex lint (no full parser) that every declared `//| input:` name appears as a `tali.get`/`tali.value` read in the body (and ideally that reads have a matching declaration), so the debuggable/no-silent-failure claim actually holds, the one place OJS is structurally stronger. Correct the critique text: OJS surfaces undefined-ref and cycle errors loudly and located at the cell, so drop fail silently and obscure.
- **Tradeoffs:** Explicit annotations are more verbose than OJS and the author must maintain them as cells change. Switching the initial run to topo order slightly diverges from the 'producer-before-consumer authoring convention' the code documents, though it can only fix, never break, a correct document. (skeptic-found downside: The entry frames explicit annotations as strictly debuggable and parser-free while missing the reciprocal SILENT failure they introduce: because the validator never parses the JS body, it cannot detect drift between the declared `//| input:` list and the code's actual `tali.get`/`tali.value` reads. A cell reading an undeclared name silently never re-runs (under-reactivity); a declared-but-unused input costs a spurious re-run. This is the same class of silent defect the entry pins on OJS, and OJS is immune to it (graph == code). Two secondary misses: fix (1) as literally worded (use r.graph.order) re-runs the WHOLE graph, not just fresh cells, on every incremental mount; and fix (2)'s inline placeholder risks a false missing-input for names a Python `ojs_define` supplies at runtime, the exact case reactive.rs already suppresses its warning for.)
- **Invariant check:** Annotations live in the .tmd source; the validator is read-only and click-to-source-located; the runtime graph is browser-only and never writes back. Fully compatible with block-level incremental updates (the graph is rebuilt when fresh cells mount). (possible violation flagged: Fix (1) as literally stated (make the initial run use r.graph.order instead of document order) would, on an incremental block mount, re-run every cell in the global graph rather than only the freshly mounted ones, breaking the block-level-incremental invariant (re-run only the edited cell plus its downstream) and re-firing side effects on already-mounted cells. It is avoidable: iterate the fresh set in topo order via r.graph.order.filter(c => fresh.includes(c) && cyclic-excluded), which equals the whole graph on a full page load but touches only fresh cells on incremental mounts. Also corpus-plus-roadmap: the change must ship pinned by a corpus doc placing a consumer above its producer; the entry does not mention pinning.)

### D141. Decide the stance on interactive kernel output (Plotly/Altair/folium/ipywidgets), which does not survive live-preview mounting today (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto renders rich interactive Jupyter output: ipywidgets via the widget manager (application/vnd.jupyter.widget-view+json + widget state), R htmlwidgets via their HTML-dependency injection, and Plotly/Altair/folium via their embedded text/html + <script>. These render and stay interactive in the static HTML.
- **Critique:** Quarto's approach drags in per-library runtimes and a require.js/widget-manager machinery, is a frequent source of 'renders in preview but blank in output' bugs, and often needs network CDNs unless self-contained embedding is forced. It is heavy and fragile, but it is a real capability Taliesin lacks.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** For a working data scientist, `import plotly.express as px; fig.show()` (or an Altair chart, or a folium map) rendering as a live pan/zoom/hover-interactive figure with zero extra syntax is the single biggest reason to reach for Quarto. It reuses the exact plotting code the author already has, across Python AND R, via one universal mechanism (the Jupyter widget MIME contract and the htmlwidgets HTML-dependency contract) that Quarto did not have to write per-library: any library that speaks those protocols works today and in the future without Quarto knowing it exists. The requirejs/widget-manager weight is the price of that generality, and embed-resources/self-contained shows Quarto already solved the offline case when the author asks for it, capturing widget-state JSON and inlining runtimes. Taliesin's native-{js} lane cannot match this for anyone with a mature plotting codebase: it demands rewriting existing Plotly/Altair analyses in Observable Plot/d3.
- **Taliesin today:** crates/server/src/kernel.rs render_media only handles MediaType Html/Png/Svg/Jpeg/Plain; application/vnd.jupyter.widget-view+json is unhandled, so ipywidgets fall through to their text/plain repr (no interactivity). Plotly/Altair emit text/html and ARE captured via the Html branch, but web-client/client.js `fragment()` builds nodes with an inert `<template>`, so on a live-preview block update any embedded `<script>` is NOT executed (it only runs on the initial SSR/static page load). There is no widget-state channel and no vendored Plotly. So interactive Python-library output is at best static-first-load-only and at worst a plain-text fallback.
- **Proposed better:** Make the stance explicit rather than accidental. Minimum: add a script-revival pass when mounting kernel-emitted output blocks in client.js (clone each <script> into a fresh executable node) so text/html interactive output works under live preview, matching the static path. Better long-term: steer authors to the native `{js}` lane for interactivity (Plot/d3 already vendored offline) and emit a located diagnostic when a cell produces a widget-view mime that Taliesin renders as a static fallback, so the degradation is visible, not silent.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but split it into two independently shippable pieces and make the stance the position of record. Piece 1 (high value, low risk, do first): an honesty/diagnostic layer. Emit a located diagnostic when a cell produces application/vnd.jupyter.widget-view+json that Taliesin renders as a static text/plain fallback (currently silent at kernel.rs:921), AND detect external <script src>/CDN references in kernel-emitted text/html and warn or fail the self-contained build, closing the existing silent offline-invariant hole in the build path. Pin both with one corpus document that contains an inline, offline, self-contained interactive figure so degradation is visible and the capability is under the regression net. Piece 2 (optional, higher risk than stated): script revival on live-preview update, gated to self-contained inline output only (no external src, so execution is deterministic and offline-safe) and hooked into the existing teardownJs/invalidation lifecycle so re-mounts do not leak or double-init. Formally adopt "no ipywidget-manager parity; steer authors to the native {js} lane" as the stated position, matching the OJS-runtime removal. Fix the entry's tradeoffs text to name lifecycle-leak and script-ordering as the real risks rather than framing it as a code-execution/security surface, since the author's own kernel scripts already run on first load.
- **Tradeoffs:** Reviving arbitrary kernel scripts is a code-execution and complexity surface, and most of these libraries pull heavy CDN runtimes that break the offline/self-contained build. Chasing ipywidget-manager parity would reintroduce exactly the third-party-runtime weight Taliesin removed with OJS. The owner may legitimately prefer to keep the clean native-{js} lane and formally NOT support ipywidgets. (skeptic-found downside: The "minimum" (clone each <script> into an executable node on block update) is necessary but not sufficient and understates the work in three ways verified against the code. (1) Ordering and external loads: Plotly/Vega output emits an inline init script that references a global (window.Plotly, vegaEmbed) which is often loaded by a separate <script src> in the same fragment; a naive clone-and-append does not guarantee the src finishes loading before the inline init runs, so revival is racy. This is precisely why htmlwidgets uses ordered HTML-dependency injection instead of raw tags. (2) Leak-on-every-edit: client.js already has a teardownJs/invalidation lifecycle (lines 836-843) for {js} cells so re-mounting does not leak WebGL contexts/RAF loops; raw kernel HTML output has NO such hook, so reviving its scripts on each block update re-executes init with no teardown, leaking listeners/plot instances on the edit-heavy hot path that is Taliesin's whole point. (3) The security framing is misaimed: the SSR/static path ALREADY executes these author-kernel scripts on first load, so revival is not a new trust boundary for the author's own document; the real risk is lifecycle/correctness, not code-execution. Separately, the static build TODAY silently ships CDN <script src> in Plotly/Altair/folium output, so the offline/self-contained invariant is already being violated in the build path, not just a future risk for the interactive path, and the entry buries that.)
- **Invariant check:** Script revival stays within the read-only live HTML view and never writes to source; block-id/sourcepos are unaffected. The offline invariant is the tension point: any solution must gate CDN-dependent output out of the self-contained build or vendor the runtime, so 'wider browser behavior' does not cost HTML-only/offline guarantees. (possible violation flagged: Two, both fixable but real as-written. (a) Corpus-plus-roadmap: no corpus or docs document references plotly/altair/ipywidgets/folium/htmlwidgets anywhere, so this capability has no pin today; the invariant requires any new capability to ship pinned by a corpus document (an inline, offline, self-contained interactive figure), and the proposal omits that pin. (b) Block-level incremental updates: reviving raw kernel scripts with no teardown hook risks duplicate init and leaks on re-mount, which would degrade the load-bearing incremental-update goal unless the revival plugs into the existing teardown/invalidation lifecycle. Not violated: HTML-only, single read-only editing surface (revival never writes to source), click-to-source, block-id/sourcepos (output block keeps its cell-derived id), and Markdown-syntax.)

### D142. Replace the Observable/OJS client runtime with a tiny native {js} enhancer (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** For any doc with `ojs`/`{ojs}` cells Quarto ships the full Observable stack to the browser: the quarto-ojs runtime (a reactive VM), the Inspector, and the Observable stdlib, plus D3/Plot pulled from the stdlib. That is hundreds of KB of always-loaded JS whether or not the reactivity is trivial.
- **Critique:** The OJS runtime is a whole reactive interpreter shipped to the reader to evaluate a handful of cells; it is heavy on first paint, opaque to debug (the dataflow lives inside a VM), and it is a third-party dependency Quarto must track and vendor. Most author reactivity is one input fanning out to a few sinks, which does not need a general reactive VM.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** OJS is a general reactive substrate Quarto did NOT write and does not maintain: the correctness of the dataflow, generators-as-cells, async cells, view(), FileAttachment, Generators, and the whole Observable stdlib are offloaded to Observable, a documented standard many authors already know from observablehq.com. That buys three things Taliesin's enhancer deliberately gives up. (1) Zero-annotation implicit reactivity: no per-cell //| input / //| name bookkeeping because the VM infers the dataflow graph, so an author can paste an Observable notebook cell and it just works. (2) True generators and animation-as-cells plus uniform cyclic-safe scheduling. (3) A large ecosystem of copy-pasteable notebooks. For a general-purpose, many-author tool the heavy runtime is the price of a maintained, general reactive layer, and shipping one shared vendored runtime that a browser caches across a whole site is a defensible choice versus hand-optimizing one author's fan-out pattern. Quarto is optimizing for breadth of expression and reuse, not for byte count on a single-author blog.
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/assets/js/qmd-js.js is a ~15 KB unminified enhancer (no reactive VM). Each `{js}` cell is emitted as `<script type="application/qmd-js">` + a target div; the enhancer runs the source in an AsyncFunction with a small scope ({get,set,value,defines,onInput,container,invalidation}). d3.min.js + plot.umd.min.js are vendored and gated on `has_js_cells` (render/mod.rs `js_cell_head`), so a page with no `{js}` cells ships neither. The Observable runtime was removed entirely.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the enhancer approach. Optional refinement: minify qmd-js.js at build time (it is currently inlined unminified) and lazy-load Plot/d3 only for the cells that reference `window.Plot`/`window.d3` rather than for any `{js}` cell, since some cells (Three.js, plain DOM) use neither.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the status as taliesin-already-better: the load-bearing decision (remove the Observable reactive VM, emit {js} as application/qmd-js script + target div, run via a small graph scheduler, gate the heavy libs) is verified in code and is genuinely better for a single-author HTML-only tool. Drop the minify refinement entirely (it saves ~4 KB gzipped against ~476 KB of libs and fights the readable/debuggable advantage that is this entry's whole thesis). Replace lazy-load Plot/d3 with build-time per-library static gating (has_d3_use vs has_plot_use vs neither), implemented conservatively (ship the lib whenever a cell body is ambiguous or references d3/Plot transitively), and pinned by a Three.js-only and a Plot-only corpus document so the gate cannot silently break a chart. A larger, honestly-bigger win than any of these is trimming vendored d3 to the module subset Plot and the corpus actually use, since d3 alone is ~273 KB. Also note (do not necessarily fix here) the missing build-time validation of {js} cell bodies as an inconsistency with Taliesin's strict-validation identity.
- **Tradeoffs:** The enhancer deliberately implements less than OJS: no implicit reactivity, no generators-as-cells, no Observable stdlib globals (FileAttachment, Generators, etc). Authors migrating an Observable notebook must rewrite cells to the explicit annotation model. (skeptic-found downside: The core (drop the VM, keep the native enhancer) holds and matches shipped code, so the status is right. But the two OPTIONAL refinements, which are the only NEW content, are both weak. (a) Minify qmd-js.js: near-zero payoff. The enhancer is 15 KB next to the ~476 KB of gated d3+Plot it sits beside (d3.min.js 273 KB, plot.umd.min.js 203 KB, both verified), gzip/brotli already takes 15 KB to ~4 KB, and minifying directly undercuts the entry's own selling point that the enhancer is readable and debuggable in DevTools (the exact thing it faults OJS for hiding in a VM). Drop this refinement. (b) Lazy-load Plot/d3 per cell is mis-framed: for the DEFAULT self-contained single-file build every script is already inlined into the one HTML file, so runtime lazy-load defers nothing (you cannot un-download an inline blob) while forcing the currently-synchronous window.Plot/window.d3 access in the AsyncFunction run loop to become async. The genuinely valuable version is BUILD-TIME per-library static gating: split the single has_js_cells gate into has_d3_use / has_plot_use so a Three.js-only or Plot-only page omits ~273 KB of unused d3. That stays inside the static-emission model but carries a text-scan false-negative risk (a d3 call reached only through a //| name helper, or an aliased reference, would be missed and the chart breaks at runtime with d3 is not defined), which is worse than shipping unused bytes, so the gate must be conservative (ship-if-unsure). Separately, the tradeoffs list omits a real gap versus Taliesin's own strict-validation differentiator: {js} bodies are eval'd via new AsyncFunction with NO build-time validation, so a broken cell ships to the reader and only surfaces as a runtime tali-js-error pre, unlike the front-matter/config that Taliesin validates up front.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure browser-side enrichment of the live HTML view; the {js} script blocks carry data-block-id/data-sourcepos like any block, gating keeps offline/self-contained builds intact, and nothing writes back to source. Respects HTML-only and single-surface invariants. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation of the core change; the {js} script blocks carry data-block-id/data-sourcepos, gating preserves offline self-contained output, and nothing writes back to source. Two conditional touches on the refinements: (1) if lazy-load is implemented as a runtime dynamic import() of a SEPARATE resource it brushes the HTML-only self-contained invariant, since the default build must inline everything into one portable file; reframing it as build-time static gating avoids this. (2) Corpus-plus-roadmap: any per-library gating must be pinned by a new corpus document (a Plot-only page and a Three.js-only page) before it counts as done, so the false-negative gate is proven by the regression net.)

### D143. Extend the ojs_define/define() kernel->JS bridge to R (currently Python-only) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's `ojs_define()` publishes values from a computation kernel into OJS and works from R, Python, and Julia, so a reader-side Observable cell can consume a data frame computed in any supported language.
- **Critique:** N/A to Quarto here (this is a Taliesin gap, not a Quarto pain): Quarto's cross-language define is broader than Taliesin's today.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto inherited and serves a genuinely polyglot scientific-publishing audience where R (tidyverse/RMarkdown lineage), Python, and Julia are first-class equals, not a Python core with bolt-ons. A cross-language kernel-to-Observable bridge is table stakes for that audience: publishing a data frame computed in R into a reader-side interactive Observable cell is a headline use case Quarto inherited directly from its RMarkdown base. Paying the per-language serialization surface (R via jsonlite, Julia via JSON) across all three kernels is the correct investment for a tool whose whole value proposition is one authoring surface over many compute languages. Shipping the bridge for only one language would alienate a large fraction of Quarto's base and undercut the polyglot promise, so Quarto's choice is right for Quarto. The entry concedes this openly (it labels the item a Taliesin gap, not a Quarto pain), which is fair and not a strawman: I verified the Python-only limitation against code (OJS_DEFINE_PREAMBLE is in KernelSpec::python's preambles only; KernelSpec::r ships preambles: &[]).
- **Taliesin today:** crates/server/src/kernel.rs defines OJS_DEFINE_PREAMBLE (a Python `define(**kwargs)` that serializes each value, with a pandas DataFrame convenience, and emits `<script type="qmd-define">`); it is bound as both `define` and `ojs_define`. But `KernelSpec::r` sets `preambles: &[]` with the code comment 'nothing for R yet'. So an R `{r}` cell has NO way to publish a value into the `{js}` reactive runtime; only Python can feed the graph. qmd-js.js bindDefines() already ingests the blob language-agnostically, so only the R-side emitter is missing.
- **Proposed better:** Add an R preamble that defines an R `define(...)`/`ojs_define(...)` emitting the identical `<script type="qmd-define">{contents:[{name,value}]}</script>` blob via IRdisplay::display_html(), with a data.frame->columnar-JSON convenience mirroring the pandas path. No client change is needed since bindDefines already accepts the shape.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship it: this is a real gap where Quarto is genuinely broader, and the fix is additive, HTML-only, no source write-back, keeps Markdown syntax, and touches none of click-to-source/block-diff/warm-server. But bake three guardrails into the proposed_better or it ships subtly broken. (1) Set auto_unbox=TRUE on the R JSON encode and state the contract explicitly: named list -> object, unnamed vector -> array, length-1 vector -> unwrapped scalar, so a scalar define does not arrive in JS as [x]. (2) Guard jsonlite-absent with a fallback or diagnostic, mirroring the Python pandas guard, since R has no stdlib serializer. (3) Reuse the exact column-oriented shape the pandas path emits ({col: [values]}) for data.frame/tibble so a {js} consumer sees identical structure regardless of source language, and decide NA/factor/Date coercions deliberately (NA -> null, factor -> labels). Because the core corpus net cannot execute R, pin this with a QMD_FAST_R-gated server-side execution test asserting the <script type=\"qmd-define\">{contents:[...]} blob shape (mirroring the existing Python kernel test) plus one browser-verified corpus doc, and state honestly in the entry that corpus-pinning here is execution-gated, not automatic. Note as a de-risking point that the qmd_define=True metadata is consumed nowhere server-side, so R's IRdisplay::display_html() losing it costs nothing.
- **Tradeoffs:** Adds an R-specific serialization surface to maintain (data.frame/tibble/factor edge cases), and R value->JSON fidelity differs from Python's. Low blast radius since it is additive and gated behind the R kernel being present. (skeptic-found downside: Four costs the drafter glossed. (1) Scalar trap, the sharpest: R has no scalar type, so jsonlite::toJSON(5) yields [5]; a {js} cell reading define('n', 5) would receive an array, not a number, unless the preamble sets auto_unbox=TRUE. Shipping the entry's 'mirror the pandas path' verbatim produces this bug. (2) R has no stdlib JSON encoder: the Python path uses stdlib json (always present) and only guards pandas, but the R path depends on jsonlite, which is external (a transitive IRkernel dep in practice, but not base R), so the preamble must guard jsonlite-absent exactly like the pandas guard or it silently cannot serialize. (3) NA/Date/factor have no clean JSON mapping (NA -> null, factor -> integer-codes vs labels, Date -> epoch vs string); the drafter waved at data.frame/tibble/factor but not these concrete traps. (4) Corpus-pinning friction: I verified the core corpus tests do NOT execute kernels (corpus.rs:318, 'R cells aren't executed here'), no automated test asserts any define blob for Python or R, and the only kernel test is Python-only and gated on QMD_FAST_PYTHON. So the 'corpus is the arbiter of done' pin is only weakly satisfiable here, verifiable by a kernel-gated server test plus manual browser check, the same limited coverage the existing Python define path already has, not by the automated core net.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure additive kernel preamble; output is the same define blob the {js} runtime already consumes; no new output format, no source write-back. HTML-only and single-surface preserved.

### D144. Deliberately omit Shiny / server-backed reactivity in favor of client-side {js} (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto supports `server: shiny` documents where reactivity runs in a live R or Python process: the rendered artifact is not a static page but an app that must be hosted on a running backend (shinyapps.io, a container, etc).
- **Critique:** Shiny docs trade the entire value of a static site for a running server: they cannot be served as plain HTML, cannot be opened from file://, and carry a real deployment/ops tax. For a single-author HTML-only tool this is a category mismatch.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Shiny is not a lapse of discipline, it is the only correct answer for a class of problem client-side cannot touch. (1) Data privacy and secrets: interactivity over a large, proprietary, or regulated dataset, a live database, or a model behind an API key requires the data and logic to stay server-side; a static page would have to ship them all to the browser. (2) Correctness: the reactive compute runs in the real R/Python env with the real libraries, so live results exactly match the static render, with no risk of a client-side reimplementation diverging from build-time output. (3) Scale: GPU inference, large simulations, and unbounded free-text-driven queries cannot be precomputed into any finite grid. (4) Adoption and single surface: it lets a data scientist author one .qmd that is both a report and a real app using the reactive vocabulary they already know (reactive(), input$, render*), meeting a large existing community where it stands. For Quarto, a multi-format publishing system for that community, Shiny is a rational scope expansion (and a deliberate opt-in alongside its own client-side path of OJS/htmlwidgets/plotly), not a category error.
- **Taliesin today:** Not built, by design. Taliesin renders to static HTML with a client-side reactive layer ({js} cells + `{{< input >}}` controls + the define bridge). There is no server process in the output; the dev server (serve.rs/serve_site.rs) exists only for live preview, not as a runtime the built page depends on.
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line: no server-backed reactivity. Where an author needs 'recompute in response to input', the intended answer is a `{js}` cell doing the compute client-side, or precomputing a parameter grid at build time and having the {js} layer index into it. Document this explicitly as a non-goal so it is a stated decision, not an omission.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the non-goal, sharpen the framing and honesty. (1) Reframe the status from "taliesin-already-better" to "correctly-scoped, deliberate non-goal": do not claim superiority over a capability you intentionally lack; claim a defensible scope boundary. Client-side is better only for Taliesin's target class (static HTML); for the Shiny-appropriate class Taliesin does not compete, and saying "better" invites the strawman it should avoid. (2) State the two real limits explicitly in tradeoffs: precompute grids do not scale (combinatorial explosion, no free/unbounded inputs), and client-side {js} must ship all data and logic to the browser, so sensitive-data / proprietary-model / live-database interactivity has no client substitute. (3) Name the specific in-house trap to forbid: never wire the preview's warm Jupyter kernel (kernel.rs) into client interactivity to fake "recompute on input"; that would turn the preview into an app runtime the built HTML cannot reproduce, breaking HTML-only and preview/build parity. (4) Point at the compliant escape hatch: build-time parameterization (render N variants from parameters) is allowed and is distinct from server-backed reactivity. (5) Pin it with the existing corpus/reactive/inputs.qmd as the sanctioned-interactivity anchor.
- **Tradeoffs:** Genuinely heavy server-side compute (a model that cannot run in-browser and cannot be precomputed) is out of reach; those authors stay on Shiny/Streamlit. This is an accepted scope boundary, not a regression. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter frames the client-side substitute too cleanly and misses two real limits. First, the "precompute a parameter grid at build time and index into it" answer suffers combinatorial explosion (curse of dimensionality: a few continuous sliders times a select is tens or hundreds of thousands of baked outputs) and cannot cover free-text or unbounded numeric inputs at all. Second, and deeper: the tradeoffs section reduces the out-of-reach case to "genuinely heavy compute," but the actual reason authors reach for Shiny is usually data privacy and secrets, not raw compute size. A client-side {js} page must ship all data and all logic to the browser, so interactivity over a proprietary dataset, a live database, or a private model behind an API key has NO client-side substitute (precomputation still materializes outputs that can leak the underlying data). That is a genuine capability Taliesin gives up, and the entry should name it rather than imply parity.)
- **Invariant check:** Directly upholds the HTML-only invariant (a Shiny app is a parallel non-HTML runtime target) and the single-surface invariant. Client-side {js} is the compliant substitute.

### D145. Wire OJS-style invalidation into the block-diff lifecycle so live edits dispose WebGL/RAF cleanly (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** OJS provides an `invalidation` promise a cell can await to tear down resources, but in Quarto's static render there is no live-edit story: a source change triggers a full re-render/reload of the page, so per-cell incremental teardown does not arise.
- **Critique:** Quarto's model never has to reconcile a long-lived interactive cell (a Three.js scene with a WebGL context and a requestAnimationFrame loop) against an in-place source edit, because it reloads. Taliesin's block-level incremental update DOES create that reconciliation problem, and a naive implementation would leak a WebGL context and a RAF loop on every keystroke-triggered re-render.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's full-document re-render-and-browser-reload on save is leak-proof by construction: browser navigation/document teardown automatically reclaims every WebGL context, RAF loop, timer, and event listener with zero author cooperation and zero framework teardown code. Quarto never has to get a scoped per-block teardown right, never ships a subtly-wrong `node.contains` scan, and never depends on authors remembering to register `invalidation.then(...)`. The OJS `invalidation` promise still covers the case that matters in a live page (a reactive cell re-running when its inputs change), so interactive authors keep a disposal hook without a reload. For a document compiler whose primary artifact is static and multi-format, consciously trading live DOM-state preservation and edit latency for a guaranteed-clean lifecycle is the robust default, not an oversight. Taliesin's incremental model is the thing that CREATES the reconciliation hazard; Quarto simply declined to take on that hazard.
- **Taliesin today:** qmd-js.js gives each cell a per-run `invalidation` promise (freshInv/resolveInv) exposed on the cell API. teardownIn(node) resolves a cell's invalidation (running the author's `invalidation.then(() => renderer.dispose())`) and splices it from the registry; resetRuntime() does the whole page. web-client/client.js calls teardownJs(el) BEFORE `el.replaceWith(node)` on every update/remove, and resetJs() before a full re-mount. This is a live-preview-specific correctness win that only exists because of the block model.
- **Proposed better:** Keep as-is; it is a load-bearing pairing of the invalidation contract with the block diff. Minor hardening: add a corpus doc that mounts a WebGL cell and asserts (via a counter the cell increments in its invalidation handler) that editing an unrelated block does not tear it down while editing the cell itself does exactly once.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the invalidation-plus-block-diff pairing as-is; the infrastructure is verified correct and load-bearing (per-run freshInv/resolveInv, dispose() driven by teardownIn scoped via node.contains with graph invalidation, resetRuntime on full_render, client teardownJs before every replaceWith/remove and resetJs before re-mount, and set_meta preserving live cells on position-only shifts). Revise the hardening: (a) move the "torn-down exactly once / unrelated edit is a no-op" assertion out of the cargo corpus net into a browser-driven regression (chrome-devtools MCP driving a real live preview, or a DOM-survival + context-count counter added to tools/live-edit-bench), since a render-level test physically cannot observe live-edit teardown; (b) do not add a redundant static WebGL corpus doc, reuse pca-geometry as the pin; (c) fix the reference exemplar itself: add renderer.forceContextLoss() to both corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd and corpus/tech-blog/_includes/three-scene.qmd and teach it in docs/guide/using/interactive.qmd + code.qmd, then have the browser test assert the active-WebGL-context count stays bounded across N rapid edits, not merely that a counter fired once. Status stays "taliesin-already-better" on the mechanism, but the shipped teardown pattern and the test location both need correction before this is genuinely airtight.
- **Tradeoffs:** Authors must actually use `invalidation.then(...)` for cleanup to fire; a cell that grabs a WebGL context without registering teardown still leaks across edits (inherent to any teardown contract). The teardown scan is O(cells) per detached block, negligible at corpus scale. (skeptic-found downside: Two holes the drafter missed. (1) The proposed assertion cannot live where proposed. The corpus regression net is a Rust render-level harness (`cargo test -p taliesin-core` renders .tmd to HTML); it cannot execute a `{js}` cell, apply a block-diff update/remove op, or read a runtime counter set in an `invalidation.then` microtask. Proving "an unrelated edit does not tear down while a self-edit tears down exactly once" requires a browser-driven test (chrome-devtools MCP against a live preview) or an extension of tools/live-edit-bench, not a static corpus doc. A corpus doc can only PIN that a WebGL cell renders, and pca-geometry already does that via corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd, so the new doc is largely redundant for pinning and cannot carry the assertion at all. (2) The reference exemplar the framework ships still leaks. corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd's invalidation handler (lines 110-115) calls cancelAnimationFrame + ctrl.dispose() + renderer.dispose() + removeEventListener but NOT renderer.forceContextLoss(). In Three.js, dispose() frees GPU buffers/textures yet does not promptly release the underlying WebGL context (it lingers until GC); browsers cap active contexts at roughly 16, so rapid live editing of the scene can still exhaust the context pool and blank earlier canvases even though the author DID register teardown. The entry's tradeoffs flag only the no-teardown-at-all case; it misses that Taliesin's own canonical teardown example is itself insufficient, which undercuts the "already better" framing precisely in the scenario the feature exists to protect.)
- **Invariant check:** Depends on and reinforces block-level incremental updates and data-block-id identity; entirely read-only DOM lifecycle management, no source write-back. Core-invariant aligned.

### D146. Server-render reactive controls from a declarative {{< input >}} shortcode instead of imperative viewof cells (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Observable inputs in Quarto are created imperatively in OJS `viewof` cells with `Inputs.range(...)`, `Inputs.select(...)`, etc; the control is instantiated in the browser by the Observable stdlib at runtime.
- **Critique:** Requiring a JS `viewof` cell (and the stdlib to instantiate it) just to get a slider or dropdown is heavyweight and non-declarative: the control does not exist until the runtime constructs it, it is not visible/accessible in the source-rendered HTML, and it depends on the Observable Inputs library.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Observable Inputs is a rich, composable, battle-tested library, and `viewof` is not Quarto ceremony but Observable's ONE reactive primitive: `viewof x = Inputs.range([0,100])` uniformly binds a value (x) to its view (the DOM node) using the exact same runtime that already handles cell deps, generators, promises, and mutable state. That single primitive buys an unbounded control set for free (date/color/file pickers, searchable tables with row selection, button groups, forms, 2D pads) with zero framework changes, and the identical code runs in an Observable notebook, Observable Framework, and Quarto, so an author who knows JS learns no new shortcode-attribute vocabulary. Where Taliesin has THREE mechanisms (data-qmd-input, //| viewof, ojs_define), Observable has one. And the critique's accessibility point partly cuts the other way: in Quarto's target use (interactive scientific reports), the output that consumes the input is itself JS-computed, so a no-JS reader gets neither the input nor the plot, meaning server-rendering the control alone buys little for that reader. Quarto also never REQUIRES Inputs: raw HTML `<input>` referenced from OJS works too, so the imperative default is a floor, not a ceiling.
- **Taliesin today:** crates/core/src/render/extension/mod.rs input_shortcode implements `{{< input name= type= ... >}}` with five types (slider/range, number, checkbox, text, select), emitting static keyboard-accessible labeled HTML controls with `data-qmd-input="name"` (slider gets a live `<output>` readout). qmd-js.js registers `[data-qmd-input]` through the SAME registerInput/scheduleFrom path as `//| viewof` cells, so a control drives the reactive graph with zero author JS. validate_input emits located diagnostics (missing name, unknown type with did-you-mean, select without options), and diagnostics/reactive.rs counts these controls as define names. `//| viewof` remains available for controls that need custom JS.
- **Proposed better:** Keep both lanes (declarative shortcode for the common controls, `//| viewof` for bespoke ones). Optional extension: a `bind=` attribute or a two-input `radio`/`toggle` type, and letting `{{< input >}}` publish an initial value into the define map so a sink cell reading it before any user interaction is order-independent.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry as taliesin-already-better: server-rendered, keyboard-accessible, click-to-source, strict-validated controls that drive the same reactive graph with zero author JS are a real, verified win over an Observable Inputs cell, and keeping //| viewof as the bespoke lane is correct. Trim the optional-extension section: (1) accept `radio` as the single clearly-worth-it breadth addition, but only with a `<fieldset>`/`<legend>` and shared-name grouping for a11y, corpus-pinned; (2) drop or defer `toggle` (redundant checkbox skin that only grows the strict-validator surface); (3) do NOT ship `bind=` until it has a concrete spec, and constrain it in writing to client-side reactive wiring only (linking two controls or a control to a define) since anything that persists a chosen value back into .tmd would break the single read-only editing surface; (4) correct the order-independence rationale: initial value is already available on first run via before-cells registration, so frame the define-map publish (if kept) honestly as tali.defines-enumeration consistency, not an ordering fix. Also fix the same-line/duplicate-name id collision. Every addition ships with its corpus document per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Tradeoffs:** The declarative set is intentionally small (five types); anything richer (a color picker, a 2D pad, linked inputs) still needs a `//| viewof` cell. The shortcode's value types are limited to what an HTML form control natively produces. (skeptic-found downside: The "publish an initial value into the define map so a sink reading it before any user interaction is order-independent" extension is largely redundant and rests on a mis-stated problem. qmd-js.js already registers every [data-qmd-input] control BEFORE any cell runs (enhance() line 304-322, explicit comment), and api.value(n) returns readValue(el) from the live DOM (line 87), so a sink using tali.value(name) already gets the input's initial value on first render regardless of source order. Publishing into r.defines only adds one niche: consistency for code that enumerates tali.defines directly (the input name is currently absent there). It fixes no ordering bug. Separately, every proposed new type/attribute enlarges the STRICT validator (validate_input/INPUT_TYPES) and the JSON schema and must be corpus-pinned, which erodes the "intentionally small (five types)" minimalism the entry itself lists as a strength; `toggle` in particular is a CSS skin of `checkbox` with no new value semantics. And a latent correctness edge the drafter missed: ctrl_id is `qin-{line_no}`, so two inputs on one source line (or two inputs sharing a `name=`) produce duplicate ids / an ambiguous `<label for>` and, for shared names, the second registerInput silently overwrites r.inputs[name].)
- **Invariant check:** Controls are server-rendered HTML in the read-only view; they carry block id/sourcepos as raw-HTML blocks and never write to source (reader interaction stays client-side). Statically validated with click-to-source. Fully invariant-compliant.

### D147. Decide how far the offline guarantee extends to author-imported heavy libraries (e.g. Three.js via esm.sh) (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto with `embed-resources: true` inlines its own runtime and dependencies, but author `import`s from a CDN inside an OJS/JS cell are equally online-dependent; Quarto makes no stronger offline guarantee for author-pulled ESM than Taliesin does.
- **Critique:** This is a shared limitation, not a Quarto-only pain: any framework that lets a cell `import()` from a URL cannot guarantee offline for that cell. The Taliesin-specific tension is that its brand promise is offline-first (KaTeX fonts vendored, d3/Plot vendored, syntax highlight server-side), yet the corpus's own 3D scenes fetch Three.js from the network at runtime.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto draws a principled line: "self-contained / embed-resources" is a build-time asset-inlining guarantee over what the compiler can statically see (script/link/img/css), not a promise to intercept arbitrary runtime module URLs. Rewriting an author's `import("https://esm.sh/three@0.163.0")` to a vendored copy would force Quarto to embed a module-graph resolver plus a bundler, pin and patch versions, and silently swap the exact URL the author wrote for a local build that might differ in version or behavior. Declining keeps the build deterministic and honors author intent: the URL you wrote is the URL that loads. Runtime code reaching the network is the author's explicit choice, and treating "did the author's own code phone home" as out of scope for a document compiler is the same separation of concerns Taliesin currently follows. Quarto is also arguably no worse than Taliesin here: OJS `require("d3")` fetches from a CDN at runtime by default, so the limitation is genuinely symmetric.
- **Taliesin today:** Taliesin vendors d3.min.js and plot.umd.min.js and gates them on `has_js_cells`. But corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd (and the tech-blog copy) do `await import("https://esm.sh/three@0.163.0")` plus OrbitControls from the same CDN. qmd-js.js's own header comment states 'Three.js is dynamically import()ed by the cell itself'. So a flagship interactive capability (WebGL scenes) silently requires network access and breaks in a truly offline/self-contained build.
- **Proposed better:** Pick an explicit policy: either (a) vendor a pinned Three.js as an optional gated asset (like d3/Plot) exposed as `window.THREE`, so 3D scenes are offline like everything else, at a size cost paid only by pages that use it; or (b) keep CDN imports but emit a build-time diagnostic when a `{js}` cell imports from an http(s) URL during a self-contained build, so the offline break is surfaced, not silent. Vendoring aligns better with the offline brand.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry, it is a genuine gap tied to the offline brand and pinned by an existing corpus doc, but reorder and correct the fix. (1) Ship option (b) first: extend the build-only import scan (build.rs `relative_specifiers`/`copy_js_imports`) to detect http(s) specifiers and emit a warning during `build`/self-contained only (not `preview`), as a diagnostic not a hard error, matching Taliesin's existing STRICT surface-don't-hide philosophy. This closes the "silent" part immediately and cheaply. (2) Add the try/catch graceful "needs network to load Three.js" fallback that the site copies already have to the reusable `corpus/_includes/three-scene.qmd`, so an offline viewer sees a message, not a dead cell. (3) Treat true vendoring (option a) as a SEPARATE, larger decision, and if pursued do it correctly: vendor `three.module.js` + the used jsm addons locally, inject an offline import map, add a fine-grained per-page "uses three" gate (NOT `has_js_cells`), and switch the corpus to bare `three`/`three/addons/` specifiers. Do not frame it as "just gate it like d3," because r163 has no global build and the coarse gate would over-ship. Net: honesty now (b + fallback), full offline later (a done right).
- **Tradeoffs:** Three.js is large (hundreds of KB) and evolves fast, so vendoring adds a maintenance/pinning burden and page weight; a diagnostic-only path keeps size down but leaves the offline gap real. Either way the owner must define what 'offline' promises for author-supplied code versus framework assets. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's PREFERRED path, option (a) "vendor Three.js and gate it like d3/Plot, exposed as window.THREE," is presented as a near drop-in but is materially harder than stated. (1) Gate granularity: d3/Plot are gated on `has_js_cells`, which fires for ANY `{js}` cell. Reusing that gate would inline ~600KB of Three.js into every page that has even a tiny Plot chart, a real regression for a performance-branded tool. Three needs a finer "this page actually uses three" gate that does not exist today. (2) No global build exists: modern Three.js (r163) ships ONLY as ESM, there is no UMD/`three.min.js` you can `<script src>` to get `window.THREE`, and the scenes also import `OrbitControls` from `examples/jsm`, an addon not in the core module. So "expose as window.THREE" cannot be done by dropping in a file like d3.min.js. The clean offline mechanism is instead a locally-vendored `three.module.js` + jsm addons behind an injected offline import map, which additionally requires the corpus to import bare `three`/`three/addons/` instead of the full esm.sh URL (an author-side source edit, permitted). The entry's tradeoffs note "large / evolves fast" but miss the concrete blocker (no global build) and the coarse-gate over-ship. Separately, the entry over-states "silent": the build is silent (no diagnostic), but the site scene copies already try/catch to a "needs network" message, while the reusable corpus include lacks that fallback, so the sharpest defect is narrower than "silently breaks.")
- **Invariant check:** Both options stay HTML-only and read-only; vendoring strengthens the self-contained/offline posture behind the offline invariant, the diagnostic option at least makes violations visible. No source write-back either way.

## Extensions, shortcodes, and filters

### D148. Expand shortcodes as a pre-parse, line-preserving Rust text pass, not as Lua functions over the Pandoc AST (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Shortcodes are Lua functions run during Pandoc's filter phase; each returns Pandoc AST (inlines or blocks), can read document metadata, and works inside metadata fields as well as the body. The mechanism is uniform with the Lua filter API.
- **Critique:** AST-level shortcodes are powerful but require a Lua runtime, run opaquely inside the batch compile, and (crucially for Taliesin) do not preserve a stable line map: an AST-inserted block does not carry the source line the author typed, which is exactly what click-to-source and block-level incremental swap key off. They also add per-run interpreter cost that fights the warm-loop goal.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's central constraint is that ONE shortcode definition must render correctly to every Pandoc writer (LaTeX, Typst, docx, epub, revealjs, HTML). Returning Pandoc AST (inlines/blocks) is the only design that is format-agnostic: a raw-HTML-emitting text pass would only ever be correct for HTML. Because Quarto is multi-format, the AST/Lua model is not a compromise, it is the correct answer to its problem. Uniformity with the Lua filter API is a second real win: shortcode authors reuse the whole Pandoc Lua toolkit (constructors, walk, `quarto.doc.add_html_dependency`, metadata access), shortcodes compose with other filters, and metadata reading enables genuinely useful capabilities Taliesin has no equivalent for, namely `{{< meta >}}`/`{{< var >}}` variable and metadata interpolation (DRY front matter, `_variables.yml`, version/env injection) and shortcodes usable inside metadata fields. One fairness caveat on the critique: the dominant Quarto per-render cost is the pandoc process spin-up plus a full document reparse, not the embedded Lua interpreter per shortcode (that part is cheap); "per-run interpreter cost" slightly misattributes where the warm-loop tax lives. And Quarto never promised click-to-source, so "does not preserve a line map" is not a Quarto failure, it is simply a property Taliesin needs and Quarto's target audience does not. For Quarto's constraints the choice is right; it is only wrong for a single-format, single-author, warm-loop tool.
- **Taliesin today:** `expand_shortcodes` (render/extension/mod.rs) runs on the raw source AFTER include resolution and BEFORE comrak parses, one invocation per line that opens+closes on that line, so the include source map stays valid. Fenced blocks and inline code spans are skipped ('code is sacred'); unknown names are left verbatim AND reported as located click-to-source warnings. Built-ins (`embed`, `video`, `input`) are pure Rust emitting raw-HTML blocks that then get a block-id/sourcepos like any block.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the pre-parse Rust model as the substrate; it is the only model that keeps the line map total. Where a shortcode legitimately needs to emit multi-line/block content, keep the current discipline of collapsing the emitted template to a single line (the removed template path already did `template.replace('\n', ' ')`) so one source line still maps to one rendered region.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the pre-parse, line-preserving Rust text pass: for an HTML-only, single-author, warm-loop tool it is correctly optimized, and it is the enabling property for click-to-source and block-level incremental swap (a line map total by construction), which no AST-return model can offer. Sharpen the entry on three points. First, foreground the honest steelman: Quarto returns AST because it is MULTI-FORMAT and needs one definition to feed every writer; Taliesin can pick the text model precisely because HTML is its only target, so this is "right tool for different constraints," not "Quarto got it wrong." Second, drop the stale `template.replace('\n', ' ')` advice: state the surviving invariant as "each built-in emits newline-free HTML for a single-line invocation" and lock it with a corpus test or a debug assertion, since the emitted string, not any removed template, is what must stay line-safe. Third, name the honest gap rather than hiding it: Taliesin has no metadata/variable-interpolation shortcode, and because line-preservation is orthogonal to metadata-reading (parse front matter first, interpolate inline), that gap is a future roadmap item the text model can absorb, not a reason to abandon it. Optionally, emit a located warning for an unterminated `{{<` so the one unsupported shape fails loudly instead of silently.
- **Tradeoffs:** A shortcode cannot span multiple source lines or wrap a block of body content the way a Lua block-shortcode can; authors needing block-level composition use `:::` divs (a first-party, source-mapped mechanism) instead. Emitting rich structure through a one-line template is more awkward than returning AST. (skeptic-found downside: The actionable remedy is stale: it tells authors to "keep the current discipline of collapsing the emitted template to a single line (the removed template path already did `template.replace('\n', ' ')`)", but that template path was deleted in f5239cb along with the whole `_extensions` system. The surviving built-ins (embed/video/input) already emit newline-free HTML by construction (hand-authored Rust string literals), so there is no "template" to collapse; the real invariant is "a built-in's emitted HTML for a one-line invocation contains no literal newline," and the real reason it matters is that `expand_in_line` returning an embedded `\n` would add lines and desync the `origins` line map from `includes::resolve` for everything downstream. Two further misses: (1) Quarto's AST model buys metadata/variable interpolation (`{{< meta >}}`/`{{< var >}}`) that Taliesin has no equivalent for, and the drafter conflates "AST model" with "can read metadata": line-preservation does NOT actually block a meta/var shortcode, since the text pass could parse front matter first and interpolate inline on one line, so the stated tradeoff ("cannot wrap a block") is real but the metadata gap is a separate, unaddressed capability hole; (2) a multi-line `{{< ...` invocation with no `>}}` on its line is silently shipped as literal text with NO warning (only fully-closed unknown names warn), so the one class of shortcode the model cannot express also fails silently.)
- **Invariant check:** Directly protects click-to-source and block-level incremental updates (line-preserving is the enabling property), stays HTML-only, keeps the Markdown substrate (shortcodes remain `{{< >}}` over CommonMark), and needs no runtime beyond the compiled binary (warm-loop intact).

### D149. Do not ship a third-party extension install/loading system (_extensions/); keep all behavior in the compiled binary (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `quarto add owner/repo` clones a GitHub repo into `_extensions/<name>/`, whose `_extension.yml` manifest contributes filters, shortcodes, formats, SCSS themes, templates, and resources; front matter references them via `filters:`, `format: <ext>-html`, `extensions:`, etc. The ecosystem (quarto-ext, journals, revealjs plugins) is the headline extensibility story.
- **Critique:** For a single author the install surface is mostly cost: extensions carry no lockfile and weak versioning, so they drift and silently break against Quarto releases. Taliesin already lived this: the one worked example (liquid-glass) targeted a `.reveal` DOM the native engine never emits, so it was dead on arrival. The manifest+loader+asset-fallback machinery is a large, always-present complexity tax paid for an ecosystem that a one-author tool does not have.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format, multi-author, institutional tool, and the extension system is its distribution mechanism, not a vanity feature. Journals (the quarto-journals org) ship one extension that targets LaTeX, HTML, and docx at once, so the core team never has to maintain hundreds of niche submission templates; the long tail lives in community-owned repos, the same model that let VS Code extensions, Pandoc filters, and LaTeX packages scale. Lua filters run on the shared Pandoc AST, so a single extension works across every output format, leverage a one-AST-to-HTML tool structurally cannot offer. For thousands of users, PR-to-core does not scale, so extensions are the pressure-release valve that lets a user add behavior without forking or waiting on a release cycle. And Quarto does stamp a source plus version into each installed manifest and ships `quarto update`, so its versioning is weak, not absent. In that context the manifest plus loader plus asset machinery is load-bearing infrastructure, and the critique is fair only because it stays scoped to the single-author stage, where none of that leverage applies.
- **Taliesin today:** Removed entirely in commit f5239cb (~2200 lines): extension_ref/find_extension_dir/load_manifest/validate_manifest/Contribution/apply_contribution/resolve_format_extension/resolve_named_extensions, the `extensions:` front-matter key (schema re-blessed), build.rs copy_resources, the serve.rs `_extensions` asset fallback, and theme.rs resolve_theme_layers. `render/extension/mod.rs` is now shortcodes-only.
- **Proposed better:** Keep it removed. If demand ever appears, reintroduce only a data-only, in-repo mechanism (declarative template shortcodes + theme-variable packs, see sibling decisions), never a code-install path. Gate any revival on a concrete corpus document that needs it, per corpus-plus-roadmap.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the third-party install/loading system removed: the verdict is correct and reinforces HTML-only, the warm-server no-per-edit-cost model, and corpus-as-arbiter (the same commit even added corpus/deck.qmd to keep deck rendering pinned after dropping the extension-based deck test). Sharpen three things. (1) Scope the Quarto critique explicitly to the single-author stage, because Quarto's extension system is a legitimate cross-format, maintenance-offloading distribution layer for a multi-author, multi-format tool; it is pure cost at Taliesin's stage, not in general. (2) Reconcile the residue rather than assert a clean sweep: either delete the vestigial _extensions/<name>/theme.css read and the dead ext() test helper, or explicitly bless that single-file read as THE sanctioned data-only theme path and bring it under strict validation (flag or did-you-mean an unknown bare theme name) with a corpus pin, so it matches the clean-break discipline applied to every other unknown key. (3) State the tradeoff honestly: there is currently no user-extensible surface at all, so the data-only revival is hypothetical and must be gated on a concrete corpus document per corpus-plus-roadmap, never shipped speculatively.
- **Tradeoffs:** No path for a stranger to package and share a feature; every genuinely new transform is a Rust change in the main repo. That is the correct trade at single-author stage but caps community contribution if the tool ever grows users. (skeptic-found downside: The removal is not as total as "removed entirely" claims, and the seam matters. theme.rs (crates/core/src/render/theme.rs, lines 40-46) still silently reads _extensions/<name>/theme.css when theme: is a bare name, with no manifest, no did-you-mean, no test coverage, and a silent fall-back to default on a miss. That is a live, undocumented, data-only extension point that both contradicts the "no per-doc _extensions read" framing and sits oddly against the STRICT clean-break stance, where an unknown key like filters: or format: x-html is flagged but an unknown bare theme name is quietly ignored. A dead ext() helper in crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs that still writes _extension.yml manifests also survives with zero callers. None of this breaks the recommendation; it actually proves the "data-only revival" path already half-exists, but the entry should own that instead of claiming a clean sweep. Separately, the entry understates its own strictness: today there is zero user-extensible surface at all, since even the kept shortcodes (embed/video/input) are compiled-in, so the data-only revival is purely hypothetical.)
- **Invariant check:** Reinforces HTML-only (format-extensions cannot smuggle in new output targets), preserves the warm-server/no-per-edit-cost model (no per-doc manifest scan), and keeps the corpus as arbiter (nothing renders that the corpus does not pin). No effect on click-to-source or the read-only surface.

### D150. Whether a single author can define a custom shortcode without a Rust change: revive the data-only `shortcodes:` template map in config (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Any user drops a Lua shortcode into `_extensions/` and immediately has `{{< myshortcode arg >}}`; the community ships `{{< youtube >}}`, `{{< fa >}}`, `{{< kbd >}}`, etc. as installable extensions.
- **Critique:** Taliesin's set is closed to `embed`/`video`/`input`; anything else (a YouTube embed, an icon, a badge) requires a Rust PR and a release. For a tool whose whole thesis is a fast personal authoring loop, needing to recompile the binary to add `{{< youtube ID >}}` is a real ergonomic gap, and 'unknown shortcode' warnings turn a reasonable author want into a diagnostic.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's shortcodes are not text substitution, they are Lua programs that run inside the Pandoc pipeline, and that is the whole point. A Quarto shortcode receives (a) the target format, so one `{{< video >}}` emits an iframe for HTML and a poster-link for PDF/docx; (b) document and project metadata, so `{{< meta >}}` / `{{< var >}}` can read config; and (c) it returns Pandoc AST, not a raw string, so its output re-enters cross-ref numbering, further shortcode expansion, and downstream filters. That is exactly what a MULTI-FORMAT, MULTI-USER tool needs: it lets thousands of users add capabilities the maintainer never imagined without waiting on a maintainer release, and it degrades gracefully across output targets. The strongest single point: a real programmable extension point has no expressiveness cliff. The moment an author wants conditional logic (the built-in `video`'s own `dark=` two-source behavior is a perfect example), Lua handles it and a data-only template map cannot. Quarto chose the general mechanism precisely because the interesting shortcodes are the ones that need logic, and building the trivial ones on top of a powerful primitive costs nothing extra.
- **Taliesin today:** No user-defined shortcodes. render_shortcode matches only the three built-in names; everything else falls through to a located 'unknown shortcode' warning. Notably the removed extension system ALREADY contained a data-only template mechanism (`shortcodes:` map name -> HTML template with `{{1}}`/`{{2}}` positional and `{{key}}` named substitution, collapsed to one line); only the extension-LOADING wrapper was deleted, not the idea.
- **Proposed better:** Add a `shortcodes:` map to `_site.yml` (and/or front matter): name -> an HTML or Markdown template string with `${1}`/`${key}` interpolation, expanded in the existing pre-parse pass and collapsed to one line to stay line-preserving. Pure data, no code execution. Validate declared names against the closed built-in set (no shadowing) and HTML-escape interpolated values by default. Pin with a `corpus/shortcodes/custom.qmd`.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry but sharpen it into a strict, HTML-only, corpus-pinned template map. Concretely: (1) Scope templates to HTML only (drop 'or Markdown') and keep the one-line-collapse line-preserving guarantee. (2) Interpolate with a single-pass tokenizer over `${1}`/`${key}` (not ascending `String::replace`), and DIAGNOSE every unfilled or unknown placeholder with a located, did-you-mean warning so the feature matches Taliesin's strict-no-silent-unknowns identity instead of the removed mechanism's silent pass-through. `${...}` over the old `{{...}}` is the right call since it avoids colliding with the `{{< >}}` delimiter. (3) HTML-escape interpolated args by default as correctness hygiene, state plainly that it is not a security boundary (single-author, no untrusted input) and that attribute/URL contexts still need care, and offer a raw opt-out only if a real need appears. (4) Validate declared names against the full reserved set embed/video/input/include (no shadowing) plus duplicate detection, and bless `shortcodes:` in KNOWN_KEYS + the generated schema. (5) Pin with a corpus doc built around a REUSE-heavy case (an icon shortcode used many times) so the DRY win is the visible justification, and note in the doc that one-off embeds are still better served by raw HTML. Frame the entry as 'data-only is the RIGHT answer for a single-format single-author tool because Quarto's Lua machinery exists to serve multi-format polymorphism and a shared ecosystem, both of which Taliesin deliberately dropped', not as ecosystem parity.
- **Tradeoffs:** Reintroduces a small config surface and a template-injection review point (escaping, `${...}` grammar, arg validation). It is strictly less expressive than Lua (no logic, no metadata reads beyond args, no block composition), which is the point but will disappoint anyone wanting conditional/loop logic. (skeptic-found downside: The feature sits in an awkward middle that the entry undersells. (1) Expressiveness cliff: a data-only map handles exactly the cases (youtube, fa, kbd) that a single author can ALSO satisfy with a one-line raw-HTML snippet or an editor abbreviation (raw inline HTML is already passed through the block model with its own id/sourcepos), and it fails at exactly the cases (the `dark=` conditional video, composed blocks) where a real extension point would earn its keep. The single-author thesis that justifies the whole tool also removes the value multiplier (one Lua file shared by thousands) that makes community shortcodes worth the machinery, so the honest win is DRY across many call sites of a fixed template, not parity with Quarto's ecosystem. (2) Strict-diagnostics gap: the revived mechanism used naive `String::replace` with no diagnostic on an unfilled or misspelled placeholder, so a typo'd `${nmae}` or a `${3}` with two args ships literal `${...}` into the page. That silently contradicts Taliesin's defining strict-validation ethos (did-you-mean, no silent unknowns) and must be fixed, not inherited. Also `${1}` before `${10}` corrupts under ascending naive replace; it needs a real single-pass interpolator. (3) Escaping is context-blind: 'HTML-escape by default' is correct for text nodes but insufficient for the attribute and URL contexts these shortcodes actually target (`src=\"...${1}\"`, `class=\"fa-${1}\"`), and since a single-author tool has NO untrusted input, the escaping is correctness/hygiene, not the security boundary the entry frames it as. (4) 'HTML or Markdown template' conflicts with 'collapse to one line': collapsing newlines to spaces destroys block Markdown, so templates must be HTML-only (as the original was) or inline-only. (5) It re-adds the config-to-pre-parse plumbing just deleted in f5239cb and forces an edit to the drift-locked KNOWN_KEYS/schema; small, but it re-couples render to config. (6) The reserved-name set must include `include` (resolved in an earlier pass, not a `render_shortcode` built-in), not just embed/video/input.)
- **Invariant check:** Data-only, so no untrusted code path and no new output format (HTML-only intact). Line-preserving expansion keeps click-to-source and incremental swap valid. Ships pinned by a corpus doc (corpus-plus-roadmap). Preview stays read-only. Keeps the Markdown/`{{< >}}` substrate.

### D151. Provide metadata/variable interpolation shortcodes ({{< meta >}} / {{< var >}}) for DRY authoring (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `{{< meta some.key >}}` interpolates a front-matter value into the body, `{{< var key >}}` reads a project `_variables.yml`, and `{{< env VAR >}}` reads an environment variable, so a version string, product name, or release date lives in one place and is referenced everywhere.
- **Critique:** Taliesin has none of these, so an author repeating a version number, dataset size, or title across a document must hand-edit every occurrence, and there is no single source of truth for a value that also appears in front matter. This is a common, low-glamour authoring need that Markdown alone cannot serve.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's meta/var/env is not a bolt-on, it is the natural payoff of its architecture. Quarto sits on Pandoc, whose document model already carries an arbitrary, nested metadata tree, and it already layers a project config plane (_variables.yml, _metadata.yml, profile-merged front matter). Given that infrastructure exists for other reasons, exposing it back into the body via {{< meta dotted.key >}} / {{< var key >}} is nearly free and composes with Quarto's templating and multi-format output (the same version string flows into HTML, PDF, and DOCX from one source). Because Quarto deliberately tolerates arbitrary metadata keys, meta has a real home for custom scalars (product name, dataset size), which is exactly the ergonomic that makes it useful, and env has a legitimate CI/CD use (inject a git SHA or build number at pipeline time) that is reproducible within that pipeline even if not across machines. So each of the three is a coherent, low-cost consequence of an arbitrary-metadata, multi-format, project-config design, not an accident.
- **Taliesin today:** Not built. Grep confirms no `meta`/`var`/`env` shortcode; only `embed`/`video`/`input`/`include`. Front matter is available as the leading `---` block but the shortcode pass currently runs before comrak extracts it, so nothing reads it back into the body.
- **Proposed better:** Add `{{< meta dotted.key >}}` (reads the doc's own front matter) and `{{< var key >}}` (reads a project `_variables.yml`), expanded in the same pre-parse pass. Cheaply parse just the front-matter block first so `meta` has values; a missing key becomes a located warning, not a silent blank. Defer `{{< env >}}` (portability/secrets risk) or gate it behind an explicit allowlist. Pin with a corpus doc exercising a front-matter round-trip.
- **Revised recommendation:** Ship it, but reprioritize and tighten. (1) Lead with {{< var key >}} reading a project _variables.yml, since that namespace is exempt from the closed-key validator and is the correct home for the DRY custom scalars the critique cites (version, dataset size, product name); define its behavior in single-file mode (sibling _variables.yml or simply site-only) and wire _variables.yml into the dev-server file watcher so live preview re-renders on edit. (2) Scope {{< meta dotted.key >}} to the doc's own front matter for echoing KNOWN identity keys, and, to make custom values usable without tripping the validator, add ONE sanctioned validator-exempt bag whose immediate children are not linted (mirror how format: sub-keys are already exempt, e.g. a params: block), so authors have a first-class home for custom metadata meta can read. (3) Implement via the existing frontmatter::front_matter_block helper (no new ordering work needed). (4) Guard non-scalar and multi-line values: warn (located) and do not interpolate, preserving one-line-in-one-line-out and thus click-to-source. (5) Decide escaping explicitly and default to safe: treat the value as literal text (escape Markdown-active characters) unless an author opts into raw. (6) Keep env deferred/gated as proposed. (7) Pin a corpus doc that exercises a known-key meta echo, a var round-trip, a missing-key located warning, and a multi-line-value rejection.
- **Tradeoffs:** Introduces an ordering wrinkle (front matter must be parsed before body expansion), and `var`/`_variables.yml` adds one config file. `env` is deliberately excluded/gated because reading arbitrary environment into a rendered page is a footgun and hurts build reproducibility. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter inverts the priority of the two mechanisms and misses why. Taliesin's clean-break strict validator (frontmatter.rs KNOWN_KEYS is a CLOSED set; validate_front_matter flags every unknown top-level key with a did-you-mean warning) means a custom scalar like `version:` or `product:` in front matter TRIPS the validator. So {{< meta ... >}} works cleanly only for the ~15 already-known identity keys (title, subtitle, author, date, description), which is the narrow case of echoing the title into the body, not the DRY case the critique actually cites (a version number or dataset size repeated across a doc). Those custom values have NO validator-clean home in front matter.
