That makes {{< var >}} reading a separate _variables.yml namespace the MORE important half, not the add-on, because _variables.yml sidesteps the closed-key-set check entirely. Three further gaps: (1) the invariant_check overstates 'one line in, one line out' as unconditional, but a YAML block scalar (`key: |` literal or `>` folded) yields a multi-line value whose interpolation injects newlines mid-line and breaks the line-preserving source map, so the implementation must reject/flatten non-scalar and multi-line values with a warning; (2) escaping semantics are undecided: because expansion is pre-parse into the Markdown buffer, an interpolated value is parsed AS Markdown, so a filename with underscores italicizes and a value with backticks or raw HTML is interpreted, which is a footgun for values meant literally; (3) for live preview, editing _variables.yml must be wired into the notify file watcher or the var interpolation goes stale, and 'var' has no defined home in single-file (non-site) mode.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure text interpolation into HTML/Markdown, still line-preserving (one line in, one line out), so click-to-source holds. No output-format change (HTML-only). Data-only, no code execution. Read-only preview unaffected. Corpus-pinned per roadmap. (possible violation flagged: No fixed invariant (HTML-only, read-only preview, Markdown/shortcode syntax retained, block-level incremental, warm server, corpus-pinned) is violated: meta/var are new shortcode NAMES inside the already-sanctioned {{< >}} syntax, data-only with no code execution and no write-back. The one real invariant risk is click-to-source: line-preservation holds ONLY for single-line scalar values, so the implementation MUST guard against multi-line/block-scalar YAML values (warn and skip, do not inject) or it breaks the sourcepos map. Separately, note a design-commitment tension (not one of the listed hard invariants): {{< meta >}} over custom keys collides with the strict clean-break front-matter validator, which is why var/_variables.yml should lead.)

### D152. Deliberately offer no user filter API (arbitrary AST transforms); keep every transform first-party Rust (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `filters:` runs arbitrary Lua (and JSON) filters over the Pandoc AST, with `at: pre-quarto`/`post-quarto` ordering. This is Quarto's deepest hook: crossref, callouts, and most first-party features are themselves filters, and users write their own to rewrite any node.
- **Critique:** Lua filters are Quarto's most powerful extension point and its most fragile: they run untrusted code, ordering between filters is a frequent source of surprising bugs, they break across Quarto/Pandoc versions, and they operate on an AST with no notion of the author's source line. A source-mapped, incrementally-diffed live view cannot safely expose an arbitrary AST-rewrite hook without losing the very block-id/sourcepos guarantees that make it special.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Filters are not a wart, they are the load-bearing generalization that makes Quarto's own crossref and callouts AND a whole `quarto add` community ecosystem share ONE dogfooded mechanism, so a user's extension has exactly the same power as a maintainer's feature (no second-class citizen). Because a filter transforms the Pandoc AST, one filter is authored once and applies across every output format (HTML, LaTeX, docx, ePub): that is the correct abstraction for a multi-format batch publisher, which is Quarto's actual design target, not a live source-mapped editor. `at: pre-quarto`/`post-quarto` is explicit pipeline-ordering control (a mitigation, not only a source, of ordering bugs), and the 'untrusted code' worry is really the ordinary trust model of any deliberately-installed build dependency (npm/cargo). The critique's 'no notion of source line' point judges Quarto against a goal it never adopted.
- **Taliesin today:** No filter API and no `filters:` key anywhere (verified). Every transform is first-party Rust that emits blocks carrying data-block-id + data-sourcepos: `:::` divs (divs.rs), figures (figure.rs), citations/xref (cite.rs), theorems, deck. This is intrinsic to the architecture, not an omission.
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line: do NOT add a server-side AST-filter runtime. Offer the two-tier substitute instead, a DATA tier (declarative template shortcodes, sibling decision) for content injection, and a CLIENT tier (the `taliEnhancers` DOM registry, sibling decision) for behavior. If an author repeatedly needs a structural transform, promote it to first-party Rust pinned by a corpus doc rather than opening a plugin seam.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the conclusion (refuse an ARBITRARY server-side AST-filter runtime): it is correct and Taliesin already embodies it. But sharpen three things. (1) Flag the dependency: the DATA tier (user-definable template shortcodes) is not built (shortcodes are a fixed built-in set), so today the only real escape hatch is the CLIENT tier, and the entry's 'we offer a substitute' claim is partly a promise. (2) Name the CLIENT tier's own limit: taliEnhancers-injected structure is sourcepos-blind and un-clickable, so it is a weaker hatch, not a full substitute. (3) Correct the invariant argument, which currently overclaims: refusing an ARBITRARY AST rewrite is genuinely sourcepos-driven, but a CONSTRAINED block-to-blocks transform whose outputs inherit the input block's data-sourcepos by construction (exactly how first-party callout/figure wrappers already work) would NOT break sourcepos totality. The honest reasons to still refuse a constrained seam are pragmatic (API-surface stability, warm-loop performance and sandbox safety, single-author ROI), not invariant safety. Framing it that way keeps a future constrained, corpus-pinned seam an open option instead of foreclosing it on an invariant claim that only covers the arbitrary case. Impact medium, confidence high.
- **Tradeoffs:** The extensibility ceiling is real: a transform Taliesin has not built (say, wrapping every table in a custom widget) has no user-space escape hatch and must wait for a core change. That is a genuine loss of power versus Quarto, accepted to keep the invariants total. (skeptic-found downside: The entry oversells its 'two-tier substitute'. The CLIENT tier (taliEnhancers) only mutates already-mounted DOM, so any STRUCTURE it injects carries no data-sourcepos and is invisible to click-to-source and to the block diff: it is invariant-safe (never writes source, runs post-mount, has teardown/reset) but a strictly weaker, source-map-blind hatch, not a true substitute for a structural transform. And the DATA tier it leans on (user-definable template shortcodes) does not exist yet: today's shortcodes are a fixed built-in set (embed/video/input), unknown ones are left verbatim with a warning. So the entry currently rests on an unlanded sibling proposal plus 'the author will write Rust', a single-author bottleneck it frames as a timeless virtue rather than a scope-contingent one.)
- **Invariant check:** An arbitrary AST hook would threaten data-block-id/data-sourcepos totality (the corpus-enforced contract) and click-to-source; refusing it protects them. No new output format. Warm-loop and read-only surface preserved. The proposed substitutes are themselves invariant-safe.

### D153. Treat the re-mount-aware client enhancer registry (taliEnhancers) as the public behavior-extension contract (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Client behavior comes from format JS plus raw script injection (revealjs plugins, `include-after-body`). None of it is designed around a live incremental preview, because Quarto reloads the whole page on every edit, so a Quarto JS hook only needs to run once at load.
- **Critique:** Because Quarto has no live block-swap, its client scripts assume a one-shot DOMContentLoaded world; anything that decorated the DOM must be manually re-run after dynamic changes. Taliesin's incremental preview re-mounts individual blocks, so a naive load-once script silently stops decorating swapped-in content. That mismatch is exactly the failure the liquid-glass extension hit.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's full-reload model is deliberate and coherent, not an oversight. (1) Quarto targets N output formats (HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs, epub); its extension value lives at the Pandoc/Lua/shortcode BUILD layer, so most extensions transform content at compile time and never touch runtime DOM, meaning a run-once client model costs them nothing. (2) A full page reload guarantees every third-party library sees a fresh DOM exactly once, so unmodified, non-idempotent libraries (chart libs, tooltip libs, highlighters that append nodes and register global listeners) work with zero author discipline. An idempotent-enhancer contract inverts this: it requires every decorator to be re-run-safe, which is HARDER for exactly the broad universe of off-the-shelf libraries. (3) Full reload needs no re-mount contract, no teardown/leak management, and no stale-partial-DOM edge cases, and behaves identically in preview and final output. Quarto trades preview latency (a reload) for client simplicity and maximal library compatibility, the right trade when the product is author-once-render-to-many with a large extension ecosystem. Taliesin only pays for a re-mount contract because it chose block-level incremental preview, which is a different, narrower product bet.
- **Taliesin today:** `window.taliEnhancers.register(fn)` (assets/js/code-enhance/01-registry.js): an idempotent `fn(root)` that runs after every (re)mount in preview, on DOMContentLoaded in static build, and once immediately on late registration. Mermaid, lightbox, scrolly, walkthrough, and the `{js}` reactive runtime all register through it; a `qmdEnhancers` back-compat alias exists. This survived the extension purge intentionally.
- **Proposed better:** Formalize and document `taliEnhancers` as THE public client extension contract: authors load their own JS via `include-after-body` and register an idempotent enhancer, indistinguishable from core's. Add a short reference page and a corpus doc that registers a trivial enhancer and asserts it re-runs after a block swap, so the re-mount contract is pinned, not just conventional.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry (Taliesin genuinely is better here and the mechanism is real and already validator-sanctioned via include-after-body), but sharpen the plan on four points. (1) Ship a paired unmount hook OR explicitly scope the contract to stateless, idempotent DOM decoration and document that resource-holding extensions must use the {js} invalidation path, not the enhancer registry; do not market it as THE complete client contract while it is mount-only. (2) Fix the pin: re-run-after-block-swap is RUNTIME browser behavior and cannot be asserted by cargo test -p taliesin-core (static render). Split it: a JS/registry unit test for idempotency + late-register catch-up + re-run semantics, a browser harness for the real block swap (like the vscode relay / live-edit-bench), and a corpus doc only for the narrow fact that the include-after-body enhancer script is EMITTED. (3) Document the performance contract (root = whole #tali-root, re-scanned every op-burst, guard with a data-attribute) and the static-vs-live root difference (document.body vs #tali-root). (4) To honor Taliesin's strict/did-you-mean identity, surface a thrown enhancer in the dev-menu diagnostic, not only console.error. With these, the entry is accurate rather than optimistic.
- **Tradeoffs:** It is behavior-only (DOM decoration), not a content/structure hook, and enhancers must be written idempotent or they double-apply on re-mount; that discipline is on the author. It also runs author JS in the page, but only JS the author themselves added, not fetched third-party code. (skeptic-found downside: The registry is MOUNT-ONLY: it exposes register(fn) but no paired teardown/unmount. Confirmed in code that even Taliesin's own {js} runtime needed a SEPARATE teardown path (window.taliJs.teardown, driven by invalidation and called from client.js teardownJs), NOT taliEnhancers. So calling taliEnhancers THE public client extension contract oversells it: it is only half the lifecycle. A third-party enhancer that attaches a ResizeObserver, timer, listener, or WebGL context to a block will LEAK on every edit (its block-id changes, the node is replaced, nothing cleans up), which is exactly the leak teardownJs was written to prevent for {js}. Second missed cost: root passed to enhancers is the WHOLE #tali-root (client.js:32), re-scanned on every op-burst; the idempotency data-attribute guard prevents double-WORK but not the O(document) re-SCAN, so N author enhancers times doc size times edit frequency is a real cliff the tradeoffs section omits. Third: root differs between modes (live gets #tali-root, static gets document.body), an inconsistency a formal contract must pin down. Fourth: indistinguishable-from-core is aspirational; core's enhancers were written idempotent on purpose, and a naive author wrapping a non-idempotent third-party lib double-applies on the FIRST re-mount, the precise failure Quarto's reload avoids for free.)
- **Invariant check:** Client-only and read-only: an enhancer decorates rendered DOM, never writes back to source, so the single-editing-surface holds. It is the mechanism that KEEPS behavior working under block-level incremental swap. HTML-only and warm-loop untouched; corpus pin brings it under the regression net.

### D154. No code-install path: every executed byte is the compiled binary plus the author's own repo (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `quarto add owner/repo` and `quarto use template` fetch and run arbitrary Lua filters, shortcodes, and JS from a GitHub repo with no signing, no lockfile, and only git-tag-level versioning; trust is 'you ran code from a stranger's repo'.
- **Critique:** This is a real supply-chain surface: an extension update can change behavior or exfiltrate on next render, pins are by convention, and there is no integrity check. For a personal authoring tool that surface buys little and risks much.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a general, multi-format publisher for a large, heterogeneous community, and the long tail of needs (per-journal templates, institutional themes, RevealJS plugins, domain notation filters) is genuinely unbounded and domain-specific: curating all of it into one binary is impossible, so an extension mechanism is the only tractable way to cover it. Its trust model is not a new or reckless boundary; it matches the scientific-computing stack its users already inhabit (pip, CRAN, GitHub R packages, TeX packages, LaTeX \write18, Pandoc Lua filters all execute third-party code). Critically, `quarto add owner/repo` VENDORS the extension into the project's `_extensions/` folder, which is committed to the project repo: the code is right there, diffable, code-reviewable, and pinned by your own git history exactly as strongly as any vendored dependency. It does NOT re-fetch or auto-update on each render; the code is static until you deliberately run `quarto update`. So the trust decision is a one-time explicit act at add-time (and again at explicit update-time), the extension is auditable in your own tree, and per-project pinning is effectively a git commit hash, not mere convention. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** There is no install command and no third-party code loading (removed in f5239cb). Behavior comes from the compiled binary; the only author-supplied code is JS the author themselves places via `include-after-body` and registers through `taliEnhancers`. Front-matter includes are path-traversal-guarded (safe_join) to the project root.
- **Proposed better:** Preserve this as an explicit design property: any future extensibility (template shortcodes, theme packs, metadata vars) must be DATA-only and in-repo, so 'what runs' stays exactly 'the signed binary + files you can see in git'. Make it a stated invariant so a future plugin proposal is measured against it.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the status (taliesin-already-better is verified: no add/install/use/update subcommand; extension loading removed in f5239cb; author code only via taliEnhancers + safe_join-guarded include files). REVISE three things. (1) Reframe the invariant from DATA-only to a PROVENANCE invariant: no install/add/use command and no remote or third-party code fetch, so every executed byte is either the compiled binary or a file the author authored and committed to the project, reviewed as their own source. This correctly includes the shipped author-JS path instead of contradicting it. Add the boundary to hold: that author code runs in the READ-ONLY preview (taliEnhancers, include-after-body/in-header text) and must never gain a path to write the .tmd source. (2) Fix the critique clause: drop or qualify exfiltrate on next render, because Quarto vendors extensions into committed _extensions/ and does not silently re-fetch per render; the fair, sharper criticism is the fetch-time gap (no signing, no integrity check when you add/update) plus the missing per-project lockfile, while acknowledging the vendored code is itself auditable and git-pinned. (3) Per corpus-plus-roadmap, pin the invariant with a guard test so it is enforced not merely stated: assert the CLI exposes no add/install/use subcommand and that a render performs no network fetch, alongside the existing strict-unknown-key rejection. Expand tradeoffs to name the own-code cross-project-reuse cost, not just no borrowing from strangers.
- **Tradeoffs:** The flip side of the closed-set and no-filter decisions: no ecosystem, no one-command feature install, and the author cannot borrow a stranger's transform without vendoring source. The safety is bought with reduced reach. (skeptic-found downside: The specific wording DATA-only is self-contradicting: Taliesin already ships an executable-code escape hatch the entry itself relies on (author JS via include-after-body text/file registered through taliEnhancers, verified in code-enhance/01-registry.js + qmd-js.js). That is arbitrary browser code, not data, so a literal DATA-only invariant would retroactively forbid the very mechanism cited as proof Taliesin is safer. The real property is provenance (no install command, no remote fetch; every executed byte is the binary or an author-authored, git-committed file), not a data-vs-code capability line. Also missed in tradeoffs: the absence of any extension concept costs the SINGLE author too, not just would-be borrowers, since there is no first-class way to share their own reusable theme/shortcode code across their blog + book + slides beyond manual copy, {{< include >}}, or a git submodule. And safe_join is a containment/portability nicety, not a trust boundary in a single-author threat model where the author trusts their own repo, so leaning on it in the trust story slightly overstates its role.)
- **Invariant check:** No untrusted execution keeps the warm-server/kernel model predictable and the build reproducible; data-only extensibility cannot introduce a new output target (HTML-only) or a write-back path (read-only surface). Consistent with keeping all capability corpus-pinned.

### D155. Reject format-as-extension; the format set is a closed enum, with theming as the only data-only remainder (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** low, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** A custom output format is an extension: `format: acm-pdf` (or `-html`) inherits a base format and bundles templates, SCSS, filters, and metadata, so a journal or house style ships as an installable format.
- **Critique:** Format-as-extension is inseparable from Quarto's multi-target compiler: it exists to parameterize LaTeX/Word/HTML variants. Most of its weight (templates for non-HTML targets, per-format filter stacks) is meaningless for an HTML-only tool and would only invite the multi-format complexity Taliesin exists to avoid.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Format-as-extension is Quarto's package manager for complete, reproducible house styles, and its core value is target-neutral rather than a LaTeX/Word artifact. Even restricted to HTML, a format bundles a theme (SCSS), Lua filters and shortcodes, DEFAULT METADATA (toc, section numbering, citation style, code-tools), and pinned dependencies into ONE versioned, installable unit an author selects with a single `format:` key and updates via `quarto update`. Quarto ships real HTML-only format extensions (journal HTML templates, closeread scrollytelling), proving the mechanism packages browser behavior, not just print targets. The win a per-project stylesheet cannot match: discovery plus versioning plus one-word inheritance across many documents and many authors, so a whole community converges on a maintained look-and-behavior without each person re-wiring includes. A stylesheet gives you the look; a format gives you the look, the behavior, the default settings, and a distribution channel as one named thing. (skeptic judged the critique unfair or a strawman)
- **Taliesin today:** `DocFormat` is a closed 2-variant enum (`Html`, `Reveal`); book/site are handled at the site layer, not as formats. Extension themes and `resolve_theme_layers` were removed with the extension system. Author styling is served data-only today: the `css:` front-matter key (doc_includes.rs) plus the `--tali-*` CSS-variable themes (theme.rs).
- **Proposed better:** Keep formats closed. Treat the legitimate remainder, house-style theming, as a data-only concern already covered by `css:` + `--tali-*` variables; if authors want shareable looks, ship them as a documented convention of a variable-override stylesheet referenced from config, never as a code-bearing format extension. No new machinery needed.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the decision: formats are a closed enum, not extensions, and this directly enforces HTML-only. Taliesin already matches it (DocFormat = Html|Reveal, model.rs:113-120), so "taliesin-already-better" stands. But sharpen the entry text on three points. (1) Correct the factual claim: extension THEMES were NOT fully removed; theme.rs:43-47 still reads `_extensions/<name>/theme.css`. Decide explicitly between documenting-plus-corpus-pinning that surviving data-only path or deleting it for a genuine clean break, rather than asserting removal. (2) Recognize the convention already ships end to end: per-doc `css:` front matter AND a project-wide `_site.yml` `css:` key (site/mod.rs:276) already inject a house-style stylesheet, so "no new machinery needed" is true and understated. Reframe the deliverable as "document plus corpus-pin the existing css/theme paths," not "invent a convention." (3) Stop equating "house style" with "theming." Acknowledge that Taliesin deliberately gives up packaging default front-matter settings and shortcodes as a selectable unit (fine at single-author scope), instead of claiming the legitimate remainder is fully covered. Net: verdict is keep-formats-closed and already-better, with the justification corrected and the honest capability caveat stated.
- **Tradeoffs:** No way to package a named, inheritable 'format' others select by one key; a shared house style is a stylesheet the author wires up per project rather than a one-word `format:` value. Acceptable given HTML-only, but less turnkey than Quarto's named formats. (skeptic-found downside: Two things the drafter missed. (1) A factual error that cuts both ways: `taliesin_current` says extension themes were removed, but `crates/core/src/render/theme.rs:43-47` STILL resolves a bare `theme: <name>` to `_extensions/<name>/theme.css` as a live, data-only path. So the "documented theme-pack convention" the proposal wants to ship is roughly already implemented (via that resolver plus the per-doc `css:` and the project-wide `_site.yml` `css:` key at site/mod.rs:276), it is just undocumented and un-corpus-pinned; and a supposedly-removed system left a live tendril that muddies the clean-break story. (2) The bigger conceptual gap: a Quarto format packages default SETTINGS (numbered sections, toc, citation style, figure numbering) plus filters and shortcodes, not just CSS. The `css:`/`--tali-*`/`_extensions/theme.css` paths carry only look, never default front-matter. The entry quietly narrows "house style" down to "theming" so the remainder fits the existing data-only path, then calls it fully covered. For a single-author tool that loss is acceptable and deliberate, but it is a real capability gap, not merely "less turnkey" as the tradeoffs field frames it.)
- **Invariant check:** Directly enforces HTML-only (the closed enum is the guardrail against a second compiler path). Theming stays data-only (no untrusted code), preview read-only, click-to-source/incremental untouched. A theme-pack convention would be corpus-pinnable.

## Diagnostics, validation, and error UX

### D156. Make `check` a static document publish-gate, not an install doctor (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** `quarto check` inspects the INSTALLATION: it prints versions and probes Pandoc, the Deno/TypeScript runtime, the R+knitr engine, the Python+Jupyter engine, and TinyTeX/LaTeX, reporting whether each works. It is an environment doctor. Quarto has no single command that statically lints a document's xrefs, links, anchors, or front matter as a pre-publish gate; those surface (if at all) only during a full `quarto render`.
- **Critique:** The name `quarto check` invites the expectation of a document linter, but it only answers 'is my toolchain installed'. A broken `@fig-` reference, a dead relative link, a duplicate heading id, or an alt-less image ships silently in a green build; you find them by eye or in production. There is no fast, non-executing 'is this document publishable' gate.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** The critique's central claim is accurate and holds: `quarto check` is genuinely an installation doctor (versions + Pandoc + Deno/TS + R/knitr + Python/Jupyter + TinyTeX probes), and Quarto has no fast, non-executing command that statically gates a document's xrefs/links/anchors/front matter before publish. Two overstatements to keep the steelman honest: (1) a broken `@fig-` reference is not fully silent in Quarto, it renders a visible `?fig-x` placeholder and emits a stderr warning, so it degrades rather than vanishing; (2) Quarto DOES validate YAML front matter and `_quarto.yml` against shipped JSON schemas during render and can error, so front matter is not entirely unchecked. The strongest case FOR Quarto's choice: it targets a genuinely different and, for a multi-format tool, more common failure. Quarto renders PDF/Word/HTML/ePub across an enormous toolchain surface, and the number-one new-user failure is 'render won't run at all' (missing LaTeX, wrong kernel), which no document linter can diagnose. Naming that triage tool `check` is defensible because in Quarto the RENDER is the document gate: `quarto render` executes cells and with `execute: error: false` (default) a code-cell exception fails the build, catching a whole defect class (runtime execution errors) that a static linter cannot. So Quarto's `check` (environment) plus `render` (execution + content gate) is a coherent two-command split, not an oversight.
- **Taliesin today:** `taliesin check <file|dir>` (crates/server/src/check.rs) renders in memory with no kernel and runs the whole diagnostics/ battery: xrefs, duplicate heading ids, internal + cross-page anchors, local assets/media/links, the {js} reactive graph (dangling inputs + cycles), a11y (heading skips, unnamed interactives, alt-less images), KaTeX render failures, citations-without-bibliography, and YAML parse + unknown-key lint. It exits non-zero on any finding and is corpus-pinned by check_superset_has_no_false_positives_across_corpus. 'A green check means publishable.'
- **Proposed better:** Hold the design and lean in: `check` is the marquee CI / pre-publish command. Keep every diagnostics/ validator reachable from it (already true) and document the 'green = publishable' contract as a load-bearing promise, not an incidental tool.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep and promote `check` as the marquee CI / pre-publish gate (Taliesin is genuinely better than Quarto here, verified: cmd_check renders in-memory with no kernel, runs the full diagnostics battery, xrefs, dup heading ids, in-page + cross-page anchors, local assets/media/links, {js} reactive dangling-inputs + cycles, a11y heading-skips/unnamed-interactives/alt-less-images, KaTeX render failures, citations-without-bibliography, YAML parse + unknown-key lint, exits non-zero on any finding, and is corpus-pinned by check_superset_has_no_false_positives_across_corpus). But REVISE the documented contract: replace the flat 'green = publishable' promise with 'green = statically publishable: no static defects' and publish an explicit non-coverage list (runtime code-cell execution, ids produced only at runtime, external link liveness, visual/layout correctness). Document the honest two-stage CI gate: `check` for the fast static pass, `build` (which executes cells / replays freeze) for the execution pass, so the promise you make load-bearing is one the tool actually keeps. Keep the zero-false-positive corpus pin as the ratchet. Minor framing fix: findings are located as file:line that feed EDITOR navigation, not browser Alt-click click-to-source, so describe the reinforcement accurately. This turns the entry from a naive 'we already won' into a defensible, honestly-scoped promise.
- **Tradeoffs:** The promise is only as strong as the validator set; a defect class with no validator (see the value-domain-validation entry) silently weakens 'publishable'. Keeping zero false positives across a growing corpus is ongoing work. (skeptic-found downside: The execution gap, which the drafter's tradeoffs section misses entirely. `check` is deliberately static and kernel-free (crates/server/src/check.rs line 1: 'static, kernel-free document linting'), so a green `check` does NOT mean the document actually renders: a `{python}`/`{r}` cell that throws, a cold build with no `_freeze` cache to replay, or a broken kernel are all outside the gate. The word 'publishable' overclaims by conflating static publishability with a fully executed render. Quarto's render-as-gate model actually catches these because it runs the cells. Concretely: the anchors validator (crates/core/src/diagnostics/anchors.rs) deliberately skips xref targets that 'may target an id emitted only by code-cell execution (which static check does not run)', so a cross-reference that would only resolve at runtime is neither verified nor flagged, it just passes green. Also out of scope by design and worth naming in the contract: external link liveness (validate_local_links explicitly never fetches http/mailto/absolute links, links.rs lines 63-64) and visual/layout correctness. So the honest contract is 'green check = no STATIC defects, statically publishable' not a flat 'publishable', and the marquee CI story should pair `check` (fast, static) with `build` (executes cells, catches the runtime class) as an explicit two-stage gate.)
- **Invariant check:** Pure read-only static analysis over the block model: no source writes, HTML-only, corpus-pinned, and every finding is located so it reinforces click-to-source.

### D157. Validate front matter against a CLOSED vocabulary with no Quarto-tolerance tier (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto validates front matter against a large, mostly-permissive JSON schema and can surface unknown-key warnings and even 'did you mean' hints (terminal and the VS Code YAML intelligence server). But the schema is a broad superset: many project-, format-, and passthrough keys are optional or forwarded to Pandoc, so a fair number of typo'd or unsupported keys pass without error, and validation is non-fatal.
- **Critique:** Because the vocabulary is huge and tolerant by design (Quarto aims to accept a superset and forward the rest), a key Quarto does not act on can sit in your front matter doing nothing, with no signal. The permissiveness that makes Quarto forgiving also makes silent no-ops common.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-format, extensible compiler, and its permissive-forward metadata policy is a requirement of that architecture, not laziness. Unknown top-level keys are forwarded to Pandoc as document metadata and template variables that custom templates and Lua filters legitimately consume; third-party extensions and each output format introduce their own keys; and a document may target formats or extensions not installed at lint time. Under project/profile/document layering, a key meaningless in one context is meaningful in another. A truly closed vocabulary would break the filter/template/extension ecosystem that IS Quarto's value proposition, and against thousands of users and arbitrary formats a strict closed set would generate false positives that block legitimate workflows, a worse failure mode than a silent no-op. Quarto still layers a schema plus did-you-mean over the keys it owns (strongest in the editor YAML intelligence), capturing much of the benefit without foreclosing extensibility. So permissive-forward is the only coherent policy for an open compiler: Quarto's choice is correct FOR QUARTO. The critique is fair because it never denies Quarto validates or offers hints; it correctly pins the silent-no-op to the superset/passthrough design. Its only slight unfairness is framing that permissiveness as a weakness rather than an architectural necessity, but the entry's quarto_does field concedes the design rationale, so it is steelmanned, not a strawman.
- **Taliesin today:** frontmatter.rs defines a closed KNOWN_KEYS set plus closed child sets (EXECUTE/LISTING/ABOUT/HERO/PROSE_LINT/THEOREM). validate_front_matter flags EVERY unknown top-level key and every unknown immediate child, with a Levenshtein-<=2 did-you-mean, located to the source line. It is a clean break: no Quarto-tolerance tier, any non-Taliesin key warns. It runs on every render (render/mod.rs:209), so it surfaces live in preview, not only in `check`.
- **Proposed better:** Hold the line; the clean break is right for a single-author tool. Keep the const the single source of truth: it already generates the JSON Schema and drives the validator, drift-locked by the schema bless test (schema.rs).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the closed-vocabulary clean break: it is genuinely better than Quarto for a single-author HTML-only tool, because none of Quarto's permissive-forward justifications (Pandoc passthrough, third-party template variables, uninstalled formats, open extension metadata) apply, so the closed set has near-zero legitimate false positives. Keep the const as the single, schema-bless-drift-locked source of truth. But sharpen the entry in two ways. (1) Scope the claim honestly: validation is total at the top level plus the six named nested blocks, NOT below that; state that `format:` subkeys and deeper structured children remain unlinted, so silent no-ops still exist in those regions. (2) Close the one region Taliesin (unlike Quarto) actually owns: since HTML is the only target and the deck engine is native, add a closed child set for `format: html:` (and the native deck block) so typos there get the same located did-you-mean, extend the schema bless test to cover it, and pin it with a new corpus document per corpus-plus-roadmap. Net: move from "hold the line" to "hold the line at the top, and push the same discipline into the format region Taliesin now fully owns," with the coverage claim scoped to the depth it truly reaches.
- **Tradeoffs:** A closed set means every new feature must add its key or it self-flags; forgetting is caught by tests/corpus but is friction. Authors migrating from Quarto see many warnings at once (intended, but noisy on first contact). (skeptic-found downside: The "clean break / any non-Taliesin key warns" framing overstates coverage. The closed set is total only at the top level and for six NAMED nested blocks (execute/listing/about/hero/prose-lint/theorems). Everything deeper is unlinted: `format:` subkeys entirely, plus structured children of `include-in-header:`, `author:` (affiliations), etc. I confirmed there is no FORMAT_KEYS/HTML_KEYS/DECK_KEYS set, so a typo inside `format: html:` (e.g. `tabel-of-contents: true`) is silently ignored with no did-you-mean, which is EXACTLY the Quarto silent-no-op the entry criticizes. The code comment justifies skipping `format:` because "an extension owns them," but that rationale is stale post-reveal-removal: HTML is the only output target and the deck engine is now native to core (deck::), so Taliesin owns every format option. This is therefore a closable gap Taliesin uniquely can close, not an inherent limit, and the drafter missed both the honesty gap (claiming totality it does not have) and the opportunity gap.)
- **Invariant check:** Warnings only, never blocks rendering; located for click-to-source; a single closed vocabulary layered ABOVE the kept YAML/Markdown substrate. HTML-only unaffected.

### D158. Make every diagnostic carry a did-you-mean AND a click-to-source location (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's YAML validator can include 'did you mean' suggestions and reports line numbers for YAML errors; the VS Code extension adds completion and hover. But most non-YAML diagnostics (Pandoc, knitr/Jupyter tracebacks, LaTeX) are opaque terminal text, and there is no universal 'click a warning to jump to its source line in my editor' because the browser preview is a separate rendered artifact.
- **Critique:** Suggestions and locations exist unevenly across Quarto's diagnostic sources, and the preview is a one-way rendered view: a terminal warning does not take you to the offending line; you read a number and navigate by hand.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's YAML validation is not a throwaway "can include did you mean": it is a schema-driven system. The whole config surface is described by JSON schemas, and the quarto-cli YAML intelligence turns those schemas into as-you-type completion, hover docs, AND did-you-mean, delivered as native editor diagnostics (squiggles) in the RStudio and VS Code LSP. That is arguably ahead of Taliesin on one real axis: the diagnostic appears IN the editor where the cursor is, live as you type, before any render, rather than in a browser panel after a save-and-rebuild round-trip. For non-YAML diagnostics (Pandoc, a Jupyter/knitr traceback, LaTeX), Quarto deliberately passes the underlying tool's error through verbatim rather than re-interpreting and re-locating it. That is a defensible fidelity choice: the traceback already names the failing cell and line, and faithfully re-mapping a kernel line through notebook conversion back to a source line across many languages and many output formats (PDF, Word, ePub, reveal, HTML) is lossy and fragile. Quarto also has no browser-to-editor bridge to click through because it is multi-format: when the artifact can be a PDF or a Word file, "click the rendered output to jump to source" is not generally realizable, so Quarto put navigation in the editor (the visual editor, LSP squiggles) instead of the preview. Its choice is coherent for a general multi-format compiler.
- **Taliesin today:** One shared unknown_key_message (frontmatter.rs) gives Levenshtein-<=2 did-you-mean across front-matter keys, cell options, callout kinds, input types, reactive input names (closest_owned), and CLI commands/flags. EVERY located Warning carries file:line and, in the preview, renders as a clickable row that fires gotoSource to the editor cursor (serve/mod.rs + client.js), plus a 2-line code frame (compute_diagnostics). It is the click-to-source invariant applied to diagnostics.
- **Proposed better:** Keep, and extend coverage as new value domains gain checks (value-domain entry). Ensure any new diagnostic source is constructed via Warning::at so it inherits click-to-source for free.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry as taliesin-already-better for validation/lint diagnostics (the unified Levenshtein-<=2 did-you-mean across front-matter, cell options, callout kinds, input types, reactive inputs, site config, and CLI, each rendered as a clickable located row, is real and Quarto has no browser-to-editor click-through). But sharpen three things. (a) Concede honestly that Quarto's schema-driven YAML LSP wins on the in-editor, as-you-type axis, and make the proposed extension: feed Taliesin's diagnostics INTO the editor via the VS Code companion as native LSP diagnostics/squiggles, not only as browser rows, so the finding lands where the cursor already is. (b) Close the one gap where the critique still bites Taliesin: extend Warning::at-style click-to-source to kernel tracebacks by parsing the kernel's reported line and offsetting it by the cell's sourcepos, so an execution error jumps to the exact failing .tmd line rather than the cell start. (c) Correct the copy: the code frame is currently only on the broken-YAML error, so either say so or extend with_frame to every located warning. Each addition must ship pinned by a corpus document. Keep the graceful-degradation and false-positive tradeoffs as written, and additionally note the misplaced-valid-key case (a real key at the wrong nesting level yields a misleading suggestion), which is more confusing than a plain near-neighbor.
- **Tradeoffs:** Levenshtein-<=2 occasionally suggests a near-neighbor that is not what the author meant; low harm since the key still renders. Click-to-source depends on the editor bridge being wired (VS Code companion), degrading gracefully to a plain located message otherwise. (skeptic-found downside: Two things the drafter glossed. (1) Locus and timing: Taliesin's diagnostics live in a browser dev panel and are recomputed only on save/rebuild (compute_diagnostics runs in the rebuild loop), so the finding is not where the author's eyes are (the editor) and appears only after a render round-trip, unlike Quarto's in-editor, as-you-type LSP squiggles. The entry frames this purely as Taliesin-better and never concedes the in-editor, pre-render axis where Quarto's schema LSP is genuinely ahead. (2) The claim "EVERY located Warning is click-to-source" quietly excludes the hardest, highest-value class: kernel execution tracebacks. Verified in code: a raising cell renders as a tali-error pre inside the cell's tali-output wrapper (exec.rs), surfaced by scanCellErrors (client.js) which only scrolls the preview to the cell; it is not a located did-you-mean row, and the traceback's internal line is never mapped back to the exact .tmd line, so click-to-source lands at the cell start at best. That is precisely the "opaque traceback" weakness the critique pins on Quarto, and Taliesin is only at rough parity there, not "better." Minor third point: the 2-line code frame is attached only to the broken-YAML front-matter error, not to every located warning, so "plus a 2-line code frame" overstates universality.)
- **Invariant check:** Navigates preview to editor only, never writes source; every finding located via data-sourcepos. Directly upholds the click-to-source invariant. HTML-only unaffected.

### D159. Surface warnings in the browser preview (panel + count badge + overlay), not just the terminal (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** high, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** During `quarto preview`, render warnings and cell errors go to the terminal / render log. The browser preview shows the rendered document; it does not surface a warning panel, a problem count, or a11y findings in the preview UI. You watch the terminal to know something is wrong.
- **Critique:** The signal (a warning) and the surface the author is looking at (the browser) are decoupled. On a live edit loop you can miss a broken include or a missing kernel because it scrolled past in the terminal.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's terminal-first choice has three real defenses. (1) Preview fidelity: Quarto is a multi-format engine and its preview is meant to be exactly the document that ships, so it deliberately injects almost nothing into the preview DOM (just a reload socket). A warning panel, badge, or a11y overlay would make the preview no longer WYSIWYG with the published HTML/PDF. Taliesin can afford preview-only chrome only because it renders HTML-only and strips CLIENT_JS from the build; Quarto declines that tradeoff on purpose. (2) One uniform diagnostic channel: the terminal/render log carries the full untruncated traceback, exit codes, and CI output in the same place, and it works headless. A browser badge is a lossy summary that helps nothing in CI. (3) The critique's 'you must watch the terminal' is a partial strawman for Quarto's PRIMARY workflows: in RStudio and the VS Code Quarto extension, render and cell errors ARE surfaced next to the editor (Render pane / Problems panel), i.e. exactly where you type, which is arguably a better locus than a panel inside the read-only browser. The gap Quarto genuinely leaves open is (a) advisory/a11y signals, which it surfaces nowhere, and (b) the bare-CLI + external-editor workflow, which is precisely Taliesin's target user.
- **Taliesin today:** Diagnostics are pushed over the websocket into a dev-menu panel (serve/mod.rs + client.js) with three live sources: server diagnostics (front-matter/include/kernel/render warnings), per-cell runtime errors scanned from the mounted DOM (.tali-error/.tali-js-error, each a button that scrolls to and flashes the cell), and a client-side a11y audit (including computed-CSS contrast the static pass cannot do). A collapsed dev pill shows an amber alert + count badge; a fatal render error overlays the last-good content and recovers on the next good save.
- **Proposed better:** Keep. Optionally unify severity presentation (see the JSON-diagnostic entry) so the badge can distinguish errors from advisories, and surface the same count in the build CLI summary line for preview/CI parity.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the entry: status taliesin-already-better is well-supported by code, and this is textbook 'richer browser behavior in a live HTML view'. Sharpen two things. (1) Adopt the severity split (badge/pill distinguishes hard errors like a broken include or crashed cell from advisories like a contrast miss), which is genuinely valuable because today a must-fix and a nice-to-fix look identical on the pill. (2) Reword the CLI-parity claim to be honest about asymmetry: surface only the build-COMPUTABLE subset (server diagnostics + Python cell errors + broken xrefs, which build.rs already counts as `problems`) in a non-strict success summary line, and state explicitly that the a11y/contrast audit and {js}-runtime errors are preview-only because they require a live browser. If true CI a11y parity is ever wanted, scope it as a SEPARATE, heavier feature (a headless-browser/axe-style audit pass), not as a free by-product of this entry. Add a corpus/test note that CLI-summary behavior is pinned by a build/CLI test, and keep the a11y scan debounced/idle so the diagnostic layer never taxes the warm incremental loop.
- **Tradeoffs:** The panel/badge is preview-only chrome that adds client JS which must stay lightweight. The DOM-scan for cell errors couples the panel to output markup conventions (.tali-error), which must be kept stable. (skeptic-found downside: The 'surface the same count in the build CLI summary for preview/CI parity' enhancement over-promises a parity that is physically impossible for two of the three preview sources. The client a11y/contrast audit runs in a live browser over computed CSS (getComputedStyle); there is no DOM and no computed style in the headless Rust build, so that dimension cannot be counted at build time at all. Likewise {js} reactive-cell errors surface as `.tali-js-error`, a class qmd-js.js creates at RUNTIME (lines 156, 269); the build's report_cell_errors only matches `class=\"tali-error\"` (Python cells baked into HTML), so {js} errors are invisible to the CLI by construction. The build count can therefore only ever be a strict subset (server diagnostics + Python cell errors + broken xrefs), never 'the same count'. Two smaller misses: (a) this is already partly done, build.rs tracks a `problems` count and `--strict` already prints it and fails on it, so the real gap is only a non-strict success summary line; and (b) a corpus .tmd render cannot pin a CLI stdout summary, so this enhancement needs a build/CLI test, not a corpus doc, which sits awkwardly with the 'corpus is the arbiter of done' mechanism.)
- **Invariant check:** Read-only browser surface; clicking a row navigates to source, never writes. This is exactly 'richer browser behavior in a live HTML view'. HTML-only unaffected. (possible violation flagged: No hard violation: the panel rows navigate via gotoSource and never write, the overlay only shows/dismisses, HTML-only and Markdown-substrate are untouched, and click-to-source is actively reused. One constraint to flag rather than a breach: the client a11y+contrast scan re-runs getComputedStyle over the whole mounted DOM after every render (client.js already notes at ~line 859 that the full audit is heavy and must stay debounced). Any 'richer severity / more scanning' direction must remain idle-scheduled/debounced or it regresses the block-level incremental + no-per-edit-cost warm loop, which IS a load-bearing goal. Also note the corpus-pinning mechanism mismatch above (CLI chrome is pinned by a build test, not a corpus render).)

### D160. Decide where `check` stops: static-only, no cell execution, no environment probe (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto splits the concerns: `quarto check` verifies the toolchain, and a real `quarto render` executes cells (halting on a cell error by default, since execute.error defaults to false) so runtime failures are caught only by actually running. There is no 'lint plus execute for CI without producing output' middle mode.
- **Critique:** For Taliesin, `check` is deliberately static and kernel-free, which is fast and deterministic but verifies neither that the Jupyter/R kernel is even available nor that this document's cells actually run. An author can get a green `check`, then have preview/build fail because ipykernel is missing or a cell raises. The 'publishable' promise has a hole around execution and environment.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's split is principled, not a gap. `quarto check` is a genuine environment doctor that also SMOKE-TESTS the compute stack: it runs a trivial render through each detected engine (Jupyter/knitr) to prove the machine can execute at all, a slow, stateful, once-per-setup question that does not belong bolted onto a per-document lint. `quarto render` then answers the separate per-document question by actually executing, and because `execute.error` defaults to false, a plain `quarto render` in CI already fails on any cell error, so Quarto DOES catch runtime failures in one command (the render command) with no extra mode. A "lint plus execute but discard output" middle mode would solve a non-problem in Quarto's model: the rendered artifact is the deliverable you want to inspect and deploy anyway, so throwing it away just adds a config axis for no gain. The deeper steelman the entry underweights: Taliesin already MATCHES Quarto's execution gate. `build --strict` executes cells, counts `tali-error` blocks, and exits non-zero, which is the exact analogue of `quarto render` with `execute.error: false`. So the "publishable promise has a hole around execution" framing is overstated; execution IS covered. Quarto's real, defensible position is that environment-probing and document-execution are legitimately different lifecycles and should stay separate commands, exactly the shape Taliesin converged on independently.
- **Taliesin today:** `check` calls render_document_with_includes (no exec.rs, no kernel.rs). Runtime cell errors are caught only later: `build --strict` executes and counts tali-error blocks (build.rs report_cell_errors), and the live preview shows them in the panel. There is no environment/kernel doctor at all (no equivalent of `quarto check`); a missing kernel first appears as a 'kernel unavailable' diagnostic at preview time.
- **Proposed better:** Consider two opt-in modes: `check --execute` that runs cells through the existing warm-kernel + _freeze path (an unchanged doc replays from cache, so CI catches runtime errors in one command), and a lightweight `taliesin doctor` that probes the configured QMD_FAST_PYTHON/QMD_FAST_R kernels and prints what is missing. Keep the default `check` static and fast.
- **Revised recommendation:** Do not add a third execution entry point. The execution gate already exists as `build --strict` (Taliesin's analogue of `quarto render` with execute.error:false). The genuine, narrower gaps are: (a) no single command gives execute-plus-full-lint, because the static superset runs only in `check` while execution runs only in `build --strict` (verified: `build_page_executing` calls just `validate_xrefs`), and (b) no environment preflight, though the contextual exec diagnostic already covers "why is my kernel missing." Preferred fix: unify on ONE publishable gate by having `build --strict` also run the full static-validator superset, so `build --strict` = execute + full lint + fail non-zero, while `check` stays the fast, pure, always-runnable static gate. Drop `check --execute` as redundant. If a preflight is still wanted, make `taliesin doctor` a thin wrapper that triggers the existing `Executor::diagnostic()` probe rather than new probing logic, and never advertise any mode's CI speed on the freeze cache (gitignored, cold on fresh checkout).
- **Tradeoffs:** `--execute` reintroduces kernel dependence and nondeterminism into what is currently a pure, offline gate; CI would then need a kernel. A doctor is scope the tool has so far avoided (the author manages their own interpreters). Both add surface to maintain. (skeptic-found downside: Both halves are largely redundant with capabilities that already exist. (1) `check --execute` heavily duplicates `build --strict`, which already executes cells and fails on cell errors; the only real delta is that `build --strict` skips the full static superset (a11y, dup-ids, anchors, assets, media, links, reactive, math, citations), running only xrefs. (2) The headline selling point, that the freeze cache makes it a cheap one-command CI gate, is illusory in the case that matters: `_freeze/` is gitignored and cold on a fresh CI checkout, so the first (and in CI, only) run always cold-boots the kernel and executes every cell, and errors are never cached, so the very failures you want to catch always force a live kernel run. The "replays from cache" speedup and the "catches runtime errors" purpose are in tension: replay only helps already-green cells. (3) The `doctor` duplicates the existing `Executor::diagnostic()`, which already names the failing language, the correct env var (QMD_FAST_R vs QMD_FAST_PYTHON), and the interpreter's own error, and fires contextually exactly when a doc needs a kernel it cannot get, arguably a better design than a separate probe you must remember to run. (4) Adding an opt-in `--execute` dilutes `check`'s clean invariant ("pure, offline, runnable in any CI with zero setup") and invites a false-green: users may assume the default `check` validated execution.)
- **Invariant check:** `--execute` reuses the existing exec/freeze path (freeze is a gitignored cache, no write to source); a doctor is read-only environment probing. HTML-only and single-editing-surface unaffected.

### D161. Extend validation from key NAMES to enumerated value DOMAINS (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto's schema constrains many values by type and, for enumerated keys, by an allowed value set (e.g. a known set of layout or appearance values), so some out-of-domain values are caught by schema validation, not just unknown key names.
- **Critique:** This is a place Quarto's schema validation currently covers more than Taliesin: Taliesin checks that a key EXISTS but, for most keys, not that its value is honored.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto MUST do comprehensive value-domain validation because it is a general, multi-format compiler serving thousands of authors with no single corpus to act as the arbiter of correctness. A bad enum value can silently mis-drive one of many output writers (LaTeX/Typst/Word/HTML), and unlike Taliesin there is no live HTML preview the author is staring at to catch the wrong render. The same centrally-maintained schema also doubles as the single source of truth for editor autocomplete, hover, and diagnostics in the VS Code extension and RStudio. A rich, enumerated schema is the only tractable way to give located errors across hundreds of options and dozens of formats when you cannot watch every user's output. For Quarto's scope, validating VALUES and not just key NAMES is correct engineering, not ceremony; the critique is fair and even correctly hedged ("some", "for enumerated keys").
- **Taliesin today:** The only value-domain check is validate_theorem_values (number-within must be `chapter`; numbered must be a bool or `unless-unique`). So `page-layout: fulll`, `title-block-style: nune` (only `none` is honored by detect_title_block_hidden), or an unknown top-level `format:` value pass a green check silently and render the default, i.e. the OPPOSITE of intent, exactly the failure mode validate_theorem_values was written to prevent.
- **Proposed better:** Generalize the theorems value-check into a small table of enumerated value domains (page-layout, title-block-style, the top-level format names, listing.type/sort, toc as a strict bool) and emit the same located did-you-mean when a value is off-domain. Drive it from the same consts that already back the JSON Schema enums (the schema already encodes number-within's enum), so validator and schema stay in lockstep.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the idea but tighten scope and correct the mechanism. Ship a value-domain table ONLY for genuinely closed domains where a typo silently renders the opposite of intent: title-block-style ({none, default}), page-layout ({full} plus accept inert article/custom), listing.type ({grid} plus accept inert default/table), and the strict-bool keys toc AND draft (draft is higher-stakes: draft: ture silently publishes). EXCLUDE format names (extension-extensible suffix pattern, deliberately unlinted; if ever checked, reuse the is_reveal_format pattern, never a flat enum) and listing.sort (substring-parsed field+direction, would false-positive on legitimate sort: "date desc"). Prerequisite work the entry glosses: first single-source the theorem/number-within enum so schema.rs reads the const instead of an inline literal, then drive both validator and schema from that one table, and add a sanity test coupling each honored value-set to its validator const (the value analog of schemas_are_structurally_sane), since the bless test alone does not guard parser-vs-validator drift. Each opted-in key gets a corpus pin. Frame the win as check/build honesty (a green check must not certify the opposite of intent), not as parity with Quarto's schema; all invariants (warnings-only, located, no source write, HTML-only) hold and it reinforces the existing clean-break posture set by validate_theorem_values.
- **Tradeoffs:** Requires enumerating the honored value set per key and keeping it current as features grow (same drift risk as KNOWN_KEYS, mitigated the same way via bless test). Over-tightening a key that legitimately accepts free-form strings would false-positive, so each key must be opted in deliberately. (skeptic-found downside: The drafter's candidate list is partly self-contradicting. (1) format names and listing.sort are NOT closed enums: format is extension-extensible via -deck/-revealjs suffix matching (is_reveal_format) and is DELIBERATELY left unlinted today (test format_subkeys_are_not_linted + schema leaves format as json!({})), while sort is substring-parsed free-form (!s.contains("asc")). Both are exactly the "free-form keys false-positive" case the drafter's own tradeoff warns against, yet both are listed; adding a format-name enum also reverses a documented decision. (2) The "honored set" framing is too narrow: you must also accept inert-default spellings (page-layout: article/custom, title-block-style: default) or a legitimate, harmless default spelling warns. (3) The claim that the schema enums are already backed by the same consts is false: schema.rs hardcodes "enum":["chapter"] as an inline json! literal, separate from THEOREM_NUMBER_WITHIN, so real lockstep requires FIRST single-sourcing them, and no test couples the parser's honored set to the validator const (the bless test only guards schema-vs-file). (4) Marginal value is smaller than for Quarto because the live preview visually surfaces most value mistakes instantly; the real, unambiguous gap is check/build honesty (a green check on a doc the author did not eyeball), which narrows where this earns its keep. A stronger uncited example than page-layout is draft: a typo'd draft: ture silently publishes the page (as_bool None -> unwrap_or(false)).)
- **Invariant check:** Warnings only, located, no render block, no source write; reuses the existing did-you-mean machinery. HTML-only unaffected; each new domain gets a corpus pin.

### D162. Bake a crashing cell's traceback inline and keep rendering, instead of aborting the render (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** For computational documents Quarto's execute.error defaults to false, so a cell that raises HALTS the render and prints the traceback to the terminal; you get no output document until you fix it or set error: true. It is all-or-nothing per render.
- **Critique:** One broken cell in a long document blocks previewing everything else, and the error lives in the terminal, detached from the rendered page. The default optimizes for 'do not publish a doc with a hidden error' at the cost of the live-editing loop.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto's execute.error: false is a deliberate publishing-safety default for a multi-format, reproducibility-first tool, and it is defensible on four counts. (1) Never silently ship a document with an embedded stack trace: a traceback baked into a published HTML or PDF report is both an embarrassment and a correctness hazard, so failing loudly forces the author to confront the error before it reaches a reader. (2) Fail-fast at the first raising cell yields exactly ONE diagnostic to fix, which avoids the downstream cascade the entry itself concedes. (3) Quarto renders each document against a fresh kernel and halts, so downstream cells never execute against corrupt or partial state; you never get plausible-but-wrong output. (4) The opposite behavior is a one-line opt-in (error: true globally, or #| error: true per cell), so authors demonstrating an exception in a tutorial get inline errors trivially. It is a safe default with a cheap escape hatch, not dogma, and quarto preview does surface render errors in the browser while keeping the last-good page, so it is not purely terminal-detached.
- **Taliesin today:** A crashing cell's traceback is ANSI-stripped, HTML-escaped, and baked inline as a .tali-error block (kernel.rs + exec.rs) while the rest of the document keeps rendering via the block model. The error is uncacheable (never frozen), surfaced as a clickable panel row live, logged with a located line at build, and fails build --strict. Kernel-died and per-cell timeout get their own inline markers.
- **Proposed better:** Keep the inline-and-continue model; it fits block-level incremental updates. Document build --strict as the CI gate for 'no baked tracebacks', pairing with static `check` so the two together cover static + runtime.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep inline-and-continue: it is genuinely better aligned with block-level incremental updates and the warm dev loop than Quarto's halt, and the invariant story is clean (error blocks carry data-block-id + data-sourcepos per corpus.rs:407, no source write, HTML-only, Markdown syntax untouched). But sharpen the entry past 'document --strict': (1) Surface the stale-binding hazard, not just the cascade. When an upstream same-language cell raises, mark every downstream cell as suspect (a lighter dimmed banner than .tali-error, since exec.rs keeps running them against a possibly-incomplete kernel), or at minimum document loudly that a warm-preview render after an upstream error is not trustworthy until a clean re-run. This closes the only real gap Quarto's fresh-kernel model has over Taliesin. (2) Correct the tradeoffs text: the primary risk is silent stale-state output, with the cascade secondary. (3) Frame --strict accurately (it already counts cell errors via report_cell_errors + strict_exit) and pair it with static check, as the proposal says. (4) Note honestly that the kernel-side .tali-error path is pinned by unit tests, not a corpus doc (the {js} path has corpus/reactive/js-error.qmd, but a deliberately-erroring Python cell cannot be a reliable CI corpus fixture without a guaranteed kernel), so under corpus-plus-roadmap the arbiter of done here is weaker than ideal.
- **Tradeoffs:** Inline errors mean a broken doc can be built to HTML with a visible traceback unless --strict is used; the author must opt into strictness for CI. Continuing past an error can cascade (a later cell depending on the failed one also errors), producing several findings from one root cause. (skeptic-found downside: The tradeoffs section names only the visible cascade (a downstream cell that depends on the failed one ALSO errors, producing N findings from one root cause). It misses the more insidious case, which is specific to Taliesin's warm-kernel-plus-continue combination that I confirmed in exec.rs: a plain exception leaves the kernel ALIVE, so downstream same-language cells still execute, and they can run against a STALE binding (the variable the crashed cell was meant to reassign still holds its previous value from an earlier successful run). Those cells do not error; they emit output that looks valid but is silently wrong, with only the single upstream .tali-error block as a signal. This is exactly the warm-kernel fragility the project already recognizes ('kernel variable state is never cached ... that is what makes Quarto per-cell cache fragile'), and it is the one place Quarto's fresh-kernel-plus-halt model is genuinely safer. So inline-and-continue trades Quarto's guaranteed-consistent-but-halted document for a possibly-inconsistent-but-complete one.)
- **Invariant check:** Error outputs render as blocks carrying data-block-id/data-sourcepos like any other, preserving incremental swap + click-to-source; no source write. HTML-only unaffected.

### D163. Enrich the machine-readable diagnostic stream with severity, stable rule ids, and an explain layer (Proposed (revised))

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Quarto render/preview emit human terminal text; there is no stable, documented machine-readable diagnostic stream for third-party CI or editors to consume (integration is the bespoke VS Code extension), and no stable rule-id / 'explain' catalog for its diagnostics.
- **Critique:** Neither tool ships a rich diagnostic protocol today, but this is a cheap place for Taliesin to pull decisively ahead, and its own two diagnostic channels have already diverged.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Quarto is a multi-engine orchestrator (Pandoc + knitr + Jupyter + a Deno/TypeScript layer), so most of its diagnostics are pass-through errors from engines it does not own: Pandoc parse errors, R/knitr tracebacks, Python exceptions. Owning a single stable rule-id catalog over borrowed, versioned error vocabularies would be a leaky, perpetually-drifting abstraction, so Quarto rationally declined it. For editor integration it invested in the standard, interoperable channel instead of a bespoke one: the quarto-language-server speaks LSP, and LSP diagnostics already carry severity, line+column ranges, a `code` (rule id) and `codeDescription.href` (explain link), consumable by ANY LSP editor, not just VS Code. Quarto also publishes a comprehensive JSON Schema for its YAML options (the very capability Taliesin cloned in schema.rs), which is itself a documented machine-readable contract. So Quarto's diagnostics are richer than 'human terminal text' implies. The one thing it genuinely lacks, a CLI-consumable non-editor JSON stream with Quarto-owned stable rule ids, is a direct consequence of being a delegating multi-engine tool. Taliesin can own such a catalog precisely because it is a single self-contained renderer with its own validators; that is a structural asymmetry, not laziness on Quarto's part.
- **Taliesin today:** `check --format json` emits a [{file,line,message}] array with a pipe-safe {"error":...} envelope (check.rs). But that Diagnostic struct has only file/line/message: NO severity (a11y advisories and broken xrefs are indistinguishable in JSON, and `check` treats every finding as a 'problem' with a single non-zero exit), no column, and no stable rule id. The live-preview Diagnostic (protocol.rs) DOES carry level, so the two channels are inconsistent.
- **Proposed better:** Give the check JSON diagnostic parity with (and beyond) the preview channel: add level (error|warning|advisory), a stable rule id per validator (e.g. a11y/img-alt, xref/broken, frontmatter/unknown-key), and optional column. Let a11y/contrast be advisory so CI can gate on errors while merely reporting advisories, and anchor each rule id to a docs page (a lightweight explain layer, the ergonomic of rustc --explain).
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep, but ship it sharper. (a) Add `level` (error|warning|advisory) and a stable `rule` id to the check.rs Diagnostic, sourcing the rule family per validator at the check.rs aggregation boundary (cheap, touches no construction site), and add an OPTIONAL `rule`/`level` to core Warning (default None/warning) set only at the highest-value render-channel sites (frontmatter unknown-key, cell-option, callout-kind, shortcode) so the two channels finally agree without a 58-site rewrite. (b) Align the vocabulary with LSP DiagnosticSeverity (Error/Warning/Information-as-advisory) and model the explain link on `codeDescription.href`, so the JSON is a trivial map to a future Taliesin LSP server (the real editor-interop story, made plausible by the in-flight .tmd grammar) rather than a parallel vocabulary an editor must shim. (c) Tier BOTH gates together: check exits non-zero on error/warning and zero on advisory-only, and teach `--strict` the same split so the two CI gates never disagree. (d) Drop `column` from v1: defer it until the locator can emit a true token span. (e) Honor corpus-plus-roadmap: pin a rule-id inventory doc (a test that fails if an id is renamed or removed, making the 'stable API surface' claim real) plus a test that every emitted rule id resolves to a docs anchor, so the explain layer cannot rot.
- **Tradeoffs:** A stable rule-id catalog becomes an API surface to keep backward-compatible once tools depend on it. Severity tiers force a per-validator policy call (hard error vs advisory). Minor code churn to thread the fields through both channels. (skeptic-found downside: The 'minor code churn / additive metadata' framing undersells three costs. (1) Rule-id threading is uneven: the static validators (xref, a11y, anchors, assets, links, reactive, math, cites) map to one rule family each cleanly at the check.rs aggregation boundary, but the render warning channel (doc.warnings) is a single heterogeneous stream (front-matter typos, unknown cell options, unknown callout kinds, unknown shortcodes, prose lint, missing-file and include errors). Stable ids THERE require tagging at the ~58 Warning construction sites (or fragile message-substring matching that breaks the instant a message is reworded). (2) Severity is not purely additive JSON: if a11y/contrast becomes 'advisory', the check exit code (currently non-zero on ANY finding) AND the SEPARATE `--strict` build gate (build.rs, currently fails on ANY located warning) must BOTH learn the tiers, or they disagree (check green, --strict red). It touches two exit-code contracts, not just the JSON shape. (3) `column` is the weakest field: the locator is block-line granular (a broken xref is located to its paragraph's start line, not the offending token), so an optional column would be null or imprecise in most cases and imply a precision Taliesin does not have.)
- **Invariant check:** Output-only metadata on the existing diagnostic stream: no source write, and JSON on stdout is tooling, not a new document output target. Location fields keep click-to-source. HTML-only unaffected.

### D164. Shrink the render-failure surface by staying HTML-only and re-surfacing the one silent soft-fail path (Taliesin already better)

- **Impact:** medium, **confidence:** high, **skeptic verdict:** revise
- **Quarto does:** Because Quarto targets many formats, a render can fail deep in an external toolchain: Pandoc template/filter errors, LaTeX/xelatex errors for PDF (notoriously cryptic multi-line logs), or Jupyter/knitr tracebacks. The error text is whatever the underlying tool produces, often far from the author's source.
- **Critique:** Multi-format breadth exposes the author to error surfaces from tools they did not choose to invoke, especially the LaTeX log swamp for PDF; even an author who only wants HTML pays for the possibility of those failure modes.
- **Quarto's strongest defense:** Multi-format is not accidental bloat, it is Quarto's entire thesis: one source, several first-class deliverables (HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs, ePub). For its real audience (academics, journals, textbook authors), a print-fidelity PDF is table-stakes, and LaTeX/xelatex remains the best math-and-print typesetter that exists. No HTML-to-PDF path (paged.js, Prince, Weasyprint) matches it for journal submission, so the "cryptic multi-line LaTeX log" is the price of delegating to the most capable engine, not a design mistake. Quarto also mitigates that surface (quarto check, structured error output, --debug, keeping the .tex on failure). So Quarto's choice is correct FOR QUARTO'S SCOPE, and Taliesin's is correct for a single-author HTML-only tool: the two are different scope bets, not a right-vs-wrong. One honest caveat against the critique: an HTML-only Quarto render never invokes xelatex, so an author who only wants HTML does NOT actually pay the LaTeX log swamp; the critique's "even an author who only wants HTML pays for those failure modes" is the one overstated clause (it survives only under the weak reading that the tool CAN drop them into PDF later). What an HTML-only Quarto author does still inherit is the Pandoc-mediated surface (template/Lua-filter errors far from source), which is the price of Pandoc's universality and extensibility, capabilities Taliesin also declines. So the critique is fair in thrust (breadth enlarges the failure surface) but should not imply Quarto blundered.
- **Taliesin today:** HTML-only by invariant, so there is no LaTeX/Pandoc-template/filter failure surface at all. Math is server-side KaTeX with throw_on_error=false, so a bad $...$ renders a red katex-error span inline instead of aborting; that was the one silent render path, and validate_math (diagnostics/math_render.rs) walks the block model and re-surfaces KaTeX's own title= message on the located click-to-source channel into `check`, --strict, and the preview overlay. Highlighting is syntect (no external highlighter to fail).
- **Proposed better:** Keep the HTML-only invariant; it is a large, quiet win in error UX. Continue the pattern 'any construct that can fail silently gets a static re-surfacing validator' (validate_math is the template) for any future browser feature with a soft-fail path.
- **Revised recommendation:** Keep the HTML-only invariant: it is a genuine quiet win in error UX and the steelman does not dislodge it. But correct the entry and close the gap it papers over. (1) Fix the false claim: validate_math currently reaches ONLY `check`, not `--strict` or the preview overlay (proven by grep + a build --strict that exits 0 on broken math). (2) Close it by emitting the math warning on the render pass's existing doc.warnings channel (the same channel build.rs:323-326 counts for --strict and serve/mod.rs renders into the overlay), so a broken $...$ fails a --strict CI build and shows a clickable jump-to-source overlay row, not only when someone remembers to run `check`. The scan is cheap string-matching over already-rendered HTML, so this respects the warm-server / no-per-edit-cost invariant; it is read-only and located, so click-to-source and single-editing-surface are untouched. (3) Fix the math_render.rs doc comment, which already asserts the three-channel reach it lacks. (4) Generalize the principle correctly: "every soft-fail construct gets a located static validator" must specify the validator rides doc.warnings (loop-visible in preview + --strict), or the pattern will keep shipping check-only half-coverage. Downgrade status from "taliesin-already-better (done)" to "better-in-check, loop-wiring-unfinished."
- **Tradeoffs:** A future print/PDF track must render FROM the built HTML (per invariant) so it never reintroduces the LaTeX error surface, which constrains how print is done. throw_on_error=false means a math error is a visible red span, acceptable but reliant on validate_math being run to escalate it to a diagnostic. (skeptic-found downside: The entry's factual basis is wrong, and it hides a real gap. validate_math is invoked ONLY from the `check` subcommand (check.rs), never from render/mod.rs, build.rs, or any serve path (verified by grep across all crates). Because render never appends math errors to doc.warnings, the "one silent soft-fail path" does NOT reach `--strict` or the preview overlay, contrary to the entry's taliesin_current AND the module's own doc comment (math_render.rs:7-8 both claim check/--strict/overlay). Empirically confirmed on a doc with a broken $\frac{1}{$ and a bad environment: `check` exits 1 and lists both located errors, but `build --strict` on the same file exits 0 and ships the page with red katex-error spans and no diagnostic. So a CI `--strict` gate green-lights a page with visibly broken math, and in the daily warm-preview + build loop the only in-loop signal is the red span itself, exactly the soft-fail the entry claims is re-surfaced.
